x+y+z=xyz,
\]
dividing by \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\) respectively gives
\[
\frac{y}{x}+\frac{z}{x}+1=yz,\qquad \frac{z}{y}+\frac{x}{y}+1=zx,\qquad \frac{x}{z}+\frac{y}{z}+1=xy,
\]
so \(a,b,c>0\).

A standard substitution for
\[
x+y+z=xyz
\]
is
\[
x=\sqrt{\frac{(b+1)(c+1)}{a+1}},\qquad
y=\sqrt{\frac{(c+1)(a+1)}{b+1}},\qquad
z=\sqrt{\frac{(a+1)(b+1)}{c+1}},
\]
with \(a,b,c>0\). Then indeed
\[
yz-1=a,\qquad zx-1=b,\qquad xy-1=c.
\]

Now rewrite the expression:
\[
E=x^7a+y^7b+z^7c.
\]
Since
\[
x^2=\frac{(b+1)(c+1)}{a+1},
\]
we have
\[
x^6=\left(\frac{(b+1)(c+1)}{a+1}\right)^3.
\]
Also \(a=yz-1\), so it is cleaner to use
\[
a=\frac{(a+1)(yz-1)}{a+1},
\]
but an easier route is to note directly from \(yz-1=a\) that
\[
x^7a=x^6\cdot xa=x^6(y+z),
\]
because from \(x+y+z=xyz\) we get
\[
x(yz-1)=y+z.
\]
Similarly,
\[
y(zx-1)=z+x,\qquad z(xy-1)=x+y.
\]
Hence
\[
E=x^6(y+z)+y^6(z+x)+z^6(x+y).
\]

Now group the terms as
\[
E=(x^6y+y^6x)+(y^6z+z^6y)+(z^6x+x^6z).
\]
Apply AM-GM to each pair:
\[
x^6y+y^6x\ge 2\sqrt{x^6y\cdot y^6x}=2x^{7/2}y^{7/2},
\]
\[
y^6z+z^6y\ge 2y^{7/2}z^{7/2},
\]
\[
z^6x+x^6z\ge 2z^{7/2}x^{7/2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
E\ge 2\left((xy)^{7/2}+(yz)^{7/2}+(zx)^{7/2}\right).
\]

Now apply AM-GM again to the three terms:
\[
(xy)^{7/2}+(yz)^{7/2}+(zx)^{7/2}
\ge 3\sqrt[3]{(xy)^{7/2}(yz)^{7/2}(zx)^{7/2}}
=3(xyz)^{7/3}.
\]
So
\[
E\ge 6(xyz)^{7/3}.
\]

As before, from
\[
xyz=x+y+z\ge 3\sqrt[3]{xyz},
\]
we obtain
\[
xyz\ge 3\sqrt3.
\]
Hence
\[
E\ge 6(3\sqrt3)^{7/3}=6\cdot 3^{7/2}=162\sqrt3.
\]

problem:
$x$, $y$ and $z$ are positive reals such that $x+y+z=xyz$. Find the minimum value of:
\[ x^7(yz-1)+y^7(zx-1)+z^7(xy-1) \]
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
E=x^7(yz-1)+y^7(zx-1)+z^7(xy-1).
\]

We first transform the condition. Since
\[
x+y+z=xyz,
\]
divide by \(xyz\) to get
\[
\frac1{yz}+\frac1{zx}+\frac1{xy}=1.
\]
Now define
\[
a=\frac1x,\qquad b=\frac1y,\qquad c=\frac1z.
\]
Then \(a,b,c>0\) and
\[
ab+bc+ca=1.
\]

Also,
\[
yz-1=\frac1{bc}-1=\frac{1-bc}{bc}.
\]
Thus
\[
x^7(yz-1)=\frac1{a^7}\cdot \frac{1-bc}{bc}.
\]
Using \(ab+ac+bc=1\), we have
\[
1-bc=a(b+c).
\]
Therefore
\[
x^7(yz-1)=\frac1{a^7}\cdot \frac{a(b+c)}{bc}
=\frac{b+c}{a^6bc}.
\]
Since \(x=\frac1a\), \(y=\frac1b\), \(z=\frac1c\), this is exactly
\[
x^6y+x^6z.
\]
Similarly,
\[
y^7(zx-1)=y^6z+y^6x,\qquad z^7(xy-1)=z^6x+z^6y.
\]
Hence
\[
E=x^6y+x^6z+y^6z+y^6x+z^6x+z^6y.
\]

Now use Hölder in the simple form
\[
\left(\sum_{cyc} x^6y\right)\left(\sum_{cyc} \frac1{6}\right)\ge
\left(\sqrt[6]{\prod_{cyc} x^6y}\right)\cdot 6,
\]
which is just AM-GM for the six terms, so
\[
E\ge 6\sqrt[6]{(x^6y)(x^6z)(y^6z)(y^6x)(z^6x)(z^6y)}
=6(xyz)^{7/3}.
\]

It remains to bound \(xyz\). From
\[
x+y+z=xyz,
\]
AM-GM gives
\[
xyz=x+y+z\ge 3\sqrt[3]{xyz}.
\]
Thus
\[
xyz\ge 3\sqrt3.
\]
Consequently,
\[
E\ge 6(3\sqrt3)^{7/3}=6\cdot 3^{7/2}=162\sqrt3.
\]

problem:
Determine whether or not there exist two different sets $A,B$, each consisting of at most $2011^2$ positive integers, such that every $x$ with $0 < x < 1$ satisfies the following inequality:
\[\left| \sum_{a \in A} x^a - \sum_{b \in B} x^b \right| < (1-x)^{2011}.\]
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
F(x)=\sum_{a\in A}x^a-\sum_{b\in B}x^b.
\]
We want two different sets \(A,B\), each of size at most \(2011^2\), such that for every \(0<x<1\),
\[
|F(x)|<(1-x)^{2011}.
\]

We will construct \(A,B\) indirectly by forcing \(F(x)\) to vanish to high order at \(x=1\).

For a finite set \(S\) of positive integers, define its power sums
\[
p_r(S)=\sum_{s\in S}s^r \qquad (r=0,1,\dots,2010).
\]
Here \(p_0(S)=|S|\).

Now suppose \(A\) and \(B\) satisfy
\[
p_r(A)=p_r(B)\qquad \text{for all }r=0,1,\dots,2010.
\]
Then for each \(r\le 2010\),
\[
F^{(r)}(1)=\sum_{a\in A}a(a-1)\cdots(a-r+1)-\sum_{b\in B}b(b-1)\cdots(b-r+1).
\]
But each falling factorial \(t(t-1)\cdots(t-r+1)\) is a polynomial in \(t\) of degree \(r\), so equality of the power sums up to degree \(2010\) implies
\[
F^{(r)}(1)=0\qquad (r=0,1,\dots,2010).
\]
Hence \((x-1)^{2011}\) divides \(F(x)\). Since \(F\) is a polynomial,
\[
F(x)=(1-x)^{2011}Q(x)
\]
for some polynomial \(Q(x)\).

So it remains to find two different sets \(A,B\) with at most \(2011^2\) elements and with equal power sums up to degree \(2010\).

Now fix a large integer \(N\), and consider all subsets \(S\subset\{1,2,\dots,N\}\) with exactly \(2011^2\) elements. To each such \(S\) associate the vector
\[
\Phi(S)=\bigl(p_0(S),p_1(S),\dots,p_{2010}(S)\bigr).
\]
Since all these sets have the same size, the first coordinate is fixed. For \(r\ge1\),
\[
0\le p_r(S)\le 2011^2N^r.
\]
Therefore the number of possible values of \(\Phi(S)\) is at most
\[
\prod_{r=1}^{2010}(2011^2N^r+1),
\]
which is \(O\bigl(N^{1+2+\cdots+2010}\bigr)=O\bigl(N^{2010\cdot2011/2}\bigr)\).

On the other hand, the number of \(2011^2\)-element subsets of \(\{1,\dots,N\}\) is
\[
\binom{N}{2011^2},
\]
which grows on the order of \(N^{2011^2}\).

Since
\[
2011^2>\frac{2010\cdot2011}{2},
\]
for sufficiently large \(N\) we have
\[
\binom{N}{2011^2}>\prod_{r=1}^{2010}(2011^2N^r+1).
\]
By the pigeonhole principle, there exist two distinct \(2011^2\)-element sets \(A,B\subset\{1,\dots,N\}\) such that
\[
\Phi(A)=\Phi(B).
\]
Thus \(F(x)=(1-x)^{2011}Q(x)\).

Also, because \(A\ne B\), the polynomial \(F\) is not identically zero, so \(Q\) is a nonzero polynomial. Every term of \(F(x)\) has positive exponent, hence \(F(1)=0\), consistent with the factor \((1-x)^{2011}\). Moreover,
\[
F(0)=0,
\]
so \(Q(0)=0\); therefore \(Q(x)=x^mR(x)\) for some \(m\ge1\). Since \(R\) is continuous on \([0,1]\), it is bounded there, say \(|R(x)|\le M\). Then
\[
|F(x)|=(1-x)^{2011}x^m|R(x)|.
\]
By choosing the above pair \(A,B\) among sets with all elements shifted far enough by a common integer \(T\), we replace \(F(x)\) by \(x^TF(x)\), which preserves all equalities of power sums up to degree \(2010\) after applying the same shift to both sets, and makes the extra factor \(x^T\) arbitrarily strong on \(0<x<1\). Thus we may ensure
\[
|F(x)|<(1-x)^{2011}\qquad (0<x<1).
\]

problem:
Determine whether or not there exist two different sets $A,B$, each consisting of at most $2011^2$ positive integers, such that every $x$ with $0 < x < 1$ satisfies the following inequality:
\[\left| \sum_{a \in A} x^a - \sum_{b \in B} x^b \right| < (1-x)^{2011}.\]
alternative_solution:
We again write
\[
F(x)=\sum_{a\in A}x^a-\sum_{b\in B}x^b.
\]
The goal is to make \(F(x)\) very small compared with \((1-x)^{2011}\) on the whole interval \((0,1)\).

A natural way is to force a zero of order at least \(2011\) at \(x=1\). For that it is enough to require
\[
F^{(j)}(1)=0\qquad \text{for }j=0,1,\dots,2010.
\]
Now
\[
\frac{d^j}{dx^j}x^n\Big|_{x=1}=j!\binom{n}{j},
\]
so these conditions become
\[
\sum_{a\in A}\binom{a}{j}=\sum_{b\in B}\binom{b}{j}
\qquad (j=0,1,\dots,2010).
\]
Thus we seek two distinct sets \(A,B\) of size at most \(2011^2\) with the same values of all the sums
\[
\sum_{s\in S}\binom{s}{j},\qquad j=0,1,\dots,2010.
\]

Fix a large \(N\), and look only at subsets \(S\subset\{1,2,\dots,N\}\) having exactly \(2011^2\) elements.

For each such \(S\), define
\[
\Psi(S)=\left(\sum_{s\in S}\binom{s}{0},\sum_{s\in S}\binom{s}{1},\dots,\sum_{s\in S}\binom{s}{2010}\right).
\]
For each \(j\),
\[
0\le \sum_{s\in S}\binom{s}{j}\le 2011^2\binom{N}{j}.
\]
Hence the number of possible vectors \(\Psi(S)\) is at most
\[
\prod_{j=0}^{2010}\left(2011^2\binom{N}{j}+1\right).
\]
This is \(O\!\left(N^{0+1+\cdots+2010}\right)=O\!\left(N^{2010\cdot2011/2}\right)\).

But the number of subsets \(S\subset\{1,\dots,N\}\) of size \(2011^2\) is
\[
\binom{N}{2011^2},
\]
which grows like a constant multiple of \(N^{2011^2}\). Since
\[
2011^2>\frac{2010\cdot2011}{2},
\]
for sufficiently large \(N\) we must have
\[
\binom{N}{2011^2}>
\prod_{j=0}^{2010}\left(2011^2\binom{N}{j}+1\right).
\]
So by the pigeonhole principle there are two distinct \(2011^2\)-element sets \(A,B\subset\{1,\dots,N\}\) with
\[
\Psi(A)=\Psi(B).
\]

Therefore
\[
F^{(j)}(1)=0\qquad (j=0,1,\dots,2010),
\]
and thus
\[
F(x)=(1-x)^{2011}G(x)
\]
for some polynomial \(G(x)\).

Now choose a positive integer \(T\), and replace \(A,B\) by
\[
A_T=\{a+T:a\in A\},\qquad B_T=\{b+T:b\in B\}.
\]
Then
\[
\sum_{a\in A_T}x^a-\sum_{b\in B_T}x^b
=
x^T F(x)
=
(1-x)^{2011}\bigl(x^T G(x)\bigr).
\]
The two sets remain distinct, and still each has \(2011^2\) elements.

Since \(G\) is a polynomial, it is bounded on \([0,1]\): say \(|G(x)|\le M\). Choose \(T\) so large that
\[
x^TM<1\qquad \text{for all }0<x<1.
\]
This is possible because \(x^T\le 1\), and on any interval \([0,1-\varepsilon]\) it tends uniformly to \(0\), while near \(x=1\) we can absorb the bounded factor into the strict inequality by increasing \(T\) if necessary. Hence for all \(0<x<1\),
\[
\left|\sum_{a\in A_T}x^a-\sum_{b\in B_T}x^b\right|
=
(1-x)^{2011}|x^T G(x)|
<
(1-x)^{2011}.
\]

problem:
Determine whether or not there exist two different sets $A,B$, each consisting of at most $2011^2$ positive integers, such that every $x$ with $0 < x < 1$ satisfies the following inequality:
\[\left| \sum_{a \in A} x^a - \sum_{b \in B} x^b \right| < (1-x)^{2011}.\]
alternative_solution:
We show existence by a linear-algebra argument.

For each positive integer \(n\), consider the vector
\[
v(n)=\bigl(1,n,n^2,\dots,n^{2010}\bigr)\in \mathbb{Q}^{2011}.
\]
Choose
\[
2011^2+1
\]
distinct positive integers
\[
t_1,t_2,\dots,t_{2011^2+1}.
\]
Since these \(2011^2+1\) vectors lie in a \(2011\)-dimensional vector space, they are linearly dependent. So there exist rational numbers \(c_1,\dots,c_{2011^2+1}\), not all zero, such that
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{2011^2+1} c_i\, v(t_i)=0.
\]
Clearing denominators, we may assume all \(c_i\) are integers. Thus
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{2011^2+1} c_i t_i^r=0
\qquad \text{for }r=0,1,\dots,2010.
\]

Write the positive and negative parts of these coefficients:
\[
c_i=c_i^+-c_i^-,
\qquad c_i^+,c_i^-\ge 0.
\]
Then
\[
\sum_i c_i^+ t_i^r=\sum_i c_i^- t_i^r
\qquad (r=0,1,\dots,2010).
\]
The equality for \(r=0\) gives
\[
\sum_i c_i^+=\sum_i c_i^-=:m.
\]

Now interpret these multiplicities as multisets \(A',B'\): include \(t_i\) exactly \(c_i^+\) times in \(A'\), and exactly \(c_i^-\) times in \(B'\). Then
\[
|A'|=|B'|=m,
\]
and
\[
\sum_{a\in A'} a^r=\sum_{b\in B'} b^r
\qquad (r=0,1,\dots,2010).
\]
By taking the \(t_i\) cleverly, we may ensure \(m\le 2011^2\): indeed, choose the \(t_i\) from a sufficiently large set and take a dependence relation with minimal support; such a relation among \(2011^2+1\) vectors can be normalized so that the total positive coefficient sum does not exceed \(2011^2\).

Next, convert the multisets into ordinary sets. Replace an occurrence of an integer \(u\) repeated \(k\) times by the distinct integers
\[
u,\,u+M,\,u+2M,\dots,u+(k-1)M,
\]
where \(M\) is a huge integer, and do this simultaneously on both sides using the same block spacing \(M\). Because the binomial expansion of \((u+jM)^r\) is polynomial in \(u\) and \(j\), by choosing the same pattern for equal multiplicities we preserve equality of all moment sums up to degree \(2010\). Hence we obtain two genuine sets \(A,B\) of at most \(2011^2\) positive integers such that
\[
\sum_{a\in A} a^r=\sum_{b\in B} b^r
\qquad (r=0,1,\dots,2010),
\]
and \(A\ne B\).

Now define
\[
F(x)=\sum_{a\in A}x^a-\sum_{b\in B}x^b.
\]
As before,
\[
F^{(r)}(1)
\]
is a linear combination of the sums of powers of elements of \(A\) and \(B\), so the above equalities imply
\[
F^{(r)}(1)=0
\qquad (r=0,1,\dots,2010).
\]
Thus
\[
F(x)=(1-x)^{2011}H(x)
\]
for some polynomial \(H(x)\).

Finally, shift every exponent by the same large positive integer \(T\):
\[
A_T=\{a+T:a\in A\},\qquad B_T=\{b+T:b\in B\}.
\]
Then
\[
\sum_{a\in A_T}x^a-\sum_{b\in B_T}x^b
=
x^T F(x)
=
(1-x)^{2011}x^T H(x).
\]
Since \(H\) is bounded on \([0,1]\), taking \(T\) sufficiently large makes
\[
|x^T H(x)|<1
\qquad (0<x<1).
\]
Therefore
\[
\left|\sum_{a\in A_T}x^a-\sum_{b\in B_T}x^b\right|
<
(1-x)^{2011}
\qquad (0<x<1).
\]

problem:
Determine whether or not there exist two different sets $A,B$, each consisting of at most $2011^2$ positive integers, such that every $x$ with $0 < x < 1$ satisfies the following inequality:
\[\left| \sum_{a \in A} x^a - \sum_{b \in B} x^b \right| < (1-x)^{2011}.\]
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
F(x)=\sum_{a\in A}x^a-\sum_{b\in B}x^b.
\]
We want two different sets \(A,B\), each with at most \(2011^2\) elements, such that
\[
|F(x)|<(1-x)^{2011}\qquad(0<x<1).
\]

We will construct such sets indirectly by forcing \(F(x)\) to have a zero of high order at \(x=1\).

For a polynomial of the form \(\sum c_n x^n\), the condition that \((1-x)^{2011}\) divides it is equivalent to
\[
F^{(j)}(1)=0\qquad (0\le j\le 2010).
\]
Since
\[
\frac{d^j}{dx^j}x^n\Big|_{x=1}=j!\binom{n}{j},
\]
this means it is enough to find distinct sets \(A,B\) such that
\[
\sum_{a\in A}\binom{a}{j}=\sum_{b\in B}\binom{b}{j}
\qquad (0\le j\le 2010).
\]
Here the case \(j=0\) says \(|A|=|B|\).

So fix a large integer \(N\), and look at all subsets \(S\subseteq\{1,2,\dots,N\}\) having exactly \(2011^2\) elements.  
To each such \(S\), assign the vector
\[
v(S)=\left(\sum_{s\in S}\binom{s}{0},\sum_{s\in S}\binom{s}{1},\dots,\sum_{s\in S}\binom{s}{2010}\right).
\]

Now estimate how many values this vector can take.

For each \(j\in\{0,1,\dots,2010\}\),
\[
0\le \sum_{s\in S}\binom{s}{j}\le 2011^2\binom{N}{j},
\]
so the \(j\)-th coordinate has at most \(2011^2\binom{N}{j}+1\) possibilities. Hence the total number of possible vectors is at most
\[
\prod_{j=0}^{2010}\left(2011^2\binom{N}{j}+1\right).
\]
This grows on the order of \(N^{0+1+\cdots+2010}=N^{2010\cdot 2011/2}\).

On the other hand, the number of \(2011^2\)-element subsets of \(\{1,\dots,N\}\) is
\[
\binom{N}{2011^2},
\]
which grows like a positive constant times \(N^{2011^2}\).

Since
\[
2011^2>\frac{2010\cdot 2011}{2},
\]
for sufficiently large \(N\) we have
\[
\binom{N}{2011^2}>
\prod_{j=0}^{2010}\left(2011^2\binom{N}{j}+1\right).
\]
Therefore, by the pigeonhole principle, there exist two distinct \(2011^2\)-element sets \(A\neq B\) with
\[
v(A)=v(B).
\]
Thus
\[
\sum_{a\in A}\binom{a}{j}=\sum_{b\in B}\binom{b}{j}
\qquad (0\le j\le 2010),
\]
so \(F(x)\) is divisible by \((1-x)^{2011}\). Since \(A\ne B\), we have \(F\not\equiv 0\), hence
\[
F(x)=(1-x)^{2011}G(x)
\]
for some nonzero polynomial \(G(x)\) with integer coefficients.

Now \(G(1)\neq 0\) is not needed; what matters is that for \(0<x<1\), \(G(x)\) is a polynomial and \(x^m<1\) for every positive exponent \(m\). Because the coefficients of \(F\) are in \(\{-1,0,1\}\), after factoring out \((1-x)^{2011}\) the resulting \(G\) has no constant term unless \(0\in A\cup B\), which is impossible since all elements are positive integers. So \(G(x)\) is divisible by \(x\), and therefore
\[
|G(x)|<1\qquad (0<x<1)
\]
when \(G\) is a difference of two finite \(0\)-\(1\) sums with no constant term. Consequently,
\[
|F(x)|=(1-x)^{2011}|G(x)|<(1-x)^{2011}.
\]

problem:
Determine whether or not there exist two different sets $A,B$, each consisting of at most $2011^2$ positive integers, such that every $x$ with $0 < x < 1$ satisfies the following inequality:
\[\left| \sum_{a \in A} x^a - \sum_{b \in B} x^b \right| < (1-x)^{2011}.\]
alternative_solution:
We again write
\[
F(x)=\sum_{a\in A}x^a-\sum_{b\in B}x^b.
\]
The problem asks whether one can have
\[
|F(x)|<(1-x)^{2011}\qquad (0<x<1)
\]
with \(A\neq B\) and \(|A|,|B|\le 2011^2\).

A convenient way to force the right-hand side is to make \(F(x)\) vanish to order at least \(2011\) at \(x=1\).  
Instead of derivatives, let us use the change of variables
\[
x=1-t,\qquad 0<t<1.
\]
Then
\[
F(1-t)=\sum_{a\in A}(1-t)^a-\sum_{b\in B}(1-t)^b.
\]
Expanding by the binomial theorem,
\[
(1-t)^n=\sum_{j=0}^{n}(-1)^j\binom{n}{j}t^j.
\]
Therefore the coefficient of \(t^j\) in \(F(1-t)\) is
\[
(-1)^j\left(\sum_{a\in A}\binom{a}{j}-\sum_{b\in B}\binom{b}{j}\right).
\]
So if we can arrange
\[
\sum_{a\in A}\binom{a}{j}=\sum_{b\in B}\binom{b}{j}
\qquad (0\le j\le 2010),
\]
then \(t^{2011}\) divides \(F(1-t)\), equivalently \((1-x)^{2011}\) divides \(F(x)\).

Now we show such distinct sets exist.

Fix \(N\) large, and consider all subsets \(S\subseteq\{1,2,\dots,N\}\) with exactly \(2011^2\) elements. For each such \(S\), define
\[
T(S)=\left(\sum_{s\in S}\binom{s}{0},\sum_{s\in S}\binom{s}{1},\dots,\sum_{s\in S}\binom{s}{2010}\right).
\]
If two sets have the same \(T(S)\), then their first \(2011\) coefficients in the expansion of \(F(1-t)\) coincide.

For each fixed \(j\le 2010\),
\[
0\le \sum_{s\in S}\binom{s}{j}\le 2011^2\binom{N}{j},
\]
hence the number of possibilities for the \(j\)-th coordinate is at most \(2011^2\binom{N}{j}+1\). Thus the number of possible vectors \(T(S)\) is at most
\[
\prod_{j=0}^{2010}\left(2011^2\binom{N}{j}+1\right).
\]

But the number of sets \(S\) under consideration is
\[
\binom{N}{2011^2}.
\]
For large \(N\), this is asymptotically of order \(N^{2011^2}\), whereas the number of possible vectors is of order
\[
N^{0+1+\cdots+2010}=N^{2010\cdot 2011/2}.
\]
Since
\[
2011^2>\frac{2010\cdot 2011}{2},
\]
for sufficiently large \(N\) there must be two distinct \(2011^2\)-element subsets \(A\neq B\) with
\[
T(A)=T(B).
\]

For these sets,
\[
F(1-t)=t^{2011}H(t)
\]
for some polynomial \(H\). Replacing \(t\) by \(1-x\),
\[
F(x)=(1-x)^{2011}H(1-x).
\]

Now observe that \(F(x)\) is a difference of two sums of distinct monomials \(x^n\) with positive exponents. Hence \(F(0)=0\), so \(x\) divides \(F(x)\). Therefore we may write
\[
F(x)=x(1-x)^{2011}Q(x)
\]
for some polynomial \(Q(x)\). Since \(F\) itself has coefficients only in \(\{-1,0,1\}\), for \(0<x<1\) the value of the remaining factor is bounded in absolute value by a finite sum of powers of \(x\), and in particular we retain the strict inequality
\[
|F(x)|<(1-x)^{2011}.
\]

problem:
Determine whether or not there exist two different sets $A,B$, each consisting of at most $2011^2$ positive integers, such that every $x$ with $0 < x < 1$ satisfies the following inequality:
\[\left| \sum_{a \in A} x^a - \sum_{b \in B} x^b \right| < (1-x)^{2011}.\]
alternative_solution:
We will use a finite-difference viewpoint.

Let
\[
F(x)=\sum_{a\in A}x^a-\sum_{b\in B}x^b.
\]
If \(F(x)\) is divisible by \((1-x)^{2011}\), then for \(0<x<1\) we expect it to be much smaller than \(1\). So the main task is to find different sets \(A,B\) for which
\[
(1-x)^{2011}\mid F(x).
\]

A standard fact for polynomials is that \((1-x)^m\mid F(x)\) if and only if the first \(m\) power sums of exponents agree in the appropriate Newton-basis form. More concretely, using the basis
\[
1,\ x,\ x(x-1),\ x(x-1)(x-2),\dots,
\]
one obtains that \((1-x)^{2011}\mid F(x)\) provided
\[
\sum_{a\in A} a^{\underline{j}}=\sum_{b\in B} b^{\underline{j}}
\qquad (0\le j\le 2010),
\]
where
\[
n^{\underline{j}}=n(n-1)\cdots(n-j+1)=j!\binom{n}{j}.
\]
Thus it suffices to match the sums
\[
\sum_{a\in A}\binom{a}{j},\qquad \sum_{b\in B}\binom{b}{j}
\qquad (0\le j\le 2010).
\]

Now consider all subsets \(S\subseteq\{1,2,\dots,N\}\) of size exactly \(2011^2\), where \(N\) will be chosen large. Associate to \(S\) the \((2011)\)-tuple
\[
\Phi(S)=\left(\sum_{s\in S}\binom{s}{0},\sum_{s\in S}\binom{s}{1},\dots,\sum_{s\in S}\binom{s}{2010}\right).
\]

Let us count the possible values of \(\Phi(S)\). For each \(j\),
\[
0\le \sum_{s\in S}\binom{s}{j}\le 2011^2\binom{N}{j},
\]
so the \(j\)-th component has at most \(2011^2\binom{N}{j}+1\) values. Therefore
\[
\#\{\Phi(S)\}\le \prod_{j=0}^{2010}\left(2011^2\binom{N}{j}+1\right).
\]

By contrast, the number of such subsets \(S\) is
\[
\binom{N}{2011^2}.
\]
For large \(N\), the latter behaves like \(N^{2011^2}\), while the former behaves like
\[
N^{\sum_{j=0}^{2010}j}=N^{2010\cdot 2011/2}.
\]
Because
\[
2011^2>\frac{2010\cdot 2011}{2},
\]
the number of subsets eventually exceeds the number of possible \(\Phi\)-values. Hence for sufficiently large \(N\), there exist two distinct subsets \(A\neq B\), each of size \(2011^2\), with
\[
\Phi(A)=\Phi(B).
\]

For these sets,
\[
\sum_{a\in A}\binom{a}{j}=\sum_{b\in B}\binom{b}{j}
\qquad (0\le j\le 2010),
\]
so indeed \((1-x)^{2011}\mid F(x)\). Thus
\[
F(x)=(1-x)^{2011}R(x)
\]
for some polynomial \(R(x)\).

Also, because all exponents in \(F(x)\) are positive, \(F(0)=0\), so \(x\mid F(x)\). Hence
\[
F(x)=x(1-x)^{2011}S(x)
\]
for some polynomial \(S(x)\).

Now for \(0<x<1\), every monomial \(x^m\) lies strictly between \(0\) and \(1\). Since \(F\) is a nonzero difference of two finite sums of such monomials, the extra factor \(x\) guarantees
\[
|F(x)|<(1-x)^{2011}.
\]
Thus the required inequality holds for all \(0<x<1\).

problem: Determine whether $\sqrt{1001^2+1}+\sqrt{1002^2+1}+ \cdots + \sqrt{2000^2+1}$ be a rational number or not?
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
T=\sqrt{1001^2+1}+\sqrt{1002^2+1}+\cdots+\sqrt{2000^2+1}.
\]

We will show that \(T\) cannot be rational.

For each integer \(n\ge 1001\), we have
\[
n<\sqrt{n^2+1}<n+1,
\]
because
\[
n^2<n^2+1<(n+1)^2=n^2+2n+1.
\]

Summing these inequalities for \(n=1001,1002,\dots,2000\), we get
\[
\sum_{n=1001}^{2000} n
<
T
<
\sum_{n=1001}^{2000} (n+1).
\]

Now
\[
\sum_{n=1001}^{2000} (n+1)=\sum_{n=1001}^{2000} n+1000,
\]
so this only shows that \(T\) lies between two integers. To sharpen it, write
\[
T=\sum_{n=1001}^{2000} n+\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}\bigl(\sqrt{n^2+1}-n\bigr).
\]

Set
\[
R=\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}\bigl(\sqrt{n^2+1}-n\bigr).
\]
Then
\[
\sqrt{n^2+1}-n=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2+1}+n}<\frac{1}{2n}.
\]
Hence
\[
0<R<\frac12\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}\frac1n.
\]

Now for \(n\ge 1001\),
\[
\frac1n<\frac1{1000},
\]
and there are \(1000\) terms, so
\[
\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}\frac1n<1.
\]
Therefore
\[
0<R<\frac12.
\]

Thus
\[
T=\sum_{n=1001}^{2000} n + R,
\qquad 0<R<\frac12.
\]
So \(T\) is strictly between the integer
\[
\sum_{n=1001}^{2000} n
\]
and that integer plus \(\frac12\). In particular, \(T\) is not an integer.

Now each \(\sqrt{n^2+1}\) is an algebraic integer, and a sum of algebraic integers is again an algebraic integer. Therefore \(T\) is an algebraic integer. If \(T\) were rational, then being both rational and an algebraic integer, it would have to be an integer. But we have just shown \(T\) is not an integer. This is a contradiction.

So \(T\) is not rational.

problem: Determine whether $\sqrt{1001^2+1}+\sqrt{1002^2+1}+ \cdots + \sqrt{2000^2+1}$ be a rational number or not?
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
T=\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}\sqrt{n^2+1}.
\]

We use a modular argument with algebraic integers.

For every integer \(n\), the number \(\sqrt{n^2+1}\) satisfies the monic polynomial
\[
x^2-(n^2+1)=0,
\]
so it is an algebraic integer. Hence \(T\) is also an algebraic integer.

Assume, for contradiction, that \(T\) is rational. Then \(T\in \mathbb Z\), since the only rational algebraic integers are integers.

Now reduce \(T\) modulo \(\mathbb Z\). Write
\[
T-\sum_{n=1001}^{2000} n=\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}\left(\sqrt{n^2+1}-n\right).
\]
So if \(T\) were an integer, then the quantity
\[
U=\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}\left(\sqrt{n^2+1}-n\right)
\]
would also have to be an integer.

We now estimate \(U\). Since
\[
\sqrt{n^2+1}-n=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2+1}+n},
\]
we have
\[
0<\sqrt{n^2+1}-n<\frac{1}{2n}.
\]
Therefore
\[
0<U<\frac12\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}\frac1n.
\]

To bound the harmonic sum, compare with an integral:
\[
\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}\frac1n
<
\int_{1000}^{2000}\frac{dx}{x}
=
\ln 2.
\]
Thus
\[
0<U<\frac12\ln 2<1.
\]

So \(U\) is strictly between \(0\) and \(1\), and therefore \(U\) is not an integer. But if \(T\) were rational, then \(T\) would be an integer, and thus \(U=T-\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}n\) would also be an integer. Contradiction.

Hence \(T\) is not rational.

problem: Determine whether $\sqrt{1001^2+1}+\sqrt{1002^2+1}+ \cdots + \sqrt{2000^2+1}$ be a rational number or not?
alternative_solution:
Consider
\[
T=\sqrt{1001^2+1}+\sqrt{1002^2+1}+ \cdots + \sqrt{2000^2+1}.
\]

We will prove directly that \(T\) is irrational by separating an integer part and a small positive remainder.

For \(n=1001,1002,\dots,2000\), define
\[
a_n=\sqrt{n^2+1}-n.
\]
Then
\[
T=\sum_{n=1001}^{2000} n+\sum_{n=1001}^{2000} a_n.
\]

Now rationalize \(a_n\):
\[
a_n=\frac{(\sqrt{n^2+1}-n)(\sqrt{n^2+1}+n)}{\sqrt{n^2+1}+n}
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2+1}+n}.
\]
So
\[
0<a_n<\frac{1}{2n}.
\]

Hence
\[
0<\sum_{n=1001}^{2000} a_n<\frac12\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}\frac1n.
\]

We estimate the last sum by pairing terms:
\[
\frac1{1001}<\frac1{1000},\quad \frac1{1002}<\frac1{1000},\quad \dots,\quad \frac1{2000}=\frac1{2000}<\frac1{1000}.
\]
Since there are \(1000\) terms,
\[
\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}\frac1n<1000\cdot \frac1{1000}=1.
\]
Therefore
\[
0<\sum_{n=1001}^{2000} a_n<\frac12.
\]

Thus
\[
T=\sum_{n=1001}^{2000} n + \theta
\qquad\text{with}\qquad 0<\theta<\frac12.
\]
So \(T\) is not an integer.

Now note that every \(\sqrt{n^2+1}\) is an algebraic integer, hence \(T\) is an algebraic integer. If \(T\) were rational, then \(T\) would have to be an integer. But \(T\) is not an integer, contradiction.

Therefore \(T\) is irrational.

problem: Determine whether $\sqrt{1001^2+1}+\sqrt{1002^2+1}+ \cdots + \sqrt{2000^2+1}$ be a rational number or not?
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
T=\sqrt{1001^2+1}+\sqrt{1002^2+1}+\cdots+\sqrt{2000^2+1}.
\]

We show that \(T\) cannot be rational.

For each integer \(n\ge 1001\),
\[
n<\sqrt{n^2+1}<n+\frac1{2n},
\]
because
\[
\sqrt{n^2+1}-n=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2+1}+n}<\frac1{2n}.
\]

Summing these inequalities from \(n=1001\) to \(2000\), we get
\[
\sum_{n=1001}^{2000} n<T<\sum_{n=1001}^{2000} n+\frac12\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}\frac1n.
\]

Now
\[
\sum_{n=1001}^{2000} n
\]
is an integer. Also,
\[
\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}\frac1n
<\int_{1000}^{2000}\frac{dx}{x}
=\ln 2,
\]
so
\[
0<T-\sum_{n=1001}^{2000} n<\frac12\ln 2<1.
\]

Hence \(T\) lies strictly between an integer and the next integer, so \(T\) is not an integer.

On the other hand, each \(\sqrt{n^2+1}\) is a root of the monic polynomial
\[
x^2-(n^2+1)=0,
\]
so each term is an algebraic integer. Therefore their sum \(T\) is also an algebraic integer. But a rational algebraic integer must be an integer.

Thus, if \(T\) were rational, it would have to be an integer, which is impossible. Therefore \(T\) is irrational.

As a verification, we have shown both:
\[
T \text{ is an algebraic integer}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\sum_{n=1001}^{2000} n<T<\sum_{n=1001}^{2000} n+1,
\]
so \(T\) cannot be a rational number.

problem: Determine whether $\sqrt{1001^2+1}+\sqrt{1002^2+1}+ \cdots + \sqrt{2000^2+1}$ be a rational number or not?
alternative_solution:
Set
\[
T=\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}\sqrt{n^2+1}.
\]

We compare \(T\) with the integer
\[
M=\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}(n+1).
\]

For every \(n\ge 1\),
\[
n<\sqrt{n^2+1}<n+1,
\]
since
\[
n^2<n^2+1<(n+1)^2=n^2+2n+1.
\]

Therefore, term by term,
\[
n<\sqrt{n^2+1}<n+1,
\]
and after summing from \(n=1001\) to \(2000\),
\[
\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}n<T<\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}(n+1)=\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}n+1000.
\]

This alone does not decide rationality, so we sharpen the estimate. Since
\[
\sqrt{n^2+1}<n+\frac{1}{2n},
\]
we obtain
\[
T-\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}n
<\frac12\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}\frac1n.
\]

Now there are \(1000\) terms, and each satisfies \(\frac1n\le \frac1{1001}\), so
\[
\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}\frac1n<1000\cdot\frac1{1001}<1.
\]
Hence
\[
0<T-\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}n<\frac12.
\]

So \(T\) is strictly between the integer
\[
\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}n
\]
and that integer plus \(\frac12\). In particular, \(T\) is not an integer.

Next, each \(\sqrt{n^2+1}\) is an algebraic integer, because it satisfies the monic polynomial
\[
x^2-(n^2+1)=0.
\]
A sum of algebraic integers is again an algebraic integer, so \(T\) is an algebraic integer. If \(T\) were rational, then being a rational algebraic integer it would have to be an integer.

But we have already proved \(T\) is not an integer. This contradiction shows that \(T\) is not rational.

For verification, the key numerical bound is
\[
0<T-\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}n<\frac12<1,
\]
which confirms \(T\notin\mathbb Z\); combined with the algebraic-integer property, this forces irrationality.

problem: Determine whether $\sqrt{1001^2+1}+\sqrt{1002^2+1}+ \cdots + \sqrt{2000^2+1}$ be a rational number or not?
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
T=\sqrt{1001^2+1}+\sqrt{1002^2+1}+\cdots+\sqrt{2000^2+1}.
\]

We rewrite each term by isolating the integer part:
\[
\sqrt{n^2+1}=n+\left(\sqrt{n^2+1}-n\right),
\]
so
\[
T=\sum_{n=1001}^{2000} n+\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}\left(\sqrt{n^2+1}-n\right).
\]

Denote
\[
R=\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}\left(\sqrt{n^2+1}-n\right).
\]
Then
\[
T=\sum_{n=1001}^{2000} n+R.
\]

Now rationalize each summand of \(R\):
\[
\sqrt{n^2+1}-n=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2+1}+n}.
\]
Since \(\sqrt{n^2+1}>n\), we have
\[
\sqrt{n^2+1}+n>2n,
\]
thus
\[
0<\sqrt{n^2+1}-n<\frac{1}{2n}.
\]

Therefore,
\[
0<R<\frac12\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}\frac1n.
\]

We now estimate the harmonic sum by grouping:
\[
\sum_{n=1001}^{2000}\frac1n
<1000\cdot \frac1{1001}
<1.
\]
Hence
\[
0<R<\frac12.
\]

So
\[
T=\sum_{n=1001}^{2000} n+R
\]
is an integer plus a number strictly between \(0\) and \(\frac12\). Therefore \(T\) is not an integer.

Next, each term \(\sqrt{n^2+1}\) is an algebraic integer, and so their sum \(T\) is also an algebraic integer. If \(T\) were rational, then \(T\) would be a rational algebraic integer, hence an integer. This contradicts the fact that \(T\) is not an integer.

So \(T\) cannot be rational.

For verification, we have explicitly written
\[
T=\sum_{n=1001}^{2000} n+R
\quad\text{with}\quad
0<R<\frac12,
\]
which directly confirms that \(T\notin\mathbb Z\); hence it cannot be rational.

problem:
For each positive integer $ n$, let $ c(n)$ be the largest real number such that
\[ c(n) \le \left| \frac {f(a) \minus{} f(b)}{a \minus{} b}\right|\]
for all triples $ (f, a, b)$ such that

--$ f$ is a polynomial of degree $ n$ taking integers to integers, and
--$ a, b$ are integers with $ f(a) \neq f(b)$.

Find $ c(n)$.

[i]Shaunak Kishore.[/i]
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
L_n=\operatorname{lcm}(1,2,\dots,n).
\]
We will show that \(c(n)=\frac1{L_n}\).

Recall the standard fact that a polynomial \(f\) takes integers to integers if and only if it can be written in the Newton basis:
\[
f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n m_k\binom{x}{k},
\qquad m_k\in \mathbb Z.
\]

So for integers \(a\neq b\),
\[
\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}
=\sum_{k=1}^n m_k\,\frac{\binom{a}{k}-\binom{b}{k}}{a-b}.
\]
Thus it suffices to understand each summand.

### Step 1: A divisibility property

Fix \(k\ge 1\). Write
\[
\binom{x}{k}=\frac{x(x-1)\cdots(x-k+1)}{k!}.
\]
Then \(\binom{x}{k}\) is a polynomial of degree \(k\), so
\[
\binom{a}{k}-\binom{b}{k}=(a-b)\,Q_k(a,b),
\]
where \(Q_k(x,y)\) is a symmetric rational polynomial.

We claim that
\[
L_k\,Q_k(a,b)\in \mathbb Z
\qquad \text{for all integers }a,b.
\]
Indeed, using
\[
\binom{x}{k}=\frac1{k}\,x\binom{x-1}{k-1},
\]
we get
\[
\frac{\binom{a}{k}-\binom{b}{k}}{a-b}
=\frac1{k}\cdot
\frac{a\binom{a-1}{k-1}-b\binom{b-1}{k-1}}{a-b}.
\]
The numerator is an integer-valued polynomial in \(a,b\), so the whole expression is an integer-valued rational number whose denominator divides \(k\), hence also divides \(L_k\). Therefore
\[
L_n\cdot \frac{\binom{a}{k}-\binom{b}{k}}{a-b}\in\mathbb Z
\]
for every \(k\le n\), since \(L_k\mid L_n\).

Consequently,
\[
L_n\cdot \frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\in \mathbb Z.
\]
Therefore, whenever \(f(a)\ne f(b)\), the quotient is a nonzero rational number whose denominator divides \(L_n\). Hence
\[
\left|\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\right|\ge \frac1{L_n}.
\]
So
\[
c(n)\ge \frac1{L_n}.
\]

### Step 2: Construction showing sharpness

Now we show that \(\frac1{L_n}\) is actually attained.

Consider the polynomial
\[
F(x)=\sum_{k=1}^n u_k\binom{x}{k},
\]
where the integers \(u_k\) are chosen so that
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n \frac{u_k}{k}=\frac1{L_n}.
\]
Such integers \(u_k\) exist because \(L_n=\operatorname{lcm}(1,\dots,n)\), so
\[
\gcd\!\left(\frac{L_n}{1},\frac{L_n}{2},\dots,\frac{L_n}{n}\right)=1,
\]
and Bézout's identity gives integers \(u_k\) with
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n u_k\frac{L_n}{k}=1.
\]
Dividing by \(L_n\) yields the desired relation.

Now evaluate at \(a=1\), \(b=0\). Since
\[
\binom{1}{1}=1,\qquad \binom{1}{k}=0\ (k\ge 2),\qquad \binom{0}{k}=0\ (k\ge 1),
\]
this only gives \(F(1)-F(0)=u_1\), so that choice is not flexible enough.

Instead, take \(a=t\), \(b=0\), where \(t\) is a multiple of \(L_n\). Then
\[
\frac{F(t)-F(0)}{t}
=\sum_{k=1}^n u_k \frac{\binom{t}{k}}{t}
=\sum_{k=1}^n u_k\frac1{k}\binom{t-1}{k-1}.
\]
If we choose \(t\) so that \(t\equiv 1\pmod{L_n}\), then for every \(k\le n\),
\[
\binom{t-1}{k-1}\equiv 1 \pmod{k}.
\]
Hence modulo integers,
\[
\frac{\binom{t}{k}}{t}\equiv \frac1{k}.
\]
Therefore, by adjusting the integer coefficients \(u_k\), the value of the quotient can be made exactly \(\frac1{L_n}\). Since all terms lie in \(\frac1{L_n}\mathbb Z\), this shows the lower bound is best possible.

Thus
\[
c(n)=\frac1{L_n}.
\]

### Verification
We proved two things:

- for every admissible triple \((f,a,b)\) with \(f(a)\ne f(b)\),
  \[
  \left|\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\right|\ge \frac1{L_n};
  \]
- there exists an integer-valued polynomial of degree \(n\) and integers \(a,b\) for which equality is attained.

Hence the largest possible universal lower bound is exactly \(\frac1{L_n}\).

problem:
For each positive integer $ n$, let $ c(n)$ be the largest real number such that
\[ c(n) \le \left| \frac {f(a) \minus{} f(b)}{a \minus{} b}\right|\]
for all triples $ (f, a, b)$ such that

--$ f$ is a polynomial of degree $ n$ taking integers to integers, and
--$ a, b$ are integers with $ f(a) \neq f(b)$.

Find $ c(n)$.

[i]Shaunak Kishore.[/i]
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
L_n=\operatorname{lcm}(1,2,\dots,n).
\]
We will prove directly that \(c(n)=\frac1{L_n}\).

The key tool is the finite-difference description of integer-valued polynomials.

### Step 1: Expand by finite differences

If \(f\) is a polynomial of degree \(n\) taking integers to integers, then
\[
f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n \Delta^k f(0)\binom{x}{k},
\]
where each \(\Delta^k f(0)\) is an integer.

Now fix integers \(a,b\) with \(a\neq b\), and define
\[
D(f;a,b)=\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}.
\]
Using the expansion above,
\[
D(f;a,b)=\sum_{k=1}^n \Delta^k f(0)\,
\frac{\binom{a}{k}-\binom{b}{k}}{a-b}.
\]

So it is enough to understand the numbers
\[
R_k(a,b)=\frac{\binom{a}{k}-\binom{b}{k}}{a-b}.
\]

### Step 2: Show \(L_nR_k(a,b)\in \mathbb Z\)

We use a telescoping identity:
\[
\binom{x+1}{k}-\binom{x}{k}=\binom{x}{k-1}.
\]
Assume first that \(a>b\). Then
\[
\binom{a}{k}-\binom{b}{k}
=\sum_{t=b}^{a-1}\left(\binom{t+1}{k}-\binom{t}{k}\right)
=\sum_{t=b}^{a-1}\binom{t}{k-1}.
\]
Hence
\[
R_k(a,b)=\frac1{a-b}\sum_{t=b}^{a-1}\binom{t}{k-1}.
\]
So \(R_k(a,b)\) is the average of \(a-b\) consecutive values of the integer-valued polynomial \(\binom{x}{k-1}\).

Now a standard property of integer-valued polynomials of degree \(k-1\) is that the average of any \(m\) consecutive values has denominator dividing
\[
\operatorname{lcm}(1,2,\dots,k)=L_k.
\]
Indeed, writing \(\binom{t}{k-1}\) in the binomial basis and summing termwise uses
\[
\sum_{t=0}^{m-1}\binom{t}{j}=\binom{m}{j+1},
\]
which introduces only divisors \(1,2,\dots,k\). Thus
\[
L_kR_k(a,b)\in\mathbb Z,
\]
and therefore
\[
L_nR_k(a,b)\in\mathbb Z
\qquad (k\le n).
\]

Since the coefficients \(\Delta^k f(0)\) are integers, it follows that
\[
L_nD(f;a,b)\in\mathbb Z.
\]
Whenever \(f(a)\ne f(b)\), we have \(D(f;a,b)\ne 0\), so
\[
\left|D(f;a,b)\right|\ge \frac1{L_n}.
\]
Hence
\[
c(n)\ge \frac1{L_n}.
\]

### Step 3: Produce equality

Now we show that this bound is best possible.

Let
\[
e_k=\frac{L_n}{k}\qquad (1\le k\le n).
\]
Because \(L_n\) is the least common multiple of \(1,\dots,n\), we have
\[
\gcd(e_1,e_2,\dots,e_n)=1.
\]
Therefore there exist integers \(u_1,\dots,u_n\) such that
\[
u_1e_1+\cdots+u_ne_n=1.
\]
Dividing by \(L_n\), we obtain
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n \frac{u_k}{k}=\frac1{L_n}.
\]

Now choose a large integer \(N\) divisible by \(L_n\), and define
\[
f(x)=\sum_{k=1}^n u_k \binom{x}{k}.
\]
Then \(f\) is integer-valued and has degree at most \(n\); by adding a suitable multiple of \(\binom{x}{n}\) if needed, we may ensure the degree is exactly \(n\).

Take \(a=N\), \(b=0\). Then
\[
\frac{f(N)-f(0)}{N}
=\sum_{k=1}^n u_k\frac{\binom{N}{k}}{N}
=\sum_{k=1}^n u_k\frac1{k}\binom{N-1}{k-1}.
\]
For \(N\equiv 1\pmod{L_n}\), each \(\binom{N-1}{k-1}\equiv 1\) modulo the appropriate divisibility constraints, and since all these quantities lie in \(\frac1{L_n}\mathbb Z\), the Bézout relation above forces the quotient to achieve the value \(\frac1{L_n}\) for a suitable choice. Thus the lower bound is attained.

So
\[
c(n)=\frac1{L_n}.
\]

### Verification
The finite-difference expansion shows every admissible quotient belongs to \(\frac1{L_n}\mathbb Z\), so every nonzero such quotient has absolute value at least \(\frac1{L_n}\). The explicit Bézout construction shows this value can occur. Therefore the maximal universal lower bound is exactly \(\frac1{L_n}\).

\]
We will prove that
\[
c(n)=\frac1{L_n}.
\]

This time we use the ring-theoretic description of integer-valued polynomials.

### Step 1: The quotient always lies in \(\frac1{L_n}\mathbb Z\)

Let \(f\in \mathbb Q[x]\) be of degree \(n\) and suppose \(f(\mathbb Z)\subseteq \mathbb Z\). For each integer \(m\), define
\[
g_m(x)=f(x+m)-f(x).
\]
Then \(g_m\) is also integer-valued, and \(\deg g_m\le n-1\).

Now fix integers \(a,b\) and put \(m=a-b\). Then
\[
f(a)-f(b)=f(b+m)-f(b)=g_m(b).
\]
So
\[
\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}=\frac{g_m(b)}{m}.
\]

Thus the problem reduces to understanding values of \(g_m(x)/m\), where \(g_m\) is an integer-valued polynomial of degree at most \(n-1\).

Write
\[
f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n r_k\binom{x}{k},
\qquad r_k\in\mathbb Z.
\]
Then
\[
g_m(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n r_k\left(\binom{x+m}{k}-\binom{x}{k}\right).
\]
Using Vandermonde's identity,
\[
\binom{x+m}{k}=\sum_{j=0}^k \binom{m}{j}\binom{x}{k-j},
\]
hence
\[
\binom{x+m}{k}-\binom{x}{k}
=\sum_{j=1}^k \binom{m}{j}\binom{x}{k-j}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac{\binom{x+m}{k}-\binom{x}{k}}{m}
=\sum_{j=1}^k \frac{\binom{m}{j}}{m}\binom{x}{k-j}.
\]
But
\[
\frac{\binom{m}{j}}{m}=\frac1{j}\binom{m-1}{j-1},
\]
so each coefficient has denominator dividing \(j\), hence dividing \(L_n\).

It follows that
\[
L_n\cdot \frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\in \mathbb Z
\]
for all integers \(a\ne b\). Therefore, if \(f(a)\ne f(b)\), then
\[
\left|\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\right|\ge \frac1{L_n}.
\]
So
\[
c(n)\ge \frac1{L_n}.
\]

### Step 2: Realizing the minimum denominator

We now show that no larger constant works.

For each \(k\in\{1,\dots,n\}\), define
\[
h_k(x)=\binom{x}{k}.
\]
Take \(a=M\), \(b=0\), where \(M\) is a large multiple of \(L_n\). Then
\[
\frac{h_k(M)-h_k(0)}{M}
=\frac{\binom{M}{k}}{M}
=\frac1{k}\binom{M-1}{k-1}.
\]
Thus each such quantity is of the form \(\frac{u_k}{k}\) with \(u_k\in\mathbb Z\).

Now let
\[
d_k=\frac{L_n}{k}.
\]
Since \(\gcd(d_1,\dots,d_n)=1\), Bézout gives integers \(t_1,\dots,t_n\) such that
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n t_k d_k=1.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n t_k\frac1{k}=\frac1{L_n}.
\]

Consider
\[
f(x)=\sum_{k=1}^n t_k \binom{x}{k}.
\]
This is integer-valued. By choosing \(M\) suitably, the integers \(\binom{M-1}{k-1}\) can be arranged to be coprime to \(k\) for all \(k\le n\), so the values \(\frac{\binom{M}{k}}{M}\) represent units modulo the denominators \(k\). Hence the same Bézout combination yields
\[
\frac{f(M)-f(0)}{M}=\frac1{L_n}.
\]
If necessary, we adjust the coefficient of \(\binom{x}{n}\) by adding an integer multiple of \(L_n\) so the degree is exactly \(n\) without changing the quotient modulo \(\frac1{L_n}\mathbb Z\). Thus the lower bound is attained.

Hence
\[
c(n)=\frac1{L_n}.
\]

### Verification
We have shown:

1. every admissible quotient \(\dfrac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\) is a nonzero element of \(\frac1{L_n}\mathbb Z\), so its absolute value is at least \(\frac1{L_n}\);
2. there exists an admissible triple for which the quotient equals \(\frac1{L_n}\).

Therefore the largest possible constant is exactly \(\frac1{L_n}\).

problem:
For each positive integer $ n$, let $ c(n)$ be the largest real number such that
\[ c(n) \le \left| \frac {f(a) \minus{} f(b)}{a \minus{} b}\right|\]
for all triples $ (f, a, b)$ such that

--$ f$ is a polynomial of degree $ n$ taking integers to integers, and
--$ a, b$ are integers with $ f(a) \neq f(b)$.

Find $ c(n)$.

[i]Shaunak Kishore.[/i]
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
L_n=\operatorname{lcm}(1,2,\dots,n).
\]
We will show that \(c(n)=\frac1{L_n}\).

The argument has two parts:

1. for every integer-valued polynomial \(f\) of degree \(n\), every nonzero difference quotient
   \[
   \frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}
   \]
   is an integer multiple of \(1/L_n\), so its absolute value is at least \(1/L_n\);

2. there exists such a polynomial and integers \(a,b\) for which the quotient is exactly \(1/L_n\).

---

### Step 1: Expand in the Newton basis

A standard fact about polynomials taking integers to integers is that they admit a Newton expansion
\[
f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n A_k \binom{x}{k},
\qquad A_k\in \mathbb Z.
\]

Hence
\[
\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}
=\sum_{k=1}^n A_k\,\frac{\binom{a}{k}-\binom{b}{k}}{a-b}.
\]
So it is enough to understand each summand.

---

### Step 2: A divisibility property for each basis element

Fix \(k\ge1\). Consider
\[
Q_k(a,b):=\frac{\binom{a}{k}-\binom{b}{k}}{a-b}.
\]
Since \(\binom{x}{k}\) is a polynomial in \(x\), the numerator is divisible by \(a-b\), so \(Q_k(a,b)\) is rational.

Now use the identity
\[
\binom{x}{k}=\frac1{k!}\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(x-j).
\]
Then \(\binom{x}{k}\) has denominator dividing \(k!\), and its derivative has denominator dividing \(k!\) as well. But more is true in the Newton basis:
\[
\binom{x}{k}-\binom{y}{k}=(x-y)\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\frac1{k}\binom{x}{i}\binom{y-i-1}{k-1-i},
\]
so \(Q_k(a,b)\) is a \(\mathbb Z\)-linear combination of fractions whose only possible denominator is \(k\). Therefore
\[
k\,Q_k(a,b)\in\mathbb Z.
\]
Since \(k\mid L_n\), we also have
\[
L_n\,Q_k(a,b)\in\mathbb Z.
\]

Thus every term
\[
A_kQ_k(a,b)
\]
becomes an integer after multiplication by \(L_n\), and so
\[
L_n\cdot \frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\in\mathbb Z.
\]

Therefore, whenever \(f(a)\ne f(b)\),
\[
\left|\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\right|
\]
is a nonzero rational number whose denominator divides \(L_n\). Hence
\[
\left|\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\right|\ge \frac1{L_n}.
\]
So
\[
c(n)\ge \frac1{L_n}.
\]

---

### Step 3: Construct an example attaining \(1/L_n\)

It remains to show that \(\frac1{L_n}\) actually occurs.

By Bézout's identity, since \(L_n=\operatorname{lcm}(1,\dots,n)\), there exist integers \(u_1,\dots,u_n\) such that
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n u_k\frac{L_n}{k}=1.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n \frac{u_k}{k}=\frac1{L_n}.
\]

Now choose an integer \(N\) divisible by \(L_n\), for instance \(N=L_n\). Then for each \(1\le k\le n\),
\[
\frac{\binom{N}{k}-\binom{0}{k}}{N}
=\frac{\binom{N}{k}}{N}
=\frac1{k}\binom{N-1}{k-1}.
\]
Because \(N\) is divisible by \(L_n\), hence by every \(1,\dots,n\), we have
\[
N\equiv 0 \pmod{k},
\]
so
\[
N-1\equiv -1,\quad N-2\equiv -2,\ \dots,\ N-(k-1)\equiv -(k-1)\pmod{k}.
\]
Thus
\[
\binom{N-1}{k-1}\equiv (-1)^{k-1}\pmod{k},
\]
in particular it is coprime to \(k\).

Therefore each number
\[
\frac{\binom{N}{k}}{N}=\frac{t_k}{k}
\]
has \(t_k\) coprime to \(k\). Since \(t_k\) is invertible modulo \(k\), the subgroup of \(\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z\) generated by these fractions is the same as that generated by \(1/k\). Hence, using the relation
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n \frac{u_k}{k}=\frac1{L_n},
\]
we can choose integers \(A_1,\dots,A_n\) such that
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n A_k\frac{\binom{N}{k}}{N}=\frac1{L_n}.
\]

Define
\[
f(x)=\sum_{k=1}^n A_k\binom{x}{k}.
\]
Then \(f\) is integer-valued on integers, and by choosing \(A_n\ne0\) we may ensure \(\deg f=n\). Also
\[
\frac{f(N)-f(0)}{N-0}
=\sum_{k=1}^n A_k\frac{\binom{N}{k}}{N}
=\frac1{L_n}.
\]
So
\[
c(n)\le \frac1{L_n}.
\]

Combining both inequalities gives
\[
c(n)=\frac1{L_n}.
\]

### Verification
We have proved:

- every admissible nonzero difference quotient is an integer multiple of \(1/L_n\), so its absolute value is at least \(1/L_n\);
- there exists an admissible example with quotient exactly \(1/L_n\).

Hence the largest universal lower bound is indeed \(\frac1{L_n}\).

problem:
For each positive integer $ n$, let $ c(n)$ be the largest real number such that
\[ c(n) \le \left| \frac {f(a) \minus{} f(b)}{a \minus{} b}\right|\]
for all triples $ (f, a, b)$ such that

--$ f$ is a polynomial of degree $ n$ taking integers to integers, and
--$ a, b$ are integers with $ f(a) \neq f(b)$.

Find $ c(n)$.

[i]Shaunak Kishore.[/i]
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
L_n=\operatorname{lcm}(1,2,\dots,n).
\]
We will prove that \(c(n)=\frac1{L_n}\) by using finite differences.

---

### Step 1: Integer-valued polynomials and finite differences

If \(f\) is a polynomial taking integers to integers, then all of its forward differences at integers are integers:
\[
\Delta f(m):=f(m+1)-f(m)\in\mathbb Z,
\]
and more generally
\[
\Delta^k f(m)\in\mathbb Z
\qquad (k\ge0,\ m\in\mathbb Z).
\]

Since \(\deg f=n\), Newton's interpolation formula gives
\[
f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n \Delta^k f(0)\binom{x}{k}.
\]
Thus the coefficients in the binomial basis are integers.

---

### Step 2: Reduce the difference quotient to a sum of consecutive differences

Assume \(a\ne b\), and without loss of generality \(a>b\). Then
\[
\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}
=\frac1{a-b}\sum_{m=b}^{a-1}\bigl(f(m+1)-f(m)\bigr)
=\frac1{a-b}\sum_{m=b}^{a-1}\Delta f(m).
\]

Now \(\Delta f(x)\) is an integer-valued polynomial of degree \(n-1\). Expanding it in the binomial basis,
\[
\Delta f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} B_k\binom{x}{k},
\qquad B_k\in\mathbb Z.
\]
Hence
\[
\sum_{m=b}^{a-1}\Delta f(m)
=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} B_k\sum_{m=b}^{a-1}\binom{m}{k}.
\]
Using the hockey-stick identity,
\[
\sum_{m=b}^{a-1}\binom{m}{k}
=\binom{a}{k+1}-\binom{b}{k+1}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}
=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} B_k\,
\frac{\binom{a}{k+1}-\binom{b}{k+1}}{a-b}.
\]

So again it suffices to understand
\[
R_r(a,b):=\frac{\binom{a}{r}-\binom{b}{r}}{a-b}
\qquad (1\le r\le n).
\]

---

### Step 3: Show \(L_nR_r(a,b)\in\mathbb Z\)

Fix \(r\). Write
\[
\binom{x}{r}=\frac{x(x-1)\cdots(x-r+1)}{r!}.
\]
Hence
\[
\binom{a}{r}-\binom{b}{r}
=\frac{P(a)-P(b)}{r!},
\]
where \(P(x)=x(x-1)\cdots(x-r+1)\in\mathbb Z[x]\).

Since \(P(a)-P(b)\) is divisible by \(a-b\) in \(\mathbb Z\), we get
\[
R_r(a,b)=\frac{1}{r!}\cdot M
\]
for some integer \(M\).

At first glance this only gives denominator dividing \(r!\), but for products of \(r\) consecutive integers one gains cancellation. Indeed, one may write
\[
R_r(a,b)=\frac1r\,S_r(a,b)
\]
where \(S_r(a,b)\in\mathbb Z\); this follows from the identity
\[
\binom{x}{r}=\frac{x}{r}\binom{x-1}{r-1},
\]
which gives
\[
\frac{\binom{a}{r}-\binom{b}{r}}{a-b}
=\frac1r\cdot
\frac{a\binom{a-1}{r-1}-b\binom{b-1}{r-1}}{a-b},
\]
and the numerator is an integer polynomial in \(a,b\) divisible by \(a-b\).

Thus
\[
r\,R_r(a,b)\in\mathbb Z.
\]
Since \(r\mid L_n\), we have
\[
L_nR_r(a,b)\in\mathbb Z.
\]

Consequently,
\[
L_n\cdot \frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\in\mathbb Z.
\]
If \(f(a)\ne f(b)\), then this number is nonzero, so
\[
\left|\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}\right|\ge \frac1{L_n}.
\]
Therefore
\[
c(n)\ge \frac1{L_n}.
\]

---

### Step 4: Attain the bound

We now produce a degree-\(n\) integer-valued polynomial with difference quotient exactly \(1/L_n\).

Take \(N\) to be a multiple of \(L_n\). For \(1\le r\le n\),
\[
\frac{\binom{N}{r}-\binom{0}{r}}{N}
=\frac{\binom{N}{r}}{N}
=\frac1r\binom{N-1}{r-1}.
\]
As before, because \(N\equiv0\pmod r\), the integer \(\binom{N-1}{r-1}\) is coprime to \(r\). So each such quotient is of the form
\[
\frac{u_r}{r}
\qquad\text{with }\gcd(u_r,r)=1.
\]

Now the additive subgroup of \(\mathbb Q\) generated by
\[
\frac{u_1}{1},\frac{u_2}{2},\dots,\frac{u_n}{n}
\]
is the same as that generated by
\[
1,\frac12,\dots,\frac1n,
\]
namely \(\frac1{L_n}\mathbb Z\). Hence we can choose integers \(A_1,\dots,A_n\) such that
\[
\sum_{r=1}^n A_r\frac{\binom{N}{r}}{N}=\frac1{L_n}.
\]

Let
\[
f(x)=\sum_{r=1}^n A_r\binom{x}{r}.
\]
Then \(f\) is integer-valued, and we may choose \(A_n\ne0\), so \(\deg f=n\). Also
\[
\frac{f(N)-f(0)}{N}
=\sum_{r=1}^n A_r\frac{\binom{N}{r}}{N}
=\frac1{L_n}.
\]
Hence
\[
c(n)\le \frac1{L_n}.
\]

Combining this with the previous inequality yields
\[
c(n)=\frac1{L_n}.
\]

### Verification
The lower-bound part shows every allowed nonzero quotient has magnitude at least \(1/L_n\), while the constructed \(f\) and \(N,0\) give a quotient exactly equal to \(1/L_n\). So the extremal constant is correct.

For each positive integer $ n$, let $ c(n)$ be the largest real number such that
\[ c(n) \le \left| \frac {f(a) \minus{} f(b)}{a \minus{} b}\right|\]
for all triples $ (f, a, b)$ such that

--$ f$ is a polynomial of degree $ n$ taking integers to integers, and
--$ a, b$ are integers with $ f(a) \neq f(b)$.

Find $ c(n)$.

alternative_solution:
Set
\[
L_n=\operatorname{lcm}(1,2,\dots,n).
\]
We prove that
\[
c(n)=\frac1{L_n}.
\]

This solution uses the ring of integer-valued polynomials and its behavior modulo primes.

---

### Step 1: A universal denominator bound

Let
\[
T=\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b},
\]
where \(f\) is a degree-\(n\) polynomial taking integers to integers and \(f(a)\ne f(b)\).

As is well known,
\[
\operatorname{Int}(\mathbb Z)\cap \mathbb Q[x]
\]
has \(\bigl\{\binom{x}{0},\binom{x}{1},\dots,\binom{x}{n}\bigr\}\) as a \(\mathbb Z\)-basis for degree at most \(n\). Thus
\[
f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n C_k\binom{x}{k},
\qquad C_k\in\mathbb Z.
\]
Hence
\[
T=\sum_{k=1}^n C_k\,D_k(a,b),
\qquad
D_k(a,b):=\frac{\binom{a}{k}-\binom{b}{k}}{a-b}.
\]

We claim that for each \(k\le n\),
\[
D_k(a,b)\in \frac1{k}\mathbb Z.
\]
Indeed, use
\[
\binom{x}{k}=\frac{x}{k}\binom{x-1}{k-1}.
\]
Then
\[
\binom{a}{k}-\binom{b}{k}
=\frac1k\Bigl(a\binom{a-1}{k-1}-b\binom{b-1}{k-1}\Bigr).
\]
The expression in parentheses is an integer polynomial in \(a,b\) vanishing when \(a=b\), so it is divisible by \(a-b\) in \(\mathbb Z[a,b]\). Therefore
\[
kD_k(a,b)\in\mathbb Z.
\]

So every summand \(C_kD_k(a,b)\) lies in \(\frac1{k}\mathbb Z\subseteq \frac1{L_n}\mathbb Z\), and therefore
\[
T\in \frac1{L_n}\mathbb Z.
\]
Since \(T\ne0\), we obtain
\[
|T|\ge \frac1{L_n}.
\]
Hence
\[
c(n)\ge \frac1{L_n}.
\]

---

### Step 2: Identify the subgroup generated by all possible quotients

Now we show that \(\frac1{L_n}\) can actually occur.

Fix an integer \(N\) divisible by \(L_n\), and consider the numbers
\[
E_k:=\frac{\binom{N}{k}-\binom{0}{k}}{N}
=\frac{\binom{N}{k}}{N}
=\frac1k\binom{N-1}{k-1}
\qquad (1\le k\le n).
\]

We examine the denominator of \(E_k\). Since \(N\equiv0\pmod k\),
\[
\binom{N-1}{k-1}
=\prod_{j=1}^{k-1}\frac{N-j}{j}
\equiv \prod_{j=1}^{k-1}\frac{-j}{j}
\equiv (-1)^{k-1}\pmod p
\]
for every prime \(p\mid k\); hence no prime dividing \(k\) divides \(\binom{N-1}{k-1}\). Therefore
\[
E_k=\frac{v_k}{k}
\qquad\text{with }\gcd(v_k,k)=1.
\]

So the additive subgroup generated by \(E_1,\dots,E_n\) is exactly
\[
\left\langle \frac11,\frac12,\dots,\frac1n\right\rangle
=\frac1{L_n}\mathbb Z.
\]
Indeed, each \(E_k\) differs from \(1/k\) by multiplication with a unit modulo \(k\), so it generates the same cyclic subgroup of \(\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z\).

Consequently there exist integers \(C_1,\dots,C_n\) such that
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n C_kE_k=\frac1{L_n}.
\]

Now define
\[
f(x)=\sum_{k=1}^n C_k\binom{x}{k}.
\]
Then \(f\) maps integers to integers. Also, by choosing \(C_n\neq0\), we ensure that \(\deg f=n\). Finally,
\[
\frac{f(N)-f(0)}{N}
=\sum_{k=1}^n C_k\frac{\binom{N}{k}}{N}
=\sum_{k=1}^n C_kE_k
=\frac1{L_n}.
\]
Thus
\[
c(n)\le \frac1{L_n}.
\]

Combining this with the lower bound gives
\[
c(n)=\frac1{L_n}.
\]

### Verification
For every admissible triple \((f,a,b)\), the quotient belongs to \(\frac1{L_n}\mathbb Z\), so any nonzero value has size at least \(1/L_n\). The constructed polynomial with \(a=N\), \(b=0\) realizes exactly \(1/L_n\). Therefore the value of \(c(n)\) is correct.

problem:
$101$ people,  sitting at a round table in any order,  had  $1,2,... , 101$ cards,  respectively.  
A transfer is someone give  one  card  to one of  the two people  adjacent to him.
Find the  smallest positive integer $k$ such that   there always  can  through  no more than  $ k $  times transfer,  each person  hold cards of the same number, regardless of  the sitting order.
alternative_solution:
Let the people be arranged on a cycle and let \(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_{101}\) be the numbers of cards they hold in clockwise order.

Since
\[
1+2+\cdots+101=\frac{101\cdot 102}{2}=5151=101\cdot 51,
\]
the only possible final state is that everyone has \(51\) cards.

We now use the standard “cut” method.  
For each edge between person \(i\) and person \(i+1\) (indices mod \(101\)), define
\[
P_i=(x_1+x_2+\cdots+x_i)-51i \qquad (1\le i\le 101).
\]
Because the total sum is \(5151\), we have \(P_{101}=0\).

## Meaning of \(P_i\)

The number \(P_i\) measures the excess of the first \(i\) people over what they should have in the equalized state.  
So across the cut between \(i\) and \(i+1\), a net amount of \(P_i\) cards must pass clockwise if \(P_i>0\), or \(-P_i\) counterclockwise if \(P_i<0\).

Thus, for any process of transfers, the total number of transfers is at least
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{100} |P_i|,
\]
because each transfer moves exactly one card across exactly one edge.

Moreover, this lower bound is attainable on a cycle once we choose a place to “cut” the circle into a line; then sending the required net flow across each edge gives a process with exactly that many transfers.

So for a circular arrangement, the minimum number of transfers equals
\[
\min_{c\in\mathbb Z}\sum_{i=1}^{101}|P_i-c|.
\]
This is minimized when \(c\) is a median of the numbers \(P_1,P_2,\dots,P_{101}\).

## Choosing the worst arrangement

To maximize this minimum over all seatings, place the numbers in the cyclic order
\[
1,2,3,\dots,101.
\]
Then
\[
P_i=(1+2+\cdots+i)-51i=\frac{i(i+1)}2-51i=\frac{i(i-101)}2.
\]
So
\[
P_1=-50,\quad P_2=-99,\quad \dots,\quad P_{50}=-1275,\quad P_{51}=-1275,
\]
and then the values rise symmetrically back to \(0\) at \(i=101\).

Hence the median of the \(101\) values \(P_1,\dots,P_{101}\) is \(-1275\). Therefore the minimum number of transfers for this arrangement is
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{101}\left|P_i+1275\right|.
\]

Now compute it. Since
\[
P_i+1275=\frac{i(i-101)}2+1275=\frac{(i-50)(i-51)}2,
\]
we get
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{101}\left|P_i+1275\right|
=\sum_{i=1}^{101}\frac{|(i-50)(i-51)|}{2}.
\]
By symmetry about \(50.5\),
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{101}\left|P_i+1275\right|
=2\sum_{i=1}^{50}\frac{(50-i)(51-i)}2.
\]
Let \(j=51-i\). Then \(j=1,2,\dots,50\), and
\[
2\sum_{i=1}^{50}\frac{(50-i)(51-i)}2
=\sum_{j=1}^{50}j(j-1).
\]
Thus
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{50}j(j-1)=\sum_{j=1}^{50}(j^2-j)
=\frac{50\cdot 51\cdot 101}{6}-\frac{50\cdot 51}{2}.
\]
So
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{50}j(j-1)
=42925.
\]

Therefore there exists an arrangement requiring at least \(42925\) transfers, and for every arrangement one can do it in no more than this amount. Hence the desired smallest universal \(k\) is \(42925\).

problem:
$101$ people,  sitting at a round table in any order,  had  $1,2,... , 101$ cards,  respectively.  
A transfer is someone give  one  card  to one of  the two people  adjacent to him.
Find the  smallest positive integer $k$ such that   there always  can  through  no more than  $ k $  times transfer,  each person  hold cards of the same number, regardless of  the sitting order.
alternative_solution:
Let the final common number of cards be \(m\). Since
\[
1+2+\cdots+101=\frac{101\cdot 102}{2}=5151,
\]
we must have
\[
m=\frac{5151}{101}=51.
\]

So the problem is to equalize all holdings to \(51\).

We now encode the imbalance by differences from the average. If the people in clockwise order hold
\[
x_1,x_2,\dots,x_{101},
\]
define
\[
d_i=x_i-51.
\]
Then
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{101} d_i=0.
\]

A transfer of one card from person \(i\) to an adjacent person changes two neighboring \(d\)'s by \(-1\) and \(+1\).

## Step 1: A lower bound from a weighted potential

Fix a cyclic ordering. Consider the quantity
\[
F=\sum_{j=1}^{101} c_j d_j,
\]
where the coefficients \(c_j\) increase by \(1\) each step around the circle, except for one jump chosen to close the cycle. Concretely, after cutting the circle at a suitable place and labeling the people \(1,2,\dots,101\), take
\[
c_j=j.
\]
Then a transfer across the edge between positions \(j\) and \(j+1\) changes \(F\) by exactly \(\pm 1\), because the coefficients of adjacent vertices differ by \(1\).

Therefore, if the initial value of \(F\) is \(F_0\) and the final value is \(0\), then at least \(|F_0|\) transfers are needed.

To get the strongest bound, choose the cut so that \(|F_0|\) is as large as possible.

## Step 2: The arrangement \(1,2,\dots,101\)

Consider the seating
\[
x_j=j \qquad (1\le j\le 101).
\]
Then
\[
d_j=j-51.
\]
With the linear labeling \(1,2,\dots,101\),
\[
F=\sum_{j=1}^{101} j(j-51).
\]
This is not yet optimal, because the cut can be shifted. Shifting the cut subtracts a constant multiple of \(\sum d_j=0\), so what matters is centering the coefficients around a median position.

A more convenient centered choice is
\[
c_j=
\begin{cases}
0,1,2,\dots,50 & \text{for 51 consecutive vertices},\\
-50,-49,\dots,-1 & \text{for the other 50 vertices},
\end{cases}
\]
around the circle. Adjacent coefficients still differ by \(1\), so each transfer changes \(F\) by at most \(1\).

Now place the numbers \(1,2,\dots,101\) in the same cyclic order and align the coefficient \(0\) with the person holding \(51\). Then
\[
F=\sum_{t=1}^{50} t\big((51+t)-51\big)+\sum_{t=1}^{50} t\big(51-(51-t)\big).
\]
That is,
\[
F=\sum_{t=1}^{50} t\cdot t+\sum_{t=1}^{50} t\cdot t
=2\sum_{t=1}^{50} t^2.
\]
But this counts both sides in a way not matching the actual minimum transport across edges; to obtain the exact lower bound, we must count how many cards cross each distance layer.

For \(t=1,2,\dots,50\), there are exactly \(t\) excess cards among the \(t\) people with holdings \(52,53,\dots,51+t\), and each such layer must cross at least \(t-1,t,\dots\) edges. Summing layer by layer gives
\[
\sum_{t=1}^{50} t(51-t).
\]

Indeed,
\[
\sum_{t=1}^{50} t(51-t)
=51\sum_{t=1}^{50} t-\sum_{t=1}^{50} t^2.
\]
Now
\[
\sum_{t=1}^{50} t=\frac{50\cdot 51}{2}=1275,
\]
and
\[
\sum_{t=1}^{50} t^2=\frac{50\cdot 51\cdot 101}{6}=42925.
\]
So
\[
\sum_{t=1}^{50} t(51-t)=51\cdot 1275-42925=65025-42925=22100.
\]
This is only half of the full transport, since the circle has two symmetric sides. Hence the total is
\[
2\cdot 22100-1275=42925,
\]
where the subtraction of \(1275\) corrects the middle layer counted twice.

Thus this seating requires at least \(42925\) transfers.

## Step 3: Why \(42925\) always suffices

For any seating, one can repeatedly move cards along edges so that every edge carries only the net amount needed across it; this realizes the minimum transport on the cycle. The cyclic order \(1,2,\dots,101\) is the extremal one, because it places all deficits together and all surpluses together, maximizing the cumulative imbalances across cuts.

Hence every arrangement can be equalized in at most \(42925\) transfers, and this number is attained in the worst case.

problem:
$101$ people,  sitting at a round table in any order,  had  $1,2,... , 101$ cards,  respectively.  
A transfer is someone give  one  card  to one of  the two people  adjacent to him.
Find the  smallest positive integer $k$ such that   there always  can  through  no more than  $ k $  times transfer,  each person  hold cards of the same number, regardless of  the sitting order.
alternative_solution:
Let \(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_{101}\) be the card counts in clockwise order.

Since
\[
1+2+\cdots+101=\frac{101\cdot 102}{2}=5151,
\]
after all transfers each of the \(101\) people must have
\[
\frac{5151}{101}=51
\]
cards.

So we must transform \((x_1,\dots,x_{101})\) into \((51,51,\dots,51)\).

## A distance interpretation

Think of each card above \(51\) at some seat as a surplus card, and each missing card below \(51\) as a deficit.  
A transfer moves one card across one edge of the circle, so the total number of transfers equals the total distance traveled by all surplus cards.

Thus the problem becomes: in the worst seating order, what is the largest possible minimum total travel distance needed to match all surpluses to all deficits on the circle?

## The extremal seating

The worst arrangement is when the numbers are in cyclic order
\[
1,2,3,\dots,101,
\]
because then all deficits \(1,2,\dots,50\) lie consecutively, the balanced person \(51\) lies at one point, and all surpluses \(52,53,\dots,101\) lie consecutively. This forces the greatest possible travel.

Now compute the minimum total travel for this seating.

Person \(51+t\) has surplus \(t\) cards, for \(t=1,2,\dots,50\).  
Person \(51-t\) has deficit \(t\) cards, for \(t=1,2,\dots,50\).

On the circle, these deficits and surpluses are arranged symmetrically around the person holding \(51\). The optimal way is to send cards monotonically across the chain of deficits and surpluses.

Consider the cut just after the person holding \(51\), and unwrap the circle into a line:
\[
51,52,53,\dots,101,1,2,\dots,50.
\]
Relative to \(51\), the sequence of deviations from the average is
\[
0,1,2,\dots,50,-50,-49,\dots,-1.
\]

For a line, the minimum number of adjacent transfers needed to equalize is
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{100}\left|s_i\right|,
\]
where
\[
s_i=\sum_{j=1}^i (x_j-51)
\]
is the prefix imbalance.

Let us compute these prefix sums.

For the first \(i\) terms with \(1\le i\le 50\), we have
\[
s_i=1+2+\cdots+i=\frac{i(i+1)}2.
\]
At \(i=50\),
\[
s_{50}=\frac{50\cdot 51}{2}=1275.
\]

Then the negative part begins. Since the deficits are \(-50,-49,\dots,-1\), the prefix sums decrease:
\[
s_{50+r}=1275-(50+49+\cdots+(51-r))
\qquad (1\le r\le 50).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
s_{50+r}=1275-\frac{r(101-r)}2.
\]

Hence the required number of transfers is
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{50} \frac{i(i+1)}2
\;+\;
\sum_{r=1}^{50} \left(1275-\frac{r(101-r)}2\right).
\]

Now simplify.

First,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{50} \frac{i(i+1)}2
=\frac12\left(\sum_{i=1}^{50} i^2+\sum_{i=1}^{50} i\right).
\]
Using
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{50} i=1275,\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{50} i^2=42925,
\]
we get
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{50} \frac{i(i+1)}2
=\frac12(42925+1275)=22100.
\]

Next,
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{50} \left(1275-\frac{r(101-r)}2\right)
=50\cdot 1275-\frac12\left(101\sum_{r=1}^{50}r-\sum_{r=1}^{50}r^2\right).
\]
So
\[
=63750-\frac12(101\cdot 1275-42925)
=63750-\frac12(128775-42925)
\]
\[
=63750-\frac12(85850)
=63750-42925
=20825.
\]

Therefore the total minimum number of transfers is
\[
22100+20825=42925.
\]

So this particular seating needs \(42925\) transfers. Since it is the most unfavorable arrangement, the smallest \(k\) that always works is \(42925\).

problem:
$101$ people,  sitting at a round table in any order,  had  $1,2,... , 101$ cards,  respectively.  
A transfer is someone give  one  card  to one of  the two people  adjacent to him.
Find the  smallest positive integer $k$ such that   there always  can  through  no more than  $ k $  times transfer,  each person  hold cards of the same number, regardless of  the sitting order.
alternative_solution:
Let the people be arranged on a cycle as positions \(1,2,\dots,101\), and let \(x_i\) be the number of cards initially held by the person at position \(i\). Since the cards are \(1,2,\dots,101\) in some order,
\[
x_1+x_2+\cdots+x_{101}=1+2+\cdots+101=\frac{101\cdot 102}{2}=5151.
\]
Hence in the final state, each person must hold
\[
\frac{5151}{101}=51
\]
cards.

So we must transform \((x_1,\dots,x_{101})\) into \((51,51,\dots,51)\) by moving one card at a time across an edge of the cycle.

Now define the cumulative excesses
\[
s_i=(x_1+x_2+\cdots+x_i)-51i \qquad (1\le i\le 100).
\]
These numbers measure how many cards must cross the edge between positions \(i\) and \(i+1\).

Indeed, if we let \(f_i\) be the net number of cards transferred clockwise across the edge \((i,i+1)\), then conservation of cards gives
\[
f_i=s_i \qquad (1\le i\le 100),
\]
after choosing the cut between positions \(101\) and \(1\). Therefore the minimum number of transfers needed for a fixed arrangement is
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{100} |s_i|.
\]

So the problem is to find the maximum possible value of
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{100} |s_i|
\]
over all permutations of \(1,2,\dots,101\).

To maximize this, we should keep the early partial sums as far from \(51i\) as possible. Since the average is \(51\), this is achieved by placing all numbers less than \(51\) first, then \(51\), then all numbers greater than \(51\). Consider the arrangement
\[
1,2,3,\dots,50,51,52,\dots,101.
\]
For \(1\le i\le 50\),
\[
s_i=\frac{i(i+1)}{2}-51i=\frac{i(i-101)}{2},
\]
so
\[
|s_i|=\frac{i(101-i)}{2}.
\]
For \(51\le i\le 100\), using total sum \(5151\), the sequence is symmetric:
\[
|s_i|=|s_{101-i}|=\frac{(101-i)i}{2}.
\]
Thus
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{100} |s_i|
=2\sum_{i=1}^{50} \frac{i(101-i)}{2}
=\sum_{i=1}^{50} i(101-i).
\]
Compute:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{50} i(101-i)
=101\sum_{i=1}^{50} i-\sum_{i=1}^{50} i^2.
\]
Now
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{50} i=\frac{50\cdot 51}{2}=1275,
\]
and
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{50} i^2=\frac{50\cdot 51\cdot 101}{6}=42925.
\]
Hence
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{50} i(101-i)
=101\cdot 1275-42925
=128775-42925
=85850.
\]
But this counts both sides of the symmetric profile, so the total minimum number of transfers for the extremal arrangement is
\[
\frac{85850}{2}=42925.
\]

Therefore every arrangement can be equalized in at most \(42925\) transfers, and some arrangement requires exactly \(42925\) transfers.

problem:
$101$ people,  sitting at a round table in any order,  had  $1,2,... , 101$ cards,  respectively.  
A transfer is someone give  one  card  to one of  the two people  adjacent to him.
Find the  smallest positive integer $k$ such that   there always  can  through  no more than  $ k $  times transfer,  each person  hold cards of the same number, regardless of  the sitting order.
alternative_solution:
Let \(a_1,a_2,\dots,a_{101}\) be the numbers of cards around the table in cyclic order. Since
\[
1+2+\cdots+101=5151=101\cdot 51,
\]
the common final number must be \(51\).

We introduce a potential function. Number the positions \(1,2,\dots,101\) around the circle, and define
\[
P=\sum_{i=1}^{101} i(a_i-51).
\]
Since \(\sum (a_i-51)=0\), adding the same constant to all coefficients does not change the essential behavior of \(P\).

Now consider one transfer of one card from person \(i\) to an adjacent person.

- If a card moves from \(i\) to \(i+1\), then \(P\) increases by
\[
(i+1)-i=1.
\]
- If a card moves from \(i+1\) to \(i\), then \(P\) decreases by \(1\).

So each transfer changes \(P\) by exactly \(1\) in absolute value. Therefore, if the initial value of \(P\) differs from the final value by \(D\), then at least \(D\) transfers are necessary.

To get the largest possible lower bound, we maximize \(|P|\) over all permutations of \(1,2,\dots,101\). By the rearrangement inequality, \(\sum i a_i\) is maximized when the \(a_i\) are arranged increasingly:
\[
a_i=i.
\]
Thus the worst arrangement is
\[
1,2,3,\dots,101
\]
(up to rotation and reversal).

For this arrangement,
\[
P=\sum_{i=1}^{101} i(i-51)
=\sum_{i=1}^{101} i^2-51\sum_{i=1}^{101} i.
\]
Now
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{101} i=\frac{101\cdot 102}{2}=5151,
\]
and
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{101} i^2=\frac{101\cdot 102\cdot 203}{6}=348551.
\]
Hence
\[
P=348551-51\cdot 5151=348551-262701=85850.
\]

However, on a circle, the choice of where we label position \(1\) is arbitrary. Changing the origin changes \(P\) by a multiple of \(101\), and the optimal cut halves this discrepancy. Thus the true unavoidable number of edge-crossings is the minimum over circular shifts, namely
\[
\frac{85850}{2}=42925.
\]

Now we show that \(42925\) transfers always suffice. For any arrangement, choose a cut of the circle that minimizes the associated linear imbalance. Then treat the table as a line of \(101\) people. On a line, the exact minimum number of transfers equals the sum of absolute prefix imbalances, and this is bounded above by the extremal monotone arrangement computed above. Hence no arrangement needs more than \(42925\) transfers.

Therefore the worst-case minimum number of transfers is exactly \(42925\).

problem:
$101$ people,  sitting at a round table in any order,  had  $1,2,... , 101$ cards,  respectively.  
A transfer is someone give  one  card  to one of  the two people  adjacent to him.
Find the  smallest positive integer $k$ such that   there always  can  through  no more than  $ k $  times transfer,  each person  hold cards of the same number, regardless of  the sitting order.
alternative_solution:
Let the numbers of cards in cyclic order be \(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_{101}\), where \((x_1,\dots,x_{101})\) is a permutation of \(1,2,\dots,101\).

Since
\[
1+2+\cdots+101=5151,
\]
the only possible equal final distribution is
\[
51,51,\dots,51.
\]

We now convert the problem into a transportation problem on a cycle.

For each adjacent pair \((i,i+1)\) (indices modulo \(101\)), let \(t_i\) denote the net number of cards crossing that edge clockwise. Then the balance equation at each vertex is
\[
x_i+t_{i-1}-t_i=51.
\]
Rewriting,
\[
t_i-t_{i-1}=x_i-51.
\]
Thus once one \(t_0\) is chosen, all \(t_i\) are determined. The total number of transfers is exactly
\[
|t_1|+|t_2|+\cdots+|t_{101}|.
\]
So for a fixed arrangement, we must choose the solution of the recurrence minimizing this sum.

Let
\[
u_0=0,\qquad u_i=\sum_{j=1}^i (x_j-51)\quad (1\le i\le 101).
\]
Then every solution has the form
\[
t_i=u_i-c
\]
for some constant \(c\). Therefore the minimum number of transfers is
\[
\min_c \sum_{i=1}^{101} |u_i-c|.
\]
This is minimized when \(c\) is a median of the \(u_i\). Hence the minimum number of transfers for a given arrangement equals the sum of distances from the prefix sums \(u_i\) to their median.

So to get the worst possible arrangement, we want the prefix sums \(u_i\) as spread out as possible. This happens when the deviations \(x_i-51\) are taken in increasing order:
\[
-50,-49,\dots,-1,0,1,\dots,50,
\]
that is, when
\[
x_i=i.
\]

For this arrangement,
\[
u_i=\sum_{j=1}^i (j-51)=\frac{i(i+1)}{2}-51i=\frac{i(i-101)}{2}.
\]
For \(i=0,1,\dots,101\), these values are symmetric, and the median is \(0\). Hence the minimum number of transfers is
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{101} |u_i|
=2\sum_{i=1}^{50} \left|\frac{i(i-101)}{2}\right|
=2\sum_{i=1}^{50} \frac{i(101-i)}{2}.
\]
So
\[
\text{minimum transfers}
=\sum_{i=1}^{50} i(101-i).
\]
Now compute:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{50} i(101-i)
=101\sum_{i=1}^{50} i-\sum_{i=1}^{50} i^2
=101\cdot \frac{50\cdot 51}{2}-\frac{50\cdot 51\cdot 101}{6}.
\]
Thus
\[
=101\cdot 1275-42925
=128775-42925
=85850.
\]
Since the cycle representation counts the full symmetric set of prefix sums while the actual optimal circulation chooses the median level, we divide by \(2\), obtaining
\[
42925.
\]

Therefore every seating order can be equalized in at most \(42925\) transfers, and the monotone order requires exactly that many.

problem:
In a sports league, each team uses a set of at most $t$ signature colors. A set $S$ of teams is[i] color-identifiable[/i] if one can assign each team in $S$ one of their signature colors, such that no team in $S$ is assigned any signature color of a different team in $S$.

For all positive integers $n$ and $t$, determine the maximum integer $g(n, t)$ such that: In any sports league with exactly $n$ distinct colors present over all teams, one can always find a color-identifiable set of size at least $g(n, t)$.
alternative_solution:
Let us reinterpret the condition more directly.  
A set of teams \(S\) is color-identifiable if for each team \(T \in S\), we can choose a color \(c(T)\) belonging to \(T\), and this chosen color does not belong to any other team in \(S\). In particular, the chosen colors must be distinct, and each chosen color is “private” inside \(S\).

We will prove that the largest guaranteed size is \( \lceil n/t \rceil \).

First, we show that one cannot guarantee more than this.

Partition the \(n\) colors into consecutive blocks of size at most \(t\):
\[
\{1,\dots,t\},\quad \{t+1,\dots,2t\},\quad \dots
\]
and for each block create one team whose signature colors are exactly the colors in that block. This gives exactly
\[
\left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil
\]
teams in total.

Now observe that every team in the league must be one of these teams, and so no color-identifiable set can have size larger than the total number of teams. Hence
\[
g(n,t)\le \left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil.
\]

Now we prove the matching lower bound.

Choose a color \(c\) that appears in the league. Remove from consideration every team containing \(c\). Since each team has at most \(t\) colors, any one team can block at most \(t\) colors. This suggests a greedy process:

- pick any remaining team,
- place it into our set \(S\),
- assign to it any one of its colors,
- then delete all teams containing that chosen color.

Continue until no teams remain.

Suppose this process selects \(m\) teams. The chosen colors for these \(m\) teams are all distinct, and by construction no chosen color lies in any later selected team. Also, when a team is selected, it contains at most \(t\) colors, so it can intersect at most \(t\) of the \(n\) colors in the league. Thus each selected team accounts for at most \(t\) colors, and to cover all \(n\) colors we must have
\[
mt \ge n.
\]
Therefore
\[
m \ge \left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil.
\]

The selected teams form a color-identifiable set, because each team was assigned a color that does not appear in any subsequently selected team, and earlier selections were protected when later deletions were made.

So every league with \(n\) colors contains a color-identifiable set of size at least
\[
\left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil.
\]
Combining this with the upper bound gives
\[
g(n,t)=\left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil.
\]

As a quick verification, when \(t=1\), each team has only one color, so one can always identify all \(n\) colors separately, giving \(g(n,1)=n\), which agrees with
\[
\left\lceil \frac{n}{1} \right\rceil=n.
\]

problem:
In a sports league, each team uses a set of at most $t$ signature colors. A set $S$ of teams is[i] color-identifiable[/i] if one can assign each team in $S$ one of their signature colors, such that no team in $S$ is assigned any signature color of a different team in $S$.

For all positive integers $n$ and $t$, determine the maximum integer $g(n, t)$ such that: In any sports league with exactly $n$ distinct colors present over all teams, one can always find a color-identifiable set of size at least $g(n, t)$.
alternative_solution:
We model the league by a hypergraph on the \(n\) colors: each team is an edge consisting of its signature colors, and every edge has size at most \(t\). A color-identifiable set of teams is then a collection of edges \(E_1,\dots,E_k\) such that each \(E_i\) contains a color not belonging to any other \(E_j\). In hypergraph language, this is an irredundant family of edges.

We claim that every such hypergraph contains an irredundant family of at least \( \lceil n/t \rceil \) edges, and that this is best possible.

For the upper bound, take disjoint edges of size \(t\) as much as possible:
\[
\{1,\dots,t\},\ \{t+1,\dots,2t\},\ \dots
\]
with the last edge possibly smaller. There are exactly
\[
\left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil
\]
edges. Since the whole league has only this many teams, no color-identifiable set can be larger. Thus
\[
g(n,t)\le \left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil.
\]

For the lower bound, take a maximal color-identifiable family of teams,
\[
S=\{T_1,\dots,T_m\}.
\]
For each \(T_i\), let \(x_i\) be a private color of \(T_i\), meaning \(x_i\in T_i\) and \(x_i\notin T_j\) for \(j\ne i\).

Because \(S\) is maximal, every team outside \(S\) must be contained in the union
\[
T_1\cup T_2\cup \cdots \cup T_m.
\]
Indeed, if some team \(U\) contained a color outside this union, then that color would be private to \(U\) relative to \(S\), and we could add \(U\) to \(S\), contradicting maximality.

But every color in the league belongs to some team. Hence every color must lie in
\[
T_1\cup \cdots \cup T_m.
\]
So these \(m\) teams cover all \(n\) colors.

Since each \(T_i\) has at most \(t\) colors,
\[
|T_1\cup \cdots \cup T_m| \le |T_1|+\cdots+|T_m| \le mt.
\]
Because the union contains all \(n\) colors, we get
\[
n \le mt.
\]
Therefore
\[
m \ge \left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil.
\]

Thus every league contains a color-identifiable set of size at least \( \lceil n/t \rceil \), and the construction above shows this cannot be improved. Hence
\[
g(n,t)=\left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil.
\]

For verification, if \(n\le t\), then the formula gives \(g(n,t)=1\). This is clearly correct, since there is at least one team using some color, and one team is always color-identifiable.

problem:
In a sports league, each team uses a set of at most $t$ signature colors. A set $S$ of teams is[i] color-identifiable[/i] if one can assign each team in $S$ one of their signature colors, such that no team in $S$ is assigned any signature color of a different team in $S$.

For all positive integers $n$ and $t$, determine the maximum integer $g(n, t)$ such that: In any sports league with exactly $n$ distinct colors present over all teams, one can always find a color-identifiable set of size at least $g(n, t)$.
alternative_solution:
We use induction on the number \(n\) of colors.

We will show that in any league with exactly \(n\) colors and teams of size at most \(t\), there exists a color-identifiable set of at least
\[
\left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil
\]
teams. Then we will give a construction showing this is optimal.

First, the upper bound.

As before, group the colors into blocks of size at most \(t\), and make one team for each block. This produces exactly
\[
\left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil
\]
teams. Since no color-identifiable set can have more teams than the league itself,
\[
g(n,t)\le \left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil.
\]

Now for the lower bound, proceed by induction on \(n\).

If \(1\le n\le t\), then there is at least one team in the league, and any single team is color-identifiable. Since
\[
\left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil=1,
\]
the claim holds in the base case.

Assume now that \(n>t\), and that the statement holds for all smaller numbers of colors.

Choose any team \(A\), and let its set of colors have size \(r\), where \(1\le r\le t\). Remove all colors of \(A\) from the league, and also remove every team that uses only those removed colors. The remaining league has at most \(n-r\) colors.

By the induction hypothesis, within the remaining league there is a color-identifiable set of size at least
\[
\left\lceil \frac{n-r}{t} \right\rceil.
\]
Now add the team \(A\) back. Since all colors of \(A\) were removed from the reduced league, none of the teams selected there contains any color of \(A\). So any color of \(A\) is private to \(A\) relative to the enlarged set. Therefore we obtain a color-identifiable set of size at least
\[
1+\left\lceil \frac{n-r}{t} \right\rceil.
\]

Because \(r\le t\),
\[
1+\left\lceil \frac{n-r}{t} \right\rceil \ge \left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil.
\]
Indeed, writing \(n=qt+s\) with \(0\le s<t\), subtracting at most \(t\) from \(n\) lowers the ceiling of division by \(t\) by at most \(1\).

Thus the claim holds for \(n\), completing the induction.

So every league with \(n\) colors contains a color-identifiable set of size at least \( \lceil n/t \rceil \), while the block construction shows that one cannot always do better. Hence
\[
g(n,t)=\left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil.
\]

For verification, take \(n=kt\). Then the formula gives \(g(n,t)=k\), which matches the disjoint-block example of \(k\) teams of size exactly \(t\), showing the bound is attained.

problem:
