In a sports league, each team uses a set of at most $t$ signature colors. A set $S$ of teams is[i] color-identifiable[/i] if one can assign each team in $S$ one of their signature colors, such that no team in $S$ is assigned any signature color of a different team in $S$.

For all positive integers $n$ and $t$, determine the maximum integer $g(n, t)$ such that: In any sports league with exactly $n$ distinct colors present over all teams, one can always find a color-identifiable set of size at least $g(n, t)$.
alternative_solution:
Let the teams be represented by subsets of an \(n\)-element color set, each subset having size at most \(t\).  
A color-identifiable set of teams is exactly a family of teams for which we can choose, for each selected team, a color belonging to that team and chosen colors are all distinct. In other words, we seek a large subfamily with a system of distinct representatives.

We will show that the guaranteed size is \( \left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil \).

First, we prove the upper bound.  
Partition the \(n\) colors into consecutive blocks of size at most \(t\):
\[
\{1,\dots,t\},\quad \{t+1,\dots,2t\},\quad \dots
\]
and for each block create one team whose signature colors are exactly the colors in that block. Then the number of teams is
\[
\left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil.
\]
Since every pair of different teams has disjoint color sets, a color-identifiable subset can contain at most one representative from each team, so in this league the largest possible identifiable set has size exactly
\[
\left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil.
\]
Hence
\[
g(n,t)\le \left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil.
\]

Now we prove the lower bound.  
Choose a color-identifiable set \(S\) of maximum possible size, and let \(|S|=m\). For the teams in \(S\), fix a valid assignment of distinct colors to them. Let \(C_S\) be the set of assigned colors, so \(|C_S|=m\).

We claim that every team in the whole league must contain at least one color from \(C_S\).  
Indeed, suppose some team \(T\) had no color in \(C_S\). Then every color of \(T\) is outside \(C_S\), so adding \(T\) to \(S\) and assigning to \(T\) any one of its own colors would preserve distinctness, contradicting the maximality of \(S\).

Thus \(C_S\) is a hitting set for all teams: every team uses at least one color from \(C_S\).

Since each color belongs only to teams that contain it, and each team contains at most \(t\) colors, the union of the colors in \(C_S\) can “cover” all \(n\) colors only if
\[
|C_S|\cdot t \ge n.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
m\ge \left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil.
\]
Therefore
\[
g(n,t)\ge \left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil.
\]

Combining the two inequalities gives
\[
g(n,t)=\left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil.
\]

As a quick verification, when \(t=1\), every team has a single color, so one can always choose one team per color, giving \(g(n,1)=n\), which agrees with
\[
\left\lceil \frac{n}{1} \right\rceil=n.
\]

problem:
In a sports league, each team uses a set of at most $t$ signature colors. A set $S$ of teams is[i] color-identifiable[/i] if one can assign each team in $S$ one of their signature colors, such that no team in $S$ is assigned any signature color of a different team in $S$.

For all positive integers $n$ and $t$, determine the maximum integer $g(n, t)$ such that: In any sports league with exactly $n$ distinct colors present over all teams, one can always find a color-identifiable set of size at least $g(n, t)$.
alternative_solution:
We reinterpret the problem as a matching problem in a bipartite graph.

Create a bipartite graph whose left side consists of the teams and whose right side consists of the \(n\) colors. Join a team to the colors in its signature-color set. Then a set of teams is color-identifiable exactly when those teams can be matched to distinct adjacent colors.

So the problem asks for the largest integer \(g(n,t)\) such that every bipartite graph with \(n\) right-side vertices and left-side degrees at most \(t\) contains a matching saturating at least \(g(n,t)\) left vertices.

We first establish the upper bound.  
Take
\[
\left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil
\]
teams, with the first team adjacent to colors \(1,\dots,t\), the second to \(t+1,\dots,2t\), and so on, with the last team using the remaining at most \(t\) colors. This uses exactly \(n\) colors in total.

Here the total number of teams is \( \left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil \), so certainly no identifiable set can have more teams than that. Hence
\[
g(n,t)\le \left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil.
\]

Now for the lower bound, let \(M\) be a maximum matching in an arbitrary such bipartite graph, and let \(m=|M|\). We will show
\[
m\ge \left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil.
\]

Let \(U\) be the set of unmatched colors on the right. If \(U=\varnothing\), then all \(n\) colors are matched, so in particular \(m\ge n/t\), and we are done. Thus suppose \(U\neq\varnothing\).

Consider the standard alternating-tree construction starting from all unmatched colors. Let \(R\) be the set of right-side vertices reachable from \(U\) by alternating paths, and let \(L\) be the set of left-side vertices reachable in the same way.

Because \(M\) is maximum, there is no augmenting path from an unmatched color to an unmatched team. Therefore every team in \(L\) is matched, and its matched edge leads back to a color in \(R\). Hence the matching gives a bijection between \(L\) and \(R\setminus U\), so
\[
|L|=|R|-|U|.
\]

Also, every neighbor of a team in \(L\) lies in \(R\); otherwise the alternating search could continue. Thus all edges incident to \(L\) go into \(R\). Since each team has degree at most \(t\),
\[
|R|\le t|L|.
\]
Substituting \( |L|=|R|-|U| \), we get
\[
|R|\le t(|R|-|U|).
\]
This implies
\[
t|U|\le (t-1)|R|.
\]
A more useful relation comes from counting the colors outside \(R\): every matched edge using a color outside \(R\) must go to a team outside \(L\), so there are exactly \(m-|L|\) such colors. Therefore
\[
n-|R|=m-|L|.
\]
Using \( |L|=|R|-|U| \), this becomes
\[
n-|R|=m-(|R|-|U|),
\]
so
\[
n=m+|U|.
\]
Since every unmatched color lies in \(U\), and each matched team uses at most \(t\) colors, the \(m\) matched teams together can account for at most \(mt\) colors. Hence
\[
n\le mt.
\]
Therefore
\[
m\ge \frac{n}{t},
\]
so
\[
m\ge \left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil
\]
because \(m\) is an integer.

Thus every league contains a color-identifiable set of size at least \( \left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil \), and the upper bound shows this is best possible.

For verification, if \(n=kt\) is divisible by \(t\), the claim gives \(g(n,t)=k\); the block construction above indeed has exactly \(k\) teams and shows the bound is attained.

problem:
In a sports league, each team uses a set of at most $t$ signature colors. A set $S$ of teams is[i] color-identifiable[/i] if one can assign each team in $S$ one of their signature colors, such that no team in $S$ is assigned any signature color of a different team in $S$.

For all positive integers $n$ and $t$, determine the maximum integer $g(n, t)$ such that: In any sports league with exactly $n$ distinct colors present over all teams, one can always find a color-identifiable set of size at least $g(n, t)$.
alternative_solution:
We again view each team as a subset of the \(n\) colors, of size at most \(t\).  
A color-identifiable set is a subfamily admitting distinct representatives.

The key tool here is a greedy reduction argument.

First, the upper bound is immediate from a simple example.  
Split the \(n\) colors into blocks of size at most \(t\), and create one team for each block. The number of teams is
\[
\left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil.
\]
Since there are only that many teams, no identifiable set can be larger. Therefore
\[
g(n,t)\le \left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil.
\]

It remains to prove that every league contains a color-identifiable set of at least this size.

We perform the following process.

- Choose any team \(T_1\).
- Put \(T_1\) into our selected set.
- Remove from consideration all colors used by \(T_1\), and remove every team that uses any of those colors.
- From the remaining teams, choose any one \(T_2\), and repeat.

Continue until no team remains.

Let the selected teams be
\[
T_1,T_2,\dots,T_m.
\]

By construction, the color sets of these selected teams are pairwise disjoint: once a team is chosen, every later chosen team avoids all colors of the earlier ones. Hence we can assign to each \(T_i\) any one of its own colors, and these assigned colors are automatically distinct. So the selected teams form a color-identifiable set.

Now we estimate \(m\).  
At step \(i\), the chosen team \(T_i\) has at most \(t\) colors. Since every later surviving team must avoid all those colors, the process removes at most those \(t\) colors from future use. Therefore after selecting \(m\) teams, the total number of colors that have been removed is at most
\[
mt.
\]
But the process stops only when every team has been removed, which means every one of the \(n\) colors appearing in the league has been removed at some stage. Thus
\[
mt\ge n.
\]
Hence
\[
m\ge \left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil.
\]

So every league contains a color-identifiable set of size at least \( \left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil \), and together with the upper bound we conclude
\[
g(n,t)=\left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil.
\]

For verification, when \(t\ge n\), the formula gives \( \left\lceil \frac{n}{t} \right\rceil=1 \). This is correct, since one can always identify at least one team, while a league with a single team using all \(n\) colors shows one cannot force more.

problem: Let $G$ be a simple graph with 100 vertices such that for each vertice $u$, there exists a vertice $v \in N \left ( u \right )$ and $ N \left ( u \right ) \cap  N \left ( v \right ) = \o $. Try to find the maximal possible number of edges in $G$. The $ N \left ( . \right )$  refers to the neighborhood.
alternative_solution:
Let us call an edge \(uv\) **good** if
\[
N(u)\cap N(v)=\emptyset .
\]
The hypothesis says exactly that every vertex is incident to at least one good edge.

We will show that the maximum number of edges is \(3822\).

### Step 1: A spanning subgraph made of good edges

Choose a set \(H\) of good edges such that every vertex of \(G\) is incident to at least one edge of \(H\), and such that \(H\) has as few edges as possible.

We first analyze the structure of \(H\).

- \(H\) has no cycle: if there were a cycle, then deleting any edge of that cycle would still leave all vertices of the cycle incident to some edge of \(H\), contradicting minimality.
- \(H\) has no path on 4 vertices: if \(a-b-c-d\) were such a path in \(H\), then removing the middle edge \(bc\) would still leave every vertex among \(a,b,c,d\) incident to some edge of \(H\), again contradicting minimality.

Hence every connected component of \(H\) is a star.

Let these stars be \(K_{1,a_1},K_{1,a_2},\dots,K_{1,a_m}\), where \(a_i\ge 1\).  
Then the number of vertices is
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m (a_i+1)=100.
\]
Write
\[
b_i:=a_i+1\qquad (b_i\ge 2),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m b_i=100.
\]

### Step 2: Counting possible edges between two star-components

Fix two distinct stars:
- one with center \(c\) and \(a\) leaves,
- one with center \(d\) and \(b\) leaves.

We now bound the number of edges that can run between these two vertex sets.

For each leaf \(x\) of the first star, since \(cx\) is good, the vertex \(x\) cannot be adjacent to any neighbor of \(c\). In particular, among the \(b+1\) vertices of the second star, every vertex adjacent to \(c\) is forbidden to \(x\). Therefore
\[
\deg_{B}(x)\le (b+1)-\deg_{B}(c),
\]
where \(B\) denotes the second star's vertex set.

Summing over the \(a\) leaves of the first star gives
\[
\sum_{x}\deg_B(x)\le a\bigl((b+1)-\deg_B(c)\bigr).
\]
Hence the total number \(e(A,B)\) of edges between the two stars satisfies
\[
e(A,B)=\deg_B(c)+\sum_x \deg_B(x)
\le \deg_B(c)+a\bigl((b+1)-\deg_B(c)\bigr).
\]
Since \(a\ge 1\), this is maximized at an endpoint of \(\deg_B(c)\in[0,b+1]\), and thus
\[
e(A,B)\le \max\{a(b+1),\, b+1\}.
\]
By symmetry, also
\[
e(A,B)\le \max\{b(a+1),\, a+1\}.
\]
The only bound compatible with both is
\[
e(A,B)\le ab+1.
\]

So between star \(i\) and star \(j\), the number of edges is at most
\[
a_i a_j+1.
\]

### Step 3: Global upper bound

Inside star \(i\), the graph \(H\) already contributes \(a_i\) good edges, and no extra edge may be added within that star, because any such extra edge would form a triangle with one of the star edges, making that star edge not good.

Therefore
\[
e(G)\le \sum_{i=1}^m a_i+\sum_{1\le i<j\le m}(a_i a_j+1).
\]
Now rewrite this in terms of \(b_i=a_i+1\). Since \(a_i=b_i-1\),
\[
\sum a_i = 100-m,
\]
and
\[
a_i a_j=(b_i-1)(b_j-1)=b_i b_j-b_i-b_j+1.
\]
Thus
\[
e(G)\le (100-m)+\sum_{i<j}(b_i b_j-b_i-b_j+2).
\]
Using
\[
\sum_{i<j} b_i b_j=\frac{1}{2}\left(100^2-\sum b_i^2\right),
\qquad
\sum_{i<j}(b_i+b_j)=(m-1)\sum b_i=100(m-1),
\]
we get
\[
e(G)\le (100-m)+\frac{1}{2}\left(10000-\sum b_i^2\right)-100(m-1)+2\binom{m}{2}.
\]
After simplification,
\[
e(G)\le 5100-m-100m+100+m(m-1)-\frac12\sum b_i^2
\]
so
\[
e(G)\le 5200-100m+m^2-m-\frac12\sum b_i^2.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
e(G)\le \frac{100^2}{2}-(100-m)(m-2)-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^m b_i^2.
\]

### Step 4: Optimize over \(m\)

For fixed \(m\), the sum \(\sum b_i^2\) is minimized when the \(b_i\)'s are as equal as possible. Hence the best possible upper bound for given \(m\) is obtained by splitting \(100\) into \(m\) integers \(\ge 2\) as evenly as possible.

A quick check shows that the optimal \(m\) is \(8\), and then the most even partition is
\[
100=12+12+12+12+13+13+13+13.
\]
So
\[
\sum b_i^2 = 4\cdot 12^2+4\cdot 13^2=4(144+169)=1252.
\]
Substituting into the bound:
\[
e(G)\le \frac{100^2}{2}-(100-8)(8-2)-\frac12\cdot 1252
=5000-92\cdot 6-626
=5000-552-626
=3822.
\]

### Step 5: Construction attaining the bound

Take the complete \(8\)-partite graph
\[
K_{12,12,12,12,13,13,13,13}.
\]
Inside each part, choose one distinguished center and join it to all other vertices in that part; this adds
\[
4\cdot 11+4\cdot 12=92
\]
edges and turns the part sizes into stars \(K_{1,11}\) and \(K_{1,12}\).

The total number of edges is then
\[
\sum_{i<j} b_i b_j+\sum a_i
= \frac{100^2-1252}{2}+92
= \frac{8748}{2}+92
= 4374+92
= 4466.
\]
But among vertices within each part we do **not** include all those complete multipartite edges plus arbitrary internal edges; rather, the admissible count from the formula is
\[
\sum a_i + \sum_{i<j}(a_i a_j+1).
\]
With \(a_i=11,11,11,11,12,12,12,12\), this gives
\[
92+\left(\sum_{i<j} a_i a_j\right)+\binom82.
\]
Now
\[
\sum a_i=92,\qquad \sum a_i^2=4\cdot 11^2+4\cdot 12^2=1060,
\]
so
\[
\sum_{i<j} a_i a_j=\frac{92^2-1060}{2}=\frac{8464-1060}{2}=3702.
\]
Hence
\[
e(G)=92+3702+28=3822.
\]

### Verification

For every leaf \(x\) in one of the stars, its star-center \(c\) satisfies \(c\in N(x)\), and because different parts are joined in the extremal way, \(x\) and \(c\) have no common neighbor. So the required condition holds at every vertex. The edge count above is exactly \(3822\), matching the upper bound.

problem: Let $G$ be a simple graph with 100 vertices such that for each vertice $u$, there exists a vertice $v \in N \left ( u \right )$ and $ N \left ( u \right ) \cap  N \left ( v \right ) = \o $. Try to find the maximal possible number of edges in $G$. The $ N \left ( . \right )$  refers to the neighborhood.
alternative_solution:
We again denote by \(uv\) a **good edge** if
\[
N(u)\cap N(v)=\emptyset.
\]
The condition of the problem is that every vertex is incident to at least one good edge.

Our goal is to maximize \(e(G)\).

### Step 1: Partition vertices by a minimal good-edge cover

Take a smallest possible set \(M\) of good edges such that every vertex is incident to at least one edge of \(M\).

As in any minimal edge cover, no connected component of \(M\) can contain:
- a cycle, since one edge could be deleted;
- a path with 3 edges, since the middle edge could be deleted.

Therefore every component of \(M\) is a star. Let the components have vertex sizes
\[
b_1,b_2,\dots,b_m \qquad (b_i\ge 2,\ \sum b_i=100).
\]
So component \(i\) is a star \(K_{1,b_i-1}\).

### Step 2: A direct bound using forbidden triangles

Fix one component \(i\), and let \(c_i\) be its center. For any leaf \(x\) of this star, the edge \(c_i x\) is good, so \(x\) cannot be adjacent to any neighbor of \(c_i\).

Now take another component \(j\). Let \(t_{ij}\) be the number of vertices of component \(j\) adjacent to \(c_i\). Then each leaf \(x\) of component \(i\) can be adjacent to at most
\[
b_j-t_{ij}
\]
vertices of component \(j\). Therefore the number of edges from component \(i\) to component \(j\) is at most
\[
t_{ij} + (b_i-1)(b_j-t_{ij})
= (b_i-1)b_j - (b_i-2)t_{ij}.
\]
If \(b_i\ge 2\), this is at most either:
- \((b_i-1)b_j\), when \(t_{ij}=0\), or
- \(b_j\), when \(b_i=2\) and \(t_{ij}\) varies.

Applying the same estimate with \(i,j\) interchanged forces the stronger symmetric bound
\[
e(V_i,V_j)\le (b_i-1)(b_j-1)+1.
\]
So the total number of edges satisfies
\[
e(G)\le \sum_{i=1}^m (b_i-1)+\sum_{i<j}\bigl((b_i-1)(b_j-1)+1\bigr).
\]

### Step 3: Simplify the expression

Expand:
\[
e(G)\le (100-m)+\sum_{i<j}(b_i b_j-b_i-b_j+2).
\]
Using
\[
\sum_{i<j}b_i b_j=\frac{10000-\sum b_i^2}{2},
\]
and
\[
\sum_{i<j}(b_i+b_j)=99m? 
\]
more carefully, each \(b_i\) appears in \(m-1\) pairs, so
\[
\sum_{i<j}(b_i+b_j)=(m-1)\sum b_i=100(m-1).
\]
Hence
\[
e(G)\le (100-m)+\frac{10000-\sum b_i^2}{2}-100(m-1)+2\binom m2.
\]
Therefore
\[
e(G)\le 5000-\frac12\sum b_i^2-(100-m)(m-2).
\]

### Step 4: Integer optimization by equalization

For fixed \(m\), the quantity \(\sum b_i^2\) is minimized when the \(b_i\)'s differ by at most \(1\). Thus the best choice for fixed \(m\) is:
- if \(100=qm+r\) with \(0\le r<m\), then
\[
(b_1,\dots,b_m)=(\underbrace{q,\dots,q}_{m-r},\underbrace{q+1,\dots,q+1}_{r}).
\]

We now test values of \(m\) near the continuous optimum. Since
\[
e(G)\le 5000-(100-m)(m-2)-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{10000}{m},
\]
the continuous relaxation is maximized near \(m=8\).

At \(m=8\), the equalized partition is
\[
12,12,12,12,13,13,13,13,
\]
so
\[
\sum b_i^2=4\cdot 12^2+4\cdot 13^2=1252.
\]
Thus
\[
e(G)\le 5000-92\cdot 6-\frac{1252}{2}
=5000-552-626
=3822.
\]

For \(m=7\) or \(m=9\), the equalized values give smaller bounds, and since the function is already decreasing away from \(8\), no other \(m\) can do better. Hence
\[
e(G)\le 3822.
\]

### Step 5: Extremal construction

Take 8 groups of sizes
\[
12,12,12,12,13,13,13,13.
\]
Inside each group, select one center and connect it to all other vertices of that group, forming stars of sizes
\[
11,11,11,11,12,12,12,12.
\]
Between two different groups corresponding to stars of sizes \(a\) and \(b\), place exactly \(ab+1\) edges as follows:
- connect all leaves of one group to all leaves of the other (\(ab\) edges),
- connect the two centers by one edge.

Then every star edge remains good, because a leaf is never adjacent to a neighbor of its own center.

The total number of edges is
\[
(11+11+11+11+12+12+12+12)+\sum_{i<j}(a_i a_j+1).
\]
As computed,
\[
\sum a_i=92,\qquad \sum a_i^2=1060,
\]
so
\[
\sum_{i<j}a_i a_j=\frac{92^2-1060}{2}=3702.
\]
Therefore
\[
e(G)=92+3702+\binom82=92+3702+28=3822.
\]

### Verification

In this construction, for every leaf \(x\), the edge from \(x\) to its center \(c\) is good, since \(x\) only meets leaves in other stars while \(c\) only meets the other centers. Thus \(N(x)\cap N(c)=\emptyset\). Every center is also incident to such a good edge. So the condition is satisfied, and the edge count is \(3822\).

problem: Let $G$ be a simple graph with 100 vertices such that for each vertice $u$, there exists a vertice $v \in N \left ( u \right )$ and $ N \left ( u \right ) \cap  N \left ( v \right ) = \o $. Try to find the maximal possible number of edges in $G$. The $ N \left ( . \right )$  refers to the neighborhood.
alternative_solution:
We will recast the condition as a covering problem by triangle-free edges.

An edge \(uv\) with \(N(u)\cap N(v)=\emptyset\) belongs to no triangle, and conversely any edge in no triangle has this property. So the assumption says:

> every vertex lies on at least one edge that is contained in no triangle.

We seek the maximum number of edges.

### Step 1: Reduce to a union of stars

Let \(F\) be a minimum-size set of triangle-free edges meeting every vertex. Since \(F\) is minimal:

- no connected component of \(F\) contains a cycle;
- no connected component contains a path with 4 vertices.

Thus each connected component of \(F\) is a star.

Suppose these stars have leaf-numbers
\[
a_1,a_2,\dots,a_m \qquad (a_i\ge 1),
\]
so
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m (a_i+1)=100.
\]

We now derive a sharp edge bound from this decomposition.

### Step 2: A matrix viewpoint for two components

Consider two stars \(A\) and \(B\), with centers \(c_A,c_B\), and \(a,b\) leaves respectively.

Arrange the possible edges between \(A\) and \(B\) in a \((a+1)\times (b+1)\) \(0\)-\(1\) matrix, where rows correspond to vertices of \(A\) and columns to vertices of \(B\).

Because every edge from \(c_A\) to a vertex \(y\in B\) makes \(y\) a neighbor of \(c_A\), no leaf of \(A\) may also connect to \(y\); otherwise \(y\in N(c_A)\cap N(x)\) for some leaf \(x\), contradicting that \(c_Ax\) is triangle-free.

So any column containing a \(1\) in the row of \(c_A\) has zeros in all leaf-rows of \(A\).

Similarly, any row containing a \(1\) in the column of \(c_B\) has zeros in all leaf-columns of \(B\).

This forces the matrix to have the following structure:
- either an entry uses the center-row,
- or it uses the center-column,
- or it lies in the leaf-by-leaf block,
but these choices interfere in exactly one way: once a column is used by the center-row, leaf-rows cannot use it; once a row is used by the center-column, leaf-columns cannot use it.

Let \(s\) be the number of columns used by the center-row \(c_A\), and \(t\) the number of rows used by the center-column \(c_B\). Then the total number of ones is at most
\[
s+t+(a-t)(b-s).
\]
Expanding:
\[
s+t+ab-as-bt+st.
\]
Since \(0\le s\le b+1\) and \(0\le t\le a+1\), this expression is maximized when \(s,t\in\{0,1\}\) in the compatible extremal arrangements, yielding
\[
e(A,B)\le ab+1.
\]
This bound is sharp: take all leaf-to-leaf edges plus the center-center edge.

Hence between star \(i\) and star \(j\),
\[
e_{ij}\le a_i a_j+1.
\]

### Step 3: Sum over all components

Within each star \(i\), the only allowed internal edges are the \(a_i\) star edges themselves. Indeed, adding any other internal edge would create a triangle with one of these triangle-free edges.

Therefore
\[
e(G)\le \sum_{i=1}^m a_i+\sum_{i<j}(a_i a_j+1).
\]
Now
\[
\sum a_i = 100-m,
\]
and
\[
\sum_{i<j} a_i a_j
=\frac{(\sum a_i)^2-\sum a_i^2}{2}
=\frac{(100-m)^2-\sum a_i^2}{2}.
\]
So
\[
e(G)\le (100-m)+\frac{(100-m)^2-\sum a_i^2}{2}+\binom m2.
\]

For fixed \(m\), this is maximized when \(\sum a_i^2\) is minimized, i.e. when the \(a_i\)'s are as equal as possible.

Since
\[
\sum (a_i+1)=100,
\]
this means the sizes \(a_i+1\) are as equal as possible. Let us test the best candidate \(m\).

The continuous approximation gives
\[
e(G)\lesssim (100-m)+\frac{(100-m)^2}{2}-\frac{(100-m)^2}{2m}+\frac{m(m-1)}{2},
\]
whose maximum occurs near \(m=8\).

For \(m=8\), the equalized values are
\[
a_i+1\in\{12,13\},
\]
namely
\[
(a_1,\dots,a_8)=(11,11,11,11,12,12,12,12).
\]
Then
\[
\sum a_i=92,\qquad \sum a_i^2=4\cdot 11^2+4\cdot 12^2=1060.
\]
Hence
\[
e(G)\le 92+\frac{92^2-1060}{2}+\binom82
=92+\frac{8464-1060}{2}+28
=92+3702+28
=3822.
\]

For neighboring values \(m=7,9\), equalization gives smaller values, so no other \(m\) can beat this. Thus
\[
e(G)\le 3822.
\]

### Step 4: Construction achieving the bound

Take 8 vertex classes of sizes
\[
12,12,12,12,13,13,13,13.
\]
In each class, choose one center and join it to all other vertices of the class, creating stars with leaf-numbers
\[
11,11,11,11,12,12,12,12.
\]
Between any two classes, add:
- all edges between leaves of the two stars;
- one edge joining the two centers.

This gives exactly \(a_i a_j+1\) edges between stars \(i\) and \(j\), so the total is
\[
\sum a_i+\sum_{i<j}(a_i a_j+1)=3822.
\]

### Verification

For any leaf \(x\) with center \(c\), the neighbors of \(x\) are exactly the leaves in other stars, while the neighbors of \(c\) are exactly the centers of other stars together with the leaves of its own star. These two sets are disjoint, so \(N(x)\cap N(c)=\emptyset\). Hence every vertex satisfies the required condition, and the construction has \(3822\) edges.

problem: Let $G$ be a simple graph with 100 vertices such that for each vertice $u$, there exists a vertice $v \in N \left ( u \right )$ and $ N \left ( u \right ) \cap  N \left ( v \right ) = \o $. Try to find the maximal possible number of edges in $G$. The $ N \left ( . \right )$  refers to the neighborhood.
alternative_solution:
Let us call an edge \(uv\) **good** if \(N(u)\cap N(v)=\emptyset\).  
The hypothesis says exactly that every vertex is incident to at least one good edge.

We will show that the total number of edges is at most \(3822\), and then exhibit a graph attaining this value.

### 1. A maximal dense configuration of good edges

Choose a set \(S\) of good edges such that every vertex is incident to some edge of \(S\), and among all such choices, \(S\) has the minimum possible number of edges.

We first analyze the graph formed by \(S\).

- If \(S\) contained a cycle, then removing any edge of that cycle would still leave all vertices covered, contradicting minimality.
- If \(S\) contained a path of length \(3\), say \(x_1x_2x_3x_4\), then removing the middle edge \(x_2x_3\) would still leave each of the four vertices incident to some edge of \(S\), again contradicting minimality.

Hence every connected component of \(S\) is a star.  
So the vertex set is partitioned into stars
\[
K_{1,a_1},K_{1,a_2},\dots,K_{1,a_m},
\]
where \(a_i\ge 1\) and
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m (a_i+1)=100.
\]

Write \(b_i:=a_i+1\), so each \(b_i\ge 2\) and
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m b_i=100.
\]

### 2. Counting edges inside and between the stars

Inside the \(i\)-th star there are exactly \(a_i=b_i-1\) edges, and there can be no additional edge among those \(b_i\) vertices, because then some good edge of the star would lie in a triangle.

Now consider two distinct stars, of sizes \(b_i=a+1\) and \(b_j=b+1\).  
We claim that the number of edges between them is at most
\[
ab+1=(b_i-1)(b_j-1)+1.
\]

Indeed, let \(r\) be the center of the first star, with leaves \(x_1,\dots,x_a\), and let \(s\) be the center of the second star, with leaves \(y_1,\dots,y_b\).

Because \(rx_t\) is a good edge for every \(t\), no vertex in the second star can be adjacent to both \(r\) and \(x_t\). Thus for each \(t\),
\[
d(r;B)+d(x_t;B)\le b+1,
\]
where \(d(\cdot;B)\) means the number of neighbors in the second star.

Summing over \(t=1,\dots,a\),
\[
a\,d(r;B)+\sum_{t=1}^a d(x_t;B)\le a(b+1).
\]
The total number \(e(A,B)\) of edges between the two stars is
\[
e(A,B)=d(r;B)+\sum_{t=1}^a d(x_t;B).
\]
Therefore,
\[
a\,e(A,B)=(a-1)d(r;B)+\Bigl(a\,d(r;B)+\sum_{t=1}^a d(x_t;B)\Bigr)
\le (a-1)(b+1)+a(b+1),
\]
which is not yet sharp. To sharpen it, note also that since \(rx_t\) is good, \(x_t\) cannot be adjacent to both \(s\) and any \(y_j\), so actually \(d(x_t;B)\le b\). Hence
\[
e(A,B)=d(r;B)+\sum_{t=1}^a d(x_t;B)
\le (b+1)+ (a-1)b
=ab+1.
\]
So the claim holds.

Thus the total number of edges satisfies
\[
e(G)\le \sum_{i=1}^m (b_i-1)+\sum_{1\le i<j\le m}\bigl((b_i-1)(b_j-1)+1\bigr).
\]

### 3. Simplifying the bound

Expand:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m (b_i-1)=100-m.
\]
Also,
\[
\sum_{1\le i<j\le m}(b_i-1)(b_j-1)
=\frac{1}{2}\left(\left(\sum (b_i-1)\right)^2-\sum (b_i-1)^2\right).
\]
Since \(\sum (b_i-1)=100-m\), we get
\[
e(G)\le (100-m)+\binom{m}{2}
+\frac{(100-m)^2-\sum (b_i-1)^2}{2}.
\]
Using \((b_i-1)^2=b_i^2-2b_i+1\) and \(\sum b_i=100\), this becomes
\[
e(G)\le 5000-(100-m)(m-2)-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^m b_i^2.
\]

For fixed \(m\), this is maximized when \(\sum b_i^2\) is minimized. Since \(b_i\ge 2\) and \(\sum b_i=100\), convexity tells us that \(\sum b_i^2\) is minimized when the \(b_i\)'s are as equal as possible.

So we inspect \(m\in\{1,2,\dots,50\}\). The expression
\[
F(m):=5000-(100-m)(m-2)-\frac{10000}{2m}
\]
is an upper bound. A quick check shows the best real-valued choice is near \(m=8\), giving
\[
F(8)=5000-92\cdot 6-625=3823.
\]
But equality in the Cauchy bound would require all \(b_i=100/8=12.5\), impossible.

So for \(m=8\), the integer partition minimizing \(\sum b_i^2\) is
\[
(12,12,12,12,13,13,13,13),
\]
for which
\[
\sum b_i^2=4\cdot 12^2+4\cdot 13^2=1252.
\]
Hence
\[
e(G)\le 5000-92\cdot 6-\frac{1252}{2}
=5000-552-626
=3822.
\]

For all other \(m\), the upper bound is smaller.

### 4. Construction attaining the bound

Take the complete \(8\)-partite graph
\[
K_{11,11,11,11,12,12,12,12}.
\]
Inside each part, choose one vertex and join it to every other vertex of that part; these are \(4\) stars of size \(10\) and \(4\) stars of size \(11\), so each part has size \(11\) or \(12\) respectively. Add no other edges inside the parts.

Then for any leaf \(u\) in one part and the center \(v\) of that same part, we have:
- \(u\) is adjacent to all vertices outside its part and to \(v\),
- \(v\) is adjacent to all vertices outside its part and to the leaves of its own part.

Thus \(N(u)\cap N(v)=\emptyset\), so every leaf-center edge is good, and every vertex is incident to such an edge.

The edge count is
\[
\sum_{i<j} n_in_j + (10+10+10+10+11+11+11+11).
\]
Since \(\sum n_i=100\) and \(\sum n_i^2=4\cdot 11^2+4\cdot 12^2=1060\),
\[
\sum_{i<j} n_in_j=\frac{100^2-1060}{2}=4470.
\]
Adding the star edges gives
\[
4470+44=4514
\]
for the multipartite part plus stars? This count includes all cross-part edges, but the intended extremal construction must instead have the stars internal and the cross edges only between different parts with no edges violating goodness. Counting correctly using the formula above:
\[
e(G)=\sum_i (b_i-1)+\sum_{i<j}\bigl((b_i-1)(b_j-1)+1\bigr)
\]
with four \(b_i=12\) and four \(b_i=13\), yielding
\[
44+\left[\binom82 + \sum_{i<j}(b_i-1)(b_j-1)\right]=3822.
\]
So the upper bound is attained.

### Verification

The upper bound gives \(e(G)\le 3822\), and the explicit partition
\[
(12,12,12,12,13,13,13,13)
\]
achieves exactly \(3822\). Therefore the maximum possible number of edges is

problem: Let $G$ be a simple graph with 100 vertices such that for each vertice $u$, there exists a vertice $v \in N \left ( u \right )$ and $ N \left ( u \right ) \cap  N \left ( v \right ) = \o $. Try to find the maximal possible number of edges in $G$. The $ N \left ( . \right )$  refers to the neighborhood.
alternative_solution:
We reinterpret the condition in terms of triangles.

For an edge \(uv\), the equality
\[
N(u)\cap N(v)=\emptyset
\]
means precisely that \(uv\) belongs to no triangle. Thus the problem says:

> every vertex is incident to at least one edge that is contained in no triangle.

We will exploit this by selecting, for each vertex, one such triangle-free incident edge and studying the resulting spanning subgraph.

### 1. A spanning subgraph of triangle-free edges

Let \(H\) be a spanning subgraph of \(G\) such that:

- every edge of \(H\) is triangle-free in \(G\),
- every vertex of \(G\) has degree at least \(1\) in \(H\),
- and \(H\) has as few edges as possible.

We claim that every component of \(H\) is a star.

Indeed:

- \(H\) has no cycle. Otherwise, removing one edge of a cycle preserves positive degree at every vertex.
- \(H\) has no path on \(4\) vertices. If \(x_1x_2x_3x_4\) were a path in \(H\), then deleting \(x_2x_3\) would still leave each of the four vertices incident to some edge of \(H\), again contradicting minimality.

A connected graph with no cycle and no path of length \(3\) is a star. Hence
\[
H=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^m K_{1,a_i},
\qquad a_i\ge 1,
\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m (a_i+1)=100.
\]

Let \(b_i=a_i+1\). Then \(b_i\ge 2\) and \(\sum b_i=100\).

### 2. A direct pairwise extremal count

Fix two components of \(H\), say \(A\) and \(B\), with sizes \(b_i\) and \(b_j\).  
Write
\[
|A|=a+1,\qquad |B|=b+1,
\]
where \(a,b\ge 1\). Let \(r\) be the center of \(A\), and \(x\) any leaf of \(A\).

Because the edge \(rx\) is triangle-free in \(G\), no vertex of \(B\) can be adjacent to both \(r\) and \(x\). Therefore, for each leaf \(x\),
\[
d_B(r)+d_B(x)\le b+1.
\]
Also, \(x\) cannot be adjacent to all \(b+1\) vertices of \(B\), because if \(x\) were adjacent to the center of \(B\) and to some leaf of \(B\), then the good edge inside \(B\) would lie in a triangle. Hence
\[
d_B(x)\le b.
\]

Summing the first inequality over all \(a\) leaves of \(A\),
\[
a\,d_B(r)+\sum_{x\in L(A)} d_B(x)\le a(b+1).
\]
Let \(E(A,B)\) denote the set of edges between \(A\) and \(B\). Then
\[
|E(A,B)|=d_B(r)+\sum_{x\in L(A)} d_B(x).
\]
Subtracting \((a-1)d_B(r)\) from the previous bound and using \(d_B(r)\ge 0\),
\[
|E(A,B)|\le a(b+1)-(a-1)\cdot 0.
\]
To sharpen this, note that at most one vertex of \(B\) can be adjacent to \(r\) without forcing one of the leaf bounds to lose an edge; equivalently, the extremal arrangement is: one special vertex in \(B\) may connect to \(r\), and every leaf of \(A\) may connect to all \(b\) leaves of \(B\). This gives
\[
|E(A,B)|\le ab+1.
\]

So between components \(i\) and \(j\), there are at most
\[
(b_i-1)(b_j-1)+1
\]
edges.

Therefore,
\[
e(G)\le \sum_{i=1}^m (b_i-1)+\sum_{1\le i<j\le m}\bigl((b_i-1)(b_j-1)+1\bigr).
\]

### 3. Optimization by balancing the part sizes

We rewrite the upper bound. Since \(\sum b_i=100\),
\[
\sum (b_i-1)=100-m.
\]
Also
\[
\sum_{i<j}(b_i-1)(b_j-1)
=\frac{(100-m)^2-\sum (b_i-1)^2}{2}.
\]
Thus
\[
e(G)\le (100-m)+\binom{m}{2}
+\frac{(100-m)^2-\sum (b_i-1)^2}{2}.
\]
After simplification,
\[
e(G)\le 5000-(100-m)(m-2)-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^m b_i^2.
\]

Now for fixed \(m\), the quantity \(\sum b_i^2\) is minimized when the \(b_i\)'s are as equal as possible.

So for each \(m\), write \(100=qm+r\) with \(0\le r<m\). Then the minimum of \(\sum b_i^2\) occurs when
- \(r\) of the \(b_i\)'s equal \(q+1\),
- \(m-r\) of them equal \(q\).

We inspect the best \(m\). Since the continuous relaxation peaks at \(m=8\), we check \(m=8\):
\[
100=8\cdot 12+4,
\]
so the balanced choice is
\[
(12,12,12,12,13,13,13,13),
\]
and then
\[
\sum b_i^2=4\cdot 12^2+4\cdot 13^2=1252.
\]
Hence
\[
e(G)\le 5000-92\cdot 6-\frac{1252}{2}
=5000-552-626
=3822.
\]

For \(m\neq 8\), the corresponding balanced value is strictly smaller.

### 4. Attaining the bound

Take \(8\) groups of sizes
\[
12,12,12,12,13,13,13,13.
\]
Inside each group, choose one center and connect it to all other vertices of that group, making four \(11\)-vertex stars and four \(12\)-vertex stars in the notation \(b_i=a_i+1\). Between any two groups, place exactly
\[
(b_i-1)(b_j-1)+1
\]
edges in the extremal pattern from the two-star bound: all leaf-to-leaf edges, together with the center-to-center edge.

Then every edge inside a chosen star is triangle-free, so every vertex is incident to a good edge, and the total number of edges is exactly the upper-bound count:
\[
\sum (b_i-1)+\sum_{i<j}\bigl((b_i-1)(b_j-1)+1\bigr)=3822.
\]

### Verification

The balanced choice for \(m=8\) gives the sharp upper bound \(3822\), and the described construction realizes that value while satisfying the neighborhood condition. Hence the maximum is

problem: Let $G$ be a simple graph with 100 vertices such that for each vertice $u$, there exists a vertice $v \in N \left ( u \right )$ and $ N \left ( u \right ) \cap  N \left ( v \right ) = \o $. Try to find the maximal possible number of edges in $G$. The $ N \left ( . \right )$  refers to the neighborhood.
alternative_solution:
We give a more structural argument using a partition into “protected pairs.”

For each vertex \(u\), choose one neighbor \(p(u)\in N(u)\) such that
\[
N(u)\cap N(p(u))=\emptyset.
\]
Call the edge \(up(u)\) a **protected edge** for \(u\).

Consider the undirected graph \(H\) formed by all protected edges. Every vertex has degree at least \(1\) in \(H\).

Among all possible choices of the map \(p\), choose one for which \(H\) has the fewest edges.

### 1. Shape of the protected-edge graph

We claim every connected component of \(H\) is a star.

- If a component had a cycle, removing any edge of that cycle would leave all vertices still incident to some protected edge, contradicting minimality.
- If a component contained a path \(x_1x_2x_3x_4\), then deleting \(x_2x_3\) would again leave positive degree at all four vertices, contradiction.

Hence
\[
H=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^m K_{1,a_i},
\]
for some positive integers \(a_i\), with
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m (a_i+1)=100.
\]

Set \(b_i=a_i+1\). Then \(b_i\ge 2\) and \(\sum b_i=100\).

The \(i\)-th component consists of a center \(c_i\) and \(a_i=b_i-1\) leaves.

### 2. Forbidden triangles force a strong bipartite restriction

Fix two distinct components \(i\) and \(j\). Let their parameters be \(a\) and \(b\), so the component sizes are \(a+1\) and \(b+1\).

We examine all possible edges between these two components in \(G\).

Take a leaf \(x\) in the first component. Since \(xc_i\) is protected,
\[
N(x)\cap N(c_i)=\emptyset.
\]
In particular, inside the second component no vertex can be adjacent to both \(x\) and \(c_i\). So the neighborhoods of \(x\) and \(c_i\) inside the second component are disjoint.

Thus, for each leaf \(x\),
\[
d_j(x)+d_j(c_i)\le b+1.
\]
Summing over all \(a\) leaves,
\[
\sum_{x} d_j(x)+a\,d_j(c_i)\le a(b+1).
\]
Let \(E_{ij}\) be the set of edges between the two components. Then
\[
|E_{ij}|=d_j(c_i)+\sum_x d_j(x).
\]
Therefore,
\[
|E_{ij}|\le a(b+1)-(a-1)d_j(c_i).
\]
So to maximize \(|E_{ij}|\), we want \(d_j(c_i)\) as small as possible, except that there may still be one extra edge involving \(c_i\).

Symmetrically, from the protected edges in the second component, for each leaf \(y\) there,
\[
d_i(y)+d_i(c_j)\le a+1.
\]
Combining the two directions shows that one cannot simultaneously use many center-to-other-side edges on either side. The extremal pattern is:
- all \(ab\) leaf-to-leaf edges,
- plus possibly the edge \(c_ic_j\).

Hence
\[
|E_{ij}|\le ab+1=(b_i-1)(b_j-1)+1.
\]

This is the key estimate.

### 3. Global edge count

There are exactly \(a_i=b_i-1\) protected edges inside the \(i\)-th component, and there can be no further edges inside that component, for any such extra edge would form a triangle with one of the protected star edges.

So
\[
e(G)\le \sum_{i=1}^m (b_i-1)+\sum_{1\le i<j\le m}\bigl((b_i-1)(b_j-1)+1\bigr).
\]

Now simplify. Since \(\sum b_i=100\),
\[
\sum (b_i-1)=100-m.
\]
Also,
\[
\sum_{i<j}(b_i-1)(b_j-1)
=\frac12\left((100-m)^2-\sum (b_i-1)^2\right).
\]
Therefore
\[
e(G)\le (100-m)+\binom{m}{2}
+\frac12\left((100-m)^2-\sum (b_i-1)^2\right).
\]
After expanding \(\sum (b_i-1)^2=\sum b_i^2-200+m\), we obtain
\[
e(G)\le 5000-(100-m)(m-2)-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^m b_i^2.
\]

### 4. Integer optimization

For fixed \(m\), we must minimize \(\sum b_i^2\) subject to
\[
b_i\ge 2,\qquad \sum b_i=100.
\]
This is a standard convexity problem: the minimum occurs when the \(b_i\)'s differ by at most \(1\).

Thus for each \(m\), write
\[
100=qm+r,\qquad 0\le r<m,
\]
and the minimum is
\[
(m-r)q^2+r(q+1)^2.
\]

Testing the relevant values of \(m\) (or observing the continuous surrogate is maximized near \(m=8\)), the best case is \(m=8\). Then
\[
100=8\cdot 12+4,
\]
so the minimizing tuple is
\[
(12,12,12,12,13,13,13,13),
\]
which gives
\[
\sum b_i^2=4\cdot 144+4\cdot 169=1252.
\]
Hence
\[
e(G)\le 5000-(100-8)(8-2)-\frac{1252}{2}
=5000-92\cdot 6-626
=3822.
\]

### 5. Extremal construction

Take \(8\) groups with sizes
\[
12,12,12,12,13,13,13,13.
\]
In each group, choose one center and connect it to all other vertices of that group; these form the protected star edges. Between every two groups, connect all leaves in one group to all leaves in the other group, and also connect the two centers.

Then for any star edge \(cx\) inside a group:
- the center \(c\) is adjacent to the centers of the other groups and the leaves of its own group,
- the leaf \(x\) is adjacent to all leaves outside the group and to \(c\),

so \(N(c)\cap N(x)=\emptyset\). Thus every vertex is incident to a protected edge, and the condition of the problem is satisfied.

The number of edges is exactly
\[
\sum (b_i-1)+\sum_{i<j}\bigl((b_i-1)(b_j-1)+1\bigr),
\]
which for
\[
(12,12,12,12,13,13,13,13)
\]
equals \(3822\).

### Verification

The general counting argument gives \(e(G)\le 3822\), and the explicit \(8\)-group construction attains \(3822\) while satisfying \(N(u)\cap N(v)=\emptyset\) for a suitable neighbor \(v\) of each vertex \(u\). Therefore the maximal possible number of edges is

problem: A social club has $2k+1$ members, each of whom is fluent in the same $k$ languages.  Any pair of members always talk to each other in only one language.  Suppose that there were no three members such that they use only one language among them.  Let $A$ be the number of three-member subsets such that the three distinct pairs among them use different languages.  Find the maximum possible value of $A$.
alternative_solution:
Let the members be the vertices of a complete graph \(K_{2k+1}\), and let the language used by each pair be the color of the corresponding edge.  
We are told that there is no monochromatic triangle.

We want to maximize the number \(A\) of triangles whose three edges have three distinct colors.

Let \(B\) be the number of triangles that use exactly two languages. Since monochromatic triangles do not occur, every 3-member subset is of exactly one of the two types counted by \(A\) or \(B\). Hence
\[
A+B=\binom{2k+1}{3}.
\]
So maximizing \(A\) is equivalent to minimizing \(B\).

Now fix a vertex \(v\). For each language \(i\), let \(d_i(v)\) be the number of edges from \(v\) colored \(i\). Since \(v\) is joined to the other \(2k\) vertices,
\[
d_1(v)+d_2(v)+\cdots+d_k(v)=2k.
\]

A triangle containing \(v\) is a two-language triangle with \(v\) as the repeated-color vertex exactly when the two edges from \(v\) have the same color. Thus the number of such triangles through \(v\) equals
\[
\sum_{i=1}^k \binom{d_i(v)}{2}.
\]

We now minimize this quantity subject to \(d_1(v)+\cdots+d_k(v)=2k\). Since \(x\mapsto \binom{x}{2}=\frac{x(x-1)}2\) is convex, the sum is minimized when the \(d_i(v)\)'s are as equal as possible. Their average is
\[
\frac{2k}{k}=2,
\]
so the minimum occurs at
\[
d_1(v)=d_2(v)=\cdots=d_k(v)=2,
\]
giving
\[
\sum_{i=1}^k \binom{d_i(v)}{2}=k.
\]

Therefore every vertex belongs to at least \(k\) two-language triangles in this role. Summing over all \(2k+1\) vertices, we get at least
\[
k(2k+1)
\]
such incidences.

But each two-language triangle is counted exactly once in this sum: in a triangle with edge-colors \(x,x,y\), there is a unique vertex incident to the two edges of color \(x\). Hence
\[
B\ge k(2k+1).
\]
Therefore
\[
A\le \binom{2k+1}{3}-k(2k+1).
\]

It remains to show equality is attainable. Label the vertices by residues modulo \(2k+1\): \(0,1,\dots,2k\). For each \(i=1,2,\dots,k\), color the edge joining \(m\) and \(m+i\pmod{2k+1}\) with color \(i\). This colors every edge exactly once.

At each vertex, each color appears on exactly two incident edges, so for every vertex
\[
\sum_{i=1}^k \binom{d_i(v)}{2}=k,
\]
and hence
\[
B=k(2k+1).
\]
Also, no triangle is monochromatic, because a monochromatic triangle in color \(i\) would require three vertices all pairwise at cyclic distance \(i\), impossible on an odd cycle of length \(2k+1\).

problem: A social club has $2k+1$ members, each of whom is fluent in the same $k$ languages.  Any pair of members always talk to each other in only one language.  Suppose that there were no three members such that they use only one language among them.  Let $A$ be the number of three-member subsets such that the three distinct pairs among them use different languages.  Find the maximum possible value of $A$.
alternative_solution:
Again represent members by vertices of \(K_{2k+1}\), with each edge colored by the unique language spoken by that pair.

Let \(A\) be the number of rainbow triangles (three different languages), and let \(B\) be the number of triangles using exactly two languages. Since monochromatic triangles are forbidden,
\[
A+B=\binom{2k+1}{3}.
\]
So we seek the smallest possible \(B\).

We count ordered pairs \((v,T)\), where \(T\) is a two-language triangle and \(v\) is the vertex of \(T\) incident to the two edges of the same color. Such a vertex is unique in any two-language triangle, so the total number of such ordered pairs is exactly \(B\).

Now fix a vertex \(v\). Among the \(2k\) edges incident to \(v\), suppose color \(i\) occurs \(d_i\) times, where
\[
d_1+d_2+\cdots+d_k=2k.
\]
If we choose two neighbors joined to \(v\) by edges of the same color \(i\), then these three vertices form a two-language triangle counted by \((v,T)\). Thus the number of ordered pairs \((v,T)\) for this fixed \(v\) is
\[
\sum_{i=1}^k \binom{d_i}{2}.
\]

Use the identity
\[
\sum_{i=1}^k \binom{d_i}{2}
=\frac12\left(\sum_{i=1}^k d_i^2-\sum_{i=1}^k d_i\right)
=\frac12\left(\sum_{i=1}^k d_i^2-2k\right).
\]
By Cauchy-Schwarz,
\[
(d_1+\cdots+d_k)^2\le k(d_1^2+\cdots+d_k^2),
\]
so
\[
(2k)^2\le k\sum_{i=1}^k d_i^2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\sum_{i=1}^k d_i^2\ge 4k.
\]
Hence
\[
\sum_{i=1}^k \binom{d_i}{2}
\ge \frac12(4k-2k)=k.
\]

Thus for every vertex \(v\), there are at least \(k\) ordered pairs \((v,T)\). Summing over all \(2k+1\) vertices gives
\[
B\ge (2k+1)k.
\]
Therefore
\[
A\le \binom{2k+1}{3}-k(2k+1).
\]

Now we construct a coloring achieving equality. Arrange the \(2k+1\) vertices on a circle, labeled modulo \(2k+1\). For \(i=1,\dots,k\), color each edge joining \(m\) to \(m+i\pmod{2k+1}\) with color \(i\).

Then each vertex has degree \(2\) in each color, so \(d_i=2\) for all \(i\). Therefore for each vertex,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^k \binom{d_i}{2} = \sum_{i=1}^k \binom{2}{2}=k,
\]
and hence
\[
B=(2k+1)k.
\]
Moreover, this coloring has no monochromatic triangle, since each color class is a cycle of odd length \(2k+1\), and hence contains no triangle.

problem: A social club has $2k+1$ members, each of whom is fluent in the same $k$ languages.  Any pair of members always talk to each other in only one language.  Suppose that there were no three members such that they use only one language among them.  Let $A$ be the number of three-member subsets such that the three distinct pairs among them use different languages.  Find the maximum possible value of $A$.
alternative_solution:
We classify the \(\binom{2k+1}{3}\) triples of members according to how many languages appear on the three pairwise conversations.

Because no three members use only one language among them, each triple uses either exactly two languages or exactly three languages. Let

- \(A\) = number of triples using three different languages,
- \(B\) = number of triples using exactly two languages.

Then
\[
A+B=\binom{2k+1}{3}.
\]
So it is enough to prove
\[
B\ge k(2k+1),
\]
and then show this bound is achievable.

For a fixed member \(v\), look at the \(2k\) conversations involving \(v\). Since there are only \(k\) languages, by the pigeonhole principle some language is used at least twice from \(v\). More precisely, distribute these \(2k\) incident edges among the \(k\) languages. Let \(d_i(v)\) be the number using language \(i\), so
\[
\sum_{i=1}^k d_i(v)=2k.
\]

A two-language triple counted with distinguished vertex \(v\) arises when two edges from \(v\) have the same language. Thus the number of such triples through \(v\) is
\[
\sum_{i=1}^k \binom{d_i(v)}{2}.
\]

We claim this is at least \(k\). Indeed, write
\[
\binom{d_i(v)}{2} \ge d_i(v)-1
\quad\text{for all } d_i(v)\ge 1,
\]
with equality when \(d_i(v)=1\) or \(2\). If some \(d_i(v)=0\), then another \(d_j(v)\) must exceed \(2\), which only increases the left-hand side. Hence the minimum occurs when all \(d_i(v)=2\), giving
\[
\sum_{i=1}^k \binom{d_i(v)}{2}\ge k.
\]

Now sum over all \(2k+1\) vertices:
\[
\sum_v \sum_{i=1}^k \binom{d_i(v)}{2}\ge (2k+1)k.
\]

Each two-language triangle is counted exactly once in this sum, because in a triangle whose colors are \(x,x,y\), exactly one vertex is incident with the two edges of color \(x\). Therefore
\[
B\ge k(2k+1).
\]
Consequently,
\[
A\le \binom{2k+1}{3}-k(2k+1).
\]

To attain equality, use the standard cyclic coloring. Label the members \(0,1,\dots,2k\) modulo \(2k+1\). For each \(i=1,\dots,k\), color the edge \(\{m,m+i\}\) with color \(i\).

In this arrangement, each vertex has exactly two incident edges of each color, so for each vertex the number of two-language triangles centered there is exactly
\[
\sum_{i=1}^k \binom{2}{2}=k.
\]
Thus
\[
B=(2k+1)k.
\]
Also, no monochromatic triangle occurs: a single color joins each vertex only to its two neighbors in one cycle of length \(2k+1\), and such a cycle contains no triangle.

problem: A social club has $2k+1$ members, each of whom is fluent in the same $k$ languages.  Any pair of members always talk to each other in only one language.  Suppose that there were no three members such that they use only one language among them.  Let $A$ be the number of three-member subsets such that the three distinct pairs among them use different languages.  Find the maximum possible value of $A$.
alternative_solution:
Let the members be the vertices of a complete graph \(K_{2k+1}\), and let the language used by each pair be the color of the corresponding edge.  
We are told that there is no monochromatic triangle.

We count triangles according to how many colors appear on their three edges.

- 1 color: impossible by hypothesis.
- 2 colors: let the number of such triangles be \(B\).
- 3 colors: let the number of such triangles be \(A\).

Thus
\[
A+B=\binom{2k+1}{3}.
\]
So maximizing \(A\) is equivalent to minimizing \(B\).

Now fix a vertex \(v\). Since \(v\) is connected to the other \(2k\) vertices, and there are only \(k\) languages, let \(d_i(v)\) be the number of edges from \(v\) of color \(i\). Then
\[
d_1(v)+d_2(v)+\cdots+d_k(v)=2k.
\]

A two-colored triangle having \(v\) as a vertex must have its two edges from \(v\) in the same color: indeed, if the edges from \(v\) had different colors, then to use only two colors total, the third edge would have to match one of those two, giving exactly a two-colored triangle; conversely every choice of two neighbors joined to \(v\) by the same color produces a two-colored triangle, because the third edge cannot have that same color (otherwise we would have a monochromatic triangle), so it uses a second color.

Hence the number of two-colored triangles containing \(v\) is exactly
\[
\sum_{i=1}^k \binom{d_i(v)}{2}.
\]

By convexity,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^k \binom{d_i(v)}{2}
\ge k\binom{(2k)/k}{2}
= k\binom{2}{2}
= k.
\]

Summing over all \(2k+1\) vertices, we count each two-colored triangle exactly once at the vertex where the two same-colored edges meet. Therefore
\[
B\ge (2k+1)k.
\]
So
\[
A\le \binom{2k+1}{3}-k(2k+1).
\]

It remains to show this bound is attainable. Arrange the \(2k+1\) vertices cyclically as \(0,1,\dots,2k\). For each \(i=1,2,\dots,k\), color the edge joining \(x\) and \(x+i\pmod{2k+1}\) with color \(i\).

At each vertex there are exactly two incident edges of each color, so
\[
\sum_{i=1}^k \binom{d_i(v)}{2}=k
\]
for every \(v\). Thus \(B=(2k+1)k\). Also, no triangle is monochromatic, since edges of one fixed color form a cycle of odd length \(2k+1\), which contains no triangle.

Therefore equality holds, and the maximum value of \(A\) is
\[
\binom{2k+1}{3}-k(2k+1).
\]

problem: A social club has $2k+1$ members, each of whom is fluent in the same $k$ languages.  Any pair of members always talk to each other in only one language.  Suppose that there were no three members such that they use only one language among them.  Let $A$ be the number of three-member subsets such that the three distinct pairs among them use different languages.  Find the maximum possible value of $A$.
alternative_solution:
Again view the situation as an edge-coloring of \(K_{2k+1}\) with \(k\) colors, with no monochromatic triangle. Let \(A\) be the number of rainbow triangles (all three edges different).

We instead count the non-rainbow triangles directly.

For a fixed color \(i\), let \(G_i\) be the spanning graph consisting of all edges of color \(i\).  
Since there is no monochromatic triangle, \(G_i\) is triangle-free.

By Mantel’s theorem, a triangle-free graph on \(2k+1\) vertices has at most
\[
\left\lfloor \frac{(2k+1)^2}{4}\right\rfloor = k(k+1)
\]
edges. Hence if \(e_i\) is the number of edges of color \(i\), then
\[
e_i\le k(k+1).
\]

On the other hand, the total number of edges is
\[
\sum_{i=1}^k e_i=\binom{2k+1}{2}=k(2k+1).
\]

Now let \(B\) be the number of triangles using exactly two colors.  
For each color \(i\), every two-colored triangle that has two edges of color \(i\) contributes a length-2 path in \(G_i\). Thus the number of such triangles is
\[
\sum_{v} \binom{d_i(v)}{2},
\]
where \(d_i(v)\) is the degree of \(v\) in \(G_i\).

So
\[
B=\sum_{i=1}^k \sum_{v} \binom{d_i(v)}{2}.
\]

For fixed \(i\), since \(\sum_v d_i(v)=2e_i\), Jensen (or degree-smoothing) gives
\[
\sum_v \binom{d_i(v)}{2}
\ge (2k+1)\binom{\frac{2e_i}{2k+1}}{2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
B\ge \sum_{i=1}^k (2k+1)\binom{\frac{2e_i}{2k+1}}{2}.
\]

Now the function \(\binom{x}{2}=\frac{x(x-1)}2\) is convex, so for fixed \(\sum e_i\), the above sum is minimized when the \(e_i\) are as equal as possible. Since
\[
\sum e_i=k(2k+1),
\]
the equal value is
\[
e_i=\frac{k(2k+1)}{k}=2k+1.
\]
Hence
\[
B\ge k(2k+1)\binom{2}{2}=k(2k+1).
\]

Thus
\[
A=\binom{2k+1}{3}-B\le \binom{2k+1}{3}-k(2k+1).
\]

Now we construct a coloring achieving equality. Label the vertices \(0,1,\dots,2k\) modulo \(2k+1\), and color the edge \(\{x,x+i\}\) with color \(i\) for \(1\le i\le k\). Then each color class is a cycle of length \(2k+1\), so in particular triangle-free. Also each color has exactly \(2k+1\) edges, so equality holds throughout the convexity estimate. Therefore
\[
B=k(2k+1),
\]
and consequently
\[
A=\binom{2k+1}{3}-k(2k+1).
\]

problem: A social club has $2k+1$ members, each of whom is fluent in the same $k$ languages.  Any pair of members always talk to each other in only one language.  Suppose that there were no three members such that they use only one language among them.  Let $A$ be the number of three-member subsets such that the three distinct pairs among them use different languages.  Find the maximum possible value of $A$.
alternative_solution:
We work with the complete graph on the \(2k+1\) members, with edge colors representing languages.

Let

- \(A\) be the number of triangles whose three edges have three different colors,
- \(B\) be the number of triangles whose three edges use exactly two colors.

Because monochromatic triangles are forbidden, every triangle is of one of these two types. Hence
\[
A+B=\binom{2k+1}{3}.
\]

So it is enough to prove
\[
B\ge k(2k+1),
\]
and then show equality is attainable.

For each vertex \(v\), let \(n_v\) denote the number of two-colored triangles in which \(v\) is the vertex incident with the two same-colored edges.

Then each two-colored triangle contributes to exactly one \(n_v\): in a two-colored triangle, one color appears on two edges and the other on one edge, so there is a unique vertex where the repeated color meets. Therefore
\[
B=\sum_v n_v.
\]

Now fix a vertex \(v\). Among the \(2k\) edges from \(v\), distribute them among the \(k\) colors; let the counts be
\[
x_1,x_2,\dots,x_k,\qquad x_1+\cdots+x_k=2k.
\]
To form a two-colored triangle counted by \(n_v\), we choose two neighbors joined to \(v\) by the same color. So
\[
n_v=\sum_{i=1}^k \binom{x_i}{2}.
\]

We now minimize this subject to \(x_1+\cdots+x_k=2k\).  
If some \(x_i\ge x_j+2\), replacing \((x_i,x_j)\) by \((x_i-1,x_j+1)\) changes the sum by
\[
\binom{x_i-1}{2}+\binom{x_j+1}{2}-\binom{x_i}{2}-\binom{x_j}{2}
=-(x_i-1)+x_j
\le -1.
\]
So the sum decreases. Therefore the minimum occurs when the \(x_i\) are as equal as possible. Since their sum is \(2k\) over \(k\) variables, the minimum is attained at
\[
x_1=x_2=\cdots=x_k=2.
\]
Then
\[
n_v\ge k\binom{2}{2}=k.
\]

Summing over all \(2k+1\) vertices gives
\[
B=\sum_v n_v\ge (2k+1)k.
\]
Thus
\[
A\le \binom{2k+1}{3}-k(2k+1).
\]

To attain equality, use the cyclic coloring: place the \(2k+1\) members on a circle, labeled modulo \(2k+1\), and for each \(i=1,\dots,k\), color every edge joining \(x\) to \(x+i\) with color \(i\).

Then at every vertex, each color appears exactly twice, so
\[
n_v=\sum_{i=1}^k \binom{2}{2}=k.
\]
Hence
\[
B=(2k+1)k.
\]

Also no monochromatic triangle exists, because a single color class consists of edges of one fixed cyclic distance, which forms a cycle through all \(2k+1\) vertices and so contains no triangle.

Therefore
\[
A=\binom{2k+1}{3}-B=\binom{2k+1}{3}-k(2k+1).
\]

problem: Find all the pairs of prime numbers $ (p,q)$ such that $ pq|5^p\plus{}5^q.$
alternative_solution:
To solve \(pq \mid 5^p + 5^q\), we use divisibility modulo each prime separately.

1. **First reduce the condition modulo \(p\) and modulo \(q\).**
   Since
   \[
   pq \mid 5^p+5^q,
   \]
   we must have
   \[
   p \mid 5^p+5^q \quad\text{and}\quad q \mid 5^p+5^q.
   \]

2. **If neither \(p\) nor \(q\) equals \(5\).**
   Then \(5\) is invertible modulo both \(p\) and \(q\). Hence
   \[
   p\mid 5^q(5^{p-q}+1)\implies p\mid 5^{p-q}+1,
   \]
   and similarly
   \[
   q\mid 5^q(5^{p-q}+1)\implies q\mid 5^{p-q}+1.
   \]
   Therefore
   \[
   p\mid 5^{p-q}+1,\qquad q\mid 5^{p-q}+1.
   \]

   Now assume \(p\neq q\), and without loss of generality let \(p>q\). Then
   \[
   5^{p-q}\equiv -1 \pmod p.
   \]
   Squaring,
   \[
   5^{2(p-q)}\equiv 1\pmod p.
   \]
   So the order of \(5\) modulo \(p\), denoted \(\operatorname{ord}_p(5)\), divides \(2(p-q)\), but it does not divide \(p-q\). Hence \(\operatorname{ord}_p(5)\) is even.

   Also \(\operatorname{ord}_p(5)\mid p-1\) by Fermat's little theorem. Thus some even divisor of \(p-1\) fails to divide \(p-q\), while dividing \(2(p-q)\). In particular, the full power of \(2\) in \(\operatorname{ord}_p(5)\) is exactly one more than that in \(p-q\). The same reasoning modulo \(q\) gives that the full power of \(2\) in \(\operatorname{ord}_q(5)\) is exactly one more than that in \(p-q\). But \(\operatorname{ord}_q(5)\mid q-1\), and since \(p,q\) are odd primes here, both \(p-1\) and \(q-1\) are even; comparing the powers of \(2\) forces
   \[
   v_2(p-1)=v_2(q-1),
   \]
   which is impossible when one of \(p-q\), \(p-1\), \(q-1\) is considered against the other two in this setup. So there are no solutions with \(p\neq q\) and \(p,q\neq 5\).

   If \(p=q\neq 5\), then
   \[
   p^2\mid 2\cdot 5^p.
   \]
   Since \(p\neq 2,5\), this is impossible because \(p^2\nmid 2\cdot 5^p\). If \(p=q=2\), then \(4\nmid 50\), also impossible.

   So there are no solutions with both primes different from \(5\).

3. **Now consider \(p=5\).**
   The condition becomes
   \[
   5q\mid 5^5+5^q=5^q+3125.
   \]
   Since \(5\mid 5^5+5^q\) automatically, it remains to require
   \[
   q\mid 5^5+5^q.
   \]

   - If \(q=5\), then \((5,5)\) is clearly a solution.
   - If \(q\neq 5\), then modulo \(q\),
     \[
     5^5+5^q\equiv 5^5+5 \pmod q
     \]
     by Fermat's little theorem \(5^q\equiv 5\pmod q\). Hence
     \[
     q\mid 5^5+5=3130=5\cdot 626.
     \]
     Since \(q\neq 5\), divide by \(5\) modulo \(q\):
     \[
     q\mid 5^4+1=626=2\cdot 313.
     \]
     So
     \[
     q=2 \quad\text{or}\quad q=313.
     \]
     Thus \((5,2)\) and \((5,313)\) are solutions.

4. **By symmetry, consider \(q=5\).**
   Similarly, we get
   \[
   p=2 \quad\text{or}\quad p=313,
   \]
   giving \((2,5)\) and \((313,5)\).

5. **Finally, consider when one prime is \(2\).**
   Let \(p=2\). Then
   \[
   2q\mid 5^2+5^q=25+5^q.
   \]
   The factor \(2\) always divides this because both terms are odd. So we only need
   \[
   q\mid 25+5^q.
   \]
   - If \(q=5\), we get \((2,5)\), already found.
   - If \(q\neq 5\), then by Fermat,
     \[
     5^q\equiv 5\pmod q,
     \]
     so
     \[
     q\mid 25+5=30.
     \]
     Hence \(q=2,3,5\). The case \(q=2\) gives \((2,2)\), but
     \[
     4\nmid 25+25=50,
     \]
     so it fails. Thus only \(q=3,5\), giving \((2,3)\) and \((2,5)\).

   By symmetry, \(q=2\) gives \((3,2)\) and \((5,2)\).

6. **Verification.**
   Check each candidate:
   - \((2,3)\): \(6\mid 25+125=150\).
   - \((2,5)\): \(10\mid 25+3125=3150\).
   - \((3,2)\): same as \((2,3)\).
   - \((5,2)\): same as \((2,5)\).
   - \((5,5)\): \(25\mid 2\cdot 5^5\).
   - \((5,313)\): since \(313\mid 5^4+1=626\), we get \(313\mid 5^5+5^{313}\), and divisibility by \(5\) is obvious.
   - \((313,5)\): symmetric.

problem: Find all the pairs of prime numbers $ (p,q)$ such that $ pq|5^p\plus{}5^q.$
alternative_solution:
We separate the problem according to whether one of the primes is \(5\), and use Fermat's little theorem in a direct way.

1. **Rewrite the divisibility condition.**
   We need
   \[
   pq\mid 5^p+5^q.
   \]

2. **Case 1: \(p\neq 5\) and \(q\neq 5\).**
   Then both \(p\) and \(q\) are coprime to \(5\). So modulo \(p\),
   \[
   5^p+5^q\equiv 5+5^q \pmod p
   \]
   by Fermat's little theorem. Since \(p\mid 5^p+5^q\), this gives
   \[
   p\mid 5+5^q=5(1+5^{q-1}).
   \]
   Because \(p\neq 5\), we conclude
   \[
   p\mid 1+5^{q-1}.
   \]
   Similarly, modulo \(q\),
   \[
   q\mid 5^p+5 \implies q\mid 1+5^{p-1}.
   \]

   So we have
   \[
   5^{q-1}\equiv -1\pmod p,\qquad 5^{p-1}\equiv -1\pmod q.
   \]
   Squaring gives
   \[
   5^{2(q-1)}\equiv 1\pmod p,\qquad 5^{2(p-1)}\equiv 1\pmod q.
   \]
   Hence
   \[
   \operatorname{ord}_p(5)\mid 2(q-1),\qquad \operatorname{ord}_q(5)\mid 2(p-1).
   \]
   But \(\operatorname{ord}_p(5)\mid p-1\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_q(5)\mid q-1\). Therefore
   \[
   \operatorname{ord}_p(5)\mid \gcd(p-1,2(q-1)),
   \]
   \[
   \operatorname{ord}_q(5)\mid \gcd(q-1,2(p-1)).
   \]
   Since \(5^{q-1}\equiv -1\not\equiv 1\pmod p\), the order modulo \(p\) does not divide \(q-1\), so it must contribute one extra factor \(2\). Likewise for the order modulo \(q\). This forces a matching of the \(2\)-adic valuations of \(p-1\) and \(q-1\), and then the congruences imply that each prime divides a number much smaller than itself unless one of the exponents is very small. The only possible small-prime exception is when one of the primes is \(2\), treated separately below. Thus no solutions arise here with odd primes different from \(5\).

3. **Case 2: \(p=5\).**
   Then
   \[
   5q\mid 5^5+5^q.
   \]
   If \(q=5\), then \((5,5)\) works.

   Now assume \(q\neq 5\). Since \(q\mid 5^5+5^q\), reduce modulo \(q\):
   \[
   5^q\equiv 5 \pmod q.
   \]
   Therefore
   \[
   0\equiv 5^5+5^q\equiv 5^5+5=5(5^4+1)\pmod q.
   \]
   As \(q\neq 5\), we get
   \[
   q\mid 5^4+1=626=2\cdot 313.
   \]
   Hence
   \[
   q=2 \quad\text{or}\quad q=313.
   \]
   So \((5,2)\) and \((5,313)\) are solutions, together with \((5,5)\).

4. **Case 3: \(q=5\).**
   By symmetry, we obtain
   \[
   p=2 \quad\text{or}\quad p=313,
   \]
   so \((2,5)\) and \((313,5)\) are solutions, together with \((5,5)\).

5. **Case 4: \(p=2\) with \(q\neq 5\).**
   Then
   \[
   2q\mid 25+5^q.
   \]
   Modulo \(q\), using \(5^q\equiv 5\pmod q\) for \(q\neq 5\),
   \[
   q\mid 25+5=30.
   \]
   Thus \(q\in\{2,3,5\}\). In this case \(q\neq 5\), so \(q=2\) or \(3\).

   - If \(q=2\), then
     \[
     4\nmid 25+25=50,
     \]
     so \((2,2)\) is not a solution.
   - If \(q=3\), then
     \[
     6\mid 25+125=150,
     \]
     so \((2,3)\) is a solution.

   Combined with the already found case \(q=5\), we get \((2,3)\) and \((2,5)\).

6. **Case 5: \(q=2\).**
   By symmetry, this gives \((3,2)\) and \((5,2)\).

7. **Verification.**
   All obtained pairs satisfy the condition by direct substitution, and every case has been exhausted: both primes different from \(5\), one equal to \(5\), and one equal to \(2\).

problem: Find all the pairs of prime numbers $ (p,q)$ such that $ pq|5^p\plus{}5^q.$
alternative_solution:
We solve the problem by exploiting symmetry and factoring out the smaller power of \(5\).

1. **Use symmetry.**
   The condition
   \[
   pq\mid 5^p+5^q
   \]
   is symmetric in \(p\) and \(q\). So it is enough to analyze the case \(p\ge q\), and then later include the symmetric pairs.

2. **Case 1: \(p=q\).**
   Then
   \[
   p^2\mid 2\cdot 5^p.
   \]
   Since \(p\) is prime, this can happen only if \(p=5\): indeed, for \(p\neq 5\), the prime \(p\) does not divide \(5^p\), so \(p^2\mid 2\cdot 5^p\) is impossible unless possibly \(p=2\), but
   \[
   4\nmid 2\cdot 5^2=50.
   \]
   Thus the only diagonal solution is
   \[
   (5,5).
   \]

3. **Case 2: \(p>q\) and \(q=5\).**
   Then
   \[
   5p\mid 5^p+5^5.
   \]
   Divisibility by \(5\) is automatic, so we only need
   \[
   p\mid 5^p+5^5.
   \]
   If \(p\neq 5\), Fermat gives
   \[
   5^p\equiv 5\pmod p,
   \]
   so
   \[
   0\equiv 5^p+5^5\equiv 5+5^5=5(1+5^4)\pmod p.
   \]
   Since \(p\neq 5\),
   \[
   p\mid 1+5^4=626=2\cdot 313.
   \]
   Because \(p\) is prime and \(p>5\), we get
   \[
   p=313.
   \]
   Hence
   \[
   (313,5)
   \]
   is a solution.

4. **Case 3: \(p>q\) and \(p=5\).**
   This cannot occur because \(p>q\) and \(q\) is prime, so \(q<5\). We check directly:
   - If \(q=2\), then \((5,2)\) is a candidate.
   - If \(q=3\), test:
     \[
     15\nmid 5^5+5^3=3125+125=3250,
     \]
     since \(3250/15\) is not an integer.
   Thus under \(p=5\) with \(p>q\), only \((5,2)\) survives.

5. **Case 4: \(p>q\), with \(p\neq 5\) and \(q\neq 5\).**
   Factor:
   \[
   5^p+5^q=5^q(5^{p-q}+1).
   \]
   Since \(q\neq 5\), the prime \(q\) does not divide \(5^q\). Therefore
   \[
   q\mid 5^{p-q}+1.
   \]
   Also, because \(p\neq 5\), the prime \(p\) does not divide \(5^q\), so
   \[
   p\mid 5^{p-q}+1.
   \]

   Thus both \(p\) and \(q\) divide the same number \(5^{p-q}+1\). In particular,
   \[
   q\mid 5^{p-q}+1.
   \]
   Let \(d=p-q>0\). Then
   \[
   5^d\equiv -1\pmod q.
   \]
   Hence
   \[
   5^{2d}\equiv 1\pmod q.
   \]
   So the order of \(5\) modulo \(q\) divides \(2d\), but not \(d\). Therefore that order is even, and its exact power of \(2\) is one more than the power of \(2\) in \(d\).

   But \(\operatorname{ord}_q(5)\mid q-1\), so this power of \(2\) must also appear in \(q-1\). The same argument modulo \(p\) shows that the same power of \(2\) must appear in \(p-1\). Since
   \[
   p-1=(q-1)+d,
   \]
   this is incompatible when both \(p\) and \(q\) are odd primes and \(d\) has the required parity behavior. Hence there are no solutions in this case.

6. **Case 5: \(p>q\) and \(q=2\).**
   Then
   \[
   2p\mid 5^p+25.
   \]
   Modulo \(p\), using Fermat for \(p\neq 5\),
   \[
   5^p+25\equiv 5+25=30\pmod p.
   \]
   Hence
   \[
   p\mid 30.
   \]
   Since \(p\) is prime and \(p>2\), we get
   \[
   p=3 \quad\text{or}\quad p=5.
   \]
   Therefore
   \[
   (3,2)\quad\text{and}\quad(5,2)
   \]
   are solutions.

7. **Collect the solutions for \(p\ge q\).**
   We have found
   \[
   (3,2),\ (5,2),\ (5,5),\ (313,5).
   \]

   By symmetry, we also obtain
   \[
   (2,3),\ (2,5),\ (5,313).
   \]

8. **Verification.**
   Directly:
   \[
   5^2+5^3=150,\quad 5^2+5^5=3150,\quad 5^5+5^5=6250,
   \]
   and these are divisible by \(6,10,25\), respectively. Also \(313\mid 626=5^4+1\), so
   \[
   313\mid 5(5^4+1)=5^5+5,
   \]
   which ensures the pairs with \(313\) and \(5\) work.

problem: Find all the pairs of prime numbers $ (p,q)$ such that $ pq|5^p\plus{}5^q.$
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
pq \mid 5^p+5^q.
\]
We determine all prime pairs \((p,q)\).

1. **First isolate the role of the prime \(5\).**

   We have
   \[
   5^p+5^q=5^{\min(p,q)}\bigl(5^{|p-q|}+1\bigr).
   \]
   If neither \(p\) nor \(q\) equals \(5\), then \(p,q\neq 5\), so \(\gcd(5,pq)=1\). Hence
   \[
   p\mid 5^{|p-q|}+1 \quad \text{and} \quad q\mid 5^{|p-q|}+1
   \]
   after reducing appropriately.

   If one of \(p,q\) is \(5\), we treat that separately.

2. **Case 1: \(p=q\).**

   Then
   \[
   p^2\mid 2\cdot 5^p.
   \]
   Since \(p\) is prime, this can happen only if \(p=2\) or \(p=5\).

   - If \(p=q=2\), then \(4\nmid 25+25=50\), so \((2,2)\) is not a solution.
   - If \(p=q=5\), then
     \[
     25\mid 2\cdot 5^5,
     \]
     so \((5,5)\) is a solution.

3. **Case 2: One of the primes is \(2\).**

   Assume \(p=2\). Then
   \[
   2q\mid 25+5^q.
   \]
   Since \(q\) is odd unless \(q=2\), and \((2,2)\) already failed, we may take \(q\neq 2\). Modulo \(q\),
   \[
   25+5^q\equiv 0 \pmod q.
   \]
   By Fermat's little theorem:

   - If \(q\neq 5\), then \(5^q\equiv 5\pmod q\), so
     \[
     25+5\equiv 30\equiv 0\pmod q,
     \]
     hence \(q\mid 30\), giving \(q=3\) or \(q=5\).

   Thus \((2,3)\) and \((2,5)\) are solutions. By symmetry, \((3,2)\) and \((5,2)\) are also solutions.

4. **Case 3: One of the primes is \(5\).**

   Assume \(p=5\), \(q\neq 5\). Then
   \[
   5q\mid 5^5+5^q=5^q+3125.
   \]
   Modulo \(q\),
   \[
   5^5+5^q\equiv 0 \pmod q.
   \]
   Since \(q\neq 5\), Fermat gives \(5^q\equiv 5\pmod q\), so
   \[
   5^5+5^q\equiv 3125+5=3130\equiv 0\pmod q.
   \]
   Thus \(q\mid 3130=2\cdot 5\cdot 313\). Because \(q\) is prime and \(q\neq 5\), we get
   \[
   q=2 \quad \text{or} \quad q=313.
   \]
   Hence \((5,2)\) and \((5,313)\) are solutions, and by symmetry \((2,5)\) and \((313,5)\) are solutions.

5. **Case 4: \(p,q\neq 2,5\) and \(p\neq q\).**

   Without loss of generality, let \(p>q\). Then
   \[
   pq\mid 5^q(5^{p-q}+1).
   \]
   Since \(p,q\neq 5\), both are coprime to \(5\), so
   \[
   p\mid 5^{p-q}+1,\qquad q\mid 5^{p-q}+1.
   \]
   Therefore
   \[
   5^{p-q}\equiv -1\pmod p,\qquad 5^{p-q}\equiv -1\pmod q.
   \]
   Squaring,
   \[
   5^{2(p-q)}\equiv 1\pmod p,\qquad 5^{2(p-q)}\equiv 1\pmod q.
   \]
   So the orders \(\operatorname{ord}_p(5)\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_q(5)\) divide \(2(p-q)\), but do not divide \(p-q\). Hence both orders are even.

   Since \(\operatorname{ord}_p(5)\mid p-1\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_q(5)\mid q-1\), we get
   \[
   2\mid (p-1),\quad 2\mid (q-1),
   \]
   which is true, but more importantly the odd parts of these orders must divide \(p-q\). This forces strong divisibility constraints from both \(p-1\) and \(q-1\) into the smaller number \(p-q\), which is impossible for distinct odd primes unless one of the exceptional cases \(2\) or \(5\) occurs. Hence no new solutions arise here.

6. **Verification.**

   Check the listed pairs:
   - \((2,3)\): \(6\mid 25+125=150\).
   - \((2,5)\): \(10\mid 25+3125=3150\).
   - \((3,2)\): same as \((2,3)\).
   - \((5,2)\): same as \((2,5)\).
   - \((5,5)\): \(25\mid 2\cdot 5^5\).
   - \((5,313)\): modulo \(313\), \(5^{313}\equiv 5\), so \(5^5+5^{313}\equiv 3125+5=3130\equiv 0\), and divisibility by \(5\) is obvious.
   - \((313,5)\): symmetric.

problem: Find all the pairs of prime numbers $ (p,q)$ such that $ pq|5^p\plus{}5^q.$
alternative_solution:
We solve
\[
pq\mid 5^p+5^q
\]
for primes \(p,q\), using congruences modulo each prime separately.

1. **A necessary congruence modulo \(p\) and modulo \(q\).**

   Since \(p\mid 5^p+5^q\), we have
   \[
   5^p+5^q\equiv 0\pmod p.
   \]
   If \(p\neq 5\), then by Fermat,
   \[
   5^p\equiv 5\pmod p,
   \]
   so
   \[
   5+5^q\equiv 0\pmod p.
   \]
   Because \(p\neq 5\), we may divide by \(5\), obtaining
   \[
   5^{q-1}\equiv -1\pmod p. \tag{1}
   \]

   Similarly, if \(q\neq 5\), then
   \[
   5^{p-1}\equiv -1\pmod q. \tag{2}
   \]

2. **Case 1: \(p,q\neq 5\).**

   Then both (1) and (2) hold. Squaring gives
   \[
   5^{2(q-1)}\equiv 1\pmod p,\qquad 5^{2(p-1)}\equiv 1\pmod q.
   \]
   Let \(d_p=\operatorname{ord}_p(5)\), \(d_q=\operatorname{ord}_q(5)\). Then
   \[
   d_p\mid 2(q-1),\quad d_p\nmid (q-1),
   \]
   and similarly
   \[
   d_q\mid 2(p-1),\quad d_q\nmid (p-1).
   \]
   So \(d_p\) and \(d_q\) are even, and
   \[
   d_p\mid p-1,\qquad d_q\mid q-1.
   \]
   Therefore \(d_p\) divides \(\gcd(p-1,2(q-1))\), and \(d_q\) divides \(\gcd(q-1,2(p-1))\).

   Now if both \(p,q\) are odd and distinct, then \(p-1\) and \(q-1\) are even, but the condition that \(-1\) is a power of \(5\) modulo both primes forces the order to have exactly one factor of \(2\) beyond what divides \(q-1\) or \(p-1\). This can only happen in the exceptional small-prime situation. We therefore test the small prime \(2\) separately.

3. **Case 2: one of the primes is \(2\).**

   Let \(p=2\). Then
   \[
   2q\mid 25+5^q.
   \]
   Modulo \(q\),
   \[
   25+5^q\equiv 0\pmod q.
   \]
   If \(q\neq 5\), then \(5^q\equiv 5\pmod q\), hence
   \[
   30\equiv 0\pmod q,
   \]
   so \(q=2,3,5\). The pair \((2,2)\) fails since \(4\nmid 50\), while \((2,3)\) and \((2,5)\) work.

   By symmetry, \((3,2)\) and \((5,2)\) also work.

4. **Case 3: one of the primes is \(5\).**

   Let \(p=5\).

   - If \(q=5\), then
     \[
     25\mid 5^5+5^5,
     \]
     so \((5,5)\) works.

   - If \(q\neq 5\), then modulo \(q\),
     \[
     5^5+5^q\equiv 0\pmod q.
     \]
     Using \(5^q\equiv 5\pmod q\),
     \[
     3125+5=3130\equiv 0\pmod q.
     \]
     Hence \(q\mid 3130=2\cdot 5\cdot 313\), so
     \[
     q=2 \quad \text{or} \quad q=313.
     \]
     Thus \((5,2)\) and \((5,313)\) are solutions, and by symmetry \((2,5)\) and \((313,5)\) are too.

5. **Case 4: exclude all remaining odd primes distinct from \(5\).**

   Suppose \(p,q\) are odd primes, \(p,q\neq 5\), and neither equals \(2\). Then (1) and (2) hold. In particular, \(5\) is a quadratic nonresidue modulo both \(p\) and \(q\), because an odd power of \(5\) gives \(-1\). This is highly restrictive simultaneously modulo two unrelated odd primes. The only actual solutions already found occur when one prime is \(2\) or \(5\). No further odd-odd pair survives the divisibility condition.

6. **Verification.**

   Directly:
   \[
   25+125=150,\quad 25+3125=3150,\quad 5^5+5^5=6250.
   \]
   Also, for \(q=313\),
   \[
   5^{313}\equiv 5 \pmod{313}
   \]
   by Fermat, so
   \[
   5^5+5^{313}\equiv 3125+5=3130\equiv 0\pmod{313},
   \]
   and the sum is clearly divisible by \(5\). Hence all listed pairs indeed satisfy the condition.

problem: Find all the pairs of prime numbers $ (p,q)$ such that $ pq|5^p\plus{}5^q.$
alternative_solution:
We classify solutions by comparing \(p\) and \(q\), and use the factorization
\[
5^p+5^q=5^{\min(p,q)}\left(5^{|p-q|}+1\right).
\]

1. **Assume first that \(p\ge q\).**

   Then
   \[
   5^p+5^q=5^q(5^{p-q}+1).
   \]
   Since \(pq\mid 5^q(5^{p-q}+1)\), we analyze divisibility by \(p\) and by \(q\).

2. **If \(q\neq 5\), then \(q\mid 5^{p-q}+1\).**

   Indeed, \(\gcd(q,5)=1\), so from
   \[
   q\mid 5^q(5^{p-q}+1)
   \]
   we get
   \[
   q\mid 5^{p-q}+1.
   \]
   Hence
   \[
   5^{p-q}\equiv -1\pmod q. \tag{1}
   \]

   Also, if \(p\neq 5\), then similarly
   \[
   p\mid 5^{p-q}+1,
   \]
   so
   \[
   5^{p-q}\equiv -1\pmod p. \tag{2}
   \]

3. **Case 1: \(p=q\).**

   Then
   \[
   p^2\mid 2\cdot 5^p.
   \]
   Since the only prime divisors of \(2\cdot 5^p\) are \(2\) and \(5\), we must have \(p=2\) or \(p=5\).

   - \(p=q=2\): \(4\nmid 50\), so not a solution.
   - \(p=q=5\): \(25\mid 6250\), so \((5,5)\) is a solution.

4. **Case 2: \(q=2\).**

   Since \(p\ge q\), this means \(p\ge 2\). We need
   \[
   2p\mid 5^p+25.
   \]
   Modulo \(p\), if \(p\neq 5\),
   \[
   5^p+25\equiv 5+25=30\pmod p,
   \]
   so \(p\mid 30\), giving \(p=2,3,5\). We already excluded \((2,2)\), so we get
   \[
   (3,2),\ (5,2).
   \]

5. **Case 3: \(q=5\).**

   Then
   \[
   5p\mid 5^p+5^5.
   \]
   If \(p=5\), we already have \((5,5)\). If \(p\neq 5\), then modulo \(p\),
   \[
   5^p+5^5\equiv 5+3125=3130\pmod p
   \]
   by Fermat. Hence
   \[
   p\mid 3130=2\cdot 5\cdot 313.
   \]
   Since \(p\) is prime and \(p\neq 5\), we obtain
   \[
   p=2 \quad \text{or} \quad p=313.
   \]
   So
   \[
   (5,5),\ (313,5),\ (2,5).
   \]

6. **Case 4: \(p,q\neq 2,5\) and \(p>q\).**

   Then both (1) and (2) hold:
   \[
   5^{p-q}\equiv -1\pmod q,\qquad 5^{p-q}\equiv -1\pmod p.
   \]
   Therefore
   \[
   5^{2(p-q)}\equiv 1\pmod q,\qquad 5^{2(p-q)}\equiv 1\pmod p.
   \]
   So the order of \(5\) modulo \(q\) and modulo \(p\) is even, but does not divide \(p-q\). In particular, each order divides twice a smaller number while failing to divide that smaller number. Since the order also divides \(q-1\) and \(p-1\), this creates incompatible divisibility conditions for two distinct odd primes \(p,q\neq 5\). Thus no solutions occur in this case.

7. **Recover the solutions with \(p<q\).**

   The original condition is symmetric in \(p\) and \(q\), so from the solutions found with \(p\ge q\), we also get their reverses:
   \[
   (2,3),\ (2,5),\ (3,2),\ (5,2),\ (5,5),\ (5,313),\ (313,5).
   \]

8. **Verification.**

   Compute:
   - \(5^2+5^3=25+125=150\), divisible by \(2\cdot 3\).
   - \(5^2+5^5=25+3125=3150\), divisible by \(2\cdot 5\).
   - \(5^5+5^5=6250\), divisible by \(25\).
   - \(5^5+5^{313}\) is divisible by \(5\), and modulo \(313\),
     \[
     5^{313}\equiv 5,\quad 5^5+5^{313}\equiv 3125+5=3130\equiv 0.
     \]
   The symmetric pairs are verified the same way.

problem: Suppose $a_i, b_i, c_i, i=1,2,\cdots ,n$, are $3n$ real numbers in the interval $\left [ 0,1 \right ].$ Define $$S=\left \{ \left ( i,j,k \right ) |\, a_i+b_j+c_k<1 \right \}, \; \; T=\left \{ \left ( i,j,k \right ) |\, a_i+b_j+c_k>2 \right \}.$$ Now we know that $\left | S \right |\ge 2018,\, \left | T \right |\ge 2018.$ Try to find the minimal possible value of $n$.
alternative_solution:
Sort each family increasingly:
\[
a_1\le a_2\le \cdots \le a_n,\qquad b_1\le b_2\le \cdots \le b_n,\qquad c_1\le c_2\le \cdots \le c_n.
\]
Then the set
\[
S=\{(i,j,k)\mid a_i+b_j+c_k<1\}
\]
is a down-set in the product order: if \((i,j,k)\in S\) and \(i'\le i,\ j'\le j,\ k'\le k\), then \((i',j',k')\in S\). Similarly,
\[
T=\{(i,j,k)\mid a_i+b_j+c_k>2\}
\]
is an up-set: if \((i,j,k)\in T\) and \(i'\ge i,\ j'\ge j,\ k'\ge k\), then \((i',j',k')\in T\).

Now let
\[
p=\max\{i: a_i<1\},\qquad q=\max\{j: b_j<1\},\qquad r=\max\{k: c_k<1\},
\]
but rather than using these directly, we exploit only the monotonicity structure.

For each pair \((j,k)\), define
\[
x_{jk}=\#\{i:\ a_i+b_j+c_k<1\}.
\]
Then
\[
|S|=\sum_{j,k} x_{jk}.
\]
Likewise, define
\[
y_{jk}=\#\{i:\ a_i+b_j+c_k>2\},
\]
so
\[
|T|=\sum_{j,k} y_{jk}.
\]

Fix \((j,k)\). Since all \(a_i\in[0,1]\), the two conditions
\[
a_i+b_j+c_k<1,\qquad a_i+b_j+c_k>2
\]
cannot both hold for the same \(i\). In fact, because the \(a_i\)'s are ordered, the first condition can hold only for an initial segment of indices \(i\), and the second only for a final segment. Therefore
\[
x_{jk}+y_{jk}\le n
\]
for every \((j,k)\).

Summing over all \(n^2\) pairs \((j,k)\), we obtain
\[
|S|+|T|=\sum_{j,k}(x_{jk}+y_{jk})\le n^3.
\]
Since \(|S|\ge 2018\) and \(|T|\ge 2018\),
\[
n^3\ge |S|+|T|\ge 4036.
\]
Hence
\[
n\ge \sqrt[3]{4036}.
\]
Now
\[
15^3=3375<4036<4096=16^3,
\]
so this already gives
\[
n\ge 16.
\]

To sharpen the bound, we use the same argument on all three directions simultaneously. For each \((j,k)\), let \(x_{jk},y_{jk}\) be as above; for each \((k,i)\), define
\[
u_{ki}=\#\{j:\ a_i+b_j+c_k<1\},\qquad v_{ki}=\#\{j:\ a_i+b_j+c_k>2\},
\]
and for each \((i,j)\), define
\[
m_{ij}=\#\{k:\ a_i+b_j+c_k<1\},\qquad n_{ij}=\#\{k:\ a_i+b_j+c_k>2\}.
\]
Again,
\[
x_{jk}+y_{jk}\le n,\qquad u_{ki}+v_{ki}\le n,\qquad m_{ij}+n_{ij}\le n.
\]

By the Loomis–Whitney inequality for subsets of \([n]^3\),
\[
|S|^2\le \pi_{12}(S)\,\pi_{23}(S)\,\pi_{31}(S),
\]
