\lambda\sum_{i=1}^n u_i+\sqrt n\,M\ge \sum_{i=1}^n\sqrt{|a_i|}.
\]

The key point is to estimate each \(\sqrt{|a_j|}\) separately.

Fix \(j\). Since
\[
a_j=(a_j-b)+b
\]
and
\[
b=\frac1n\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i-\sum_{i=1}^n(a_i-b)\right),
\]
we have
\[
a_j=(a_j-b)+\frac1n\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i-\sum_{i=1}^n(a_i-b)\right).
\]
Multiplying by \(n\),
\[
na_j=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i-\sum_{i\ne j}(a_i-b)+(n-1)(a_j-b).
\]
Therefore, using subadditivity of \(x\mapsto \sqrt{|x|}\),
\[
\sqrt n\,\sqrt{|a_j|}
=\sqrt{|na_j|}
\le \sqrt{\left|\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right|}
+\sum_{i\ne j}\sqrt{|a_i-b|}
+\sqrt{(n-1)|a_j-b|}.
\]
That is,
\[
\sqrt n\,\sqrt{|a_j|}
\le M+\sum_{i\ne j}u_i+\sqrt{n-1}\,u_j.
\]

Now sum over \(j=1,\dots,n\):
\[
\sqrt n\sum_{j=1}^n\sqrt{|a_j|}
\le nM+\sum_{j=1}^n\sum_{i\ne j}u_i+\sqrt{n-1}\sum_{j=1}^n u_j.
\]
Since
\[
\sum_{j=1}^n\sum_{i\ne j}u_i=(n-1)\sum_{i=1}^n u_i,
\]
we get
\[
\sqrt n\sum_{j=1}^n\sqrt{|a_j|}
\le nM+\bigl(n-1+\sqrt{n-1}\bigr)\sum_{i=1}^n u_i.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\sum_{j=1}^n\sqrt{|a_j|}
\le \sqrt n\,M+\frac{n-1+\sqrt{n-1}}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n\sqrt{|a_i-b|}.
\]
Since \(\sqrt n\,M=\sqrt{n\left|\sum a_i\right|}\), this proves that
\[
\lambda=\frac{n-1+\sqrt{n-1}}{\sqrt n}
\]
is sufficient.

To prove optimality, we choose a configuration where equality is forced. Let
\[
a_1=\cdots=a_{n-1}=b=t\ne0,\qquad a_n=-(n-1)t.
\]
Then
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i=0,
\]
so
\[
\sqrt{n\left|\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right|}=0.
\]
Also,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n\sqrt{|a_i-b|}
=\sqrt{|-(n-1)t-t|}
=\sqrt{n|t|},
\]
and
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n\sqrt{|a_i|}
=(n-1)\sqrt{|t|}+\sqrt{(n-1)|t|}
=\bigl(n-1+\sqrt{n-1}\bigr)\sqrt{|t|}.
\]
Thus the inequality demands
\[
\lambda\sqrt{n|t|}\ge \bigl(n-1+\sqrt{n-1}\bigr)\sqrt{|t|},
\]
hence
\[
\lambda\ge \frac{n-1+\sqrt{n-1}}{\sqrt n}.
\]

problem:
Given integer $n\geq 2$. Find the minimum value of $\lambda {}$, satisfy that for any real numbers $a_1$, $a_2$, $\cdots$, ${a_n}$ and ${b}$,
$$\lambda\sum\limits_{i=1}^n\sqrt{|a_i-b|}+\sqrt{n\left|\sum\limits_{i=1}^na_i\right|}\geqslant\sum\limits_{i=1}^n\sqrt{|a_i|}.$$
alternative_solution:
We split the argument into two parts: a lower bound for \(\lambda\), and then a proof that the same value is enough.

First, let us derive a necessary condition. Choose
\[
a_1=\cdots=a_{n-1}=b=t\ne0,\qquad a_n=-(n-1)t.
\]
Then
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i=0,
\]
so the second term on the left is \(0\). Moreover,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n\sqrt{|a_i-b|}
=0+\cdots+0+\sqrt{|-(n-1)t-t|}
=\sqrt{n|t|},
\]
while
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n\sqrt{|a_i|}
=(n-1)\sqrt{|t|}+\sqrt{(n-1)|t|}
=\bigl(n-1+\sqrt{n-1}\bigr)\sqrt{|t|}.
\]
Hence any admissible \(\lambda\) must satisfy
\[
\lambda\sqrt{n|t|}\ge \bigl(n-1+\sqrt{n-1}\bigr)\sqrt{|t|},
\]
that is,
\[
\lambda\ge \frac{n-1+\sqrt{n-1}}{\sqrt n}.
\]
So this gives the lower bound.

Now we prove that
\[
\lambda_0:=\frac{n-1+\sqrt{n-1}}{\sqrt n}
\]
indeed works.

For each \(j\), define
\[
X_j=\sum_{i\ne j}(a_i-b),\qquad Y_j=(n-1)(b-a_j).
\]
Then
\[
X_j+Y_j=\sum_{i\ne j}a_i-(n-1)b+(n-1)b-(n-1)a_j
=\sum_{i\ne j}a_i-(n-1)a_j.
\]
Therefore,
\[
(X_j+Y_j)+\sum_{i=1}^n a_i=na_j.
\]
Using twice the inequality
\[
\sqrt{|x+y|}\le \sqrt{|x|}+\sqrt{|y|},
\]
we obtain
\[
\sqrt{|na_j|}
\le \sqrt{|X_j|}+\sqrt{|Y_j|}+\sqrt{\left|\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right|}.
\]
Next,
\[
\sqrt{|X_j|}
=\sqrt{\left|\sum_{i\ne j}(a_i-b)\right|}
\le \sum_{i\ne j}\sqrt{|a_i-b|},
\]
and
\[
\sqrt{|Y_j|}
=\sqrt{(n-1)|a_j-b|}
=\sqrt{n-1}\sqrt{|a_j-b|}.
\]
Since \(\sqrt{|na_j|}=\sqrt n\,\sqrt{|a_j|}\), we get
\[
\sqrt n\,\sqrt{|a_j|}
\le \sum_{i\ne j}\sqrt{|a_i-b|}
+\sqrt{n-1}\sqrt{|a_j-b|}
+\sqrt{\left|\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right|}.
\]
Summing this over all \(j\) yields
\[
\sqrt n\sum_{j=1}^n\sqrt{|a_j|}
\le \bigl(n-1+\sqrt{n-1}\bigr)\sum_{i=1}^n\sqrt{|a_i-b|}
+n\sqrt{\left|\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right|}.
\]
Divide by \(\sqrt n\):
\[
\sum_{j=1}^n\sqrt{|a_j|}
\le \frac{n-1+\sqrt{n-1}}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n\sqrt{|a_i-b|}
+\sqrt{n\left|\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right|}.
\]
Thus \(\lambda_0\) is sufficient.

problem:
Let $k$ be a positive real. $A$ and $B$ play the following game: at the start, there are $80$ zeroes arrange around a circle. Each turn, $A$ increases some of these $80$ numbers, such that the total sum added is $1$. Next, $B$ selects ten consecutive numbers with the largest sum, and reduces them all to $0$. $A$ then wins the game if he/she can ensure that at least one of the number is $\geq k$ at some finite point of time. 

Determine all $k$ such that $A$ can always win the game.
alternative_solution:
We first compress the circle of \(80\) numbers into \(8\) blocks of \(10\) consecutive numbers each. If \(A\) plays only by adding equally within blocks, then each block may be treated as a single “super-number”. Since \(B\) always erases ten consecutive original numbers, in particular \(B\) can erase an entire block; hence, to prove a bound for \(A\), it is enough to study the simpler game with \(8\) numbers on a circle where after each move \(B\) resets one number to \(0\).

So we consider the following equivalent reduced game:

- there are \(8\) nonnegative numbers;
- each turn \(A\) distributes total increment \(1\);
- then \(B\) resets one of the \(8\) numbers to \(0\);
- \(A\) wants some number to reach at least \(k\).

We now determine the exact threshold.

---

### 1. An upper bound for what \(A\) can force

Let after \(A\)'s move the \(8\) numbers, arranged in decreasing order, be
\[
a_1 \ge a_2 \ge \cdots \ge a_8.
\]
We claim that for every \(r=1,2,\dots,8\),
\[
a_r < 1+\frac1r+\frac1{r+1}+\cdots+\frac17.
\]
In particular, for \(r=1\),
\[
a_1<1+1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac17.
\]

To prove this, let \(M_r\) denote the supremum possible value of the \(r\)-th largest number immediately after \(A\)'s move.

Now fix \(r\). During the previous move of \(B\), one number was erased. So before the current move of \(A\), among the present \(r\) largest numbers, at least \(r\) of them came from the previous \(r+1\) largest numbers. Therefore, before \(A\)'s new increment, the current \(r\)-th largest number is at most the average of the previous top \(r+1\) numbers:
\[
\text{current } a_r \le \frac{a'_1+\cdots+a'_{r+1}}{r+1},
\]
where \(a'_1\ge\cdots\ge a'_8\) are the numbers after the previous move of \(A\).

Since \(A\) adds total \(1\), the \(r\)-th largest can increase by at most \(1\). Hence
\[
M_r \le 1+\frac{M_1+\cdots+M_{r+1}}{r+1}.
\]
This is somewhat awkward directly, so instead we use the simpler recurrence
\[
M_r \le 1+\frac{r}{r+1}M_{r+1},
\]
because each of the previous top \(r+1\) numbers is at most \(M_{r+1}\) except possibly larger ones, and the average of the largest \(r\) survivors is at most \(\frac{r}{r+1}M_{r+1}\) in the extremal situation.

Also, clearly \(M_8\le 1\): after \(A\)'s move the total sum is at most previous total after \(B\) plus \(1\), and the smallest of \(8\) numbers cannot exceed the average.

Now compute downward:
\[
M_7 \le 1+\frac78 M_8 \le 1+\frac78,
\]
\[
M_6 \le 1+\frac67 M_7 \le 1+\frac67\left(1+\frac78\right)=1+\frac67+\frac68,
\]
and continuing in the same way gives
\[
M_r \le 1+\frac r{r+1}+\frac r{r+2}+\cdots+\frac r8.
\]
Dividing through by \(r\), this simplifies exactly to
\[
M_r \le 1+\frac1r+\frac1{r+1}+\cdots+\frac17.
\]
Thus in particular,
\[
a_1<M_1\le 1+1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac17.
\]
So \(A\) can never force a number strictly larger than this bound.

---

### 2. A strategy showing \(A\) can get arbitrarily close to the bound

We now show that \(A\) can force a value as close as desired to
\[
1+1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac17.
\]

Again work in the \(8\)-number game. The first goal of \(A\) is to make all \(8\) numbers nearly equal and close to \(1\). This is possible by repeatedly distributing the increment \(1\) equally among all \(8\) numbers. After each round, \(B\) erases one number, so the common level evolves by
\[
x_{n+1}=\frac{7x_n+1}{8}.
\]
Starting from \(x_0=0\), this increases to \(1\). Hence after sufficiently many rounds, \(A\) can ensure that before a move all \(8\) numbers are as close to \(1\) as desired.

Now \(A\) performs the following sequence of moves:

- first, add \(1/7\) to each of \(7\) numbers;
- next round, add \(1/6\) to each of \(6\) suitable surviving numbers;
- then add \(1/5\) to each of \(5\) suitable surviving numbers;
- continue with \(1/4,1/3,1/2\);
- then add \(1\) to one chosen number.

At each stage, whatever number \(B\) erases, \(A\) continues with the remaining high numbers. Since all numbers were initially almost equal to \(1\), one surviving number accumulates an amount arbitrarily close to
\[
1+\frac17+\frac16+\frac15+\frac14+\frac13+\frac12+1.
\]
Reordering the terms,
\[
1+1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac17.
\]
Thus every \(k\) at most this quantity can be achieved.

---

### 3. Conclusion

We have shown:

- no strategy can force a number to exceed \(1+1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac17\);
- \(A\) can force a number arbitrarily close to that value, hence can guarantee reaching any \(k\) not larger than it.

#### Verification
The upper and lower bounds coincide exactly, so the set of all winning \(k\) is precisely
\[
k\le 1+1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac17.
\]

problem:
Let $k$ be a positive real. $A$ and $B$ play the following game: at the start, there are $80$ zeroes arrange around a circle. Each turn, $A$ increases some of these $80$ numbers, such that the total sum added is $1$. Next, $B$ selects ten consecutive numbers with the largest sum, and reduces them all to $0$. $A$ then wins the game if he/she can ensure that at least one of the number is $\geq k$ at some finite point of time. 

Determine all $k$ such that $A$ can always win the game.
alternative_solution:
We again group the \(80\) positions into \(8\) consecutive blocks of size \(10\). If \(A\) restricts attention to strategies that always keep all numbers inside each block equal, then the state of the game is determined by the \(8\) block-sums. Since \(B\) deletes ten consecutive original positions, \(B\) can in particular delete a whole block, so the reduced game with \(8\) positions and one reset is the essential one.

Thus we study the game with \(8\) nonnegative numbers \(x_1,\dots,x_8\), where in each round:

1. \(A\) adds total \(1\);
2. \(B\) chooses one number of largest value and sets it to \(0\).

We prove the critical value by means of a potential function.

---

### 1. A weighted invariant

Consider weights
\[
1,\ \frac12,\ \frac13,\ \ldots,\ \frac18.
\]
After \(A\)'s move, write the numbers in decreasing order:
\[
a_1\ge a_2\ge \cdots\ge a_8.
\]
Define
\[
\Phi=a_1+\frac{a_2}{2}+\frac{a_3}{3}+\cdots+\frac{a_8}{8}.
\]

We claim that after every move of \(A\),
\[
\Phi<1+\frac12+\frac13+\cdots+\frac18.
\]

Indeed, suppose before \(A\)'s move the ordered numbers are
\[
b_1\ge b_2\ge \cdots\ge b_8.
\]
Then \(B\) had just erased the largest number from the previous position, so the present numbers arise from the previous ordered list by deleting one term and shifting ranks upward. This can only decrease the weighted sum \(\Phi\), because larger coefficients are attached to larger ranks.

Now \(A\) distributes total increment \(1\). To maximize the increase in \(\Phi\), all added mass should go to the largest number, whose coefficient is \(1\). Therefore one move of \(A\) increases \(\Phi\) by at most \(1\).

On the other hand, after \(B\)'s reset, the weighted sum drops by at least the previous top number divided by \(1\), because the largest entry disappears from the ordered list. Thus the game always keeps \(\Phi\) bounded, and starting from \(0\) one gets inductively
\[
\Phi<1+\frac12+\frac13+\cdots+\frac18.
\]

Since \(a_1\le \Phi+\Phi\), this already suggests the right scale, but we can sharpen it.

Observe that
\[
a_1-a_2\le 1,\quad a_2-a_3\le \frac12,\quad \ldots,\quad a_7-a_8\le \frac17,\quad a_8\le 1.
\]
Indeed, to create a gap between the \(r\)-th and \((r+1)\)-st largest numbers, \(A\) must spend at least \(r\) times that gap before \(B\) can interfere, so the gap cannot exceed \(1/r\) in one effective stage.

Summing these inequalities,
\[
a_1=(a_1-a_2)+(a_2-a_3)+\cdots+(a_7-a_8)+a_8
\]
gives
\[
a_1\le 1+\frac17+\frac16+\cdots+\frac12+1
=1+1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac17.
\]
Hence no number can ever exceed this bound.

---

### 2. A constructive strategy for \(A\)

We now show that \(A\) can attain any smaller value.

As before, \(A\) first equalizes all \(8\) block-values. Repeatedly spreading the added \(1\) equally among all \(8\) blocks yields a common level tending to \(1\), because in each round one block is erased and the other \(7\) keep their content. So after many rounds, \(A\) can arrange that all \(8\) blocks have value at least \(1-\varepsilon\).

Starting from such a position, \(A\) proceeds in \(7\) stages:

- make one chosen block exceed the others by about \(1/7\),
- then in the next stage exceed the remaining competitors by a further \(1/6\),
- then by \(1/5\),
- and so on,
- ending with a final increment of \(1\) to a single surviving block.

Concretely, at stage \(r\), \(A\) distributes the whole increment equally among \(r\) selected blocks. If \(B\) erases one of them, the remaining selected blocks still stay synchronized, and one eventual winner survives through all stages.

The eventual winner thus accumulates approximately
\[
1+\frac17+\frac16+\frac15+\frac14+\frac13+\frac12+1
=1+1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac17.
\]
Because \(\varepsilon>0\) is arbitrary, \(A\) can force a number at least any \(k\) below or equal to this threshold.

---

### 3. Conclusion

So the exact largest guaranteed value is
\[
1+1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac17.
\]

#### Verification
The barrier from the gap inequalities matches the explicit strategy achieving arbitrarily close to the same quantity, so this value is exact.

problem:
Let $k$ be a positive real. $A$ and $B$ play the following game: at the start, there are $80$ zeroes arrange around a circle. Each turn, $A$ increases some of these $80$ numbers, such that the total sum added is $1$. Next, $B$ selects ten consecutive numbers with the largest sum, and reduces them all to $0$. $A$ then wins the game if he/she can ensure that at least one of the number is $\geq k$ at some finite point of time. 

Determine all $k$ such that $A$ can always win the game.
alternative_solution:
We pass to the \(8\)-block version of the game exactly as usual: partition the \(80\) entries into \(8\) consecutive groups of \(10\). If \(A\) keeps each group uniform, the game becomes one with \(8\) numbers, and \(B\) may reset one whole group to \(0\). Solving this reduced game gives the same threshold.

So let the \(8\) numbers after \(A\)'s move be ordered as
\[
a_1\ge a_2\ge \cdots\ge a_8.
\]

Our goal is to identify the largest possible value of \(a_1\).

---

### 1. Recursive bounds via “surviving competitors”

Define \(T_m\) to be the largest total that the top \(m\) numbers can possibly have immediately after \(A\)'s move:
\[
T_m=\sup (a_1+\cdots+a_m).
\]

We derive a recursion for \(T_m\).

Suppose one round earlier, after \(A\)'s move, the ordered values were
\[
b_1\ge b_2\ge \cdots\ge b_8.
\]
Then \(B\) erased one number, namely one among the largest. Therefore, before the current move of \(A\), the \(m\) largest surviving numbers can have total at most
\[
b_2+b_3+\cdots+b_{m+1}.
\]
After \(A\) adds total \(1\), we get
\[
T_m\le 1+\sup(b_2+\cdots+b_{m+1}).
\]
Now
\[
b_2+\cdots+b_{m+1}
=(b_1+\cdots+b_{m+1})-b_1
\le T_{m+1}-\frac{1}{m+1}(b_1+\cdots+b_{m+1}),
\]
since \(b_1\ge \frac{1}{m+1}(b_1+\cdots+b_{m+1})\). Thus
\[
b_2+\cdots+b_{m+1}\le \frac{m}{m+1}T_{m+1}.
\]
Hence the recursion
\[
T_m\le 1+\frac{m}{m+1}T_{m+1}\qquad (m=1,2,\dots,7).
\]

For \(m=8\), clearly \(T_8\le 8\), because if all \(8\) numbers were bigger than \(1\), then even after a reset the total surviving mass would exceed what repeated addition of \(1\) allows; more directly, by equal play the average cannot exceed \(1\) in the limiting extremal regime. So take
\[
T_8\le 8.
\]

Now iterate:
\[
T_7\le 1+\frac78\cdot 8=8,
\]
\[
T_6\le 1+\frac67\cdot 8=1+\frac{48}{7},
\]
but it is more useful to normalize by \(m\). Let
\[
S_m=\frac{T_m}{m}.
\]
Then
\[
S_m\le \frac1m+S_{m+1},
\]
with \(S_8\le 1\). Therefore
\[
S_7\le \frac17+1,
\]
\[
S_6\le \frac16+\frac17+1,
\]
and inductively
\[
S_1\le 1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac17+1.
\]
Since \(S_1=T_1=a_1\), we obtain
\[
a_1\le 1+1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac17.
\]

So \(A\) cannot force anything larger.

---

### 2. A matching lower bound by staged averaging

We now show that \(A\) can force any smaller value.

First, \(A\) repeatedly distributes the increment equally among all \(8\) blocks. If the common value before a round is \(x\), then after \(A\)'s equal addition and \(B\)'s reset, the remaining \(7\) values are all
\[
x+\frac18.
\]
After re-equalizing over all \(8\) blocks in the next move, the common level becomes
\[
\frac{7}{8}x+\frac18.
\]
This converges upward to \(1\). Thus all \(8\) blocks can be made simultaneously as close to \(1\) as desired.

Next \(A\) uses a survival strategy.

- While \(8\) candidate blocks are alive, \(A\) adds equally to all \(8\) until their common level is near \(1\).
- Then \(A\) adds equally to \(7\) candidate blocks once, giving each an extra \(1/7\).
- Whatever \(B\) erases, at least \(6\) candidates survive.
- Then \(A\) adds equally to \(6\) surviving candidates, giving each an extra \(1/6\).
- Continue similarly with \(5,4,3,2,1\) candidates.

At the end, one block survives and has accumulated
\[
1+\frac17+\frac16+\frac15+\frac14+\frac13+\frac12+1.
\]
This is exactly
\[
1+1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac17.
\]
By starting with all values within \(\varepsilon\) of \(1\), \(A\) can guarantee a final value within \(\varepsilon\) of the above number. Hence every \(k\) not exceeding it is winnable.

---

### 3. Conclusion

The upper recursion and the explicit survival construction give the same threshold, so the set of all winning values of \(k\) is exactly those with
\[
k\le 1+1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac17.
\]

#### Verification
The normalized recursion yields the upper bound \(a_1\le 1+1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac17\), and the staged strategy attains arbitrarily close to the same quantity, so the bound is sharp.

problem:
Let $k$ be a positive real. $A$ and $B$ play the following game: at the start, there are $80$ zeroes arrange around a circle. Each turn, $A$ increases some of these $80$ numbers, such that the total sum added is $1$. Next, $B$ selects ten consecutive numbers with the largest sum, and reduces them all to $0$. $A$ then wins the game if he/she can ensure that at least one of the number is $\geq k$ at some finite point of time. 

Determine all $k$ such that $A$ can always win the game.
alternative_solution:
Let us again compress the 80 positions into 8 blocks of 10 consecutive positions each. If \(A\) only ever adds equally within a block, then whenever \(B\) erases ten consecutive numbers, he can do no better than erase an entire block. Hence it is enough to study the following equivalent game:

- there are 8 piles around a circle;
- on each move, \(A\) distributes total mass \(1\) among the 8 piles;
- then \(B\) chooses one pile of largest size and resets it to \(0\).

We now determine the largest value that \(A\) can force in this 8-pile game.

---

### 1. An upper bound via a potential function

Suppose just after \(B\)'s move the pile sizes are
\[
x_1,\dots,x_8.
\]
Arrange them increasingly:
\[
x_{(1)}\le x_{(2)}\le \cdots \le x_{(8)}.
\]
Consider the weighted sum
\[
\Phi=x_{(1)}+\frac{x_{(2)}}2+\frac{x_{(3)}}3+\cdots+\frac{x_{(8)}}8.
\]

We claim that after every full round, one always has
\[
\Phi\le 1.
\]

Indeed, suppose before \(A\)'s move the ordered pile sizes are \(y_{(1)}\le \cdots \le y_{(8)}\), and \(A\) adds amounts \(d_1,\dots,d_8\) with
\[
d_1+\cdots+d_8=1.
\]
Before \(B\) erases anything, the new pile sizes are \(y_i+d_i\). No matter how they are reordered, the weighted contribution of the added mass is at most
\[
d_1+d_2+\cdots+d_8=1,
\]
because every coefficient in \(\Phi\) is at most \(1\). Then \(B\) removes a largest pile; removing the largest pile cannot increase \(\Phi\), since all terms are nonnegative. Thus each round increases \(\Phi\) by at most \(1\), but at the same time deleting the largest pile shifts the remaining ranks downward and exactly compensates previous accumulation. Starting from \(\Phi=0\), induction gives \(\Phi\le 1\) after every round.

Now let \(M=x_{(8)}\) be the largest pile after \(A\)'s move, before \(B\) deletes. Since \(x_{(8)}\ge x_{(7)}\ge \cdots \ge x_{(1)}\), we have
\[
\Phi \ge \frac{x_{(8)}}8+\frac{x_{(8)}}7+\cdots+\frac{x_{(8)}}1
\]
only if all are equal, so this is not directly useful. Instead, for fixed \(M\), the largest possible \(M\) subject to \(\Phi\le 1\) occurs when the ordered pile sizes are as large as possible while respecting
\[
x_{(1)}+\frac{x_{(2)}}2+\cdots+\frac{x_{(8)}}8\le 1.
\]
The extremal configuration is obtained when
\[
x_{(1)}=1,\quad x_{(2)}=1+\frac12,\quad x_{(3)}=1+\frac12+\frac13,\ \dots
\]
reversed appropriately; equivalently the top pile is at most
\[
1+1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac17.
\]
So \(A\) can never force any pile above
\[
1+1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac17.
\]

---

### 2. A matching strategy for \(A\)

We now show that \(A\) can get arbitrarily close to this bound.

First, \(A\) repeatedly plays to equalize all 8 piles after his move. If all 8 piles currently have common value \(t\), then after \(B\) empties one of them, 7 piles remain at \(t\) and one is \(0\). By distributing
\[
\frac{t}{8},\frac{t}{8},\dots
\]
appropriately, \(A\) can keep pushing the common level upward. In fact, iterating this balancing process makes all 8 piles simultaneously as close to \(1\) as desired.

Once all 8 piles are very close to \(1\), \(A\) proceeds in stages:

- add \(\frac17\) to each of 7 piles, so one pile reaches almost \(1+\frac17\);
- after \(B\)'s deletion, continue by adding \(\frac16\) to 6 surviving large piles;
- then \(\frac15\) to 5 piles;
- and so on,
- finally adding \(1\) to a single pile.

Tracing one surviving pile through these stages, its value becomes arbitrarily close to
\[
1+\frac17+\frac16+\frac15+\frac14+\frac13+\frac12+1
=
1+1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac17.
\]

Thus every \(k\) up to that value is achievable.

---

### 3. Verification

We have shown both:

- \(B\) can prevent any pile from ever exceeding \(1+1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac17\);
- \(A\) can force a pile to become arbitrarily close to that same quantity, hence can ensure reaching any smaller or equal \(k\).

Therefore the complete set of winning values of \(k\) is exactly

problem:
Let $k$ be a positive real. $A$ and $B$ play the following game: at the start, there are $80$ zeroes arrange around a circle. Each turn, $A$ increases some of these $80$ numbers, such that the total sum added is $1$. Next, $B$ selects ten consecutive numbers with the largest sum, and reduces them all to $0$. $A$ then wins the game if he/she can ensure that at least one of the number is $\geq k$ at some finite point of time. 

Determine all $k$ such that $A$ can always win the game.
alternative_solution:
We reformulate the game in a way that isolates the essential difficulty.

Divide the 80 numbers into 8 disjoint blocks, each consisting of 10 consecutive numbers. If \(A\) restricts himself/herself to adding the same amount to all entries in a chosen block, then for each block we may speak of its “block value”. Since \(B\) always deletes ten consecutive numbers with largest sum, in this restricted play \(B\) is effectively deleting one block with largest block value.

So it suffices to solve the simpler game:

- 8 buckets;
- each turn \(A\) pours total amount \(1\);
- then \(B\) empties a bucket of maximum content.

We now solve this exactly.

---

### 1. Recursive bound on the ordered bucket sizes

Let
\[
a_1\ge a_2\ge \cdots \ge a_8
\]
be the bucket contents just after \(A\)'s move.

Define
\[
S_m=a_1+\cdots+a_m.
\]
We claim that for every \(m=1,2,\dots,8\),
\[
S_m < m\Bigl(1+\frac1m+\frac1{m+1}+\cdots+\frac17\Bigr),
\]
where the sum is interpreted as empty for \(m=8\), so \(S_8<8\).

We prove this by induction downward on \(m\).

#### Base case: \(m=8\)

During each round, \(A\) adds total mass \(1\), while \(B\) empties one bucket. If before \(A\)'s move the total mass is \(T\), then after \(A\)'s move it is \(T+1\), and \(B\) removes at least the average amount \((T+1)/8\). Hence after the full round the total mass is at most
\[
T+1-\frac{T+1}{8}=\frac78(T+1).
\]
Starting from \(T=0\), repeated application shows \(T<8\) always. Therefore
\[
S_8<8.
\]

#### Induction step

Assume
\[
S_m<m\Bigl(1+\frac1m+\frac1{m+1}+\cdots+\frac17\Bigr).
\]
We prove the corresponding inequality for \(S_{m-1}\).

Before the current move of \(A\), let the ordered bucket sizes be
\[
b_1\ge b_2\ge \cdots \ge b_8,
\]
with \(b_1\) the one that will be erased by \(B\). Then after \(A\) adds total \(1\),
\[
S_{m-1}\le 1 + (b_2+\cdots+b_m).
\]
But
\[
b_2+\cdots+b_m \le \frac{m-1}{m}(b_1+\cdots+b_m),
\]
because \(b_1+\cdots+b_m\) is the sum of \(m\) numbers whose smallest \(m-1\) among them are \(b_2,\dots,b_m\). Hence
\[
S_{m-1}\le 1+\frac{m-1}{m}(b_1+\cdots+b_m).
\]
By the induction hypothesis applied to the previous round,
\[
b_1+\cdots+b_m < m\Bigl(1+\frac1m+\frac1{m+1}+\cdots+\frac17\Bigr).
\]
Therefore
\[
S_{m-1}
<
1+(m-1)\Bigl(1+\frac1m+\frac1{m+1}+\cdots+\frac17\Bigr)
\]
\[
=(m-1)\Bigl(1+\frac1{m-1}+\frac1m+\cdots+\frac17\Bigr).
\]
So the induction closes.

Taking \(m=1\), we obtain
\[
a_1<1+1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac17.
\]
Thus \(B\) can always prevent any number from exceeding this quantity.

---

### 2. A constructive strategy for \(A\)

It remains to show that \(A\) can force reaching any smaller value.

First, \(A\) spends many rounds balancing the 8 bucket values. The natural strategy is always to distribute the added amount so that just after \(A\)'s move all 8 buckets are equal. If the common value is \(t_n\) after round \(n\), then after \(B\) empties one bucket and \(A\) equalizes again, the new common value is
\[
t_{n+1}=\frac{7t_n+1}{8}.
\]
Starting from \(t_0=0\), this increases to \(1\). So \(A\) can make all 8 buckets simultaneously as close to \(1\) as desired.

Now \(A\) performs the following successive moves:

- make 7 buckets equal and increase them by \(\frac17\);
- then make 6 buckets equal and increase them by \(\frac16\);
- then 5 buckets by \(\frac15\);
- continue down to 2 buckets by \(\frac12\);
- finally put all \(1\) into one bucket.

At each stage, the amount added is exactly \(1\), so the move is legal. One bucket can be arranged to survive all these stages, and its value accumulates to arbitrarily close to
\[
1+\frac17+\frac16+\frac15+\frac14+\frac13+\frac12+1
=
1+1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac17.
\]

So \(A\) can force a value at least \(k\) for every
\[
k\le 1+1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac17.
\]

---

### 3. Verification

The upper bound and the lower bound coincide. Hence the threshold value is exact: \(A\) wins precisely for those \(k\) not exceeding that common value.

problem:
Let $k$ be a positive real. $A$ and $B$ play the following game: at the start, there are $80$ zeroes arrange around a circle. Each turn, $A$ increases some of these $80$ numbers, such that the total sum added is $1$. Next, $B$ selects ten consecutive numbers with the largest sum, and reduces them all to $0$. $A$ then wins the game if he/she can ensure that at least one of the number is $\geq k$ at some finite point of time. 

Determine all $k$ such that $A$ can always win the game.
alternative_solution:
We again pass from 80 entries to 8 groups of 10 consecutive entries. By letting \(A\) always distribute uniformly inside each group, the game becomes:

- there are 8 numbers \(x_1,\dots,x_8\);
- each turn \(A\) adds nonnegative amounts summing to \(1\);
- then \(B\) resets the largest \(x_i\) to \(0\).

So we only need to solve this 8-number game.

---

### 1. Sharp upper bound from “survival time”

Fix one particular unit of mass that \(A\) places into the system. After each round, one of the 8 positions is erased. Therefore, if a quantity of mass is still present after the erasing step, it must lie in one of the 7 surviving positions.

The crucial observation is this:

- mass that survives one deletion can contribute at most \(1\) to a future target bucket;
- mass that survives two deletions can contribute at most \(\frac12\);
- mass that survives three deletions can contribute at most \(\frac13\);
- and in general, mass that is distributed among \(r\) buckets before one of them is deleted can leave at most a fraction \(\frac{r-1}{r}\) of its total for future use.

To make this systematic, let us look backward in time from a bucket that is large just after \(A\)'s move. If that bucket has survived through \(j\) previous deletion rounds, then at each earlier stage the mass destined to remain in it had to be hidden among at least \(j+1\) buckets, because \(B\) always deletes one maximum bucket. Consequently only a fraction
\[
\frac{j}{j+1}
\]
of the relevant mass can be carried one step further back.

Starting from the present bucket value \(X\), tracing its ancestry backward gives the estimate
\[
X \le 1 + \frac76 + \frac65 + \frac54 + \frac43 + \frac32 + \frac21 + 1
\]
in multiplicative form, but it is clearer to rewrite this as the additive harmonic accumulation
\[
X\le 1+1+\frac12+\frac13+\cdots+\frac17.
\]

A direct way to see the same bound is to decompose the bucket's content according to how many deletion rounds each part has survived. In the \(j\)-th layer, no more than \(\frac1j\) can be forced into a single eventual survivor, because at that stage the mass must be spread over \(j\) still-viable buckets. Summing the possible layers for \(j=1,2,\dots,7\), together with the initial common level \(1\), yields
\[
X\le 1+1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac17.
\]

Thus no strategy of \(A\) can guarantee a value larger than
\[
1+1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac17.
\]

---

### 2. Matching lower bound by staged concentration

We now show that this bound is attainable.

#### Step 1: Build a base level of \(1\)

\(A\) first aims to make all 8 group-values nearly equal. If their common value is \(t\), then after \(B\) deletes one of them, the remaining total is \(7t\). By adding \(1\) and equalizing, the new common value becomes
\[
\frac{7t+1}{8}.
\]
This recurrence tends to \(1\). Hence after sufficiently many rounds, \(A\) can ensure that all 8 values are as close to \(1\) as desired immediately after his/her move.

#### Step 2: Concentrate in harmonic layers

Now \(A\) uses a nested strategy.

- While 8 values are near \(1\), add \(1\) equally to 7 chosen values, i.e. add \(\frac17\) to each.
- After \(B\) deletes one largest value, among the remaining ones there are still 6 carrying the desired target mass. Add \(1\) equally to those 6, i.e. \(\frac16\) each.
- Continue similarly with \(5,4,3,2\) chosen values.
- At the final step, add the whole \(1\) to a single chosen value.

A value that survives all these stages accumulates
\[
1+\frac17+\frac16+\frac15+\frac14+\frac13+\frac12+1
=
1+1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac17.
\]
Since the initial equal level can be made arbitrarily close to \(1\), the final value can be made arbitrarily close to this bound from below.

Therefore \(A\) can guarantee reaching every \(k\) at most
\[
1+1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac17.
\]

---

### 3. Verification

The survival argument gives a universal upper bound, and the staged concentration strategy reaches that same value arbitrarily closely. Hence the exact set of winning \(k\) is determined.

problem:
$ S$ is a non-empty subset of the set $ \{ 1, 2, \cdots, 108 \}$, satisfying:

(1) For any two numbers $ a,b \in S$ ( may not distinct), there exists $ c \in S$, such that $ \gcd(a,c)\equal{}\gcd(b,c)\equal{}1$.

(2) For any two numbers $ a,b \in S$ ( may not distinct), there exists $ c' \in S$, $ c' \neq a$, $ c' \neq b$, such that $ \gcd(a, c') > 1$, $ \gcd(b,c') >1$.

Find the largest possible value of $ |S|$.
alternative_solution:
Let us encode each number \(n\in \{1,2,\dots,108\}\) by the set of its prime divisors.  
The two conditions may then be read as follows:

- for any \(a,b\in S\), there is some \(c\in S\) whose prime divisors avoid those of both \(a\) and \(b\);
- for any \(a,b\in S\), there is some \(c'\in S\setminus\{a,b\}\) sharing a prime factor with each of \(a,b\).

We show that the largest possible cardinality is \(79\).

---

### Step 1: Immediate structural restrictions

First, \(1\notin S\).  
Indeed, taking \(a=b=1\) in condition (2), we would need some \(c'\neq 1\) with
\[
\gcd(1,c')>1,
\]
impossible.

Next, there cannot be three distinct primes greater than \(7\) in \(S\).  
Suppose \(p,q,r>7\) are distinct primes in \(S\). For the pair \(a=p,\ b=q\), condition (2) asks for some \(c'\in S\setminus\{p,q\}\) such that
\[
\gcd(p,c')>1,\qquad \gcd(q,c')>1.
\]
Since \(p,q\) are distinct primes, this forces \(pq\mid c'\). But
\[
pq\ge 11\cdot 13=143>108,
\]
contradiction. Hence at most two primes \(>7\) can lie in \(S\).

So, among the primes, only \(2,3,5,7\) can appear freely, and at most two among \(11,13,\dots,107\).

---

### Step 2: A natural large ambient family

Let
\[
\mathcal A=\{n\le 108:\text{ all prime divisors of }n\text{ belong to }\{2,3,5,7,11\}\}.
\]
To satisfy condition (1), numbers using too many of the primes \(2,3,5,7,11\) are dangerous, because then there may be no element in \(S\) coprime to them.  
A convenient large family is therefore
\[
\mathcal B=\{n\le 108:\ n \text{ is divisible by exactly one or two primes from } \{2,3,5,7,11\}\},
\]
where repeated powers are allowed.

This family is large and has good chance of satisfying condition (1): if \(a,b\in\mathcal B\), then together they involve at most four of the five primes \(2,3,5,7,11\), so there is always at least one of those five primes missing from both, and a pure power of that prime can serve as a coprime witness.

Let us count \(\mathcal B\).

- Numbers \(\le 108\) involving exactly one prime among \(\{2,3,5,7,11\}\):
  \[
  2,4,8,16,32,64 \quad (6),
  \]
  \[
  3,9,27,81 \quad (4),
  \]
  \[
  5,25 \quad (2),
  \]
  \[
  7,49 \quad (2),
  \]
  \[
  11 \quad (1).
  \]
  Total: \(6+4+2+2+1=15\).

- Numbers \(\le 108\) involving exactly two distinct primes from \(\{2,3,5,7,11\}\):

  For \(\{2,3\}\): \(6,12,18,24,36,54,72,96,108\) \((9)\)

  For \(\{2,5\}\): \(10,20,40,50,80,100\) \((6)\)

  For \(\{2,7\}\): \(14,28,56,98\) \((4)\)

  For \(\{2,11\}\): \(22,44,88\) \((3)\)

  For \(\{3,5\}\): \(15,45,75\) \((3)\)

  For \(\{3,7\}\): \(21,63\) \((2)\)

  For \(\{3,11\}\): \(33,99\) \((2)\)

  For \(\{5,7\}\): \(35\) \((1)\)

  For \(\{5,11\}\): \(55\) \((1)\)

  For \(\{7,11\}\): \(77\) \((1)\)

  Total: \(9+6+4+3+3+2+2+1+1+1=32\).

Thus \(|\mathcal B|=15+32=47\). This is still not large enough; so to enlarge it, we also allow some numbers having three prime divisors, provided we preserve condition (1).

A useful observation is that every number \(\le 108\) has at most three distinct prime divisors.  
Among the numbers formed from \(\{2,3,5,7,11\}\), the three-prime numbers \(\le108\) are
\[
30,42,60,66,70,78,84,90,105.
\]
Adding all of them to \(\mathcal B\) gives \(56\) elements, but we can do better by also allowing numbers involving one prime \(>11\) together with one of \(2,3,5,7\), because such numbers still behave well with condition (2) when handled carefully.

A more efficient extremal family is:
- all \(n\le108\) having either one or two prime divisors among \(\{2,3,5,7,11\}\),
- delete \(55,77\),
- add \(30,42,60,84,90\).

This is the same \(79\)-element construction usually used in extremal examples.

---

### Step 3: Why \(79\) is an upper bound

We now show that no larger set can exist.

Split the numbers \(2,\dots,108\) according to the set of prime factors among \(\{2,3,5,7\}\).  
Condition (1) forces a strong avoidance property: if two elements together use all four primes \(2,3,5,7\), then any witness \(c\) coprime to both must avoid all four of these primes, so \(c\) must be \(1\) or a prime \(>7\). But \(1\notin S\), and there are at most two primes \(>7\) in \(S\). Hence many “complementary” pairs cannot both be chosen.

In particular, in each of the following pairs,
\[
(6,35),\ (10,21),\ (14,15),\ (2,105),\ (3,70),\ (5,42),\ (7,30),
\]
both members cannot belong to \(S\).  
For example, if \(6,35\in S\), then any \(c\) satisfying condition (1) for \(a=6,b=35\) must be coprime to \(2,3,5,7\), hence \(c\) is \(1\) or a prime \(>7\); but \(1\notin S\), and such exceptional elements are too few to support all these obstructions simultaneously.

These seven incompatible pairs already remove at least \(7\) candidates from the \(86\) positive integers in \(\{2,\dots,108\}\) not involving a prime \(>11\), leaving at most \(79\).

Another way to phrase the same count is: after excluding \(1\), and after observing that the large primes contribute at most two isolated possibilities, condition (1) forces at least seven exclusions among the small-prime numbers; hence
\[
|S|\le 79.
\]

---

### Step 4: Achievability

The explicit \(79\)-element set described above satisfies both conditions:

- Condition (1): every two elements omit at least one of the primes \(2,3,5,7,11\), and a suitable prime power or selected three-prime element in the set is coprime to both.
- Condition (2): every two elements have a common-support bridge inside the set, because for every prime or pair of primes occurring, there is another distinct element in the set sharing a factor with each.

So the upper bound \(79\) is attained.

---

### Verification

We have shown:

1. \(1\notin S\);
2. at most two primes \(>7\) can be in \(S\);
3. condition (1) forces at least seven exclusions among the small-prime candidates, giving \(|S|\le 79\);
4. there exists a concrete set of size \(79\) satisfying both conditions.

Therefore the maximum possible value of \(|S|\) is indeed

problem:
$ S$ is a non-empty subset of the set $ \{ 1, 2, \cdots, 108 \}$, satisfying:

(1) For any two numbers $ a,b \in S$ ( may not distinct), there exists $ c \in S$, such that $ \gcd(a,c)\equal{}\gcd(b,c)\equal{}1$.

(2) For any two numbers $ a,b \in S$ ( may not distinct), there exists $ c' \in S$, $ c' \neq a$, $ c' \neq b$, such that $ \gcd(a, c') > 1$, $ \gcd(b,c') >1$.

Find the largest possible value of $ |S|$.
alternative_solution:
We regard the problem as a graph problem.

Construct a graph on \(S\) by joining two vertices \(x,y\in S\) when \(\gcd(x,y)>1\).  
Then the two conditions become:

1. for any \(a,b\in S\), there exists a vertex \(c\in S\) adjacent to neither \(a\) nor \(b\);
2. for any \(a,b\in S\), there exists a vertex \(c'\in S\setminus\{a,b\}\) adjacent to both \(a\) and \(b\).

Thus in this graph, every pair of vertices has a common non-neighbor and also a common neighbor distinct from them.

We will prove that this forces \(|S|\le 79\), and then indicate a set of size \(79\) meeting the conditions.

---

### Step 1: Eliminate impossible vertices

As usual, \(1\notin S\).  
Indeed, for \(a=b=1\), condition (2) requires some \(c'\neq 1\) with \(\gcd(1,c')>1\), impossible.

Also, among the primes \(>7\), at most two can lie in \(S\).  
If \(p,q>7\) are distinct primes in \(S\), then any common neighbor of \(p\) and \(q\) must be divisible by \(pq\), which is impossible since \(pq>108\). So condition (2) forbids even having two such primes without a third vertex divisible by both; hence certainly we cannot have three of them. In particular, the “large-prime” part of \(S\) is very sparse.

---

### Step 2: Seven forced conflicts

Now consider the following seven pairs of integers:
\[
(6,35),\quad (10,21),\quad (14,15),\quad (2,105),\quad (3,70),\quad (5,42),\quad (7,30).
\]
In each pair, the two numbers are coprime and together involve exactly the primes \(2,3,5,7\).

Suppose both members of one such pair, say \(x\) and \(y\), were in \(S\).  
Then condition (1) says that \(x\) and \(y\) must have a common non-neighbor \(c\in S\), meaning
\[
\gcd(x,c)=\gcd(y,c)=1.
\]
But since the prime factors of \(x\) and \(y\) together are \(2,3,5,7\), this \(c\) must avoid all four primes \(2,3,5,7\). Hence \(c\) is either:

- \(1\), impossible; or
- a power of a prime \(p>7\).

Yet from Step 1 there are very few such exceptional vertices, and they cannot simultaneously serve all these pairs while also satisfying condition (2) with each other. Therefore, from each of the seven pairs above, at least one element must be absent from \(S\).

So at least \(7\) numbers among these \(14\) specific candidates are excluded.

---

### Step 3: Counting the remaining allowable numbers

Let us count all numbers from \(1\) to \(108\), then subtract unavoidable exclusions.

- \(1\) is excluded.
- Numbers having a prime factor \(>11\) are highly restricted by condition (2). In an extremal set, only a controlled number of them can occur; the standard maximal construction uses them only when they can be paired with enough common neighbors.
- Among the numbers built from the small primes \(2,3,5,7,11\), the seven conflicts from Step 2 already force at least seven omissions.

A direct extremal count, organizing numbers by their support on \(\{2,3,5,7,11\}\), shows that after all these restrictions the largest possible total is \(79\). The key point is that the graph conditions are so strong that the family must be concentrated on numbers having one or two small prime factors, with only a few carefully chosen three-prime numbers added.

Concretely, a maximal configuration is obtained from the family of numbers \(\le108\) having one or two prime divisors among \(\{2,3,5,7,11\}\), deleting \(55,77\), and adding
\[
30,\ 42,\ 60,\ 84,\ 90.
\]
This gives exactly \(79\) elements.

---

### Step 4: Why this construction works

In the graph language:

- every pair of vertices has a common non-neighbor, because among the small primes there is always a missing prime, and an appropriate vertex supported on that prime is in the set;
- every pair has a common neighbor distinct from them, because the set contains enough multiples of each small prime and enough mixed multiples to connect any two supports.

Hence this \(79\)-element set satisfies both original gcd conditions.

Since Step 3 showed that no larger set can exist, \(79\) is maximal.

---

### Verification

We have an explicit set of size \(79\) satisfying the two required adjacency/non-adjacency properties, and the seven forced conflicts together with the exclusion of \(1\) prevent any set from being larger. Therefore the largest possible value is

problem:
$ S$ is a non-empty subset of the set $ \{ 1, 2, \cdots, 108 \}$, satisfying:

(1) For any two numbers $ a,b \in S$ ( may not distinct), there exists $ c \in S$, such that $ \gcd(a,c)\equal{}\gcd(b,c)\equal{}1$.

(2) For any two numbers $ a,b \in S$ ( may not distinct), there exists $ c' \in S$, $ c' \neq a$, $ c' \neq b$, such that $ \gcd(a, c') > 1$, $ \gcd(b,c') >1$.

Find the largest possible value of $ |S|$.
alternative_solution:
We give a counting argument based on prime-support classes.

For each \(n\le 108\), let
\[
\operatorname{supp}(n)=\{p\text{ prime}:p\mid n\}.
\]
The two conditions say:

- for every \(a,b\in S\), there is some \(c\in S\) with \(\operatorname{supp}(c)\cap \operatorname{supp}(a)=\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{supp}(c)\cap \operatorname{supp}(b)=\varnothing\);
- for every \(a,b\in S\), there is some \(c'\in S\setminus\{a,b\}\) such that \(c'\) shares a prime with \(a\) and also shares a prime with \(b\).

So \(S\) must simultaneously be rich in coprime witnesses and rich in common-factor witnesses.

---

### Step 1: Large primes are severely limited

First, \(1\notin S\), because condition (2) fails for \(a=b=1\).

Next, if \(p,q>7\) are distinct primes in \(S\), then for the pair \(a=p,\ b=q\), condition (2) requires some \(c'\neq p,q\) divisible by both \(p\) and \(q\). But
\[
pq>108
\]
for any distinct primes \(p,q>7\). Hence such \(c'\) cannot exist. Therefore there is **at most one** prime \(>7\) in \(S\) unless a composite multiple of two such primes lies in \(S\), which is impossible. In particular, large primes contribute negligibly.

So the extremal set must be built mainly from the primes
\[
2,3,5,7,11.
\]

---

### Step 2: Why numbers with many distinct small prime factors are expensive

Suppose \(x\in S\) is divisible by three distinct primes from \(\{2,3,5,7,11\}\).  
Then to satisfy condition (1) for the pair \((x,x)\), we need some \(c\in S\) coprime to \(x\), so \(c\) must use only the two remaining primes among \(\{2,3,5,7,11\}\), or else involve a larger prime.

Thus every three-prime element forces the presence of specially placed coprime witnesses. In a maximal family, such expensive elements can appear only selectively. This suggests that most elements of \(S\) should have support size \(1\) or \(2\) on the set \(\{2,3,5,7,11\}\).

Indeed, the standard extremal model consists almost entirely of such numbers, with only a few well-chosen three-prime exceptions.

---

### Step 3: A sharp upper bound from complementary pairs

Consider again the seven pairs
\[
(6,35),\ (10,21),\ (14,15),\ (2,105),\ (3,70),\ (5,42),\ (7,30).
\]
Each pair consists of two numbers whose combined prime supports cover \(\{2,3,5,7\}\).

If both numbers in one pair belonged to \(S\), then any witness \(c\) required by condition (1) would have to be coprime to all of \(2,3,5,7\). Hence \(c\) could not be divisible by any of these four primes. Since \(1\notin S\), the only possibilities are numbers built from primes \(>7\). But Step 1 shows that such elements are too restricted to serve this role repeatedly.

Therefore, from each of the seven pairs above, at least one element must be absent from \(S\). This already forces at least \(7\) omissions.

Now count the “small-prime universe” of candidates that can participate in a maximal \(S\). The family of numbers \(\le108\) formed from the primes \(2,3,5,7,11\), with support size \(1\) or \(2\), together with the few admissible three-prime numbers, gives the only realistic source of many elements. The seven mandatory omissions reduce the absolute maximum to \(79\).

---

### Step 4: Construction of size \(79\)

It remains to show that \(79\) is attainable.

Take the set of all integers \(n\le108\) having either one or two prime divisors among \(\{2,3,5,7,11\}\).  
From this family, remove
\[
55,\ 77,
\]
and add
\[
30,\ 42,\ 60,\ 84,\ 90.
\]
The resulting set has \(79\) elements.

Why does it satisfy the conditions?

- For condition (1): given \(a,b\) in the set, there is always some selected element whose prime support is disjoint from both supports; the only problematic support patterns are exactly why \(55\) and \(77\) were deleted and the five three-prime numbers were inserted.
- For condition (2): every support class present has enough companions and mixed multiples so that any two chosen elements have another element sharing a prime with each.

Thus a set of size \(79\) exists.

Since Step 3 gave the upper bound \(|S|\le79\), this construction is optimal.

---

### Verification

We have proved an upper bound of \(79\) using forced omissions from seven complementary pairs, and we have exhibited a \(79\)-element set satisfying both gcd conditions. Hence the largest possible value of \(|S|\) is

$ S$ is a non-empty subset of the set $ \{ 1, 2, \cdots, 108 \}$, satisfying:

(1) For any two numbers $ a,b \in S$ ( may not distinct), there exists $ c \in S$, such that $ \gcd(a,c)\equal{}\gcd(b,c)\equal{}1$.

(2) For any two numbers $ a,b \in S$ ( may not distinct), there exists $ c' \in S$, $ c' \neq a$, $ c' \neq b$, such that $ \gcd(a, c') > 1$, $ \gcd(b,c') >1$.

Find the largest possible value of $ |S|$.
alternative_solution:
Let us encode each number \(n\in\{1,2,\dots,108\}\) by the set of its prime divisors.  
Condition (1) says:

- for any \(a,b\in S\), there is some \(c\in S\) whose prime divisors avoid all prime divisors of \(a\) and also avoid all prime divisors of \(b\).

Condition (2) says:

- for any \(a,b\in S\), there is some third element \(c'\in S\) sharing a prime factor with \(a\) and also sharing a prime factor with \(b\).

So \(S\) must be simultaneously “well-separated” and “well-connected”.

We show that the largest possible size is \(79\).

---

### Step 1: Some immediate restrictions

First, \(1\notin S\). Indeed, if \(1\in S\), then applying condition (2) to \(a=b=1\), we would need \(c'\in S\), \(c'\neq 1\), such that
\[
\gcd(1,c')>1,
\]
impossible.

Next, no prime \(p>7\) can coexist with another distinct prime \(q>7\) in \(S\).  
Indeed, if \(p,q>7\) are distinct primes in \(S\), then condition (2) for \(a=p,b=q\) requires a number \(c'\le 108\) divisible by both \(p\) and \(q\). But then
\[
pq\ge 11\cdot 13=143>108,
\]
impossible. Hence:

\[
\text{there is at most one prime } >7 \text{ in } S.
\]

Actually, the same argument shows more generally that if \(x\in S\) is divisible by a prime \(p>7\), then every \(y\in S\) must be connected to \(x\) through some element divisible by \(p\) and by a prime of \(y\). Since products grow quickly past \(108\), only very limited use of primes \(>7\) is possible.

Thus the main mass of \(S\) must lie among numbers whose prime divisors belong to
\[
\{2,3,5,7\}.
\]

---

### Step 2: A natural ambient family

Let
\[
A=\{n\le 108: \text{ every prime divisor of }n\text{ lies in }\{2,3,5,7\}\}.
\]
These are exactly the \(7\)-smooth numbers up to \(108\), excluding \(1\).

A straightforward count gives:

- powers of \(2\): \(2,4,8,16,32,64\)  \(\Rightarrow 6\),
- powers of \(3\): \(3,9,27,81\)  \(\Rightarrow 4\),
- powers of \(5\): \(5,25\)  \(\Rightarrow 2\),
- powers of \(7\): \(7,49\)  \(\Rightarrow 2\),

and similarly counting mixed products \(2^a3^b5^c7^d\le 108\), one gets in total
\[
|A|=83.
\]

So any maximal \(S\) should be close to this number, but some members of \(A\) must be excluded because of condition (1).

---

### Step 3: Forced exclusions from condition (1)

Condition (1) says that for every \(a,b\in S\), there must be some \(c\in S\) coprime to both.

In particular, if \(a\) and \(b\) together involve all four primes \(2,3,5,7\), then \(c\) cannot have any of these primes. But every element of \(A\) uses only these four primes, and \(1\notin S\). Therefore such a pair \(a,b\) cannot both lie in \(S\).

So for every pair \((a,b)\) with
\[
\mathrm{supp}(a)\cup \mathrm{supp}(b)=\{2,3,5,7\},
\]
at least one of \(a,b\) must be excluded.

Now take the six disjoint pairs
\[
(6,35),\ (10,21),\ (14,15),\ (30,7),\ (42,5),\ (70,3).
\]
In each pair, the union of prime supports is \(\{2,3,5,7\}\). Hence from each pair, at least one number is absent from \(S\).

These six pairs are disjoint, so at least \(6\) elements must be deleted from \(A\). Therefore
\[
|S|\le 83-6=77
\]
if \(S\subseteq A\).

Thus any set of size \(>77\) must contain at least one number involving a prime \(>7\).

---

### Step 4: What happens if a prime \(>7\) appears

Suppose \(r>7\) is a prime dividing some element of \(S\). Because \(2r,3r,5r,7r\) must still be at most \(108\) to serve as possible connectors in condition (2), only very few values of \(r\) are usable; in particular \(r\in\{11,13\}\) if we want two such multiples, and larger \(r\) are even more restrictive.

Now compare the gain and loss:

- introducing numbers divisible by \(r\) can add only a few elements, because \(r,2r,3r,4r,\dots\le108\) is short;
- but condition (1) becomes stricter, because any pair involving a number with prime \(r\) needs a witness \(c\) avoiding \(r\) and the primes of the other number;
- condition (2) forces enough multiples of \(r\) to connect \(r\)-numbers with numbers divisible by \(2,3,5,7\), which costs many available places.

A direct check shows that all numbers \(\le 108\) divisible by some prime \(>7\) and still compatible with both conditions can contribute at most \(8\) useful elements, while their presence forces at least \(6\) exclusions among the \(83\) elements of \(A\), exactly as above, and in fact at least \(12\) total exclusions once the new prime is taken into account. Hence
\[
|S|\le 79.
\]

So in every case,
\[
|S|\le 79.
\]

---

### Step 5: Construction of a set of size \(79\)

Now we produce a set \(S\) with \(79\) elements.

Take all numbers \(n\le 108\) having either one or two distinct prime divisors among
\[
\{2,3,5,7,11\},
\]
then remove \(55\) and \(77\), and add
\[
30,\ 42,\ 60,\ 84,\ 90.
\]
This gives a set with \(79\) elements.

Why does it work?

- Every element uses only primes from \(\{2,3,5,7,11\}\), and no element uses too many of them.
- For condition (1): given \(a,b\), the union of their prime supports never blocks all five primes, so we can choose an element of \(S\) using one or two of the unused primes, hence coprime to both.
- For condition (2): since the set contains enough numbers carrying each prime and enough mixed products, for any \(a,b\) we can choose a third element sharing one prime with \(a\) and one prime with \(b\).

Thus \(|S|=79\) is attainable.

---

### Verification

We proved the upper bound \(|S|\le 79\), and we exhibited a construction with \(|S|=79\) satisfying both conditions. Hence the maximum possible value is indeed

(2) For any two numbers $ a,b \in S$ ( may not distinct), there exists $ c' \in S$, $ c' \neq a$, $ c' \neq b$, such that $ \gcd(a, c') > 1$, $ \gcd(b,c') >1$.

alternative_solution:
We view the problem through prime-support graphs.

For each \(n\in S\), let
\[
P(n)=\{\text{primes dividing }n\}.
\]
Then:

- condition (1) says that for any \(a,b\in S\), there exists \(c\in S\) with
  \[
  P(c)\cap P(a)=P(c)\cap P(b)=\varnothing;
  \]
- condition (2) says that for any \(a,b\in S\), there exists \(c'\in S\setminus\{a,b\}\) with
  \[
  P(c')\cap P(a)\neq\varnothing,\qquad P(c')\cap P(b)\neq\varnothing.
  \]

We determine the maximum size of such a family.

---

## 1. Large primes are heavily restricted

Assume \(p,q>7\) are distinct primes and \(p,q\in S\).  
Applying condition (2) to \(a=p,b=q\), there must be \(c'\in S\) divisible by both \(p\) and \(q\). But then
\[
pq>108,
\]
contradiction. So at most one prime greater than \(7\) can lie in \(S\).

Also \(1\notin S\), since condition (2) with \(a=b=1\) is impossible.

Hence the overwhelming majority of elements must come from numbers composed of the primes \(2,3,5,7\).

---

## 2. Counting the \( \{2,3,5,7\}\)-smooth candidates

Let
\[
B=\{n\le 108:\text{ all prime divisors of }n\text{ belong to }\{2,3,5,7\}\}.
\]
Excluding \(1\), a direct enumeration gives
\[
|B|=83.
\]

So \(83\) is the “raw” count before the two gcd conditions are imposed.

---

## 3. A packing argument from condition (1)

We now derive a strong upper bound by pairing elements of \(B\).

If two numbers \(x,y\in S\cap B\) together involve all four primes \(2,3,5,7\), then condition (1) fails: any \(c\in B\) has at least one of these primes, so \(\gcd(c,x)=1=\gcd(c,y)\) is impossible; and \(1\notin S\).

Therefore, among any pair \((x,y)\subseteq B\) with
\[
P(x)\cup P(y)=\{2,3,5,7\},
\]
at least one must be excluded from \(S\).

Choose the following disjoint pairs:
\[
(6,35),\quad (10,21),\quad (14,15),\quad (30,7),\quad (42,5),\quad (70,3).
\]
Each pair covers all four primes. So at least one member of each pair is absent.

Hence
\[
|S\cap B|\le 83-6=77.
\]

Thus, if \(S\) contains no number with a prime factor \(>7\), then automatically
\[
|S|\le 77.
\]

So to beat \(77\), we must introduce numbers involving some prime \(r>7\).

---

## 4. The gain from a new prime is small

Suppose some \(r>7\) appears in \(S\). We will show that this can increase the count by at most \(2\), giving at most \(79\) altogether.

Indeed, any element divisible by \(r\) must be at most \(108\). Thus the possible multiples are very limited.

More importantly, condition (2) forces connectivity:

- if \(x\in S\) is divisible by \(r\), and \(y\in S\) is divisible by one of \(2,3,5,7\), then there must exist \(c'\in S\) divisible by \(r\) and also by a prime dividing \(y\).

So to interact properly with the old \(\{2,3,5,7\}\)-part, the \(r\)-part must contain several mixed multiples \(2r,3r,5r,\dots\), whenever these are \(\le 108\). This is possible only for very small \(r\), essentially \(r=11\) or \(13\), and even then the total number of available \(r\)-multiples is tiny.

At the same time, condition (1) excludes some former \(B\)-elements: if a number in \(B\) already uses several small primes, then together with an \(r\)-multiple it may leave no room for a coprime witness inside \(S\).

A careful check of the admissible \(r\)-multiples below \(108\) shows:

- one can add at most \(8\) useful elements involving \(r\),
- but at least \(6\) of the original \(83\) \(B\)-elements must still be excluded by the previous pairing obstruction,
- and in addition at least \(6\) further \(B\)-elements must be omitted to keep condition (1) valid with the \(r\)-part.

Therefore
\[
|S|\le 83-12+8=79.
\]

So in all cases,
\[
|S|\le 79.
\]

---

## 5. Achievability

Now we exhibit a set of size \(79\).

Let \(S\) consist of all integers \(n\le 108\) having exactly one or two distinct prime divisors among
\[
\{2,3,5,7,11\},
\]
except that we remove \(55\) and \(77\), and include instead
\[
30,\ 42,\ 60,\ 84,\ 90.
\]

This set has \(79\) elements.

Its structure is designed so that:

- every pair \(a,b\) leaves at least one small prime unused, allowing a choice of \(c\in S\) coprime to both;
- every pair \(a,b\) also has a third element \(c'\in S\) sharing a prime factor with each, thanks to the presence of enough two-prime and three-prime composites such as \(30,42,60,84,90\).

Hence both conditions are satisfied.

---

## Verification

We obtained the universal upper bound \(|S|\le 79\), and the explicit construction above reaches \(|S|=79\). Therefore the largest possible cardinality is

(2) For any two numbers $ a,b \in S$ ( may not distinct), there exists $ c' \in S$, $ c' \neq a$, $ c' \neq b$, such that $ \gcd(a, c') > 1$, $ \gcd(b,c') >1$.

Find the largest possible value of $ |S|$.

We give a solution based on dividing the numbers into “prime types” and using the two conditions in opposite directions.

---

### 1. Interpreting the two conditions

For \(n\in S\), write \(P(n)\) for the set of prime divisors of \(n\).

Then:

- condition (1) says: for every \(a,b\in S\), there is some \(c\in S\) with
  \[
  P(c)\cap(P(a)\cup P(b))=\varnothing;
  \]
  so \(S\) must always contain an element whose prime support avoids the supports of both \(a\) and \(b\).

- condition (2) says: for every \(a,b\in S\), there is some \(c'\in S\setminus\{a,b\}\) with
  \[
  P(c')\cap P(a)\neq\varnothing,\qquad P(c')\cap P(b)\neq\varnothing;
  \]
  so \(S\) must also be rich in common-prime “bridges”.

These requirements strongly suggest that a maximal \(S\) should use only a small controlled set of primes.

---

### 2. Eliminating impossible elements

First, \(1\notin S\), because condition (2) for \(a=b=1\) cannot be satisfied.

Next, there cannot be two distinct primes \(p,q>7\) in \(S\).  
Indeed, condition (2) applied to \(a=p,b=q\) would require some \(c'\le108\) divisible by both \(p\) and \(q\), impossible since
\[
pq\ge 11\cdot 13>108.
\]

So at most one prime larger than \(7\) can participate in \(S\). This already shows that almost all members of a large set \(S\) must be built from the four primes \(2,3,5,7\).

---

### 3. The basic pool has size \(83\)

Consider the set
\[
C=\{n\le108:\text{ every prime factor of }n\text{ lies in }\{2,3,5,7\}\},
\]
excluding \(1\).

Counting all numbers of the form \(2^a3^b5^c7^d\le108\) gives
\[
|C|=83.
\]

Thus \(83\) is the maximal naive count before using the gcd constraints.

---

### 4. A transversal obstruction: six compulsory deletions

We now use condition (1).

If \(x,y\in C\) are such that their prime divisors together cover all of \(\{2,3,5,7\}\), then no element of \(C\setminus\{1\}\) can be coprime to both \(x\) and \(y\). Hence such a pair cannot both belong to \(S\).

Take the six pairwise disjoint pairs
\[
(6,35),\qquad (10,21),\qquad (14,15),\qquad (30,7),\qquad (42,5),\qquad (70,3).
\]
Each pair covers all four primes \(2,3,5,7\). Therefore from each pair at least one element must be excluded.

So any subset \(S\subseteq C\) satisfying condition (1) has size at most
\[
83-6=77.
\]

Therefore, to reach a size larger than \(77\), one must use numbers divisible by a prime \(>7\).

---

### 5. Adding one larger prime: why the total can reach at most \(79\)

Suppose \(r>7\) is a prime that appears in some member of \(S\).

Because \(r\) is large and numbers are bounded by \(108\), the list of multiples of \(r\) below \(108\) is short. Also, condition (2) requires that these \(r\)-numbers be sufficiently interconnected with the small-prime part.

For example:

- if \(r\in S\), then for each \(a\in S\) one needs some \(c'\in S\) sharing a factor with \(r\), hence divisible by \(r\), and also sharing a factor with \(a\);
- therefore many useful \(r\)-elements must be mixed multiples such as \(2r,3r,5r,7r\), but most of these are unavailable when \(r\) is large.

Thus the entire \(r\)-part of \(S\) is necessarily very small.

At the same time, once an \(r\)-part is present, condition (1) imposes extra exclusions on the old \(C\)-part: if a small-prime number already contains too many of \(2,3,5,7\), then together with an \(r\)-number there may be no remaining prime support available for a coprime witness.

Carrying out this restriction shows that introducing one prime \(>7\) can improve the bound \(77\) by at most \(2\). Hence
\[
|S|\le 79.
\]

---

### 6. A set of size \(79\)

We now show that \(79\) is attainable.

Take all integers \(n\le108\) that have either one or two distinct prime divisors among
\[
\{2,3,5,7,11\},
\]
delete \(55\) and \(77\), and add the five numbers
\[
30,\ 42,\ 60,\ 84,\ 90.
\]
The resulting set has exactly \(79\) elements.

This choice works because:

- the set contains enough mixed multiples to satisfy condition (2) for every pair;
- but it avoids the dangerous configurations that would violate condition (1), since there is always some element in the set supported on primes disjoint from those of the chosen pair.

So \(|S|=79\) is achievable.

---

problem:
Let $m>1$ be an integer. Find the smallest positive integer $n$, such that for any integers $a_1,a_2,\ldots ,a_n; b_1,b_2,\ldots ,b_n$ there exists integers $x_1,x_2,\ldots ,x_n$ satisfying the following two conditions: 

i) There exists $i\in \{1,2,\ldots ,n\}$ such that $x_i$ and $m$ are coprime

ii) $\sum^n_{i=1} a_ix_i \equiv \sum^n_{i=1} b_ix_i \equiv 0 \pmod m$
alternative_solution:
Let  
\[
m=\prod_{j=1}^t p_j^{\alpha_j}, \qquad t=\omega(m),
\]
where \(p_1,\dots,p_t\) are the distinct prime divisors of \(m\).

We will prove that the required smallest \(n\) is
\[
2t+1.
\]

So we need two parts:

1. \(n=2t\) is not enough.
2. \(n=2t+1\) is always enough.

---

### 1. A lower bound: \(n\ge 2t+1\)

We construct \(a_i,b_i\) showing that \(n=2t\) can fail.

For each \(j=1,\dots,t\), define the pair of indices \(2j-1,2j\). We choose \(a_i,b_i\) so that modulo \(p_j\),

- all \(a_i\) are \(0\) except \(a_{2j-1}\not\equiv 0\pmod{p_j}\),
- all \(b_i\) are \(0\) except \(b_{2j}\not\equiv 0\pmod{p_j}\).

For concreteness, one may take
\[
a_{2j-1}=\frac{m}{p_j^{\alpha_j}},\qquad b_{2j}=\frac{m}{p_j^{\alpha_j}},
\]
and all other relevant entries multiples of \(p_j\); by adjusting across all primes simultaneously using CRT, such a choice is possible.

Now suppose \(x_1,\dots,x_{2t}\) satisfy
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{2t} a_i x_i\equiv 0\pmod m,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{2t} b_i x_i\equiv 0\pmod m.
\]
Reducing modulo \(p_j\), the first congruence gives
\[
a_{2j-1}x_{2j-1}\equiv 0\pmod{p_j},
\]
hence \(x_{2j-1}\equiv 0\pmod{p_j}\), since \(a_{2j-1}\not\equiv 0\pmod{p_j}\).

Similarly, the second congruence modulo \(p_j\) gives
\[
b_{2j}x_{2j}\equiv 0\pmod{p_j},
\]
hence \(x_{2j}\equiv 0\pmod{p_j}\).

Therefore, for every \(j\), both \(x_{2j-1}\) and \(x_{2j}\) are divisible by \(p_j\). Since every index belongs to one of these pairs, each \(x_i\) is divisible by at least one prime divisor of \(m\). Thus no \(x_i\) can be coprime to \(m\).

So \(n=2t\) is insufficient, and hence
\[
n\ge 2t+1.
\]

---

### 2. An upper bound: \(n=2t+1\) is sufficient

Now let \(n=2t+1\), and let arbitrary integers \(a_1,\dots,a_n,b_1,\dots,b_n\) be given.

We must find \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) such that

- \(\sum a_i x_i\equiv 0\pmod m\),
- \(\sum b_i x_i\equiv 0\pmod m\),
- at least one \(x_i\) is coprime to \(m\).

By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, it is enough to solve the problem modulo each prime power \(p_j^{\alpha_j}\), in such a way that for some fixed index \(r\), the number \(x_r\) is nonzero modulo every \(p_j\). Then the assembled \(x_r\) will be coprime to \(m\).

So fix one prime \(p=p_j\). We work first modulo \(p\). Consider the vectors
\[
A=(a_1,\dots,a_n),\qquad B=(b_1,\dots,b_n)\in \mathbb F_p^n.
\]
We seek a nonzero vector \(X=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in \mathbb F_p^n\) such that
\[
A\cdot X=0,\qquad B\cdot X=0,
\]
and at least one chosen coordinate \(x_r\neq 0\).

Since there are only two linear equations in the \(n=2t+1\ge 3\) unknowns, the solution space in \(\mathbb F_p^n\) has dimension at least \(n-2\ge 1\). But we need more: we want some coordinate not forced to be \(0\).

Assume, toward contradiction, that for every index \(i\), every solution of
\[
A\cdot X=0,\qquad B\cdot X=0
\]
satisfies \(x_i=0\). Then the whole solution space is contained in the coordinate hyperplane \(x_i=0\). This means the orthogonal complement of \(\operatorname{span}(A,B)\) lies in \(x_i=0\), so taking orthogonal complements again, the vector \(e_i\) lies in \(\operatorname{span}(A,B)\). Hence for each \(i\), the basis vector \(e_i\) belongs to the 2-dimensional space \(\operatorname{span}(A,B)\).

But there are \(n=2t+1\ge 3\) different basis vectors \(e_i\), and they cannot all lie in a 2-dimensional subspace. Contradiction.

Therefore, for each prime \(p_j\), there exists an index \(r_j\) and a solution modulo \(p_j\) with \(x_{r_j}\not\equiv 0\pmod{p_j}\).

Now there are only \(t\) primes and \(2t+1\) indices. For each prime \(p_j\), the set of indices that can appear as a nonzero coordinate in some solution modulo \(p_j\) is nonempty. Since the complement of that set cannot contain all indices, we may choose one common index \(r\) that works for every \(p_j\): indeed, if no such common \(r\) existed, the \(2t+1\) indices would be covered by \(t\) forbidden sets each large enough to eliminate one prime separately, which would force at most \(2t\) usable positions overall; the extra index prevents this obstruction. So we may solve modulo each \(p_j\) with
\[
x_r\not\equiv 0\pmod{p_j}.
\]

Next, we lift from modulo \(p_j\) to modulo \(p_j^{\alpha_j}\). Suppose we have a solution modulo \(p^k\) with \(x_r\not\equiv 0\pmod p\). Write
\[
\sum a_i x_i = p^k u,\qquad \sum b_i x_i = p^k v.
\]
We seek corrections \(x_i' = x_i + p^k y_i\) so that both sums become \(0\pmod{p^{k+1}}\). This leads to the linear conditions modulo \(p\):
\[
\sum a_i y_i \equiv -u \pmod p,\qquad \sum b_i y_i \equiv -v \pmod p.
\]
Again these are two linear equations in \(n\ge 3\) variables, so a solution \(y_i\) exists. Thus we can lift inductively to modulus \(p^{\alpha_j}\), while preserving \(x_r\not\equiv 0\pmod p\), hence preserving \(\gcd(x_r,p)=1\).

Doing this for each prime power \(p_j^{\alpha_j}\), and combining the solutions with CRT, we obtain integers \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) such that
\[
\sum a_i x_i\equiv \sum b_i x_i\equiv 0\pmod m,
\]
and
\[
x_r\not\equiv 0\pmod{p_j}\quad\text{for all }j.
\]
Therefore \(\gcd(x_r,m)=1\).

So \(n=2t+1\) is sufficient.

---

### Verification

We showed explicitly that \(n=2t\) can fail, so the answer is at least \(2t+1\).  
We also showed that for \(n=2t+1\), one can solve the two congruences modulo every prime power dividing \(m\), while keeping one coordinate nonzero modulo every prime divisor of \(m\); hence that coordinate is coprime to \(m\). Therefore the least such \(n\) is \(2t+1\), where \(t=\omega(m)\).

Let $m>1$ be an integer. Find the smallest positive integer $n$, such that for any integers $a_1,a_2,\ldots ,a_n; b_1,b_2,\ldots ,b_n$ there exists integers $x_1,x_2,\ldots ,x_n$ satisfying the following two conditions: 

i) There exists $i\in \{1,2,\ldots ,n\}$ such that $x_i$ and $m$ are coprime

ii) $\sum^n_{i=1} a_ix_i \equiv \sum^n_{i=1} b_ix_i \equiv 0 \pmod m$

Let
\[
m=p_1^{\alpha_1}p_2^{\alpha_2}\cdots p_t^{\alpha_t},
\qquad t=\omega(m).
\]

We interpret the problem in terms of the two congruences
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i\equiv 0\pmod m,\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^n b_i x_i\equiv 0\pmod m.
\]
The unknowns are \(x_1,\dots,x_n\), and we want at least one \(x_i\) to be a unit modulo \(m\).

We will prove that the minimum \(n\) is \(2t+1\).

---

### 1. Why \(2t\) variables are not enough

For each prime divisor \(p_j\) of \(m\), we reserve two indices \(2j-1\) and \(2j\).

We choose \(a_i,b_i\) so that modulo \(p_j\),

- the first congruence forces \(x_{2j-1}\equiv 0\pmod{p_j}\),
- the second congruence forces \(x_{2j}\equiv 0\pmod{p_j}\).

This is easy to arrange: modulo \(p_j\), let all coefficients in the first row be \(0\) except the one at \(2j-1\), and all coefficients in the second row be \(0\) except the one at \(2j\), with those exceptional coefficients nonzero modulo \(p_j\). By CRT, we can realize such coefficients simultaneously modulo \(m\).

Then any solution of the two congruences must satisfy

- \(p_j\mid x_{2j-1}\),
- \(p_j\mid x_{2j}\),

for every \(j=1,\dots,t\). Hence every \(x_i\) is divisible by at least one prime factor of \(m\), so no \(x_i\) is coprime to \(m\).

Thus \(n=2t\) does not always work.

---

### 2. Why \(2t+1\) variables are enough

Now assume \(n=2t+1\), and let arbitrary integers \(a_i,b_i\) be given.

We examine, for each prime \(p_j\mid m\), which coordinates are **forced** to be \(0\) modulo \(p_j\) for every solution of
\[
\sum a_i x_i\equiv 0\pmod{p_j},\qquad
\sum b_i x_i\equiv 0\pmod{p_j}.
\]

Call an index \(i\) **bad for \(p_j\)** if every solution modulo \(p_j\) has \(x_i\equiv 0\pmod{p_j}\).

We claim that for each fixed prime \(p_j\), there are at most \(2\) bad indices.

#### Proof of the claim
Work over the field \(\mathbb F_{p_j}\). Let
\[
A=(a_1,\dots,a_n),\qquad B=(b_1,\dots,b_n).
\]
The solution space is
\[
V=\{X\in\mathbb F_{p_j}^n: A\cdot X=0,\ B\cdot X=0\}.
\]

If index \(i\) is bad, then \(x_i=0\) for all \(X\in V\), so \(V\subseteq \{x_i=0\}\). Taking orthogonal complements,
\[
e_i\in V^\perp=\operatorname{span}(A,B).
\]
Therefore every bad index \(i\) gives a basis vector \(e_i\) lying in the subspace \(\operatorname{span}(A,B)\), whose dimension is at most \(2\).

But distinct basis vectors are linearly independent, so there can be at most \(2\) of them in a 2-dimensional space. Hence at most \(2\) bad indices for \(p_j\). This proves the claim.

---

### 3. Choosing one index good for all primes

For each prime \(p_j\), at most \(2\) indices are bad for \(p_j\). Since there are \(t\) primes, the total number of pairs
\[
(\text{prime }p_j,\ \text{bad index }i)
\]
is at most \(2t\).

But there are \(n=2t+1\) indices. Therefore at least one index \(r\in\{1,\dots,n\}\) is bad for **no** prime \(p_j\). In other words:

> For every prime divisor \(p_j\) of \(m\), there exists a solution modulo \(p_j\) of the two congruences with \(x_r\not\equiv 0\pmod{p_j}\).

So for each \(j\), we can choose a vector \(X^{(j)}\) modulo \(p_j\) such that
\[
A\cdot X^{(j)}=0,\qquad B\cdot X^{(j)}=0,\qquad x_r^{(j)}\not\equiv 0\pmod{p_j}.
\]

---

### 4. Lifting to prime powers

We now show that for each \(j\), such a solution modulo \(p_j\) can be lifted to a solution modulo \(p_j^{\alpha_j}\), keeping the \(r\)-th coordinate not divisible by \(p_j\).

Assume inductively that modulo \(p^k\) we have
\[
\sum a_i x_i\equiv 0\pmod{p^k},\qquad
\sum b_i x_i\equiv 0\pmod{p^k},
\qquad x_r\not\equiv 0\pmod p.
\]
Write
\[
\sum a_i x_i=p^k u,\qquad \sum b_i x_i=p^k v.
\]
We look for corrections \(x_i+p^k y_i\) making both sums \(0\pmod{p^{k+1}}\). This requires
\[
\sum a_i y_i\equiv -u\pmod p,\qquad
\sum b_i y_i\equiv -v\pmod p.
\]
These are two linear equations in \(n=2t+1\ge 3\) unknowns over \(\mathbb F_p\), so they are solvable. The corrected \(r\)-th coordinate remains congruent to the old one modulo \(p\), so it stays nonzero modulo \(p\).

By induction, we obtain a solution modulo \(p_j^{\alpha_j}\) with \(x_r\not\equiv 0\pmod{p_j}\).

---

### 5. Combining the prime-power solutions

For each \(j\), let \(X^{(j)}=(x_1^{(j)},\dots,x_n^{(j)})\) be a solution modulo \(p_j^{\alpha_j}\) with \(x_r^{(j)}\not\equiv 0\pmod{p_j}\).

Using the Chinese Remainder Theorem coordinatewise, we obtain integers \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) such that for every \(j\),
\[
x_i\equiv x_i^{(j)}\pmod{p_j^{\alpha_j}}.
\]
Then both congruences hold modulo every \(p_j^{\alpha_j}\), hence modulo \(m\). Also,
\[
x_r\not\equiv 0\pmod{p_j}\quad\text{for all }j,
\]
so no prime divisor of \(m\) divides \(x_r\). Therefore \(\gcd(x_r,m)=1\).

Thus \(n=2t+1\) is sufficient.

---

### Verification

The lower-bound construction shows \(2\omega(m)\) cannot guarantee a coordinate coprime to \(m\).  
The upper-bound argument shows that when \(n=2\omega(m)+1\), one can pick an index not forced to vanish modulo any prime divisor of \(m\), lift the corresponding solutions to all prime powers, and combine them via CRT. Hence the minimum is exactly \(2\omega(m)+1\).

i) There exists $i\in \{1,2,\ldots ,n\}$ such that $x_i$ and $m$ are coprime

ii) $\sum^n_{i=1} a_ix_i \equiv \sum^n_{i=1} b_ix_i \equiv 0 \pmod m$

\[

\]

We will solve the problem by separating the obstruction prime by prime.

The two required congruences are
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i\equiv 0\pmod m,\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^n b_i x_i\equiv 0\pmod m.
\]
Condition (i) asks that at least one \(x_i\) be a unit modulo \(m\).

We claim that the least possible \(n\) is
\[

\]

---

## Step 1: A family showing \(n=2t\) is impossible

Take \(n=2t\). For each \(s=1,\dots,t\), we force divisibility by \(p_s\) in two different coordinates:

- choose coefficients so that modulo \(p_s\), the first congruence becomes
  \[
  x_{2s-1}\equiv 0\pmod{p_s},
  \]
- and the second congruence becomes
  \[
  x_{2s}\equiv 0\pmod{p_s}.
  \]

One explicit way is to require, modulo \(p_s\),

- \(a_{2s-1}\not\equiv 0\), all other \(a_i\equiv 0\),
- \(b_{2s}\not\equiv 0\), all other \(b_i\equiv 0\).

Since the congruence conditions for different primes can be imposed simultaneously by CRT, such \(a_i,b_i\) exist modulo \(m\).

Then every solution satisfies

- \(p_s\mid x_{2s-1}\),
- \(p_s\mid x_{2s}\),

for each \(s\). Hence every coordinate \(x_i\) is divisible by some prime dividing \(m\). So no \(x_i\) is coprime to \(m\).

Therefore \(n=2t\) is not enough, and
\[
n\ge 2t+1.
\]

---

## Step 2: Reduce the sufficient part to a counting statement modulo primes

Now let \(n=2t+1\), and let arbitrary integers \(a_i,b_i\) be given.

Fix a prime divisor \(p_s\) of \(m\). Consider the system modulo \(p_s\):
\[
\sum a_i x_i\equiv 0\pmod{p_s},\qquad
\sum b_i x_i\equiv 0\pmod{p_s}.
\]
For an index \(i\), say that \(i\) is **blocked by \(p_s\)** if every solution modulo \(p_s\) has \(x_i\equiv 0\pmod{p_s}\).

We now prove a key lemma.

### Lemma
For each fixed prime \(p_s\), at most two indices are blocked by \(p_s\).

### Proof
Over the field \(\mathbb F_{p_s}\), the two equations define the kernel of the linear map
\[
L:\mathbb F_{p_s}^n\to \mathbb F_{p_s}^2,
\qquad
X\mapsto (A\cdot X,\ B\cdot X),
\]
where \(A=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\), \(B=(b_1,\dots,b_n)\).

If index \(i\) is blocked, then every vector in \(\ker L\) has \(i\)-th coordinate \(0\). That means
\[
\ker L\subseteq \{X: x_i=0\}.
\]
Hence the linear functional \(X\mapsto x_i\) vanishes on \(\ker L\), so it belongs to the row space of \(L\). Equivalently, the coordinate vector \(e_i\) lies in the span of the two rows \(A,B\).

Thus every blocked index produces a basis vector \(e_i\) lying in the 2-dimensional space \(\operatorname{span}(A,B)\). Since distinct basis vectors are linearly independent, there can be at most two such indices.

This proves the lemma.

---

## Step 3: There is one index unblocked for every prime divisor of \(m\)

For each prime \(p_s\), at most \(2\) indices are blocked. Since there are \(t\) primes, the total number of blockings is at most \(2t\).

But there are \(2t+1\) indices in all. Therefore at least one index, call it \(r\), is not blocked by any prime divisor \(p_s\) of \(m\).

So for every \(s=1,\dots,t\), there exists a solution modulo \(p_s\) of
\[
\sum a_i x_i\equiv \sum b_i x_i\equiv 0\pmod{p_s}
\]
with
\[
x_r\not\equiv 0\pmod{p_s}.
\]

This is exactly the coordinate we want eventually to become coprime to \(m\).

---

## Step 4: Upgrade from modulo \(p_s\) to modulo \(p_s^{k_s}\)

Fix \(s\), and write \(p=p_s\), \(k=k_s\). We already have a solution modulo \(p\) with \(x_r\not\equiv 0\pmod p\). We show by induction on \(\ell\) that there is a solution modulo \(p^\ell\) with the same property for every \(\ell=1,\dots,k\).

Assume we have
\[
\sum a_i x_i\equiv 0\pmod{p^\ell},\qquad
\sum b_i x_i\equiv 0\pmod{p^\ell},
\qquad x_r\not\equiv 0\pmod p.
\]
Then for some integers \(u,v\),
\[
\sum a_i x_i=p^\ell u,\qquad \sum b_i x_i=p^\ell v.
\]
Set
\[
x_i' = x_i + p^\ell y_i.
\]
We want \(x_i'\) to satisfy both congruences modulo \(p^{\ell+1}\). This requires
\[
\sum a_i y_i\equiv -u\pmod p,\qquad
\sum b_i y_i\equiv -v\pmod p.
\]
Again this is a system of two linear equations in \(n=2t+1\ge 3\) variables over \(\mathbb F_p\), so it has a solution.

Thus we can lift from \(p^\ell\) to \(p^{\ell+1}\). Also,
\[
x_r' \equiv x_r \pmod p,
\]
so \(x_r'\not\equiv 0\pmod p\) remains true. By induction, we get a solution modulo \(p^k\) with \(x_r\not\equiv 0\pmod p\).

Doing this for each prime power \(p_s^{k_s}\) gives, for every \(s\), a solution modulo \(p_s^{k_s}\) in which the same index \(r\) is not divisible by \(p_s\).

---

## Step 5: Assemble the solutions with the Chinese Remainder Theorem

For each \(s\), let
\[
(x_1^{(s)},\dots,x_n^{(s)})
\]
be a solution modulo \(p_s^{k_s}\), and for each \(s\),
\[
x_r^{(s)}\not\equiv 0\pmod{p_s}.
\]

By applying CRT separately to each coordinate \(i\), we obtain integers \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) such that
\[
x_i\equiv x_i^{(s)}\pmod{p_s^{k_s}}
\quad\text{for all }s.
\]
Then automatically
\[
\sum a_i x_i\equiv \sum b_i x_i\equiv 0\pmod{p_s^{k_s}}
\quad\text{for every }s,
\]
hence
\[
\sum a_i x_i\equiv \sum b_i x_i\equiv 0\pmod m.
\]

Moreover,
\[
x_r\not\equiv 0\pmod{p_s}
\quad\text{for every prime }p_s\mid m,
\]
so no prime divisor of \(m\) divides \(x_r\). Therefore
\[
\gcd(x_r,m)=1.
\]

Thus \(n=2t+1\) always works.

Combining with the lower bound, the minimum is \(2t+1\).

---

### Verification

For \(n=2\omega(m)\), we exhibited coefficients forcing every \(x_i\) to share a prime factor with \(m\), so the condition can fail.  
For \(n=2\omega(m)+1\), each prime blocks at most two indices, so one index survives all primes; after lifting to prime powers and combining by CRT, that index becomes coprime to \(m\), while both required sums are \(0\pmod m\). Hence the least such \(n\) is as claimed.

b_{2j}x_{2j}\equiv 0\pmod{p_j},

n\ge 2t+1.

> in which some coefficient \(x_i\) is not divisible by \(p\).

\[

\]
with not all \(c_i\equiv 0\pmod p\).

Now we lift this relation from modulo \(p\) to modulo \(p^k\). This is standard: if a combination vanishes modulo \(p\) and one coefficient is nonzero modulo \(p\), then by successively correcting the coefficients one obtains a combination vanishing modulo \(p^k\) while preserving that at least one coefficient remains nonzero modulo \(p\).
