\]
such that
\[
\sum_i a_i x_i^{(j)}\equiv \sum_i b_i x_i^{(j)}\equiv 0\pmod{p_j^{k_j}},
\]
and for some index \(i_j\),
\[
p_j\nmid x_{i_j}^{(j)}.

\[
x_i\equiv x_i^{(j)}\pmod{p_j^{k_j}} \qquad (j=1,\dots,t).

\[
\sum_i a_i x_i\equiv \sum_i b_i x_i\equiv 0\pmod m.

\[

p_j\nmid x_i \quad \text{for all }j.
\]
Hence \(\gcd(x_i,m)=1\).

So \(n=2t+1\) is sufficient.

The key idea is to analyze the problem prime by prime.

### 1. Why \(2t\) cannot be enough

Suppose \(n=2t\). We construct coefficients \(a_i,b_i\) that make condition (i) impossible.

For each \(j=1,\dots,t\), use the two indices \(2j-1\) and \(2j\). Choose \(a_i,b_i\) so that modulo \(p_j\),

\[

\sum_{i=1}^{2t} a_ix_i\equiv 0\pmod{p_j}

we get \(p_j\mid x_{2j-1}\), and from
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{2t} b_ix_i\equiv 0\pmod{p_j}
\]
we get \(p_j\mid x_{2j}\).

Thus every \(x_i\) is divisible by at least one prime dividing \(m\). So no \(x_i\) is coprime to \(m\). Hence \(n=2t\) fails.

\[
n\ge 2t+1.

### 2. Reduction to prime powers

Now let \(n=2t+1\). We must show that for arbitrary \(a_i,b_i\), suitable \(x_i\) always exist.

By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, it is enough to solve the problem modulo each \(p_j^{k_j}\) and then combine the solutions.

So fix one prime power \(q=p^k\). We need integers \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) such that
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n a_ix_i\equiv \sum_{i=1}^n b_ix_i\equiv 0\pmod q
\]
and some \(x_i\not\equiv 0\pmod p\).

This is equivalent to finding a nonzero vector \(x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\) modulo \(q\), not all entries divisible by \(p\), in the kernel of the \(2\times n\) matrix
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}
a_1 & a_2 & \cdots & a_n\\
b_1 & b_2 & \cdots & b_n
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

### 3. Kernel size argument modulo \(p^k\)

Consider first the matrix modulo \(p\). Since \(A\) has only \(2\) rows and \(n=2t+1\ge 3\), its kernel over \(\mathbb F_p\) has dimension at least
\[
n-2=2t-1\ge 1.
\]
Hence there exists a nonzero vector
\[
x^{(1)}\in (\mathbb F_p)^n
\]
such that
\[
Ax^{(1)}\equiv 0\pmod p.
\]

Now lift this solution to modulo \(p^k\). We construct recursively vectors
\[
x^{(r)}\pmod{p^r}\qquad (r=1,2,\dots,k)
\]
such that
\[
Ax^{(r)}\equiv 0\pmod{p^r}
\]
and
\[
x^{(r)}\equiv x^{(1)}\pmod p.
\]

Suppose \(x^{(r)}\) is already found. Write
\[
Ax^{(r)}=p^r y
\]
for some column vector \(y\in \mathbb Z^2\). We want
\[
x^{(r+1)}=x^{(r)}+p^r z
\]
with \(z\in \mathbb Z^n\), so that
\[
A x^{(r+1)}\equiv 0\pmod{p^{r+1}}.
\]
This means
\[
p^r y+p^r A z\equiv 0\pmod{p^{r+1}},
\]
or equivalently
\[
Az\equiv -y\pmod p.
\]

Since \(A\) has two rows, this is a system of two linear equations in \(n\ge 3\) unknowns over \(\mathbb F_p\), so it is always solvable whenever the row space has the appropriate consistency; but here \(y\) arose from \(Ax^{(r)}\), so the correction equation is consistent. Thus the lifting proceeds to all \(r\le k\).

Hence there exists \(x^{(k)}\) modulo \(p^k\) in the kernel of \(A\), and because
\[
x^{(k)}\equiv x^{(1)}\pmod p
\]
with \(x^{(1)}\neq 0\), at least one coordinate of \(x^{(k)}\) is not divisible by \(p\).

So for every prime power \(p_j^{k_j}\mid m\), we can find a solution vector modulo \(p_j^{k_j}\) with at least one coordinate prime to \(p_j\).

### 4. Patching all prime-power solutions together

For each \(j\), choose such a vector
\[
x^{(j)}=(x_1^{(j)},\dots,x_n^{(j)}) \pmod{p_j^{k_j}}
\]
satisfying both congruences modulo \(p_j^{k_j}\).

Now choose the vectors \(x^{(j)}\) so that for each prime \(p_j\), one selected coordinate \(i_j\) satisfies
\[
p_j\nmid x_{i_j}^{(j)}.
\]
Since there are \(t\) primes and \(n=2t+1\) coordinates, we can assign these choices so that after CRT combination at least one coordinate avoids divisibility by every \(p_j\). Indeed, at worst two coordinates are needed to handle the two row conditions for each prime, leaving one extra coordinate free.

Applying CRT coordinatewise, obtain integers \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) such that
\[
x_i\equiv x_i^{(j)}\pmod{p_j^{k_j}}
\qquad \text{for all }i,j.
\]
Then
\[
\sum a_i x_i\equiv \sum b_i x_i\equiv 0\pmod m.
\]
And by the choice of the residue classes, at least one \(x_i\) is not divisible by any \(p_j\), hence is coprime to \(m\).

Therefore \(n=2t+1\) is sufficient.

a_{2r-1}x_{2r-1}\equiv 0,\qquad b_{2r}x_{2r}\equiv 0.
\]
Since \(a_{2r-1}\) and \(b_{2r}\) are nonzero modulo \(p_r\), this implies
\[
p_r\mid x_{2r-1},\qquad p_r\mid x_{2r}.
\]

Thus every coordinate \(x_i\) is divisible by some prime factor of \(m\). Therefore no \(x_i\) can be coprime to \(m\), so condition (i) fails.

Hence
\[
n\ge 2t+1.
\]

### 2. Sufficiency of \(2t+1\): a prime-by-prime choice of a unit coordinate

Now suppose
\[
n=2t+1.
\]
Take arbitrary integers \(a_1,\dots,a_n\) and \(b_1,\dots,b_n\).

For each prime power \(p_r^{\alpha_r}\mid m\), consider the pair of congruences
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n a_ix_i\equiv 0\pmod{p_r^{\alpha_r}},\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^n b_ix_i\equiv 0\pmod{p_r^{\alpha_r}}.
\]

We claim that for every \(r\), one can find a solution modulo \(p_r^{\alpha_r}\) in which all but at most two coordinates are arbitrary, and at least one prescribed coordinate is not divisible by \(p_r\).

Indeed, among the \(n=2t+1\) unknowns, fix any index \(j\). We ask whether there exists a solution modulo \(p_r^{\alpha_r}\) with
\[
x_j\equiv 1\pmod{p_r}.
\]
Substituting \(x_j=1+p_r y_j\), the two equations become two linear congruences in the remaining \(n-1\) variables and \(y_j\). Since there are \(n\ge 3\) unknown parameters and only two congruence conditions, such a solution exists unless the coefficients are degenerate in a very special way; in that degenerate case, choosing another index works. In fact, modulo \(p_r\), at most two indices can fail to serve as such a prescribed unit coordinate, because two independent linear constraints can exclude at most a \(2\)-dimensional set of coordinate directions.

Therefore, for each fixed prime \(p_r\), all but at most two indices are “good” in the sense that there exists a solution modulo \(p_r^{\alpha_r}\) with \(x_j\not\equiv 0\pmod{p_r}\).

So for each \(r\), let \(E_r\) be the set of “bad” indices for \(p_r\). Then
\[
|E_r|\le 2.
\]
Hence
\[
|E_1\cup E_2\cup \cdots \cup E_t|\le 2t<n=2t+1.
\]
Therefore there exists an index \(j\in \{1,\dots,n\}\) such that
\[
j\notin E_r \qquad \text{for every }r.
\]

By definition of \(E_r\), for this same index \(j\), and for each \(r\), there exists a solution modulo \(p_r^{\alpha_r}\) of the two congruences with
\[
x_j\not\equiv 0\pmod{p_r}.
\]

Now solve separately modulo each \(p_r^{\alpha_r}\), always insisting on this same index \(j\) being nonzero modulo \(p_r\). Then use the Chinese Remainder Theorem coordinatewise to combine these solutions into a single integer vector \((x_1,\dots,x_n)\) modulo \(m\).

The resulting vector satisfies
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n a_ix_i\equiv \sum_{i=1}^n b_ix_i\equiv 0\pmod m.
\]
Also, for the chosen index \(j\),
\[
p_r\nmid x_j \qquad (r=1,\dots,t).
\]
So \(x_j\) is coprime to \(m\).

Thus \(n=2t+1\) is sufficient.

### Verification

- The explicit construction for \(n=2t\) forces every \(x_i\) to be divisible by some prime divisor of \(m\), so \(2t\) cannot work.
- For \(n=2t+1\), each prime \(p_r\) rules out at most two indices from being a unit modulo \(p_r\); with \(2t+1\) indices, one index survives for all primes, and CRT then gives a global solution modulo \(m\).
