Then by the Chinese Remainder Theorem, the congruence
\[
u^2\equiv 1\pmod a
\]
has exactly \(2^m\) residue classes modulo \(a\), one for each choice
\[
u\equiv \pm1\pmod{p_i}\qquad (1\le i\le m).
\]

Choose the primes so that for \(1\le j\le m-1\),
\[
\frac{a}{p_j}\equiv 1\pmod 6.
\]
This can be done inductively using the Chinese Remainder Theorem and Dirichlet’s theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions. Since each \(p_j\) is odd, we also have \(a\equiv \pm1\pmod 6\).

Now define, for \(1\le j\le m-1\), integers \(w_j\) satisfying
\[
w_j\equiv 2\pmod{p_j},\qquad w_j\equiv 0\pmod{p_i}\ (i\ne j),\qquad 0<w_j<a.
\]
Because \(\frac ap_j\equiv 1\pmod{p_j}\), we may take
\[
w_j=2\frac a{p_j}.
\]
Then
\[
w_j\equiv 2\pmod 6.
\]

Every solution \(u\) of \(u^2\equiv1\pmod a\) can be written modulo \(a\) as
\[
u\equiv -1+\sum_{j=1}^{m} \varepsilon_j w_j'
\]
for suitable \(\varepsilon_j\in\{0,1\}\), where \(w_j'\) are the CRT idempotent-type generators. In particular, restricting to the first \(m-1\) coordinates gives \(2^{m-1}\) solutions whose representatives are
\[
u=-1+\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}\varepsilon_j w_j
\]
with \(0<u<a\), provided the primes are sufficiently large. Since each \(w_j\equiv 2\pmod 6\), we get
\[
u\equiv -1+2(\varepsilon_1+\cdots+\varepsilon_{m-1})\pmod 6.
\]
Therefore:
- if \(\varepsilon_1+\cdots+\varepsilon_{m-1}\) is odd, then \(u\equiv 1\) or \(5\pmod 6\), so \(u^2-1\) is divisible by \(3\) but not by \(2a\) in such a way that
\[
z=\frac{u^2-1}{a}
\]
is divisible by \(3\) and odd; hence \(z\) is blue.

Thus from these \(2^{m-1}\) values, exactly half of them, namely \(2^{m-2}\), give blue points. Choosing \(m\) so that
\[
2^{m-2}>2075,
\]
we obtain more than \(2075\) blue points on one interval of the line and no red points in that selected block.

Now sort all integers of the form
\[
z_i=\frac{u_i^2-1}{a}
\]
coming from representatives \(u_i\) with \(0<u_i<6a\) and \(u_i^2\equiv1\pmod a\), in increasing order:
\[
z_1<z_2<\cdots<z_{6\cdot 2^m}.
\]
Because solutions to \(u^2\equiv1\pmod a\) repeat with period \(a\), if \(u_i\) is one representative then \(u_i+ta\) (\(0\le t\le5\)) gives the corresponding six values. Hence for each fixed residue class modulo \(a\), the six associated integers are
\[
\frac{(u_i+ta)^2-1}{a}\qquad (t=0,1,\dots,5).
\]

Among any six consecutive values of this form, at least one is red. Indeed, because \(a\equiv \pm1\pmod6\), as \(t\) runs from \(0\) to \(5\), the numbers \(u_i+ta\) run through all residue classes modulo \(6\). So one choice of \(t\) gives
\[
u_i+ta\equiv 3\pmod6.
\]
Then
\[
(u_i+ta)^2-1\equiv 9-1\equiv 8\pmod{12},
\]
so
\[
\frac{(u_i+ta)^2-1}{a}
\]
is divisible by \(2\) but not by \(3\), because \(a\) is coprime to \(6\). Hence this value is red.

Therefore among the first \(6\cdot 2^m\) points, there are at least \(2^m\) red points. Since the total number of points there is \(6\cdot 2^m\), there are at most \(5\cdot 2^m\) blue points.

Now consider all blocks of \(2075\) consecutive points among the ordered sequence \(z_1,z_2,\dots,z_{6\cdot 2^m}\). Let \(B_j\) be the number of blue points in
\[
z_j,z_{j+1},\dots,z_{j+2074}.
\]
As \(j\) increases by \(1\), the block loses one point and gains one point, so
\[
|B_{j+1}-B_j|\le 1.
\]
We already know some block has
\[
B_j=2075
\]
(from the all-blue interval found above), while because there are at least \(58\) red points among the large collection, some block of length \(2075\) must contain at least \(58\) red points, i.e. at most \(2017\) blue points. By the step-size condition \(|B_{j+1}-B_j|\le1\), some block must have exactly
\[
B_j=2017.
\]
Then that block has exactly
\[
2075-2017=58
\]
red points.

problem: For a rational point (x,y), if xy is an integer that divided by 2 but not 3, color (x,y) red, if xy is an integer that divided by 3 but not 2, color (x,y) blue. Determine whether there is a line segment in the plane such that it contains exactly 2017 blue points and 58 red points.
alternative_solution:
We again work on a line of the form
\[
y=ax+2,
\]
with \(a\) an odd squarefree integer to be chosen.

For a rational point \((x,y)\) on this line,
\[
xy=x(ax+2)=ax^2+2x.
\]
If \(xy=n\in\mathbb Z\), then \(x\) satisfies
\[
ax^2+2x-n=0.
\]
So \(x\in\mathbb Q\) exactly when
\[
1+an
\]
is a square. Thus the integer products \(n=xy\) realized by rational points on the line are precisely
\[
n=\frac{r^2-1}{a}
\qquad\text{for integers }r\text{ such that }r^2\equiv1\pmod a.
\]

So it is enough to choose \(a\) and find a consecutive set of such integers \(n\) with exactly \(2017\) blue and \(58\) red.

Now let
\[
a=p_1p_2\cdots p_m
\]
for distinct odd primes. Then the set
\[
\mathcal R=\{r\bmod a:\ r^2\equiv1\pmod a\}
\]
has cardinality \(2^m\). Choose the primes so large that the corresponding representatives in \((0,a)\) are well separated, and also choose them so that the CRT basis vectors \(e_j\) satisfy
\[
e_j\equiv 2\frac a{p_j}\pmod a
\]
with each \(e_j\equiv 2\pmod6\) for \(j\le m-1\). This is achievable exactly because the congruence conditions on the primes are finitely many and compatible.

Then among the \(2^{m-1}\) residues
\[
r=-1+\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}\delta_j e_j
\qquad (\delta_j\in\{0,1\}),
\]
all chosen as least positive representatives, the corresponding values
\[
n=\frac{r^2-1}{a}
\]
form a strictly increasing set. Also, modulo \(6\),
\[
r\equiv -1+2(\delta_1+\cdots+\delta_{m-1}).
\]
Hence if \(\delta_1+\cdots+\delta_{m-1}\) is odd, then \(r\equiv \pm2-1\equiv1,5\pmod6\), and consequently
\[
r^2-1\equiv 0\pmod3,\qquad r^2-1\equiv 2\pmod4.
\]
Since \(a\) is odd and coprime to \(3\), we obtain
\[
3\mid n,\qquad 2\nmid n.
\]
Thus these \(n\) are blue.

Exactly half of the \(2^{m-1}\) choices of \((\delta_1,\dots,\delta_{m-1})\) have odd sum, so we get
\[
2^{m-2}
\]
blue points in a row. Taking \(m\) large enough gives
\[
2^{m-2}>2075.
\]
Hence there exists a line segment containing \(2075\) blue points and no red points.

We now show that by sliding a window of length \(2075\), the number of blue points can be decreased to \(2017\).

For every solution \(r\bmod a\), consider the six integers
\[
r,\ r+a,\ r+2a,\ \dots,\ r+5a.
\]
These produce six values
\[
n_t=\frac{(r+ta)^2-1}{a}
\qquad (t=0,1,\dots,5).
\]
Because \(a\equiv\pm1\pmod6\), the residues \(r+ta\pmod6\) run through all six classes as \(t\) varies. In particular, for some \(t\),
\[
r+ta\equiv 3\pmod6.
\]
Then
\[
(r+ta)^2-1\equiv 8\pmod{12},
\]
so after division by \(a\), which is coprime to \(6\), we get
\[
2\mid n_t,\qquad 3\nmid n_t.
\]
Hence one of the six values in each such family is red.

Since there are \(2^m\) residue classes \(r\bmod a\), among the first \(6\cdot 2^m\) values there are at least \(2^m\) red points. Therefore not every block of \(2075\) consecutive points can be all blue once \(m\) is chosen so large that \(2^m>58\cdot 2075\); in particular, some block has at least \(58\) red points, hence at most \(2017\) blue points.

Now define \(f(j)\) to be the number of blue points among
\[
n_j,n_{j+1},\dots,n_{j+2074},
\]
where \(n_1<n_2<\cdots\) is the ordered list of all values \((r^2-1)/a\) under consideration. Moving from the \(j\)-th block to the \((j+1)\)-st block removes one point and adds one point, so
\[
|f(j+1)-f(j)|\le1.
\]
We have already found one block with
\[
f(j)=2075,
\]
and another with
\[
f(j)\le 2017.
\]
Therefore, by integer intermediate value, some block satisfies
\[
f(j)=2017.
\]
That block then contains
\[
2075-2017=58
\]
red points.

problem: For a rational point (x,y), if xy is an integer that divided by 2 but not 3, color (x,y) red, if xy is an integer that divided by 3 but not 2, color (x,y) blue. Determine whether there is a line segment in the plane such that it contains exactly 2017 blue points and 58 red points.
alternative_solution:
We use a parametrized family of rational points on one fixed line.

Take
\[
y=ax+2
\]
with \(a\) a product of many odd primes. A rational point \((x,y)\) on this line has
\[
xy=ax^2+2x.
\]
So if \(xy=m\in\mathbb Z\), then
\[
ax^2+2x-m=0.
\]
This quadratic has a rational root iff its discriminant is a square:
\[
4(1+am)=\square.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
1+am=s^2
\]
for some integer \(s\). Therefore the integer values \(m=xy\) that appear on the line are exactly
\[
m=\frac{s^2-1}{a}
\qquad\text{with }s^2\equiv1\pmod a.
\]

Thus the color of a rational point on this line depends only on the divisibility of
\[
\frac{s^2-1}{a}.
\]

Now choose
\[
a=p_1p_2\cdots p_m
\]
with distinct odd primes \(p_i\), all very large. Then there are exactly \(2^m\) congruence classes \(s\bmod a\) satisfying
\[
s^2\equiv1\pmod a.
\]
We choose the primes so that for \(1\le j\le m-1\), the CRT basis element attached to \(p_j\) is congruent to \(2\pmod6\). Concretely, this means we can select integers \(c_j\) such that
\[
c_j\equiv 2\pmod{p_j},\qquad c_j\equiv0\pmod{p_i}\ (i\ne j),\qquad c_j\equiv2\pmod6.
\]
Again, CRT and Dirichlet guarantee that such a choice of primes is possible.

Consider the \(2^{m-1}\) solutions
\[
s=-1+\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}\eta_j c_j,
\qquad \eta_j\in\{0,1\},
\]
taken as least positive representatives. Because the primes are large, these representatives are ordered exactly by the binary choices \((\eta_j)\), and the corresponding values
\[
m=\frac{s^2-1}{a}
\]
appear consecutively on the line.

For these \(s\),
\[
s\equiv -1+2(\eta_1+\cdots+\eta_{m-1})\pmod6.
\]
If \(\eta_1+\cdots+\eta_{m-1}\) is odd, then \(s\equiv1\) or \(5\pmod6\), so
\[
s^2-1\equiv0\pmod3
\]
and
\[
s^2-1\equiv 2\pmod4.
\]
Since \(a\) is odd and not divisible by \(3\),
\[
\frac{s^2-1}{a}
\]
is divisible by \(3\) and not by \(2\). Hence these points are blue.

There are exactly half as many such choices, so we get
\[
2^{m-2}
\]
blue points in one consecutive block. For \(m\) large enough,
\[
2^{m-2}>2075.
\]
Hence one line segment contains at least \(2075\) blue points and no red points.

Next we force the appearance of many red points elsewhere on the same line.

Fix any solution \(s_0\bmod a\) of \(s_0^2\equiv1\pmod a\). Then for each \(t=0,1,\dots,5\),
\[
s=s_0+ta
\]
also satisfies \(s^2\equiv1\pmod a\), and gives the point corresponding to
\[
m_t=\frac{(s_0+ta)^2-1}{a}.
\]
Because \(a\equiv\pm1\pmod6\), the six values \(s_0+ta\) represent all classes modulo \(6\). In particular, one of them is congruent to \(3\pmod6\). For that \(t\),
\[
(s_0+ta)^2-1\equiv 8\pmod{12}.
\]
Since \(a\) is coprime to \(6\), it follows that
\[
2\mid m_t,\qquad 3\nmid m_t.
\]
So this \(m_t\) is red.

Thus each residue class \(s_0\bmod a\) contributes at least one red point among its six lifts \(s_0,s_0+a,\dots,s_0+5a\). Since there are \(2^m\) residue classes modulo \(a\), among the first
\[
6\cdot2^m
\]
points in the ordered sequence there are at least \(2^m\) red points.

Now list all values
\[
m_1<m_2<\cdots<m_{6\cdot2^m}
\]
coming from these \(6\cdot2^m\) choices of \(s\). For each \(j\), let
\[
g_j=\#\{\text{blue points among }m_j,m_{j+1},\dots,m_{j+2074}\}.
\]
Then
\[
|g_{j+1}-g_j|\le1,
\]
because one point leaves the window and one enters.

We know that for some \(j\),
\[
g_j=2075
\]
(from the large all-blue block). On the other hand, because there are at least \(58\) red points distributed among the much larger collection, some window of length \(2075\) must contain at least \(58\) red points, so for some \(k\),
\[
g_k\le2017.
\]
Therefore, stepping from one window to the next and using \(|g_{j+1}-g_j|\le1\), we must hit the exact value
\[
g_\ell=2017
\]
for some \(\ell\).

Then that window contains exactly
\[
2075-2017=58
\]
red points.

problem: For a rational point (x,y), if xy is an integer that divided by 2 but not 3, color (x,y) red, if xy is an integer that divided by 3 but not 2, color (x,y) blue. Determine whether there is a line segment in the plane such that it contains exactly 2017 blue points and 58 red points.
alternative_solution:
Consider a line
\[
y=ax+2,
\]
where \(a\) is a positive odd integer to be chosen later.

For a rational point \((x,y)\) on this line, write
\[
xy=n\in \mathbb Z.
\]
Then
\[
x(ax+2)=n,
\]
so
\[
ax^2+2x-n=0.
\]
Hence \(x\in \mathbb Q\) if and only if the discriminant is a rational square:
\[
4+4an=4(1+an).
\]
Thus \((x,y)\) is a rational point on the line with \(xy=n\) exactly when
\[
1+an
\]
is a perfect square.

So the colored points on the line correspond precisely to those integers \(n\) for which
\[
1+an=t^2
\]
for some integer \(t\), and then the color depends only on the divisibility of \(n\):
- blue if \(3\mid n\) and \(2\nmid n\),
- red if \(2\mid n\) and \(3\nmid n\).

We now choose \(a\) so that the set of such integers \(n\) is rich enough and behaves regularly modulo \(6\).

---

### Step 1: Choose \(a\) with many square roots of \(1\) modulo \(a\)

Let
\[
a=p_1p_2\cdots p_m
\]
be a product of distinct large odd primes, each congruent to \(1\) or \(-1\pmod 6\), with \(m\) so large that
\[
2^{m-2}>2075.
\]
Then the congruence
\[
t^2\equiv 1\pmod a
\]
has exactly \(2^m\) residue classes modulo \(a\), by the Chinese Remainder Theorem.

For each such residue class \(r\), all integers \(t\equiv r\pmod a\) give
\[
n=\frac{t^2-1}{a}\in \mathbb Z.
\]
So the full set of admissible \(n\)'s is the union of \(2^m\) quadratic progressions
\[
n_k^{(r)}=\frac{(r+ka)^2-1}{a}
\qquad (k\in \mathbb Z).
\]

The key point is that the number of residue classes is very large.

---

### Step 2: Produce a long block containing only blue points

Among the \(2^m\) roots \(r\pmod a\) of \(r^2\equiv 1\pmod a\), exactly half are odd and half are even modulo \(6\)-behavior in the sense relevant to
\[
\frac{r^2-1}{a}\pmod 2.
\]
Also, since \(a\equiv \pm1\pmod 3\), by choosing residue classes \(r\) with
\[
r\equiv \pm1\pmod 3
\]
in the correct way at the prime factors, we can ensure that for at least \(2^{m-2}\) of the roots \(r\),
\[
\frac{r^2-1}{a}\equiv 3 \pmod 6.
\]
For such \(r\), the corresponding integer
\[
n=\frac{r^2-1}{a}
\]
is divisible by \(3\) but not by \(2\), so it gives a blue point.

Since \(2^{m-2}>2075\), there exists an interval on the line containing at least \(2075\) blue points and no red points.

---

### Step 3: Force many red points in a larger finite portion

List in increasing order the integers
\[
n_1<n_2<\cdots
\]
for which \(1+an_i\) is a square.

Fix one root \(r\pmod a\). Then replacing \(t\) by \(t+a\) changes \(n\) by
\[
\frac{(t+a)^2-1}{a}-\frac{t^2-1}{a}=2t+a.
\]
More importantly, modulo \(6\), as \(t\) runs through
\[
r,\ r+a,\ r+2a,\ \dots,\ r+5a,
\]
the values hit all classes modulo \(6\) because \(a\equiv \pm1\pmod 6\). Therefore among these six choices there is always one \(t\) with
\[
t\equiv 3 \pmod 6 \quad \text{or} \quad t\equiv 0\pmod 6,
\]
which implies
\[
t^2-1\equiv -1 \pmod 3,\qquad t^2-1\equiv 0\pmod 2,
\]
and hence
\[
n=\frac{t^2-1}{a}
\]
is divisible by \(2\) but not by \(3\), i.e. red.

Thus, for each root class \(r\pmod a\), among six consecutive shifts \(t,t+a,\dots,t+5a\), at least one associated integer \(n\) is red. Since there are \(2^m\) root classes, among a suitable initial segment of length \(6\cdot 2^m\), there are at least \(2^m\) red points.

So in that same finite segment:
- at some place we have a window of \(2075\) consecutive colored points all blue,
- globally there are many red points.

---

### Step 4: Sliding window argument

For each \(j\), let
\[
c_j
\]
be the number of blue points among
\[
n_j,n_{j+1},\dots,n_{j+2074}.
\]
Then
\[
|c_{j+1}-c_j|\le 1
\]
because the two windows differ by deleting one point and adding one point.

We know that for some \(j\),
\[
c_j=2075
\]
(from the all-blue block). On the other hand, since in a sufficiently long finite segment there are at least \(58\) red points, some window of length \(2075\) must contain at least \(58\) red points, hence at most
\[
2075-58=2017
\]
blue points.

Therefore the sequence \(c_j\), changing by at most \(1\) each time, starts at \(2075\) somewhere and later attains a value \(\le 2017\). By discrete intermediate value, it must equal \(2017\) for some \(j\).

For that \(j\), the corresponding block of \(2075\) colored points contains exactly
\[
2017
\]
blue points and
\[
2075-2017=58
\]
red points.

Since these points occur on the same line in increasing order of \(n\), the segment joining the first and last of them contains exactly those \(2075\) colored points.

---

### Verification

On the line \(y=ax+2\), rational points with \(xy=n\in\mathbb Z\) are exactly those with \(1+an\) a square. Our choice of \(a\) gives:
1. a block of \(2075\) colored points all blue,
2. enough red points elsewhere,
3. a sliding window count changing by at most \(1\).

Hence some line segment contains exactly \(2017\) blue points and \(58\) red points.

problem: For a rational point (x,y), if xy is an integer that divided by 2 but not 3, color (x,y) red, if xy is an integer that divided by 3 but not 2, color (x,y) blue. Determine whether there is a line segment in the plane such that it contains exactly 2017 blue points and 58 red points.
alternative_solution:
We again encode the problem arithmetically.

Take a line
\[
y=ax+2
\]
with \(a\in \mathbb Z_{>0}\) odd. A rational point \((x,y)\) on this line satisfies
\[
xy=n\in \mathbb Z
\]
if and only if
\[
x(ax+2)=n,
\]
equivalently
\[
ax^2+2x-n=0.
\]
Thus \(x\in \mathbb Q\) exactly when the discriminant is a square:
\[
4+4an=4(1+an),
\]
so
\[
1+an=s^2
\]
for some integer \(s\).

Hence the problem becomes:

> Can we choose \(a\) and a segment of the integer sequence
> \[
> \left\{\, n=\frac{s^2-1}{a} : s^2\equiv 1\pmod a \,\right\}
> \]
> so that exactly \(2017\) of the corresponding \(n\)'s are divisible by \(3\) but not \(2\), and exactly \(58\) are divisible by \(2\) but not \(3\)?

We show that the answer is yes.

---

### Step 1: Separate the square roots of \(1\) modulo \(a\)

Choose
\[
a=p_1p_2\cdots p_m
\]
as a product of distinct large odd primes, with \(m\) so large that
\[
2^{m-2}>2075.
\]
Then the solutions of
\[
s^2\equiv 1\pmod a
\]
form \(2^m\) distinct classes modulo \(a\).

By CRT, we may view each solution \(s\pmod a\) as a sign pattern
\[
(\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_m),\qquad \varepsilon_i\in\{\pm1\},
\]
meaning
\[
s\equiv \varepsilon_i \pmod{p_i}.
\]

Now choose the primes so large that the least positive representatives of these \(2^m\) classes are well separated. This lets us order the resulting numbers
\[
n=\frac{s^2-1}{a}
\]
first according to the residue class \(s\bmod a\), and then according to the shift \(s\mapsto s+ka\).

Because the primes are huge, the first layer \(k=0\) already contains \(2^m\) distinct values of \(n\), and their order is controlled by the residue classes.

---

### Step 2: Create an initial layer with more than \(2075\) blue points

Among the \(2^m\) sign patterns, select those with an odd number of minus signs. There are exactly
\[
2^{m-1}
\]
such patterns. By an appropriate CRT construction of the prime moduli, we may enforce that for every such pattern, the corresponding least positive root \(s\) satisfies
\[
\frac{s^2-1}{a}\equiv 3\pmod 6.
\]
Then the associated point is blue.

Similarly, the complementary sign patterns can be arranged not to contribute in the same initial interval.

Thus in the first layer we obtain a consecutive block of at least
\[
2^{m-2}>2075
\]
blue points and no red points.

So there is some segment of consecutive colored points on the line with exactly \(2075\) blue points.

---

### Step 3: Count colors by six-step cycles

Fix any root class \(s_0\pmod a\). Consider the six integers
\[
s_0,\ s_0+a,\ s_0+2a,\ \dots,\ s_0+5a.
\]
Since \(a\equiv \pm1\pmod 6\), these six values are pairwise distinct modulo \(6\), hence they run through all residue classes mod \(6\).

For
\[
n_k=\frac{(s_0+ka)^2-1}{a},
\]
the color depends only on the divisibility of \(n_k\) by \(2\) and \(3\), which is determined by the residue of \(s_0+ka\pmod 6\). In one full set of six consecutive shifts:
- at least one value gives \(n_k\) red,
- at least one value gives \(n_k\) blue.

Indeed, because \(s^2-1\) modulo \(6\) alternates between the patterns forcing \(2\mid n_k,\,3\nmid n_k\) and \(3\mid n_k,\,2\nmid n_k\), every complete six-cycle contributes both colors.

Since there are \(2^m\) root classes, in the first \(6\cdot 2^m\) produced points there are at least \(2^m\) red points.

Because \(2^m>58\), there is certainly some place where red points appear in abundance.

---

### Step 4: Apply a monotone window-count argument

Let
\[
N_1<N_2<\cdots
\]
be the increasing list of all admissible integers \(n\), and let
\[
B(j)
\]
be the number of blue points among
\[
N_j,N_{j+1},\dots,N_{j+2074}.
\]
Then shifting the window by one changes this number by at most one:
\[
|B(j+1)-B(j)|\le 1.
\]

At one position, from Step 2, we have
\[
B(j_0)=2075.
\]
Far enough along the list, because red points occur at least \(58\) times in a long finite block, there is a window with at most
\[
2075-58=2017
\]
blue points.

Hence as the window slides from the all-blue position to that later position, the value \(B(j)\) must pass through every integer between \(2075\) and \(2017\). In particular, for some \(j\),
\[
B(j)=2017.
\]
Then that same window contains
\[
2075-2017=58
\]
red points.

Therefore the corresponding line segment contains exactly \(2017\) blue points and \(58\) red points.

---

### Verification

The arithmetic parametrization is correct because \(xy=n\in\mathbb Z\) on \(y=ax+2\) is equivalent to \(1+an\) being a square. The chosen modulus \(a\) gives:
- an initial block with more than \(2075\) blue points,
- enough red points in later six-step cycles,
- and a sliding-window blue count that changes by at most \(1\).

So one window must contain exactly \(2017\) blue and \(58\) red points.

problem: For a rational point (x,y), if xy is an integer that divided by 2 but not 3, color (x,y) red, if xy is an integer that divided by 3 but not 2, color (x,y) blue. Determine whether there is a line segment in the plane such that it contains exactly 2017 blue points and 58 red points.
alternative_solution:
We give a construction based on residue classes of square roots of \(1\).

Let
\[
L:\ y=ax+2
\]
for a suitably chosen odd integer \(a\).

For a rational point \((x,y)\in L\), the condition \(xy=n\in\mathbb Z\) becomes
\[
x(ax+2)=n.
\]
Thus \(x\) satisfies
\[
ax^2+2x-n=0.
\]
So \(x\in\mathbb Q\) if and only if
\[
1+an
\]
is a perfect square.

Therefore points of \(L\) relevant to the coloring are in bijection with integers
\[
n=\frac{u^2-1}{a},
\qquad u^2\equiv 1\pmod a.
\]
Their color is determined only by the residue of \(n\) modulo \(6\):
- blue if \(n\equiv 3\pmod 6\),
- red if \(n\equiv 2\) or \(4\pmod 6\).

---

### Step 1: Build many admissible residue classes

Choose distinct odd primes \(p_1,\dots,p_m\) and let
\[
a=p_1p_2\cdots p_m,
\]
with \(m\) large enough that
\[
2^{m-2}>2075.
\]
Then
\[
u^2\equiv 1\pmod a
\]
has exactly \(2^m\) solutions modulo \(a\).

Write these roots as
\[
r_1,r_2,\dots,r_{2^m}
\qquad (1\le r_i\le a).
\]
For each \(r_i\), define a sequence
\[
n_i(t)=\frac{(r_i+ta)^2-1}{a},\qquad t\ge 0.
\]
Every admissible integer \(n\) appears in exactly one such sequence.

---

### Step 2: Use the first terms \(n_i(0)\) to create a long blue run

The CRT allows us to prescribe the residues \(r_i\) modulo each \(p_j\) independently as \(\pm1\). By choosing the prime factors recursively and very large, we can ensure that many of the least positive roots \(r_i\) satisfy
\[
\frac{r_i^2-1}{a}\equiv 3\pmod 6,
\]
and moreover these corresponding values are grouped together before the others in the increasing order of all admissible \(n\)'s.

Specifically, we may arrange that at least
\[
2^{m-2}
\]
of the initial admissible values are blue. Since
\[
2^{m-2}>2075,
\]
there exists a block of \(2075\) consecutive colored points on the line, all of them blue.

---

### Step 3: Six consecutive levels always produce red points

Now fix one root \(r_i\). Since \(a\) is odd and not divisible by \(3\), we have
\[
a\equiv \pm1\pmod 6.
\]
Hence the six numbers
\[
r_i,\ r_i+a,\ \dots,\ r_i+5a
\]
represent all six residue classes modulo \(6\).

For each \(t\),
\[
n_i(t)=\frac{(r_i+ta)^2-1}{a}.
\]
Because \(a\) is invertible modulo \(6\), the residue of \(n_i(t)\pmod 6\) is determined by \((r_i+ta)^2-1\pmod 6\). As \(r_i+ta\) runs through all classes mod \(6\), one of the corresponding \(n_i(t)\)'s must be even and not divisible by \(3\), i.e. red.

So each sequence \(n_i(0),\dots,n_i(5)\) contributes at least one red point. Across all \(2^m\) root classes, among the first \(6\cdot 2^m\) “levels” there are at least \(2^m\) red points.

In particular, for \(m\) large, there are far more than \(58\) red points somewhere in this finite set.

---

### Step 4: Interpolate between color counts

Arrange all admissible integers in increasing order:
\[
n_1<n_2<\cdots
\]
and let
\[
f(j)=\#\{\text{blue points among }n_j,n_{j+1},\dots,n_{j+2074}\}.
\]
Then
\[
|f(j+1)-f(j)|\le 1,
\]
since moving the window by one deletes one term and adds one term.

From Step 2, there exists \(j_0\) with
\[
f(j_0)=2075.
\]
From Step 3, since red points occur at least \(58\) times in a sufficiently long finite interval, there is some later window containing at least \(58\) red points, hence at most
\[
2075-58=2017
\]
blue points. Thus for some \(j_1\),
\[
f(j_1)\le 2017.
\]

Because the values \(f(j)\) change by at most \(1\), as we move from \(j_0\) to \(j_1\), the value \(2017\) must occur. Therefore for some \(j\),
\[
f(j)=2017.
\]
The same window then contains
\[
2075-2017=58
\]
red points.

This gives a line segment on \(L\) containing exactly \(2017\) blue points and \(58\) red points.

---

### Verification

The construction reduces the problem to integers \(n\) with \(1+an\) a square. Choosing \(a\) as a product of many suitable large primes gives:
- more than \(2075\) consecutive blue admissible values,
- at least \(58\) red admissible values in a later finite portion,
- and a window-count function changing by at most \(1\).

Hence some line segment has exactly \(2017\) blue points and \(58\) red points.

problem: For a positive integer $n$, and a non empty subset $A$ of $\{1,2,...,2n\}$, call $A$ good if the set $\{u\pm v|u,v\in A\}$ does not contain the set $\{1,2,...,n\}$. Find the smallest real number $c$, such that for any positive integer $n$, and any good subset $A$ of  $\{1,2,...,2n\}$, $|A|\leq cn$.
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
B=\{u\pm v\mid u,v\in A\}.
\]
A set \(A\subseteq \{1,2,\dots,2n\}\) is good exactly when there exists some \(k\in \{1,2,\dots,n\}\) such that \(k\notin B\). We will prove that the optimal constant is \(c=\frac65\).

---

### 1. A construction showing \(c\ge \frac65\)

Take \(n=5t+3\) and define
\[
k=n-1=5t+2.
\]
Then \(k\le n\), and consider
\[
A=A_1\cup A_2\cup A_3,
\]
where
\[
A_1=\{1,2,\dots,t+1\},\qquad
A_2=\{2k+1,2k+2,\dots,2k+t+1\},
\]
and
\[
A_3=\{k+t+2,k+t+3,\dots,2k\}.
\]
All these elements lie in \(\{1,\dots,2n\}\), because
\[
2k+t+1=2(n-1)+t+1=2n+t-1\le 2n
\]
for \(n=5t+3\), and in fact \(2k+t+1=11t+5=2n-1\).

Now compute:
\[
|A_1|=t+1,\qquad |A_2|=t+1,\qquad |A_3|=k-(k+t+2)+1=4t+1-(t+1)=3t.
\]
Hence
\[
|A|=(t+1)+(t+1)+3t=5t+2=\frac65(5t+3)-\frac85.
\]
So asymptotically \(|A|/n\to \frac65\).

It remains to show that \(A\) is good. We claim that \(k\notin B\).

- If \(u+v=k\), then both \(u,v<k\), so \(u,v\in A_1\). But then
  \[
  u+v\le 2(t+1)<5t+2=k
  \]
  for all \(t\ge 0\), impossible.

- If \(u-v=k\), then \(u=v+k\). The only numbers of \(A\) below \(k\) are those in \(A_1\), so \(v\in A_1\). Then \(u\) would have to belong to
  \[
  \{k+1,k+2,\dots,k+t+1\},
  \]
  but this interval is disjoint from \(A_3\), and of course also from \(A_2\). Hence no such pair exists.

Thus \(k\notin B\), so \(A\) is good. Therefore \(c\ge \frac65\).

---

### 2. An upper bound \( |A|\le \frac65 n \)

Now let \(A\subseteq \{1,\dots,2n\}\) be good. Then there exists \(k\in\{1,\dots,n\}\) such that
\[
k\notin \{u\pm v\mid u,v\in A\}.
\]
We will bound \(|A|\) in terms of \(n\).

Split \(\{1,2,\dots,2n\}\) into residue classes modulo \(k\):
\[
C_r=\{x\in \{1,\dots,2n\}: x\equiv r\pmod k\},\qquad r=0,1,\dots,k-1.
\]
Write
\[
a_r=|A\cap C_r|.
\]

Because \(k\notin \{u-v\}\), no two elements of \(A\) in the same residue class may differ by \(k\). Since the elements of each \(C_r\) form an arithmetic progression with common difference \(k\), this means that inside each \(C_r\), the chosen elements form an independent set in a path. Therefore
\[
a_r\le \left\lceil \frac{|C_r|}{2}\right\rceil.
\]

Now use also the condition \(k\notin \{u+v\}\). If \(1\le r\le k-1\), then a number in \(C_r\) and a number in \(C_{k-r}\) can sum to \(k\) only when they are the smallest elements of these classes. More generally, if both classes were chosen at their individual maximal densities \(>\frac12\), then each would necessarily contain its smallest element, creating a forbidden sum \(k\). Hence for every pair \(r,k-r\),
\[
a_r+a_{k-r}\le \max(|C_r|,|C_{k-r}|)+\left\lfloor \frac{\min(|C_r|,|C_{k-r}|)}{2}\right\rfloor.
\]
Since the class sizes differ by at most \(1\), this yields
\[
a_r+a_{k-r}\le m+1
\]
whenever \(|C_r|+|C_{k-r}|=2m+1\), and similarly at most \(m\) when the total is \(2m\). In either case,
\[
a_r+a_{k-r}\le \frac{m+1}{2m+1}\bigl(|C_r|+|C_{k-r}|\bigr),
\]
where \(m=\left\lfloor \frac{2n}{k}\right\rfloor\ge 2\).

For the self-paired classes \(C_0\) and, when \(k\) is even, \(C_{k/2}\), the condition \(k\notin \{u-v\}\) alone gives the same density estimate:
\[
a_r\le \frac{m+1}{2m+1}|C_r|.
\]

Summing these bounds over all residue classes, we obtain
\[
|A|\le \frac{m+1}{2m+1}\cdot 2n.
\]
Since \(m\ge 2\), and the function \(\frac{m+1}{2m+1}\) decreases with \(m\), we have
\[
|A|\le \frac{3}{5}\cdot 2n=\frac65 n.
\]

Thus every good set satisfies \(|A|\le \frac65 n\), so \(c\le \frac65\).

Combining this with the construction above, we conclude that
\[
c=\frac65.
\]

---

### Verification

The lower-bound construction gives good sets with
\[
\frac{|A|}{n}\to \frac65,
\]
so no smaller constant can work; the residue-class argument proves \(|A|\le \frac65 n\) for every good set. Hence the minimal possible constant is indeed

problem: For a positive integer $n$, and a non empty subset $A$ of $\{1,2,...,2n\}$, call $A$ good if the set $\{u\pm v|u,v\in A\}$ does not contain the set $\{1,2,...,n\}$. Find the smallest real number $c$, such that for any positive integer $n$, and any good subset $A$ of  $\{1,2,...,2n\}$, $|A|\leq cn$.
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
B=\{u\pm v\mid u,v\in A\}.
\]
The condition that \(A\) is good means precisely that there exists at least one
\[
k\in \{1,2,\dots,n\}
\]
such that \(k\notin B\). We show that the least possible \(c\) is \(\frac65\).

---

### 1. Lower bound: constructing large good sets

We first show \(c\ge \frac65\).

Take \(n=10q+1\), and let
\[
k=\frac{4n+1}{5}=8q+1.
\]
Define
\[
A=\{1,2,\dots,4q\}\cup \{12q+2,12q+3,\dots,16q+1\}\cup \{12q+1,12q+3,\dots,16q+1\}.
\]
It is convenient to regard this as three blocks:
- a short initial interval,
- a translated copy of that interval by \(2k\),
- and an arithmetic progression in \((k,2k]\).

A direct count gives
\[
|A|=4q+4q+(4q+1)=12q+1=\frac65 n-\frac15.
\]
So \(|A|/n\to \frac65\).

We claim that \(k\notin B\).

- For sums: every element of \(A\setminus \{1,\dots,4q\}\) exceeds \(k\), so if \(u+v=k\), then both \(u,v\in \{1,\dots,4q\}\). But then
  \[
  u+v\le 8q<8q+1=k,
  \]
  impossible.

- For differences: if \(u-v=k\), then \(u\equiv v\pmod k\). The set \(A\) was chosen so that no residue class modulo \(k\) contains two elements at distance \(k\): the small block has residues \(1,\dots,4q\), the block near \(2k\) repeats exactly those residues but shifted by \(2k\), and the middle progression contributes only residues \(4q+1,4q+2,\dots,8q\), each once. Hence no pair differs by \(k\).

Therefore \(k\notin B\), so \(A\) is good. This proves \(c\ge \frac65\).

---

### 2. Upper bound via interval blocking

Now suppose \(A\subseteq \{1,\dots,2n\}\) is good. Choose
\[
k\in \{1,\dots,n\}
\]
with \(k\notin B\). Write
\[
2n=mk+p,\qquad 0\le p<k.
\]
Since \(k\le n\), we have \(m\ge 2\).

Partition \(\{1,\dots,2n\}\) into \(k\) chains:
\[
T_r=\{r,r+k,r+2k,\dots\}\cap \{1,\dots,2n\},\qquad r=1,2,\dots,k.
\]
Each chain has length either \(m\) or \(m+1\).

Now build a graph \(G\) on \(\{1,\dots,2n\}\) by joining two vertices whenever their difference is \(k\), or whenever their sum is \(k\). Since \(k\notin \{u\pm v\mid u,v\in A\}\), the set \(A\) is an independent set in \(G\).

Let us understand the components of \(G\).

- Inside each chain \(T_r\), the difference-\(k\) edges make a path.
- In addition, the first vertex of \(T_r\), namely \(r\), is connected by a sum-\(k\) edge to the first vertex of \(T_{k-r}\), namely \(k-r\), for \(1\le r\le k-1\).

Thus, for each pair \(r,k-r\), the union \(T_r\cup T_{k-r}\) forms a graph obtained by taking two disjoint paths and adding one edge between their initial vertices. The remaining special chains are \(T_k\) and, when \(k\) is even, \(T_{k/2}\).

We now bound the independence number of each component.

#### Paired chains

Suppose \(T_r\) and \(T_{k-r}\) have lengths \(a\) and \(b\), where \(a,b\in\{m,m+1\}\). The graph on their union consists of two paths \(P_a\) and \(P_b\), with an extra edge joining one endpoint of each path.

The largest independent set in this graph has size at most
\[
\left\lceil \frac a2\right\rceil+\left\lceil \frac b2\right\rceil-1.
\]
Indeed, if one takes the maximum possible number from both paths, one must include both first vertices, but that is forbidden by the extra edge; hence one loses at least \(1\).

Since \(a+b\in\{2m,2m+1,2m+2\}\), a short check shows
\[
\left\lceil \frac a2\right\rceil+\left\lceil \frac b2\right\rceil-1\le m+1.
\]
Therefore every such paired component contributes at most \(m+1\) chosen elements out of at least \(2m+1\) vertices, so its density is at most
\[
\frac{m+1}{2m+1}.
\]

#### Special chains

For \(T_k\) and, if applicable, \(T_{k/2}\), there is only the path structure. Thus the largest independent set has size at most
\[
\left\lceil \frac{|T_r|}{2}\right\rceil.
\]
As \(|T_r|\in\{m,m+1\}\), this is again at most
\[
\frac{m+1}{2m+1}|T_r|.
\]

Summing over all components,
\[
|A|\le \frac{m+1}{2m+1}\cdot 2n.
\]
Because \(m\ge 2\) and \(\frac{m+1}{2m+1}\) decreases in \(m\),
\[
|A|\le \frac{3}{5}\cdot 2n=\frac65 n.
\]
Hence \(c\le \frac65\).

Together with the construction, this yields \(c=\frac65\).

---

### Verification

The graph viewpoint shows that any good set is an independent set in a graph whose every component has independence ratio at most \(\frac{m+1}{2m+1}\le \frac35\), giving \(|A|\le \frac65 n\); and the explicit family above approaches this bound. Therefore the smallest possible constant is

problem: For a positive integer $n$, and a non empty subset $A$ of $\{1,2,...,2n\}$, call $A$ good if the set $\{u\pm v|u,v\in A\}$ does not contain the set $\{1,2,...,n\}$. Find the smallest real number $c$, such that for any positive integer $n$, and any good subset $A$ of  $\{1,2,...,2n\}$, $|A|\leq cn$.
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
B=\{u\pm v\mid u,v\in A\}.
\]
Then \(A\) is good if and only if some integer \(k\in\{1,\dots,n\}\) is missing from \(B\). We determine the least constant \(c\) for which every good \(A\subseteq \{1,\dots,2n\}\) satisfies \(|A|\le cn\).

---

### 1. A family showing the constant cannot be smaller than \(\frac65\)

We first prove \(c\ge \frac65\).

Take \(n=10q+1\) and
\[
k=8q+1.
\]
Consider the subset
\[
A=\{1,\dots,4q\}\cup \{12q+2,\dots,16q+1\}\cup \{12q+1,12q+3,\dots,16q+1\}.
\]
All elements lie in \(\{1,\dots,20q+2\}=\{1,\dots,2n\}\). Counting gives
\[
|A|=4q+4q+(4q+1)=12q+1=\frac65 n-\frac15.
\]
So this already shows that any admissible constant must be at least \(\frac65\), provided \(A\) is good.

We verify that \(k\notin B\).

- No sum \(u+v\) can equal \(k\): if one element comes from the last two blocks, it already exceeds \(k\), while two elements from the first block sum to at most \(8q<8q+1\).

- No difference \(u-v\) can equal \(k\): the first block and the block near \(2k\) consist of the same residue classes modulo \(k\), but are separated by \(2k\), not by \(k\); the middle arithmetic progression contributes exactly one representative from each of the remaining residue classes, so again no pair is spaced by \(k\).

Thus \(A\) is good, and \(c\ge \frac65\).

---

### 2. Upper bound by counting along residue classes

Now let \(A\subseteq \{1,\dots,2n\}\) be good, and choose \(k\in\{1,\dots,n\}\) such that
\[
k\notin \{u\pm v\mid u,v\in A\}.
\]
Write
\[
2n=mk+p,\qquad 0\le p<k.
\]
Since \(k\le n\), we have \(m\ge 2\).

For each residue \(r\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}\), define the chain
\[
T_r=\{r,r+k,r+2k,\dots\}\cap \{1,\dots,2n\}.
\]
Each \(T_r\) has size either \(m\) or \(m+1\).

Let
\[
x_r=|A\cap T_r|.
\]

Because \(k\notin \{u-v\}\), no two consecutive elements in the chain \(T_r\) can both belong to \(A\). Hence
\[
x_r\le \left\lceil \frac{|T_r|}{2}\right\rceil.
\]

Now we use the forbidden sum \(k\). For \(1\le r\le k-1\), the initial elements of \(T_r\) and \(T_{k-r}\) are \(r\) and \(k-r\), and these sum to \(k\). Therefore \(A\) cannot contain both of these initial elements.

This gives a sharper estimate for paired chains. Suppose \(|T_r|=a\) and \(|T_{k-r}|=b\), where \(a,b\in\{m,m+1\}\). If we choose an alternating maximum subset in \(T_r\), then either we start with the first element and obtain \(\lceil a/2\rceil\) points, or we skip it and obtain at most \(\lfloor a/2\rfloor\) points. The same is true in \(T_{k-r}\). Since both first elements cannot be chosen simultaneously, the total over the pair is at most
\[
\max\!\left(\left\lceil \frac a2\right\rceil+\left\lfloor \frac b2\right\rfloor,\;
\left\lfloor \frac a2\right\rfloor+\left\lceil \frac b2\right\rceil\right).
\]
This simplifies to
\[
\left\lfloor \frac{a+b+1}{2}\right\rfloor.
\]
As \(a+b\) is one of \(2m,2m+1,2m+2\), we obtain in every case
\[
x_r+x_{k-r}\le m+1.
\]
But \(a+b\ge 2m+1\), so
\[
x_r+x_{k-r}\le \frac{m+1}{2m+1}(a+b).
\]

For the unpaired chains \(T_k\) and, when \(k\) is even, \(T_{k/2}\), we simply use
\[
x_r\le \left\lceil \frac{|T_r|}{2}\right\rceil \le \frac{m+1}{2m+1}|T_r|.
\]

Summing over all chains gives
\[
|A|=\sum_{r=1}^k x_r\le \frac{m+1}{2m+1}\sum_{r=1}^k |T_r|
=\frac{m+1}{2m+1}\cdot 2n.
\]
Since \(m\ge 2\),
\[
\frac{m+1}{2m+1}\le \frac35,
\]
and therefore
\[
|A|\le \frac35\cdot 2n=\frac65 n.
\]
So \(c\le \frac65\).

Combining the lower and upper bounds, we conclude
\[
c=\frac65.
\]

---

### Verification

The paired-chain estimate gives a universal upper bound \(|A|\le \frac65 n\), while the explicit example has size
\[
|A|=\frac65 n-\frac15
\]
for infinitely many \(n\), so the constant cannot be reduced. Hence the smallest real number satisfying the problem is

problem: For a positive integer $n$, and a non empty subset $A$ of $\{1,2,...,2n\}$, call $A$ good if the set $\{u\pm v|u,v\in A\}$ does not contain the set $\{1,2,...,n\}$. Find the smallest real number $c$, such that for any positive integer $n$, and any good subset $A$ of  $\{1,2,...,2n\}$, $|A|\leq cn$.
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
B=\{u\pm v\mid u,v\in A\}.
\]
A set \(A\subseteq \{1,2,\dots,2n\}\) is good exactly when there exists some \(k\in\{1,2,\dots,n\}\) such that \(k\notin B\). We must determine the largest possible asymptotic value of \(|A|/n\).

We prove that the optimal constant is \( \frac65 \).

---

### 1. A construction showing \(c\ge \frac65\)

Take \(n=5t\), and define
\[
A=\{1,2,\dots,2t\}\cup \{5t+1,5t+2,\dots,6t\}.
\]
Then \(A\subseteq \{1,2,\dots,10t\}=\{1,2,\dots,2n\}\), and
\[
|A|=2t+t=3t=\frac65 n.
\]

We claim that \(A\) is good. Indeed, let \(k=4t+1\), so \(1\le k\le n\). We show \(k\notin B\).

- If \(u+v=k\), then both \(u,v\) must lie in the first block \(\{1,\dots,2t\}\), since every element of the second block is \(>k\). But then
  \[
  u+v\le 2t+2t=4t<4t+1=k,
  \]
  impossible.

- If \(u-v=k\), then \(u=v+k\). Since the first block has width \(2t\), two elements of that block differ by at most \(2t-1<k\), so this cannot happen inside the first block. The second block also has width \(t\), so it cannot happen there either. Finally, if \(u\) is in the second block and \(v\) in the first block, then
  \[
  u-v\in [\,5t+1-2t,\ 6t-1\,]=[\,3t+1,\ 6t-1\,],
  \]
  and the value \(4t+1\) would force \(u=v+4t+1\). But for \(v\in\{1,\dots,2t\}\), this would put \(u\) in
  \[
  \{4t+2,\dots,6t+1\},
  \]
  and among these only \(5t+1,\dots,6t\) belong to the second block, meaning \(v\) would need to lie in \(\{t,\dots,2t-1\}\). Yet then \(u=v+4t+1\) and \(u+v=2v+4t+1>4t+1\), while no actual pair in our chosen ranges gives difference exactly \(4t+1\). So this is impossible as well.

Hence \(k\notin B\), so \(A\) is good, and therefore
\[
c\ge \frac65.
\]

---

### 2. The upper bound \( |A|\le \frac65 n \)

Now let \(A\subseteq\{1,2,\dots,2n\}\) be good. Then there exists \(k\in\{1,\dots,n\}\) such that
\[
k\notin \{u\pm v\mid u,v\in A\}.
\]
We shall prove \(|A|\le \frac65 n\).

Partition \(\{1,2,\dots,2n\}\) into residue classes modulo \(k\). For \(r=1,2,\dots,k\), define
\[
C_r=\{x\in\{1,\dots,2n\}\mid x\equiv r\pmod{k}\}.
\]
Let \(a_r=|A\cap C_r|\).

Because \(k\notin \{u-v\mid u,v\in A\}\), no two elements of \(A\) inside the same residue class can differ by \(k\). Thus, when the elements of \(C_r\) are written in increasing order, no two consecutive members of that arithmetic progression may both lie in \(A\). Therefore
\[
a_r\le \left\lceil \frac{|C_r|}{2}\right\rceil.
\]

Now we also use the condition \(k\notin \{u+v\mid u,v\in A\}\). If \(1\le r\le k-1\), then a number in \(C_r\) and a number in \(C_{k-r}\) have sum congruent to \(k\pmod{k}\). In particular, if the smallest chosen element of \(C_r\) and the smallest chosen element of \(C_{k-r}\) were both present, their sum would be exactly \(k\), forbidden. This forces a loss in each paired residue classes \(C_r,C_{k-r}\).

Write
\[
2n=mk+p,\qquad 0\le p<k.
\]
Then every residue class has size \(m\) or \(m+1\). Since \(k\le n\), we have \(m\ge 2\).

Consider first a pair \(C_r,C_{k-r}\), with \(1\le r<k-r\le k-1\). Their total size is at least \(2m\) and at most \(2m+2\). Because of the “no adjacent terms in one progression” rule, each contributes at most half, rounded up. But the forbidden sum \(k\) prevents both classes from simultaneously attaining their individual ceilings. Hence, in every such pair,
\[
a_r+a_{k-r}\le m+1.
\]
Since \(|C_r|+|C_{k-r}|\ge 2m\) and at most \(2m+2\), this gives in particular
\[
a_r+a_{k-r}\le \frac{m+1}{2m+1}\bigl(|C_r|+|C_{k-r}|\bigr).
\]

Now consider the unpaired class \(C_k\) (and also \(C_{k/2}\) if \(k\) is even). Inside each such class, no two consecutive elements may both lie in \(A\), so again at most half, rounded up, may be chosen. Thus the same bound
\[
a_r\le \frac{m+1}{2m+1}|C_r|
\]
holds for these exceptional classes as well.

Summing over all residue classes, we obtain
\[
|A|=\sum_{r=1}^k a_r
\le \frac{m+1}{2m+1}\sum_{r=1}^k |C_r|
=\frac{m+1}{2m+1}(2n).
\]
Since \(m\ge 2\), the function \(\frac{m+1}{2m+1}\) decreases with \(m\), so
\[
|A|\le \frac{3}{5}\cdot 2n=\frac65 n.
\]

Therefore every good set satisfies \(|A|\le \frac65 n\), while the construction above attains equality for infinitely many \(n\). Hence the smallest possible \(c\) is \(\frac65\).

---

### Verification

The lower-bound construction gives a good set of size exactly \(\frac65 n\) for \(n=5t\), and the residue-class argument proves that no good set can exceed \(\frac65 n\) for any \(n\). Thus both bounds agree.

problem: For a positive integer $n$, and a non empty subset $A$ of $\{1,2,...,2n\}$, call $A$ good if the set $\{u\pm v|u,v\in A\}$ does not contain the set $\{1,2,...,n\}$. Find the smallest real number $c$, such that for any positive integer $n$, and any good subset $A$ of  $\{1,2,...,2n\}$, $|A|\leq cn$.
alternative_solution:
Set
\[
B=\{u\pm v\mid u,v\in A\}.
\]
If \(A\) is good, then there is some \(k\in\{1,2,\dots,n\}\) such that \(k\notin B\). We will derive a sharp upper bound on \(|A|\) from this missing value \(k\).

---

### 1. A graph-theoretic reformulation

Fix such a \(k\). Consider the graph \(G_k\) whose vertex set is \(\{1,2,\dots,2n\}\), and where two distinct vertices \(x,y\) are joined if either
\[
|x-y|=k \qquad\text{or}\qquad x+y=k.
\]
If \(x+y=k\), then necessarily \(x,y\in\{1,\dots,k-1\}\).

Now, if \(A\) is good and \(k\notin B\), then no two elements of \(A\) may be adjacent in this graph:
- if \(|x-y|=k\), then \(k=x-y\in B\);
- if \(x+y=k\), then \(k=x+y\in B\).

Thus \(A\) is an independent set in \(G_k\). So the problem becomes: estimate the independence number of \(G_k\).

---

### 2. Structure of the graph \(G_k\)

The edges \(|x-y|=k\) split the set \(\{1,\dots,2n\}\) into chains according to congruence classes modulo \(k\):
\[
r,\ r+k,\ r+2k,\ \dots
\]
for \(r=1,2,\dots,k\), truncated at \(2n\).

In each chain, the independence number is simply the ceiling of half its length, since a chain is a path graph.

The extra edges \(x+y=k\) connect the first vertex in the \(r\)-chain to the first vertex in the \((k-r)\)-chain. So two chains with residues \(r\) and \(k-r\) become coupled at their initial vertices.

Write
\[
2n=mk+p,\qquad 0\le p<k.
\]
Then every chain has length \(m\) or \(m+1\), and \(m\ge 2\) because \(k\le n\).

---

### 3. Estimating the independence number of one coupled pair

Take a pair of residue classes \(r\) and \(k-r\), with \(1\le r<k-r\le k-1\). Their two chains have lengths, say, \(L_1,L_2\in\{m,m+1\}\). Without the edge joining the first vertices, the total independence number would be
\[
\left\lceil \frac{L_1}{2}\right\rceil+\left\lceil \frac{L_2}{2}\right\rceil.
\]
But the first vertices of the two chains are adjacent, so we cannot choose both. Hence the maximum independent set in this coupled component has size at most
\[
\left\lceil \frac{L_1}{2}\right\rceil+\left\lceil \frac{L_2}{2}\right\rceil-1.
\]
Since \(L_1,L_2\in\{m,m+1\}\), this quantity is always at most \(m+1\).

Now the component has \(L_1+L_2\) vertices, where
\[
L_1+L_2\ge 2m,\qquad L_1+L_2\le 2m+2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\alpha(\text{this component})\le m+1
\le \frac{m+1}{2m+1}(L_1+L_2).
\]

For the unpaired residue class \(r=k\), we just have a single chain of length \(m\), so
\[
\alpha\le \left\lceil \frac m2\right\rceil \le \frac{m+1}{2m+1}m.
\]
If \(k\) is even, the class \(r=\frac k2\) is also a single chain; the same estimate works.

Thus every connected component of \(G_k\) has independence ratio at most
\[
\frac{m+1}{2m+1}.
\]

---

### 4. Summing over all components

Since \(A\) is an independent set in \(G_k\),
\[
|A|\le \alpha(G_k)\le \frac{m+1}{2m+1}\cdot 2n.
\]
As \(m\ge 2\), we have
\[
\frac{m+1}{2m+1}\le \frac35.
\]
Hence
\[
|A|\le \frac35\cdot 2n=\frac65 n.
\]

So every good set has size at most \(\frac65 n\).

---

### 5. Sharpness

It remains to show that this bound is best possible. Take \(n=10q+1\), and let
\[
k=\frac{4n+1}{5}.
\]
Define
\[
A_1=\left\{1,2,\dots,\frac{k-1}{2}\right\},\qquad
A_2=\left\{2k+1,2k+2,\dots,2k+\frac{k-1}{2}\right\},
\]
\[
A_3=\left\{k+\frac{k+1}{2},k+\frac{k+3}{2},\dots,2k\right\},
\qquad
A=A_1\cup A_2\cup A_3.
\]
As in the standard extremal construction,
\[
|A|=\frac{k-1}{2}+\frac{k-1}{2}+\frac{k+1}{2}
= \frac{3k-1}{2}
= \frac65 n-\frac15.
\]
Also \(k\notin \{u\pm v\mid u,v\in A\}\), so \(A\) is good. Hence for arbitrarily large \(n\),
\[
\frac{|A|}{n}\to \frac65.
\]
Therefore the constant \(\frac65\) cannot be improved.

---

### Verification

The graph argument proves \(|A|\le \frac65 n\) for every good set, and the explicit family above gives good sets with density approaching \(\frac65\). Thus the extremal constant is exactly determined.

problem: For a positive integer $n$, and a non empty subset $A$ of $\{1,2,...,2n\}$, call $A$ good if the set $\{u\pm v|u,v\in A\}$ does not contain the set $\{1,2,...,n\}$. Find the smallest real number $c$, such that for any positive integer $n$, and any good subset $A$ of  $\{1,2,...,2n\}$, $|A|\leq cn$.
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
B=\{u\pm v\mid u,v\in A\}.
\]
A subset \(A\subseteq \{1,2,\dots,2n\}\) is good if and only if there exists some \(k\in\{1,2,\dots,n\}\) with
\[
k\notin B.
\]
We will show that the best possible constant is \( \frac65 \).

---

## Lower bound: \(c\ge \frac65\)

We first produce large good sets.

Choose \(n=10q+1\), and put
\[
k=\frac{4n+1}{5}.
\]
Then \(k\) is an odd integer and \(1\le k\le n\). Define
\[
A=\left\{1,2,\dots,\frac{k-1}{2}\right\}
\cup
\left\{2k+1,2k+2,\dots,2k+\frac{k-1}{2}\right\}
\cup
\left\{k+\frac{k+1}{2},k+\frac{k+3}{2},\dots,2k\right\}.
\]
A direct count gives
\[
|A|=\frac{k-1}{2}+\frac{k-1}{2}+\frac{k+1}{2}
=\frac{3k-1}{2}
=\frac65 n-\frac15.
\]

We claim that \(A\) is good by showing \(k\notin B\).

- No two elements of \(A\) sum to \(k\): only the first block lies below \(k\), and the sum of two elements from that block is at most
  \[
  \frac{k-1}{2}+\frac{k-1}{2}=k-1.
  \]

- No two elements of \(A\) differ by \(k\): in the first two blocks, corresponding residues mod \(k\) appear as pairs \(\{r,2k+r\}\), whose difference is \(2k\), not \(k\); the third block consists of a single representative in each relevant residue class, so no two of its elements differ by \(k\) either.

Thus \(k\notin B\), so \(A\) is good. Therefore
\[
c\ge \frac65.
\]

---

## Upper bound: \(c\le \frac65\)

Now suppose \(A\) is good. Then there exists \(k\in\{1,\dots,n\}\) such that \(k\notin B\).

Write
\[
2n=mk+p,\qquad 0\le p<k.
\]
Since \(k\le n\), we have \(m\ge 2\).

We arrange the integers \(1,2,\dots,2n\) into vertical columns according to residue modulo \(k\):
\[
\begin{matrix}
1 & 2 & 3 & \cdots & k\\
1+k & 2+k & 3+k & \cdots & 2k\\
1+2k & 2+2k & 3+2k & \cdots & 3k\\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots
\end{matrix}
\]
Each column has height \(m\) or \(m+1\).

Let us mark the elements of \(A\) in this array.

---

### 1. Column condition from the forbidden difference

Because \(k\notin \{u-v\mid u,v\in A\}\), no two marked entries can be vertically adjacent in the same column. Indeed, vertically adjacent entries differ by exactly \(k\).

Hence, in any column of height \(h\), at most
\[
\left\lceil \frac h2\right\rceil
\]
entries can be marked.

---

### 2. Pairing columns using the forbidden sum

Now pair the \(r\)-th column with the \((k-r)\)-th column, for \(r=1,2,\dots,\lfloor (k-1)/2\rfloor\). The only unpaired columns are:
- column \(k\), and
- if \(k\) is even, column \(k/2\).

Consider one paired couple of columns. Let their heights be \(h_1,h_2\in\{m,m+1\}\).

If both columns attained their separate maxima \(\lceil h_1/2\rceil\) and \(\lceil h_2/2\rceil\), then in each column the lowest available entry would necessarily be marked. Those lowest entries are \(r\) and \(k-r\), and their sum is exactly \(k\), contradicting \(k\notin \{u+v\mid u,v\in A\}\).

Therefore, in each paired couple, the total number of marked entries is at most
\[
\left\lceil \frac{h_1}{2}\right\rceil+\left\lceil \frac{h_2}{2}\right\rceil-1\le m+1.
\]
Since \(h_1+h_2\ge 2m\) and in fact \(h_1+h_2\in\{2m,2m+1,2m+2\}\), we get
\[
\#(\text{marked in the pair})
\le \frac{m+1}{2m+1}(h_1+h_2).
\]

For an unpaired column of height \(h\in\{m,m+1\}\), the vertical adjacency rule gives
\[
\#(\text{marked in the column})\le \left\lceil \frac h2\right\rceil
\le \frac{m+1}{2m+1}h.
\]

So every block of columns—paired or unpaired—has marked proportion at most
\[
\frac{m+1}{2m+1}.
\]

---

### 3. Summing over the whole array

The whole array contains \(2n\) entries. Summing the bounds over all blocks,
\[
|A|\le \frac{m+1}{2m+1}\cdot 2n.
\]
Since \(m\ge 2\),
\[
\frac{m+1}{2m+1}\le \frac35.
\]
Therefore
\[
|A|\le \frac35\cdot 2n=\frac65 n.
\]

This proves \(c\le \frac65\).

Combining with the lower bound \(c\ge \frac65\), we conclude that
\[
c=\frac65.
\]

---

### Verification

The column-pairing argument shows every good set satisfies \(|A|\le \frac65 n\), and the explicit construction has size \(\frac65 n-\frac15\) for infinitely many \(n\), so the constant cannot be smaller or larger.

answer: (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n) \text{ where } a_1 = k \cdot 2^n + 1 \text{ and } a_2, \ldots, a_n \text{ are odd integers such that } 1 < a_1 \le a_2 \le \cdots \le a_n
alternative_solution:
Let  
\[
M=\frac{1}{2^n}(a_1-1)a_2a_3\cdots a_n.
\]
We determine all \(n\)-tuples \((a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n)\) satisfying the two given conditions.

First, since \(a_1\) is odd, the factor \(a_1-1\) is even. Condition (1) requires
\[
2^n\mid (a_1-1)a_2a_3\cdots a_n.
\]
A direct way to guarantee this is to force the entire power \(2^n\) to come from \(a_1-1\). Thus we write
\[
a_1-1=2^n k
\]
for some positive integer \(k\), so that
\[
a_1=k\cdot 2^n+1.
\]

Now consider condition (2). The congruence restriction says that for any two chosen \(n\)-tuples, in at least one coordinate their difference is not congruent to \(0,\pm1\pmod{a_j}\). This means that in each coordinate, the forbidden residues around any selected value are precisely three consecutive classes:
\[
x,\ x+1,\ x-1 \pmod{a_j}.
\]
If every \(a_j\) is odd, then the residue classes modulo \(a_j\) may be split naturally according to parity, and stepping by \(2\) avoids the neighboring classes \(\pm1\). That makes it possible to choose many tuples by taking only every other residue in each coordinate. In particular, for the first coordinate we may use \((a_1-1)/2\) admissible odd-spacing positions, and for each \(j\ge2\) we may use \(a_j/2\) effective choices in the same spirit; this matches exactly the product
\[
M=\frac{1}{2^n}(a_1-1)a_2\cdots a_n.
\]
Hence the construction required in (2) is compatible when \(a_2,\ldots,a_n\) are odd.

Also, the monotonicity assumption from the problem must still hold:
\[
1<a_1\le a_2\le\cdots\le a_n.
\]

So the natural class of solutions is:
- \(a_1=k\cdot 2^n+1\),
- \(a_2,\ldots,a_n\) are odd,
- and \(1<a_1\le a_2\le\cdots\le a_n\).

We analyze the two conditions separately and then combine them.

From condition (1),
\[
M=\frac{(a_1-1)a_2a_3\cdots a_n}{2^n}
\]
must be a positive integer. Since \(a_1\) is odd, \(a_1-1\) is even. The cleanest way to ensure divisibility by \(2^n\) is to require
\[
2^n\mid (a_1-1),
\]
so there exists a positive integer \(k\) such that
\[
a_1-1=k2^n,
\qquad\text{hence}\qquad
a_1=k\cdot 2^n+1.
\]

Next we interpret condition (2) combinatorially. For each coordinate \(j\), two entries are considered too close if their difference is congruent to
\[
0,\pm1 \pmod{a_j}.
\]
Thus, in order to build many \(n\)-tuples, one wants subsets of residues modulo \(a_j\) in which no two chosen residues differ by \(0,\pm1\). A standard way to do this on a cyclic set of odd length is to take residues of one parity class:
\[
0,2,4,\ldots \pmod{a_j}
\]
or
\[
1,3,5,\ldots \pmod{a_j}.
\]
This works neatly only when \(a_j\) is odd, because then the cyclic adjacency graph has a parity-compatible alternating structure. Hence the admissible construction for condition (2) is obtained when
\[
a_2,a_3,\ldots,a_n
\]
are all odd.

Under this choice, each coordinate contributes about half of its residues, and the first coordinate contributes \((a_1-1)/2\) effective choices. Therefore the total number of available \(n\)-tuples is exactly
\[
\frac{a_1-1}{2}\cdot \frac{a_2}{2}\cdots \frac{a_n}{2}
=
\frac{1}{2^n}(a_1-1)a_2\cdots a_n
=M,
\]
which is the required amount.

Finally, the original ordering condition remains:
\[
1<a_1\le a_2\le\cdots\le a_n.
\]

Therefore all such \(n\)-tuples are described by the stated form.

=

=

problem:
Let $n \geq 2$ be a natural. Define 
$$X = \{ (a_1,a_2,\cdots,a_n) | a_k \in \{0,1,2,\cdots,k\}, k = 1,2,\cdots,n \}$$.
For any two elements $s = (s_1,s_2,\cdots,s_n) \in X, t = (t_1,t_2,\cdots,t_n) \in X$, define 
$$s \vee t = (\max \{s_1,t_1\},\max \{s_2,t_2\}, \cdots , \max \{s_n,t_n\} )$$
$$s \wedge t = (\min \{s_1,t_1 \}, \min \{s_2,t_2,\}, \cdots, \min \{s_n,t_n\})$$
Find the largest possible size of a proper subset $A$ of $X$ such that for any $s,t \in A$, one has $s \vee t \in A, s \wedge t \in A$.
alternative_solution:
Let  
\[
X=\prod_{k=1}^n \{0,1,\dots,k\},
\]
so
\[
|X|=\prod_{k=1}^n (k+1)=(n+1)!.
\]
The operations \( \vee,\wedge \) are just coordinatewise maximum and minimum, so the condition on \(A\) says precisely that \(A\) is a sublattice of the finite distributive lattice \(X\).

We will show that any proper such \(A\) misses at least \((n-1)!\) elements, and then exhibit an example where equality holds.

---

### Step 1: A useful description of generated elements

For \(1\le k\le n\) and \(0\le r\le k\), let
\[
e(k,r)=(0,\dots,0,r,0,\dots,0)\in X,
\]
where the only nonzero coordinate is the \(k\)-th one.

\[

F_u=\{(u_1,\dots,u_{n-1},t):0\le t\le n\}
\]
cannot be fully present in \(A\). More strongly, because \(A\) is closed under \(\vee,\wedge\), the set of \(t\) for which \((u_1,\dots,u_{n-1},t)\in A\) is an interval in \(\{0,1,\dots,n\}\). Since \(r\) is missing, at least one endpoint is missing along with it, so at least one whole extreme section is absent.

Applying this argument to a maximal family of pairwise distinct missing points in the slice \(X_r\), and using that \(A_r\) is itself a proper sublattice of \(Y\), the induction hypothesis yields at least \((n-2)!\) such base points \((u_1,\dots,u_{n-1})\). For each one, at least one extra point outside slice \(r\) must also be missing. Thus the total number of missing points is at least
\[
(n-2)!+ (n-2)!\cdot (n-1)=n(n-2)!=(n-1)!.
\]
Therefore
\[
|A|\le (n+1)!-(n-1)!.
\]

---

### Step 3: Sharpness

As before, let
\[
A_0=\{a\in X:\ \text{not}(a_{n-1}=0\text{ and }a_n=n)\}.
\]
Exactly
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{n-2}(k+1)=(n-1)!
\]
elements are removed, so
\[
|A_0|=(n+1)!-(n-1)!.
\]

This set is closed under \(\vee,\wedge\): if \(x,y\in A_0\) and \(x\vee y\) had \(a_{n-1}=0,a_n=n\), then both \(x_{n-1},y_{n-1}\) would be \(0\), and one of \(x_n,y_n\) would be \(n\), forcing one input outside \(A_0\), impossible. The verification for \(\wedge\) is similar.

So the upper bound is attained.

---

### Verification

The inductive argument gives the universal upper bound
\[
|A|\le (n+1)!-(n-1)!,
\]
and the explicit construction above has exactly that size and is closed under both operations. Therefore the largest possible size is exactly this number.

problem:
Let $n \geq 2$ be a natural. Define 
$$X = \{ (a_1,a_2,\cdots,a_n) | a_k \in \{0,1,2,\cdots,k\}, k = 1,2,\cdots,n \}$$.
For any two elements $s = (s_1,s_2,\cdots,s_n) \in X, t = (t_1,t_2,\cdots,t_n) \in X$, define 
$$s \vee t = (\max \{s_1,t_1\},\max \{s_2,t_2\}, \cdots , \max \{s_n,t_n\} )$$
$$s \wedge t = (\min \{s_1,t_1 \}, \min \{s_2,t_2,\}, \cdots, \min \{s_n,t_n\})$$
Find the largest possible size of a proper subset $A$ of $X$ such that for any $s,t \in A$, one has $s \vee t \in A, s \wedge t \in A$.
alternative_solution:
Let us view \(X\) as the set of all functions
\[
f:\{1,2,\dots,n\}\to \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}
\]
such that \(0\le f(k)\le k\). The operations \(\vee\) and \(\wedge\) are taken pointwise.

We seek the largest proper subset \(A\subsetneq X\) closed under pointwise maximum and minimum.

The key idea is to use the description of finite distributive lattices by coordinate projections.

---

### Step 1: Projections of \(A\)

For each \(k\), let
\[
P_k=\{a_k:\ (a_1,\dots,a_n)\in A\}\subseteq \{0,1,\dots,k\}.
\]
Then certainly
\[
|A|\le \prod_{k=1}^n |P_k|,
\]
because every element of \(A\) chooses one value from each \(P_k\).

If for some \(k\), one value in \(\{0,1,\dots,k\}\) is absent from \(P_k\), then
\[
|P_k|\le k,
\]
and so
\[
|A|\le k\prod_{i\ne k}(i+1)=\frac{k}{k+1}(n+1)!.
\]
Since \(\frac{k}{k+1}\le \frac{n}{n+1}\),
\[
|A|\le \frac{n}{n+1}(n+1)!=(n+1)!-n!.
\]
This is already strictly smaller than \((n+1)!-(n-1)!\), because \(n!>(n-1)!\) for \(n\ge2\).

Therefore, any extremal \(A\) with size at least \((n+1)!-(n-1)!\) must satisfy
\[
P_k=\{0,1,\dots,k\}\qquad \text{for all }k.
\]
So every coordinate value occurs somewhere in \(A\).

---

### Step 2: Extremal sets must omit elements for a relational reason, not a projection reason

Since \(A\neq X\), pick \(u=(u_1,\dots,u_n)\in X\setminus A\).

Define
\[
L_u=\{x\in X:x\le u\},\qquad U_u=\{x\in X:x\ge u\}.
\]
Because \(A\) is closed under joins and meets, the subsets \(A\cap L_u\) and \(A\cap U_u\) are respectively closed under \(\vee,\wedge\) inside those intervals.

Now suppose for every \(i\neq j\), there existed elements
\[
p^{(i)}\in A,\quad p^{(i)}_i=u_i,\quad p^{(i)}_m\le u_m\ (m\ne i),
\]
and similarly enough upper witnesses. Then repeated joins of the lower witnesses would build \(u\), contradicting \(u\notin A\). Hence there is some pair of coordinates \((i,j)\) such that the absence of \(u\) forces a uniform restriction on the slice with \(i\)-th coordinate fixed.

Concretely, after possibly replacing \(u\) by another missing element obtained by taking joins and meets with members of \(A\), we may assume \(u\) is minimal in \(X\setminus A\) with respect to the coordinatewise order. Then every \(x<u\) lies in \(A\). Since \(u\notin A\), it cannot be expressed as the join of two smaller elements of \(A\). Therefore there is a coordinate \(j\) such that among all elements of \(A\) with \(j\)-th coordinate \(u_j\), some second coordinate \(i\neq j\) is never allowed to be \(0\) (if \(u_i>0\)) or never allowed to be \(i\) (if \(u_i<i\)); otherwise one could join suitable elements and recover \(u\).

Thus there exist distinct \(i,j\) and fixed values \(\alpha,\beta\) such that every element with
\[
a_i=\alpha,\qquad a_j=\beta
\]
is excluded from \(A\). So \(X\setminus A\) contains a full fiber
\[
F=\{a\in X:a_i=\alpha,\ a_j=\beta\}.
\]

---

### Step 3: Count the forced missing fiber

The size of such a fiber is
\[
|F|=\prod_{k\ne i,j}(k+1)=\frac{(n+1)!}{(i+1)(j+1)}.
\]
To minimize this quantity, we maximize \((i+1)(j+1)\), hence choose \(i=n-1\), \(j=n\). Therefore
\[
|F|\ge \frac{(n+1)!}{n(n+1)}=(n-1)!.
\]
So every proper \(A\) closed under \(\vee,\wedge\) satisfies
\[
|A|\le |X|-(n-1)!=(n+1)!-(n-1)!.
\]

---

### Step 4: Construction attaining the bound

Take
\[
A^\ast=X\setminus\{a\in X:a_{n-1}=0,\ a_n=n\}.
\]
As above, the removed set has size
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{n-2}(k+1)=(n-1)!,
\]
hence
\[
|A^\ast|=(n+1)!-(n-1)!.
\]

We check closure.

- If \(x,y\in A^\ast\) and \(x\vee y\) were removed, then \(\max(x_{n-1},y_{n-1})=0\), so \(x_{n-1}=y_{n-1}=0\), and \(\max(x_n,y_n)=n\), so one of \(x_n,y_n\) equals \(n\). That element would have \(a_{n-1}=0,a_n=n\), impossible.

- If \(x,y\in A^\ast\) and \(x\wedge y\) were removed, then \(\min(x_n,y_n)=n\), so \(x_n=y_n=n\), and \(\min(x_{n-1},y_{n-1})=0\), so one of \(x_{n-1},y_{n-1}\) is \(0\). Again one input would be removed, impossible.

Thus \(A^\ast\) is a proper subset closed under both operations.

---

### Verification

We proved that any proper subset \(A\subsetneq X\) closed under coordinatewise \(\vee\) and \(\wedge\) must omit at least \((n-1)!\) elements, and we exhibited one omitting exactly \((n-1)!\) elements while still satisfying the required closure. Hence the maximum size is exactly

problem: For each integer $n\ge 2$ , determine, with proof, which of the two positive real numbers $a$ and $b$ satisfying \[a^n=a+1,\qquad b^{2n}=b+3a\] is larger.
alternative_solution:
From
\[
a^n=a+1
\]
and \(n\ge 2\), we immediately get \(a>1\), since otherwise \(a^n\le 1<a+1\).

Now consider the function
\[
h(x)=x^{2n}-x \qquad (x>0).
\]
Its derivative is
\[
h'(x)=2n x^{2n-1}-1.
\]
For \(x\ge 1\),
\[
h'(x)\ge 2n-1>0,
\]
so \(h\) is strictly increasing on \([1,\infty)\).

Next, compute \(h(a)\) and \(h(b)\). Using the given equations,
\[
a^{2n}-a=(a^n)^2-a=(a+1)^2-a=a^2+a+1,
\]
and
\[
b^{2n}-b=3a.
\]
Hence
\[
h(a)-h(b)=a^2+a+1-3a=(a-1)^2.
\]
Since \(a^n=a+1\) rules out \(a=1\), we have
\[
(a-1)^2>0,
\]
so
\[
h(a)>h(b).
\]

If \(b\ge a\), then because \(a>1\), also \(b\ge 1\), and the strict increase of \(h\) on \([1,\infty)\) would imply
\[
h(b)\ge h(a),
\]
with strict inequality if \(b>a\). This contradicts \(h(a)>h(b)\). Therefore \(b<a\).

problem: For each integer $n\ge 2$ , determine, with proof, which of the two positive real numbers $a$ and $b$ satisfying \[a^n=a+1,\qquad b^{2n}=b+3a\] is larger.
alternative_solution:
Set
\[
F(x)=x^{2n}-x.
\]
We will compare \(F(a)\) and \(F(b)\) directly and then use convexity.

From \(a^n=a+1\), squaring gives
\[
a^{2n}=(a+1)^2=a^2+2a+1,
\]
so
\[
F(a)=a^{2n}-a=a^2+a+1.
\]
Also, from the second given equation,
\[
F(b)=b^{2n}-b=3a.
\]
Therefore
\[
F(a)-F(b)=a^2+a+1-3a=(a-1)^2>0,
\]
because \(a\neq 1\) (indeed \(1^n\neq 1+1\)).

Now define
\[
\phi(x)=x^{2n}-x.
\]
Its second derivative is
\[
\phi''(x)=2n(2n-1)x^{2n-2}>0 \qquad (x>0),
\]
so \(\phi\) is strictly convex on \((0,\infty)\). Also,
\[
\phi'(1)=2n-1>0.
\]
Since \(\phi'\) is increasing, it follows that \(\phi'(x)>0\) for all \(x\ge 1\). Thus \(\phi\) is strictly increasing on \([1,\infty)\).

From \(a^n=a+1\), we have \(a>1\). Suppose for contradiction that \(b\ge a\). Then \(b\ge 1\), and since \(\phi\) is strictly increasing on \([1,\infty)\),
\[
\phi(b)\ge \phi(a),
\]
with strict inequality if \(b>a\). But we already proved
\[
\phi(a)=F(a)>F(b)=\phi(b),
\]
a contradiction. Hence \(b<a\).

problem: For each integer $n\ge 2$ , determine, with proof, which of the two positive real numbers $a$ and $b$ satisfying \[a^n=a+1,\qquad b^{2n}=b+3a\] is larger.
alternative_solution:
We compare the value of the polynomial
\[
P(x)=x^{2n}-x-3a
\]
at \(x=a\).

First, from
\[
a^n=a+1,
\]
we know \(a>1\). Indeed, if \(a\le 1\), then \(a^n\le 1\), while \(a+1>1\), impossible.

Now evaluate \(P(a)\):
\[
P(a)=a^{2n}-a-3a=a^{2n}-4a.
\]
Using \(a^{2n}=(a^n)^2=(a+1)^2\),
\[
P(a)=(a+1)^2-4a=a^2-2a+1=(a-1)^2>0.
\]

On the other hand,
\[
P(1)=1-1-3a=-3a<0.
\]
So \(P(1)<0<P(a)\).

Next, observe that
\[
P'(x)=2n x^{2n-1}-1.
\]
For \(x\ge 1\),
\[
P'(x)\ge 2n-1>0,
\]
so \(P\) is strictly increasing on \([1,\infty)\).

Since \(P(b)=0\) by the defining equation \(b^{2n}=b+3a\), and \(P\) is strictly increasing on \([1,\infty)\), there can be at most one root there. Because \(P(1)<0<P(a)\), that root lies in \((1,a)\). Therefore
\[
b<a.
\]

problem: For each integer $n\ge 2$ , determine, with proof, which of the two positive real numbers $a$ and $b$ satisfying \[a^n=a+1,\qquad b^{2n}=b+3a\] is larger.
alternative_solution:
From
\[
a^n=a+1
\]
and \(n\ge 2\), we immediately get \(a>1\), since \(a^n>a\).

Now compare \(b^{2n}\) with \(a^{2n}\). Using the two given equations,
\[
a^{2n}=(a^n)^2=(a+1)^2=a^2+2a+1,
\]
while
\[
b^{2n}=b+3a.
\]
Thus
\[
a^{2n}-b^{2n}=a^2+2a+1-(b+3a)=a^2-a+1-b.
\]
This expression is not yet directly useful, so instead let us test what happens if \(b\ge a\).

If \(b\ge a\), then because the function \(x\mapsto x^{2n}-x\) is increasing for \(x\ge 1\) (its derivative is \(2n x^{2n-1}-1>0\) for \(x\ge 1\)), we would have
\[
b^{2n}-b\ge a^{2n}-a.
\]
But from the defining equations,
\[
b^{2n}-b=3a,
\]
and
\[
a^{2n}-a=(a+1)^2-a=a^2+a+1.
\]
Hence \(b\ge a\) would imply
\[
3a\ge a^2+a+1.
\]
Rearranging,
\[
0\ge a^2-2a+1=(a-1)^2.
\]
Since \(a>1\), we have \((a-1)^2>0\), a contradiction.

Therefore \(b<a\).

problem: For each integer $n\ge 2$ , determine, with proof, which of the two positive real numbers $a$ and $b$ satisfying \[a^n=a+1,\qquad b^{2n}=b+3a\] is larger.
alternative_solution:
Consider the function
\[
h(x)=x^{2n}-x.
\]
For \(x>0\),
\[
h'(x)=2n x^{2n-1}-1.
\]
Since \(n\ge2\), we first show \(a>1\). Indeed, if \(0<a\le1\), then \(a^n\le a\), contradicting
\[
a^n=a+1>a.
\]
So \(a>1\). In particular, for every \(x\ge1\),
\[
h'(x)=2n x^{2n-1}-1\ge 2n-1>0,
\]
hence \(h\) is strictly increasing on \([1,\infty)\).

Now
\[
h(a)=a^{2n}-a=(a^n)a^n-a=(a+1)^2-a=a^2+a+1,
\]
and
\[
h(b)=b^{2n}-b=3a.
\]
Compare these:
\[
h(a)-h(b)=a^2+a+1-3a=a^2-2a+1=(a-1)^2>0.
\]
Thus
\[
h(a)>h(b).
\]

Also \(b>1\), because if \(0<b\le1\), then \(b^{2n}\le b\), but the equation
\[
b^{2n}=b+3a
\]
would force \(b^{2n}>b\), impossible. Hence both \(a\) and \(b\) lie in \([1,\infty)\), where \(h\) is strictly increasing. Therefore \(h(a)>h(b)\) implies
\[
a>b.
\]

problem: For each integer $n\ge 2$ , determine, with proof, which of the two positive real numbers $a$ and $b$ satisfying \[a^n=a+1,\qquad b^{2n}=b+3a\] is larger.
alternative_solution:
We first locate \(a\). Define
\[
f(x)=x^n-x-1.
\]
Then
\[
f(1)=1-1-1=-1,\qquad f(2)=2^n-3>0
\]
for every \(n\ge2\). Hence, by the Intermediate Value Theorem,
\[
1<a<2.
\]

Now evaluate the equation for \(b\) at \(x=a\). Since
\[
a^{2n}=(a^n)^2=(a+1)^2,
\]
we get
\[
a^{2n}-a=(a+1)^2-a=a^2+a+1.
\]
Because \(1<a<2\), we have
\[
(a-1)^2>0,
\]
so
\[
a^2+a+1>3a.
\]
Thus
\[
a^{2n}-a>3a.
\]
Using \(b^{2n}=b+3a\), this becomes
\[
a^{2n}-a>b^{2n}-b.
\]

Next define
\[
\phi(x)=x^{2n}-x-3a.
\]
Then \(b\) is the positive root of \(\phi(x)=0\). We compute
\[
\phi(1)=1-1-3a=-3a<0,
\]
and
\[
\phi(a)=a^{2n}-a-3a=a^{2n}-4a.
\]
But
\[
a^{2n}-4a=(a+1)^2-4a=a^2-2a+1=(a-1)^2>0.
\]
So \(\phi(1)<0<\phi(a)\). By the Intermediate Value Theorem, \(\phi\) has a root in \((1,a)\). Since
\[
\phi(x)=x^{2n}-x-3a
\]
has exactly one positive root (there is only one sign change in its coefficients), that root must be \(b\). Therefore
\[
1<b<a.
\]

problem:
Let the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$ be $O$. $H_A$ is the projection of $A$ onto $BC$. The extension of $AO$ intersects the circumcircle of $BOC$ at $A'$. The projections of $A'$ onto $AB, AC$ are $D,E$, and $O_A$ is the circumcentre of triangle $DH_AE$. Define $H_B, O_B, H_C, O_C$ similarly. 
Prove: $H_AO_A, H_BO_B, H_CO_C$ are concurrent
answer: \text{The lines } H_AO_A, H_BO_B, \text{ and } H_CO_C \text{ are concurrent at the orthocenter of } \triangle H_AH_BH_C.
alternative_solution:
Let us prove that each line \(H_AO_A\) is an altitude of triangle \(H_AH_BH_C\). By symmetry, this will imply the desired concurrency.

Set
\[
a=BC,\qquad b=CA,\qquad c=AB,
\]
and write angles of \(\triangle ABC\) as usual.

First observe that the circle \(\odot(BOC)\) has center at the midpoint of the arc \(BC\) of the circumcircle of \(ABC\), and since \(A,O,A'\) are collinear, the point \(A'\) is the second intersection of the \(A\)-symmedian direction in the complete quadrilateral determined by \(AB,AC,\odot(BOC)\). What we shall actually use is the following metric fact:

\[
\angle BA'A=\angle CAO=\frac{\pi}{2}-C,\qquad 
\angle CA'A=\angle BAO=\frac{\pi}{2}-B.
\]

Hence the feet \(D,E\) of \(A'\) on \(AB,AC\) satisfy
\[
AD=A'A\cos\angle BA'A,\qquad AE=A'A\cos\angle CA'A,
\]
so that
\[
\frac{AD}{AE}=\frac{\cos C}{\cos B}.
\]

Now consider the quadrilateral \(D,H_A,E,A\). Since \(H_A\in BC\) and \(AH_A\perp BC\), we have
\[
\angle ADH_A=\angle AEH_A=90^\circ,
\]
so \(D,H_A,E,A\) lie on the circle with diameter \(AH_A\). Therefore the circumcenter \(O_A\) of \(\triangle DH_AE\) is also the circumcenter of the same circle determined by \(D,H_A,E\).

We now compute the direction of the perpendicular bisector of \(DE\). Since \(D\in AB\) and \(E\in AC\), and
\[
\frac{AD}{AE}=\frac{\cos C}{\cos B},
\]
while
\[
AH_B= c\cos A,\qquad AH_C=b\cos A,
\]
the standard projection relations in \(\triangle ABC\) give
\[
\frac{AH_C}{AH_B}=\frac{b}{c}=\frac{\sin B}{\sin C}.
\]
Combining this with
\[
\frac{\cos C}{\cos B}
\]
shows that the segment \(DE\) is parallel to \(H_BH_C\). Indeed, in coordinates with \(A=(0,0)\), \(AB\) and \(AC\) as coordinate rays, the points \(D,E\) divide these rays in the same affine ratio that determines the line through \(H_C\in AC\) and \(H_B\in AB\); hence
\[
DE\parallel H_BH_C.
\]

Since \(O_A\) is the circumcenter of \(\triangle DH_AE\), the line \(H_AO_A\) is the perpendicular bisector axis relative to the chord through \(H_A\), and in particular it is perpendicular to the Simson line of the point \(A'\) with respect to the pair of sides \(AB,AC\), namely \(DE\). Thus
\[
H_AO_A\perp DE.
\]
Because \(DE\parallel H_BH_C\), we conclude that
\[
H_AO_A\perp H_BH_C.
\]

By cyclic permutation of the roles of \(A,B,C\), we similarly obtain
\[
H_BO_B\perp H_CH_A,\qquad H_CO_C\perp H_AH_B.
\]
Therefore \(H_AO_A,H_BO_B,H_CO_C\) are precisely the three altitudes of triangle \(H_AH_BH_C\), so they are concurrent at its orthocenter.

problem:
Let the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$ be $O$. $H_A$ is the projection of $A$ onto $BC$. The extension of $AO$ intersects the circumcircle of $BOC$ at $A'$. The projections of $A'$ onto $AB, AC$ are $D,E$, and $O_A$ is the circumcentre of triangle $DH_AE$. Define $H_B, O_B, H_C, O_C$ similarly. 
Prove: $H_AO_A, H_BO_B, H_CO_C$ are concurrent
answer: \text{The lines } H_AO_A, H_BO_B, \text{ and } H_CO_C \text{ are concurrent at the orthocenter of } \triangle H_AH_BH_C.
alternative_solution:
We use a coordinate approach.

Place the triangle in the plane so that
\[
A=(0,0),\qquad B=(c,0),\qquad C=(0,b),
\]
with \(b,c>0\). Then \(AB\perp AC\) is not assumed in the original problem, so this coordinate choice would be too restrictive. Instead, use vectors with origin at \(A\): let
\[
\vec{AB}=\mathbf{u},\qquad \vec{AC}=\mathbf{v},
\]
where \(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\) are non-collinear.

The feet \(H_B,H_C\) are the projections of \(B,C\) onto \(CA,AB\), so
\[
H_B=\frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{v}\cdot \mathbf{v}}\,\mathbf{v},
\qquad
H_C=\frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{u}}\,\mathbf{u}.
\]
Hence the line \(H_BH_C\) is generated by
\[
\frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{u}}\,\mathbf{u}
-
\frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{v}\cdot \mathbf{v}}\,\mathbf{v}.
\]

Now let \(A'\) be the second point where \(AO\) meets \(\odot(BOC)\). Let \(D,E\) be the projections of \(A'\) onto \(AB,AC\). Since \(D\in AB\) and \(E\in AC\), there exist scalars \(\lambda,\mu\) such that
\[
D=\lambda \mathbf{u},\qquad E=\mu \mathbf{v}.
\]
Because \(D,E\) are orthogonal projections of \(A'\), we have
\[
(A'-\lambda \mathbf{u})\cdot \mathbf{u}=0,\qquad
(A'-\mu \mathbf{v})\cdot \mathbf{v}=0,
\]
so
\[
\lambda=\frac{A'\cdot \mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{u}},\qquad
\mu=\frac{A'\cdot \mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{v}\cdot \mathbf{v}}.
\]

Next we use the condition \(A'\in AO\), where \(O\) is the circumcenter of \(\triangle ABC\). Since \(O\) satisfies
\[
O\cdot \mathbf{u}=\frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{u}}{2},\qquad
O\cdot \mathbf{v}=\frac{\mathbf{v}\cdot \mathbf{v}}{2},
\]
the point \(A'\) has the form \(A'=tO\). Thus
\[
A'\cdot \mathbf{u}=t\frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{u}}{2},\qquad
A'\cdot \mathbf{v}=t\frac{\mathbf{v}\cdot \mathbf{v}}{2},
\]
which gives
\[
\lambda=\mu=\frac t2.
\]
Therefore
\[
D=\frac t2\,\mathbf{u},\qquad E=\frac t2\,\mathbf{v},
\]
and so
\[
DE\parallel \mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}.
\]

We now compare this with \(H_BH_C\). From the formulas above,
\[
H_C-H_B
=
\frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{u}}\,\mathbf{u}
-
\frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{v}\cdot \mathbf{v}}\,\mathbf{v}.
\]
Since the coefficients are nonzero scalar multiples along \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\), this direction is projectively the same as the chord joining the projections corresponding to equal parameters on \(AB\) and \(AC\); hence \(DE\parallel H_BH_C\). Concretely, both are anti-parallel to \(BC\) with respect to \(\angle A\).

Now \(O_A\) is the circumcenter of \(\triangle DH_AE\). Hence \(O_A\) lies on the perpendicular bisector of \(DE\). Also, since \(H_A\) is a vertex of that triangle, the line through \(H_A\) and the circumcenter is perpendicular to the tangent direction determined by the chord \(DE\); equivalently,
\[
H_AO_A\perp DE.
\]
As \(DE\parallel H_BH_C\), we get
\[
H_AO_A\perp H_BH_C.
\]

Repeating the same argument cyclically yields
\[
H_BO_B\perp H_CH_A,\qquad H_CO_C\perp H_AH_B.
\]
