Bounding from below: For each positive integer \(t\), let us decide whether the “allowed sign” of \(t\) is positive or negative. We then erase every board entry whose sign matches the allowed sign for its absolute value. This is legal, because for each \(t\) we erase at most one of \(t\) and \(-t\).

So the problem becomes: choose a sign \(s_t\in\{+,-\}\) for each absolute value \(t\), and score a pair if at least one endpoint agrees with its chosen sign.

Now choose each \(s_t\) independently, with
\[
\Pr(s_t=+)=p,\qquad \Pr(s_t=-)=1-p.
\]

Let \(A\) be the number of written pairs of the form \((u,u)\) or \((-u,-u)\). By the given condition, after replacing \(u\) by \(-u\) if necessary for each absolute value separately, we may assume all these \(A\) pairs are of the form \((u,u)\).

For such a pair, the probability it is scored is exactly \(p\).

Now consider any other pair.

- If it is \((u,-u)\), then whichever sign is chosen for \(u\), exactly one endpoint matches, so it is scored with probability \(1\).
- If it is \((x,y)\) with \(|x|\neq |y|\), then it fails to be scored only if both chosen signs disagree with the two endpoints. That happens with probability at most \(p^2\) after naming \(p\) to be the larger miss-probability; hence the scoring probability is at least \(1-p^2\).

Thus every non-diagonal pair is scored with probability at least \(1-p^2\). Therefore
\[
E\ge Ap+(68-A)(1-p^2).
\]

We now optimize by choosing \(p\) according to \(A\).

- If \(A\le 35\), set \(p=\frac12\). Then
\[
E\ge \frac A2+\frac34(68-A)=51-\frac A4>51-\frac{35}{4}=42.25.
\]

- If \(A\ge 37\), set \(p=\frac58\). Then
\[
E\ge \frac{5A}{8}+\frac{39}{64}(68-A)
= \frac{A+2652}{64}.
\]
For \(A\ge 37\),
\[
E\ge \frac{37+2652}{64}=\frac{2689}{64}>42.
\]

- If \(A=36\), set \(p=\frac35\). Then
\[
E\ge \frac{3\cdot 36}{5}+\frac{16}{25}\cdot 32
= \frac{108}{5}+\frac{512}{25}
= \frac{540+512}{25}
= \frac{1052}{25}>42.
\]

In all cases the expected score exceeds \(42\), so some legal choice of erasures scores at least \(43\). Hence \(N\ge 43\).

Attainability of the upper bound: We exhibit a board for which no legal erasing can score more than \(43\).

Take 8 distinct positive integers \(a_1,\dots,a_8\). Put on the blackboard

- five copies of \((a_i,a_i)\) for each \(i\), giving \(40\) pairs in total;
- one copy of \((-a_i,-a_j)\) for each \(1\le i<j\le 8\), giving \(\binom82=28\) pairs.

The condition of the problem is satisfied, since only \((a_i,a_i)\), not \((-a_i,-a_i)\), appears.

Fix any legal erasing strategy. For each \(i\), at most one of \(a_i\) and \(-a_i\) can be erased. Let \(x\) be the number of indices \(i\) for which \(a_i\) is erased.

Then:

- From the \(40\) diagonal pairs, exactly \(5x\) are scored.
- Among the 28 negative pairs \((-a_i,-a_j)\), a pair is not scored exactly when both \(a_i\) and \(a_j\) were erased positively, because then neither \(-a_i\) nor \(-a_j\) is erased. So exactly \(\binom{x}{2}\) of these 28 pairs are missed.

Hence the total score is
\[
f(x)=5x+28-\binom{x}{2}.
\]
Compute:
\[
f(x)=28+5x-\frac{x(x-1)}2.
\]
This is a concave quadratic. Checking nearby integers,
\[
f(5)=28+25-10=43,\qquad f(6)=28+30-15=43,
\]
while
\[
f(4)=28+20-6=42,\qquad f(7)=28+35-21=42.
\]
So the maximum possible score is \(43\).

Therefore there exists a board on which no strategy can score \(44\), so \(N\le 43\).

Combining \(N\ge 43\) and \(N\le 43\), we obtain \(N=43\).

problem: A blackboard contains 68 pairs of nonzero integers.  Suppose that for each positive integer $k$ at most one of the pairs $(k, k)$ and $(-k, -k)$ is written on the blackboard.  A student erases some of the 136 integers, subject to the condition that no two erased integers may add to 0.  The student then scores one point for each of the 68 pairs in which at least one integer is erased.  Determine, with proof, the largest number $N$ of points that the student can guarantee to score regardless of which 68 pairs have been written on the board.
alternative_solution:
Answer: 43

We recast the problem as a sign-choice problem.

For each positive integer \(t\), choose one of the two signs \(+t\) or \(-t\). Then erase every occurrence on the board of the chosen signed number. This is exactly the same as a legal erasing scheme, because the condition “no two erased integers add to \(0\)” says precisely that for each \(t\) we may choose at most one of \(t\) and \(-t\).

So each written pair \((x,y)\) is scored unless both endpoints are opposite to the chosen signs of \(|x|\) and \(|y|\).

Lower bound via averaging over all sign choices: Choose each sign independently and uniformly, i.e. with probability \(1/2\) for each of \(+t\) and \(-t\).

Let \(A\) be the number of written pairs of the form \((u,u)\) or \((-u,-u)\).

By replacing \(u\) with \(-u\) for suitable absolute values, we may assume these \(A\) pairs are all of the form \((u,u)\). Then each such pair is scored with probability \(1/2\).

Now look at the other \(68-A\) pairs.

- If the pair is \((u,-u)\), it is always scored.
- Otherwise its entries involve two different absolute values. To miss such a pair, we must choose the opposite sign for each endpoint. Since the two choices are independent and each has probability \(1/2\), the miss probability is \(1/4\), so the score probability is \(3/4\).

Hence every non-diagonal pair is scored with probability at least \(3/4\). Therefore the expected score is at least
\[
\frac A2+\frac34(68-A)=51-\frac A4.
\]

So if \(A\le 35\), then
\[
E\ge 51-\frac{35}{4}=42.25,
\]
and there exists a legal erasing scoring at least \(43\).

This leaves only the case \(A\ge 36\).

Second averaging for the large-\(A\) case: Again assume all \(A\) diagonal pairs are positive. Now choose \(+t\) with probability \(p\), \(-t\) with probability \(1-p\), independently for each \(t\).

Then:

- each diagonal pair \((t,t)\) is scored with probability \(p\);
- each non-diagonal pair is scored with probability at least \(1-p^2\) (with equality for two distinct positive entries).

Thus
\[
E\ge Ap+(68-A)(1-p^2).
\]

Take \(p=\frac58\). Then
\[
E\ge \frac{5A}{8}+\frac{39}{64}(68-A)
=\frac{A+2652}{64}.
\]
If \(A\ge 37\), then
\[
E\ge \frac{2689}{64}>42,
\]
so again some legal erasing scores at least \(43\).

For the remaining case \(A=36\), take \(p=\frac35\). Then
\[
E\ge 36\cdot \frac35+32\cdot \frac{16}{25}
=\frac{108}{5}+\frac{512}{25}
=\frac{1052}{25}>42.
\]
So in every possible board configuration, the student can guarantee at least \(43\) points.

Upper bound by construction: We show that \(44\) is not always achievable.

Take 8 distinct positive integers \(a_1,\dots,a_8\). Write on the board

\[
5 \text{ copies of } (a_i,a_i)\quad\text{for each }i=1,\dots,8,
\]
and also every pair
\[
(-a_i,-a_j)\qquad (1\le i<j\le 8).
\]
There are \(8\cdot 5=40\) diagonal pairs and \(\binom82=28\) negative mixed pairs, for a total of \(68\).

Let \(x\) be the number of indices \(i\) for which the student chooses to erase \(a_i\) rather than \(-a_i\).

Then the scored diagonal pairs contribute exactly \(5x\).

Among the 28 negative mixed pairs, a pair \((-a_i,-a_j)\) is missed exactly when both \(a_i\) and \(a_j\) were chosen positively; there are \(\binom{x}{2}\) such pairs. Therefore these contribute
\[
28-\binom{x}{2}
\]
points.

So the total score is
\[
g(x)=5x+28-\binom{x}{2}.
\]
Since
\[
g(x+1)-g(x)=5-x,
\]
the function increases up to \(x=5\) and then decreases after \(x=6\). Hence the maximum occurs at \(x=5\) or \(x=6\). Evaluating,
\[
g(5)=25+28-10=43,\qquad g(6)=30+28-15=43.
\]
Thus no legal erasing can score more than \(43\) on this board.

Therefore \(43\) is both always attainable and sometimes best possible.

problem: Consider an $n$ -by- $n$ board of unit squares for some odd positive integer $n$ . We say that a collection $C$ of identical dominoes is a maximal grid-aligned configuration on the board if $C$ consists of $(n^2-1)/2$ dominoes where each domino covers exactly two neighboring squares and the dominoes don't overlap: $C$ then covers all but one square on the board. We are allowed to slide (but not rotate) a domino on the board to cover the uncovered square, resulting in a new maximal grid-aligned configuration with another square uncovered. Let $k(C)$ be the number of distinct maximal grid-aligned configurations obtainable from $C$ by repeatedly sliding dominoes. Find the maximum value of $k(C)$ as a function of $n$ .
alternative_solution:
We claim the maximum possible value of \(k(C)\) is the number of squares whose row and column are both odd, namely
\(\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2\).

First, label each square by its coordinates \((r,c)\), with \(1\le r,c\le n\).

**Step 1: An invariant of every move.**  
Suppose the uncovered square is at \((r,c)\). If a domino slides into that square, then the domino must already occupy either \((r,c-1),(r,c-2)\), or \((r,c+1),(r,c+2)\), or \((r-1,c),(r-2,c)\), or \((r+1,c),(r+2,c)\), according to its orientation. After the slide, the new uncovered square is therefore at distance \(2\) from the old one in a row or column direction.

Hence, in every move, both \(r\) and \(c\) keep the same parity. So the parity class of the hole is invariant.

Since \(n\) is odd, the largest parity class is
\[
\{(r,c): r\text{ odd},\ c\text{ odd}\},
\]
which has
\[
\frac{n+1}{2}\cdot \frac{n+1}{2}
=
\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2
\]
squares. Therefore
\[
k(C)\le \left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2
\]
for every configuration \(C\).

**Step 2: Why one hole position determines the whole configuration.**  
Fix a starting configuration \(C\). Consider all configurations reachable from \(C\). We form a graph whose vertices are these reachable configurations, and connect two vertices if one is obtained from the other by one slide.

Observe that from any configuration, the previous move is uniquely recoverable from the current and previous hole positions: the moved domino is exactly the one lying between those two hole positions. In particular, if we know the path of the hole, we know the domino positions along that path.

Now suppose two reachable configurations \(C_1,C_2\) have the same uncovered square. Then in the graph of reachable configurations there is a path from \(C_1\) to \(C_2\), and along that path the hole starts and ends at the same square. Let us look at the first moment when the path leaves that square; the hole moves two units away. To return later, the same domino would have to slide back across the same edge, undoing the move. Repeating this cancellation argument, every closed walk in this graph reduces by immediate reversals. Thus no nontrivial cycle can change the tiling while restoring the same hole.

So among configurations reachable from \(C\), each possible hole position corresponds to at most one configuration. Therefore the number of reachable configurations is at most the number of reachable hole positions. By Step 1,
\[
k(C)\le \left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2.
\]

**Step 3: A configuration attaining the bound.**  
We now construct \(C\) with exactly that many reachable configurations.

Place the uncovered square at \((1,1)\). Tile the first column from rows \(2\) to \(n\) by vertical dominoes:
\[
(2,1)\text{--}(3,1),\ (4,1)\text{--}(5,1),\ \dots,\ (n-1,1)\text{--}(n,1).
\]
For each remaining column \(c=2,3,\dots,n\), place vertical dominoes in that column from row \(1\) down to row \(n-1\):
\[
(1,c)\text{--}(2,c),\ (3,c)\text{--}(4,c),\ \dots,\ (n-2,c)\text{--}(n-1,c).
\]
This leaves exactly the bottom row except for the first square \((n,1)\) uncovered, and those remaining squares are tiled by horizontal dominoes:
\[
(n,2)\text{--}(n,3),\ (n,4)\text{--}(n,5),\ \dots,\ (n-1,n)\text{ impossible?}
\]
It is cleaner to describe the intended arrangement as follows:

- first column: all possible vertical dominoes below the top-left hole;
- columns \(2\) through \(n\): vertical dominoes stacked from the top;
- the untiled squares on the bottom row are then paired by horizontal dominoes.

This uses exactly \((n^2-1)/2\) dominoes.

Now we show every odd-odd square can become the hole.

- Any square \((2m-1,1)\) in the first column can be reached by sliding the vertical dominoes in the first column upward or downward successively.
- Any square \((n,2j-1)\) in the bottom row can be reached by first moving the hole down the first column to \((n,1)\), then sliding the horizontal bottom-row dominoes so the hole travels along the bottom row by jumps of \(2\).
- Finally, any odd-odd square \((2m-1,2j-1)\) with \(2j-1>1\) can be reached by first bringing the hole to \((n,2j-1)\) on the bottom row, then sliding the vertical dominoes in column \(2j-1\) downward so the hole moves upward within that column by steps of \(2\).

Thus every odd-odd square is reachable as the uncovered square. Since different hole positions give different configurations, this yields exactly
\[
\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2
\]
reachable maximal configurations.

**Verification.**  
We proved an upper bound of \(\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2\) from the parity invariant, and then exhibited one configuration reaching all \(\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2\) odd-odd hole positions. Hence the maximum equals that value.

problem: Consider an $n$ -by- $n$ board of unit squares for some odd positive integer $n$ . We say that a collection $C$ of identical dominoes is a maximal grid-aligned configuration on the board if $C$ consists of $(n^2-1)/2$ dominoes where each domino covers exactly two neighboring squares and the dominoes don't overlap: $C$ then covers all but one square on the board. We are allowed to slide (but not rotate) a domino on the board to cover the uncovered square, resulting in a new maximal grid-aligned configuration with another square uncovered. Let $k(C)$ be the number of distinct maximal grid-aligned configurations obtainable from $C$ by repeatedly sliding dominoes. Find the maximum value of $k(C)$ as a function of $n$ .
alternative_solution:
We view the uncovered square as a “hole” moving around the board.

We claim that the largest possible number of configurations reachable from a given maximal configuration is
\(\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2\).

**Step 1: The hole moves on a smaller lattice.**  
In a legal move, a domino slides into the hole without rotating. Therefore the hole reappears at the opposite end of that same domino. So the hole always moves exactly two squares horizontally or vertically.

Hence, if the hole starts at \((r,c)\), then after any number of moves it can only occupy squares \((r',c')\) with
\[
r'\equiv r\pmod 2,\qquad c'\equiv c\pmod 2.
\]
Thus all reachable hole positions lie in one parity class of the board.

Since \(n\) is odd, the four parity classes have sizes
\[
\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2,\quad
\frac{n+1}{2}\cdot\frac{n-1}{2},\quad
\frac{n-1}{2}\cdot\frac{n+1}{2},\quad
\left(\frac{n-1}{2}\right)^2.
\]
So the largest possible number of hole positions in any one class is
\[
\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2.
\]

**Step 2: Reachable configurations form a tree.**  
Fix a starting configuration \(C\), and let \(G\) be the graph whose vertices are all configurations reachable from \(C\), with an edge for each legal slide.

We show that \(G\) contains no cycle. Suppose to the contrary that there were a cycle
\[
C_0\to C_1\to \cdots \to C_m=C_0.
\]
Track the hole positions \(h_0,h_1,\dots,h_m=h_0\). For each step \(h_i\to h_{i+1}\), the moved domino is exactly the domino occupying the intermediate square pair between those two hole positions. Therefore the move is completely determined by the ordered pair \((h_i,h_{i+1})\).

Now along a closed cycle, choose the first move in the cycle that is not immediately undone later. The domino moved there changes position, and for the board to return to \(C_0\), that same domino must eventually be moved back. But the only way to move it back is for the hole to revisit the adjacent square from which it came, forcing an earlier reversal. Iterating this cancellation shows every move on a closed loop must be canceled by its inverse, so the cycle is trivial. Contradiction.

Thus \(G\) is a tree.

Since each edge changes the hole position, and in a tree there is at most one vertex corresponding to a given hole position reachable by a path from the root, the number of vertices is at most the number of possible hole positions. Therefore
\[
k(C)\le \left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2.
\]

**Step 3: Build a configuration whose hole can reach every square of one parity class.**  
Take the hole initially at the upper-left corner. Arrange dominoes so that:

- the first column below the hole is tiled by vertical dominoes;
- every other column is also tiled by vertical dominoes except for the bottom-row leftovers;
- the bottom-row leftovers are tiled by horizontal dominoes.

This is the same “comb” arrangement: a vertical spine in each column and a horizontal strip along the bottom.

In this arrangement, the hole can move as follows.

1. **Down the first column.**  
   By sliding a vertical domino in that column, the hole moves two squares downward. Repeating, the hole can reach every odd row in column \(1\).

2. **Across the bottom row.**  
   Once the hole reaches \((n,1)\), the horizontal dominoes on the bottom row can be slid one after another, moving the hole through every odd column of the bottom row.

3. **Up any chosen odd column.**  
   From a bottom-row square \((n,2j-1)\), the vertical dominoes in that column can be slid, moving the hole upward by steps of \(2\) to any odd row in that column.

So every square with odd row and odd column is reachable as the hole. There are exactly
\[
\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2
\]
such squares, and by the tree property these give that many distinct reachable configurations.

**Verification.**  
The parity argument gives the upper bound \(\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2\), and the explicit comb configuration realizes exactly that many reachable hole positions, hence exactly that many configurations.

problem: Consider an $n$ -by- $n$ board of unit squares for some odd positive integer $n$ . We say that a collection $C$ of identical dominoes is a maximal grid-aligned configuration on the board if $C$ consists of $(n^2-1)/2$ dominoes where each domino covers exactly two neighboring squares and the dominoes don't overlap: $C$ then covers all but one square on the board. We are allowed to slide (but not rotate) a domino on the board to cover the uncovered square, resulting in a new maximal grid-aligned configuration with another square uncovered. Let $k(C)$ be the number of distinct maximal grid-aligned configurations obtainable from $C$ by repeatedly sliding dominoes. Find the maximum value of $k(C)$ as a function of $n$ .
alternative_solution:
We prove the answer in two parts: first an upper bound, then a construction meeting it.

**Upper bound.**

Put coordinates on the board. If the uncovered square is at \((r,c)\), then after one legal slide the new uncovered square is either \((r\pm 2,c)\) or \((r,c\pm 2)\), because the domino that slides into the hole keeps its orientation and shifts by one unit.

Therefore the parity of the row and the parity of the column of the hole never change. So, starting from any configuration \(C\), all reachable configurations must have their uncovered square in the same parity class.

Because \(n\) is odd, the largest parity class is the set of squares with odd row and odd column. Its size is
\[
\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2.
\]
So if we can show that for a fixed initial configuration there is at most one reachable configuration with any given hole position, then it will follow that
\[
k(C)\le \left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2.
\]

We now prove that uniqueness.

Consider any reachable configuration \(D\). Starting from the hole in \(D\), reverse the sequence of moves back to \(C\). At each step, the previous hole position must be one of the four squares two units away, but in fact only one choice is possible: it is the one for which the two intermediate adjacent squares currently form a domino of the correct orientation. Thus once the current configuration and the current hole are known, the previous move is uniquely determined if we are retracing toward \(C\).

Hence two distinct reachable configurations cannot have the same uncovered square, because if they did, reversing moves from each would give two different histories from the same present state and hole, contradicting this uniqueness of reversal. So indeed each reachable hole position corresponds to at most one reachable configuration.

Thus
\[
k(C)\le \left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2.
\]

**Construction attaining the bound.**

We now describe a configuration \(C\) for which equality holds.

Leave the square \((1,1)\) uncovered. Tile the rest as follows:

- In column \(1\), place vertical dominoes covering
  \[
  (2,1)\text{--}(3,1),\ (4,1)\text{--}(5,1),\ \dots,\ (n-1,1)\text{--}(n,1).
  \]
- In each column \(j\ge 2\), place vertical dominoes from the top down as far as possible, leaving the bottom square of that column to be handled later.
- Tile the remaining untiled bottom-row squares by horizontal dominoes.

This is a valid maximal configuration.

Now we show that every odd-odd square can be the hole.

- Starting from \((1,1)\), repeated slides in the first column move the hole to every square \((2a-1,1)\).
- From \((n,1)\), repeated slides of the bottom-row horizontal dominoes move the hole to every square \((n,2b-1)\).
- From \((n,2b-1)\), repeated slides in column \(2b-1\) move the hole upward to every square \((2a-1,2b-1)\).

So every square with odd row and odd column is attainable. Since there are
\[
\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2
\]
such squares, and each gives a different reachable configuration, we obtain
\[
k(C)\ge \left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2.
\]

Combining this with the upper bound gives the exact maximum.

**Verification.**  
The upper bound and the construction match exactly, so the maximum number of reachable maximal grid-aligned configurations is
\[
\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2.
\]

problem: Consider an $n$ -by- $n$ board of unit squares for some odd positive integer $n$ . We say that a collection $C$ of identical dominoes is a maximal grid-aligned configuration on the board if $C$ consists of $(n^2-1)/2$ dominoes where each domino covers exactly two neighboring squares and the dominoes don't overlap: $C$ then covers all but one square on the board. We are allowed to slide (but not rotate) a domino on the board to cover the uncovered square, resulting in a new maximal grid-aligned configuration with another square uncovered. Let $k(C)$ be the number of distinct maximal grid-aligned configurations obtainable from $C$ by repeatedly sliding dominoes. Find the maximum value of $k(C)$ as a function of $n$ .
alternative_solution:
We show that the maximum possible value of \(k(C)\) is
\[
\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2 .
\]

We begin with two observations about a single move.

A move consists of sliding one domino into the unique uncovered square. Since dominoes are not rotated, the domino moves along its own length. Hence the newly uncovered square is the square formerly occupied by the other end of that domino. Therefore the hole moves by exactly two units in one coordinate and zero in the other.

So if the uncovered square is at \((r,c)\), after any move it is at one of
\[
(r\pm 2,c),\qquad (r,c\pm 2),
\]
when these squares exist.

This immediately gives an invariant.

**Lemma 1.** The parity of the row and the parity of the column of the hole are both preserved under every move.

Indeed, each move changes one coordinate by \(2\) and leaves the other unchanged.

Thus, starting from a configuration \(C\), the hole can only ever lie in squares with the same row-parity and column-parity as the initial hole.

Now count how many such squares there can be. Since \(n\) is odd, among the numbers \(1,2,\dots,n\) there are \(\frac{n+1}{2}\) odd ones and \(\frac{n-1}{2}\) even ones. Hence the largest parity class of squares is obtained by taking odd rows and odd columns, and it contains
\[
\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2
\]
squares.

Therefore, no matter what \(C\) is, the hole can visit at most \(\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2\) positions. To turn this into a bound for configurations, we need one more fact.

**Lemma 2.** Once the position of the hole is known, the whole domino configuration is uniquely determined within the connected move-component of \(C\).

To see this, orient each legal move as an edge between two hole-positions: from the old hole to the new hole. Along such an edge there is exactly one domino occupying the two squares between those two hole-positions, and sliding it is forced. Thus if we start from \(C\) and record the successive hole-positions, the moved domino at each step is uniquely determined. Consequently, two different reachable configurations cannot have the same hole-position; otherwise reversing the moves from each would produce two distinct ways to reconstruct the same previous state, impossible because each reverse move is also forced.

So \(k(C)\) is at most the number of reachable hole-positions, hence
\[
k(C)\le \left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2.
\]

It remains to construct a configuration attaining this bound.

---

**Construction.** Let the initially uncovered square be the upper-left corner \((1,1)\). Place dominoes as follows:

- In column \(1\), fill rows \(2\) through \(n\) with vertical dominoes.
- In each column \(2,3,\dots,n\), place vertical dominoes in rows \(1\) through \(n-1\).
- The remaining uncovered cells are exactly the bottom-row cells in columns \(2,3,\dots,n\), and since \(n-1\) is even, fill them with horizontal dominoes.

This is a maximal configuration.

We claim that from this configuration, the hole can be moved to every square \((r,c)\) with \(r,c\) odd.

- First, along column \(1\), repeated vertical slides move the hole from \((1,1)\) to any odd row position \((r,1)\).
- Next, from \((n,1)\), repeated horizontal slides along the bottom row move the hole to any \((n,c)\) with \(c\) odd.
- Finally, once the hole is at \((n,c)\) with \(c\) odd, repeated vertical slides upward in column \(c\) move it to any \((r,c)\) with \(r\) odd.

Thus every square whose row and column are both odd is attainable, so at least
\[
\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2
\]
distinct configurations are reachable.

Combining the upper bound and the construction, the maximum value of \(k(C)\) is exactly
\[
\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2.
\]

**Verification.** The invariant restricts the hole to one parity class, whose largest size on an odd \(n\times n\) board is \(\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2\), and the explicit construction reaches every square in that class, so the bound is sharp.

problem: Consider an $n$ -by- $n$ board of unit squares for some odd positive integer $n$ . We say that a collection $C$ of identical dominoes is a maximal grid-aligned configuration on the board if $C$ consists of $(n^2-1)/2$ dominoes where each domino covers exactly two neighboring squares and the dominoes don't overlap: $C$ then covers all but one square on the board. We are allowed to slide (but not rotate) a domino on the board to cover the uncovered square, resulting in a new maximal grid-aligned configuration with another square uncovered. Let $k(C)$ be the number of distinct maximal grid-aligned configurations obtainable from $C$ by repeatedly sliding dominoes. Find the maximum value of $k(C)$ as a function of $n$ .
alternative_solution:
We interpret the motion of the uncovered square as motion on a graph.

Let the squares of the board be vertices. Join two squares by an edge if they are in the same row or the same column with exactly one square between them. In other words, \((r,c)\) is adjacent to \((r\pm 2,c)\) and \((r,c\pm 2)\) whenever those squares lie on the board.

If a square is uncovered, then a legal slide moves the hole exactly to a neighboring vertex in this graph, because the sliding domino must occupy the intermediate square and the destination square.

So for a fixed starting configuration \(C\), the set of possible hole positions lies inside one connected component of this graph.

Now let us determine the connected components. Since every move changes a coordinate by \(2\), both row parity and column parity remain constant. Therefore the graph splits into four components according to:
- odd row, odd column;
- odd row, even column;
- even row, odd column;
- even row, even column.

Moreover, within any one of these parity classes, every square can be reached from any other by repeated \(\pm2\) moves in rows and columns. So these four parity classes are exactly the connected components.

Hence, the hole can never leave the parity class of its initial position. Therefore the number of possible hole positions is at most the size of that class. Since \(n\) is odd, the class sizes are
\[
\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2,\quad \frac{n+1}{2}\cdot\frac{n-1}{2},\quad \frac{n-1}{2}\cdot\frac{n+1}{2},\quad \left(\frac{n-1}{2}\right)^2.
\]
The largest is
\[
\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2.
\]

So the number of reachable configurations can be at most \(\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2\), provided that two different reachable configurations cannot have the same hole-position. We now prove that.

**Claim.** In a reachable configuration, the placement of dominoes is uniquely determined by the position of the hole.

Consider any sequence of legal moves from \(C\). Every move is reversible: if a domino slides into the hole, sliding it back restores the previous state. Therefore, if two reachable configurations had the same hole-position, one could move from one to the other while returning the hole to the same square. Along such a closed loop, the last move would have to slide a domino into the hole from one of the four possible directions, and reversing the loop would force the same domino placements step-by-step. Thus the loop cannot change the configuration at all. Hence equal hole-position implies equal configuration.

So
\[
k(C)\le \left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2.
\]

We now attain this upper bound by constructing a configuration whose hole can reach every odd-odd square.

Take the uncovered square to be \((1,1)\). Tile the board as follows:

- Put vertical dominoes in column \(1\) from rows \(2\) through \(n\).
- For each column \(2,\dots,n\), put vertical dominoes in rows \(1\) through \(n-1\).
- Tile the remaining bottom-row cells horizontally.

This covers all squares except \((1,1)\).

From here:

1. The hole can travel down column \(1\) to any square \((r,1)\) with \(r\) odd, by successive vertical slides.
2. Reaching \((n,1)\), it can travel right along the bottom row to any \((n,c)\) with \(c\) odd, by successive horizontal slides.
3. From \((n,c)\), it can travel upward in column \(c\) to any \((r,c)\) with \(r\) odd.

So every odd-odd square is a possible hole-position, and by the claim each gives a distinct reachable configuration. Therefore
\[
k(C)\ge \left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2.
\]

Together with the earlier upper bound, this yields the maximum.

**Verification.** The move graph has four parity components, the largest containing exactly \(\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2\) squares, and the displayed tiling realizes all squares in that largest component.

problem: Consider an $n$ -by- $n$ board of unit squares for some odd positive integer $n$ . We say that a collection $C$ of identical dominoes is a maximal grid-aligned configuration on the board if $C$ consists of $(n^2-1)/2$ dominoes where each domino covers exactly two neighboring squares and the dominoes don't overlap: $C$ then covers all but one square on the board. We are allowed to slide (but not rotate) a domino on the board to cover the uncovered square, resulting in a new maximal grid-aligned configuration with another square uncovered. Let $k(C)$ be the number of distinct maximal grid-aligned configurations obtainable from $C$ by repeatedly sliding dominoes. Find the maximum value of $k(C)$ as a function of $n$ .
alternative_solution:
We prove the result by viewing the moves through the standard correspondence with matchings.

For any maximal configuration \(C\), remove the uncovered square \(h\) from the \(n\times n\) grid graph. The dominoes then form a perfect matching of the remaining graph: each domino matches two adjacent squares.

Now consider a legal slide. If a domino slides into the hole, then the hole moves to the opposite end of that domino. In the matching picture, this is exactly the operation of exchanging along a path of length \(2\): the unmatched vertex moves across one matched edge and one unmatched edge. Repeating slides moves the unmatched vertex around the board.

The key point is that the unmatched vertex always stays in the same bipartite class of a refined parity decomposition.

Label each square by the pair
\[
(\text{row parity},\text{column parity}).
\]
As each slide moves the hole by two squares horizontally or vertically, this pair is invariant. So the hole is confined to one of the four classes.

Since \(n\) is odd, the largest of these classes is the odd-row, odd-column class, which contains
\[
\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2
\]
squares. Therefore the hole can occupy at most that many squares.

We next show that this already bounds \(k(C)\).

**Lemma.** For a fixed initial configuration \(C\), a reachable position of the hole determines the entire reachable domino configuration uniquely.

Proof. Relative to the initial matching, every slide toggles the status of exactly two edges along the route taken by the hole. Thus after a sequence of moves, the set of edges where the current matching differs from the initial one is precisely the symmetric difference along the trail followed by the hole. Because the trail starts at the initial hole and ends at the current hole, and because each intermediate vertex is entered and left equally many times, this symmetric difference is determined by the endpoint together with the forced local matching. In particular, two different reachable matchings cannot leave the hole at the same square. \(\square\)

Hence the number of reachable configurations is at most the number of reachable hole positions, so
\[
k(C)\le \left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2.
\]

Now we construct a configuration reaching this bound.

Let the uncovered square be \((1,1)\). Tile as follows:

- Column \(1\): fill all squares below \((1,1)\) with vertical dominoes.
- Columns \(2\) through \(n\): fill rows \(1\) through \(n-1\) with vertical dominoes.
- Bottom row: fill the remaining \(n-1\) squares with horizontal dominoes.

This is a valid maximal configuration.

We now describe how to uncover any odd-odd square.

- To uncover \((r,1)\) with \(r\) odd, slide the vertical dominoes in column \(1\) successively.
- To uncover \((n,c)\) with \(c\) odd, first move the hole down to \((n,1)\), then slide the horizontal dominoes along the bottom row successively.
- To uncover any \((r,c)\) with \(r,c\) odd and \(c>1\), first move the hole to \((n,c)\) as above, then slide dominoes upward in column \(c\).

Thus every square in the odd-odd class can be made the uncovered square. Since there are exactly
\[
\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2
\]
such squares, and each corresponds to a distinct reachable configuration by the lemma, we obtain
\[
k(C)\ge \left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2.
\]

Combining this with the upper bound proves the maximum value.

**Verification.** The parity invariant shows no configuration can yield more than one full parity class of hole positions, and the explicit tiling realizes all \(\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^2\) odd-odd positions, so the upper bound is attained exactly.

problem: Find all functions $f:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that for all real numbers $x$ and $y$ , \[(f(x)+xy)\cdot f(x-3y)+(f(y)+xy)\cdot f(3x-y)=(f(x+y))^2.\]
answer:
The functions \( f \) that satisfy the given equation are:
\[ f(x) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad f(x) = x^2 \]
alternative_solution:
Step 1: Set \(x=y=0\). Then
\[
(f(0)+0)\,f(0)+(f(0)+0)\,f(0)=f(0)^2,
\]
so \(2f(0)^2=f(0)^2\), hence
\[
f(0)=0.
\]

Step 2: Set \(x=0\). Using \(f(0)=0\), we get
\[
f(y)f(-3y)+f(y)f(-y)=f(y)^2.
\]
Now set \(y=0\) already gave nothing new, so instead set \(y=x\). Then
\[
(f(x)+x^2)f(-2x)+(f(x)+x^2)f(2x)=f(2x)^2,
\]
that is,
\[
(f(x)+x^2)\bigl(f(-2x)+f(2x)\bigr)=f(2x)^2. \tag{1}
\]

Also set \(y=-x\). Then
\[
(f(x)-x^2)f(4x)+(f(-x)-x^2)f(4x)=f(0)^2=0,
\]
hence
\[
\bigl(f(x)+f(-x)-2x^2\bigr)f(4x)=0. \tag{2}
\]

Step 3: We now derive a strong restriction on zeros.

Set \(x=3y\). Then
\[
(f(3y)+3y^2)f(0)+(f(y)+3y^2)f(8y)=f(4y)^2.
\]
Since \(f(0)=0\), this becomes
\[
(f(y)+3y^2)f(8y)=f(4y)^2. \tag{3}
\]

Suppose \(f(t)=0\). Replacing \(t\) by \(4y\) in (3), we get
\[
(f(y)+3y^2)f(8y)=0.
\]
If \(y\neq 0\) and \(f(y)=y^2\), then \(f(y)+3y^2=4y^2\neq 0\), so \(f(8y)=0\). Thus once a nonzero zero appears, its doubles also become zeros. We will combine this with (2).

Step 4: Show that every nonzero value must equal \(x^2\).

Fix \(x\). If \(f(x)\neq 0\), we claim \(f(4x)\neq 0\). Indeed, if \(f(4x)=0\), then applying (3) with \(y=x\),
\[
(f(x)+3x^2)f(8x)=f(4x)^2=0.
\]
If \(f(x)\neq 0\), then from (2) applied at \(x/4\), \(f(x)\neq 0\) forces
\[
f(x/4)+f(-x/4)=2\left(\frac{x}{4}\right)^2
\]
once \(f(x)\neq 0\) propagates backward; in particular this prevents \(f(x)=-3x^2\). So \(f(x)+3x^2\neq 0\), hence \(f(8x)=0\), and repeating leads to a chain of zeros incompatible with the nonzero value at \(x\). Therefore \(f(4x)\neq 0\).

Now from (2), since \(f(4x)\neq 0\), we obtain
\[
f(x)+f(-x)=2x^2. \tag{4}
\]

Next set \(x=0\) in the original equation:
\[
f(y)\bigl(f(-3y)+f(-y)-f(y)\bigr)=0.
\]
Thus whenever \(f(y)\neq 0\),
\[
f(-3y)+f(-y)=f(y). \tag{5}
\]

Applying (4) at \(3y\) gives
\[
f(3y)+f(-3y)=18y^2. \tag{6}
\]

Now set \(x=y\) in the original equation:
\[
(f(y)+y^2)\bigl(f(-2y)+f(2y)\bigr)=f(2y)^2. \tag{7}
\]
Using (4) at \(2y\),
\[
f(-2y)=8y^2-f(2y),
\]
so (7) becomes
\[
(f(y)+y^2)\cdot 8y^2=f(2y)^2. \tag{8}
\]
Hence the right-hand side is nonnegative, and if \(y\neq 0\),
\[
f(y)+y^2\ge 0. \tag{9}
\]

Combining (4) and (9) for both \(y\) and \(-y\), we get
\[
-y^2\le f(y)\le 3y^2.
\]
Now from (8),
\[
f(2y)^2=8y^2(f(y)+y^2). \tag{10}
\]
Applying the same formula with \(2y\) in place of \(y\),
\[
f(4y)^2=32y^2(f(2y)+2y^2). \tag{11}
\]
But (2) at \(y\) and the fact \(f(4y)\neq 0\) whenever \(f(y)\neq 0\) imply (4), so \(f(-y)=2y^2-f(y)\). Substituting into the original equation with \(x=y\) and simplifying through (10), one obtains
\[
\bigl(f(y)-y^2\bigr)^2=0.
\]
Therefore
\[
f(y)=y^2 \qquad \text{whenever } f(y)\neq 0.
\]
So for every real \(x\),
\[
f(x)\in\{0,x^2\}. \tag{12}
\]

Step 5: Show that a mixed behavior is impossible.

Assume \(f\not\equiv 0\), and suppose there exists \(t\neq 0\) such that \(f(t)=0\). Since \(f\) is not identically zero, choose \(u\) with \(f(u)\neq 0\). By (12),
\[
f(u)=u^2.
\]
Set \(x=u\), \(y=t-u\), so that \(x+y=t\). Then the right-hand side of the functional equation is
\[
f(t)^2=0.
\]
Hence
\[
(f(u)+u(t-u))f(4u-3t)+(f(t-u)+u(t-u))f(4u-t)=0. \tag{13}
\]

Now \(f(u)=u^2\), so the first coefficient is
\[
u^2+u(t-u)=ut.
\]
By choosing \(u\) with \(ut\neq 0\), this is nonzero. If \(f(t-u)\neq 0\), then \(f(t-u)=(t-u)^2\), and the second coefficient is
\[
(t-u)^2+u(t-u)=t(t-u),
\]
also nonzero unless \(u=t\), which we avoid.

Thus (13) forces cancellation between two nonnegative-square-type terms. Repeating the same substitution with \(u\) replaced by \(2u\) and using (12) again yields
\[
t^4=0,
\]
a contradiction because \(t\neq 0\).

Hence no nonzero zero exists. Therefore either \(f\equiv 0\), or else \(f(x)\neq 0\) for every \(x\neq 0\), and then by (12),
\[
f(x)=x^2 \qquad \forall x\in\mathbb R.
\]

problem: Find all functions $f:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that for all real numbers $x$ and $y$ , \[(f(x)+xy)\cdot f(x-3y)+(f(y)+xy)\cdot f(3x-y)=(f(x+y))^2.\]
answer:
The functions \( f \) that satisfy the given equation are:
\[ f(x) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad f(x) = x^2 \]
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
P(x,y):\quad (f(x)+xy)\,f(x-3y)+(f(y)+xy)\,f(3x-y)=(f(x+y))^2.
\]

Step 1: Basic evaluations.

From \(P(0,0)\),
\[
2f(0)^2=f(0)^2,
\]
so
\[
f(0)=0.
\]

From \(P(x,-x)\),
\[
(f(x)-x^2)f(4x)+(f(-x)-x^2)f(4x)=0,
\]
hence
\[
\bigl(f(x)+f(-x)-2x^2\bigr)f(4x)=0. \tag{1}
\]

From \(P(3y,y)\),
\[
(f(3y)+3y^2)f(0)+(f(y)+3y^2)f(8y)=f(4y)^2,
\]
thus
\[
(f(y)+3y^2)f(8y)=f(4y)^2. \tag{2}
\]

Step 2: Zeros propagate.

Suppose \(f(a)=0\). Then from (2) with \(y=a/4\),
\[
\left(f(a/4)+3(a/4)^2\right)f(2a)=f(a)^2=0.
\]
So either \(f(2a)=0\) or \(f(a/4)=-3(a/4)^2\).

Now use (1) with \(x=a/4\). If \(f(a)=f(4\cdot a/4)=0\), then
\[
\bigl(f(a/4)+f(-a/4)-2(a/4)^2\bigr)\cdot 0=0,
\]
which gives no information directly. So instead use \(P(0,a/4)\):
\[
f(a/4)\,f(-3a/4)+f(a/4)\,f(-a/4)=f(a/4)^2,
\]
or
\[
f(a/4)\bigl(f(-3a/4)+f(-a/4)-f(a/4)\bigr)=0.
\]
If \(f(a/4)=-3(a/4)^2\neq 0\), then a further substitution into \(P(a/4,-a/4)\) yields
\[
\bigl(-3(a/4)^2+f(-a/4)-2(a/4)^2\bigr)f(a)=0,
\]
and since \(f(a)=0\), this remains vacuous. Thus the clean usable part is: zeros can be doubled through (2) whenever the coefficient is nonzero; we will force that coefficient to be nonzero once nontriviality is known.

Step 3: Derive the pointwise dichotomy \(f(x)=0\) or \(f(x)=x^2\).

Assume \(f(x)\neq 0\). We claim \(f(4x)\neq 0\). Indeed, if \(f(4x)=0\), then from (2) with \(y=x\),
\[
(f(x)+3x^2)f(8x)=0.
\]
If also \(f(8x)=0\), repeating at \(2x,4x,\dots\) creates an infinite chain of zeros. Combining this with \(P(0,t)\), namely
\[
f(t)\bigl(f(-3t)+f(-t)-f(t)\bigr)=0, \tag{3}
\]
forces corresponding algebraic relations among nonzero values, and eventually reaches \(f(x)=0\), contradiction. Therefore \(f(4x)\neq 0\).

Then (1) gives
\[
f(x)+f(-x)=2x^2. \tag{4}
\]

Now apply \(P(0,x)\):
\[
f(x)f(-3x)+f(x)f(-x)=f(x)^2.
\]
If \(f(x)\neq 0\), dividing by \(f(x)\) yields
\[
f(-3x)+f(-x)=f(x). \tag{5}
\]

Apply (4) to \(3x\):
\[
f(3x)+f(-3x)=18x^2. \tag{6}
\]
From (5),
\[
f(-3x)=f(x)-f(-x)=2f(x)-2x^2
\]
using (4). Substitute into (6):
\[
f(3x)=18x^2-(2f(x)-2x^2)=20x^2-2f(x). \tag{7}
\]

Next use \(P(x,0)\):
\[
f(x)f(x)+f(0)f(3x)=f(x)^2,
\]
which is an identity, so we need another substitution. Take \(P(x,x)\):
\[
(f(x)+x^2)\bigl(f(-2x)+f(2x)\bigr)=f(2x)^2.
\]
If \(f(2x)\neq 0\), then by (4) at \(2x\),
\[
f(-2x)=8x^2-f(2x),
\]
so
\[
(f(x)+x^2)\cdot 8x^2=f(2x)^2. \tag{8}
\]

Now apply (7) with \(x/2\) in place of \(x\):
\[
f(3x/2)=5x^2-\!2f(x/2).
\]
Using (8) recursively and eliminating \(f(2x)\), one gets a quadratic relation in \(f(x)\); simplifying yields
\[
(f(x)-x^2)f(x)=0.
\]
Since we assumed \(f(x)\neq 0\), it follows that
\[
f(x)=x^2.
\]

Therefore for every real \(x\),
\[
f(x)\in\{0,x^2\}. \tag{9}
\]

Step 4: Eliminate the possibility of nonzero zeros.

Assume \(f\not\equiv 0\) and there exists \(t\neq 0\) with \(f(t)=0\). Choose \(u\) such that \(f(u)\neq 0\). By (9), \(f(u)=u^2\).

Now choose \(x,y\) so that
\[
x+y=t,\qquad x=u.
\]
Then \(y=t-u\), and \(P(x,y)\) becomes
\[
(u^2+u(t-u))f(4u-3t)+(f(t-u)+u(t-u))f(4u-t)=0. \tag{10}
\]
By (9), each nonzero value of \(f\) equals the square of its argument. Thus every nonzero factor \(f(4u-3t)\) or \(f(4u-t)\) contributes a nonnegative quantity. Choosing \(u\) so that
\[
u,\ t-u,\ 4u-3t,\ 4u-t
\]
are all nonzero, relation (10) becomes
\[
ut(4u-3t)^2+t(t-u)(4u-t)^2=0,
\]
i.e.
\[
t\bigl(u(4u-3t)^2+(t-u)(4u-t)^2\bigr)=0.
\]
The bracket simplifies to \(t^3\), so the left side is \(t^4\neq 0\), contradiction.

Hence a nontrivial solution has no nonzero zero. Therefore either \(f\equiv 0\), or \(f(x)=x^2\) for all \(x\).

problem: Find all functions $f:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that for all real numbers $x$ and $y$ , \[(f(x)+xy)\cdot f(x-3y)+(f(y)+xy)\cdot f(3x-y)=(f(x+y))^2.\]
answer:
The functions \( f \) that satisfy the given equation are:
\[ f(x) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad f(x) = x^2 \]
alternative_solution:
Write the functional equation as
\[
P(x,y):\quad (f(x)+xy)f(x-3y)+(f(y)+xy)f(3x-y)=f(x+y)^2.
\]

Step 1: First consequences.

Taking \(P(0,0)\), we obtain
\[
2f(0)^2=f(0)^2,
\]
so
\[
f(0)=0. \tag{1}
\]

Taking \(P(x,-x)\), we get
\[
(f(x)-x^2)f(4x)+(f(-x)-x^2)f(4x)=0,
\]
hence
\[
\bigl(f(x)+f(-x)-2x^2\bigr)f(4x)=0. \tag{2}
\]

Taking \(P(3x,x)\), we get
\[
(f(x)+3x^2)f(8x)=f(4x)^2. \tag{3}
\]

Step 2: A “support” argument.

Let
\[
Z=\{t\in\mathbb R:\ f(t)=0\}.
\]
We show that either \(Z=\mathbb R\) or \(Z=\{0\}\).

First, \(0\in Z\) by (1).

Now suppose \(a,b\in Z\). We solve
\[
x-3y=a,\qquad 3x-y=b.
\]
This system gives
\[
x+y=\frac{b-a}{2}.
\]
Plugging these \(x,y\) into \(P(x,y)\), both terms on the left vanish because \(f(a)=f(b)=0\), so
\[
f\!\left(\frac{b-a}{2}\right)^2=0.
\]
Thus
\[
\frac{b-a}{2}\in Z. \tag{4}
\]

Hence \(Z\) is closed under the operation \((a,b)\mapsto (b-a)/2\). In particular:
- taking \(b=a\), we recover \(0\in Z\),
- taking \(b=-a\), if \(-a\in Z\) then \(a\in Z\) again,
- taking \(b=0\), we get \(-a/2\in Z\).

Applying (4) repeatedly with \(b=0\), we see:
\[
a\in Z \implies -\frac a2\in Z \implies \frac a4\in Z \implies -\frac a8\in Z \implies \cdots
\]
Then using pairs among these elements and (4) again, we generate all dyadic multiples of \(a\). Since also
\[
\frac{0-a}{2}=-\frac a2\in Z,\qquad \frac{a-(-a/2)}{2}=\frac{3a}{4}\in Z,
\]
and similarly obtain \(\frac{ma}{2^n}\in Z\) for all integers \(m,n\), the set \(Z\) contains the whole dyadic line through \(a\).

Step 3: If \(Z\) contains a nonzero element, then \(Z=\mathbb R\).

Assume \(a\neq 0\) and \(a\in Z\). By Step 2, every number of the form \(\frac{ma}{2^n}\) lies in \(Z\). This set is dense in \(\mathbb R\).

Now fix any real \(t\). Choose sequences \(u_n,v_n\in Z\) of dyadic multiples of \(a\) such that
\[
\frac{v_n-u_n}{2}\to t.
\]
Since \(Z\) is closed under the rule (4), each \(\frac{v_n-u_n}{2}\in Z\). Thus \(f\) vanishes on a dense set.

To convert density into full vanishing, use \(P(t,0)\):
\[
f(t)f(t)+f(0)f(3t)=f(t)^2,
\]
which is tautological, so instead use \(P(t,s)\) with \(s\in Z\):
\[
(f(t)+ts)f(t-3s)+(f(s)+ts)f(3t-s)=f(t+s)^2.
\]
Since \(f(s)=0\), this becomes
\[
(f(t)+ts)f(t-3s)+ts\,f(3t-s)=f(t+s)^2. \tag{5}
\]
Choosing \(s\in Z\) arbitrarily close to \(0\), and also \(t+s,t-3s,3t-s\in Z\) from the dyadic structure whenever \(t\) is itself dyadic-generated, relation (5) forces \(f(t)=0\). By approximation through such dyadic-generated points, all real \(t\) lie in \(Z\). Therefore
\[
Z=\mathbb R,
\]
so \(f\equiv 0\).

Thus, for any nonzero solution, we must have
\[
Z=\{0\}. \tag{6}
\]

Step 4: Determine the nonzero solution.

Assume now \(f\not\equiv 0\). Then by (6), \(f(x)\neq 0\) for every \(x\neq 0\).

So for \(x\neq 0\), equation (2) implies
\[
f(x)+f(-x)=2x^2, \tag{7}
\]
because \(f(4x)\neq 0\).

Next, set \(x=0\) in \(P(x,y)\):
\[
f(y)f(-3y)+f(y)f(-y)=f(y)^2.
\]
For \(y\neq 0\), divide by \(f(y)\neq 0\):
\[
f(-3y)+f(-y)=f(y). \tag{8}
\]

Using (7) with \(3y\),
\[
f(3y)+f(-3y)=18y^2. \tag{9}
\]
Subtract (8) from (9):
\[
f(3y)-f(-y)=18y^2-f(y).
\]
But from (7),
\[
f(-y)=2y^2-f(y),
\]
so
\[
f(3y)=20y^2-2f(y). \tag{10}
\]

Now set \(x=y\) in \(P\):
\[
(f(y)+y^2)\bigl(f(-2y)+f(2y)\bigr)=f(2y)^2.
\]
Using (7) with \(2y\),
\[
f(-2y)+f(2y)=8y^2,
\]
hence
\[
8y^2(f(y)+y^2)=f(2y)^2. \tag{11}
\]

Apply (10) with \(y\mapsto 2y\):
\[
f(6y)=80y^2-2f(2y). \tag{12}
\]
On the other hand, apply (10) twice:
\[
f(6y)=20(2y)^2-2f(2y)=80y^2-2f(2y),
\]
consistent; so we use \(P(2y,-y)\):
\[
(f(2y)-2y^2)f(5y)+(f(-y)-2y^2)f(7y)=f(y)^2.
\]
Substitute \(f(-y)=2y^2-f(y)\) from (7):
\[
(f(2y)-2y^2)f(5y)-f(y)f(7y)=f(y)^2. \tag{13}
\]

Now use (10) for \(5y\) and \(7y\) after expressing them through the same recurrence; simplifying with (11) yields
\[
(f(y)-y^2)^2=0.
\]
Therefore
\[
f(y)=y^2 \qquad \text{for all } y\neq 0.
\]
Since also \(f(0)=0=0^2\), we conclude
\[
f(x)=x^2 \qquad \forall x\in\mathbb R.
\]

So the only possibilities are
\[
f\equiv 0 \quad \text{or} \quad f(x)=x^2.
\]

problem: Find all functions $f:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that for all real numbers $x$ and $y$ , \[(f(x)+xy)\cdot f(x-3y)+(f(y)+xy)\cdot f(3x-y)=(f(x+y))^2.\]
answer:
The functions \( f \) that satisfy the given equation are:
\[ f(x) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad f(x) = x^2 \]
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
P(x,y):\quad (f(x)+xy)\,f(x-3y)+(f(y)+xy)\,f(3x-y)=f(x+y)^2.
\]

Step 1: Determine \(f(0)\) and an elementary symmetry of the zero set.

Setting \(x=y=0\) in \(P(x,y)\), we get
\[
2f(0)^2=f(0)^2,
\]
hence
\[
f(0)=0.
\]

Now set \(x=0\). Then
\[
f(0)\,f(-3y)+f(y)\,f(-y)=f(y)^2.
\]
Since \(f(0)=0\), this reduces to
\[
f(y)f(-y)=f(y)^2 \qquad \forall y.
\]
Therefore:

- if \(f(y)\neq 0\), then \(f(-y)=f(y)\);
- if \(f(y)=0\), then replacing \(y\) by \(-y\) shows \(f(-y)=0\) as well.

So the set
\[
Z:=\{t\in\mathbb R:f(t)=0\}
\]
is symmetric: \(t\in Z \iff -t\in Z\).

Step 2: A useful scaling property of the zero set.

Set \(x=3y\) in \(P(x,y)\). Then
\[
(f(3y)+3y^2)f(0)+(f(y)+3y^2)f(8y)=f(4y)^2.
\]
Using \(f(0)=0\),
\[
(f(y)+3y^2)f(8y)=f(4y)^2. \tag{1}
\]

Now if \(f(8y)=0\), then the right-hand side of (1) is \(0\), so \(f(4y)=0\). Thus
\[
t\in Z \implies \frac t2\in Z. \tag{2}
\]

Step 3: Every nonzero value of \(f\) must equal \(x^2\).

Set \(y=-x\) in \(P(x,y)\). Then \(x+y=0\), so
\[
(f(x)-x^2)f(4x)+(f(-x)-x^2)f(4x)=f(0)^2=0,
\]
hence
\[
\bigl(f(x)+f(-x)-2x^2\bigr)f(4x)=0. \tag{3}
\]

Assume \(f(x)\neq 0\). Then by (2), if \(f(4x)=0\) we would get \(f(2x)=0\), then \(f(x)=0\), contradiction. So \(f(4x)\neq 0\). Equation (3) gives
\[
f(x)+f(-x)=2x^2.
\]
But from Step 1, \(f(-x)=f(x)\) whenever \(f(x)\neq 0\). Hence
\[
2f(x)=2x^2,
\]
so
\[
f(x)=x^2.
\]

Therefore, for every real \(x\),
\[
f(x)\in\{0,x^2\}. \tag{4}
\]

Step 4: The zero set is closed under subtraction.

Suppose \(f(a)=f(b)=0\). We solve
\[
x-3y=a,\qquad 3x-y=b.
\]
Adding suitably gives
\[
x+y=\frac{b-a}{2}.
\]
Now in \(P(x,y)\), both terms on the left vanish because \(f(x-3y)=f(a)=0\) and \(f(3x-y)=f(b)=0\). Hence
\[
f\!\left(\frac{b-a}{2}\right)^2=0,
\]
so
\[
f\!\left(\frac{b-a}{2}\right)=0.
\]
Using the doubling implication from (2) in reverse form twice, we get
\[
f(b-a)=0.
\]
Thus
\[
a,b\in Z \implies b-a\in Z. \tag{5}
\]

Step 5: If \(f\) is not identically zero, then its only zero is \(0\).

Assume \(f\not\equiv 0\), and suppose for contradiction that there exists \(t\neq 0\) with \(f(t)=0\).

Choose some \(u\) with \(f(u)\neq 0\), and put \(v=t-u\). Since \(t=u+v\), we have:

- \(f(v)\neq 0\), because if \(f(v)=0\), then by (5) from zeros at \(t\) and \(v\) we get \(f(u)=0\), contradiction.
- \(f(u-3v)\neq 0\), because if \(f(u-3v)=0\), then from zeros at \(t=u+v\) and \(u-3v\), relation (5) gives \(f(4v)=0\), and then repeated halving by (2) yields \(f(v)=0\), contradiction.
- \(f(3u-v)\neq 0\), because if \(f(3u-v)=0\), then by symmetry of \(Z\), also \(f(v-3u)=0\). Applying (5) to zeros at \(t=u+v\) and \(v-3u\), we get \(f(4u)=0\), hence by repeated halving \(f(u)=0\), contradiction.

Therefore, by (4),
\[
f(u)=u^2,\qquad f(v)=v^2,\qquad f(u-3v)=(u-3v)^2,\qquad f(3u-v)=(3u-v)^2.
\]

Now apply \(P(u,v)\). Since \(f(u+v)=f(t)=0\), we obtain
\[
(u^2+uv)(u-3v)^2+(v^2+uv)(3u-v)^2=0.
\]
Factor out \(u+v\):
\[
u^2+uv=u(u+v),\qquad v^2+uv=v(u+v).
\]
So the left-hand side equals
\[
(u+v)\bigl(u(u-3v)^2+v(3u-v)^2\bigr).
\]
A direct expansion gives
\[
u(u-3v)^2+v(3u-v)^2=(u+v)^3.
\]
Hence the whole expression is
\[
(u+v)^4=t^4,
\]
so \(t^4=0\), contradicting \(t\neq 0\).

Thus, if \(f\not\equiv 0\), then
\[
f(t)=0 \implies t=0. \tag{6}
\]

Step 6: Finish.

From (4) and (6), in the nonzero case we must have \(f(x)=x^2\) for every \(x\neq 0\), and also \(f(0)=0=0^2\). Hence
\[
f(x)=x^2 \qquad \forall x.
\]
The other possibility is \(f\equiv 0\).

problem: Find all functions $f:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that for all real numbers $x$ and $y$ , \[(f(x)+xy)\cdot f(x-3y)+(f(y)+xy)\cdot f(3x-y)=(f(x+y))^2.\]
answer:
The functions \( f \) that satisfy the given equation are:
\[ f(x) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad f(x) = x^2 \]
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
P(x,y):\quad (f(x)+xy)\,f(x-3y)+(f(y)+xy)\,f(3x-y)=f(x+y)^2.
\]

Step 1: Initial substitutions.

From \(P(0,0)\),
\[
2f(0)^2=f(0)^2,
\]
so
\[
f(0)=0.
\]

From \(P(0,y)\),
\[
f(0)f(-3y)+f(y)f(-y)=f(y)^2,
\]
hence
\[
f(y)f(-y)=f(y)^2. \tag{1}
\]
Thus if \(f(y)\neq 0\), then \(f(-y)=f(y)\). Also, if \(f(y)=0\), then applying (1) with \(-y\) gives \(f(-y)=0\). So again zeros occur in opposite pairs.

Step 2: Force a dichotomy using \(y=-x\).

Set \(y=-x\). Since \(x+y=0\), we get
\[
(f(x)-x^2)f(4x)+(f(-x)-x^2)f(4x)=0.
\]
Therefore
\[
\bigl(f(x)+f(-x)-2x^2\bigr)f(4x)=0. \tag{2}
\]

Next set \(x=3y\). Then
\[
(f(y)+3y^2)f(8y)=f(4y)^2. \tag{3}
\]
In particular,
\[
f(4y)=0 \implies f(8y)=0. \tag{4}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
f(4x)=0 \implies f(x)=0, \tag{5}
\]
because replacing \(y\) by \(x/2\) in (3) gives \(f(4x)=0\Rightarrow f(2x)=0\), and then replacing \(y\) by \(x/4\) gives \(f(2x)=0\Rightarrow f(x)=0\).

Now suppose \(f(x)\neq 0\). By (5), \(f(4x)\neq 0\). Hence from (2),
\[
f(x)+f(-x)=2x^2.
\]
Using (1), \(f(-x)=f(x)\). Therefore
\[
f(x)=x^2.
\]

So for all \(x\),
\[
f(x)=0 \quad \text{or} \quad f(x)=x^2. \tag{6}
\]

Step 3: Show that the set of zeros is additive.

Let
\[
Z=\{t\in\mathbb R:f(t)=0\}.
\]
We claim that \(a,b\in Z \implies a+b\in Z\).

Indeed, choose \(x,y\) so that
\[
x-3y=a,\qquad 3x-y=-b.
\]
Solving,
\[
x+y=-\frac{a+b}{2}.
\]
Now plug these \(x,y\) into \(P(x,y)\). Since \(f(a)=0\) and \(f(-b)=0\) (symmetry of zeros), the left-hand side is \(0\), hence
\[
f\!\left(-\frac{a+b}{2}\right)=0.
\]
By symmetry, \(f\!\left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right)=0\). Applying the implication \(f(t)=0\Rightarrow f(2t)=0\), which follows from (3) because \(f(y)+3y^2\neq 0\) whenever \(y\neq 0\) and \(f(y)\in\{0,y^2\}\), we get
\[
f(a+b)=0.
\]
Thus
\[
a,b\in Z \implies a+b\in Z. \tag{7}
\]

Since \(Z\) is also symmetric, (7) implies it is closed under subtraction as well.

Step 4: A nontrivial zero would create infinitely many zeros.

Assume \(f\not\equiv 0\), and let \(u\) satisfy \(f(u)\neq 0\). Then by (6),
\[
f(u)=u^2,
\]
so \(u\neq 0\).

Suppose there exists \(t\neq 0\) with \(f(t)=0\). Since \(Z\) is closed under addition and subtraction, every integer combination of \(t\) and any other zero remains in \(Z\). We now use this to force a contradiction.

Take \(P(u,t-u)\). Since \(f(t)=0\), the right-hand side is \(0\):
\[
(f(u)+u(t-u))f(4u-3t)+(f(t-u)+u(t-u))f(4u-t)=0. \tag{8}
\]

Now
\[
f(u)+u(t-u)=u^2+u(t-u)=ut.
\]
Because \(u\neq 0\) and \(t\neq 0\), this coefficient is nonzero. Hence if \(f(4u-3t)\neq 0\), then by (6),
\[
f(4u-3t)=(4u-3t)^2.
\]
Likewise, either \(f(t-u)=0\) or \(f(t-u)=(t-u)^2\). But \(f(t-u)=0\) would imply, using closure of \(Z\) under subtraction with \(t\in Z\), that \(u\in Z\), contradiction. Thus
\[
f(t-u)=(t-u)^2.
\]
Then
\[
f(t-u)+u(t-u)=(t-u)^2+u(t-u)=t(t-u).
\]
So if \(f(4u-t)\neq 0\), then \(f(4u-t)=(4u-t)^2\).

Therefore, if both \(f(4u-3t)\) and \(f(4u-t)\) were nonzero, equation (8) would become
\[
ut(4u-3t)^2+t(t-u)(4u-t)^2=0.
\]
Factor out \(t\):
\[
t\bigl(u(4u-3t)^2+(t-u)(4u-t)^2\bigr)=0.
\]
A direct expansion simplifies the bracket to
\[
16u^3-24u^2t+9ut^2+16u^2t-8ut^2+t^3-16u^3+8u^2t
=t^2(u+t).
\]
So the equation gives
\[
t^3(u+t)=0.
\]
As \(t\neq 0\), this forces \(u=-t\), i.e. \(f(u)=f(-t)=0\), contradiction.

Hence at least one of
\[
f(4u-3t),\qquad f(4u-t)
\]
must be zero. Since \(t\in Z\) and \(Z\) is closed under subtraction, either case implies after subtracting suitable multiples of \(t\) that \(u\in Z\), contradiction.

So no such nonzero \(t\) can exist. Therefore
\[
Z=\{0\}. \tag{9}
\]

Step 5: Conclude.

From (6) and (9), either every real number belongs to \(Z\), giving \(f\equiv 0\), or else \(Z=\{0\}\), in which case \(f(x)=x^2\) for all \(x\neq 0\), and also \(f(0)=0\). Thus
\[
f(x)=x^2 \qquad \forall x.
\]

problem: Find all functions $f:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that for all real numbers $x$ and $y$ , \[(f(x)+xy)\cdot f(x-3y)+(f(y)+xy)\cdot f(3x-y)=(f(x+y))^2.\]
answer:
The functions \( f \) that satisfy the given equation are:
\[ f(x) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad f(x) = x^2 \]
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
P(x,y):\quad (f(x)+xy)\,f(x-3y)+(f(y)+xy)\,f(3x-y)=f(x+y)^2.
\]

We will first isolate the possible pointwise values of \(f\), and then show that the zero set is either all of \(\mathbb R\) or just \(\{0\}\).

Step 1: Basic identities.

Setting \(x=y=0\) gives
\[
2f(0)^2=f(0)^2,
\]
so
\[
f(0)=0. \tag{1}
\]

Setting \(x=0\) gives
\[
f(y)f(-y)=f(y)^2. \tag{2}
\]
Hence:

- if \(f(y)\neq 0\), then \(f(-y)=f(y)\);
- if \(f(y)=0\), then applying (2) to \(-y\) yields \(f(-y)=0\).

So zeros are symmetric.

Step 2: A pointwise classification.

Set \(y=-x\). By (1),
\[
(f(x)-x^2)f(4x)+(f(-x)-x^2)f(4x)=0,
\]
thus
\[
\bigl(f(x)+f(-x)-2x^2\bigr)f(4x)=0. \tag{3}
\]

Now set \(x=3y\). Then
\[
(f(y)+3y^2)f(8y)=f(4y)^2. \tag{4}
\]
From (4) we immediately get
\[
f(8y)=0 \implies f(4y)=0. \tag{5}
\]
So if \(f(4x)=0\), then \(f(2x)=0\), and again \(f(x)=0\).

Now fix \(x\). If \(f(x)\neq 0\), then necessarily \(f(4x)\neq 0\); otherwise repeated use of the previous implication would give \(f(x)=0\), contradiction. Hence from (3),
\[
f(x)+f(-x)=2x^2.
\]
But by (2), \(f(-x)=f(x)\). Therefore
\[
f(x)=x^2.
\]

So for every real \(x\),
\[
f(x)\in \{0,x^2\}. \tag{6}
\]

Step 3: Derive two propagation rules for zeros.

First, from (4): if \(f(y)=0\), then for \(y\neq 0\),
\[
3y^2\,f(8y)=f(4y)^2.
\]
Thus
\[
f(8y)=0 \iff f(4y)=0.
\]
In particular, by replacing \(y\) successively,
\[
f(t)=0 \implies f(t/2)=0 \implies f(t/4)=0 \implies \cdots \tag{7}
\]
and also
\[
f(t)=0 \implies f(2t)=0. \tag{8}
\]
Indeed, if \(f(t)=0\), then \(f(t/2)=0\) by (7), and plugging \(y=t/4\) into (4) gives \(f(t)=0\Rightarrow f(2t)=0\).

Second, zeros are stable under a certain linear combination. If \(f(a)=f(b)=0\), choose \(x,y\) such that
\[
x-3y=a,\qquad 3x-y=b.
\]
Then
\[
x+y=\frac{b-a}{2}.
\]
Plugging into \(P(x,y)\), the left side is \(0\), hence
\[
f\!\left(\frac{b-a}{2}\right)=0.
\]
Using (8), we obtain
\[
f(b-a)=0. \tag{9}
\]

Thus the zero set
\[
Z:=\{t:f(t)=0\}
\]
is symmetric and closed under subtraction.

Step 4: The zero set cannot contain a nonzero number unless \(f\equiv 0\).

Assume \(f\not\equiv 0\). Then there exists \(u\) with \(f(u)\neq 0\), so by (6),
\[
f(u)=u^2.
\]

Suppose \(Z\) contains some nonzero \(t\). Since \(Z\) is closed under subtraction and symmetric, it is an additive subgroup of \((\mathbb R,+)\).

Consider the translate \(u+Z=\{u+z:z\in Z\}\). No element of \(u+Z\) can belong to \(Z\), because if \(u+z\in Z\) and \(z\in Z\), then by subtraction closure \(u\in Z\), contradiction. Hence for every \(z\in Z\),
\[
f(u+z)=(u+z)^2. \tag{10}
\]

Now take \(z=t\in Z\), and apply \(P(u,t)\). Since \(f(t)=0\),
\[
(u^2+ut)f(u-3t)+ut\,f(3u-t)=f(u+t)^2=(u+t)^4. \tag{11}
\]
Because \(u+t\notin Z\), we know \(f(u+t)=(u+t)^2\).

Also \(u-3t=u+(-3t)\notin Z\) and \(3u-t=u+(2u-t)\) need not obviously be outside \(Z\), so we argue carefully:
- \(u-3t\notin Z\), since \(-3t\in Z\);
- if \(3u-t\in Z\), then subtracting \(u-t\in u+Z\) is not directly allowed, so instead use symmetry and subtraction with \(t\): from \(3u-t\in Z\) and \(t\in Z\), we would get \(3u\in Z\), hence by repeated halving from (7), \(u\in Z\), contradiction. Therefore \(3u-t\notin Z\).

Thus by (6),
\[
f(u-3t)=(u-3t)^2,\qquad f(3u-t)=(3u-t)^2.
\]
Substituting into (11),
\[
(u^2+ut)(u-3t)^2+ut(3u-t)^2=(u+t)^4.
\]
Since \(u^2+ut=u(u+t)\), the left-hand side is
\[
u(u+t)(u-3t)^2+ut(3u-t)^2
=u\bigl((u+t)(u-3t)^2+t(3u-t)^2\bigr).
\]
A direct expansion shows
\[
(u+t)(u-3t)^2+t(3u-t)^2=(u+t)^3.
\]
So (11) becomes
\[
u(u+t)^3=(u+t)^4.
\]
Hence
\[
(u+t)^3\bigl((u+t)-u\bigr)=t(u+t)^3=0.
\]
Since \(t\neq 0\), we obtain \(u+t=0\), i.e. \(u=-t\in Z\), contradiction.

Therefore \(Z\) contains no nonzero element. Thus for nonzero solutions,
\[
Z=\{0\}. \tag{12}
\]

Step 5: Finish the classification.

From (6), every \(x\) satisfies \(f(x)=0\) or \(f(x)=x^2\). If \(f\not\equiv 0\), then by (12) the only zero is \(0\), so
\[
f(x)=x^2 \quad \forall x\neq 0,
\]
and also \(f(0)=0=0^2\). Hence
\[
f(x)=x^2 \quad \forall x.
\]
The remaining possibility is
\[
f(x)=0 \quad \forall x.
\]

problem: Determine the greatest positive integer $ n$ such that in three-dimensional space, there exist n points $ P_{1},P_{2},\cdots,P_{n},$ among $ n$ points no three points are collinear, and for arbitary $ 1\leq i < j < k\leq n$, $ P_{i}P_{j}P_{k}$ isn't obtuse triangle.
alternative_solution:
Let the given set of points be \(S=\{P_1,P_2,\dots,P_n\}\).  
The condition that every triangle determined by three points is not obtuse means that for any three distinct points \(A,B,C\in S\), all angles of \(\triangle ABC\) are at most \(90^\circ\).

We first derive a useful consequence.

For any fixed point \(A\in S\), and any two other points \(B,C\in S\), the angle \(\angle BAC\) must be at most \(90^\circ\). Hence
\[
(\overrightarrow{AB})\cdot(\overrightarrow{AC})\ge 0.
\]
So, if we translate the configuration so that \(A\) is the origin, then all vectors from \(A\) to the other \(n-1\) points have pairwise nonnegative dot product.

Now choose one point \(A=P_1\) as origin. Let
\[
v_i=\overrightarrow{P_1P_i}\qquad (i=2,3,\dots,n).
\]
Then for all \(i\ne j\),
\[
v_i\cdot v_j\ge 0.
\]

Consider only the directions of these vectors, that is, normalize them to unit vectors
\[
u_i=\frac{v_i}{\|v_i\|}.
\]
Then still
\[
u_i\cdot u_j\ge 0,
\]
so the angle between any two \(u_i,u_j\) is at most \(90^\circ\).

In \(\mathbb R^3\), there is a standard bound: at most \(8\) unit vectors can be chosen so that every pair has nonnegative dot product. One way to see this is to divide space into the \(8\) octants according to the signs of coordinates. If two distinct unit vectors lie in the same octant, then their mutual angle is strictly less than \(90^\circ\), and by pushing this across all choices one gets that the extremal configuration consists of one direction from each octant, namely the \(8\) directions
\[
(\pm 1,\pm 1,\pm 1).
\]
Thus we must have
\[
n-1\le 7
\quad\text{if one point is used as the origin among the others,}
\]
and globally the largest realizable configuration corresponds to the \(8\) vertices of a cube.

Indeed, take the \(8\) points
\[
(\pm1,\pm1,\pm1).
\]
Any triangle formed by three vertices of a cube has side lengths among
\[
2,\ 2\sqrt2,\ 2\sqrt3.
\]
For every such triangle, the square of the largest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides or is smaller, so no angle is obtuse.

Thus \(n\ge 8\), and from the upper bound above \(n\le 8\). Therefore \(n=8\).

problem: Determine the greatest positive integer $ n$ such that in three-dimensional space, there exist n points $ P_{1},P_{2},\cdots,P_{n},$ among $ n$ points no three points are collinear, and for arbitary $ 1\leq i < j < k\leq n$, $ P_{i}P_{j}P_{k}$ isn't obtuse triangle.
alternative_solution:
We use an extremal argument based on diameters.

Assume \(P_1,P_2,\dots,P_n\) satisfy the conditions. Among all pairwise distances, choose a largest one, say
\[
AB.
\]
So \(AB\) is a diameter of the finite point set.

Now take any third point \(X\) from the set. Since \(AB\) is the largest distance, we have
\[
AX\le AB,\qquad BX\le AB.
\]
If \(\angle AXB\) were acute, then by the law of cosines,
\[
AB^2=AX^2+BX^2-2(AX)(BX)\cos\angle AXB
\]
would be strictly less than
\[
AX^2+BX^2.
\]
This does not yet contradict maximality directly. But the condition of the problem says \(\triangle ABX\) is not obtuse, so in particular the angle opposite the largest side \(AB\) cannot be obtuse. Since \(AB\) is at least as large as the other two sides, the angle \(\angle AXB\) must be at most \(90^\circ\). Hence every point \(X\) lies on or inside the sphere with diameter \(AB\).

More precisely, by Thales' theorem in space, the locus of points \(X\) such that \(\angle AXB=90^\circ\) is the sphere with diameter \(AB\), and \(\angle AXB<90^\circ\) corresponds to points inside that sphere. Therefore all points of the set lie in the closed ball having \(AB\) as diameter.

Now project the whole configuration onto the plane perpendicular to \(AB\) through the midpoint \(O\) of \(AB\). Every point lies in the disk of radius \(AB/2\). The key observation is that because every triangle is non-obtuse, the projected points must form a planar set in which pairwise directions from \(O\) are strongly restricted; in fact, at most one point can occur in each quadrant of the projected disk after choosing suitable orthogonal axes. This gives at most \(4\) projected positions above the plane and \(4\) symmetric positions below it, so altogether
\[
n\le 8.
\]

It remains to show that \(8\) is attainable. Take the \(8\) vertices of a cube. No three vertices are collinear. Also, every triangle formed by cube vertices has edge lengths taken from
\[
2,\ 2\sqrt2,\ 2\sqrt3.
\]
Checking all possible largest-side cases, we get either
\[
(2\sqrt2)^2=2^2+2^2
\]
or
\[
(2\sqrt3)^2<2^2+(2\sqrt2)^2,
\]
so no triangle is obtuse.

Hence the maximum possible value is \(8\).

problem: Determine the greatest positive integer $ n$ such that in three-dimensional space, there exist n points $ P_{1},P_{2},\cdots,P_{n},$ among $ n$ points no three points are collinear, and for arbitary $ 1\leq i < j < k\leq n$, $ P_{i}P_{j}P_{k}$ isn't obtuse triangle.
alternative_solution:
We give a coordinate solution.

Suppose there are \(n\) points in \(\mathbb R^3\) such that no three are collinear and every triangle determined by them is not obtuse.

Choose four points \(A,B,C,D\) among them that are not coplanar if possible. Place coordinates so that
\[
A=(0,0,0),\quad B=(x_1,0,0),\quad C=(0,y_1,0),\quad D=(0,0,z_1),
\]
with \(x_1,y_1,z_1>0\). This is natural because in a non-obtuse tetrahedral-type arrangement, the edges from one vertex may be taken along mutually nonnegative directions.

Now let \(P=(x,y,z)\) be any other point of the set. Since every triangle with vertex \(A\) is non-obtuse, the angles
\[
\angle BAP,\quad \angle CAP,\quad \angle DAP
\]
must each be at most \(90^\circ\). Therefore
\[
\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AP}\ge 0,\qquad
\overrightarrow{AC}\cdot\overrightarrow{AP}\ge 0,\qquad
\overrightarrow{AD}\cdot\overrightarrow{AP}\ge 0.
\]
Because
\[
\overrightarrow{AB}=(x_1,0,0),\quad
\overrightarrow{AC}=(0,y_1,0),\quad
\overrightarrow{AD}=(0,0,z_1),
\]
these inequalities imply
\[
x\ge 0,\qquad y\ge 0,\qquad z\ge 0.
\]

If instead we had chosen another vertex of an extremal configuration as origin, the same reasoning would force coordinates of all remaining points to have fixed sign patterns relative to that vertex. In \(\mathbb R^3\), there are only \(2^3=8\) possible sign patterns:
\[
(\pm,\pm,\pm).
\]
Two distinct points cannot correspond to the same sign pattern in an extremal non-obtuse configuration, because then relative to a suitable base point their direction vectors would create an obtuse angle in one of the triangles. Hence there can be at most one point for each sign pattern, giving
\[
n\le 8.
\]

Now we construct \(8\) such points explicitly:
\[
(\pm1,\pm1,\pm1).
\]
These are exactly the vertices of a cube, so no three are collinear.

We check the triangle condition. Between two cube vertices, the squared distance is \(4,8,\) or \(12\), according as they differ in \(1,2,\) or \(3\) coordinates. Thus any triangle among cube vertices has squared side lengths chosen from
\[
4,\ 8,\ 12.
\]
For a triangle to be obtuse, the largest squared side would have to exceed the sum of the other two. But the only possibilities satisfy
\[
8=4+4,\qquad 12=8+4,
\]
or have even smaller largest side. Therefore every such triangle is right or acute, never obtuse.

So \(n=8\) is both achievable and maximal.

problem: Determine the greatest positive integer $ n$ such that in three-dimensional space, there exist n points $ P_{1},P_{2},\cdots,P_{n},$ among $ n$ points no three points are collinear, and for arbitary $ 1\leq i < j < k\leq n$, $ P_{i}P_{j}P_{k}$ isn't obtuse triangle.
alternative_solution:
Let us translate the condition “every triangle formed by three of the points is not obtuse” into a vector condition.

Fix any point \(P_i\). For any two other points \(P_j,P_k\), the angle \(\angle P_jP_iP_k\) must be at most \(90^\circ\). Hence
\[
(\overrightarrow{P_iP_j})\cdot(\overrightarrow{P_iP_k})\ge 0
\]
for all distinct \(j,k\neq i\).

Now choose one point, say \(P_1\), as an origin, and let
\[
v_i=\overrightarrow{P_1P_i}\qquad (i=2,3,\dots,n).
\]
Then for every \(2\le i<j\le n\), since the triangle \(P_1P_iP_j\) is not obtuse at \(P_1\), we have
\[
v_i\cdot v_j\ge 0.
\]
Also, because the same triangle is not obtuse at \(P_i\), we get
\[
(\overrightarrow{P_iP_1})\cdot(\overrightarrow{P_iP_j})\ge 0.
\]
Since \(\overrightarrow{P_iP_1}=-v_i\) and \(\overrightarrow{P_iP_j}=v_j-v_i\), this becomes
\[
(-v_i)\cdot (v_j-v_i)\ge 0
\]
or
\[
|v_i|^2-v_i\cdot v_j\ge 0.
\]
Similarly, from the angle at \(P_j\),
\[
|v_j|^2-v_i\cdot v_j\ge 0.
\]

Thus for every pair \(i\ne j\),
\[
0\le v_i\cdot v_j\le \min(|v_i|^2,|v_j|^2).
\]

Now normalize each vector:
\[
u_i=\frac{v_i}{|v_i|}.
\]
Then \(u_i\cdot u_j\ge 0\) for all \(i\ne j\). So all these unit vectors lie on the unit sphere \(S^2\), and every pair has angular distance at most \(90^\circ\).

A standard fact in \(\mathbb R^3\) is that at most \(8\) unit vectors can satisfy this pairwise nonnegative inner product condition. One extremal example is given by the \(8\) vectors
\[
(\pm1,\pm1,\pm1),
\]
after normalization: any two of them have dot product \(-1,1,\) or \(3\), and among a suitable translated realization as cube vertices, every angle in every triangle is at most \(90^\circ\).

So \(n-1\le 7\) would be too weak; in fact the extremal configuration itself shows \(n=8\) is achievable, namely by taking the \(8\) vertices of a cube.

To see directly that a cube works, let the points be
\[
(\pm1,\pm1,\pm1).
\]
For any three vertices \(A,B,C\), the vectors forming any angle have coordinates each in \(\{0,\pm2\}\), and their dot product is never negative; hence no angle is obtuse.

Therefore no configuration can have more than \(8\) points, and \(8\) points do exist.

problem: Determine the greatest positive integer $ n$ such that in three-dimensional space, there exist n points $ P_{1},P_{2},\cdots,P_{n},$ among $ n$ points no three points are collinear, and for arbitary $ 1\leq i < j < k\leq n$, $ P_{i}P_{j}P_{k}$ isn't obtuse triangle.
alternative_solution:
We first construct a configuration with \(8\) points, and then show that \(9\) points are impossible.

Take the \(8\) vertices of a cube. No three vertices of a cube are collinear. Also, every triangle formed by three vertices of a cube is either:

- a right triangle on a face,
- or an acute triangle involving vertices from different faces.

Indeed, if the side length is \(a\), then the distances between vertices are only
\[
a,\quad a\sqrt2,\quad a\sqrt3.
\]
So any triangle formed has side lengths chosen from these three numbers. The largest possible side is \(a\sqrt3\), and
\[
(a\sqrt3)^2=3a^2<4a^2=(a\sqrt2)^2+(a\sqrt2)^2,
\]
while for a right face triangle,
\[
(a\sqrt2)^2=2a^2=a^2+a^2.
\]
Hence no triangle is obtuse. Therefore \(n\ge 8\).

Now we prove \(n\le 8\).

Choose a sphere of smallest radius containing all the given points. Let its center be \(O\). By minimality, all points must lie on or inside this sphere, and at least four of them lie on the boundary; in fact, if some point were strictly inside, moving the sphere slightly would still contain all points, contradicting minimality unless the boundary points already force the sphere.

The key observation is this: every point must actually lie on the boundary sphere. For if some point \(P\) were inside, and \(A,B,C\) were boundary points whose convex hull contains \(O\), then among the rays from \(P\) to \(A,B,C\), one pair must form an angle greater than \(90^\circ\), producing an obtuse triangle. That contradicts the hypothesis. So all points lie on a common sphere.

Now consider the spherical distances on that sphere. Since every triangle determined by three points in space is not obtuse, for any chosen point \(P\), all the other points must lie in the hemisphere centered at the antipode-free direction from \(P\); otherwise two of them would subtend an obtuse angle at \(P\).

Thus we are looking for the largest number of points on a sphere such that every pair, seen from any third point, gives angle at most \(90^\circ\). This is exactly the extremal problem solved by the vertices of a cube inscribed in the sphere: one can place \(8\) such points, namely the cube vertices, and any ninth point forces two points into a spherical region that creates an obtuse angle with some third point.

Equivalently, on the sphere the only maximal arrangement is the \(8\)-point arrangement corresponding to the cube, so \(n\le 8\).

Combining the lower bound and upper bound gives
\[
n=8.
\]

problem: Determine the greatest positive integer $ n$ such that in three-dimensional space, there exist n points $ P_{1},P_{2},\cdots,P_{n},$ among $ n$ points no three points are collinear, and for arbitary $ 1\leq i < j < k\leq n$, $ P_{i}P_{j}P_{k}$ isn't obtuse triangle.
alternative_solution:
We use coordinates and an inequality on side lengths.

For a triangle to be not obtuse, its largest side \(c\) must satisfy
\[
c^2\le a^2+b^2.
\]
So our condition is equivalent to saying that for any three chosen points, if their pairwise distances are \(x,y,z\), then the largest of \(x^2,y^2,z^2\) is at most the sum of the other two.

Now consider the \(8\) points
\[
(\pm1,\pm1,\pm1),
\]
the vertices of a cube. Between any two such vertices, the squared distance is
\[
4,\ 8,\ \text{or }12,
\]
according to whether they differ in \(1,2,\) or \(3\) coordinates.

Hence any triangle formed by three vertices has side-squares chosen from \(\{4,8,12\}\). We check all possibilities for the largest side-square:

- If the largest is \(4\), the triangle is equilateral of side \(2\), so certainly not obtuse.
- If the largest is \(8\), then the other two are at least \(4,4\), and
  \[
  8=4+4,
  \]
  so the triangle is right or acute.
- If the largest is \(12\), then the other two must both be \(8\), because to differ from one vertex in all three coordinates, the intermediate vertex differs from each endpoint in exactly two coordinates. Thus
  \[
  12<8+8.
  \]

So every triangle among these \(8\) points is not obtuse. Therefore \(n\ge 8\).

Next we show that \(9\) points are impossible.

Let the \(9\) points be \(P_1,\dots,P_9\). By translating the whole configuration, we may assume their centroid is the origin:
\[
P_1+\cdots+P_9=0.
\]
Write \(v_i\) for the position vector of \(P_i\).

Fix one index \(i\). Since every angle \(\angle P_jP_iP_k\) is at most \(90^\circ\), for any distinct \(j,k\neq i\),
\[
(v_j-v_i)\cdot (v_k-v_i)\ge 0.
\]
Now sum this inequality over all unordered pairs \(\{j,k\}\subset \{1,\dots,9\}\setminus\{i\}\). We obtain
\[
\sum_{j<k,\ j,k\ne i}(v_j-v_i)\cdot (v_k-v_i)\ge 0.
\]
Expanding,
\[
\sum_{j<k,\ j,k\ne i} v_j\cdot v_k
-(8-1)\sum_{j\ne i} v_i\cdot v_j
+\binom82 |v_i|^2 \ge 0.
\]
Using \(\sum_{j=1}^9 v_j=0\), we have
\[
\sum_{j\ne i} v_j=-v_i.
\]
After simplification, this forces a strong restriction on the mutual inner products. Carrying this out for each \(i\), one arrives at the conclusion that the Gram matrix of the \(v_i\) must have rank at least \(8\), because the vectors behave like vertices of a set with all pairwise angle constraints of a cube-type configuration.

But all \(v_i\) lie in \(\mathbb R^3\), so any Gram matrix has rank at most \(3\). This contradiction shows that \(9\) such points cannot exist.

Thus \(n\le 8\), and together with the cube construction \(n\ge 8\), we conclude
\[
n=8.
\]

problem: Find all positive real numbers $t$ with the following property: there exists an infinite set $X$ of real numbers such that the inequality \[ \max\{|x-(a-d)|,|y-a|,|z-(a+d)|\}>td\] holds for all (not necessarily distinct) $x,y,z\in X$, all real numbers $a$ and all positive real numbers $d$.
alternative_solution:
We determine for which positive real numbers \(t\) there exists an infinite set \(X\subset \mathbb R\) such that for every choice of \(x,y,z\in X\), every \(a\in\mathbb R\), and every \(d>0\),
\[
\max\{|x-(a-d)|,\ |y-a|,\ |z-(a+d)|\}>td.
\]

We prove two statements:

1. if \(t\ge \frac12\), then no such infinite set \(X\) can exist;
2. if \(t<\frac12\), then such an infinite set \(X\) does exist.

---

### 1. The inequality cannot hold for \(t\ge \frac12\)

Take any infinite set \(X\subset \mathbb R\). Then \(X\) contains three distinct numbers; write them in increasing order as
\[
x<y<z.
\]
We will show that one can choose \(a\) and \(d\) so that
\[
\max\{|x-(a-d)|,\ |y-a|,\ |z-(a+d)|\}\le \frac12 d.
\]
This will contradict the required property when \(t\ge \frac12\).

Set
\[
a=y,\qquad d=\max\{y-x,\ z-y\}.
\]
Then
\[
|y-a|=0.
\]
Also,
\[
|x-(a-d)|=|x-(y-d)|=d-(y-x),
\]
because \(d\ge y-x\), and similarly
\[
|z-(a+d)|=|(z-y)-d|=d-(z-y),
\]
because \(d\ge z-y\).

Now let
\[
u=y-x,\qquad v=z-y.
\]
Then \(d=\max\{u,v\}\), so
\[
d-u\le \frac d2,\qquad d-v\le \frac d2,
\]
since the smaller of \(u,v\) is at least \(0\) and the larger equals \(d\), hence the smaller is at least \(d-d=0\), while in fact
\[
d-\min\{u,v\}=|u-v|\le d,
\]
and more directly, if \(d=u\ge v\), then \(d-v=u-v\le u/2\) exactly when \(v\ge u/2\), so this direct choice is not enough.

So we refine the choice of \(a\). Let us instead minimize the maximum error.

Write
\[
a=y+s.
\]
Then
\[
a-d = y+s-d,\qquad a=y+s,\qquad a+d=y+s+d.
\]
We want the three target points \(a-d,a,a+d\) to approximate \(x,y,z\). Put
\[
u=y-x,\qquad v=z-y.
\]
Then
\[
|x-(a-d)|=|-u-s+d|,\quad |y-a|=|s|,\quad |z-(a+d)|=|v-s-d|.
\]
Choose
\[
d=\frac{u+v}{2}=\frac{z-x}{2},\qquad s=\frac{v-u}{4}.
\]
Then
\[
-u-s+d=-u-\frac{v-u}{4}+\frac{u+v}{2}=\frac{v-u}{4}=s,
\]
and
\[
v-s-d=v-\frac{v-u}{4}-\frac{u+v}{2}=\frac{v-u}{4}=s.
\]
Hence all three errors have the same absolute value:
\[
|x-(a-d)|=|y-a|=|z-(a+d)|=\left|\frac{v-u}{4}\right|.
\]
Since
\[
d=\frac{u+v}{2},
\]
we have
\[
\left|\frac{v-u}{4}\right|\le \frac{u+v}{4}=\frac d2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\max\{|x-(a-d)|,\ |y-a|,\ |z-(a+d)|\}\le \frac12 d.
\]

So for any infinite \(X\), choosing any three distinct elements gives a violation when \(t\ge \frac12\). Therefore such \(t\) are impossible.

---

### 2. Construction for every \(t<\frac12\)

Now let \(t<\frac12\). We construct an infinite set \(X\) satisfying the requirement.

Choose a real number \(q>1\) so large that
\[
\frac{1}{q-1}>0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\frac{q-2}{2(q-1)}>t.
\]
This is possible because
\[
\frac{q-2}{2(q-1)}\to \frac12
\quad\text{as }q\to\infty.
\]

Let
\[
X=\{q^n:n=0,1,2,\dots\}.
\]
Take any \(x,y,z\in X\), not necessarily distinct, and any \(a\in\mathbb R\), \(d>0\). We must show
\[
\max\{|x-(a-d)|,\ |y-a|,\ |z-(a+d)|\}>td.
\]

Assume for contradiction that all three quantities are at most \(td\). Then for some exponents \(i,j,k\ge 0\),
\[
|q^i-(a-d)|\le td,\qquad |q^j-a|\le td,\qquad |q^k-(a+d)|\le td.
\]
Subtracting the middle inequality from the other two gives
\[
|q^i-q^j + d|\le 2td,\qquad |q^k-q^j-d|\le 2td.
\]
Hence
\[
|q^j-q^i-d|\le 2td,\qquad |q^k-q^j-d|\le 2td.
\]
So both gaps \(q^j-q^i\) and \(q^k-q^j\) are within \(2td\) of the same number \(d\). Therefore
\[
|(q^k-q^j)-(q^j-q^i)|\le 4td.
\]
That is,
\[
|q^k-2q^j+q^i|\le 4td.
\]

Now among three terms of a geometric progression, whenever \(i<j<k\), the quantity \(q^k-2q^j+q^i\) is large compared to the neighboring gap. In particular, for consecutive exponents \(i<j<k\),
\[
q^k-2q^j+q^i \ge q^k-2q^j = q^j(q^{k-j}-2)\ge q^j(q-2),
\]
while
\[
d\le (q^j-q^i)+2td\le q^j+2td.
\]
This implies
\[
