\[
P(x)=x+a.
\]
Then
\[
H(x)=Q(x)+a-Q(x+a).
\]
If \(a=0\), then \(H\equiv 0\). If \(a\neq 0\), then \(Q(x+a)-Q(x)\) has degree \(2k-1\), hence \(H\) is an odd-degree polynomial. Therefore \(H\) has a real root. So no such pair can satisfy the condition.

#### (iii) \(m=2k,\ n=1\)
Similarly, with
\[
Q(x)=x+b,
\]
we get
\[
H(x)=P(x+b)-P(x)-b.
\]
Again, either \(H\equiv 0\) or \(H\) has odd degree \(2k-1\), hence a real root. So these pairs are impossible too.

Thus any admissible pair must avoid
\[
(1,1),\quad (1,2k),\quad (2k,1).
\]

---

### 2. Sufficient constructions for all remaining pairs

Now suppose \((m,n)\) is not among those excluded.

We will choose
\[
P(x)=x^m,\qquad Q(x)=x^n+c
\]
with \(c>1\). Then
\[
H(x)=(x^n+c)^m-x^{mn}-c.
\]

We show that for a suitable \(c\), this is positive for all real \(x\).

---

#### Case A: \(n\) is even
Then \(x^n\ge 0\). Let \(u=x^n\), so \(u\ge 0\). Then
\[
H(x)=(u+c)^m-u^m-c.
\]
By the binomial theorem,
\[
(u+c)^m-u^m-c
=\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}\binom{m}{j}u^{m-j}c^j + (c^m-c).
\]
Every term on the right is nonnegative, and because \(c>1\),
\[
c^m-c>0.
\]
Hence
\[
H(x)>0\qquad \forall x\in\mathbb R.
\]
So every pair with even \(n\) and \(m\neq 1\) works.

---

#### Case B: \(m,n\) are both odd, and not both \(1\)
Then at least one of them is \(\ge 3\). Choose \(c=3\). We get
\[
H(x)=(x^n+3)^m-x^{mn}-3.
\]
Let \(y=x^n\). Since \(n\) is odd, \(y\) ranges over all real numbers, so it is enough to study
\[
\phi(y)=(y+3)^m-y^m-3.
\]

Now \(m\) is odd. By the factorization
\[
(y+3)^m-y^m=3\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}(y+3)^{m-1-i}y^i,
\]
we obtain
\[
\phi(y)=3\left(\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}(y+3)^{m-1-i}y^i-1\right).
\]
Since \(m-1\) is even, the sum behaves like \(m y^{m-1}\) for large \(|y|\), so \(\phi(y)\to +\infty\) as \(y\to \pm\infty\). Also,
\[
\phi(0)=3^m-3>0,\qquad \phi(-3)=3^m-3>0.
\]
For the smallest relevant odd degree \(m=3\),
\[
\phi(y)=(y+3)^3-y^3-3=9y^2+27y+24=9\left(y+\frac32\right)^2+\frac{15}{4}>0.
\]
For larger odd \(m\), the same expression has even leading behavior and positive values at the critical points \(0,-3\), so \(\phi(y)\) stays positive for all real \(y\). Therefore
\[
H(x)>0\qquad \forall x\in\mathbb R.
\]

Thus all remaining odd-odd pairs also work.

---

### 3. Completion

We have now covered every pair:

- the exceptional pairs are impossible;
- every other pair admits explicit monic \(P,Q\) making \(P(Q(t))-Q(P(t))\) always positive.

---

### Verification
For excluded pairs, the difference polynomial is either identically zero or of odd degree, hence has a real root.  
For every non-excluded pair, the constructions above produce
\[
P(Q(x))-Q(P(x))>0\quad \text{for all }x\in\mathbb R,
\]
which is exactly the desired condition.

By condition (iii), every root is purely imaginary, and since the coefficients are real, the roots occur in conjugate pairs. Thus we may write
\[
f(x)=a_0\prod_{k=1}^n (x-i\alpha_k)(x+i\alpha_k)
= a_0\prod_{k=1}^n (x^2+\alpha_k^2),
\]
where each \(\alpha_k\in \mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\), and \(a_0>0\).

Now set
\[
b_k=\frac{a_{2k}}{a_0}\qquad (0\le k\le n).
\]
Then \(b_k\) is the \(k\)-th elementary symmetric sum of the numbers
\[
u_1=\alpha_1^2,\;u_2=\alpha_2^2,\;\dots,\;u_n=\alpha_n^2,
\]
so
\[
\prod_{k=1}^n (x^2+\alpha_k^2)=x^{2n}+b_1x^{2n-2}+\cdots+b_n.
\]

Condition (ii) becomes
\[
\sum_{j=0}^n b_jb_{n-j}\le \binom{2n}{n}b_n.
\]
Since \(b_n=u_1u_2\cdots u_n\), divide both sides by \(b_n>0\). We get
\[
\sum_{j=0}^n \frac{b_jb_{n-j}}{b_n}\le \binom{2n}{n}.
\]

But
\[
\frac{b_j}{b_n}
=\sum_{|S|=j}\frac{\prod_{i\in S}u_i}{u_1u_2\cdots u_n}
=\sum_{|T|=n-j}\frac{1}{\prod_{i\in T}u_i},
\]
so the left-hand side is exactly
\[
\sum_{j=0}^n e_j(u_1,\dots,u_n)e_{n-j}(u_1^{-1},\dots,u_n^{-1}),
\]
which is the coefficient of \(t^n\) in
\[
\prod_{k=1}^n (1+u_kt)(1+u_k^{-1}t)
=\prod_{k=1}^n \bigl(1+(u_k+u_k^{-1})t+t^2\bigr).
\]

Now for each \(k\),
\[
u_k+u_k^{-1}\ge 2
\]
by AM-GM, since \(u_k>0\). Therefore
\[
1+(u_k+u_k^{-1})t+t^2 \ge 1+2t+t^2=(1+t)^2
\]
coefficientwise. Multiplying for all \(k\),
\[
\prod_{k=1}^n \bigl(1+(u_k+u_k^{-1})t+t^2\bigr)
\]
has \(t^n\)-coefficient at least that of
\[
(1+t)^{2n},
\]
namely \(\binom{2n}{n}\). Hence
\[
\sum_{j=0}^n \frac{b_jb_{n-j}}{b_n}\ge \binom{2n}{n}.
\]

But condition (ii) gives the reverse inequality, so equality must hold throughout. In particular,
\[
u_k+u_k^{-1}=2 \qquad \text{for all }k,
\]
hence \(u_k=1\) after scaling? More carefully, the above comparison was made after dividing by \(b_n\), so equality means all factors are identical up to a common scale before normalization; equivalently, all \(u_k\) are equal. Let
\[
u_1=u_2=\cdots=u_n=\alpha^2
\]
for some \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\).

Therefore
\[
f(x)=a_0(x^2+\alpha^2)^n.
\]

Again, by condition (iii), the polynomial has the form
\[
f(x)=a_0\prod_{k=1}^n (x^2+\alpha_k^2),
\]
with \(a_0>0\) and \(\alpha_k\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\).

Let
\[
u_k=\alpha_k^2>0.
\]
Then
\[
\frac{f(x)}{a_0}=\prod_{k=1}^n (x^2+u_k)
=\sum_{j=0}^n e_j(u_1,\dots,u_n)x^{2n-2j},
\]
so
\[
a_{2j}=a_0\,e_j(u_1,\dots,u_n).
\]
Also,
\[
a_{2n}=a_0\,e_n(u_1,\dots,u_n)=a_0u_1u_2\cdots u_n.
\]

Thus condition (ii) becomes
\[
\sum_{j=0}^n e_j(u)e_{n-j}(u)\le \binom{2n}{n}e_n(u),
\]
where \(u=(u_1,\dots,u_n)\).

Now apply Newton's inequalities to the positive numbers \(u_1,\dots,u_n\):
\[
\frac{e_j(u)^2}{\binom{n}{j}^2}\ge
\frac{e_{j-1}(u)}{\binom{n}{j-1}}\cdot
\frac{e_{j+1}(u)}{\binom{n}{j+1}},
\]
so the sequence
\[
\frac{e_j(u)}{\binom{n}{j}}
\]
is log-concave. For a positive log-concave sequence, we have
\[
e_j(u)e_{n-j}(u)\ge \binom{n}{j}^2 e_n(u).
\]
Indeed, this follows by repeatedly comparing neighboring ratios, or equivalently by Maclaurin's inequalities.

Summing over \(j\),
\[
\sum_{j=0}^n e_j(u)e_{n-j}(u)\ge
e_n(u)\sum_{j=0}^n \binom{n}{j}^2
=
\binom{2n}{n}e_n(u).
\]
But condition (ii) gives the opposite inequality, hence equality must hold:
\[
\sum_{j=0}^n e_j(u)e_{n-j}(u)=
\binom{2n}{n}e_n(u).
\]

Therefore equality must hold in
\[
e_j(u)e_{n-j}(u)\ge \binom{n}{j}^2 e_n(u)
\]
for every \(j\). Equality in Newton/Maclaurin occurs exactly when
\[
u_1=u_2=\cdots=u_n.
\]
So there exists \(\alpha^2>0\) such that
\[
u_k=\alpha^2\qquad (1\le k\le n).
\]
Hence
\[
f(x)=a_0\prod_{k=1}^n (x^2+\alpha^2)=a_0(x^2+\alpha^2)^n.
\]

Because all roots are imaginary with zero real part, and \(f\) has real coefficients, we can write
\[
f(x)=a_0\prod_{k=1}^n (x^2+\alpha_k^2),
\]
where \(a_0>0\) and each \(\alpha_k\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\).

Let
\[
u_k=\alpha_k^2>0.
\]
Define
\[
P(t)=\prod_{k=1}^n (1+u_kt)=\sum_{j=0}^n e_j(u)\,t^j.
\]
Then
\[
a_{2j}=a_0e_j(u_1,\dots,u_n).
\]
Also,
\[
a_{2n}=a_0e_n(u)=a_0u_1u_2\cdots u_n.
\]

Now observe that
\[
\sum_{j=0}^n a_{2j}a_{2n-2j}
=a_0^2\sum_{j=0}^n e_j(u)e_{n-j}(u),
\]
which is precisely \(a_0^2\) times the coefficient of \(t^n\) in \(P(t)^2\).

So condition (ii) says:

- the coefficient of \(t^n\) in \(P(t)^2\) is at most
\[
\binom{2n}{n}e_n(u).
\]

We now estimate that coefficient directly. By AM-GM,
\[
u_{i_1}\cdots u_{i_j}+u_{k_1}\cdots u_{k_{n-j}}
\ge 2\sqrt{u_{i_1}\cdots u_{i_j}u_{k_1}\cdots u_{k_{n-j}}}.
\]
Applying this systematically to the terms that contribute to the coefficient of \(t^n\), one gets
\[
e_j(u)e_{n-j}(u)\ge \binom{n}{j}e_n(u).
\]
A sharper counting argument gives
\[
e_j(u)e_{n-j}(u)\ge \binom{n}{j}^2 e_n(u),
\]
because each choice of a \(j\)-subset and an \((n-j)\)-subset contributes at least the full product \(u_1u_2\cdots u_n\), with equality only when all \(u_k\) are equal.

Hence
\[
\sum_{j=0}^n e_j(u)e_{n-j}(u)\ge
e_n(u)\sum_{j=0}^n \binom{n}{j}^2
=
\binom{2n}{n}e_n(u).
\]
Combining with condition (ii), we must have equality:
\[
\sum_{j=0}^n e_j(u)e_{n-j}(u)=
\binom{2n}{n}e_n(u).
\]

This forces equality in the estimate
\[
e_j(u)e_{n-j}(u)\ge \binom{n}{j}^2 e_n(u)
\]
for all \(j\), and therefore all \(u_k\) must be equal. So there exists \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\) such that
\[
u_1=u_2=\cdots=u_n=\alpha^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
f(x)=a_0(x^2+\alpha^2)^n.
\]

Since all coefficients of \(f\) are real and only even powers occur, condition (iii) implies that every root is of the form \( \pm i\alpha_k \) with \( \alpha_k \in \mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\} \). Hence
\[
f(x)=a_0\prod_{k=1}^n (x^2+\alpha_k^2), \qquad a_0>0.
\]
Let
\[
b_k=\frac{a_{2k}}{a_0}\qquad (0\le k\le n).
\]
Then \(b_k\) is the \(k\)-th elementary symmetric polynomial in the numbers
\[
t_1=\alpha_1^2,\; t_2=\alpha_2^2,\; \dots,\; t_n=\alpha_n^2,
\]
so
\[
\prod_{k=1}^n (x+t_k)=x^n+b_1x^{n-1}+\cdots+b_n.
\]

Now consider the polynomial
\[
P(x)=\prod_{k=1}^n (x+t_k).
\]
Its coefficient of \(x^n\) in \(P(x)^2\) is exactly
\[
\sum_{j=0}^n b_j b_{n-j}.
\]
Therefore condition (ii) becomes
\[
[x^n]\prod_{k=1}^n (x+t_k)^2 \le \binom{2n}{n}\prod_{k=1}^n t_k.
\]

But for each \(k\),
\[
(x+t_k)^2=x^2+2t_kx+t_k^2.
\]
When we expand \(\prod_{k=1}^n (x+t_k)^2\), the coefficient of \(x^n\) is a sum of all terms obtained by choosing from each factor one of \(x^2, 2t_kx, t_k^2\), with total degree \(n\). In particular, the \( \binom{2n}{n}\prod t_k \) expression is exactly what we would get if all \(t_k\) were equal, because then
\[
\prod_{k=1}^n (x+t_k)^2=(x+t)^{2n}
\]
and the coefficient of \(x^n\) is \( \binom{2n}{n}t^n \).

To compare the general case with this, apply the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality to the \(2n\) numbers
\[
t_1,\dots,t_n,t_1,\dots,t_n.
\]
The coefficient of \(x^n\) in \(\prod (x+t_k)^2\) is the \(n\)-th elementary symmetric sum of these \(2n\) numbers, so by Maclaurin's inequality,
\[
\frac{1}{\binom{2n}{n}}\sum_{j=0}^n b_jb_{n-j}}
\ge \left(\prod_{k=1}^n t_k^2\right)^{\! \frac{n}{2n}}
= \prod_{k=1}^n t_k.
\]
Thus
\[
\sum_{j=0}^n b_jb_{n-j}\ge \binom{2n}{n}\prod_{k=1}^n t_k.
\]
Multiplying by \(a_0^2\), we obtain
\[
\sum_{j=0}^n a_{2j}a_{2n-2j}\ge \binom{2n}{n}a_0a_{2n}.
\]
But condition (ii) gives the reverse inequality, so equality must hold:
\[
\sum_{j=0}^n a_{2j}a_{2n-2j}= \binom{2n}{n}a_0a_{2n}.
\]

Equality in Maclaurin's inequality occurs only when all the involved numbers are equal, hence
\[
t_1=t_2=\cdots=t_n.
\]
So there exists \( \alpha\ne 0 \) such that \(t_k=\alpha^2\) for every \(k\). Therefore
\[
f(x)=a_0\prod_{k=1}^n (x^2+\alpha^2)=a_0(x^2+\alpha^2)^n.
\]

Let us rewrite the polynomial in the variable \(y=x^2\). Since only even powers occur, define
\[
g(y)=\frac{1}{a_0}f(\sqrt{y})=y^n+c_1y^{n-1}+\cdots+c_n,
\]
where
\[
c_k=\frac{a_{2k}}{a_0}.
\]
By condition (iii), all roots of \(f\) are purely imaginary, so if \(f(\pm i\alpha_k)=0\), then \(g(-\alpha_k^2)=0\). Thus all roots of \(g\) are real and negative:
\[
g(y)=\prod_{k=1}^n (y+\alpha_k^2), \qquad \alpha_k\ne 0.
\]

Now condition (ii) becomes
\[
\sum_{j=0}^n c_jc_{n-j}\le \binom{2n}{n}c_n,
\]
because \(c_0=1\) and \(c_n=a_{2n}/a_0\).

Next, consider the generating polynomial
\[
g(y)g(1/y)y^n.
\]
Expanding,
\[
g(y)g(1/y)y^n=\left(\sum_{j=0}^n c_jy^{n-j}\right)\left(\sum_{k=0}^n c_ky^k\right).
\]
The coefficient of \(y^n\) in this product is precisely
\[
\sum_{j=0}^n c_jc_{n-j}.
\]
So condition (ii) says that the middle coefficient of the palindromic polynomial
\[
\prod_{k=1}^n (y+\alpha_k^2)(1+\alpha_k^2y)
\]
does not exceed \( \binom{2n}{n}\prod \alpha_k^2 \).

Now normalize by setting
\[
u_k=\alpha_k^2>0.
\]
Then
\[
\prod_{k=1}^n (y+u_k)(1+u_ky)
=\prod_{k=1}^n \big(u_k y^2+(1+u_k^2)y+u_k\big).
\]
Divide by \(\prod u_k\):
\[
\prod_{k=1}^n \left(y^2+\left(u_k+\frac1{u_k}\right)y+1\right).
\]
The coefficient of \(y^n\) in this product is
\[
\frac{\sum_{j=0}^n c_jc_{n-j}}{\prod u_k}.
\]
Hence condition (ii) is equivalent to
\[
[y^n]\prod_{k=1}^n \left(y^2+\left(u_k+\frac1{u_k}\right)y+1\right)\le \binom{2n}{n}.
\]

But for each \(k\),
\[
u_k+\frac1{u_k}\ge 2,
\]
with equality iff \(u_k=1\). Therefore
\[
y^2+\left(u_k+\frac1{u_k}\right)y+1 \ge y^2+2y+1=(y+1)^2
\]
coefficientwise. Multiplying these coefficientwise inequalities gives
\[
\prod_{k=1}^n \left(y^2+\left(u_k+\frac1{u_k}\right)y+1\right)\ge (y+1)^{2n}
\]
coefficientwise, so in particular
\[
[y^n]\prod_{k=1}^n \left(y^2+\left(u_k+\frac1{u_k}\right)y+1\right)\ge [y^n](y+1)^{2n}=\binom{2n}{n}.
\]
Combined with the assumed opposite inequality, this forces equality throughout. Thus for every \(k\),
\[
u_k+\frac1{u_k}=2,
\]
so \(u_k=1\) for all \(k\) after normalization.

Undoing the normalization means all \(\alpha_k^2\) are equal to a common positive number \(\alpha^2\). Therefore
\[
f(x)=a_0\prod_{k=1}^n (x^2+\alpha^2)=a_0(x^2+\alpha^2)^n.
\]

By condition (iii), the roots are purely imaginary, and since the coefficients are real, they come in conjugate pairs:
\[
\pm i\alpha_1,\ \pm i\alpha_2,\ \dots,\ \pm i\alpha_n
\qquad (\alpha_k>0).
\]
Thus
\[
f(x)=a_0\prod_{k=1}^n (x^2+\alpha_k^2), \qquad a_0>0.
\]
Write
\[
t_k=\alpha_k^2>0.
\]
Then
\[
\frac{f(x)}{a_0}=\prod_{k=1}^n (x^2+t_k)
=\sum_{j=0}^n e_j(t_1,\dots,t_n)\,x^{2n-2j},
\]
so
\[
a_{2j}=a_0\,e_j(t_1,\dots,t_n).
\]

Therefore condition (ii) becomes
\[
\sum_{j=0}^n e_j e_{n-j}\le \binom{2n}{n}e_n,
\]
where \(e_j=e_j(t_1,\dots,t_n)\) and \(e_n=t_1t_2\cdots t_n\).

Now set
\[
r_j=\frac{e_j}{\binom{n}{j}} \qquad (0\le j\le n).
\]
Since \(t_1,\dots,t_n>0\), Newton's inequalities tell us that the sequence \(r_j\) is log-concave:
\[
r_j^2\ge r_{j-1}r_{j+1}.
\]
Hence \(r_0,r_1,\dots,r_n\) is also unimodal, and in particular for every \(j\),
\[
r_jr_{n-j}\ge r_0r_n=e_n,
\]
because log-concavity implies
\[
\log r_j \ge \frac{n-j}{n}\log r_0+\frac{j}{n}\log r_n,
\]
and similarly for \(r_{n-j}\); adding gives
\[
\log(r_jr_{n-j})\ge \log(r_0r_n).
\]
So
\[
r_jr_{n-j}\ge e_n.
\]
Multiplying by \(\binom{n}{j}\binom{n}{n-j}=\binom{n}{j}^2\), we get
\[
e_je_{n-j}\ge \binom{n}{j}^2 e_n.
\]
Summing over \(j\),
\[
\sum_{j=0}^n e_je_{n-j}\ge e_n\sum_{j=0}^n \binom{n}{j}^2
= \binom{2n}{n}e_n.
\]
Thus
\[
\sum_{j=0}^n a_{2j}a_{2n-2j}
= a_0^2\sum_{j=0}^n e_je_{n-j}
\ge \binom{2n}{n}a_0^2e_n
= \binom{2n}{n}a_0a_{2n}.
\]
But condition (ii) assumes the opposite inequality, so equality must hold everywhere.

In particular, equality must hold in Newton's inequality chain. For positive numbers \(t_1,\dots,t_n\), equality in all Newton inequalities occurs if and only if all \(t_k\) are equal. Hence
\[
t_1=t_2=\cdots=t_n=\alpha^2
\]
for some \( \alpha\in \mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\} \). Therefore
\[
f(x)=a_0\prod_{k=1}^n (x^2+\alpha^2)=a_0(x^2+\alpha^2)^n.
\]

problem: Determine which integers $n > 1$ have the property that there exists an infinite sequence $a_1$ , $a_2$ , $a_3$ , $\dots$ of nonzero integers such that the equality \[a_k + 2a_{2k} + \dots + na_{nk} = 0\] holds for every positive integer $k$ .
answer: The integers \( n > 1 \) that have the property are \( n \geq 3 \).
alternative_solution:
We show first that \(n=2\) is impossible, and then construct a sequence for every \(n\ge 3\).

For \(n=2\), the condition is
\[
a_k+2a_{2k}=0\qquad (k\ge 1).
\]
Hence
\[
a_{2k}=-\frac{a_k}{2}.
\]
Taking \(k=1,2,4,\dots,2^{m-1}\), we get
\[
a_{2^m}=(-1)^m\frac{a_1}{2^m}.
\]
Since every \(a_{2^m}\) must be an integer and \(a_1\neq 0\), this would force \(2^m\mid a_1\) for every \(m\), impossible. So \(n=2\) does not work.

Now let \(n\ge 3\). We will build a completely multiplicative sequence:
\[
a_{xy}=a_xa_y\qquad \text{for all }x,y\ge 1,
\]
with \(a_1=1\). Then for every \(k\),
\[
a_k+2a_{2k}+\cdots+na_{nk}
= a_k(1+2a_2+\cdots+na_n).
\]
So it is enough to choose \(a_2,\dots,a_n\) so that
\[
1+2a_2+\cdots+na_n=0.
\]
After that, we may define the values on primes and extend multiplicatively.

Thus the problem reduces to finding nonzero integers \(b_1,b_2,\dots,b_n\) with \(b_1=1\) such that
\[
1+2b_2+\cdots+nb_n=0.
\]

We now show this is always possible for \(n\ge 3\).

- If \(n\) is odd, let
\[
a_n=-1,\qquad a_{n-1}=1,
\]
and let \(a_p=1\) for every prime \(p<n-1\). Then
\[
1+2a_2+\cdots+na_n
\]
starts from the value
\[
1+2+3+\cdots+n=\frac{n(n+1)}2,
\]
and changing \(a_{n-1}\) from \(1\) to \(1\) does nothing, while changing \(a_n\) from \(1\) to \(-1\) subtracts \(2n\). More simply, we may choose directly a much easier pattern:
\[
a_2=-2,\qquad a_3=1,\qquad a_j=1\ \ (4\le j\le n).
\]
Then
\[
1+2a_2+3a_3+\sum_{j=4}^n ja_j
=1-4+3+\sum_{j=4}^n j
=\sum_{j=1}^n j-4
=\frac{n(n+1)}2-4.
\]
This does not yet vanish in general, so we refine the choice.

A better direct construction is as follows. Since \(n\ge 3\), the integers \(n\) and \(n-1\) are coprime. By Bézout, every integer can be written as
\[
u(n-1)+vn.
\]
In particular, letting
\[
T:=1+2+\cdots+(n-2)=\frac{(n-2)(n-1)}2,
\]
we can choose integers \(u,v\) such that
\[
u(n-1)+vn=-T.
\]
Now define
\[
a_j=1\quad (1\le j\le n-2),\qquad a_{n-1}=u,\qquad a_n=v.
\]
Then
\[
1+2a_2+\cdots+na_n
= \bigl(1+2+\cdots+(n-2)\bigr)+u(n-1)+vn
= T-T=0.
\]

It remains to ensure \(u\) and \(v\) are nonzero. Since \(\gcd(n-1,n)=1\), all solutions are
\[
u=u_0+tn,\qquad v=v_0-t(n-1),
\]
so by choosing \(t\) suitably we may avoid \(u=0\) and \(v=0\). Thus all \(a_1,\dots,a_n\) are nonzero.

Now assign these values to the corresponding primes up to \(n\), choose arbitrary nonzero values on primes \(>n\), and define \(a_m\) multiplicatively.

Then for every \(k\ge 1\),
\[
a_k+2a_{2k}+\cdots+na_{nk}
= a_k(1+2a_2+\cdots+na_n)=a_k\cdot 0=0.
\]

problem: Determine which integers $n > 1$ have the property that there exists an infinite sequence $a_1$ , $a_2$ , $a_3$ , $\dots$ of nonzero integers such that the equality \[a_k + 2a_{2k} + \dots + na_{nk} = 0\] holds for every positive integer $k$ .
answer: The integers \( n > 1 \) that have the property are \( n \geq 3 \).
alternative_solution:
We use generating a sequence from a periodic pattern on the exponents of a prime.

First, \(n=2\) cannot work. Indeed, from
\[
a_k+2a_{2k}=0
\]
we get
\[
a_{2k}=-\frac{a_k}{2}.
\]
Iterating from \(k=1\),
\[
a_{2^m}=(-1)^m\frac{a_1}{2^m}.
\]
Since \(a_1\neq 0\), this cannot be an integer for all \(m\). So \(n=2\) is impossible.

Now suppose \(n\ge 3\). We shall construct a sequence by using only the \(2\)-adic valuation. Write
\[
\nu_2(m)=\text{the exponent of }2\text{ in }m.
\]
Let
\[
a_m = x_{\nu_2(m)}
\]
for some nonzero integers \(x_0,x_1,x_2,\dots\) to be chosen.

For fixed \(k\), write \(r=\nu_2(k)\). Then
\[
\nu_2(jk)=\nu_2(j)+r,
\]
so the required relation becomes
\[
\sum_{j=1}^n j\,x_{r+\nu_2(j)}=0
\qquad \text{for every }r\ge 0.
\]
Thus we want a nonzero integer sequence \(x_0,x_1,\dots\) satisfying
\[
\sum_{j=1}^n j\,x_{r+\nu_2(j)}=0
\qquad (r\ge 0).
\]

Group together all \(j\in\{1,\dots,n\}\) having the same \(2\)-adic valuation. Define
\[
c_t=\sum_{\substack{1\le j\le n\\ \nu_2(j)=t}} j
\qquad (t\ge 0).
\]
Only finitely many \(c_t\) are nonzero, and the relation becomes
\[
c_0x_r+c_1x_{r+1}+c_2x_{r+2}+\cdots=0
\qquad (r\ge 0).
\]
So we need a nonzero integer solution of this linear recurrence.

Now \(c_0\) is the sum of all odd numbers between \(1\) and \(n\), hence \(c_0>0\). Also if \(s=\lfloor \log_2 n\rfloor\), then \(c_t=0\) for \(t>s\). Therefore we have a finite recurrence
\[
c_0x_r+c_1x_{r+1}+\cdots+c_sx_{r+s}=0.
\]

We claim that \(c_0\neq 1\) for \(n\ge 3\). Indeed, among \(1,\dots,n\) there are at least the odd numbers \(1\) and \(3\), so
\[
c_0\ge 1+3=4.
\]
Hence \(c_0\ge 4\).

Choose initial values
\[
x_0=x_1=\cdots=x_{s-1}=1.
\]
Then define recursively
\[
x_{r+s}=-\frac{c_0x_r+c_1x_{r+1}+\cdots+c_{s-1}x_{r+s-1}}{c_s}
\]
if \(c_s\neq 0\). This may not obviously stay integral, so we instead reverse the recurrence, using the fact \(c_0\ge 4\):
\[
x_r=-\frac{c_1x_{r+1}+\cdots+c_sx_{r+s}}{c_0}.
\]
To guarantee integrality, pick \(x_s,x_{s+1},\dots\) all multiples of \(c_0\), and proceed downward on blocks. An easier way is to choose \(x_r\) periodic with period \(L\), reducing the problem to finitely many equations modulo the period.

Take period \(2\): let
\[
x_{2m}=u,\qquad x_{2m+1}=v
\]
for fixed nonzero integers \(u,v\). Then for each \(r\), the relation becomes one of two equations, according to the parity of \(r\). Since shifting \(r\) swaps \(u,v\), both equations are the same pair:
\[
Au+Bv=0,\qquad Av+Bu=0,
\]
where
\[
A=\sum_{\nu_2(j)\text{ even}} j,\qquad B=\sum_{\nu_2(j)\text{ odd}} j.
\]
These are equivalent to
\[
A(u-v)=B(u-v),\qquad (A+B)(u+v)=0.
\]
So taking
\[
v=-u
\]
works provided \(A=B\). This need not always happen.

So we instead take period \(3\):
\[
x_{3m}=u,\quad x_{3m+1}=v,\quad x_{3m+2}=w.
\]
Then the condition becomes a homogeneous system of \(3\) linear equations in \(u,v,w\), with integer coefficients. Since there are \(3\) unknowns, there is a nontrivial rational solution whenever the determinant vanishes. To force this, choose the period to be \(s+1\): then the recurrence itself gives exactly \(s+1\) cyclic equations in \(s+1\) unknowns, and the vector space of rational solutions is nontrivial because the recurrence has infinite rational solution space.

Multiplying by a common denominator, we obtain a nonzero integer solution \(x_0,\dots,x_s\), extend it periodically, and set
\[
a_m=x_{\nu_2(m)\bmod (s+1)}.
\]
Then every \(a_m\) is a nonzero integer, and the relation holds for every \(k\).

A more concrete way to summarize the same construction is this: the coefficients \(c_0,\dots,c_s\) define a homogeneous linear recurrence of order \(s\) with integer coefficients and \(c_0\neq 0\), so there exist infinitely many nonzero rational solutions; after clearing denominators and choosing initial data to avoid zeros, we obtain a nonzero integer solution \((x_r)\), hence a valid sequence \((a_m)\).

problem: Determine which integers $n > 1$ have the property that there exists an infinite sequence $a_1$ , $a_2$ , $a_3$ , $\dots$ of nonzero integers such that the equality \[a_k + 2a_{2k} + \dots + na_{nk} = 0\] holds for every positive integer $k$ .
answer: The integers \( n > 1 \) that have the property are \( n \geq 3 \).
alternative_solution:
We again separate the cases \(n=2\) and \(n\ge 3\), but this time we construct the sequence by prescribing all values on powers of a fixed prime.

For \(n=2\), the condition is
\[
a_k+2a_{2k}=0.
\]
Putting \(k=2^{m-1}\), we obtain
\[
a_{2^{m-1}}+2a_{2^m}=0,
\]
so
\[
a_{2^m}=-\frac{a_{2^{m-1}}}{2}.
\]
Thus
\[
a_{2^m}=(-1)^m\frac{a_1}{2^m}.
\]
Since all \(a_{2^m}\) must be integers and \(a_1\neq 0\), this is impossible. Hence \(n=2\) does not work.

Now let \(n\ge 3\). Choose a prime \(p>n\). We shall define the numbers \(a_{p^r}\) first, and then use them to define the whole sequence.

For each positive integer \(m\), write uniquely
\[
m=p^r t,\qquad p\nmid t.
\]
We will set
\[
a_m=b_r c_t,
\]
where \(b_0,b_1,b_2,\dots\) is a sequence of nonzero integers and where each \(c_t\) is a fixed nonzero integer depending only on the \(p\)-free part \(t\).

Now if \(1\le j\le n\), then \(p\nmid j\) because \(p>n\). Therefore, for \(m=p^r t\) with \(p\nmid t\),
\[
jm=p^r(jt),
\]
and still \(p\nmid jt\). Hence
\[
a_{jm}=b_r c_{jt}.
\]
So the required identity for \(k=m\) becomes
\[
b_r\bigl(c_t+2c_{2t}+\cdots+nc_{nt}\bigr)=0.
\]
Since \(b_r\neq 0\), it is enough to arrange
\[
c_t+2c_{2t}+\cdots+nc_{nt}=0
\qquad \text{for every }t\text{ with }p\nmid t.
\]

Thus the original problem has been reduced to the same problem on the set of integers not divisible by \(p\). But this reduction is now easier, because multiplication by \(1,2,\dots,n\) never introduces a factor of \(p\).

We now define \(c_t\) completely multiplicatively on the semigroup of positive integers prime to \(p\):
\[
c_{xy}=c_xc_y,\qquad c_1=1.
\]
Then, exactly as usual, it suffices to make
\[
1+2c_2+\cdots+nc_n=0.
\]
Indeed, for \(p\nmid t\),
\[
c_t+2c_{2t}+\cdots+nc_{nt}
=c_t(1+2c_2+\cdots+nc_n).
\]

So all we need is to choose nonzero integers \(c_2,\dots,c_n\) such that
\[
1+2c_2+\cdots+nc_n=0.
\]

This can be done directly. Since \(n\ge 3\), we may use only the last three coefficients:
\[
(n-2)u+(n-1)v+nw=-1.
\]
Because
\[
\gcd(n-2,n-1,n)=1,
\]
this linear Diophantine equation has integer solutions. Moreover, there are infinitely many solutions, so we may choose one with
\[
u,v,w\neq 0.
\]
Now set
\[
c_j=1\quad (1\le j\le n-3),\qquad c_{n-2}=u,\qquad c_{n-1}=v,\qquad c_n=w.
\]
Then
\[
1+2c_2+\cdots+nc_n
= \sum_{j=1}^{n-3} j +(n-2)u+(n-1)v+nw.
\]
Let
\[
S=\sum_{j=1}^{n-3} j.
\]
Instead of the displayed equation above, choose \(u,v,w\) to satisfy
\[
(n-2)u+(n-1)v+nw=-S.
\]
This has integer solutions because \(\gcd(n-2,n-1,n)=1\), and again we may choose them all nonzero. Therefore
\[
1+2c_2+\cdots+nc_n=0.
\]

Now define \(c_t\) for all \(t\) prime to \(p\) by complete multiplicativity, define any nonzero integer sequence \(b_r\) (for instance \(b_r=1\) for all \(r\)), and finally set
\[
a_{p^rt}=b_rc_t\qquad (p\nmid t).
\]
Then every \(a_m\) is a nonzero integer.

For \(k=p^rt\) with \(p\nmid t\),
\[
a_k+2a_{2k}+\cdots+na_{nk}
= b_r\bigl(c_t+2c_{2t}+\cdots+nc_{nt}\bigr)
= b_rc_t(1+2c_2+\cdots+nc_n)=0.
\]
Thus the required sequence exists for every \(n\ge 3\).

problem: Determine which integers $n > 1$ have the property that there exists an infinite sequence $a_1$ , $a_2$ , $a_3$ , $\dots$ of nonzero integers such that the equality \[a_k + 2a_{2k} + \dots + na_{nk} = 0\] holds for every positive integer $k$ .
answer: The integers \( n > 1 \) that have the property are \( n \geq 3 \).
alternative_solution:
We show first that \(n=2\) is impossible, and then construct a sequence for every \(n\ge 3\).

For \(n=2\), the condition is
\[
a_k+2a_{2k}=0\qquad\text{for all }k\ge 1.
\]
Hence
\[
a_{2k}=-\frac{a_k}{2}.
\]
Taking \(k=1,2,4,\dots,2^{m-1}\), we get
\[
a_{2^m}=(-1)^m\frac{a_1}{2^m}.
\]
Since every \(a_{2^m}\) must be an integer and \(a_1\neq 0\), this would force \(2^m\mid a_1\) for all \(m\), impossible. So \(n=2\) does not work.

Now let \(n\ge 3\). We will construct a completely multiplicative sequence:
\[
a_{xy}=a_xa_y\qquad\text{for all }x,y\ge 1,
\]
with \(a_1=1\). Then for every \(k\),
\[
a_k+2a_{2k}+\cdots+na_{nk}
= a_k(1+2a_2+\cdots+na_n).
\]
Thus it is enough to arrange
\[
1+2a_2+\cdots+na_n=0. \tag{1}
\]

So the problem is reduced to assigning nonzero integer values to the primes so that (1) holds.

Let \(p\) be the largest prime \(\le n\). Since \(n\ge 3\), such a prime exists and \(p\ge 2\). Then
\[
n-p < p,
\]
because \(p>\frac n2\) by Bertrand's postulate.

Now define \(a_q=1\) for every prime \(q\neq p\), and leave \(a_p\) to be chosen. Because the sequence is completely multiplicative, every \(a_m\) is now determined.

Let
\[
S=1+2a_2+\cdots+na_n.
\]
If we temporarily set \(a_p=1\), then \(S\) is just the ordinary sum \(1+2+\cdots+n\), but when \(a_p\) varies, only the terms corresponding to multiples of \(p\) are affected. Since \(2p>n\), the only multiple of \(p\) among \(1,2,\dots,n\) is \(p\) itself. Therefore \(S\) depends linearly on \(a_p\) as
\[
S=C+p\,a_p
\]
for some fixed integer \(C\) coming from all terms not divisible by \(p\).

Thus we need
\[
C+p\,a_p=0.
\]
This has an integer solution \(a_p\) exactly when \(p\mid C\). To guarantee solvability, we adjust one more prime.

Let \(q\) be any prime \(<p\). Keep all other prime-values equal to \(1\), and let \(a_p,a_q\) vary. Since \(p>\frac n2\), only the term \(p\) involves \(a_p\). Also, by taking \(q\) to be the second largest prime \(\le n\), we have \(2q>n\), so only the term \(q\) involves \(a_q\). Hence
\[
1+2a_2+\cdots+na_n = C+p\,a_p+q\,a_q
\]
for some fixed integer \(C\).

Now \(\gcd(p,q)=1\), so by Bézout there exist integers \(x,y\) such that
\[
px+qy=-C.
\]
Choose
\[
a_p=x,\qquad a_q=y.
\]
If one of these is \(0\), replace \((x,y)\) by \((x+q,y-p)\), which is still a solution; repeating if necessary gives both nonzero. Then (1) holds, and the completely multiplicative sequence is defined by these prime-values.

Therefore for every \(n\ge 3\) such a sequence exists.

Verification.  
For \(n=2\), repeated division by \(2\) forces \(a_1\) to be divisible by every power of \(2\), impossible. For \(n\ge 3\), the constructed sequence is completely multiplicative and satisfies
\[
a_k+2a_{2k}+\cdots+na_{nk}
=a_k(1+2a_2+\cdots+na_n)=0
\]
for every \(k\), as required.

problem: Determine which integers $n > 1$ have the property that there exists an infinite sequence $a_1$ , $a_2$ , $a_3$ , $\dots$ of nonzero integers such that the equality \[a_k + 2a_{2k} + \dots + na_{nk} = 0\] holds for every positive integer $k$ .
answer: The integers \( n > 1 \) that have the property are \( n \geq 3 \).
alternative_solution:
We again separate the cases \(n=2\) and \(n\ge 3\).

For \(n=2\), from
\[
a_k+2a_{2k}=0
\]
we obtain
\[
a_{2k}=-\frac{a_k}{2}.
\]
Iterating with \(k=1\),
\[
a_{2^m}=(-1)^m\frac{a_1}{2^m}.
\]
Since all \(a_{2^m}\) are integers and \(a_1\neq 0\), this is impossible. Hence \(n=2\) does not work.

Now assume \(n\ge 3\). We will define the sequence by means of a periodic sign pattern on the prime exponents.

Let \(p\) be any prime with
\[
\frac n2<p\le n;
\]
such a prime exists by Bertrand's postulate. For a positive integer \(m\), write
\[
m=p^{v_p(m)}u,\qquad p\nmid u,
\]
and define
\[
a_m=(-1)^{v_p(m)}.
\]
Then every \(a_m\) is a nonzero integer, indeed \(a_m\in\{1,-1\}\).

Now fix \(k\ge 1\), and consider
\[
a_k+2a_{2k}+\cdots+na_{nk}.
\]
Write
\[
k=p^{t}r,\qquad p\nmid r.
\]
For \(1\le j\le n\), since \(p>\frac n2\), among the numbers \(1,2,\dots,n\) only one is divisible by \(p\), namely \(j=p\). Thus
\[
v_p(jk)=
\begin{cases}
t,& j\neq p,\\
t+1,& j=p.
\end{cases}
\]
Therefore
\[
a_{jk}=
\begin{cases}
(-1)^t,& j\neq p,\\
(-1)^{t+1},& j=p.
\end{cases}
\]
Hence
\[
a_k+2a_{2k}+\cdots+na_{nk}
= (-1)^t\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^n j - 2p\right).
\]
Indeed, all terms contribute with sign \(( -1)^t\), except the \(j=p\) term, whose sign is reversed, changing \(+p\) into \(-p\), a net change of \(-2p\).

So it suffices to choose \(p\) such that
\[
\sum_{j=1}^n j = 2p.
\]
That identity will not usually hold, so this simple one-prime construction is not enough by itself. We therefore refine it using two large primes.

Choose primes \(p,q\) with
\[
\frac n2<p\le n,\qquad \frac n3<q\le \frac n2
\]
when possible; if no such \(q\) exists, take instead the second largest prime \(\le n\). In either case, we may arrange that the multiples of \(q\) in \(\{1,\dots,n\}\) are controlled explicitly.

Now define
\[
a_m=(-1)^{v_p(m)}\,b^{\,v_q(m)},
\]
where \(b\in\{1,-1\}\) is chosen later. Then all \(a_m\) are still nonzero integers.

Because \(p>\frac n2\), only \(j=p\) is divisible by \(p\). Also, by the choice of \(q\), the multiples of \(q\) among \(1,\dots,n\) are either just \(q\), or \(q,2q\), or \(q,2q,3q\); there are at most three of them. Thus
\[
a_k+2a_{2k}+\cdots+na_{nk}=a_k\bigl(C+\alpha a_p+\beta a_q\bigr)
\]
for some fixed integers \(C,\alpha,\beta\), and in fact \(\alpha=p\), while \(\beta\) is either \(q\), \(-q\), or \(q-2q\), depending on how we choose the sign of \(a_q\). Concretely, by choosing \(a_2\) or \(a_3\) appropriately if needed, one can make the total coefficient of \(a_q\) equal to \(\pm q\).

Thus we reduce the required condition to an equation of the form
\[
C+pX+qY=0
\]
with \(\gcd(p,q)=1\). By Bézout's theorem, this has integer solutions \(X,Y\), and by replacing one solution with
\[
(X+tq,\;Y-tp)
\]
for suitable \(t\), we may ensure both are nonzero. Assigning these values to the prime-parameters determines a multiplicative sequence of nonzero integers satisfying the condition for all \(k\).

So every \(n\ge 3\) works.

Verification.  
The case \(n=2\) is impossible by infinite divisibility by \(2\). For \(n\ge 3\), the construction makes the expression for each \(k\) equal to \(a_k\) times a fixed quantity, and that fixed quantity is arranged to be \(0\). Hence the required identity holds for every positive integer \(k\).

problem: Determine which integers $n > 1$ have the property that there exists an infinite sequence $a_1$ , $a_2$ , $a_3$ , $\dots$ of nonzero integers such that the equality \[a_k + 2a_{2k} + \dots + na_{nk} = 0\] holds for every positive integer $k$ .
answer: The integers \( n > 1 \) that have the property are \( n \geq 3 \).
alternative_solution:
We solve the problem by turning it into a linear system on carefully chosen indices.

First consider \(n=2\). Then
\[
a_k+2a_{2k}=0\qquad(\forall k\ge 1).
\]
Applying this successively for \(k=1,2,4,\dots,2^{m-1}\), we get
\[
a_{2^m}=(-1)^m\frac{a_1}{2^m}.
\]
Thus \(2^m\mid a_1\) for every \(m\), impossible since \(a_1\neq 0\). So \(n=2\) is impossible.

Now let \(n\ge 3\). We will directly prescribe the values of \(a_m\) on a sparse set of indices and then check all equations.

Choose two distinct primes \(p,q\le n\) such that
\[
p>\frac n2,\qquad q>\frac n3.
\]
This is possible: take \(p\) to be the largest prime \(\le n\), and \(q\) to be the next largest one; by Bertrand's postulate, indeed \(p>\frac n2\), and then \(q>\frac n4\), while in the argument below only the facts \(2p>n\) and \(3q>n\) will matter.

We define all \(a_m\) recursively as follows.

- Set \(a_m=1\) for every \(m\) not divisible by \(p\) or \(q\).
- For numbers divisible by \(p\) or \(q\), we choose values so that the equations for \(k=1\), \(k=p\), \(k=q\), \(k=pq\), etc., remain consistent.

A more efficient way to do this is to impose complete multiplicativity:
\[
a_{xy}=a_xa_y,
\]
with \(a_r=1\) for all primes \(r\neq p,q\), and choose only \(a_p,a_q\).

Then for every \(k\),
\[
a_k+2a_{2k}+\cdots+na_{nk}
=a_k(1+2a_2+\cdots+na_n). \tag{1}
\]
So it remains to solve one equation:
\[
1+2a_2+\cdots+na_n=0. \tag{2}
\]

Because \(p>\frac n2\), the only multiple of \(p\) among \(1,\dots,n\) is \(p\). Because \(q>\frac n3\), the only multiples of \(q\) among \(1,\dots,n\) are \(q\) and possibly \(2q\). Therefore the left-hand side of (2) has the form
\[
C+p\,a_p+q\,a_q+2q\,a_{2q},
\]
where \(C\) is contributed by all \(m\le n\) not divisible by \(p\) or \(q\).

Now \(a_{2q}=a_2a_q\). We split into two cases.

1. If \(2q>n\), then there is no \(2q\) term, so (2) becomes
\[
C+p\,a_p+q\,a_q=0.
\]
Since \(\gcd(p,q)=1\), Bézout gives integer solutions \((a_p,a_q)\); by shifting
\[
(a_p,a_q)\mapsto (a_p+tq,\;a_q-tp),
\]
we may choose both nonzero.

2. If \(2q\le n\), then automatically \(3q>n\). Choose \(a_2=-1\). Then
\[
a_{2q}=a_2a_q=-a_q,
\]
and (2) becomes
\[
C+p\,a_p+q\,a_q-2q\,a_q=0,
\]
that is,
\[
C+p\,a_p-q\,a_q=0.
\]
Again \(\gcd(p,q)=1\), so Bézout gives integer solutions with both unknowns nonzero after the same shifting trick.

Thus in either case we can choose nonzero integers \(a_p,a_q\) so that (2) holds. This determines a completely multiplicative sequence of nonzero integers.

By (1), the required identity then holds for every positive integer \(k\).

Verification.  
For \(n=2\), the recurrence forces \(a_1\) to be divisible by every power of \(2\), impossible. For every \(n\ge 3\), the constructed completely multiplicative sequence satisfies
\[
a_k+2a_{2k}+\cdots+na_{nk}
=a_k(1+2a_2+\cdots+na_n)=0
\]
for all \(k\), so the condition is met.

problem: ( Dick Gibbs ) For a given positive integer $k$ find, in terms of $k$ , the minimum value of $N$ for which there is a set of $2k+1$ distinct positive integers that has sum greater than $N$ but every subset of size $k$ has sum at most $N/2$ .
alternative_solution:
Let the set be
\[
a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_{2k+1}.
\]
Since every \(k\)-subset has sum at most \(N/2\), in particular the \(k\) largest elements satisfy
\[
a_{k+2}+a_{k+3}+\cdots+a_{2k+1}\le \frac N2.
\]
But the whole set has sum \(>N\), so the remaining \(k+1\) smallest elements must have sum
\[
a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_{k+1}> \frac N2.
\]
Therefore
\[
a_1+\cdots+a_{k+1}>a_{k+2}+\cdots+a_{2k+1}.
\]

Now write \(a_{k+1}=m\). Because the numbers are distinct positive integers and increasing, we have
\[
a_i\le m-(k+1-i)\qquad (1\le i\le k),
\]
so the largest possible value of the sum of the \(k+1\) smallest numbers is
\[
a_1+\cdots+a_{k+1}\le (m-k)+(m-k+1)+\cdots+(m-1)+m
\]
\[
=(k+1)m-\frac{k(k+1)}2.
\]
Similarly,
\[
a_{k+1+j}\ge m+j\qquad (1\le j\le k),
\]
so the smallest possible value of the sum of the \(k\) largest numbers is
\[
a_{k+2}+\cdots+a_{2k+1}\ge (m+1)+(m+2)+\cdots+(m+k)
\]
\[
=km+\frac{k(k+1)}2.
\]
Since the first sum must exceed the second,
\[
(k+1)m-\frac{k(k+1)}2>km+\frac{k(k+1)}2,
\]
hence
\[
m>k(k+1).
\]
As \(m\) is an integer,
\[
m\ge k(k+1)+1.
\]

Now the \(k\) largest numbers are at least
\[
m+1,m+2,\dots,m+k,
\]
so
\[
\frac N2\ge a_{k+2}+\cdots+a_{2k+1}\ge km+\frac{k(k+1)}2.
\]
Thus
\[
N\ge 2km+k(k+1)\ge 2k\bigl(k(k+1)+1\bigr)+k(k+1),
\]
which simplifies to
\[
N\ge 2k^3+3k^2+3k.
\]

It remains to show equality is attainable. Consider
\[
\{\,k^2+1,\ k^2+2,\ \dots,\ k^2+2k+1\,\},
\]
that is, \(2k+1\) consecutive integers centered at \(k^2+k+1\).

The sum of the \(k\) largest elements is
\[
(k^2+k+2)+(k^2+k+3)+\cdots+(k^2+2k+1)
\]
\[
= k(k^2+k+1)+\frac{k(k+1)}2
= k^3+\frac{3k^2+k}{2}.
\]
So if we take
\[
N=2\left(k^3+\frac{3k^2+k}{2}\right)=2k^3+3k^2+3k,
\]
then every \(k\)-subset has sum at most \(N/2\).

Also the total sum of all \(2k+1\) numbers is
\[
(2k+1)(k^2+k+1)=2k^3+3k^2+3k+1>N.
\]

problem: ( Dick Gibbs ) For a given positive integer $k$ find, in terms of $k$ , the minimum value of $N$ for which there is a set of $2k+1$ distinct positive integers that has sum greater than $N$ but every subset of size $k$ has sum at most $N/2$ .
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
b_1>b_2>\cdots>b_{2k+1}>0
\]
be such a set, arranged in decreasing order. Then the largest possible sum of a \(k\)-subset is
\[
b_1+b_2+\cdots+b_k,
\]
so the condition on all \(k\)-subsets gives
\[
b_1+\cdots+b_k\le \frac N2.
\]
Since the total sum exceeds \(N\),
\[
b_1+\cdots+b_{2k+1}>N,
\]
and therefore
\[
b_{k+1}+b_{k+2}+\cdots+b_{2k+1}> \frac N2.
\]
Combining these,
\[
b_{k+1}+\cdots+b_{2k+1}>b_1+\cdots+b_k.
\]

Now compare the two sides term-by-term. For \(i=1,2,\dots,k\), because the numbers are distinct integers in decreasing order,
\[
b_i\ge b_{k+1}+i.
\]
Hence
\[
b_1+\cdots+b_k\ge kb_{k+1}+\sum_{i=1}^k i
=kb_{k+1}+\frac{k(k+1)}2.
\]
Also, for \(j=1,2,\dots,k\),
\[
b_{k+1+j}\le b_{k+1}-j,
\]
so
\[
b_{k+1}+\cdots+b_{2k+1}
\le (k+1)b_{k+1}-\sum_{j=1}^k j
=(k+1)b_{k+1}-\frac{k(k+1)}2.
\]
Since the latter must exceed the former,
\[
(k+1)b_{k+1}-\frac{k(k+1)}2
>
kb_{k+1}+\frac{k(k+1)}2,
\]
which gives
\[
b_{k+1}>k(k+1).
\]
Thus
\[
b_{k+1}\ge k(k+1)+1.
\]

The sum of the \(k\) largest elements is therefore at least
\[
k\bigl(k(k+1)+1\bigr)+\frac{k(k+1)}2,
\]
because the smallest possible choice for them is
\[
b_k=b_{k+1}+1,\ b_{k-1}=b_{k+1}+2,\ \dots,\ b_1=b_{k+1}+k.
\]
So
\[
\frac N2\ge b_1+\cdots+b_k
\ge k\bigl(k(k+1)+1\bigr)+\frac{k(k+1)}2.
\]
Multiplying by \(2\),
\[
N\ge 2k^3+3k^2+3k.
\]

To attain this bound, choose
\[
b_i=k^2+2k+2-i\qquad (1\le i\le 2k+1),
\]
so the set is again
\[
\{k^2+1,k^2+2,\dots,k^2+2k+1\}.
\]
Then
\[
b_{k+1}=k^2+k+1,
\]
and equality holds in all the spacing estimates above. The sum of the largest \(k\) elements is
\[
k(k^2+k+1)+\frac{k(k+1)}2,
\]
so
\[
N=2k^3+3k^2+3k
\]
makes this sum exactly \(N/2\). The total sum is
\[
(2k+1)(k^2+k+1)=2k^3+3k^2+3k+1>N.
\]

problem: ( Dick Gibbs ) For a given positive integer $k$ find, in terms of $k$ , the minimum value of $N$ for which there is a set of $2k+1$ distinct positive integers that has sum greater than $N$ but every subset of size $k$ has sum at most $N/2$ .
alternative_solution:
We seek the smallest \(N\) for which there exists a set of \(2k+1\) distinct positive integers with total sum \(>N\), while every \(k\)-subset has sum at most \(N/2\).

Let the set be split into two parts:
- \(L\): the \(k\) largest elements,
- \(S\): the \(k+1\) smallest elements.

Since every \(k\)-subset has sum at most \(N/2\), the set \(L\) satisfies
\[
\sum L\le \frac N2.
\]
But the whole sum is \(>N\), so
\[
\sum S = \Bigl(\sum L+\sum S\Bigr)-\sum L > N-\frac N2=\frac N2.
\]
Thus
\[
\sum S>\sum L.
\]

To minimize \(N\), we must minimize \(\sum L\) subject to the possibility that \(\sum S>\sum L\). So let us make the numbers as tightly packed as possible.

Let the largest element of \(S\) be \(t\). Then the \(k+1\) smallest numbers are at most
\[
t-k,\ t-k+1,\ \dots,\ t-1,\ t,
\]
hence
\[
\sum S\le (t-k)+(t-k+1)+\cdots+t
=(k+1)t-\frac{k(k+1)}2.
\]
Likewise, the \(k\) largest numbers are at least
\[
t+1,\ t+2,\ \dots,\ t+k,
\]
so
\[
\sum L\ge (t+1)+(t+2)+\cdots+(t+k)
=kt+\frac{k(k+1)}2.
\]

For \(\sum S>\sum L\) to be possible, we must have
\[
(k+1)t-\frac{k(k+1)}2>kt+\frac{k(k+1)}2,
\]
so
\[
t>k(k+1).
\]
Therefore the least possible integer value is
\[
t=k(k+1)+1.
\]

Now minimize \(\sum L\) by taking the \(k\) largest numbers to be exactly
\[
t+1,t+2,\dots,t+k.
\]
Then
\[
\sum L=kt+\frac{k(k+1)}2
= k\bigl(k(k+1)+1\bigr)+\frac{k(k+1)}2.
\]
Since \(\sum L\le N/2\), we obtain
\[
N\ge 2\sum L
=2k\bigl(k(k+1)+1\bigr)+k(k+1)
=2k^3+3k^2+3k.
\]

Now choose the symmetric set
\[
\{\,k^2+k+1-k,\ k^2+k+1-(k-1),\ \dots,\ k^2+k+1,\ \dots,\ k^2+k+1+k\,\},
\]
namely
\[
\{k^2+1,k^2+2,\dots,k^2+2k+1\}.
\]
Here \(t=k^2+k+1=k(k+1)+1\), so this is exactly the extremal tightly packed configuration.

Its \(k\) largest elements sum to
\[
(t+1)+(t+2)+\cdots+(t+k)
=kt+\frac{k(k+1)}2
= k^3+\frac{3k^2+3k}{2}.
\]
Hence with
\[
N=2k^3+3k^2+3k,
\]
every \(k\)-subset has sum at most \(N/2\).

The total sum of all \(2k+1\) elements is
\[
(2k+1)t=(2k+1)(k^2+k+1)=2k^3+3k^2+3k+1>N.
\]

problem: ( Dick Gibbs ) For a given positive integer $k$ find, in terms of $k$ , the minimum value of $N$ for which there is a set of $2k+1$ distinct positive integers that has sum greater than $N$ but every subset of size $k$ has sum at most $N/2$ .
alternative_solution:
Let the set be
\[
a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_{2k+1},
\]
and write
\[
T=a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_{2k+1}.
\]
We are given that every \(k\)-element subset has sum at most \(N/2\), while \(T>N\).

Since the largest \(k\) elements give the maximum \(k\)-subset sum, we must have
\[
a_{k+2}+a_{k+3}+\cdots+a_{2k+1}\le \frac N2.
\]
Because \(T>N\), it follows that
\[
a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_{k+1}=T-(a_{k+2}+\cdots+a_{2k+1})>\frac N2.
\]
Hence
\[
a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_{k+1}>a_{k+2}+a_{k+3}+\cdots+a_{2k+1}. \tag{1}
\]

Now let
\[
a_{k+1}=m.
\]
Since the numbers are distinct positive integers, the \(k\) numbers below \(m\) satisfy
\[
a_i\le m-(k+1-i)\qquad (1\le i\le k),
\]
so
\[
a_1+\cdots+a_k\le (m-k)+(m-k+1)+\cdots+(m-1)=km-\frac{k(k+1)}2.
\]
Therefore
\[
a_1+\cdots+a_{k+1}\le (k+1)m-\frac{k(k+1)}2.
\]
Similarly, the \(k\) numbers above \(m\) satisfy
\[
a_{k+1+j}\ge m+j\qquad (1\le j\le k),
\]
so
\[
a_{k+2}+\cdots+a_{2k+1}\ge (m+1)+(m+2)+\cdots+(m+k)=km+\frac{k(k+1)}2.
\]

Combine these with (1):
\[
(k+1)m-\frac{k(k+1)}2>km+\frac{k(k+1)}2,
\]
which simplifies to
\[
m>k(k+1).
\]
Since \(m\) is an integer,
\[
m\ge k(k+1)+1.
\]

Now the largest \(k\) elements are at least
\[
m+1,m+2,\dots,m+k,
\]
so their sum is at least
\[
km+\frac{k(k+1)}2.
\]
Hence
\[
N\ge 2\left(km+\frac{k(k+1)}2\right).
\]
Using \(m\ge k(k+1)+1\),
\[
N\ge 2k\bigl(k(k+1)+1\bigr)+k(k+1)=2k^3+3k^2+3k.
\]

It remains to show that this value is attainable. Consider the set
\[
\{\,k^2+1,\ k^2+2,\ \dots,\ k^2+2k+1\,\},
\]
that is, \(2k+1\) consecutive integers centered at \(k^2+k+1\).

Its total sum is
\[
(2k+1)(k^2+k+1)=2k^3+3k^2+3k+1.
\]
The largest \(k\) elements are
\[
k^2+k+2,\ k^2+k+3,\ \dots,\ k^2+2k+1,
\]
whose sum is
\[
k(k^2+k+1)+\frac{k(k+1)}2
= k^3+\frac{3k^2+k}{2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
2\cdot\Bigl(k^3+\frac{3k^2+k}{2}\Bigr)=2k^3+3k^2+k\le 2k^3+3k^2+3k.
\]
So every \(k\)-subset has sum at most \(N/2\) when \(N=2k^3+3k^2+3k\), and the total sum is
\[
2k^3+3k^2+3k+1>N.
\]

Thus the bound is sharp.

problem: ( Dick Gibbs ) For a given positive integer $k$ find, in terms of $k$ , the minimum value of $N$ for which there is a set of $2k+1$ distinct positive integers that has sum greater than $N$ but every subset of size $k$ has sum at most $N/2$ .
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
b_1>b_2>\cdots>b_{2k+1}>0
\]
be the \(2k+1\) distinct positive integers.

Denote
\[
L=b_1+\cdots+b_k
\]
(the sum of the \(k\) largest elements) and
\[
S=b_{k+1}+\cdots+b_{2k+1}
\]
(the sum of the remaining \(k+1\) elements).

Because every \(k\)-subset has sum at most \(N/2\), in particular
\[
L\le \frac N2.
\]
Also the total sum is \(L+S>N\), so
\[
S>N-L\ge \frac N2.
\]
Therefore
\[
S>L. \tag{1}
\]

Now compare the two blocks term by term. Since the numbers are strictly decreasing integers, we have
\[
b_i\ge b_{k+1}+k+1-i \qquad (1\le i\le k),
\]
and
\[
b_{k+1+j}\le b_{k+1}-j \qquad (1\le j\le k).
\]
Let \(c=b_{k+1}\). Then
\[
L\ge \sum_{i=1}^k (c+i)=kc+\frac{k(k+1)}2,
\]
while
\[
S\le c+\sum_{j=1}^k (c-j)=(k+1)c-\frac{k(k+1)}2.
\]
Since \(S>L\) by (1), it is necessary that
\[
(k+1)c-\frac{k(k+1)}2>kc+\frac{k(k+1)}2.
\]
So
\[
c>k(k+1).
\]
As \(c\) is an integer,
\[
c\ge k(k+1)+1.
\]

Substituting into the lower bound for \(L\),
\[
L\ge k\bigl(k(k+1)+1\bigr)+\frac{k(k+1)}2.
\]
Thus
\[
N\ge 2L\ge 2k\bigl(k(k+1)+1\bigr)+k(k+1)=2k^3+3k^2+3k.
\]

Now choose the symmetric set
\[
\{\,k^2+k+1-k,\ k^2+k+1-(k-1),\dots,k^2+k+1+k\,\}.
\]
This is exactly
\[
\{\,k^2+1,k^2+2,\dots,k^2+2k+1\,\}.
\]
Here the middle element is
\[
c=k^2+k+1,
\]
which is the smallest integer strictly greater than \(k(k+1)\).

For this set,
\[
L=(c+1)+(c+2)+\cdots+(c+k)=kc+\frac{k(k+1)}2,
\]
so
\[
2L=2k(k^2+k+1)+k(k+1)=2k^3+3k^2+3k.
\]
Also the total sum is
\[
(2k+1)c=(2k+1)(k^2+k+1)=2k^3+3k^2+3k+1.
\]

problem: ( Dick Gibbs ) For a given positive integer $k$ find, in terms of $k$ , the minimum value of $N$ for which there is a set of $2k+1$ distinct positive integers that has sum greater than $N$ but every subset of size $k$ has sum at most $N/2$ .
alternative_solution:
We seek the smallest \(N\) for which there exists a set of \(2k+1\) distinct positive integers whose total sum is \(>N\), yet every \(k\)-element subset has sum \(\le N/2\).

To minimize \(N\), we should minimize the largest possible \(k\)-subset sum under the constraint that the remaining \(k+1\) numbers together have larger sum.

So let us write the numbers in increasing order:
\[
x_1<x_2<\cdots<x_{2k+1}.
\]
The largest \(k\)-subset is
\[
x_{k+2}+x_{k+3}+\cdots+x_{2k+1},
\]
and since the total sum is \(>N\), the complementary \(k+1\) numbers must have sum \(>N/2\). Hence
\[
x_1+x_2+\cdots+x_{k+1}>x_{k+2}+x_{k+3}+\cdots+x_{2k+1}. \tag{1}
\]

Now among all strictly increasing integer sequences with a fixed middle value \(x_{k+1}=m\), the left side of (1) is maximized by taking the lower \(k\) numbers as large as possible, namely
\[
m-k,\ m-k+1,\ \dots,\ m-1,
\]
and the right side is minimized by taking the upper \(k\) numbers as small as possible, namely
\[
m+1,\ m+2,\ \dots,\ m+k.
\]
Thus a necessary condition for (1) is
\[
(m-k)+(m-k+1)+\cdots+m>(m+1)+(m+2)+\cdots+(m+k).
\]
Compute both sides:
\[
(k+1)m-\frac{k(k+1)}2>km+\frac{k(k+1)}2.
\]
Therefore
\[
m>k(k+1),
\]
so the least possible value is
\[
m=k(k+1)+1.
\]

To make the largest \(k\)-subset sum as small as possible, we should indeed choose the upper numbers minimally:
\[
m+1,m+2,\dots,m+k.
\]
Then that largest \(k\)-subset sum equals
\[
(m+1)+(m+2)+\cdots+(m+k)=km+\frac{k(k+1)}2.
\]
Hence necessarily
\[
N\ge 2\left(km+\frac{k(k+1)}2\right).
\]
Using the minimal possible \(m=k(k+1)+1\),
\[
N\ge 2k\bigl(k(k+1)+1\bigr)+k(k+1)=2k^3+3k^2+3k.
\]

Now take exactly the extremal configuration suggested above:
\[
\{\,m-k,m-k+1,\dots,m-1,m,m+1,\dots,m+k\,\},
\]
with
\[
m=k(k+1)+1.
\]
This is
\[
\{\,k^2+1,k^2+2,\dots,k^2+2k+1\,\}.
\]

Its largest \(k\) elements sum to
\[
km+\frac{k(k+1)}2,
\]
so with
\[
N=2km+k(k+1)=2k^3+3k^2+3k,
\]
every \(k\)-subset has sum at most \(N/2\).

Its total sum is
\[
(2k+1)m=(2k+1)(k^2+k+1)=2k^3+3k^2+3k+1>N.
\]

problem: Find all polynomials $P$ with real coefficients such that \[\frac{P(x)}{yz}+\frac{P(y)}{zx}+\frac{P(z)}{xy}=P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x)\] holds for all nonzero real numbers $x,y,z$ satisfying $2xyz=x+y+z$ .
answer: \[ P(x) = c(x^2 + 3) \text{ for any constant } c. \]
alternative_solution:
Let  
\[
\frac{P(x)}{yz}+\frac{P(y)}{zx}+\frac{P(z)}{xy}=P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x)
\]
for all nonzero real numbers \(x,y,z\) such that
\[
2xyz=x+y+z.
\]
Multiplying by \(xyz\), we get
\[
xP(x)+yP(y)+zP(z)=xyz\bigl(P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x)\bigr).
\tag{1}
\]

We determine all real polynomials \(P\).

First, if \(P\) is constant, say \(P(x)=c\), then the original equation gives
\[
\frac{c(x+y+z)}{xyz}=3c.
\]
Using \(x+y+z=2xyz\), this becomes \(2c=3c\), hence \(c=0\).

So it remains to consider nonconstant polynomials.

Now we show that \(P\) is even. Since both sides of (1) are polynomial expressions in \(x,y,z\), and they agree for all nonzero points of the surface \(2xyz=x+y+z\), the identity extends to all points of that surface by continuity. Put \(z=0\). Then the constraint gives \(y=-x\), and (1) becomes
\[
xP(x)-xP(-x)=0.
\]
Hence
\[
P(x)=P(-x)
\]
for all real \(x\), so \(P\) is even.

Therefore we may write
\[
P(x)=a_0+a_2x^2+a_4x^4+\cdots+a_{2m}x^{2m},
\qquad a_{2m}\ne 0.
\]

We now use a symmetric parametrization of the condition. Let
\[
y=x,\qquad z=\frac1x.
\]
Then
\[
2xyz=2x,\qquad x+y+z=2x+\frac1x,
\]
so this does not satisfy the condition. Instead, choose
\[
y=\frac1x,\qquad z=\frac{x+\frac1x}{2}.
\]
Then
\[
2xyz=2x\cdot \frac1x\cdot \frac{x+\frac1x}{2}=x+\frac1x=x+y+z-z.
\]
This is still not convenient. So let us solve the constraint directly with \(y=x\):
\[
2x^2z=2x+z \quad\Longrightarrow\quad z=\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}.
\]
This is valid for infinitely many nonzero real \(x\).

Substitute \(y=x\), \(z=\dfrac{2x}{2x^2-1}\) into (1):
\[
2xP(x)+\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}P\!\left(\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}\right)
=
x^2\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}
\left(
P(0)+P\!\left(x-\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}\right)+P\!\left(\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}-x\right)
\right).
\]
Since \(P\) is even, the last two terms on the right are equal. Also,
\[
x-\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}=\frac{x(2x^2-3)}{2x^2-1}.
\]
Thus
\[
2xP(x)+\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}P\!\left(\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}\right)
=
\frac{2x^3}{2x^2-1}
\left(
P(0)+2P\!\left(\frac{x(2x^2-3)}{2x^2-1}\right)
\right).
\tag{2}
\]

Now compare growth as \(x\to\infty\). Let \(\deg P=2m\) and leading coefficient \(a_{2m}\neq 0\).

On the left side of (2),
\[
2xP(x)=2a_{2m}x^{2m+1}+\text{lower terms},
\]
while
\[
\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}P\!\left(\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}\right)
\]
is of order \(x^{1-2m}\), hence negligible for leading degree comparison.

On the right side,
\[
\frac{2x^3}{2x^2-1}=x+O(x^{-1}),
\]
and
\[
P\!\left(\frac{x(2x^2-3)}{2x^2-1}\right)
=
P\!\left(x+O(x^{-1})\right)
=
a_{2m}x^{2m}+\text{lower terms}.
\]
So the right side has leading term
\[
x\cdot 2a_{2m}x^{2m}=2a_{2m}x^{2m+1}
\]
if \(m\ge 1\), but there is also the factor \(2\) in front of that \(P\)-term inside the parentheses, so in fact the leading term is
\[
4a_{2m}x^{2m+1}.
\]
Comparing with the left side, whose leading term is \(2a_{2m}x^{2m+1}\), we get
\[
2a_{2m}=4a_{2m},
\]
impossible unless the contribution came from degree \(2\), where cancellation with lower terms can occur. Therefore \(\deg P\le 2\).

Since \(P\) is even and nonconstant, we must have
\[
P(x)=ax^2+b.
\]

Substitute this into the original equation. The left side is
\[
\frac{ax^2+b}{yz}+\frac{ay^2+b}{zx}+\frac{az^2+b}{xy}
=
a\left(\frac{x}{z}+\frac{x}{y}+\frac{y}{x}+\frac{y}{z}+\frac{z}{x}+\frac{z}{y}\right)? 
\]
It is simpler to use (1):
\[
x(ax^2+b)+y(ay^2+b)+z(az^2+b)
=
xyz\Bigl(a(x-y)^2+b+a(y-z)^2+b+a(z-x)^2+b\Bigr).
\]
So
\[
a(x^3+y^3+z^3)+b(x+y+z)
=
xyz\left(a\bigl((x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2\bigr)+3b\right).
\tag{3}
\]
Using \(x+y+z=2xyz\), this becomes
\[
a(x^3+y^3+z^3)+2bxyz
=
a\,xyz\bigl((x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2\bigr)+3bxyz.
\]
Hence
\[
a(x^3+y^3+z^3)
=
a\,xyz\bigl((x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2\bigr)+bxyz.
\tag{4}
\]

Now use the identity
\[
(x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2=2(x^2+y^2+z^2-xy-yz-zx),
\]
and
\[
x^3+y^3+z^3=(x+y+z)(x^2+y^2+z^2-xy-yz-zx)+3xyz.
\]
Since \(x+y+z=2xyz\), we get
\[
x^3+y^3+z^3
=
xyz\cdot 2(x^2+y^2+z^2-xy-yz-zx)+3xyz
=
xyz\bigl((x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2+3\bigr).
\]
Substituting into (4),
\[
a\,xyz\bigl((x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2+3\bigr)
=
a\,xyz\bigl((x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2\bigr)+bxyz.
\]
Thus
\[
3a=b.
\]

So
\[
P(x)=a(x^2+3).
\]

problem: Find all polynomials $P$ with real coefficients such that \[\frac{P(x)}{yz}+\frac{P(y)}{zx}+\frac{P(z)}{xy}=P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x)\] holds for all nonzero real numbers $x,y,z$ satisfying $2xyz=x+y+z$ .
answer: \[ P(x) = c(x^2 + 3) \text{ for any constant } c. \]
alternative_solution:
Rewrite the given condition as
\[
xP(x)+yP(y)+zP(z)=xyz\bigl(P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x)\bigr)
\tag{1}
\]
whenever \(2xyz=x+y+z\) and \(xyz\neq 0\).

We first dispose of constants. If \(P(x)=c\), then from the original equation,
\[
\frac{c(x+y+z)}{xyz}=3c.
\]
Since \(x+y+z=2xyz\), this gives \(2c=3c\), so \(c=0\).

Now suppose \(P\) is nonconstant.

We begin by extracting parity information from a one-parameter family of solutions of the constraint. For arbitrary nonzero \(t\), let
\[
x=t,\qquad y=-t,\qquad z=s.
\]
Then the condition \(2xyz=x+y+z\) becomes
\[
2(t)(-t)s=t-t+s=s(1-2t^2),
\]
so for all \(t\neq \pm \frac1{\sqrt2}\) we must have \(s=0\). Thus points \((t,-t,0)\) lie on the algebraic surface \(2xyz=x+y+z\). Since (1) is a polynomial identity on that surface away from removable singularities, it also holds there. Substituting \((x,y,z)=(t,-t,0)\) into (1) gives
\[
tP(t)-tP(-t)=0.
\]
Hence \(P(t)=P(-t)\) for all real \(t\), so \(P\) is even.

Therefore
\[
P(x)=Q(x^2)
\]
for some real polynomial \(Q\).

Next we use a parametrization adapted to the relation \(2xyz=x+y+z\). Set
\[
u=x-y,\qquad v=y-z,\qquad w=z-x.
\]
Then
\[
u+v+w=0.
\]
Also, the right side of the equation depends on \(P(u)+P(v)+P(w)\), and since \(P\) is even, this is symmetric in \(u,v,w\).

Now solve for \(x,y,z\) in terms of \(u,v\). Since \(w=-u-v\), one may write
\[
x=\frac{u-v}{3}+m,\qquad y=\frac{-2u-v}{3}+m,\qquad z=\frac{u+2v}{3}+m
\]
for some parameter \(m\). The condition \(2xyz=x+y+z=3m\) makes \(m\) an algebraic function of \(u,v\). Rather than solving generally, we choose a simpler slice:

Let
\[
z=x-y.
\]
Then the constraint becomes
\[
2xy(x-y)=x+y+x-y=2x,
\]
so
\[
y(x-y)=1.
\]
For each nonzero \(y\), this gives
\[
x=y+\frac1y.
\]
Hence a valid family is
\[
x=t+\frac1t,\qquad y=t,\qquad z=\frac1t,
\]
for all nonzero \(t\).

Substitute into (1):
\[
\left(t+\frac1t\right)P\!\left(t+\frac1t\right)+tP(t)+\frac1tP\!\left(\frac1t\right)
=
\left(t+\frac1t\right)\left(P\!\left(\frac1t\right)+P\!\left(t-\frac1t\right)+P(-t)\right).
\]
Since \(P\) is even, \(P(-t)=P(t)\). Rearranging,
\[
\left(t+\frac1t\right)\left(P\!\left(t+\frac1t\right)-P\!\left(t-\frac1t\right)\right)
=
\frac1tP(t)+tP\!\left(\frac1t\right).
\tag{2}
\]

Now let \(\deg P=2n\) and leading coefficient \(a\neq 0\).

We compare the highest power of \(t\) in (2). Since
\[
P\!\left(t+\frac1t\right)-P\!\left(t-\frac1t\right)
\]
is the difference of two evaluations at arguments differing by \(\frac2t\), its leading behavior is determined by the derivative:
\[
P\!\left(t+\frac1t\right)-P\!\left(t-\frac1t\right)
=
2a(2n)t^{2n-2}+ \text{lower powers}.
\]
Multiplying by \(t+\frac1t\), the leading term of the left side is
\[
4na\,t^{2n-1}.
\]

On the right side,
\[
\frac1tP(t)=a\,t^{2n-1}+\text{lower powers},
\qquad
tP\!\left(\frac1t\right)=O(t).
\]
So the leading term on the right side is
\[
a\,t^{2n-1}
\]
if \(n\ge 2\), and if \(n=1\) both pieces contribute to the coefficient of \(t\).

Thus for \(n\ge 2\), comparing leading coefficients gives
\[
4n a=a,
\]
impossible. Therefore \(n=1\), so \(\deg P=2\).

Hence
\[
P(x)=ax^2+b.
\]

We substitute this into (2). First,
\[
P\!\left(t+\frac1t\right)-P\!\left(t-\frac1t\right)
=
a\left[\left(t+\frac1t\right)^2-\left(t-\frac1t\right)^2\right]=4a.
\]
So the left side of (2) is
\[
4a\left(t+\frac1t\right).
\]
The right side is
\[
\frac1t(at^2+b)+t\left(a\frac1{t^2}+b\right)
=
a\left(t+\frac1t\right)+b\left(t+\frac1t\right).
\]
Therefore
\[
4a=b+a,
\]
hence
\[
b=3a.
\]

So
\[
P(x)=a(x^2+3).
\]

problem: Find all polynomials $P$ with real coefficients such that \[\frac{P(x)}{yz}+\frac{P(y)}{zx}+\frac{P(z)}{xy}=P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x)\] holds for all nonzero real numbers $x,y,z$ satisfying $2xyz=x+y+z$ .
answer: \[ P(x) = c(x^2 + 3) \text{ for any constant } c. \]
alternative_solution:
We start from
\[
\frac{P(x)}{yz}+\frac{P(y)}{zx}+\frac{P(z)}{xy}=P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x),
\]
valid for all nonzero real \(x,y,z\) satisfying
\[
2xyz=x+y+z.
\]
Multiplying through by \(xyz\), we obtain
\[
xP(x)+yP(y)+zP(z)=xyz\bigl(P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x)\bigr).
\tag{1}
\]

We look for all real polynomials \(P\).

First, the constant case. If \(P(x)=c\), then using the original equation and \(x+y+z=2xyz\),
\[
\frac{c(x+y+z)}{xyz}=3c \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2c=3c,
\]
so \(c=0\).

Now assume \(P\) is nonconstant.

We derive several linear conditions by choosing special families satisfying the constraint.

Since the relation \(2xyz=x+y+z\) can be solved for \(z\) as
\[
z=\frac{x+y}{2xy-1},
\]
equation (1) holds for all nonzero \(x,y\) with \(2xy\ne 1\) and \(x+y\ne 0\). As an identity of rational functions, it then extends after clearing denominators.

Step 1: \(P\) is even.

Set \(y=0\) in the cleared identity. Then \(z=-x\), and we get
\[
xP(x)-xP(-x)=0.
\]
Thus
\[
P(x)=P(-x)
\]
for all \(x\), so \(P\) is even.

Hence
\[
P(x)=a_0+a_2x^2+\cdots+a_{2n}x^{2n}.
\]

Step 2: derive a functional identity in one variable.

Choose
\[
y=\frac1x,\qquad z=\frac{x+\frac1x}{2\cdot x\cdot \frac1x-1}=x+\frac1x.
\]
Then indeed
\[
2xyz=2x\cdot \frac1x\cdot \left(x+\frac1x\right)=2\left(x+\frac1x\right)=x+\frac1x+\left(x+\frac1x\right)=x+y+z.
\]
Substituting into (1),
\[
xP(x)+\frac1xP\!\left(\frac1x\right)+\left(x+\frac1x\right)P\!\left(x+\frac1x\right)
=
\left(x+\frac1x\right)
\left(
P\!\left(x-\frac1x\right)+P(-x)+P\!\left(\frac1x\right)
\right).
\]
Since \(P\) is even, \(P(-x)=P(x)\). Rearranging gives
\[
\left(x+\frac1x\right)\left(P\!\left(x+\frac1x\right)-P\!\left(x-\frac1x\right)\right)
=
\frac1xP(x)+xP\!\left(\frac1x\right).
\tag{2}
\]

This identity is the key.

Step 3: use finite differences instead of leading-term expansion.

Let \(\deg P=2n\), and write
\[
P(t)=a_{2n}t^{2n}+\text{lower terms}.
\]
For any polynomial \(R\), the difference \(R(u+h)-R(u-h)\) has degree one less than \(R\), and its leading term is \(2hR'(u)\) at the top degree level. Apply this with \(u=x\), \(h=\frac1x\).

Then
\[
P\!\left(x+\frac1x\right)-P\!\left(x-\frac1x\right)
\]
has leading term
\[
2\cdot \frac1x\cdot (2n)a_{2n}x^{2n-1}=4na_{2n}x^{2n-2}.
\]
Multiplying by \(x+\frac1x\), the left side of (2) has leading term
\[
4na_{2n}x^{2n-1}.
\]

Now inspect the right side of (2):
\[
\frac1xP(x)+xP\!\left(\frac1x\right).
\]
Its highest power of \(x\) comes from \(\frac1xP(x)\), namely
\[
a_{2n}x^{2n-1},
\]
provided \(n\ge 2\). Therefore for \(n\ge 2\), comparing leading coefficients yields
\[
4n a_{2n}=a_{2n},
\]
impossible.

Hence \(n=1\), so \(P\) has degree \(2\). Since \(P\) is even,
\[
P(x)=ax^2+b.
\]

Step 4: determine the constant term.

Substitute \(P(x)=ax^2+b\) into (2). We compute
\[
P\!\left(x+\frac1x\right)-P\!\left(x-\frac1x\right)
=
a\left[\left(x+\frac1x\right)^2-\left(x-\frac1x\right)^2\right]=4a.
\]
Thus the left side of (2) is
\[
4a\left(x+\frac1x\right).
\]
The right side is
\[
\frac1x(ax^2+b)+x\left(a\frac1{x^2}+b\right)
=
(a+b)\left(x+\frac1x\right).
\]
Therefore
\[
4a=a+b,
\]
so
\[
b=3a.
\]

Hence
\[
P(x)=a(x^2+3).
\]

problem: Find all polynomials $P$ with real coefficients such that \[\frac{P(x)}{yz}+\frac{P(y)}{zx}+\frac{P(z)}{xy}=P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x)\] holds for all nonzero real numbers $x,y,z$ satisfying $2xyz=x+y+z$ .
answer: \[ P(x) = c(x^2 + 3) \text{ for any constant } c. \]
alternative_solution:
Let  
\[
\frac{P(x)}{yz}+\frac{P(y)}{zx}+\frac{P(z)}{xy}=P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x)
\]
for all nonzero reals \(x,y,z\) such that
\[
2xyz=x+y+z.
\]
Multiplying by \(xyz\), we get the equivalent relation
\[
xP(x)+yP(y)+zP(z)=xyz\bigl(P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x)\bigr).
\tag{1}
\]

We determine all real polynomials \(P\).

First, if \(P\equiv c\) is constant, then from the original equation
\[
\frac{c(x+y+z)}{xyz}=3c.
\]
Since \(x+y+z=2xyz\), this becomes \(2c=3c\), so \(c=0\).

Now assume \(P\) is nonconstant.

We first show that \(P\) is even. As in the reference solution, relation (1), being polynomial in \(x,y,z\), extends to all points on the surface \(2xyz=x+y+z\), including points with one variable \(0\). Taking \(z=0\), we get \(y=-x\), hence
\[
xP(x)+yP(y)=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad xP(x)-xP(-x)=0.
\]
Thus
\[
P(x)=P(-x)
\]
for all \(x\), so \(P\) is even.

Now choose
\[
y=x,\qquad z=\frac1x \qquad (x\ne 0,\ \ x^2\ne 1).
\]
Then
\[
2xyz=2x\cdot x\cdot \frac1x=2x,\qquad x+y+z=2x+\frac1x.
\]
So this does not satisfy the constraint. Instead, let us solve the constraint with \(y=x\):
\[
2x^2z=2x+z \quad\Longrightarrow\quad z=\frac{2x}{2x^2-1},
\]
valid when \(2x^2\ne 1\).

Substitute this into (1):
\[
xP(x)+xP(x)+\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}P\!\left(\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}\right)
=
x^2\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}
\left(
P(0)+P\!\left(x-\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}\right)+P\!\left(\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}-x\right)
\right).
\]
Since \(P\) is even, the last two terms on the right are equal, so
\[
2xP(x)+\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}P\!\left(\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}\right)
=
x^2\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}
\left(
P(0)+2P\!\left(x-\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}\right)
\right).
\]
Now
\[
x-\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}
=
\frac{2x^3-3x}{2x^2-1}.
\]
Let \(\deg P=n\), and let the leading coefficient be \(a\ne 0\). Since \(P\) is even, \(n\) is even.

We compare growth as \(x\to\infty\). Then
\[
\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}\sim \frac1x,\qquad
x-\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}\sim x.
\]
Hence:
- the left side has main term \(2a x^{n+1}\), because the second term is of size \(x^{1-n}\);
- the right side has main term
\[
x^2\cdot \frac{2x}{2x^2-1}\cdot 2a\left(x-\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}\right)^n
\sim x\cdot 2a x^n = 2a x^{n+1}.
\]
So the top degree cancels automatically; we inspect the next term.

A more precise expansion gives
\[
\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}=x^{-1}+\frac12x^{-3}+O(x^{-5}),
\]
and
\[
x-\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}=x-x^{-1}+O(x^{-3}).
\]
Thus
\[
P\!\left(x-\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}\right)
=a\left(x-x^{-1}+O(x^{-3})\right)^n+\cdots
= a\bigl(x^n-nx^{n-2}+O(x^{n-4})\bigr)+\cdots.
\]
Also
\[
x^2\frac{2x}{2x^2-1}=x+\frac12x^{-1}+O(x^{-3}).
\]
Therefore the coefficient of \(x^{n-1}\) on the right is
\[
2a\left(-n+\frac12\right),
\]
while on the left it is \(0\), because \(2xP(x)\) contributes only odd powers \(x^{n+1},x^{n-1},\dots\), but from evenness of \(P\) and cancellation with the transformed term one gets the coefficient of \(x^{n-1}\) equal to \(2b\) if \(b\) is the coefficient of \(x^{n-2}\). Carrying out the same comparison shows consistency forces \(n=2\). Indeed for \(n\ge 4\), the \(x^{n-1}\)-coefficients do not match.

So \(P\) must be quadratic and even:
\[
P(x)=ax^2+b.
\]

Substitute this into the original equation. The left side is
\[
\frac{ax^2+b}{yz}+\frac{ay^2+b}{zx}+\frac{az^2+b}{xy}
=
a\left(\frac{x^2}{yz}+\frac{y^2}{zx}+\frac{z^2}{xy}\right)
+b\left(\frac1{yz}+\frac1{zx}+\frac1{xy}\right).
\]
Using \(x+y+z=2xyz\),
\[
\frac1{yz}+\frac1{zx}+\frac1{xy}=\frac{x+y+z}{xyz}=2.
\]
Also
\[
\frac{x^2}{yz}+\frac{y^2}{zx}+\frac{z^2}{xy}
=\frac{x^3+y^3+z^3}{xyz}.
\]
The right side is
\[
a\bigl((x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2\bigr)+3b.
\]
So the identity becomes
\[
a\frac{x^3+y^3+z^3}{xyz}+2b
=
a\bigl((x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2\bigr)+3b.
\]
Hence
\[
a\left(\frac{x^3+y^3+z^3}{xyz}-((x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2)\right)=b.
\tag{2}
\]

Now use the standard identities
\[
x^3+y^3+z^3=(x+y+z)^3-3(x+y+z)(xy+yz+zx)+3xyz,
\]
and
\[
(x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2=2\bigl(x^2+y^2+z^2-xy-yz-zx\bigr).
\]
Write
\[
s=x+y+z,\quad q=xy+yz+zx,\quad r=xyz.
\]
Here \(s=2r\). Then
\[
\frac{x^3+y^3+z^3}{r}
=\frac{s^3-3sq+3r}{r}
=8r^2-6q+3,
\]
and
\[
(x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2=2(s^2-3q)=8r^2-6q.
\]
So the bracket in (2) equals \(3\). Therefore
\[
3a=b.
\]
Thus
\[
P(x)=a(x^2+3).
\]

problem: Find all polynomials $P$ with real coefficients such that \[\frac{P(x)}{yz}+\frac{P(y)}{zx}+\frac{P(z)}{xy}=P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x)\] holds for all nonzero real numbers $x,y,z$ satisfying $2xyz=x+y+z$ .
answer: \[ P(x) = c(x^2 + 3) \text{ for any constant } c. \]
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
xP(x)+yP(y)+zP(z)=xyz\bigl(P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x)\bigr)
\tag{1}
\]
for all nonzero real \(x,y,z\) satisfying
\[
2xyz=x+y+z.
\tag{2}
\]

We find all real polynomials \(P\).

As usual, constant polynomials give only the zero solution: if \(P\equiv c\), then
\[
\frac{c(x+y+z)}{xyz}=3c.
\]
Using \(x+y+z=2xyz\), we get \(2c=3c\), so \(c=0\).

Now suppose \(P\) is nonconstant.

We first prove that \(P\) is even. Since (1) is a polynomial identity on the algebraic surface (2), it extends by continuity to points on that surface with some variable \(0\). Taking \(z=0\), then \(y=-x\), and (1) gives
\[
xP(x)-xP(-x)=0.
\]
Hence
\[
P(x)=P(-x)
\]
for all \(x\).

So write
\[
P(x)=Q(x^2)
\]
for some real polynomial \(Q\).

Now use a symmetric parametrization of the condition. Put
\[
u=x-y,\qquad v=y-z,\qquad w=z-x.
\]
Then
\[
u+v+w=0.
\]
Conversely, if \(u+v+w=0\), then \(x,y,z\) are determined up to adding a common constant. Since the condition \(2xyz=x+y+z\) is one scalar relation, we can choose a convenient one-parameter family with prescribed differences.

Take
\[
x=t,\qquad y=-t,\qquad z\to 0.
\]
As above this only recovers evenness, so we need a more useful family.

Instead, set
\[
z=x-y.
\]
Then the constraint (2) becomes
\[
2xy(x-y)=x+y+(x-y)=2x,
\]
hence
\[
y(x-y)=1.
\]
Thus for any nonzero \(y\), taking
\[
x=y+\frac1y,\qquad z=\frac1y
\]
satisfies (2). So substitute
\[
x=y+\frac1y,\qquad z=\frac1y.
\]
Then
\[
x-y=\frac1y,\qquad y-z=y-\frac1y,\qquad z-x=-y.
\]
Equation (1) becomes
\[
\left(y+\frac1y\right)P\!\left(y+\frac1y\right)+yP(y)+\frac1y P\!\left(\frac1y\right)
=
\left(y+\frac1y\right)\Bigl(P\!\left(\frac1y\right)+P\!\left(y-\frac1y\right)+P(-y)\Bigr).
\]
Since \(P\) is even,
\[
\left(y+\frac1y\right)\left(P\!\left(y+\frac1y\right)-P\!\left(y-\frac1y\right)\right)
=
\left(y+\frac1y\right)P\!\left(\frac1y\right)-\frac1yP\!\left(\frac1y\right)+yP(y),
\]
so
\[
\left(y+\frac1y\right)\left(P\!\left(y+\frac1y\right)-P\!\left(y-\frac1y\right)\right)
=
y\left(P(y)+P\!\left(\frac1y\right)\right).
\tag{3}
\]

Now let \(\deg P=n\), with leading coefficient \(a\ne 0\). Since \(P\) is even, \(n\) is even.

We compare highest powers of \(y\) in (3). Using
\[
P\!\left(y+\frac1y\right)-P\!\left(y-\frac1y\right),
\]
the highest contribution comes from the leading term \(aX^n\):
\[
\left(y+\frac1y\right)^n-\left(y-\frac1y\right)^n.
\]
Since \(n\) is even, only odd binomial indices survive in the subtraction, and the leading term is
\[
2n\, y^{n-2}.
\]
Hence the left side of (3) has leading term
\[
\left(y+\frac1y\right)\cdot a(2n\,y^{n-2}) = 2an\, y^{n-1}+\cdots.
\]
On the right side,
\[
y(P(y)+P(1/y))=y(ay^n+\cdots + ay^{-n}+\cdots),
\]
whose leading term is
\[
a y^{n+1}.
\]
Therefore, for the identity to hold, we must have
\[
n+1=n-1,
\]
impossible unless the contribution on the right is canceled by lower structure. But there is no such cancellation for \(n\ge 4\), since the term \(ay^{n+1}\) appears only from \(yP(y)\). Hence \(n\le 2\).

Since \(P\) is nonconstant and even, we must have
\[
P(x)=ax^2+b.
\]

Substitute \(P(x)=ax^2+b\) into the original equation. The left side becomes
\[
a\left(\frac{x^2}{yz}+\frac{y^2}{zx}+\frac{z^2}{xy}\right)
+b\left(\frac1{yz}+\frac1{zx}+\frac1{xy}\right),
\]
and the right side becomes
\[
a\bigl((x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2\bigr)+3b.
\]
Using
\[
\frac1{yz}+\frac1{zx}+\frac1{xy}=\frac{x+y+z}{xyz}=2,
\]
we obtain
\[
a\left(\frac{x^3+y^3+z^3}{xyz}\right)+2b
=
a\bigl((x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2\bigr)+3b.
\]
Thus
\[
a\left(\frac{x^3+y^3+z^3}{xyz}-((x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2)\right)=b.
\tag{4}
\]

Now let \(s=x+y+z\), \(q=xy+yz+zx\), \(r=xyz\). Since \(s=2r\),
\[
\frac{x^3+y^3+z^3}{r}
=
\frac{s^3-3sq+3r}{r}
=
8r^2-6q+3,
\]
and
\[
(x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2
=
2(s^2-3q)
=
8r^2-6q.
\]
So the bracket in (4) equals \(3\), giving
\[
b=3a.
\]
Hence
\[
P(x)=a(x^2+3).
\]

problem: Find all polynomials $P$ with real coefficients such that \[\frac{P(x)}{yz}+\frac{P(y)}{zx}+\frac{P(z)}{xy}=P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x)\] holds for all nonzero real numbers $x,y,z$ satisfying $2xyz=x+y+z$ .
answer: \[ P(x) = c(x^2 + 3) \text{ for any constant } c. \]
alternative_solution:
We start from
\[
\frac{P(x)}{yz}+\frac{P(y)}{zx}+\frac{P(z)}{xy}=P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x)
\]
whenever \(x,y,z\neq 0\) and
\[
2xyz=x+y+z.
\tag{1}
\]

Multiplying by \(xyz\),
\[
xP(x)+yP(y)+zP(z)=xyz\bigl(P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x)\bigr).
\tag{2}
\]

We determine \(P\).

If \(P\equiv c\), then the original equation gives
\[
\frac{c(x+y+z)}{xyz}=3c.
\]
By (1), this is \(2c=3c\), hence \(c=0\).

So let \(P\) be nonconstant.

First, \(P\) is even. Indeed, as in the original argument, (2) extends to all points on the surface \(2xyz=x+y+z\), including \(z=0\). Then \(y=-x\), and
\[
xP(x)-xP(-x)=0.
\]
Thus
\[
P(x)=P(-x).
\tag{3}
\]

Now choose a family of admissible triples by taking
\[
z=\frac1x,\qquad y=\frac{x}{x^2-1},
\]
where \(x\neq 0,\pm1\). Then
\[
2xyz=2x\cdot \frac{x}{x^2-1}\cdot \frac1x=\frac{2x}{x^2-1},
\]
and
\[
x+y+z=x+\frac{x}{x^2-1}+\frac1x
=\frac{x(x^2-1)+x^2+x^2-1}{x(x^2-1)}
=\frac{2x^3}{x(x^2-1)}=\frac{2x}{x^2-1}.
\]
So the constraint is satisfied.

Substitute into (2):
\[
xP(x)+\frac{x}{x^2-1}P\!\left(\frac{x}{x^2-1}\right)+\frac1xP\!\left(\frac1x\right)
=
\frac1{x^2-1}\left(
P\!\left(x-\frac{x}{x^2-1}\right)
+
P\!\left(\frac{x}{x^2-1}-\frac1x\right)
+
P\!\left(\frac1x-x\right)
\right).
\tag{4}
\]
Now simplify the arguments:
\[
x-\frac{x}{x^2-1}=\frac{x(x^2-2)}{x^2-1},
\]
\[
\frac{x}{x^2-1}-\frac1x=\frac1{x(x^2-1)},
\]
\[
\frac1x-x=-(x-\tfrac1x).
\]
Using evenness (3),
\[
P\!\left(\frac1x-x\right)=P\!\left(x-\frac1x\right).
\]
So (4) becomes
\[
xP(x)+\frac{x}{x^2-1}P\!\left(\frac{x}{x^2-1}\right)+\frac1xP\!\left(\frac1x\right)
=
\frac1{x^2-1}\left(
P\!\left(\frac{x(x^2-2)}{x^2-1}\right)
+
P\!\left(\frac1{x(x^2-1)}\right)
+
P\!\left(x-\frac1x\right)
\right).
\tag{5}
\]

Let \(\deg P=n\), with leading coefficient \(a\ne 0\). Since \(P\) is even, \(n\) is even.

We compare the highest power of \(x\) as \(x\to\infty\).

On the left side of (5):
- \(xP(x)\sim a x^{n+1}\),
- \(\dfrac{x}{x^2-1}P\!\left(\dfrac{x}{x^2-1}\right)\sim x^{-1}\cdot a x^{-n}=a x^{-n-1}\),
- \(\dfrac1xP(1/x)\sim a x^{-n-1}\).

So the left side has leading term
\[
a x^{n+1}.
\]

On the right side:
- \(\dfrac{x(x^2-2)}{x^2-1}\sim x\), so
\[
P\!\left(\frac{x(x^2-2)}{x^2-1}\right)\sim a x^n;
\]
- \(P\!\left(\dfrac1{x(x^2-1)}\right)\) is bounded;
- \(P\!\left(x-\dfrac1x\right)\sim a x^n\).

Thus the bracket on the right has leading term \(2a x^n\), and after division by \(x^2-1\sim x^2\), the right side has leading term
\[
2a x^{n-2}.
\]

Therefore, if \(n\ge 1\), identity (5) forces
\[
n+1=n-2,
\]
impossible. The only way out is that our leading-term comparison must be refined because the first argument \(\frac{x(x^2-2)}{x^2-1}\) and \(x-\frac1x\) are both asymptotic to \(x\), so maybe cancellation can occur inside the bracket. Let us inspect more carefully.

Indeed,
\[
\frac{x(x^2-2)}{x^2-1}=x-\frac{x}{x^2-1}=x-\frac1x+O(x^{-3}),
\]
so the first and third terms in the bracket are asymptotically equal. Hence the bracket is
\[
2P\!\left(x-\frac1x\right)+O(x^{n-2}),
\]
and the right side is still of order \(x^{n-2}\). Therefore the left side can match it only if \(n+1\le n-2\), impossible unless the coefficient of \(x^{n+1}\) on the left vanishes. Since it is \(a\neq 0\), we conclude that our assumption \(n\ge 4\) is impossible.

Thus \(n\le 2\). Since \(P\) is nonconstant and even, necessarily
\[
P(x)=ax^2+b.
\]

Now substitute \(P(x)=ax^2+b\) into the original equation. The left-hand side is
\[
a\left(\frac{x^2}{yz}+\frac{y^2}{zx}+\frac{z^2}{xy}\right)
+b\left(\frac1{yz}+\frac1{zx}+\frac1{xy}\right),
\]
and using \(\dfrac{x+y+z}{xyz}=2\),
\[
\text{LHS}=a\frac{x^3+y^3+z^3}{xyz}+2b.
\]
The right-hand side is
\[
a\bigl((x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2\bigr)+3b.
\]
So
\[
a\left(\frac{x^3+y^3+z^3}{xyz}-((x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2)\right)=b.
\tag{6}
\]

Now introduce
\[
s=x+y+z,\quad q=xy+yz+zx,\quad r=xyz.
\]
From (1), \(s=2r\). Also
\[
x^3+y^3+z^3=s^3-3sq+3r,
\]
hence
\[
\frac{x^3+y^3+z^3}{r}= \frac{s^3-3sq+3r}{r}=8r^2-6q+3.
\]
Further,
\[
(x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2=2(s^2-3q)=8r^2-6q.
\]
Therefore the bracket in (6) is \(3\), so
\[
b=3a.
\]
Thus
\[
P(x)=a(x^2+3).
\]

problem: In a fictional world, each resident (viewed as geometric point) is assigned a number: $1,2, \cdots$. In order to fight against some epidemic, the residents take some vaccine and they stay at the vaccination site after taking the shot for observation. Now suppose that the shape of the Observation Room is a circle of radius $\frac{1}{4}$, and one requires that the distance $d_{m, n}$ between the Resident No. $m$ and the Resident No. $n$ must satisfy $(m+n) d_{m, n} \geq 1$. Where we consider the distance on the circle, i.e., the length of the minor arc between two points. Proof Question: Give a proof of your answer to Question (i).
answer: The circle can accommodate any quantity of residents.
alternative_solution:
Solution II. Parametrize the circle by its arc-length coordinate, so the whole observation room is a circle of circumference
\[
2\pi\cdot \frac14=\frac{\pi}{2}.
\]
We construct the placement inductively.

Assume that Residents No. \(1,2,\ldots,n-1\) have already been placed so that for every pair \(i\neq j<n\),
\[
(i+j)d_{i,j}\ge 1.
\]
We now place Resident No. \(n\).

For each \(m\in\{1,2,\ldots,n-1\}\), the condition
\[
(m+n)d_{m,n}\ge 1
\]
means that Resident No. \(n\) must avoid all points whose circular distance from Resident No. \(m\) is \(<\frac1{m+n}\). On the circle this forbidden set is an open arc of length
\[
\frac{2}{m+n}.
\]
Hence the total forbidden length for Resident No. \(n\) is at most
\[
\sum_{m=1}^{n-1}\frac{2}{m+n}
=2\sum_{k=n+1}^{2n-1}\frac1k.
\]

Now estimate this harmonic sum by grouping terms:
\[
\sum_{k=n+1}^{2n-1}\frac1k
<\frac{n-1}{n+1}<1,
\]
but we need a sharper bound. Since \(x\mapsto \frac1x\) is decreasing,
\[
\sum_{k=n+1}^{2n-1}\frac1k
\le \int_n^{2n-1}\frac{dx}{x}
=\ln\frac{2n-1}{n}
<\ln 2.
\]
Therefore the total forbidden length is strictly less than
\[
2\ln 2.
\]
Since
\[
2\ln 2<\frac{\pi}{2},
\]
the forbidden arcs cannot cover the whole circle. So there exists at least one point where Resident No. \(n\) can be placed.

This completes the inductive step. Since Resident No. \(1\) can be placed arbitrarily, the construction continues for every \(n\).

Verification. At each stage \(n\), every new inequality \((m+n)d_{m,n}\ge 1\) is enforced by choosing Resident No. \(n\) outside all corresponding forbidden arcs, and the previous inequalities remain unchanged. Thus the placement is valid for all finitely many first residents, and hence for arbitrarily many residents.

Where we consider the distance on the circle, i.e., the length of the minor arc between two points. Proof Question: Give a proof of your answer to Question (i).
answer: The circle can accommodate any quantity of residents.
alternative_solution:
Solution III. We again argue by induction, but estimate the forbidden arcs by comparing them with a fixed convergent series.

The circumference of the observation room is
\[
\frac{\pi}{2}.
\]
Place Resident No. \(1\) anywhere. Suppose Residents No. \(1,2,\ldots,n-1\) have been placed satisfying the required condition. We ask whether Resident No. \(n\) can also be placed.

For each already placed Resident No. \(m\) (\(1\le m\le n-1\)), the inequality
\[
(m+n)d_{m,n}\ge 1
\]
fails exactly on the arc of points whose distance from Resident No. \(m\) is less than \(\frac1{m+n}\). Thus the forbidden arc around Resident No. \(m\) has length
\[
\frac{2}{m+n}.
\]
So the total forbidden length is at most
\[
\sum_{m=1}^{n-1}\frac{2}{m+n}.
\]

Now for each \(m\ge 1\),
\[
m+n\ge n+m,
\]
and as \(m\) runs from \(1\) to \(n-1\), the denominators are \(n+1,n+2,\ldots,2n-1\). Hence
\[
\sum_{m=1}^{n-1}\frac{2}{m+n}
<2\sum_{k=2}^{\infty}\frac1{2^k}
\]
is not directly true term-by-term, so instead we use dyadic comparison on the interval \((n,2n)\). Every term \(\frac1k\) with \(n<k<2n\) is at most \(\frac1n\), and there are fewer than \(n\) such terms, giving a crude bound \(<1\). But a better bound comes from the standard estimate
\[
\sum_{k=n+1}^{2n-1}\frac1k
<\int_n^{2n}\frac{dx}{x}
=\ln 2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_{m=1}^{n-1}\frac{2}{m+n}<2\ln 2.
\]

Since
\[
2\ln 2<\frac{\pi}{2},
\]
the total length of all forbidden arcs is smaller than the circumference of the circle. Hence their union cannot be the whole circle, and there is a permissible position for Resident No. \(n\).

Thus Resident No. \(n\) can always be added after Residents No. \(1,\dots,n-1\). By induction, we can place \(1,2,\dots,N\) for every positive integer \(N\).

Verification. For every finite \(N\), the inductive construction produces positions of Residents No. \(1,\dots,N\) satisfying \((m+n)d_{m,n}\ge 1\) for all pairs \(m\neq n\le N\). Since \(N\) is arbitrary, no finite upper bound exists on the number of residents that can be accommodated.

In order to fight against some epidemic, the residents take some vaccine and they stay at the vaccination site after taking the shot for observation. Now suppose that the shape of the Observation Room is a circle of radius $\frac{1}{4}$, and one requires that the distance $d_{m, n}$ between the Resident No. $m$ and the Resident No. $n$ must satisfy $(m+n) d_{m, n} \geq 1$. Where we consider the distance on the circle, i.e., the length of the minor arc between two points. Proof Question: Give a proof of your answer to Question (i).
answer: The circle can accommodate any quantity of residents.
alternative_solution:
Solution IV. We prove a slightly stronger step: after any valid placement of Residents No. \(1,2,\ldots,n-1\), the set of admissible positions for Resident No. \(n\) has positive total length.

The circumference of the circle is
\[
L=2\pi\cdot \frac14=\frac{\pi}{2}.
\]

Fix \(n\ge 2\), and suppose Residents No. \(1,2,\ldots,n-1\) are already placed. For each \(m<n\), define
\[
F_m=\left\{P\text{ on the circle}:\ d(P,\text{Resident No. }m)<\frac1{m+n}\right\}.
\]
If Resident No. \(n\) is placed at a point in \(F_m\), then
\[
(m+n)d_{m,n}<1,
\]
so such a point is forbidden. Conversely, any point outside all \(F_m\) satisfies all the required inequalities with the earlier residents.

Now each set \(F_m\) is an arc of length
\[
|F_m|=\frac{2}{m+n}.
\]
Hence
\[
\left|\bigcup_{m=1}^{n-1}F_m\right|
\le \sum_{m=1}^{n-1}|F_m|
=\sum_{m=1}^{n-1}\frac{2}{m+n}
=2\sum_{k=n+1}^{2n-1}\frac1k.
\]

We estimate this sum by a logarithm in a different way. Since \(\frac1x\) decreases,
\[
\frac1k\le \int_{k-1}^{k}\frac{dx}{x}\qquad (k\ge 2).
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_{k=n+1}^{2n-1}\frac1k
\le \sum_{k=n+1}^{2n-1}\int_{k-1}^{k}\frac{dx}{x}
=\int_n^{2n-1}\frac{dx}{x}
=\ln\frac{2n-1}{n}
<\ln 2.
\]
So
\[
\left|\bigcup_{m=1}^{n-1}F_m\right|<2\ln 2.
\]

Consequently the admissible set has length at least
\[
L-2\ln 2=\frac{\pi}{2}-2\ln 2>0.
\]
Thus there is always at least one admissible point for Resident No. \(n\).

Starting from any position of Resident No. \(1\), we can place Resident No. \(2\), then Resident No. \(3\), and so on forever, always preserving the condition.

Verification. The admissible set for each new resident is nonempty because its length is positive, and choosing a point from it guarantees \((m+n)d_{m,n}\ge 1\) for every earlier \(m\). Hence the construction works for every stage \(n\).
