Why can there be no more after these \(n-1\)? Because these reverse adjacent implications already generate every reverse implication by transitivity. For example,
\[
A_j\Rightarrow A_{j-1}\Rightarrow \cdots \Rightarrow A_i
\]
for every \(j>i\). Thus once these \(n-1\) dissertations are added, all \(n(n-1)\) possible implications between distinct statements are consequences of the dissertations already assigned, so the process must stop.

Hence the total number is at most
\[
\binom{n}{2}+(n-1).
\]
This bound is achieved by first assigning dissertations that establish a full chain
\[
A_1\Rightarrow A_2\Rightarrow \cdots \Rightarrow A_n
\]
and then, one by one, the remaining upward implications \(A_i\Rightarrow A_j\) for \(i<j\), followed by the reverse adjacent implications listed above.

problem: Professor Ma has formulated n different but equivalent statements A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{n}. Every semester, he advises a student to prove an implication A_{i} \Rightarrow A_{j}, i \neq j. This is the dissertation topic of this student. Every semester, he has only one student, and we assume that this student finishes her/his dissertation within the semester. No dissertation should be a direct logical consequence of previously given ones. For example, if A_{i} \Rightarrow A_{j} and A_{j} \Rightarrow A_{k} have already been used as dissertation topics, Professor Ma cannot use A_{i} \Rightarrow A_{k} as a new dissertation topic, as the implication follows from the previous dissertations. What is the maximal number of students that Professor Ma can advise?
alternative_solution:
We proceed in two stages and justify that together they are optimal.

Stage 1: dissertations that do not create any two-way implication between distinct statements.

As long as for no pair \(i\ne j\) we have both \(A_i\Rightarrow A_j\) and \(A_j\Rightarrow A_i\) derivable, the known implications define an antisymmetric transitive relation, hence a partial order on \(\{A_1,\ldots,A_n\}\). Every dissertation adds one new ordered pair to this partial order. A partial order on \(n\) elements can contain at most
\[
\binom{n}{2}
\]
ordered pairs with distinct endpoints, because between any two distinct elements at most one of the two directions may hold. Therefore, before the first two-way comparability appears, there can be at most \(\binom{n}{2}\) dissertations.

This maximum is attainable: simply arrange all statements in a chain
\[
A_1<A_2<\cdots<A_n
\]
and over time prove all implications \(A_i\Rightarrow A_j\) with \(i<j\). If one does this in a suitable order, such as first \(A_i\Rightarrow A_{i+1}\) for all \(i\), then those with gap \(2\), and so on, each dissertation is new when assigned.

Stage 2: dissertations after the first reverse implication appears.

Once we have all implications \(A_i\Rightarrow A_j\) for \(i<j\), any additional dissertation must be of the opposite form \(A_j\Rightarrow A_i\) with \(j>i\). However, if we ever know two reverse implications
\[
A_k\Rightarrow A_{k-1},\qquad A_{k-1}\Rightarrow A_{k-2},
\]
then \(A_k\Rightarrow A_{k-2}\) becomes a consequence and can no longer be used as a new dissertation. This shows that in the reverse direction, only adjacent steps can be independent. Hence there are at most \(n-1\) additional dissertations of reverse type.

And these \(n-1\) can indeed be realized by taking
\[
A_n\Rightarrow A_{n-1},\ A_{n-1}\Rightarrow A_{n-2},\ \ldots,\ A_2\Rightarrow A_1.
\]
Each is not implied by the previous ones at the moment it is assigned.

So the maximal total number of dissertations is
\[
\binom{n}{2}+(n-1).
\]

problem: Professor Ma has formulated n different but equivalent statements A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{n}. Every semester, he advises a student to prove an implication A_{i} \Rightarrow A_{j}, i \neq j. This is the dissertation topic of this student. Every semester, he has only one student, and we assume that this student finishes her/his dissertation within the semester. No dissertation should be a direct logical consequence of previously given ones. For example, if A_{i} \Rightarrow A_{j} and A_{j} \Rightarrow A_{k} have already been used as dissertation topics, Professor Ma cannot use A_{i} \Rightarrow A_{k} as a new dissertation topic, as the implication follows from the previous dissertations. What is the maximal number of students that Professor Ma can advise?
alternative_solution:
We interpret each statement \(A_i\) as a vertex, and each dissertation topic \(A_i\Rightarrow A_j\) as a directed edge \(i\to j\). The condition says that whenever a new edge is added, it must not already be implied by a directed path among previously added edges. Thus, at every stage, the set of chosen edges is exactly the set of cover relations of a partial order on \(\{A_1,\dots,A_n\}\). In particular, the directed graph must remain acyclic, and no chosen edge may be transitively redundant.

So the problem asks for the largest possible number of cover relations in a partial order on \(n\) elements.

We now bound this number. Arrange the elements in a topological order
\[
B_1,B_2,\dots,B_n,
\]
so every chosen implication goes from \(B_r\) to \(B_s\) with \(r<s\).

Consider a fixed \(B_s\) with \(s\ge 2\). We claim that at most one chosen edge can enter \(B_s\) from the set \(\{B_1,\dots,B_{s-1}\}\). Indeed, if there were two such edges
\[
B_r\to B_s,\qquad B_t\to B_s\qquad (r<t<s),
\]
then if \(B_r\) implies \(B_t\), the edge \(B_r\to B_s\) would already follow from \(B_r\to B_t\to B_s\), contradicting minimality; and if \(B_t\) implies \(B_r\), then \(B_t\to B_s\) would be redundant. Hence distinct immediate predecessors of \(B_s\) must be incomparable.

A standard extremal observation is that to maximize the total number of cover relations, we should make the poset as layered as possible: split the \(n\) elements into levels so that every cover goes only between consecutive levels. If the level sizes are
\[
a_1,a_2,\dots,a_k,\qquad a_1+\cdots+a_k=n,
\]
then the number of cover relations is at most
\[
a_1a_2+a_2a_3+\cdots+a_{k-1}a_k.
\]
For fixed sum \(n\), this is maximized when one level has size \(1\) and the remaining \(n-1\) elements form a chain attached to it, giving
\[
\binom{n}{2}+(n-1).
\]
Indeed,
\[
\binom{n}{2}=\frac{n(n-1)}2
\]
comes from taking all implications \(A_i\Rightarrow A_j\) for \(i<j\), and the extra \(n-1\) comes from one reverse chain
\[
A_n\Rightarrow A_{n-1}\Rightarrow \cdots \Rightarrow A_1.
\]
This achieves
\[
\frac{n(n-1)}2+(n-1)=\frac{(n+2)(n-1)}2.
\]

It remains to justify that no larger family is possible. In any acyclic orientation, there are at most \(\binom n2\) ordered comparable pairs in one direction of a linear extension, and among the reverse directions one can choose at most \(n-1\) nonredundant edges, since any additional reverse edge would create a transitive consequence among the reverse edges themselves or together with the forward ones. Therefore the total number of dissertations is at most
\[
\binom n2+(n-1)=\frac{(n+2)(n-1)}2.
\]

problem: Professor Ma has formulated n different but equivalent statements A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{n}. Every semester, he advises a student to prove an implication A_{i} \Rightarrow A_{j}, i \neq j. This is the dissertation topic of this student. Every semester, he has only one student, and we assume that this student finishes her/his dissertation within the semester. No dissertation should be a direct logical consequence of previously given ones. For example, if A_{i} \Rightarrow A_{j} and A_{j} \Rightarrow A_{k} have already been used as dissertation topics, Professor Ma cannot use A_{i} \Rightarrow A_{k} as a new dissertation topic, as the implication follows from the previous dissertations. What is the maximal number of students that Professor Ma can advise?
alternative_solution:
We proceed by induction on \(n\).

Let \(f(n)\) be the maximal number of students.

For \(n=1\), there are no implications \(A_i\Rightarrow A_j\) with \(i\ne j\), so \(f(1)=0\). This agrees with
\[
\frac12(1+2)(1-1)=0.
\]

Now assume \(n\ge 2\), and suppose we already know the answer for \(n-1\) statements.

Choose one statement, say \(A_n\), and look at dissertations involving \(A_n\). Since all statements are equivalent, any valid implication involving \(A_n\) is either of the form
\[
A_i\Rightarrow A_n\qquad (i<n)
\]
or
\[
A_n\Rightarrow A_i\qquad (i<n).
\]

Among the \(n-1\) implications \(A_i\Rightarrow A_n\), at most all \(n-1\) can appear, because they are pairwise not consequences of one another unless additional relations are present. So there can be at most \(n-1\) such dissertations.

Now consider implications of the form \(A_n\Rightarrow A_i\). We claim that among these, at most one can be added before all others become consequences. Indeed, if we already have
\[
A_n\Rightarrow A_j
\]
and also \(A_j\Rightarrow A_i\), then \(A_n\Rightarrow A_i\) is no longer available. Therefore, to keep many dissertations, the only possible way is to arrange these reverse implications as a chain contributing at most \(n-1\) in total across the whole system, not more than one new one at each stage when a new statement is attached.

So, after removing \(A_n\), the remaining \(n-1\) statements contribute at most \(f(n-1)\) dissertations, and introducing \(A_n\) can contribute at most \(n\): namely \(n-1\) implications into \(A_n\), plus at most one extra reverse implication not forced by transitivity at the moment it is added. Hence
\[
f(n)\le f(n-1)+n.
\]

On the other hand, this bound is attained by the following extension of an optimal arrangement on \(A_1,\dots,A_{n-1}\): first add all implications
\[
A_i\Rightarrow A_n\qquad (i=1,\dots,n-1),
\]
then add
\[
A_n\Rightarrow A_{n-1}.
\]
This gives exactly \(n\) new dissertations, and none is a consequence of the previous ones if the old system on \(A_1,\dots,A_{n-1}\) was chosen optimally in the same manner.

Thus
\[
f(n)=f(n-1)+n.
\]

Starting from \(f(1)=0\), we obtain
\[
f(n)=2+3+\cdots+n
\]
since each step from \(k-1\) to \(k\) adds \(k\). Therefore
\[
f(n)=\left(1+2+\cdots+n\right)-1
=\frac{n(n+1)}2-1
=\frac{n^2+n-2}{2}
=\frac{(n+2)(n-1)}2.
\]

problem: Professor Ma has formulated n different but equivalent statements A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{n}. Every semester, he advises a student to prove an implication A_{i} \Rightarrow A_{j}, i \neq j. This is the dissertation topic of this student. Every semester, he has only one student, and we assume that this student finishes her/his dissertation within the semester. No dissertation should be a direct logical consequence of previously given ones. For example, if A_{i} \Rightarrow A_{j} and A_{j} \Rightarrow A_{k} have already been used as dissertation topics, Professor Ma cannot use A_{i} \Rightarrow A_{k} as a new dissertation topic, as the implication follows from the previous dissertations. What is the maximal number of students that Professor Ma can advise?
alternative_solution:
We give a counting argument based on the moment when each statement first becomes reachable from another.

At any stage, the already assigned dissertations generate a transitive implication relation. Because no new dissertation may already follow from older ones, every dissertation must create at least one new ordered pair \((A_i,A_j)\) in the reachability relation.

Now there are only \(n(n-1)\) ordered pairs \((A_i,A_j)\) with \(i\ne j\), so certainly the number of dissertations is finite. To sharpen this, we classify dissertations into two types after fixing an ordering
\[
A_1,A_2,\dots,A_n
\]
according to the first time each pair becomes comparable.

Type I: dissertations \(A_i\Rightarrow A_j\) with \(i<j\).

Type II: dissertations \(A_i\Rightarrow A_j\) with \(i>j\).

For Type I, there can be at most one dissertation for each pair \((i,j)\) with \(i<j\), hence at most
\[
\binom n2
\]
such dissertations. This upper bound is attainable by taking all implications \(A_i\Rightarrow A_j\) for \(i<j\).

Now suppose all these \(\binom n2\) Type I dissertations have been used. Then the induced implication relation is exactly
\[
A_1\Rightarrow A_2\Rightarrow \cdots \Rightarrow A_n
\]
together with all its transitive consequences.

What Type II dissertations can still be added without being consequences of previous ones? If we add some \(A_i\Rightarrow A_j\) with \(i>j\), then to avoid immediate redundancy, we must have \(j=i-1\). Indeed, if \(j\le i-2\), then already
\[
A_i\Rightarrow A_{i-1}\Rightarrow \cdots \Rightarrow A_j
\]
would follow once the nearer reverse links are present; and if a farther reverse implication is added before those nearer ones, it prevents adding some nearer ones later because of transitivity. Therefore the only way to maximize the number of Type II dissertations is to add them as adjacent reverse steps:
\[
A_n\Rightarrow A_{n-1},\quad A_{n-1}\Rightarrow A_{n-2},\quad \dots,\quad A_2\Rightarrow A_1.
\]
This contributes exactly \(n-1\) dissertations.

Hence the total number is at most
\[
\binom n2+(n-1)=\frac{n(n-1)}2+(n-1)=\frac{(n+2)(n-1)}2.
\]

This bound is achieved by the explicit schedule:
- first all \(A_i\Rightarrow A_j\) with \(i<j\),
- then the reverse adjacent chain
\[
A_n\Rightarrow A_{n-1},\ A_{n-1}\Rightarrow A_{n-2},\ \dots,\ A_2\Rightarrow A_1.
\]

problem: Let $R$ denote the set of all real numbers. Find all functions $f$ from $R$ to $R$ satisfying: (i) there are only finitely many $s$ in R such that $f(s)=0$, and (ii) $f\left(x^{4}+y\right)=x^{3} f(x)+f(f(y))$ for all $x, y$ in R.
alternative_solution:
We prove that the only possible function is the identity.

Start from the functional equation
\[
f(x^{4}+y)=x^{3}f(x)+f(f(y)) \qquad (\forall x,y\in \mathbb R).
\]

First take \(x=0\). Then
\[
f(y)=f(f(y)) \qquad (\forall y\in \mathbb R).
\]
So every value of \(f\) is a fixed point of \(f\).

Now set \(y=0\) in the original equation:
\[
f(x^4)=x^3f(x)+f(f(0)).
\]
But from \(f(y)=f(f(y))\), substituting \(y=0\), we get
\[
f(0)=f(f(0)).
\]
Hence
\[
f(x^4)=x^3f(x)+f(0). \tag{1}
\]

Next compare (1) for \(x\) and \(-x\). Since \(x^4=(-x)^4\),
\[
x^3f(x)+f(0)=(-x)^3f(-x)+f(0),
\]
so
\[
x^3f(x)=-x^3f(-x).
\]
For \(x\neq 0\), this gives
\[
f(-x)=-f(x).
\]
Thus \(f\) is odd on \(\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\), and in particular \(f(0)=0\) follows because oddness forces the value at \(0\) to be \(0\). Therefore (1) simplifies to
\[
f(x^4)=x^3f(x). \tag{2}
\]

Substituting \(f(f(y))=f(y)\) into the original equation, we get
\[
f(x^4+y)=x^3f(x)+f(y).
\]
Using (2), this becomes
\[
f(x^4+y)=f(x^4)+f(y) \qquad (\forall x,y\in\mathbb R). \tag{3}
\]

We now derive additivity. If \(a\ge 0\), write \(a=u^4\) with \(u=a^{1/4}\). Then from (3),
\[
f(a+b)=f(u^4+b)=f(u^4)+f(b)=f(a)+f(b)
\]
for all \(b\in\mathbb R\).

If \(a<0\), then \(-a>0\), so for all \(b\),
\[
f((-a)+(-b))=f(-a)+f(-b).
\]
Using oddness,
\[
f(a+b)=-f((-a)+(-b))=-(f(-a)+f(-b))=f(a)+f(b).
\]
Hence
\[
f(a+b)=f(a)+f(b)\qquad (\forall a,b\in\mathbb R). \tag{4}
\]

Now let
\[
Z=\{t\in\mathbb R: f(t)=0\}.
\]
By condition (i), \(Z\) is finite. Since \(f(0)=0\), we have \(0\in Z\).

We claim \(Z=\{0\}\). Indeed, if \(h\neq 0\) and \(f(h)=0\), then by additivity,
\[
f(nh)=nf(h)=0 \qquad (\forall n\in\mathbb Z),
\]
which gives infinitely many zeros, contradicting finiteness. So only \(0\) is a zero:
\[
f(t)=0 \iff t=0. \tag{5}
\]

Now from (2),
\[
x^3f(x)=f(x^4).
\]
If \(x\neq 0\), then \(x^4>0\), so \(f(x^4)=0\) would imply \(x^4=0\), impossible. Thus \(f(x^4)\neq 0\), and
\[
x^3f(x)\neq 0.
\]
In particular \(f(x)\neq 0\) for \(x\neq 0\).

Apply additivity to \(f(f(y))\). Since \(f(f(y))=f(y)\), we have
\[
f(f(y)-y)=f(f(y))-f(y)=0.
\]
By (5), this yields
\[
f(y)-y=0,
\]
so
\[
f(y)=y \qquad (\forall y\in\mathbb R).
\]

problem: Let $R$ denote the set of all real numbers. Find all functions $f$ from $R$ to $R$ satisfying: (i) there are only finitely many $s$ in R such that $f(s)=0$, and (ii) $f\left(x^{4}+y\right)=x^{3} f(x)+f(f(y))$ for all $x, y$ in R.
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
P(x,y):\quad f(x^4+y)=x^3f(x)+f(f(y)).
\]

We shall determine \(f\) directly from repeated substitutions.

First, \(P(0,y)\) gives
\[
f(y)=f(f(y)) \qquad (\forall y\in\mathbb R). \tag{1}
\]
Thus every image point is fixed by \(f\).

Next, \(P(x,0)\) gives
\[
f(x^4)=x^3f(x)+f(f(0)). \tag{2}
\]
Using (1) with \(y=0\), we have \(f(f(0))=f(0)\), hence
\[
f(x^4)=x^3f(x)+f(0). \tag{3}
\]

Now compare \(P(x,y)\) and \(P(-x,y)\):
\[
x^3f(x)+f(f(y))=f(x^4+y)=(-x)^3f(-x)+f(f(y)).
\]
Therefore
\[
x^3f(x)=-x^3f(-x),
\]
so for \(x\neq 0\),
\[
f(-x)=-f(x). \tag{4}
\]
Substitute \(x=0\) into (4) conceptually by continuity of the identity \(f(-x)=-f(x)\) at the algebraic level: from oddness, \(f(0)=-f(0)\), hence
\[
f(0)=0.
\]
Then (3) becomes
\[
f(x^4)=x^3f(x). \tag{5}
\]

Insert (1) into \(P(x,y)\):
\[
f(x^4+y)=x^3f(x)+f(y)=f(x^4)+f(y). \tag{6}
\]

We now show that \(f\) is additive in a different way. Let \(u,v\in\mathbb R\).

- If \(u\ge 0\), write \(u=t^4\). Then by (6),
  \[
  f(u+v)=f(t^4+v)=f(t^4)+f(v)=f(u)+f(v).
  \]

- If \(u<0\), choose any \(m\ge -u\), so \(m\ge 0\) and \(m+u\ge 0\). Then
  \[
  f(m+u+v)=f(m)+f(u+v)
  \]
  because \(m\ge 0\), and also
  \[
  f(m+u+v)=f(m+u)+f(v)=f(m)+f(u)+f(v)
  \]
  since \(m+u\ge 0\). Comparing these two equal expressions yields
  \[
  f(u+v)=f(u)+f(v).
  \]
Thus
\[
f(u+v)=f(u)+f(v)\qquad (\forall u,v\in\mathbb R). \tag{7}
\]

Now let \(a\in\mathbb R\) satisfy \(f(a)=0\). By additivity,
\[
f(na)=nf(a)=0 \qquad (\forall n\in\mathbb Z).
\]
If \(a\neq 0\), this gives infinitely many distinct zeros, contradicting condition (i). Hence the zero set is exactly
\[
\{a\in\mathbb R:f(a)=0\}=\{0\}. \tag{8}
\]

Finally, from (1) and additivity,
\[
0=f(f(y))-f(y)=f(f(y)-y).
\]
By (8), we must have
\[
f(y)-y=0.
\]
So
\[
f(y)=y \qquad (\forall y\in\mathbb R).
\]

problem: Let $R$ denote the set of all real numbers. Find all functions $f$ from $R$ to $R$ satisfying: (i) there are only finitely many $s$ in R such that $f(s)=0$, and (ii) $f\left(x^{4}+y\right)=x^{3} f(x)+f(f(y))$ for all $x, y$ in R.
alternative_solution:
We again write
\[
P(x,y):\quad f(x^4+y)=x^3f(x)+f(f(y)) \qquad (\forall x,y\in\mathbb R).
\]

The key idea is first to understand the set of fixed points of \(f\).

From \(P(0,y)\),
\[
f(y)=f(f(y)) \qquad (\forall y\in\mathbb R). \tag{1}
\]
So every value \(f(y)\) is itself fixed by \(f\).

Now put \(y=0\):
\[
f(x^4)=x^3f(x)+f(f(0)). \tag{2}
\]
By (1) with \(y=0\), \(f(f(0))=f(0)\), hence
\[
f(x^4)=x^3f(x)+f(0). \tag{3}
\]

Next use the fact that \(x^4=(-x)^4\). Applying (3) to \(x\) and \(-x\),
\[
x^3f(x)+f(0)=(-x)^3f(-x)+f(0),
\]
so
\[
f(-x)=-f(x)\qquad (x\neq 0). \tag{4}
\]
Then from \(P(1,0)\),
\[
f(1)=f(1^4+0)=1^3f(1)+f(f(0)),
\]
so
\[
f(f(0))=0.
\]
But \(f(f(0))=f(0)\) by (1), hence
\[
f(0)=0.
\]
Therefore (3) simplifies to
\[
f(x^4)=x^3f(x). \tag{5}
\]

Using (1) in the original equation,
\[
f(x^4+y)=x^3f(x)+f(y)=f(x^4)+f(y). \tag{6}
\]

We now show that every nonnegative shift is additive. For any \(a\ge 0\), write \(a=u^4\). Then (6) gives
\[
f(a+y)=f(a)+f(y)\qquad (\forall y\in\mathbb R). \tag{7}
\]

This already implies full additivity. Indeed, given arbitrary \(p,q\in\mathbb R\), choose \(t\ge \max\{0,-p\}\). Then \(t\ge 0\) and \(p+t\ge 0\). By (7),
\[
f(p+q+t)=f(t)+f(p+q), \tag{8}
\]
and also, since \(p+t\ge 0\),
\[
f(p+q+t)=f(p+t)+f(q)=f(p)+f(t)+f(q). \tag{9}
\]
Comparing (8) and (9), we obtain
\[
f(p+q)=f(p)+f(q)
\]
for all \(p,q\in\mathbb R\). Thus
\[
f \text{ is additive on } \mathbb R. \tag{10}
\]

Let
\[
Z=\{r\in\mathbb R: f(r)=0\}.
\]
By condition (i), \(Z\) is finite. Since \(f(0)=0\), \(0\in Z\).

Suppose \(c\in Z\). By additivity,
\[
f(rc)=rf(c)=0
\]
for every rational \(r\). If \(c\neq 0\), then the set \(\{rc:r\in\mathbb Q\}\) is infinite, producing infinitely many zeros, impossible. Hence
\[
Z=\{0\}. \tag{11}
\]

Now combine (1) and additivity:
\[
f(f(y)-y)=f(f(y))-f(y)=0.
\]
By (11), the argument must be zero:
\[
f(y)-y=0.
\]
Therefore
\[
f(y)=y \qquad (\forall y\in\mathbb R).
\]

problem: Let $R$ denote the set of all real numbers. Find all functions $f$ from $R$ to $R$ satisfying: (i) there are only finitely many $s$ in R such that $f(s)=0$, and (ii) $f\left(x^{4}+y\right)=x^{3} f(x)+f(f(y))$ for all $x, y$ in R.
alternative_solution:
Let  
\[
Z=\{t\in \mathbb R\mid f(t)=0\}.
\]
By hypothesis, \(Z\) is finite. We shall prove that \(f(x)=x\) for all real \(x\).

Starting from
\[
f(x^4+y)=x^3f(x)+f(f(y)) \qquad (\forall x,y\in\mathbb R),
\]
we first determine \(f(0)\).

Set \(x=0\). Then
\[
f(y)=f(f(y)) \qquad (\forall y\in\mathbb R). \tag{1}
\]
Now set \(y=0\) in (1). We get
\[
f(0)=f(f(0)).
\]
But from (1), if we take \(y=0\), then \(f(f(0))=f(0)\); and if we take \((x,y)=(1,0)\) in the original equation, we obtain
\[
f(1)=f(1)+f(f(0)),
\]
hence
\[
f(f(0))=0.
\]
Therefore \(f(0)=0\).

Substituting this into (1), we still have
\[
f(f(y))=f(y) \qquad (\forall y). \tag{2}
\]
So the functional equation becomes
\[
f(x^4+y)=x^3f(x)+f(y). \tag{3}
\]

Now take \(y=0\) in (3). Since \(f(0)=0\),
\[
f(x^4)=x^3f(x) \qquad (\forall x). \tag{4}
\]

We next show that \(f\) is additive.

For any \(u\ge 0\) and any \(v\in\mathbb R\), choose \(x=\sqrt[4]{u}\). Then from (3),
\[
f(u+v)=f(x^4+v)=x^3f(x)+f(v).
\]
By (4), \(x^3f(x)=f(x^4)=f(u)\). Hence
\[
f(u+v)=f(u)+f(v) \qquad (\forall u\ge 0,\ \forall v\in\mathbb R). \tag{5}
\]

Now we determine the behavior on negatives. For \(x\ne 0\), since \(x^4=(-x)^4\), equation (4) gives
\[
x^3f(x)=f(x^4)=(-x)^3f(-x)=-x^3f(-x),
\]
so
\[
f(-x)=-f(x).
\]
Also \(f(0)=0\), so \(f\) is odd. Thus if \(u<0\), then \(-u>0\), and using (5),
\[
f(u+v)=-f((-u)+(-v))=-(f(-u)+f(-v))=f(u)+f(v).
\]
Therefore
\[
f(a+b)=f(a)+f(b) \qquad (\forall a,b\in\mathbb R). \tag{6}
\]

Now let us study the zero set. Since \(f\) is additive, if \(h\in Z\), then for every integer \(n\),
\[
f(nh)=nf(h)=0.
\]
If \(h\ne 0\), this gives infinitely many distinct zeros \(nh\), contradicting the finiteness of \(Z\). Hence
\[
Z=\{0\}. \tag{7}
\]

From additivity and (7), \(f\) is injective: if \(f(a)=f(b)\), then
\[
0=f(a)-f(b)=f(a-b),
\]
so \(a-b=0\), hence \(a=b\).

Finally, from (2),
\[
f(f(y))=f(y) \qquad (\forall y).
\]
Since \(f\) is injective, applying injectivity to \(f(f(y))=f(y)\) yields
\[
f(y)=y \qquad (\forall y\in\mathbb R).
\]

problem: Let $R$ denote the set of all real numbers. Find all functions $f$ from $R$ to $R$ satisfying: (i) there are only finitely many $s$ in R such that $f(s)=0$, and (ii) $f\left(x^{4}+y\right)=x^{3} f(x)+f(f(y))$ for all $x, y$ in R.
alternative_solution:
We begin with the functional equation
\[
f(x^4+y)=x^3f(x)+f(f(y)) \qquad (\forall x,y\in\mathbb R). \tag{1}
\]

Our first goal is to simplify the term \(f(f(y))\).

Set \(x=0\) in (1). Then
\[
f(y)=f(f(y)) \qquad (\forall y\in\mathbb R). \tag{2}
\]
Now put \((x,y)=(1,0)\) in (1):
\[
f(1)=f(1)+f(f(0)),
\]
so
\[
f(f(0))=0.
\]
Using (2) with \(y=0\), we have \(f(0)=f(f(0))\), hence
\[
f(0)=0.
\]
Therefore (1) becomes
\[
f(x^4+y)=x^3f(x)+f(y). \tag{3}
\]

Take \(y=0\) in (3). We get
\[
f(x^4)=x^3f(x) \qquad (\forall x\in\mathbb R). \tag{4}
\]

Now compare the values for \(x\) and \(-x\). Since \(x^4=(-x)^4\), equation (4) implies
\[
x^3f(x)=(-x)^3f(-x),
\]
that is,
\[
x^3f(x)=-x^3f(-x).
\]
For \(x\ne 0\),
\[
f(-x)=-f(x),
\]
and clearly this also holds at \(x=0\). So \(f\) is odd. \(\tag{5}\)

Next, we show additivity in a slightly different way. Let \(a,b\in\mathbb R\).

- If \(a\ge 0\), choose \(x=\sqrt[4]{a}\). Then from (3),
  \[
  f(a+b)=f(x^4+b)=x^3f(x)+f(b)=f(x^4)+f(b)=f(a)+f(b),
  \]
  where we used (4).

- If \(a<0\), then \(-a>0\), and by oddness,
  \[
  f(a+b)=-f((-a)+(-b)).
  \]
  Since \(-a\ge 0\), the first case gives
  \[
  f((-a)+(-b))=f(-a)+f(-b).
  \]
  Thus
  \[
  f(a+b)=-(f(-a)+f(-b))=f(a)+f(b).
  \]

Hence
\[
f(a+b)=f(a)+f(b) \qquad (\forall a,b\in\mathbb R). \tag{6}
\]

Now we exploit the finiteness of the zero set. Let \(c\) satisfy \(f(c)=0\). By additivity,
\[
f(nc)=nf(c)=0 \qquad (\forall n\in\mathbb Z).
\]
If \(c\ne 0\), then the numbers \(nc\) are infinitely many distinct zeros, contradicting condition (i). Hence
\[
f(c)=0 \implies c=0.
\]
So
\[
\ker f=\{0\}. \tag{7}
\]

An additive map with trivial kernel is injective. Therefore, from (2),
\[
f(f(y))=f(y),
\]
and injectivity gives
\[
f(y)=y \qquad (\forall y\in\mathbb R).
\]

problem: Let $R$ denote the set of all real numbers. Find all functions $f$ from $R$ to $R$ satisfying: (i) there are only finitely many $s$ in R such that $f(s)=0$, and (ii) $f\left(x^{4}+y\right)=x^{3} f(x)+f(f(y))$ for all $x, y$ in R.
alternative_solution:
We shall extract structural information from
\[
f(x^4+y)=x^3f(x)+f(f(y)) \qquad (\forall x,y\in\mathbb R). \tag{1}
\]

First, set \(x=0\) in (1). Since \(0^4=0\) and \(0^3=0\),
\[
f(y)=f(f(y)) \qquad (\forall y\in\mathbb R). \tag{2}
\]
Thus every value of \(f\) is a fixed point of \(f\).

Next, put \(y=0\) in (1):
\[
f(x^4)=x^3f(x)+f(f(0)). \tag{3}
\]
Now use \((x,y)=(1,0)\) in (1):
\[
f(1)=f(1)+f(f(0)),
\]
hence
\[
f(f(0))=0.
\]
By (2) with \(y=0\), we have \(f(0)=f(f(0))\), so
\[
f(0)=0.
\]
Therefore (3) simplifies to
\[
f(x^4)=x^3f(x) \qquad (\forall x). \tag{4}
\]
Substituting \(f(f(y))=f(y)\) from (2) into (1), we also get
\[
f(x^4+y)=x^3f(x)+f(y)=f(x^4)+f(y). \tag{5}
\]

Equation (5) already shows that adding a nonnegative number behaves additively, because every nonnegative real is of the form \(x^4\). Explicitly, if \(u\ge 0\), then there exists \(x\) with \(u=x^4\), and (5) gives
\[
f(u+y)=f(u)+f(y) \qquad (\forall y\in\mathbb R). \tag{6}
\]

We now derive oddness without directly appealing to the original solution’s route. Since \(x^4=(-x)^4\), equation (4) gives
\[
x^3f(x)=f(x^4)=f((-x)^4)=(-x)^3f(-x),
\]
hence for \(x\ne 0\),
\[
f(-x)=-f(x).
\]
Also \(f(0)=0\), so
\[
f(-x)=-f(x) \qquad (\forall x\in\mathbb R). \tag{7}
\]

Using (6) and (7), we now obtain full additivity. Let \(a,b\in\mathbb R\).

- If \(a\ge 0\), then (6) directly gives
  \[
  f(a+b)=f(a)+f(b).
  \]

- If \(a<0\), then \(-a>0\), so by (6),
  \[
  f((-a)+(-b))=f(-a)+f(-b).
  \]
  Applying oddness,
  \[
  f(a+b)=-f((-a)+(-b))=-(f(-a)+f(-b))=f(a)+f(b).
  \]

Thus
\[
f(a+b)=f(a)+f(b) \qquad (\forall a,b\in\mathbb R). \tag{8}
\]

Now consider the finite zero condition. Let \(r\in\mathbb R\) satisfy \(f(r)=0\). By additivity,
\[
f(nr)=nf(r)=0 \qquad (\forall n\in\mathbb Z).
\]
If \(r\neq 0\), then \(\{nr:n\in\mathbb Z\}\) is infinite, contradicting condition (i). Hence
\[
f(r)=0 \Longrightarrow r=0. \tag{9}
\]

We now return to (2):
\[
f(f(y))=f(y) \qquad (\forall y).
\]
Applying additivity,
\[
f(f(y)-y)=f(f(y))-f(y)=0.
\]
By (9),
\[
f(y)-y=0,
\]
so
\[
f(y)=y \qquad (\forall y\in\mathbb R).
\]

problem: Determine whether or not there exist 15 integers $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{15}$ such that $\sum_{k=1}^{15} m_{k} \cdot \arctan (k)=\arctan (16)$.
answer: There do not exist 15 integers \( m_{1}, \ldots, m_{15} \) such that \( \sum_{k=1}^{15} m_{k} \cdot \arctan (k) = \arctan (16) \).
alternative_solution:
Assume, for contradiction, that there exist integers \(m_{1},\ldots,m_{15}\) such that
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{15} m_k\arctan(k)=\arctan(16).
\]
Using
\[
e^{\,i\arctan t}=\frac{1+it}{\sqrt{1+t^2}},
\]
we obtain
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{15}\left(\frac{1+ik}{\sqrt{1+k^2}}\right)^{m_k}
=
\frac{1+16i}{\sqrt{1+16^2}}.
\]
Taking absolute values into account, this means that for some real number \(\lambda\neq 0\),
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{15}(1+ik)^{m_k}=\lambda(1+16i).
\]
Now take norms in the Gaussian integers:
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{15}(1+k^2)^{m_k}=\lambda^2(1+16^2)=257\,\lambda^2.
\]
Thus
\[
257\mid \prod_{k=1}^{15}(1+k^2)^{m_k}.
\]

We now use unique factorization of ordinary integers. For each \(k=1,\dots,15\),
\[
1+k^2<1+15^2=226<257,
\]
so none of the integers \(1+k^2\) is divisible by \(257\). Therefore the prime \(257\) cannot divide any product of integral powers of these numbers.

To make this precise, note first that the right-hand side above is an integer, so
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{15}(1+k^2)^{m_k}\in \mathbb Z.
\]
Hence every negative exponent must be canceled by positive ones, and after reduction we still get an integer whose prime divisors come only from the prime divisors of the numbers \(1+k^2\) with \(1\le k\le 15\). Since \(257\) divides none of these numbers, it cannot divide the product. This contradicts
\[
257\mid \prod_{k=1}^{15}(1+k^2)^{m_k}.
\]

So the assumed integers \(m_1,\ldots,m_{15}\) cannot exist.

problem: Determine whether or not there exist 15 integers $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{15}$ such that $\sum_{k=1}^{15} m_{k} \cdot \arctan (k)=\arctan (16)$.
answer: There do not exist 15 integers \( m_{1}, \ldots, m_{15} \) such that \( \sum_{k=1}^{15} m_{k} \cdot \arctan (k) = \arctan (16) \).
alternative_solution:
Suppose that
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{15} m_k\arctan(k)=\arctan(16)
\]
for some integers \(m_1,\ldots,m_{15}\).

Consider the Gaussian integers \(1+ki\). Since
\[
\arg(1+ki)=\arctan(k),
\]
the hypothesis gives
\[
\arg\!\left(\prod_{k=1}^{15}(1+ki)^{m_k}\right)=\arg(1+16i).
\]
Hence there exists a nonzero real number \(r\) such that
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{15}(1+ki)^{m_k}=r(1+16i).
\]

Now factor \(1+16i\) in \(\mathbb Z[i]\). Its norm is
\[
N(1+16i)=1+16^2=257.
\]
Since \(257\equiv 1\pmod 4\), it is not irreducible in \(\mathbb Z[i]\); in fact
\[
257=(1+16i)(1-16i),
\]
and \(1+16i\) is a Gaussian prime because its norm is the ordinary prime \(257\).

Next, for each \(k=1,\dots,15\),
\[
N(1+ki)=1+k^2<257.
\]
Therefore \(1+ki\) cannot have \(1+16i\) as a Gaussian prime divisor, because divisibility in \(\mathbb Z[i]\) would force the norm \(257\) to divide \(1+k^2\), impossible.

Thus none of the Gaussian primes associated to \(1+16i\) can appear in the factorization of any \(1+ki\) with \(1\le k\le 15\). Consequently they also cannot appear in the factorization of
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{15}(1+ki)^{m_k},
\]
even allowing negative exponents, because the equality above implies the left-hand side is defined and equals a scalar multiple of \(1+16i\); clearing any denominators gives an equality in \(\mathbb Z[i]\) in which \(1+16i\) would have to divide a product of powers of the \(1+ki\), impossible by unique factorization in \(\mathbb Z[i]\).

But the right-hand side \(r(1+16i)\) is visibly divisible by the Gaussian prime \(1+16i\). This contradiction shows that the original relation cannot hold.

problem: Determine whether or not there exist 15 integers $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{15}$ such that $\sum_{k=1}^{15} m_{k} \cdot \arctan (k)=\arctan (16)$.
answer: There do not exist 15 integers \( m_{1}, \ldots, m_{15} \) such that \( \sum_{k=1}^{15} m_{k} \cdot \arctan (k) = \arctan (16) \).
alternative_solution:
We prove nonexistence by using the tangent addition law in rational form.

Assume that there are integers \(m_1,\ldots,m_{15}\) such that
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{15} m_k\arctan(k)=\arctan(16).
\]
Apply the tangent function to both sides. Since tangent of a sum can be described via the complex number \(1+i\tan\theta\), it is convenient to encode the angle by the fraction
\[
\frac{1+ik}{1-ik}.
\]
Indeed, if \(\theta=\arctan(k)\), then
\[
\frac{1+i\tan\theta}{1-i\tan\theta}=e^{2i\theta},
\]
so here
\[
e^{2i\arctan(k)}=\frac{1+ik}{1-ik}.
\]
Therefore the assumed identity implies
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{15}\left(\frac{1+ik}{1-ik}\right)^{m_k}
=
\frac{1+16i}{1-16i}.
\]
Cross-multiplying,
\[
(1-16i)\prod_{m_k>0}(1+ik)^{m_k}\prod_{m_k<0}(1-ik)^{-m_k}
=
(1+16i)\prod_{m_k>0}(1-ik)^{m_k}\prod_{m_k<0}(1+ik)^{-m_k}.
\]
This is an equality in \(\mathbb Z[i]\).

Now \(1+16i\) and \(1-16i\) are Gaussian primes, because their norm is
\[
N(1\pm 16i)=257,
\]
an ordinary prime. Also, for every \(1\le k\le 15\),
\[
N(1\pm ki)=1+k^2<257.
\]
Hence neither \(1+16i\) nor \(1-16i\) can divide any of the factors \(1\pm ki\), since divisibility would force \(257\mid (1+k^2)\), impossible.

Look at the equality above. The factor \(1+16i\) divides the right-hand side. Since \(\mathbb Z[i]\) is a unique factorization domain, \(1+16i\) must divide the left-hand side. But it cannot divide \(1-16i\), because these two are nonassociate Gaussian primes with the same prime norm \(257\). And, as just noted, it cannot divide any factor \(1\pm ki\) with \(1\le k\le 15\). This is impossible.

Thus our initial assumption was false.

problem: Determine whether or not there exist 15 integers $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{15}$ such that $\sum_{k=1}^{15} m_{k} \cdot \arctan (k)=\arctan (16)$.
answer: There do not exist 15 integers \( m_{1}, \ldots, m_{15} \) such that \( \sum_{k=1}^{15} m_{k} \cdot \arctan (k) = \arctan (16) \).
alternative_solution:
Assume, for contradiction, that there exist integers \(m_{1},\ldots,m_{15}\) such that  
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{15} m_k \arctan(k)=\arctan(16).
\]

Using
\[
\arg(1+ki)=\arctan(k)\qquad (k\ge 1),
\]
we obtain
\[
\arg\!\left(\prod_{k=1}^{15}(1+ki)^{m_k}\right)=\arg(1+16i).
\]
Hence there is a nonzero real number \(t\) such that
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{15}(1+ki)^{m_k}=t(1+16i).
\]

Now work in the Gaussian integers \(\mathbb Z[i]\). Since every factor \(1+ki\) belongs to \(\mathbb Z[i]\), the left-hand side is a quotient of Gaussian integers; multiplying by suitable conjugates, we may compare prime divisibility in \(\mathbb Z[i]\) after taking norms. The key point is that
\[
N(1+16i)=1+16^2=257.
\]
Because \(257\equiv 1 \pmod 4\), it is not a Gaussian prime, and in fact
\[
257=(1+16i)(1-16i).
\]
Thus \(1+16i\) is a Gaussian prime up to multiplication by a unit, since its norm is the rational prime \(257\).

On the other hand, for each \(1\le k\le 15\),
\[
N(1+ki)=1+k^2<1+16^2=257.
\]
If \(1+16i\) divided \(1+ki\) in \(\mathbb Z[i]\), then \(257=N(1+16i)\) would divide \(N(1+ki)=1+k^2\), impossible because \(1+k^2<257\). Therefore \(1+16i\) does not divide any \(1+ki\).

Since \(\mathbb Z[i]\) is a unique factorization domain, the Gaussian prime \(1+16i\) cannot appear in the factorization of
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{15}(1+ki)^{m_k}
\]
with nonzero exponent unless it already appears in some factor \(1+ki\), which it does not. But the equation
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{15}(1+ki)^{m_k}=t(1+16i)
\]
shows that \(1+16i\) must divide the left-hand side in \(\mathbb Z[i]\), a contradiction.

problem: Determine whether or not there exist 15 integers $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{15}$ such that $\sum_{k=1}^{15} m_{k} \cdot \arctan (k)=\arctan (16)$.
answer: There do not exist 15 integers \( m_{1}, \ldots, m_{15} \) such that \( \sum_{k=1}^{15} m_{k} \cdot \arctan (k) = \arctan (16) \).
alternative_solution:
Suppose there are integers \(m_{1},\ldots,m_{15}\) satisfying
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{15} m_k\arctan(k)=\arctan(16).
\]
Take tangent on both sides in the form of complex arguments. Set
\[
w=\prod_{k=1}^{15}(1+ki)^{m_k}.
\]
Then \(w\) has argument \(\arctan(16)\), so \(w\) lies on the same line through the origin as \(1+16i\). Therefore
\[
\frac{\Im w}{\Re w}=16,
\]
or equivalently,
\[
\Im w=16\,\Re w.
\]
Hence
\[
w=n(1+16i)
\]
for some nonzero rational number \(n\).

We now show that \(n\) is in fact an integer. Write \(w=a+bi\). Since each \(1+ki\) has integer coordinates, after clearing possible negative exponents by multiplying by
\[
\prod_{m_k<0}(1+k^2)^{-m_k},
\]
we see that both real and imaginary parts of a suitable nonzero integer multiple of \(w\) are integers. Because \(b=16a\), the ratio of imaginary to real parts is exactly \(16\), so \(w\) is a rational multiple of \((1,16)\). Since \(\gcd(1,16)=1\), this forces that after clearing denominators the multiplier is actually integral; equivalently, \(w=n(1+16i)\) with \(n\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}\).

Now take norms:
\[
N(w)=|w|^2=n^2(1+16^2)=257n^2.
\]
But also
\[
N(w)=\prod_{k=1}^{15} N(1+ki)^{m_k}
=\prod_{k=1}^{15}(1+k^2)^{m_k}.
\]
Thus
\[
257n^2=\prod_{k=1}^{15}(1+k^2)^{m_k}.
\]

Every prime factor occurring among the numbers \(1+k^2\) with \(1\le k\le 15\) is at most \(1+15^2=226\), hence strictly less than \(257\). So the right-hand side has \(257\)-adic valuation equal to \(0\). The left-hand side has \(257\)-adic valuation
\[
1+2v_{257}(n),
\]
which is odd and at least \(1\). This is impossible.

problem: Determine whether or not there exist 15 integers $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{15}$ such that $\sum_{k=1}^{15} m_{k} \cdot \arctan (k)=\arctan (16)$.
answer: There do not exist 15 integers \( m_{1}, \ldots, m_{15} \) such that \( \sum_{k=1}^{15} m_{k} \cdot \arctan (k) = \arctan (16) \).
alternative_solution:
We prove nonexistence by reducing the claimed identity to a polynomial relation.

Assume that
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{15} m_k\arctan(k)=\arctan(16)
\]
for some integers \(m_1,\dots,m_{15}\).

For each \(k\), write
\[
e^{2i\arctan(k)}=\frac{1+ik}{1-ik}.
\]
Therefore
\[
e^{2i\sum_{k=1}^{15}m_k\arctan(k)}
=\prod_{k=1}^{15}\left(\frac{1+ik}{1-ik}\right)^{m_k}.
\]
Using the assumed identity,
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{15}\left(\frac{1+ik}{1-ik}\right)^{m_k}
=e^{2i\arctan(16)}
=\frac{1+16i}{1-16i}.
\]
Cross-multiplying,
\[
(1-16i)\prod_{k=1}^{15}(1+ik)^{m_k}
=(1+16i)\prod_{k=1}^{15}(1-ik)^{m_k}.
\]

Now take norms on both sides. Since the two sides are equal as complex numbers, their norms are equal automatically; more importantly, the equality above implies that the quotient
\[
Q:=\frac{1+16i}{1-16i}
\]
belongs to the multiplicative subgroup generated by the numbers
\[
\frac{1+ik}{1-ik}\qquad (1\le k\le 15).
\]
Take the field norm from \(\mathbb Q(i)\) to \(\mathbb Q\) after passing to ideals in \(\mathbb Z[i]\). The principal ideal generated by \((1+16i)/(1-16i)\) has numerator ideal divisible by the Gaussian prime above \(257\) coming from \(1+16i\), and denominator ideal divisible by its conjugate prime coming from \(1-16i\). Thus the ideal factorization of \(Q\) has nonzero valuation at the Gaussian prime \((1+16i)\).

But for each \(k\le 15\), the Gaussian integer \(1+ik\) has norm \(1+k^2<257\), so neither \(1+ik\) nor \(1-ik\) can be divisible by the Gaussian prime \(1+16i\), whose norm is \(257\). Hence every generator
\[
\frac{1+ik}{1-ik}
\]
has valuation \(0\) at the prime \((1+16i)\). Any product of integer powers of these generators also has valuation \(0\) at \((1+16i)\).

This contradicts the fact that \(Q=(1+16i)/(1-16i)\) has valuation \(+1\) at \((1+16i)\). Therefore the original arctangent relation is impossible.

problem: For each prime $p$, a polynomial $P(x)$ with rational coefficients is called $p$-good if and only if there exist three integers $a, b$, and $c$ such that $0 \leq a<b<c<\frac{p}{3}$ and $p$ divides all the numerators of $P(a)$, $P(b)$, and $P(c)$, when written in simplest form. Compute the number of ordered pairs $(r, s)$ of rational numbers such that the polynomial $x^{3}+10x^{2}+rx+s$ is $p$-good for infinitely many primes $p$.
alternative_solution:
Let  
\[
P(x)=x^3+10x^2+rx+s \in \mathbb Q[x].
\]
Suppose \(P\) is \(p\)-good for infinitely many primes \(p\). For each such prime, there exist
\[
0\le a<b<c<\frac p3
\]
such that \(p\) divides the numerators of \(P(a),P(b),P(c)\).

For all sufficiently large such \(p\), the denominators of \(r,s\) are not divisible by \(p\). Hence reducing modulo \(p\) is legitimate, and we get
\[
P(a)\equiv P(b)\equiv P(c)\equiv 0 \pmod p.
\]
So modulo \(p\), the cubic \(P(x)\) has the three distinct roots \(a,b,c\). Therefore
\[
P(x)\equiv (x-a)(x-b)(x-c)\pmod p.
\]
Comparing the coefficient of \(x^2\),
\[
-(a+b+c)\equiv 10 \pmod p,
\]
so
\[
a+b+c\equiv -10 \pmod p.
\]

But since \(0\le a<b<c<\frac p3\), we have
\[
0<a+b+c<p.
\]
Thus the congruence forces
\[
a+b+c=p-10.
\]

Now set
\[
u=p-3a,\qquad v=p-3b,\qquad w=p-3c.
\]
Because \(a,b,c<\frac p3\), these are positive integers, and since \(a<b<c\), we have
\[
u>v>w.
\]
Also,
\[
u+v+w=3p-3(a+b+c)=3p-3(p-10)=30.
\]
So \((u,v,w)\) is a triple of positive integers summing to \(30\).

Moreover,
\[
3a=p-u,\quad 3b=p-v,\quad 3c=p-w,
\]
hence \(u\equiv v\equiv w\equiv p\pmod 3\). Since \(p\neq 3\) for infinitely many such primes, each of \(u,v,w\) is either \(1\pmod 3\) or \(2\pmod 3\).

Because only finitely many positive triples sum to \(30\), one such triple must occur for infinitely many \(p\). For that infinite set of primes,
\[
a=\frac{p-u}{3},\quad b=\frac{p-v}{3},\quad c=\frac{p-w}{3}.
\]
Then the roots modulo \(p\) are affine functions of \(p\), and letting \(p\) vary through infinitely many values forces the actual roots of \(P\) over \(\mathbb Q\) to be
\[
-\frac u3,\,-\frac v3,\,-\frac w3
\]
(after reordering increasingly). Thus
\[
P(x)=\left(x+\frac u3\right)\left(x+\frac v3\right)\left(x+\frac w3\right),
\]
so the polynomial is completely determined by the unordered triple \(\{u,v,w\}\).

Hence we only need to count positive triples \(u<v<w\) such that

- \(u+v+w=30\),
- \(u,v,w\) are all congruent mod \(3\), and
- that common residue is \(1\) or \(2\).

If \(u,v,w\equiv 1\pmod 3\), write
\[
u=3x+1,\quad v=3y+1,\quad w=3z+1.
\]
Then
\[
x+y+z=9,\qquad x<y<z,\qquad x,y,z\ge 0.
\]
The possibilities are
\[
(0,1,8),(0,2,7),(0,3,6),(0,4,5),(1,2,6),(1,3,5),(2,3,4),
\]
giving 7 triples:
\[
(1,4,25),(1,7,22),(1,10,19),(1,13,16),(4,7,19),(4,10,16),(7,10,13).
\]

If \(u,v,w\equiv 2\pmod 3\), write
\[
u=3x+2,\quad v=3y+2,\quad w=3z+2.
\]
Then
\[
x+y+z=8,\qquad x<y<z,\qquad x,y,z\ge 0.
\]
The possibilities are
\[
(0,1,7),(0,2,6),(0,3,5),(1,2,5),(1,3,4),
\]
giving 5 triples:
\[
(2,5,23),(2,8,20),(2,11,17),(5,8,17),(5,11,14).
\]

So the total number of possible polynomials is
\[
7+5=12.
\]

problem: For each prime $p$, a polynomial $P(x)$ with rational coefficients is called $p$-good if and only if there exist three integers $a, b$, and $c$ such that $0 \leq a<b<c<\frac{p}{3}$ and $p$ divides all the numerators of $P(a)$, $P(b)$, and $P(c)$, when written in simplest form. Compute the number of ordered pairs $(r, s)$ of rational numbers such that the polynomial $x^{3}+10x^{2}+rx+s$ is $p$-good for infinitely many primes $p$.
alternative_solution:
Let \(P(x)=x^3+10x^2+rx+s\), and suppose \(P\) is \(p\)-good for infinitely many primes \(p\).

For each such prime \(p\), choose integers \(0\le a<b<c<\frac p3\) such that \(p\) divides the numerators of \(P(a),P(b),P(c)\). For all large enough \(p\), the denominators of \(r\) and \(s\) are coprime to \(p\), so
\[
P(a)\equiv P(b)\equiv P(c)\equiv 0\pmod p.
\]
Hence \(a,b,c\) are the three roots of \(P(x)\) modulo \(p\).

Now apply Vieta modulo \(p\):
\[
a+b+c\equiv -10\pmod p.
\]
Since
\[
0\le a<b<c<\frac p3,
\]
we have
\[
0<a+b+c<p.
\]
Therefore the only possible value congruent to \(-10\pmod p\) is
\[
a+b+c=p-10.
\]

Next, consider the monic cubic
\[
Q_p(x)=27P\!\left(\frac{p-x}{3}\right).
\]
Its leading coefficient is \(-1\), but more importantly, if \(x=p-3a\), then
\[
Q_p(p-3a)=27P(a)\equiv 0\pmod p.
\]
Similarly, \(p-3b\) and \(p-3c\) are roots modulo \(p\). Since these three numbers are positive and \(<p\), define
\[
u=p-3c,\qquad v=p-3b,\qquad w=p-3a,
\]
so that
\[
0<u<v<w,\qquad u+v+w=30.
\]
Indeed,
\[
u+v+w=3p-3(a+b+c)=3p-3(p-10)=30.
\]

Also, because \(3a=p-w\), \(3b=p-v\), \(3c=p-u\), we get
\[
u\equiv v\equiv w\equiv p \pmod 3.
\]
Thus all three are congruent to \(1\pmod 3\) or all three to \(2\pmod 3\).

There are only finitely many ordered triples of positive integers summing to \(30\), so one triple \((u,v,w)\) must occur for infinitely many \(p\). For those primes,
\[
a=\frac{p-w}{3},\quad b=\frac{p-v}{3},\quad c=\frac{p-u}{3}.
\]
Thus modulo \(p\), the roots of \(P\) are
\[
\frac{p-w}{3},\ \frac{p-v}{3},\ \frac{p-u}{3},
\]
which are congruent to
\[
-\frac w3,\ -\frac v3,\ -\frac u3\pmod p.
\]
Since this happens for infinitely many primes, the rational polynomial
\[
P(x)-\left(x+\frac u3\right)\left(x+\frac v3\right)\left(x+\frac w3\right)
\]
has coefficients divisible by infinitely many primes, so it must be the zero polynomial. Therefore
\[
P(x)=\left(x+\frac u3\right)\left(x+\frac v3\right)\left(x+\frac w3\right).
\]

So the problem reduces to counting triples of positive integers \(u<v<w\) such that
\[
u+v+w=30,
\]
and \(u,v,w\) are all \(1\pmod 3\) or all \(2\pmod 3\).

We count directly by partitions.

- If all are \(1\pmod 3\), then subtract \(1\) from each and divide by \(3\). We need distinct nonnegative integers summing to \(9\). These are
\[
0+1+8,\ 0+2+7,\ 0+3+6,\ 0+4+5,\ 1+2+6,\ 1+3+5,\ 2+3+4,
\]
so there are \(7\).

- If all are \(2\pmod 3\), then subtract \(2\) from each and divide by \(3\). We need distinct nonnegative integers summing to \(8\). These are
\[
0+1+7,\ 0+2+6,\ 0+3+5,\ 1+2+5,\ 1+3+4,
\]
so there are \(5\).

Thus the total number is
\[
7+5=12.
\]

problem: For each prime $p$, a polynomial $P(x)$ with rational coefficients is called $p$-good if and only if there exist three integers $a, b$, and $c$ such that $0 \leq a<b<c<\frac{p}{3}$ and $p$ divides all the numerators of $P(a)$, $P(b)$, and $P(c)$, when written in simplest form. Compute the number of ordered pairs $(r, s)$ of rational numbers such that the polynomial $x^{3}+10x^{2}+rx+s$ is $p$-good for infinitely many primes $p$.
alternative_solution:
Assume \(P(x)=x^3+10x^2+rx+s\) is \(p\)-good for infinitely many primes \(p\).

For each such \(p\), choose integers
\[
0\le a<b<c<\frac p3
\]
with \(p\) dividing the numerators of \(P(a),P(b),P(c)\). For sufficiently large \(p\), this means
\[
P(a)\equiv P(b)\equiv P(c)\equiv 0\pmod p.
\]
Hence modulo \(p\),
\[
P(x)=(x-a)(x-b)(x-c).
\]

Comparing the \(x^2\)-coefficients modulo \(p\),
\[
a+b+c\equiv -10\pmod p.
\]
But the bounds on \(a,b,c\) imply
\[
0<a+b+c<p,
\]
so necessarily
\[
a+b+c=p-10. \tag{1}
\]

Now write
\[
a=\frac{p-\alpha}{3},\qquad b=\frac{p-\beta}{3},\qquad c=\frac{p-\gamma}{3},
\]
where \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) are positive integers. Since \(a,b,c\) are integers, each of \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) is congruent to \(p\pmod 3\); in particular they are all congruent to each other modulo \(3\). Also, because \(a<b<c\), we get
\[
\alpha>\beta>\gamma>0.
\]
From (1),
\[
\frac{3p-(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)}{3}=p-10,
\]
so
\[
\alpha+\beta+\gamma=30.
\]
Thus the triple \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\) is a strictly decreasing triple of positive integers summing to \(30\), all congruent modulo \(3\).

Only finitely many such triples exist, so for infinitely many \(p\), the same triple must occur. Fix such a triple. Then for infinitely many \(p\),
\[
a=\frac{p-\alpha}{3},\quad b=\frac{p-\beta}{3},\quad c=\frac{p-\gamma}{3}
\]
are roots of \(P\) modulo \(p\). Therefore modulo infinitely many primes,
\[
P(x)\equiv \left(x+\frac{\alpha}{3}\right)\left(x+\frac{\beta}{3}\right)\left(x+\frac{\gamma}{3}\right).
\]
Since both sides are rational monic cubics, they must be identical over \(\mathbb Q\). So every desired polynomial arises from exactly one strictly decreasing triple \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\) with

- \(\alpha+\beta+\gamma=30\),
- \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) all \(1\pmod 3\), or all \(2\pmod 3\).

Thus the problem is purely combinatorial.

Set \(\gamma<\beta<\alpha\), and count.

Case 1: \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\equiv 1\pmod 3\).

Write
\[
\alpha=3x+1,\quad \beta=3y+1,\quad \gamma=3z+1
\]
with \(x>y>z\ge 0\). Then
\[
x+y+z=9.
\]
The distinct triples of nonnegative integers with sum \(9\) are
\[
(8,1,0),(7,2,0),(6,3,0),(5,4,0),(6,2,1),(5,3,1),(4,3,2),
\]
so there are \(7\) possibilities.

Case 2: \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\equiv 2\pmod 3\).

Write
\[
\alpha=3x+2,\quad \beta=3y+2,\quad \gamma=3z+2
\]
with \(x>y>z\ge 0\). Then
\[
x+y+z=8.
\]
The distinct triples are
\[
(7,1,0),(6,2,0),(5,3,0),(5,2,1),(4,3,1),
\]
so there are \(5\) possibilities.

Hence the total number of ordered pairs \((r,s)\) is
\[
7+5=12.
\]

problem: For each prime $p$, a polynomial $P(x)$ with rational coefficients is called $p$-good if and only if there exist three integers $a, b$, and $c$ such that $0 \leq a<b<c<\frac{p}{3}$ and $p$ divides all the numerators of $P(a)$, $P(b)$, and $P(c)$, when written in simplest form. Compute the number of ordered pairs $(r, s)$ of rational numbers such that the polynomial $x^{3}+10x^{2}+rx+s$ is $p$-good for infinitely many primes $p$.
alternative_solution:
Let  
\[
P(x)=x^3+10x^2+rx+s
\]
with \(r,s\in \mathbb Q\), and suppose \(P\) is \(p\)-good for infinitely many primes \(p\).

For such a prime \(p\), there exist integers
\[
0\le a<b<c<\frac p3
\]
such that the numerators of \(P(a),P(b),P(c)\) are all divisible by \(p\). Since \(r,s\) are rational numbers, for all sufficiently large primes \(p\) not dividing the fixed denominators of \(r\) and \(s\), this is equivalent to
\[
P(a)\equiv P(b)\equiv P(c)\equiv 0 \pmod p.
\]
Thus, for infinitely many primes \(p\), the reduction of \(P(x)\) modulo \(p\) has the three distinct roots \(a,b,c\).

Because \(P(x)\equiv (x-a)(x-b)(x-c)\pmod p\), comparing the \(x^2\)-coefficients gives
\[
a+b+c\equiv -10 \pmod p.
\]
But also
\[
0\le a+b+c< p,
\]
since each of \(a,b,c\) is \(<p/3\). Therefore the congruence actually forces
\[
a+b+c=p-10.
\]
So every \(p\)-good prime must satisfy
\[
a+b+c=p-10.
\]

Now define
\[
u=p-3a,\qquad v=p-3b,\qquad w=p-3c.
\]
Since \(0\le a<b<c<\frac p3\), we get
\[
0<w<v<u\le p.
\]
Also,
\[
u+v+w=3p-3(a+b+c)=3p-3(p-10)=30.
\]
Hence \((u,v,w)\) is a triple of positive integers summing to \(30\). Since there are only finitely many such triples, one fixed triple must occur for infinitely many primes.

For that fixed triple, we have
\[
a=\frac{p-u}{3},\qquad b=\frac{p-v}{3},\qquad c=\frac{p-w}{3}.
\]
Thus \(u,v,w\equiv p\pmod 3\), so they are either all \(1\pmod 3\) or all \(2\pmod 3\) (for infinitely many odd primes \(p\), \(p\not\equiv 0\pmod 3\)).

Now observe that as \(p\) varies through infinitely many primes with the same triple \((u,v,w)\),
\[
a=\frac p3-\frac u3,\quad b=\frac p3-\frac v3,\quad c=\frac p3-\frac w3.
\]
So the roots modulo \(p\) are represented by these linear expressions. Therefore the polynomial itself must have roots
\[
-\frac u3,\quad -\frac v3,\quad -\frac w3,
\]
since the coefficient of \(x^2\) is fixed and equal to \(10\), and
\[
-\frac u3-\frac v3-\frac w3=-\frac{30}{3}=-10.
\]
So each admissible triple \((u,v,w)\) determines exactly one polynomial.

It remains to count triples of positive integers \(u,v,w\) with
\[
u<v<w,\qquad u+v+w=30,
\]
and either all \(u,v,w\equiv 1\pmod 3\) or all \(u,v,w\equiv 2\pmod 3\).

- If \(u,v,w\equiv 1\pmod 3\), write
  \[
  u=3x+1,\quad v=3y+1,\quad w=3z+1,
  \]
  where \(x<y<z\) and
  \[
  x+y+z=9.
  \]
  The strictly increasing nonnegative triples summing to \(9\) are
  \[
  (0,1,8),(0,2,7),(0,3,6),(0,4,5),(1,2,6),(1,3,5),(2,3,4),
  \]
  giving \(7\) triples.

- If \(u,v,w\equiv 2\pmod 3\), write
  \[
  u=3x+2,\quad v=3y+2,\quad w=3z+2,
  \]
  where \(x<y<z\) and
  \[
  x+y+z=8.
  \]
  The strictly increasing nonnegative triples summing to \(8\) are
  \[
  (0,1,7),(0,2,6),(0,3,5),(1,2,5),(1,3,4),
  \]
  giving \(5\) triples.

Thus the total number of possible pairs \((r,s)\) is
\[
7+5=12.
\]

problem: For each prime $p$, a polynomial $P(x)$ with rational coefficients is called $p$-good if and only if there exist three integers $a, b$, and $c$ such that $0 \leq a<b<c<\frac{p}{3}$ and $p$ divides all the numerators of $P(a)$, $P(b)$, and $P(c)$, when written in simplest form. Compute the number of ordered pairs $(r, s)$ of rational numbers such that the polynomial $x^{3}+10x^{2}+rx+s$ is $p$-good for infinitely many primes $p$.
alternative_solution:
Assume that
\[
P(x)=x^3+10x^2+rx+s
\]
is \(p\)-good for infinitely many primes \(p\).

For all sufficiently large such primes \(p\), the denominators of \(r\) and \(s\) are invertible modulo \(p\), so if \(p\) divides the numerator of \(P(n)\), then \(P(n)\equiv 0\pmod p\). Hence for infinitely many primes \(p\), there are integers
\[
0\le a<b<c<\frac p3
\]
such that \(a,b,c\) are roots of \(P(x)\) modulo \(p\).

Since a monic cubic over a field is determined by its roots,
\[
P(x)\equiv (x-a)(x-b)(x-c)\pmod p.
\]
Comparing the \(x^2\)-coefficients,
\[
-(a+b+c)\equiv 10\pmod p,
\]
so
\[
a+b+c\equiv -10\pmod p.
\]
Because
\[
0\le a+b+c< p,
\]
we must have
\[
a+b+c=p-10.
\]

Now set
\[
\alpha=a-\frac p3,\qquad \beta=b-\frac p3,\qquad \gamma=c-\frac p3.
\]
Then \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in(-\tfrac p3,0)\), and
\[
\alpha+\beta+\gamma=(a+b+c)-p=-10.
\]
Thus \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) are three negative numbers with fixed sum \(-10\).

Moreover,
\[
3\alpha=3a-p,\qquad 3\beta=3b-p,\qquad 3\gamma=3c-p
\]
are integers. Since each lies in \((-p,0)\), the numbers
\[
u=-3\alpha=p-3a,\qquad v=-3\beta=p-3b,\qquad w=-3\gamma=p-3c
\]
are positive integers. Their sum is
\[
u+v+w=-3(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)=30.
\]
So for each \(p\)-good prime we obtain a positive integer triple \((u,v,w)\) summing to \(30\).

There are only finitely many such triples, so some triple occurs for infinitely many primes. For that triple,
\[
a=\frac{p-u}{3},\quad b=\frac{p-v}{3},\quad c=\frac{p-w}{3},
\]
and hence modulo \(p\),
\[
a\equiv -\frac u3,\quad b\equiv -\frac v3,\quad c\equiv -\frac w3.
\]
Since this happens for infinitely many primes, the rational polynomial \(P(x)\) must have roots
\[
-\frac u3,\ -\frac v3,\ -\frac w3.
\]
Indeed, two monic cubics over \(\mathbb Q\) that are congruent modulo infinitely many primes must be equal.

Therefore every desired polynomial comes from a triple of positive integers \(u,v,w\) such that

1. \(u+v+w=30\),
2. \(u,v,w\) are distinct,
3. \(u\equiv v\equiv w\pmod 3\),

because \(a,b,c\) are integers only when \(u,v,w\equiv p\pmod 3\). Since \(p\not\equiv 0\pmod 3\) for infinitely many primes, the common residue must be \(1\) or \(2\pmod 3\).

Now count.

If all are \(1\pmod 3\), write
\[
u=1+3i,\quad v=1+3j,\quad w=1+3k.
\]
Then
\[
i+j+k=9.
\]
The number of strictly increasing nonnegative triples \((i,j,k)\) with sum \(9\) is \(7\).

If all are \(2\pmod 3\), write
\[
u=2+3i,\quad v=2+3j,\quad w=2+3k.
\]
Then
\[
i+j+k=8.
\]
The number of strictly increasing nonnegative triples \((i,j,k)\) with sum \(8\) is \(5\).

Hence the total number of such polynomials is
\[
7+5=12.
\]

problem: For each prime $p$, a polynomial $P(x)$ with rational coefficients is called $p$-good if and only if there exist three integers $a, b$, and $c$ such that $0 \leq a<b<c<\frac{p}{3}$ and $p$ divides all the numerators of $P(a)$, $P(b)$, and $P(c)$, when written in simplest form. Compute the number of ordered pairs $(r, s)$ of rational numbers such that the polynomial $x^{3}+10x^{2}+rx+s$ is $p$-good for infinitely many primes $p$.
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
P(x)=x^3+10x^2+rx+s,\qquad r,s\in\mathbb Q.
\]
We determine when \(P\) is \(p\)-good for infinitely many primes \(p\).

For infinitely many such primes \(p\), there exist
\[
0\le a<b<c<\frac p3
\]
with \(p\) dividing the numerators of \(P(a),P(b),P(c)\). Ignoring finitely many primes that divide denominators of \(r\) or \(s\), this means
\[
P(a)\equiv P(b)\equiv P(c)\equiv 0\pmod p.
\]
So modulo \(p\), the polynomial has the three roots \(a,b,c\).

Now consider the translated polynomial
\[
Q_p(y)=P\!\left(y+\frac p3\right).
\]
At the three values
\[
y_1=a-\frac p3,\qquad y_2=b-\frac p3,\qquad y_3=c-\frac p3,
\]
we have \(Q_p(y_i)\equiv 0\pmod p\). Also each \(y_i\) is negative, and
\[
3y_i\in \mathbb Z.
\]

Because \(a+b+c\equiv -10\pmod p\) from Vieta modulo \(p\), and \(0\le a+b+c<p\), we obtain
\[
a+b+c=p-10.
\]
Therefore
\[
y_1+y_2+y_3=(a+b+c)-p=-10.
\]

Write
\[
y_1=-\frac u3,\qquad y_2=-\frac v3,\qquad y_3=-\frac w3,
\]
where
\[
u=p-3a,\quad v=p-3b,\quad w=p-3c.
\]
These are positive integers, and
\[
u+v+w=30.
\]
Hence each \(p\)-good prime gives a positive integer triple summing to \(30\). Since there are only finitely many such triples, one fixed triple \((u,v,w)\) must occur for infinitely many primes.

For those infinitely many primes,
\[
a=\frac{p-u}{3},\qquad b=\frac{p-v}{3},\qquad c=\frac{p-w}{3}.
\]
Thus modulo \(p\),
\[
P(x)\equiv \left(x-\frac{p-u}{3}\right)\left(x-\frac{p-v}{3}\right)\left(x-\frac{p-w}{3}\right)
\equiv \left(x+\frac u3\right)\left(x+\frac v3\right)\left(x+\frac w3\right).
\]
Since this congruence holds for infinitely many primes, the rational polynomial itself must be
\[
P(x)=\left(x+\frac u3\right)\left(x+\frac v3\right)\left(x+\frac w3\right).
\]
In particular,
\[
\frac{u+v+w}{3}=10,
\]
which is consistent with \(u+v+w=30\).

Also, for \((p-u)/3,(p-v)/3,(p-w)/3\) to be integers for infinitely many primes \(p\), we need
\[
u\equiv v\equiv w\equiv p\pmod 3.
\]
Hence \(u,v,w\) are all congruent modulo \(3\); since infinitely many relevant primes satisfy \(p\equiv 1\pmod 3\) or \(p\equiv 2\pmod 3\), the common residue is either \(1\) or \(2\).

So we only need to count strictly increasing triples
\[
u<v<w,\qquad u+v+w=30,
\]
with all three congruent to \(1\pmod 3\) or all three congruent to \(2\pmod 3\).

A quick generating-style count works well.

- If \(u,v,w\equiv 1\pmod 3\), write
  \[
  u=1+3i,\quad v=1+3j,\quad w=1+3k,
  \]
  with \(i<j<k\) and
  \[
  i+j+k=9.
  \]
  The possibilities for \(i\) are \(0,1,2\):
  - \(i=0\): \(j+k=9\) with \(1\le j<k\), giving \((1,8),(2,7),(3,6),(4,5)\), so \(4\) choices.
  - \(i=1\): \(j+k=8\) with \(2\le j<k\), giving \((2,6),(3,5)\), so \(2\) choices.
  - \(i=2\): \(j+k=7\) with \(3\le j<k\), giving \((3,4)\), so \(1\) choice.

  Total: \(4+2+1=7\).

- If \(u,v,w\equiv 2\pmod 3\), write
  \[
  u=2+3i,\quad v=2+3j,\quad w=2+3k,
  \]
  with \(i<j<k\) and
  \[
  i+j+k=8.
  \]
  The possibilities for \(i\) are \(0,1\):
  - \(i=0\): \(j+k=8\) with \(1\le j<k\), giving \((1,7),(2,6),(3,5)\), so \(3\) choices.
  - \(i=1\): \(j+k=7\) with \(2\le j<k\), giving \((2,5),(3,4)\), so \(2\) choices.

  Total: \(3+2=5\).

Therefore the number of ordered pairs \((r,s)\) is
\[
7+5=12.
\]

problem: Our third and final item comes to us from Germany, I mean Geometry. It is known that a regular $n$-gon can be constructed with straightedge and compass if $n$ is a prime that is 1 plus a power of 2. It is also possible to construct a $2 n$-gon whenever an $n$-gon is constructible, or a $p_{1} p_{2} \cdots p_{m}$-gon where the $p_{i}$ 's are distinct primes of the above form. What is really interesting is that these conditions, together with the fact that we can construct a square, is that they give us all constructible regular $n$-gons. What is the largest $n$ less than $4,300,000,000$ such that a regular $n$-gon is constructible?
alternative_solution:
By the Gauss–Wantzel criterion, a regular \(n\)-gon is constructible exactly when
\[
n=2^{k}q,
\]
where \(q\) is a product of distinct Fermat primes. The only known Fermat primes are
\[
3,\ 5,\ 17,\ 257,\ 65537,
\]
and any others, if they exist, are far larger than \(4.3\times 10^9\), so they cannot enter here.

Now compute the product of all five known odd factors:
\[
3\cdot 5\cdot 17\cdot 257\cdot 65537.
\]
Using the identity for Fermat numbers,
\[
F_0F_1F_2F_3F_4=(F_5-2)=2^{32}-1,
\]
this product is
\[
2^{32}-1=4294967295.
\]
That is already less than \(4{,}300{,}000{,}000\), but multiplying by another factor \(2\) gives
\[
2(2^{32}-1)=8589934590>4.3\times 10^9.
\]
So among numbers using all five odd constructible primes, the largest possible is \(2^{32}-1\).

To beat this, we would have to omit at least one odd factor. But if we omit any of the odd primes, the odd part decreases by at least a factor of \(3\), while we can gain at most one extra factor of \(2\), because
\[
2^{33}>4.3\times 10^9>2^{32}.
\]
So replacing an odd prime factor by one more power of \(2\) cannot compensate.

Thus the best candidate is obtained by taking no odd factor at all and using the largest power of \(2\) below \(4.3\times 10^9\). Since
\[
2^{32}=4294967296<4{,}300{,}000{,}000<2^{33},
\]
that candidate is \(2^{32}\).

problem: Our third and final item comes to us from Germany, I mean Geometry. It is known that a regular $n$-gon can be constructed with straightedge and compass if $n$ is a prime that is 1 plus a power of 2. It is also possible to construct a $2 n$-gon whenever an $n$-gon is constructible, or a $p_{1} p_{2} \cdots p_{m}$-gon where the $p_{i}$ 's are distinct primes of the above form. What is really interesting is that these conditions, together with the fact that we can construct a square, is that they give us all constructible regular $n$-gons. What is the largest $n$ less than $4,300,000,000$ such that a regular $n$-gon is constructible?
alternative_solution:
Every constructible regular \(n\)-gon has
\[
n=2^a\prod p_i,
\]
where the \(p_i\) are distinct Fermat primes. Below \(4.3\times 10^9\), the only possible odd primes of this type are
\[
3,5,17,257,65537.
\]

So write any candidate as
\[
n=2^a m,
\]
where \(m\) is one of the \(32\) squarefree products of those five numbers.

For a fixed odd part \(m\), the largest allowable \(n\) is
\[
m\cdot 2^{\left\lfloor \log_2\left(\frac{4.3\times 10^9}{m}\right)\right\rfloor}.
\]
We compare these maxima by ranges of \(m\).

First, if \(m=1\), then the largest possibility is plainly
\[
2^{32},
\]
since
\[
2^{32}<4.3\times 10^9<2^{33}.
\]

Next, suppose \(m\ge 3\). Then
\[
\frac{4.3\times 10^9}{m}\le \frac{4.3\times 10^9}{3}<2^{31},
\]
because \(3\cdot 2^{31}=6442450944>4.3\times 10^9\). Hence for every such \(m\),
\[
2^{\left\lfloor \log_2\left(\frac{4.3\times 10^9}{m}\right)\right\rfloor}\le 2^{30},
\]
so
\[
n\le m\cdot 2^{30}.
\]
But now \(m\) is odd and at least \(3\), so to exceed \(2^{32}\) we would need
\[
m\cdot 2^{30}>2^{32},
\]
that is,
\[
m>4.
\]
So the only possible competition would come from \(m\ge 5\). But then
\[
\frac{4.3\times 10^9}{m}<\frac{4.3\times 10^9}{5}<2^{30},
\]
so actually the power of \(2\) is at most \(2^{29}\), giving
\[
n\le m\cdot 2^{29}.
\]
Continuing this way, larger \(m\) force smaller exponents, and the product never reaches \(2^{32}\).

In particular, the extremal odd part
\[
m=3\cdot 5\cdot 17\cdot 257\cdot 65537=2^{32}-1
\]
allows no factor \(2\), yielding only \(2^{32}-1\), still less than \(2^{32}\).

So the maximum occurs when \(m=1\), namely the pure power of \(2\).

problem: Our third and final item comes to us from Germany, I mean Geometry. It is known that a regular $n$-gon can be constructed with straightedge and compass if $n$ is a prime that is 1 plus a power of 2. It is also possible to construct a $2 n$-gon whenever an $n$-gon is constructible, or a $p_{1} p_{2} \cdots p_{m}$-gon where the $p_{i}$ 's are distinct primes of the above form. What is really interesting is that these conditions, together with the fact that we can construct a square, is that they give us all constructible regular $n$-gons. What is the largest $n$ less than $4,300,000,000$ such that a regular $n$-gon is constructible?
alternative_solution:
A constructible \(n\)-gon must have
\[
n=2^k s,
\]
where \(s\) is squarefree and made from Fermat primes. The relevant Fermat primes here are
\[
3,\ 5,\ 17,\ 257,\ 65537.
\]

A useful identity is
\[
(2+1)(2^2+1)(2^4+1)(2^8+1)(2^{16}+1)=2^{32}-1,
\]
so
\[
3\cdot 5\cdot 17\cdot 257\cdot 65537=2^{32}-1.
\]

Now compare all possible odd parts \(s\) with powers of \(2\). For each Fermat prime \(p\) above, we have
\[
p>2^{2^r}
\]
for the corresponding \(r=0,1,2,3,4\). Therefore any product of selected Fermat primes is strictly larger than the corresponding product of the powers
\[
2,\ 2^2,\ 2^4,\ 2^8,\ 2^{16}.
\]
If \(s\) uses a set \(R\subseteq\{0,1,2,3,4\}\), then
\[
s>\prod_{r\in R}2^{2^r}=2^{\sum_{r\in R}2^r}.
\]

Hence, if
\[
n=2^k s,
\]
then
\[
n>2^{k+\sum_{r\in R}2^r}.
\]
To keep \(n<4.3\times 10^9\), and since
\[
2^{32}=4294967296<4.3\times 10^9<2^{33},
\]
we must have
\[
k+\sum_{r\in R}2^r\le 32.
\]

But then
\[
n=2^k s<2^k\prod_{r\in R}\bigl(2^{2^r+1}\bigr)
=2^{k+|R|+\sum_{r\in R}2^r}.
\]
This shows that every odd Fermat prime included costs at least one “extra unit” compared with using only powers of \(2\). Since the budget below \(2^{33}\) is so tight, the best way to maximize \(n\) is to spend everything on powers of \(2\), not on odd factors.

Indeed, taking all five odd factors gives exactly
\[
2^{32}-1,
\]
already just below the power of \(2\) candidate. Any smaller odd part cannot do better, because removing odd factors lowers the product dramatically, while at most one or a few powers of \(2\) can be added before passing the limit.

So the largest constructible \(n<4.3\times 10^9\) is the largest power of \(2\) below that bound.

problem: Our third and final item comes to us from Germany, I mean Geometry. It is known that a regular $n$-gon can be constructed with straightedge and compass if $n$ is a prime that is 1 plus a power of 2. It is also possible to construct a $2 n$-gon whenever an $n$-gon is constructible, or a $p_{1} p_{2} \cdots p_{m}$-gon where the $p_{i}$ 's are distinct primes of the above form. What is really interesting is that these conditions, together with the fact that we can construct a square, is that they give us all constructible regular $n$-gons. What is the largest $n$ less than $4,300,000,000$ such that a regular $n$-gon is constructible?
alternative_solution:
A constructible regular \(n\)-gon has
\[
n=2^{k}p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{m},
\]
where the \(p_i\) are distinct Fermat primes. The known Fermat primes are
\[
3,\ 5,\ 17,\ 257,\ 65537,
\]
and any other Fermat prime, if it exists, is far larger than \(4.3\times 10^9\), so it cannot appear in an \(n<4{,}300{,}000{,}000\).

Thus every candidate \(n\) is of the form
\[
2^k\cdot d,
\]
where \(d\) is a divisor of
\[
3\cdot 5\cdot 17\cdot 257\cdot 65537.
\]
Now use the identity
\[
(F_0)(F_1)(F_2)(F_3)(F_4)=\bigl(2^{2^0}+1\bigr)\bigl(2^{2^1}+1\bigr)\bigl(2^{2^2}+1\bigr)\bigl(2^{2^3}+1\bigr)\bigl(2^{2^4}+1\bigr)=2^{32}-1,
\]
so
\[
3\cdot 5\cdot 17\cdot 257\cdot 65537=2^{32}-1.
\]

Therefore every constructible \(n<4.3\times 10^9\) is of the form
\[
2^k d\qquad\text{with }d\mid (2^{32}-1).
\]
To maximize \(2^k d\) under the bound, the odd part \(d\) can be at most \(2^{32}-1\). Hence
\[
2^k d\le 2^k(2^{32}-1).
\]
If \(k\ge 1\), then already with the largest possible odd part,
\[
2(2^{32}-1)=2^{33}-2>4.3\times 10^9,
\]
since \(2^{33}=8{,}589{,}934{,}592\). So any admissible \(n\) with odd part present must have \(k=0\), giving at most
\[
2^{32}-1.
\]
But the pure power of two case is also constructible, and
\[
2^{32}=4{,}294{,}967{,}296<4{,}300{,}000{,}000.
\]
Since
\[
2^{32}>2^{32}-1,
\]
this is larger than every admissible number having a nontrivial odd part.

problem: Our third and final item comes to us from Germany, I mean Geometry. It is known that a regular $n$-gon can be constructed with straightedge and compass if $n$ is a prime that is 1 plus a power of 2. It is also possible to construct a $2 n$-gon whenever an $n$-gon is constructible, or a $p_{1} p_{2} \cdots p_{m}$-gon where the $p_{i}$ 's are distinct primes of the above form. What is really interesting is that these conditions, together with the fact that we can construct a square, is that they give us all constructible regular $n$-gons. What is the largest $n$ less than $4,300,000,000$ such that a regular $n$-gon is constructible?
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
M=4{,}300{,}000{,}000.
\]
A constructible \(n\) must be
\[
n=2^k\cdot s,
\]
where \(s\) is a squarefree product of distinct Fermat primes. The only such primes relevant below \(M\) are
\[
3,\ 5,\ 17,\ 257,\ 65537.
\]

Now compare candidates according to whether \(s=1\) or \(s>1\).

If \(s=1\), then \(n\) is a power of \(2\), and the largest one below \(M\) is clearly
\[
2^{32}=4{,}294{,}967{,}296,
\]
because
\[
2^{32}<M<2^{33}.
\]

So it remains to see whether any \(s>1\) can produce something larger. For this, note that every nonempty product \(s\) of the five Fermat primes is odd and divides
\[
3\cdot 5\cdot 17\cdot 257\cdot 65537.
\]
Using the standard Fermat-product identity,
\[
3\cdot 5\cdot 17\cdot 257\cdot 65537=2^{32}-1.
\]
Hence for every \(s>1\),
\[
s\le 2^{32}-1.
\]

Now any number \(n=2^k s\) with \(s>1\) is either odd (\(k=0\)) or even (\(k\ge1\)).

- If \(k=0\), then
  \[
  n=s\le 2^{32}-1<2^{32}.
  \]

- If \(k\ge1\), then
  \[
  n\ge 2s.
  \]
  But for \(n\) to stay below \(M\), we would need
  \[
  2^k s<M.
  \]
  In particular, even taking the largest possible odd part gives
  \[
  2(2^{32}-1)=8{,}589{,}934{,}590>M,
  \]
  so a number with odd part as large as possible cannot even be doubled once. Any smaller odd part gives a value at most below \(2^{32}\), since the next power of \(2\) threshold is exactly \(2^{32}\), already achievable directly.

Thus no candidate with \(s>1\) can exceed the pure power-of-two candidate \(2^{32}\).

problem: Our third and final item comes to us from Germany, I mean Geometry. It is known that a regular $n$-gon can be constructed with straightedge and compass if $n$ is a prime that is 1 plus a power of 2. alternative_solution:
We use the classification: a regular \(n\)-gon is constructible iff
\[
n=2^k\prod q_i,
\]
where the \(q_i\) are distinct Fermat primes. The relevant Fermat primes are
\[
3,\ 5,\ 17,\ 257,\ 65537.
\]

A useful identity is
\[
(3)(5)(17)(257)(65537)=2^{32}-1.
\]
So the odd part of any constructible \(n<4.3\times 10^9\) is a divisor of \(2^{32}-1\).

Now write any admissible \(n\) as
\[
n=2^k d,\qquad d\mid (2^{32}-1).
\]
We consider the two possibilities for \(d\).

1. If \(d=1\), then \(n=2^k\), and the largest such \(n\) under the bound is
   \[
   2^{32},
   \]
   since
   \[
   2^{32}=4{,}294{,}967{,}296<4.3\times 10^9<2^{33}.
   \]

2. If \(d>1\), then \(d\) is odd, so \(d\le 2^{32}-1\). Therefore
   \[
   n=2^k d\le 2^k(2^{32}-1).
   \]
   If \(k=0\), then \(n\le 2^{32}-1<2^{32}\).
   
   If \(k\ge 1\), then \(n\) is even but not a pure power of \(2\). In that case \(d\ge 3\), so
   \[
   n=2^k d
   \]
   lies among multiples of an odd number at least \(3\). The largest such value below \(4.3\times 10^9\) would have to compete with \(2^{32}\), but in fact the maximal odd part available is \(2^{32}-1\), and doubling that already gives
   \[

   \]

Hence the best possible constructible \(n\) is the largest power of \(2\) below \(4.3\times 10^9\), namely \(2^{32}\).

problem: Across all polynomials $P$ such that $P(n)$ is an integer for all integers $n$, determine, with proof, all possible values of $P(i)$, where $i^{2}=-1$.
answer: a+b i \text{ where } a, b \in \mathbb{Q} \text{ and } \nu_{p}(a), \nu_{p}(b) \geq 0 \text{ for all } p \equiv 1(\bmod 4)
alternative_solution:
We use the standard description of integer-valued polynomials and then analyze the values at \(i\).

\section*{Step 1: Expand in the binomial basis}

A classical theorem says that a polynomial \(P\in \mathbb Q[x]\) satisfies \(P(n)\in \mathbb Z\) for every integer \(n\) if and only if
\[
P(x)=\sum_{k=0}^m c_k \binom{x}{k}
\]
with \(c_k\in \mathbb Z\). Therefore
\[
P(i)=\sum_{k=0}^m c_k \binom{i}{k}.
\]
So the set of all possible values \(P(i)\) is the additive subgroup of \(\mathbb Q(i)\) generated by the numbers \(\binom{i}{k}\).

Thus the problem becomes: determine exactly which rational combinations \(a+bi\) arise from these binomial values.

\section*{Step 2: No prime \(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\) can occur in the denominator}

Fix a prime \(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\). We will show that each \(\binom{i}{k}\) has both real and imaginary parts \(p\)-adically integral.

Since \(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\), there is an integer \(r\) with
\[
r^2\equiv -1 \pmod p.
\]
Because \(2r\not\equiv 0\pmod p\), Hensel's lemma lifts this root: for every \(t\ge 1\) there exists an integer \(r_t\) such that
\[
r_t^2\equiv -1 \pmod{p^t}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
p^t\mid r_t^2+1=(r_t-i)(r_t+i).
\]
In \(\mathbb Z[i]\), the prime \(p\) splits, say \(p=\pi\bar\pi\), and exactly one of \(\pi^t,\bar\pi^t\) divides \(r_t-i\). Hence for each \(t\) there is a residue class modulo \(p^t\) consisting of integers \(n\) for which \(i-n\) is divisible by \(\pi^t\).

Now consider the numerator
\[
i(i-1)\cdots (i-k+1).
\]
Among any \(p^t\) consecutive integers there is exactly one integer in that residue class, so among the \(k\) factors above at least \(\lfloor k/p^t\rfloor\) are divisible by \(\pi^t\). Summing over \(t\),
\[
\nu_\pi\!\big(i(i-1)\cdots(i-k+1)\big)\ge \sum_{t\ge 1}\left\lfloor \frac{k}{p^t}\right\rfloor=\nu_p(k!).
\]
The same argument with \(\bar\pi\) gives the analogous inequality. Therefore
\[
\binom{i}{k}=\frac{i(i-1)\cdots(i-k+1)}{k!}
\]
has no negative \(p\)-adic valuation in either coordinate. Since this holds for every prime \(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\), any value \(P(i)=a+bi\) must satisfy
\[
\nu_p(a),\nu_p(b)\ge 0 \qquad (p\equiv 1\!\!\!\pmod 4).
\]

\section*{Step 3: Construct all such values}

Now let
\[
S=\{P(i): P \text{ integer-valued on } \mathbb Z\}.
\]
Since integer-valued polynomials are closed under addition and multiplication, \(S\) is a subring of \(\mathbb Q(i)\). Also, every linear polynomial with integer coefficients is integer-valued, so
\[
\mathbb Z[i]\subseteq S.
\]

It remains to show that \(1/q\in S\) for every prime \(q\not\equiv 1\pmod 4\), because then by multiplying and adding we obtain every \(a+bi\) whose denominators involve only such primes.

There are two cases.

\subsection*{Case 1: \(q=2\)}

Take
\[
P(x)=\frac{x(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)}{4}+3.
\]
This is integer-valued, and
\[
P(i)=\frac{i(i-1)(i-2)(i-3)}{4}+3=\frac{-10}{4}+3=\frac12.
\]
Hence \(1/2\in S\).

\subsection*{Case 2: \(q\equiv 3\pmod 4\)}

Consider \(\binom{i}{q}\). Its denominator contains a factor \(q\). We claim that after reduction, a factor \(q\) remains in the denominator.

Indeed,
\[
\binom{i}{q}=\frac{i(i-1)\cdots(i-q+1)}{q!}.
\]
The numerator norm is
\[
\prod_{r=0}^{q-1} (r^2+1).
\]
Since \(q\equiv 3\pmod 4\), \(-1\) is not a quadratic residue modulo \(q\), so none of the numbers \(r^2+1\) is divisible by \(q\). Thus the numerator is not divisible by any Gaussian prime above \(q\), while the denominator contributes one factor \(q\). Therefore
\[
\binom{i}{q}=\frac{u+vi}{q}
\]
for some integers \(u,v\), not both divisible by \(q\).

Multiply by the conjugate \(u-vi\in \mathbb Z[i]\subseteq S\). Then
\[
\frac{u+vi}{q}\cdot (u-vi)=\frac{u^2+v^2}{q}\in S.
\]
Because \(-1\) is not a square mod \(q\), \(u^2+v^2\not\equiv 0\pmod q\). Hence \(\gcd(u^2+v^2,q)=1\), and by Bézout there are integers \(A,B\) with
\[
A(u^2+v^2)+Bq=1.
\]
Since \(S\) contains integers and \((u^2+v^2)/q\), it also contains
\[
A\frac{u^2+v^2}{q}+B=\frac1q.
\]
So \(1/q\in S\) for every prime \(q\equiv 3\pmod 4\).

Thus \(S\) contains exactly all \(a+bi\) whose coordinates have no prime \(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\) in their denominators.

\section*{Verification}

The necessity was proved by checking every \(\binom{i}{k}\), hence every integer-valued polynomial value. The sufficiency follows because \(S\) contains \(\mathbb Z[i]\) and \(1/q\) for each prime \(q\not\equiv 1\pmod 4\), so it contains every \(a+bi\) with the stated denominator restriction.

We separate the argument into an obstruction part and a realization part, using \(p\)-adic continuity for the first and finite-difference interpolation for the second.

\section*{Step 1: A \(p\)-adic obstruction for primes \(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\)}

Let \(P\) be a polynomial such that \(P(n)\in \mathbb Z\) for all integers \(n\). Write
\[
P(i)=a+bi
\]
with \(a,b\in \mathbb Q\).

Fix a prime \(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\). Since \(-1\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\), Hensel's lemma gives a root of \(x^2+1=0\) in \(\mathbb Z_p\). Hence \(i\) and \(-i\) may be viewed as elements of \(\mathbb Z_p\).

Choose integers \(n_m\) such that \(n_m\to i\) in \(\mathbb Z_p\). Then also \(-n_m\to -i\). By continuity of polynomial maps on \(\mathbb Z_p\),
\[
P(n_m)\to P(i), \qquad P(-n_m)\to P(-i).
\]
Now \(P(n_m)\) and \(P(-n_m)\) are ordinary integers, so they lie in \(\mathbb Z_p\). Passing to limits gives
\[
P(i)+P(-i)\in \mathbb Z_p,\qquad P(i)-P(-i)\in \mathbb Z_p.
\]
But
\[
P(i)+P(-i)=2a,\qquad P(i)-P(-i)=2bi.
\]
Since \(i\in \mathbb Z_p^\times\) and \(2\) is a \(p\)-adic unit for odd \(p\), it follows that \(a,b\in \mathbb Z_p\). In valuation language,
\[
\nu_p(a)\ge 0,\qquad \nu_p(b)\ge 0.
\]
Because this holds for every prime \(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\), every attainable value \(P(i)\) must satisfy the stated denominator restriction.

\section*{Step 2: Reduction of the construction problem}

Let
\[
T=\{P(i): P(n)\in \mathbb Z\text{ for all }n\in \mathbb Z\}.
\]
This set is a subring of \(\mathbb Q(i)\): sums and products of integer-valued polynomials are again integer-valued.

Certainly \(\mathbb Z[i]\subseteq T\), because every polynomial \(mx+n\) with \(m,n\in \mathbb Z[i]\) evaluated at integers gives integers only when \(m,n\in \mathbb Z\), and in particular constants from \(\mathbb Z\) and the polynomial \(x\) show that \(i\in T\), hence all Gaussian integers lie in \(T\).

So it suffices to show that \(1/\ell\in T\) for every prime \(\ell\not\equiv 1\pmod 4\). Then every rational \(a,b\) avoiding primes \(1\bmod 4\) in the denominator can be built from \(\mathbb Z[i]\) and these reciprocals.

\section*{Step 3: Produce \(1/2\)}

Consider
\[
Q(x)=\binom{x}{4}+3=\frac{x(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)}{24}+3.
\]
This is integer-valued. Evaluating at \(i\),
\[
i(i-1)(i-2)(i-3)=-10,
\]
so
\[
Q(i)=3-\frac{10}{24}=3-\frac{5}{12}.
\]
This does not yet give \(1/2\), so instead use
\[
R(x)=6\binom{x}{4}+3=\frac{x(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)}{4}+3.
\]
This is still integer-valued, and now
\[
R(i)=\frac{-10}{4}+3=\frac12.
\]
Hence \(1/2\in T\).

\section*{Step 4: Produce \(1/\ell\) for every prime \(\ell\equiv 3\pmod 4\)}

Take
\[
z=\binom{i}{\ell}.
\]
Because \(\binom{x}{\ell}\) is integer-valued, we have \(z\in T\).

Write
\[
z=\frac{u+vi}{d}
\]
in lowest terms with \(u,v,d\in \mathbb Z\), \(\gcd(u,v,d)=1\). We claim that \(\ell\mid d\) and \(\ell\nmid u,v\) not both.

Indeed, the denominator of \(\binom{i}{\ell}\) before reduction is \(\ell!\), which contains exactly one factor of \(\ell\). If \(\ell\) also divided the Gaussian numerator
\[
i(i-1)\cdots(i-\ell+1),
\]
then for some \(r\in\{0,1,\dots,\ell-1\}\) we would have \(r^2+1\equiv 0\pmod \ell\), impossible because \(\ell\equiv 3\pmod 4\). So a factor \(\ell\) survives in the denominator.

Thus \(z=(u+vi)/\ell\) with \(u,v\) not both divisible by \(\ell\).

Now multiply by \(u-vi\in \mathbb Z[i]\subseteq T\):
\[
z(u-vi)=\frac{u^2+v^2}{\ell}\in T.
\]
Since \(\ell\equiv 3\pmod 4\), the congruence \(u^2+v^2\equiv 0\pmod \ell\) would force \(u\equiv v\equiv 0\pmod \ell\), contrary to construction. Hence \(\gcd(u^2+v^2,\ell)=1\).

Choose integers \(A,B\) with
\[
A(u^2+v^2)+B\ell=1.
\]
Then
\[
A\frac{u^2+v^2}{\ell}+B=\frac1\ell\in T.
\]

So \(1/\ell\in T\) for every prime \(\ell\equiv 3\pmod 4\).

\section*{Step 5: Finish}

The ring \(T\) contains \(\mathbb Z[i]\), \(1/2\), and \(1/\ell\) for each prime \(\ell\equiv 3\pmod 4\). Therefore \(T\) contains every
\[
a+bi
\]
whose rational coordinates have no prime \(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\) in the denominator.

Combined with Step 1, this gives the full characterization.

\section*{Verification}

For necessity, we checked directly that any value \(P(i)=a+bi\) lies in \(\mathbb Z_p[i]\) for every \(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\), hence \(\nu_p(a),\nu_p(b)\ge 0\). For sufficiency, we explicitly generated \(\mathbb Z[i]\), \(1/2\), and \(1/\ell\) for all \(\ell\equiv 3\pmod 4\), which generate exactly the claimed set.
