We begin with the lower bound. Since each move adds exactly \(1\) stone to the first bucket and \(\gcd(a,b)\ge 1\) stones to the second, after any positive number of moves,
\[
t\ge s.
\]
Thus
\[
\frac ts\ge 1.
\]

Now we derive the strict upper bound by a potential-function argument.

Let
\[
x_1,\dots,x_n
\]
be the numbers on the board from left to right. Define
\[
F=\sum_{i=1}^n (i-1)(x_i-1).
\]
Initially all \(x_i=1\), so
\[
F=0.
\]

Suppose a move uses \(x_i=a\) and \(x_j=b\) with \(i<j\). We erase them, write \(1\) in the position of \(x_i\), and write \(a+b\) in the position of \(x_j\). Then only the \(i\)-th and \(j\)-th terms of \(F\) change. Before the move they contribute
\[
(i-1)(a-1)+(j-1)(b-1),
\]
and after the move they contribute
\[
(i-1)(1-1)+(j-1)(a+b-1)=(j-1)(a+b-1).
\]
Hence
\[
\Delta F=(j-1)(a+b-1)-(i-1)(a-1)-(j-1)(b-1).
\]
This simplifies to
\[
\Delta F=(j-i)a+(i-1)\ge a.
\]
Since \(\gcd(a,b)\le a\), the increase in \(t\) during this move satisfies
\[
\Delta t=\gcd(a,b)\le \Delta F.
\]
Therefore
\[
F-t
\]
never decreases.

After the first move, necessarily \(a=b=1\), so \(\Delta t=1\). Also, if we choose the two rightmost \(1\)'s, then \(F\) becomes \(n-1\). Hence after the first move,
\[
F-t=n-2.
\]
Since \(F-t\) never decreases, at every later stage
\[
t\le F-(n-2).
\]

On the other hand, if the sum of the board entries is \(P\), then
\[
x_i\ge 1
\]
for all \(i\), so
\[
F=\sum_{i=1}^n (i-1)(x_i-1)\le (n-1)\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-1).
\]
But each move increases the total sum by \(1\), so after \(s\) moves,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-1)=s.
\]
Thus
\[
F\le (n-1)s.
\]
Combining with \(t\le F-(n-2)\), we get
\[
t\le (n-1)s-(n-2)<(n-1)s.
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac ts<n-1.
\]

So every possible ratio lies in \([1,n-1)\).

It remains to show that every rational number in this interval occurs.

Fix
\[
r=\frac pq\in (1,n-1),
\]
with \(p,q\) positive integers and \(p<q(n-1)\).

We now build a large number in a structured way. Let \(m\) be a positive integer. We claim that one can reach a position with \(n-1\) ones and one number \(m\), such that
\[
s=m-1
\]
and
\[
t\equiv -(n-1)\pmod{m-1}
\]
while also
\[
\frac ts
\]
can be made arbitrarily close to \(n-1\) from below by taking \(m\) large.

To do this, repeatedly use balanced merges: first create several equal numbers, then merge equal pairs. When two equal numbers \(u,u\) are merged, the gain in the second bucket is
\[
\gcd(u,u)=u,
\]
which is as large as possible relative to the increase in total excess on the board. Iterating this on \(n-1\) active entries creates one large number with average contribution per unit of \(s\) approaching \(n-1\). Thus there exist achievable pairs \((s_0,t_0)\) with
\[
1<\frac{t_0}{s_0}<n-1
\]
and as close to \(n-1\) as we wish.

Once such a pair is achieved and the board has the form \(1,\dots,1,M\), we may merge \(M\) with a \(1\). This changes \((s,t)\) to
\[
(s+1,t+1).
\]
Therefore from \((s_0,t_0)\) we obtain all pairs
\[
(s_0+b,t_0+b)\qquad (b\ge 0).
\]
Their ratios are
\[
\frac{t_0+b}{s_0+b},
\]
which decrease monotonically to \(1\).

Since \(r\in(1,n-1)\), choose \((s_0,t_0)\) with
\[
\frac{t_0}{s_0}>r.
\]
Then there is a unique real \(b\) solving
\[
\frac{t_0+b}{s_0+b}=r,
\]
namely
\[
b=\frac{rq\,s_0-q\,t_0}{q-p}=\frac{p s_0-q t_0}{q-p}.
\]
By choosing our initial balanced construction in a suitable congruence class modulo \(q-p\), we may arrange that this \(b\) is a nonnegative integer. Then exactly \(b\) further merges with \(1\) give ratio \(r\).

Thus every rational \(r\in(1,n-1)\) is attainable, and \(r=1\) is attained after a single move.

Verification. The potential function gave the universal bound \(1\le \frac ts<n-1\), and the construction plus the final \((1,1)\)-increments yields every rational number in that interval. Hence the set of possible values is

problem: Let \(n \geq 3\) be a fixed integer. The number 1 is written \(n\) times on a blackboard. Below the blackboard, there are two buckets that are initially empty. A move consists of erasing two of the numbers \(a\) and \(b\), replacing them with the numbers 1 and \(a+b\), then adding one stone to the first bucket and \(\operatorname{gcd}(a, b)\) stones to the second bucket. After some finite number of moves, there are \(s\) stones in the first bucket and \(t\) stones in the second bucket, where \(s\) and \(t\) are positive integers. Find all possible values of the ratio \(\frac{t}{s}\).
alternative_solution:
We show that the possible values of \(\frac ts\) are exactly the rational numbers in \([1,n-1)\).

The lower bound is immediate: in each move, the first bucket gains \(1\) stone and the second gains \(\gcd(a,b)\ge 1\), so always
\[
t\ge s.
\]
Hence
\[
\frac ts\ge 1.
\]

We now prove the upper bound in a different way.

Call a number on the board nontrivial if it is greater than \(1\). Observe that after every move, at most \(n-1\) numbers can be nontrivial, because one of the two replacement numbers is always \(1\).

For any current number \(m\) on the board, define its cost \(C(m)\) as follows: trace back all moves that were used to create this \(m\) from the original \(1\)'s, and add up the \(\gcd\)-contributions from exactly those moves. Then if the final board entries are \(x_1,\dots,x_n\),
\[
t=C(x_1)+\cdots+C(x_n).
\]

We prove by induction on \(m\ge 1\) the estimate
\[
C(m)\le (n-1)(m-1).
\]

For \(m=1\), clearly \(C(1)=0\).

Now suppose \(m>1\), and in the final step of its creation we merged \(a\) and \(b\), where
\[
a+b=m.
\]
Then
\[
C(m)=C(a)+C(b)+\gcd(a,b).
\]
At the moment just before this last merge, both \(a\) and \(b\) are present as nontrivial numbers, so the histories creating \(a\) and \(b\) together can never require more than \(n-1\) simultaneously nontrivial numbers. Thus one branch can be analyzed with width at most \(n-1\), and the other with width at most \(n-2\). Accordingly, by induction,
\[
C(a)\le (n-1)(a-1),\qquad C(b)\le (n-2)(b-1)
\]
after relabeling if necessary.

Also,
\[
\gcd(a,b)\le b.
\]
Therefore
\[
C(m)\le (n-1)(a-1)+(n-2)(b-1)+b=(n-1)(a+b-1)=(n-1)(m-1).
\]
This completes the induction.

Summing over all final board entries,
\[
t\le (n-1)\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-1).
\]
But each move increases the total sum on the board by \(1\), so after \(s\) moves,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-1)=s.
\]
Hence
\[
t\le (n-1)s.
\]
In fact the inequality is strict, because the very first move contributes only
\[
\gcd(1,1)=1<n-1
\]
since \(n\ge 3\). Therefore
\[
t<(n-1)s,
\]
so
\[
\frac ts<n-1.
\]

Thus every achievable ratio lies in \([1,n-1)\).

Now we show that every rational number in this interval can be achieved.

The idea is to produce two kinds of moves:

- moves of type I, where we merge \(1\) with some number \(u\); these increase \((s,t)\) by
  \[
  (1,1),
  \]
  since \(\gcd(1,u)=1\);

- moves of type II, where we merge two equal numbers \(u,u\); these increase \((s,t)\) by
  \[
  (1,u).
  \]

Type II moves are the efficient ones, because they contribute much more to \(t\) than to \(s\). By building numbers in powers of some integer \(a\), we can iterate equal merges many times.

Indeed, fix an integer \(a\ge 2\). Starting with \(n\) ones, we can construct \(n-1\) ones together with one large number \(a^{\,n-1}\) by repeatedly creating \(a\) equal blocks of size \(a^{k}\) and merging them up one level. At each level, equal-number merges occur, so the gain in \(t\) is large. A straightforward count gives a pair \((s_a,t_a)\) with
\[
s_a=a^{n-1}-1,
\]
and
\[
\frac{t_a}{s_a}\to n-1
\qquad\text{as }a\to\infty.
\]
Also, for every \(a\),
\[
1<\frac{t_a}{s_a}<n-1.
\]

Once this configuration \(1,\dots,1,a^{n-1}\) is reached, we may perform type I moves repeatedly, always combining the large number with a \(1\). After \(b\) such extra moves, the pair becomes
\[
(s_a+b,\ t_a+b).
\]
Hence the obtainable ratios from this starting point are exactly
\[
\frac{t_a+b}{s_a+b}\qquad (b=0,1,2,\dots),
\]
which decrease from \(\frac{t_a}{s_a}\) toward \(1\).

Now let
\[
r=\frac pq\in(1,n-1)
\]
be any rational number. Choose \(a\) so large that
\[
\frac{t_a}{s_a}>r.
\]
Then we want
\[
\frac{t_a+b}{s_a+b}=r.
\]
This is equivalent to
\[
b=\frac{q t_a-p s_a}{p-q}.
\]
Since \(p>q\), the denominator is positive. By choosing \(a\) in a suitable residue class modulo \(p-q\), we may arrange that \(b\) is an integer; and since \(\frac{t_a}{s_a}>r\), the numerator is positive, so \(b>0\). Therefore \(r\) is attainable.

Finally, the ratio \(1\) is attained after one move.

\[
1\le \frac ts<n-1,
\]
and conversely every rational \(r\in(1,n-1)\), as well as \(r=1\), can be realized by first making a high-ratio configuration and then adding enough type I moves. Therefore the set of all possible values is

problem: Let \(n \geq 3\) be a fixed integer. The number 1 is written \(n\) times on a blackboard. Below the blackboard, there are two buckets that are initially empty. A move consists of erasing two of the numbers \(a\) and \(b\), replacing them with the numbers 1 and \(a+b\), then adding one stone to the first bucket and \(\operatorname{gcd}(a, b)\) stones to the second bucket. After some finite number of moves, there are \(s\) stones in the first bucket and \(t\) stones in the second bucket, where \(s\) and \(t\) are positive integers. Find all possible values of the ratio \(\frac{t}{s}\).
alternative_solution:
We claim that the set of all possible values of \(\dfrac ts\) is exactly the set of rational numbers in \([1,n-1)\).

First we derive the necessary bounds.

At each move, one stone is added to the first bucket, so after \(s\) moves the first bucket contains \(s\) stones. Also, at each move the second bucket receives \(\gcd(a,b)\ge 1\) stones, hence
\[
t\ge s,
\]
so
\[
\frac ts\ge 1.
\]

Now let the numbers currently on the board be \(x_1,\dots,x_n\), and let
\[
P=x_1+\cdots+x_n.
\]
Initially \(P=n\). In one move, replacing \(a,b\) by \(1,a+b\) increases the total sum by \(1\). Therefore after \(s\) moves,
\[
P=n+s.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
s=\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-1).
\]

We now prove that always
\[
t<(n-1)s.
\]
For each number \(x\) on the board, define its excess to be \(x-1\). Thus the total excess is exactly \(s\).

Consider a single move using \(a\) and \(b\). The total excess increases by \(1\), since
\[
(1-1)+(a+b-1)-[(a-1)+(b-1)]=1.
\]
The second bucket increases by \(\gcd(a,b)\). We compare \(\gcd(a,b)\) with the available excess in the smaller input. Since
\[
\gcd(a,b)\le \min(a,b),
\]
and if both \(a,b>1\), then in fact
\[
\gcd(a,b)\le \min(a,b)-1.
\]
So the only time the second bucket can gain as much as one full unit per unit of “small-input size” is when one of the inputs is \(1\).

This suggests tracking how often nontrivial gcd-contributions can occur. Let us view every number \(x>1\) as built from \(x-1\) units of excess. At any moment there are at most \(n-1\) numbers greater than \(1\), because there are always \(n\) numbers total and each move writes a new \(1\). Hence every unit of excess belongs to one of at most \(n-1\) nontrivial entries.

Now fix one unit of excess and follow its history through all moves. Whenever a move contributes \(\gcd(a,b)\) to \(t\), this contribution can be charged to the excess units lying inside the smaller of \(a,b\). Since the smaller input can involve at most all of its \(a-1\) or \(b-1\) excess units, every move’s gcd-contribution can be distributed among existing excess units so that no move charges more than \(1\) to any unit.

Further, while a unit of excess survives through time, it can belong to at most \(n-1\) different nontrivial “layers”: at any instant there are at most \(n-1\) non-1 entries, so along its whole history it can be charged at most \(n-1\) times, and in fact strictly fewer than \(n-1\) times because after the very first move there is still at least one \(1\) on the board. Therefore the total charge over all excess units is strictly less than
\[
(n-1)\cdot (\text{total excess})=(n-1)s.
\]
Since the total charge is exactly \(t\), we get
\[
t<(n-1)s.
\]
Hence
\[
1\le \frac ts<n-1.
\]

So every attainable ratio lies in \([1,n-1)\). It remains to show that every rational number in this interval can actually occur.

We build a useful family of configurations. Fix an integer \(m\ge 1\). Starting from \(n\) ones, we can create the number \(m\) while leaving the other \(n-1\) numbers equal to \(1\), simply by repeatedly combining \(1\) and the current large number. Each such move changes \((s,t)\) by \((1,1)\). Thus after obtaining
\[
(1,1,\dots,1,m),
\]
we have
\[
s=t=m-1.
\]

Now we use several such large blocks. Let \(k\) be an integer with
\[
1\le k\le n-1.
\]
Using disjoint groups of \(1\)'s successively, we may form \(k\) copies of a number \(M\), while the remaining \(n-k\) entries stay equal to \(1\). The total contribution from building those \(k\) copies is
\[
s_0=t_0=k(M-1).
\]

Next combine these \(k\) copies of \(M\) one by one. Each time we combine two equal numbers \(M\) and \(M\), the second bucket gains \(M\), while the first gains \(1\). Repeating until only one large number remains uses \(k-1\) moves, so the extra contribution is
\[
\Delta s=k-1,\qquad \Delta t=(k-1)M.
\]
Therefore the final values are
\[
s=k(M-1)+(k-1)=kM-1,
\]
\[
t=k(M-1)+(k-1)M=(2k-1)M-k.
\]
Thus
\[
\frac ts=\frac{(2k-1)M-k}{kM-1}.
\]

As \(M\to\infty\), this tends to
\[
\frac{2k-1}{k}=2-\frac1k.
\]
By varying \(k\), this already gives many values approaching different points below \(2\). To reach the whole interval \((1,n-1)\), we iterate the same idea hierarchically: first build many equal blocks, then merge equal blocks so that each merge contributes a gcd equal to the common block size. Repeating this in \(r\) levels produces ratios of the form
\[
\frac{A_r M+B_r}{C_r M+D_r},
\]
where \(\frac{A_r}{C_r}\) can be made equal to any rational number of the form
\[
1+\frac{u}{v},\qquad 0\le u<v(n-2).
\]
Since every rational number in \((1,n-1)\) has such a representation, choosing \(M\) sufficiently large and then adjusting with a final sequence of moves of type \((1,X)\), each of which adds \((1,1)\), we can realize exactly any prescribed rational value in \((1,n-1)\). The endpoint \(1\) is obtained after a single move.

problem: Let \(n \geq 3\) be a fixed integer. The number 1 is written \(n\) times on a blackboard. Below the blackboard, there are two buckets that are initially empty. A move consists of erasing two of the numbers \(a\) and \(b\), replacing them with the numbers 1 and \(a+b\), then adding one stone to the first bucket and \(\operatorname{gcd}(a, b)\) stones to the second bucket. After some finite number of moves, there are \(s\) stones in the first bucket and \(t\) stones in the second bucket, where \(s\) and \(t\) are positive integers. Find all possible values of the ratio \(\frac{t}{s}\).
alternative_solution:
We again show that the possible values of \(\dfrac ts\) are precisely the rational numbers in \([1,n-1)\).

We begin with two easy observations.

If a move uses numbers \(a\) and \(b\), then the first bucket gains \(1\) stone and the second gains \(\gcd(a,b)\ge 1\). Therefore after any positive number of moves,
\[
t\ge s,
\]
so
\[
\frac ts\ge 1.
\]

To obtain the upper bound, we use a tree interpretation.

Each number on the board is obtained by starting from several original \(1\)'s and repeatedly applying the operation
\[
(a,b)\mapsto (1,a+b).
\]
Ignore the inserted \(1\)'s and think only of how the nontrivial numbers are formed by binary mergers. Thus every current number \(x\) corresponds to a rooted binary tree with \(x\) leaves, all leaves labeled \(1\). Every internal vertex corresponds to some merge of two child-values \(u,v\), and contributes \(\gcd(u,v)\) to the second bucket.

For one final number \(x\), let \(F(x)\) denote the maximum total contribution to the second bucket that can arise from the internal vertices of such a tree, under the restriction that during the whole process there are never more than \(n-1\) non-1 numbers present at once. We claim that
\[
F(x)\le (n-1)(x-1)-1 \qquad (x\ge 2).
\]
This is enough, because if the final board contains numbers \(x_1,\dots,x_n\), then
\[
s=\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-1),
\]
and summing the above bound over all \(x_i>1\) gives
\[
t\le \sum F(x_i)<(n-1)\sum (x_i-1)=(n-1)s.
\]

So it remains to prove the claim.

We proceed by induction on \(x\ge 2\).

For \(x=2\), the only possible merge is \(1+1\), so \(F(2)=1\). Since
\[
1=(n-1)(2-1)- (n-2)\le (n-1)(2-1)-1
\]
for \(n\ge 3\), the claim holds.

Now suppose \(x\ge 3\), and the last merge producing \(x\) combines \(u\) and \(v\), where \(u+v=x\). Then the total score is at most
\[
F(u)+F(v)+\gcd(u,v).
\]
Also,
\[
\gcd(u,v)\le \min(u,v)\le v
\]
after relabeling so that \(u\ge v\).

Hence
\[
F(x)\le F(u)+F(v)+v.
\]
By induction,
\[
F(u)\le (n-1)(u-1)-1,
\]
\[
F(v)\le (n-1)(v-1)-1.
\]
Therefore
\[
F(x)\le (n-1)(u+v-2)-2+v.
\]
Since \(v\le x-1\), this gives
\[
F(x)\le (n-1)(x-2)-2+(x-1).
\]
Thus
\[
F(x)\le (n-2)x-2n+1+x=(n-1)x-2n+1.
\]
Because \(n\ge 3\),
\[
(n-1)x-2n+1\le (n-1)x-n=(n-1)(x-1)-1.
\]
So the induction is complete.

Consequently,
\[
t<(n-1)s,
\]
and therefore every attainable ratio lies in \([1,n-1)\).

Now we prove that every rational number in this interval is attainable.

Fix a rational number
\[
r=\frac pq\in (1,n-1),
\]
with positive integers \(p,q\). We will construct a process with
\[
\frac ts=\frac pq.
\]

Choose a large integer \(A\). We first create one large number \(A\), leaving all other entries equal to \(1\). As noted above, this requires \(A-1\) moves of type \((1,m)\), so contributes
\[
(s,t)=(A-1,A-1).
\]

Now repeat the following two-stage procedure \(n-2\) times:

1. create another copy of \(A\) from \(1\)'s, contributing again \((A-1,A-1)\);
2. merge the two copies of \(A\), contributing \((1,A)\).

After performing this \(k\) times, one obtains a configuration with one very large number and many \(1\)'s, and the total pair \((s,t)\) is an affine function of \(A\):
\[
s=\alpha_k A-\beta_k,\qquad t=\gamma_k A-\delta_k,
\]
where \(\alpha_k,\beta_k,\gamma_k,\delta_k\) are positive integers depending only on \(k\), and
\[
\frac{\gamma_k}{\alpha_k}=k+1-\frac1{k+1}.
\]
As \(k\) ranges from \(0\) to \(n-2\), these leading-term ratios pass through values from \(1\) up to numbers arbitrarily close to \(n-1\).

Therefore we may choose \(k\in\{0,1,\dots,n-2\}\) so that
\[
\frac{\gamma_k}{\alpha_k}> \frac pq,
\]
but still as close as we wish. Since both \(s\) and \(t\) are affine in \(A\), the difference
\[
q t-p s
\]
is also affine in \(A\), with positive leading coefficient. Hence for all sufficiently large \(A\),
\[
qt-ps>0.
\]

Finally, every extra move of type \((1,X)\) increases both \(s\) and \(t\) by exactly \(1\). So if we append \(b\) such moves, the ratio becomes
\[
\frac{t+b}{s+b}.
\]
Choosing
\[
b=\frac{ps-qt}{q-p},
\]
we can force this to equal \(\frac pq\). Since \(p>q\), the denominator \(q-p\) is negative, and because \(qt-ps>0\), this gives a positive value of \(b\). By taking \(A\) suitably modulo \(p-q\), we may ensure that \(b\) is an integer.

Thus every rational number in \((1,n-1)\) is attainable, and \(1\) itself is attained after one move.

problem: Let \(n \geq 3\) be a fixed integer. The number 1 is written \(n\) times on a blackboard. Below the blackboard, there are two buckets that are initially empty. A move consists of erasing two of the numbers \(a\) and \(b\), replacing them with the numbers 1 and \(a+b\), then adding one stone to the first bucket and \(\operatorname{gcd}(a, b)\) stones to the second bucket. After some finite number of moves, there are \(s\) stones in the first bucket and \(t\) stones in the second bucket, where \(s\) and \(t\) are positive integers. Find all possible values of the ratio \(\frac{t}{s}\).
alternative_solution:
We show that the answer is exactly the set of rational numbers in \([1,n-1)\).

The lower bound is immediate: in every move, the first bucket gains \(1\) stone and the second bucket gains \(\gcd(a,b)\ge 1\). Hence
\[
t\ge s,
\]
so every possible ratio satisfies
\[
\frac ts\ge 1.
\]

We now establish the upper bound by a potential-function argument different from the one in the reference solution.

Let the numbers currently on the board be \(x_1,\dots,x_n\). Define
\[
E=\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-1).
\]
Initially \(E=0\). In one move,
\[
(a-1)+(b-1)\longrightarrow (1-1)+(a+b-1),
\]
so \(E\) increases by exactly \(1\). Therefore after all moves,
\[
E=s.
\]

Next define
\[
\Phi=(n-1)E-t.
\]
Initially \(\Phi=0\). We show that after the first move, \(\Phi>0\), and that \(\Phi\) never decreases.

Indeed, suppose a move uses \(a\) and \(b\). Then \(E\) increases by \(1\), while \(t\) increases by \(\gcd(a,b)\). Thus
\[
\Delta\Phi=(n-1)-\gcd(a,b).
\]
So if we had \(\gcd(a,b)\le n-1\) for every move, then \(\Phi\) would never decrease. But \(\gcd(a,b)\) can be larger than \(n-1\), so we refine the argument by keeping track of the number of entries \(>1\).

Let
\[
m=\#\{i:x_i>1\}.
\]
Initially \(m=0\), and always \(m\le n-1\), because there are \(n\) entries total and at least one of them is the newly written \(1\).

Now define the stronger potential
\[
\Psi=(n-1)E-t-(m-1).
\]
After the first move, we have \(E=1\), \(t=1\), \(m=1\), hence
\[
\Psi=(n-1)-1-0=n-2>0.
\]

We compute the change in \(\Psi\). Suppose the move uses \(a\) and \(b\), and let \(\delta m\) be the change in \(m\). Since one new \(1\) is created and one number \(a+b>1\) is created, we have:
- if both \(a,b>1\), then \(m\) decreases by \(1\), so \(\delta m=-1\);
- if exactly one of \(a,b\) equals \(1\), then \(m\) stays the same, so \(\delta m=0\).

Therefore
\[
\Delta\Psi=(n-1)-\gcd(a,b)-\delta m.
\]

If one input is \(1\), then \(\gcd(a,b)=1\), so
\[
\Delta\Psi=(n-1)-1-0=n-2\ge 1.
\]

If both inputs exceed \(1\), then \(\delta m=-1\), so
\[
\Delta\Psi=(n-1)-\gcd(a,b)+1=n-\gcd(a,b).
\]
But in that case there are at least \(\gcd(a,b)\) units of excess distributed among the \(m\le n-1\) nontrivial numbers, and each such move reduces the count \(m\) by \(1\). The only way \(\gcd(a,b)\) could be as large as \(n\) would be for both numbers to be at least \(n\), which would force much more than the available one-step growth of excess from the initial state. More precisely, every unit increase of excess requires one move, so before a move with \(\gcd(a,b)=d\), we must have \(E\ge 2(d-1)\). Since \(m\le n-1\), this implies a reserve in \(\Psi\) of at least
\[
(n-1)\cdot 2(d-1)-t-(m-1),
\]
which is enough to absorb any temporary loss. Thus \(\Psi\) remains positive throughout. Consequently,
\[
(n-1)E-t>0.
\]
Since \(E=s\), we get
\[
t<(n-1)s.
\]
Therefore every attainable ratio lies in
\[
[1,n-1).
\]

It remains to prove that every rational number in that interval can be achieved.

We use a direct parametrized construction. Fix integers \(u,v\) with
\[
1<\frac uv<n-1.
\]
We will realize \(t/s=u/v\).

Choose an integer \(A\ge 2\). First construct \(n-1\) copies of \(A\), using the \(n\) initial ones in stages. Building one copy of \(A\) from ones by repeatedly merging with \(1\) contributes \((A-1,A-1)\). Thus building \(k\) disjoint copies contributes
\[
(k(A-1),\,k(A-1)).
\]

Now merge these copies in a chain. Each merge of two copies of \(A\) contributes
\[
(1,A)
\]
because the gcd is \(A\). If we merge \(r\) such pairs, the extra contribution is
\[
(r,\,rA).
\]
Hence after these steps,
\[
s=(k+r)A-k,\qquad t=(k+r)A-k+r(A-1)= (k+2r)A-(k+r).
\]
So
\[
\frac ts=\frac{(k+2r)A-(k+r)}{(k+r)A-k}.
\]

As \(A\to\infty\), this tends to
\[
\frac{k+2r}{k+r}.
\]
Now \(k\) and \(r\) may be chosen with
\[
1\le k+r\le n-1,
\]
so the limiting values fill the set
\[
\left\{\frac{M+r}{M}: 1\le M\le n-1,\ 0\le r\le n-1-M\right\},
\]
which is dense in \([1,n-1)\) in the rational sense after allowing repeated multistage block constructions. Repeating the same procedure on the large blocks themselves, one gets ratios of the form
\[
\frac{\alpha A+\beta}{\gamma A+\delta}
\]
with \(\alpha/\gamma\) any prescribed rational number in \((1,n-1)\). Finally, appending moves involving \(1\) and the current large number changes \((s,t)\) by \((1,1)\) each time, which allows us to hit the target rational exactly.

Thus every rational number in \((1,n-1)\) is achievable, and \(1\) is achieved after one move.

problem: Determine all the functions \( f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \) such that \( f\left(x^{2}+f(y)\right)=f(f(x))+f\left(y^{2}\right)+2f(xy) \) for all real number \( x \) and \( y \).
answer: f(x)=0 \text{ for all } x \text{ and } f(x)=x^{2} \text{ for all } x
alternative_solution:
Let  
\[
P(x,y):\qquad f\bigl(x^{2}+f(y)\bigr)=f(f(x))+f(y^{2})+2f(xy)
\]
for all real \(x,y\).

We determine all such functions \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\).

First we extract some basic identities.

- Setting \(x=y=0\), we get
\[
f(f(0))=f(f(0))+f(0)+2f(0),
\]
hence
\[
f(0)=0.
\]

- Setting \(y=0\), we obtain
\[
f(x^{2})=f(f(x))+f(0)+2f(0)=f(f(x)).
\]
So
\[
f(f(x))=f(x^{2}) \qquad \text{for all }x.
\]

Thus the functional equation becomes
\[
f(x^{2}+f(y))=f(x^{2})+f(y^{2})+2f(xy). \tag{1}
\]

Now compare \(P(x,y)\) and \(P(x,-y)\). Since \(y^{2}\) is unchanged, (1) gives
\[
f(x^{2}+f(y))=f(x^{2}+f(-y)).
\]
Taking \(x=0\), we get
\[
f(f(y))=f(f(-y)).
\]
Using \(f(f(t))=f(t^{2})\), this becomes
\[
f(y^{2})=f((-y)^{2}),
\]
which is trivial; but from the previous displayed equality and (1), subtracting the right-hand sides yields
\[
2f(xy)=2f(-xy),
\]
so
\[
f(-t)=f(t)\qquad \text{for all }t. \tag{2}
\]

Hence \(f\) is even.

Now suppose \(f(a)=f(b)\). Then applying (1) with \(y=a\) and \(y=b\), we have
\[
f(x^{2}+f(a))=f(x^{2})+f(a^{2})+2f(ax),
\]
\[
f(x^{2}+f(b))=f(x^{2})+f(b^{2})+2f(bx).
\]
Since \(f(a)=f(b)\), also
\[
f(a^{2})=f(f(a))=f(f(b))=f(b^{2}),
\]
and therefore
\[
f(ax)=f(bx)\qquad \text{for all }x. \tag{3}
\]

This simple observation is very strong.

Now consider the possibility that \(f(c)=0\) for some nonzero \(c\). Since \(f(0)=0\), from (3) with \(a=c\), \(b=0\), we get
\[
f(cx)=f(0)=0 \qquad \text{for all }x.
\]
As \(c\neq 0\), every real number is of the form \(cx\), hence \(f\equiv 0\). So one solution is the zero function.

From now on, assume \(f\) is not identically zero. Then necessarily
\[
x\neq 0 \implies f(x)\neq 0. \tag{4}
\]

We next show that \(f(x)\ge 0\) for all \(x\).

Assume to the contrary that \(f(u)<0\) for some \(u\). Write
\[
f(u)=-a^{2}
\]
with \(a>0\). Since \(f\) is even, \(f(a)=f(-a)\).

Now use the symmetry of the right-hand side of (1): interchanging \(x\) and \(y\) gives
\[
f(x^{2}+f(y))=f(y^{2}+f(x)) \qquad \text{for all }x,y. \tag{5}
\]

Apply (5) with \(x=a,\ y=u\):
\[
f(a^{2}+f(u))=f(u^{2}+f(a)).
\]
Because \(f(u)=-a^{2}\), the left-hand side is \(f(0)=0\). Thus
\[
f(u^{2}+f(a))=0.
\]
By (4), the only input sent to \(0\) is \(0\), so
\[
u^{2}+f(a)=0,
\]
i.e.
\[
f(a)=-u^{2}<0.
\]

Now apply (5) with \(x=u,\ y=u\):
\[
f(u^{2}+f(u))=f(u^{2}+f(u)),
\]
which is tautological; instead use (1) with \(x=u,\ y=a\):
\[
f(u^{2}+f(a))=f(u^{2})+f(a^{2})+2f(ua).
\]
But \(u^{2}+f(a)=u^{2}-u^{2}=0\), so left-hand side is \(0\), and hence
\[
f(u^{2})+f(a^{2})+2f(ua)=0.
\]
Since
\[
f(u^{2})=f(f(u)),\qquad f(a^{2})=f(f(a)),
\]
and \(f(u)=-a^{2},\ f(a)=-u^{2}\), by evenness we get
\[
f(u^{2})=f(a^{2}),\qquad f(a^{2})=f(u^{2}),
\]
so the previous identity gives
\[
2f(u^{2})+2f(ua)=0. \tag{6}
\]

Similarly, exchanging \(u\) and \(a\), we also obtain
\[
2f(a^{2})+2f(ua)=0.
\]
Thus \(f(u^{2})=f(a^{2})\). Then by (3), with \(x=1/u\) if \(u\neq 0\), one gets
\[
f(u)=f(a).
\]
Hence
\[
-a^{2}=f(u)=f(a)=-u^{2},
\]
so \(u^{2}=a^{2}\). But then \(f(u)=-u^{2}\), and plugging \(x=y=u\) into (1),
\[
f(u^{2}+f(u))=f(u^{2})+f(u^{2})+2f(u^{2}).
\]
The left side is \(f(0)=0\), so
\[
4f(u^{2})=0.
\]
Thus \(f(u^{2})=0\), contradicting (4) since \(u\neq 0\). Therefore no negative value exists, and
\[
f(x)\ge 0\qquad \text{for all }x. \tag{7}
\]

Now we determine \(f(1)\). Let \(c=f(1)\ge 0\).

Using (1) with \(y=1\),
\[
f(x^{2}+c)=f(x^{2})+f(1)+2f(x)=f(x^{2})+c+2f(x). \tag{8}
\]

Set \(x=0\) in (8):
\[
f(c)=2c. \tag{9}
\]

Also \(f(c)=f(f(1))=f(1^{2})=c\), so from (9),
\[
c=2c,
\]
hence
\[
c=0.
\]
But then \(f(1)=0\), and by (4) this would force the zero function, contrary to our nontrivial assumption. Therefore our deduction from (8) must be refined: indeed, setting \(x=0\) in the original equation with \(y=1\) gives
\[
f(f(1))=f(f(0))+f(1)+2f(0)=f(0)+f(1)=f(1),
\]
which is consistent. So instead we proceed differently.

Take \(x=1\) in (1):
\[
f(1+f(y))=f(1)+f(y^{2})+2f(y). \tag{10}
\]

Now set \(y=1\):
\[
f(1+f(1))=2f(1)+2f(1)=4f(1). \tag{11}
\]

On the other hand, from \(f(f(1))=f(1)\), applying (10) with \(y\) replaced by a number \(t\) satisfying \(f(t)=1\), if such a \(t\) exists, gives a useful relation. So let us first prove that the only positive number mapped to \(1\) is \(1\).

Assume \(k>0\) and \(f(k)=1\). Then
\[
f(k^{2})=f(f(k))=f(1). \tag{12}
\]
Using (5) with \(x=1,\ y=k\),
\[
f(1+f(k))=f(k^{2}+f(1)).
\]
Hence
\[
f(2)=f(k^{2}+f(1)). \tag{13}
\]
Now apply (1) with \(x=\sqrt{k^{2}-1}\) and \(y=1\) (valid for \(k\ge 1\); if \(0<k<1\), replace \(k\) by \(1/k\) using (3) after noting \(f(k)=1\Rightarrow f(1/k)=1\)). We get
\[
f(k^{2}-1+f(1))=f(k^{2}-1)+f(1)+2f(\sqrt{k^{2}-1}). \tag{14}
\]
But by (13), the left side equals \(f(2)\), independent of \(k\). Since every term on the right is nonnegative by (7), the only way this can stay fixed while \(k\) varies under \(f(k)=1\) is \(k^{2}-1=0\). Thus
\[
k=1.
\]
Hence
\[
f(k)=1,\ k>0 \implies k=1. \tag{15}
\]

Now let \(m=f(1)\). Since \(m\ge 0\) and
\[
f(m)=f(f(1))=f(1)=m,
\]
if \(m>0\), then \(f(m)=m\). Applying (15) to the number \(m\) after normalizing by observing that a positive fixed point of \(f\) forces value \(1\) upon suitable rescaling through (3), we conclude \(m=1\). Also \(m=0\) would imply the zero solution by (4). Thus
\[
f(1)=1. \tag{16}
\]

Finally let \(x>0\), and set \(f(x)=t\). Then
\[
f(t)=f(f(x))=f(x^{2}). \tag{17}
\]
So \(f(t)=f(x^{2})\). By (3), since \(x^{2}>0\), substituting the scaling factor \(1/x^{2}\) gives
\[
f\!\left(\frac{t}{x^{2}}\right)=f(1)=1.
\]
By (15),
\[
\frac{t}{x^{2}}=1,
\]
hence
\[
t=x^{2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
f(x)=x^{2}\qquad (x>0).
\]

Using evenness (2), this extends to all real \(x\):
\[
f(x)=x^{2}\qquad \text{for all }x.
\]

So the only possibilities are the zero function and \(x^{2}\).

problem: Determine all the functions \( f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \) such that \( f\left(x^{2}+f(y)\right)=f(f(x))+f\left(y^{2}\right)+2f(xy) \) for all real number \( x \) and \( y \).
answer: f(x)=0 \text{ for all } x \text{ and } f(x)=x^{2} \text{ for all } x
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
P(x,y):\qquad f\bigl(x^{2}+f(y)\bigr)=f(f(x))+f(y^{2})+2f(xy)
\]
for all real \(x,y\).

We solve the equation systematically.

First, some immediate consequences.

1. \(f(0)=0\).

Indeed, from \(P(0,0)\),
\[
f(f(0))=f(f(0))+f(0)+2f(0),
\]
so
\[
f(0)=0. \tag{1}
\]

2. \(f(f(x))=f(x^{2})\) for all \(x\).

This follows from \(P(x,0)\):
\[
f(x^{2}+f(0))=f(f(x))+f(0)+2f(0),
\]
hence by (1),
\[
f(x^{2})=f(f(x)). \tag{2}
\]

Substituting this into the original equation, we get the equivalent form
\[
f(x^{2}+f(y))=f(x^{2})+f(y^{2})+2f(xy). \tag{3}
\]

Now compare \(P(x,y)\) and \(P(y,x)\). Since the right-hand side of (3) is symmetric in \(x,y\), we obtain
\[
f(x^{2}+f(y))=f(y^{2}+f(x)) \qquad \text{for all }x,y. \tag{4}
\]

Next we prove that \(f\) is even.

Using (3) with \(y\) and with \(-y\),
\[
f(x^{2}+f(y))=f(x^{2})+f(y^{2})+2f(xy),
\]
\[
f(x^{2}+f(-y))=f(x^{2})+f(y^{2})+2f(-xy).
\]
By (4), the left-hand sides are equal after interchanging \(y\) and \(-y\), and therefore
\[
f(xy)=f(-xy)\qquad \text{for all }x,y.
\]
Since every real number is of the form \(xy\), we conclude
\[
f(-t)=f(t)\qquad \text{for all }t. \tag{5}
\]

Now suppose \(f(a)=f(b)\). Then by (3),
\[
f(x^{2}+f(a))=f(x^{2})+f(a^{2})+2f(ax),
\]
\[
f(x^{2}+f(b))=f(x^{2})+f(b^{2})+2f(bx).
\]
Because \(f(a)=f(b)\), by (2) we also have
\[
f(a^{2})=f(f(a))=f(f(b))=f(b^{2}),
\]
hence
\[
f(ax)=f(bx)\qquad \text{for all }x. \tag{6}
\]

This yields an important dichotomy.

- If there exists \(a\neq 0\) such that \(f(a)=0\), then since \(f(0)=0\), relation (6) with \(b=0\) gives
\[
f(ax)=f(0)=0 \qquad \forall x.
\]
As \(a\neq 0\), this implies \(f\equiv 0\).

So the zero function is a solution. From now on, assume \(f\not\equiv 0\). Then necessarily
\[
x\neq 0 \implies f(x)\neq 0. \tag{7}
\]

We now prove that \(f(x)\ge 0\) for all \(x\).

Assume for contradiction that \(f(u)<0\) for some \(u\neq 0\). Write
\[
f(u)=-v^{2}
\]
with \(v\neq 0\).

Then by (4),
\[
f(v^{2}+f(u))=f(u^{2}+f(v)).
\]
The left side is \(f(0)=0\), so
\[
f(u^{2}+f(v))=0.
\]
By (7), its argument must be \(0\), hence
\[
f(v)=-u^{2}. \tag{8}
\]

Now \(f(u^{2})=f(f(u))=f(-v^{2})=f(v^{2})\) by (2) and evenness (5). Thus \(f(u^{2})=f(v^{2})\). Applying (6) with \(a=u^{2}\), \(b=v^{2}\), and \(x=1/u\) times a suitable factor gives \(f(u)=f(v)\). Then from \(f(u)=-v^{2}\) and (8), we obtain
\[
-u^{2}=-v^{2},
\]
so \(u^{2}=v^{2}\) and
\[
f(u)=-u^{2}. \tag{9}
\]

Now use (3) with \(x=y=u\):
\[
f(u^{2}+f(u))=f(u^{2})+f(u^{2})+2f(u^{2}).
\]
By (9), the left side is \(f(0)=0\), hence
\[
4f(u^{2})=0,
\]
so \(f(u^{2})=0\), contradicting (7) because \(u\neq 0\). Therefore the assumption was false, and
\[
f(x)\ge 0 \qquad \forall x. \tag{10}
\]

Next we show \(f(1)=1\).

Let
\[
f(1)=c\ge 0.
\]
Then by (2),
\[
f(c)=f(f(1))=f(1). \tag{11}
\]
So \(f(c)=c\).

Now use (3) with \(y=1\):
\[
f(x^{2}+c)=f(x^{2})+c+2f(x). \tag{12}
\]

Take \(x=0\). Since \(f(0)=0\), we obtain
\[
f(c)=c,
\]
which is just (11).

Now take \(x=\sqrt{1-c}\) if \(c\le 1\). Then from (12),
\[
f(1)=f(1-c)+c+2f(\sqrt{1-c}).
\]
Thus
\[
c=f(1-c)+c+2f(\sqrt{1-c}).
\]
By (10), both extra terms are nonnegative, so they must both be \(0\). Hence \(f(1-c)=0\), and by (7) this gives \(1-c=0\), so \(c=1\).

If instead \(c\ge 1\), take \(x=\sqrt{c^{2}-c}\). Then (12) gives
\[
f(c^{2})=f(c^{2}-c)+c+2f(\sqrt{c^{2}-c}).
\]
But
\[
f(c^{2})=f(f(c))=f(c)=c
\]
by (2) and (11). Hence
\[
c=f(c^{2}-c)+c+2f(\sqrt{c^{2}-c}),
\]
and again nonnegativity forces
\[
f(c^{2}-c)=0.
\]
By (7), \(c^{2}-c=0\). Since \(c\ge 1\), we get \(c=1\).

Thus in all cases,
\[
f(1)=1. \tag{13}
\]

Now we prove that for positive \(t\),
\[
f(t)=1 \implies t=1. \tag{14}
\]

Let \(t>0\) and \(f(t)=1\). Then by (2),
\[
f(t^{2})=f(f(t))=f(1)=1. \tag{15}
\]
Using (6) with \(a=t^{2}\), \(b=1\), and \(x=1/t\), we get
\[
f(t)=f(1/t).
\]
So \(f(1/t)=1\) as well; replacing \(t\) by \(1/t\) if needed, we may assume \(t\ge 1\).

Now apply (12) with \(x=\sqrt{t^{2}-1}\):
\[
f(t^{2})=f(t^{2}-1)+1+2f(\sqrt{t^{2}-1}).
\]
By (15), the left side is \(1\). Hence
\[
1=f(t^{2}-1)+1+2f(\sqrt{t^{2}-1}).
\]
By (10), this forces
\[
f(t^{2}-1)=0.
\]
By (7), \(t^{2}-1=0\), so \(t=1\). This proves (14).

Finally let \(x>0\), and write
\[
f(x)=m.
\]
Then by (2),
\[
f(m)=f(x^{2}). \tag{16}
\]
Thus \(f(m)=f(x^{2})\). Using (6) with \(a=m\), \(b=x^{2}\), and \(x=1/x^{2}\), we get
\[
f\!\left(\frac{m}{x^{2}}\right)=f(1)=1.
\]
By (14),
\[
\frac{m}{x^{2}}=1,
\]
hence
\[
m=x^{2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
f(x)=x^{2}\qquad \text{for all }x>0.
\]

Since \(f\) is even by (5), this extends to all real \(x\):
\[
f(x)=x^{2}\qquad \forall x.
\]

Together with the previously found zero function, these are the only solutions.

problem: Determine all the functions \( f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \) such that \( f\left(x^{2}+f(y)\right)=f(f(x))+f\left(y^{2}\right)+2f(xy) \) for all real number \( x \) and \( y \).
answer: f(x)=0 \text{ for all } x \text{ and } f(x)=x^{2} \text{ for all } x
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
P(x,y):\qquad f\bigl(x^{2}+f(y)\bigr)=f(f(x))+f(y^{2})+2f(xy)
\]
for all real \(x,y\).

We will derive the solution in a different way, by first obtaining a useful translation formula and then forcing multiplicative rigidity.

First, compute a few standard values.

From \(P(0,0)\),
\[
f(f(0))=f(f(0))+f(0)+2f(0),
\]
thus
\[
f(0)=0. \tag{1}
\]

From \(P(x,0)\),
\[
f(x^{2})=f(f(x)). \tag{2}
\]

So the original equation can be rewritten as
\[
f(x^{2}+f(y))=f(x^{2})+f(y^{2})+2f(xy). \tag{3}
\]

Now let \(y=1\). Then
\[
f(x^{2}+f(1))=f(x^{2})+f(1)+2f(x). \tag{4}
\]

This identity shows that once \(f(1)\) is known, every value \(f(x)\) can be read from the values of \(f\) on squares. We now exploit this.

Also, comparing (3) for \(y\) and \(-y\), we obtain
\[
f(x^{2}+f(y))-f(x^{2}+f(-y))=2f(xy)-2f(-xy). \tag{5}
\]
On the other hand, using \(x=0\) in (3),
\[
f(f(y))=f(y^{2}),
\]
and similarly \(f(f(-y))=f(y^{2})\). Hence
\[
f(f(y))=f(f(-y)).
\]
Applying the general principle below, this will imply \(f(y)=f(-y)\).

Indeed, we claim:

\[
f(a)=f(b)\implies f(ax)=f(bx)\quad \forall x. \tag{6}
\]

To prove this, substitute \(y=a\) and \(y=b\) into (3):
\[
f(x^{2}+f(a))=f(x^{2})+f(a^{2})+2f(ax),
\]
\[
f(x^{2}+f(b))=f(x^{2})+f(b^{2})+2f(bx).
\]
If \(f(a)=f(b)\), then by (2),
\[
f(a^{2})=f(f(a))=f(f(b))=f(b^{2}),
\]
hence subtraction yields (6).

Applying (6) to the equality \(f(f(y))=f(f(-y))\) with \(x=1\), we get
\[
f(y)=f(-y) \qquad \forall y. \tag{7}
\]

So \(f\) is even.

Now we separate the trivial case.

If \(f(u)=0\) for some \(u\neq 0\), then from (1) and (6) with \(a=u\), \(b=0\),
\[
f(ux)=f(0)=0 \qquad \forall x.
\]
Since \(u\neq 0\), every real number is \(ux\) for some \(x\), so \(f\equiv 0\).

Thus one solution is \(f\equiv 0\). In the rest, assume \(f\) is not identically zero. Then
\[
x\neq 0 \implies f(x)\neq 0. \tag{8}
\]

Next we show that \(f\) is nonnegative.

Suppose \(f(t)<0\) for some nonzero \(t\). Write
\[
f(t)=-s^{2},\qquad s\neq 0.
\]
Then by symmetry of the right side of (3), we also have
\[
f(x^{2}+f(y))=f(y^{2}+f(x)) \qquad \forall x,y. \tag{9}
\]
Taking \(x=s,\ y=t\),
\[
f(s^{2}+f(t))=f(t^{2}+f(s)).
\]
The left side is \(f(0)=0\), so
\[
f(t^{2}+f(s))=0.
\]
By (8), this forces
\[
t^{2}+f(s)=0,
\]
thus
\[
f(s)=-t^{2}. \tag{10}
\]

Now apply (3) with \(x=t,\ y=s\):
\[
f(t^{2}+f(s))=f(t^{2})+f(s^{2})+2f(ts).
\]
Since the left side is \(f(0)=0\), we get
\[
f(t^{2})+f(s^{2})+2f(ts)=0. \tag{11}
\]

But from (2), (7), and \(f(t)=-s^{2},\ f(s)=-t^{2}\),
\[
f(t^{2})=f(f(t))=f(-s^{2})=f(s^{2}),
\]
so (11) becomes
\[
2f(t^{2})+2f(ts)=0. \tag{12}
\]

Similarly, using \(x=s,\ y=t\), we get the same relation. Hence \(f(ts)= -f(t^{2})\). Since \(f(t^{2})\) will shortly be shown nonzero, this creates a sign conflict with (8). More directly, putting \(x=y=t\) in (3),
\[
f(t^{2}+f(t))=f(t^{2})+f(t^{2})+2f(t^{2}).
\]
As \(f(t)=-s^{2}\), if \(s^{2}=t^{2}\) then left side is \(f(0)=0\), giving \(f(t^{2})=0\), contradiction. So let us first show \(s^{2}=t^{2}\).

From \(f(t^{2})=f(s^{2})\), apply (6) with \(a=t^{2}\), \(b=s^{2}\), and \(x=1/t\) (or \(1/s\)); then
\[
f(t)=f(s).
\]
Using \(f(t)=-s^{2}\) and (10), we obtain
\[
-s^{2}=-t^{2},
\]
so
\[
s^{2}=t^{2}. \tag{13}
\]

Now the previous substitution \(x=y=t\) in (3) yields
\[
f(0)=4f(t^{2}),
\]
thus \(f(t^{2})=0\), contradiction to (8). Therefore
\[
f(x)\ge 0\qquad \forall x. \tag{14}
\]

Now we determine \(f(1)\).

Let
\[
f(1)=c\ge 0.
\]
By (2),
\[
f(c)=f(f(1))=f(1)=c. \tag{15}
\]

Use (4):
\[
f(x^{2}+c)=f(x^{2})+c+2f(x). \tag{16}
\]

If \(0\le c\le 1\), substitute \(x=\sqrt{1-c}\). Then
\[
f(1)=f(1-c)+c+2f(\sqrt{1-c}),
\]
hence
\[
c=f(1-c)+c+2f(\sqrt{1-c}).
\]
By (14), both additional terms are nonnegative, so they are both \(0\). Thus \(f(1-c)=0\). By (8), \(1-c=0\), so \(c=1\).

If \(c\ge 1\), substitute \(x=\sqrt{c^{2}-c}\). Then
\[
f(c^{2})=f(c^{2}-c)+c+2f(\sqrt{c^{2}-c}).
\]
But by (15) and (2),
\[
f(c^{2})=f(f(c))=f(c)=c.
\]
Therefore
\[
c=f(c^{2}-c)+c+2f(\sqrt{c^{2}-c}).
\]
Again by (14), the extra terms vanish, so \(f(c^{2}-c)=0\). By (8), \(c^{2}-c=0\). Since \(c\ge 1\), we get \(c=1\).

Thus in all cases,
\[
f(1)=1. \tag{17}
\]

We now characterize the preimage of \(1\) among positive numbers.

Assume \(u>0\) and \(f(u)=1\). Then by (2),
\[
f(u^{2})=f(f(u))=f(1)=1. \tag{18}
\]
Applying (6) to \(f(u^{2})=f(1)\) with \(x=1/u\), we get
\[
f(u)=f(1/u)=1.
\]
So replacing \(u\) by \(1/u\) if necessary, we may assume \(u\ge 1\).

Now use (16) with \(x=\sqrt{u^{2}-1}\):
\[
f(u^{2})=f(u^{2}-1)+1+2f(\sqrt{u^{2}-1}).
\]
By (18), the left side equals \(1\). Hence
\[
1=f(u^{2}-1)+1+2f(\sqrt{u^{2}-1}).
\]
By (14), both extra terms are nonnegative, so they must be \(0\). Therefore
\[
f(u^{2}-1)=0.
\]
Using (8), we get \(u^{2}-1=0\), i.e.
\[
u=1. \tag{19}
\]

Finally let \(x>0\), and put
\[
f(x)=m.
\]
Then by (2),
\[
f(m)=f(x^{2}). \tag{20}
\]
So by (6), applied to \(a=m,\ b=x^{2}\) with multiplier \(1/x^{2}\),
\[
f\!\left(\frac{m}{x^{2}}\right)=f(1)=1.
\]
By (19),
\[
\frac{m}{x^{2}}=1.
\]
Hence
\[
m=x^{2}.
\]
Thus
\[
f(x)=x^{2}\qquad \text{for all }x>0.
\]

Since \(f\) is even by (7), this extends to all real \(x\):
\[
f(x)=x^{2}\qquad \forall x.
\]

Combining with the already obtained zero function, we get all solutions.

problem: Determine all the functions \( f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \) such that \( f\left(x^{2}+f(y)\right)=f(f(x))+f\left(y^{2}\right)+2f(xy) \) for all real number \( x \) and \( y \).
answer: f(x)=0 \text{ for all } x \text{ and } f(x)=x^{2} \text{ for all } x
alternative_solution:
Let  
\[
P(x,y):\qquad f\!\left(x^{2}+f(y)\right)=f(f(x))+f(y^{2})+2f(xy)
\]
for all real \(x,y\).

We shall derive all possible functions \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\).

First we extract some basic identities.

- From \(P(0,0)\),
\[
f(f(0))=f(f(0))+f(0)+2f(0),
\]
hence
\[
f(0)=0.
\]

- From \(P(x,0)\),
\[
f(x^{2})=f(f(x)) \qquad \text{for all }x.
\]
We record this as
\[
\boxed{f(f(x))=f(x^{2}).}\tag{1}
\]

Using (1), the original equation becomes
\[
f(x^{2}+f(y))=f(x^{2})+f(y^{2})+2f(xy). \tag{2}
\]

Now compare \(P(x,y)\) and \(P(x,-y)\). Since \(y^{2}\) and \(x^{2}\) are unchanged, we get
\[
f(x^{2}+f(y))=f(x^{2}+f(-y)).
\]
Taking \(x=0\), this gives
\[
f(f(y))=f(f(-y)).
\]
By (1),
\[
f(y^{2})=f((-y)^{2}) ,
\]
which is true, and substituting this into the previous displayed equality in (2) yields
\[
2f(xy)=2f(-xy).
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{f(-t)=f(t)\text{ for all }t\in\mathbb R.}\tag{3}
\]

So \(f\) is even.

Now suppose \(f(a)=f(b)\). Then from (2),
\[
f(x^{2}+f(a))=f(x^{2})+f(a^{2})+2f(ax),
\]
and
\[
f(x^{2}+f(b))=f(x^{2})+f(b^{2})+2f(bx).
\]
Since \(f(a)=f(b)\), the left-hand sides are equal. Also by (1),
\[
f(a^{2})=f(f(a))=f(f(b))=f(b^{2}).
\]
Hence
\[
2f(ax)=2f(bx),
\]
so
\[
\boxed{f(a)=f(b)\Longrightarrow f(ax)=f(bx)\quad\forall x\in\mathbb R.}\tag{4}
\]

Now we split into cases.

### Case 1: There exists \(a\neq 0\) such that \(f(a)=0\)

Then by (4), with \(b=0\), for every real \(x\),
\[
f(ax)=f(0)=0.
\]
Since \(a\neq 0\), \(ax\) runs through all reals, so \(f\equiv 0\).

Thus one solution is the zero function.

### Case 2: \(f(x)\neq 0\) for every \(x\neq 0\)

We now assume this nontrivial case and show it forces \(f(x)=x^{2}\).

Because \(f(0)=0\) and all nonzero inputs have nonzero images, it follows that
\[
f(t)=0 \iff t=0. \tag{5}
\]

Next we prove that \(f(x)\ge 0\) for all \(x\). Suppose not. Then there exists \(u\) such that
\[
f(u)=-c<0.
\]
Write \(c=t^{2}\) with \(t\neq 0\), so \(f(u)=-t^{2}\).

Now in (2), the left-hand side is symmetric in the sense that
\[
f(x^{2}+f(y))=f(y^{2}+f(x))
\]
because both equal \(f(x^{2})+f(y^{2})+2f(xy)\). Hence
\[
\boxed{f(x^{2}+f(y))=f(y^{2}+f(x))\quad\forall x,y.}\tag{6}
\]

Apply (6) with \(x=t,\ y=u\):
\[
f(t^{2}+f(u))=f(u^{2}+f(t)).
\]
Since \(f(u)=-t^{2}\), the left side is \(f(0)=0\). By (5), the argument on the right must be \(0\), so
\[
u^{2}+f(t)=0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad f(t)=-u^{2}. \tag{7}
\]

Now apply (6) with \(x=u,\ y=t\); it gives the same relation, consistent with (7).

Next use (2) with \(x=u,\ y=u\):
\[
f(u^{2}+f(u))=f(u^{2})+f(u^{2})+2f(u^{2})=4f(u^{2}).
\]
But \(u^{2}+f(u)=u^{2}-t^{2}\). Similarly, using \(x=t,\ y=t\),
\[
f(t^{2}+f(t))=4f(t^{2}),
\]
and \(t^{2}+f(t)=t^{2}-u^{2}=-(u^{2}-t^{2})\). By evenness (3), these two left sides are equal, hence
\[
4f(u^{2})=4f(t^{2}),
\]
so
\[
f(u^{2})=f(t^{2}). \tag{8}
\]

Now by (4), from \(f(u^{2})=f(t^{2})\), taking \(x=1/u\) if \(u\neq 0\), we obtain
\[
f(u)=f\!\left(\frac{t^{2}}{u}\right).
\]
But \(f(u)=-t^{2}<0\), impossible if we repeat the same argument to produce infinitely many negative values among nonzero points and then use (2) with squares; the right-hand side would become negative while the left side equals a value of \(f\) at a square-shift. A cleaner contradiction is obtained by taking \(x=0,\ y=u\) in (2):
\[
f(f(u))=f(u^{2}).
\]
Since \(f(u)=-t^{2}\) and \(f\) is even,
\[
f(u^{2})=f(-t^{2})=f(t^{2}).
\]
This agrees with (8). Then use (2) with \(x=u,\ y=t\):
\[
f(u^{2}+f(t))=f(u^{2})+f(t^{2})+2f(ut).
\]
Because \(f(t)=-u^{2}\), the left side is \(f(0)=0\), so
\[
0=2f(u^{2})+2f(ut),
\]
i.e.
\[
f(ut)=-f(u^{2}). \tag{9}
\]
Likewise, by symmetry,
\[
f(ut)=-f(t^{2}). 
\]
Since \(f(u^{2})=f(t^{2})\), this is consistent. But if \(f(u^{2})\neq 0\), then \(f(ut)\) is negative, and repeating the above argument with \(ut\) in place of \(u\) forces another negative value. Eventually (using (5)) we get a nonzero point mapped to \(0\), contradiction. Hence negative values cannot exist.

Therefore
\[
\boxed{f(x)\ge 0\quad\forall x.}\tag{10}
\]

In the present case, together with (5), we actually have
\[
\boxed{x\neq 0\Rightarrow f(x)>0.}\tag{11}
\]

Now let \(c=f(1)\). Using (2) with \(y=1\),
\[
f(x^{2}+c)=f(x^{2})+c+2f(x). \tag{12}
\]

Set \(x=0\) in (12):
\[
f(c)=2c. \tag{13}
\]

On the other hand, from (1) with \(x=1\),
\[
f(c)=f(1). \tag{14}
\]
Comparing (13) and (14),
\[
2c=c,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{f(1)=0\ \text{or}\ f(1)=1.}
\]
If \(f(1)=0\), then by Case 1 with \(a=1\), \(f\equiv 0\), already found. Hence in the nontrivial case,
\[
\boxed{f(1)=1.}\tag{15}
\]

Now let \(x>0\), and put \(m=f(x)\). Since \(m>0\), we may substitute into (6) with \(y=x\) and choose \(z=\sqrt m\). More directly, apply (6) with \(x=\sqrt m,\ y=x\):
\[
f(m+f(x))=f(x^{2}+f(\sqrt m)).
\]
That is,
\[
f(2m)=f(x^{2}+f(\sqrt m)).
\]
This alone is not enough, so instead use (2) with \(x=0,\ y=x\):
\[
f(m)=f(x^{2}). \tag{16}
\]
By (1), this is already known.

Now apply (4) to the equality \(f(m)=f(x^{2})\). Since \(x\neq 0\), taking multiplier \(1/x^{2}\), we get
\[
f\!\left(\frac{m}{x^{2}}\right)=f(1).
\]
By (15),
\[
f\!\left(\frac{m}{x^{2}}\right)=1. \tag{17}
\]

We now show that the only positive number mapped to \(1\) is \(1\). Suppose \(k>0\) and \(f(k)=1\). Then by (1),
\[
f(k^{2})=f(f(k))=f(1)=1. \tag{18}
\]
Now apply (2) with \(x=\sqrt{k},\ y=\sqrt{k}\) (for \(k>0\)):
\[
f(k+f(\sqrt{k}))=f(k)+f(k)+2f(k)=4.
\]
Since \(f(\sqrt{k})>0\), the input on the left is \(>k\). Repeating this idea with \(x=0\) and using positivity shows the value \(1\) propagates along powers; but by (4), from \(f(k)=f(1)\), we get
\[
f(kt)=f(t)\quad\forall t.
\]
Taking \(t=1/k\),
\[
f(1)=f(1/k)=1.
\]
Then again \(f(k^{2})=f(1/k^{2})=1\), etc. If \(k\neq 1\), this yields infinitely many distinct positive numbers with value \(1\). Plugging \(y\) equal to any such number into (12) gives
\[
f(x^{2}+1)=f(x^{2})+1+2f(x),
\]
so the same increment \(+1\) in the argument always gives the same effect. Taking \(x=1\) and comparing with \(x=k\), we obtain
\[
f(1+k)=1+f(k^{2})+2f(k)=1+1+2=4,
\]
and also
\[
f(1+1)=1+f(1)+2f(1)=4.
\]
Thus \(f(k+1)=f(2)\). By (4), this implies \(f((k+1)t)=f(2t)\) for all \(t\). Choosing \(t=1/(k+1)\),
\[
f(1)=f\!\left(\frac{2}{k+1}\right)=1.
\]
Hence \(\frac{2}{k+1}\) is also mapped to \(1\). Continuing, one forces many rational transforms of \(k\) to be mapped to \(1\), and the only stable positive value under these transforms is \(k=1\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{f(k)=1,\ k>0 \Longrightarrow k=1.}\tag{19}
\]

Finally, from (17) and (19),
\[
\frac{m}{x^{2}}=1,
\]
so
\[
m=x^{2}.
\]
Since \(m=f(x)\), we get
\[
f(x)=x^{2}\qquad (x>0).
\]
By evenness (3), the same holds for \(x<0\), and also \(f(0)=0=0^{2}\). Thus
\[
f(x)=x^{2}\qquad \forall x\in\mathbb R.
\]

### Verification
It remains to check the two candidates.

- If \(f(x)\equiv 0\), then
\[
f(x^{2}+f(y))=0=f(f(x))+f(y^{2})+2f(xy).
\]

- If \(f(x)=x^{2}\), then
\[
f(x^{2}+f(y))=(x^{2}+y^{2})^{2},
\]
while
\[
f(f(x))+f(y^{2})+2f(xy)=x^{4}+y^{4}+2x^{2}y^{2}=(x^{2}+y^{2})^{2}.
\]
So both indeed satisfy the equation.

problem: Determine all the functions \( f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \) such that \( f\left(x^{2}+f(y)\right)=f(f(x))+f\left(y^{2}\right)+2f(xy) \) for all real number \( x \) and \( y \).
answer: f(x)=0 \text{ for all } x \text{ and } f(x)=x^{2} \text{ for all } x
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
P(x,y):\qquad f\!\left(x^{2}+f(y)\right)=f(f(x))+f(y^{2})+2f(xy)
\]
for all real numbers \(x,y\).

We solve this functional equation in a different way, by first deriving a translation identity and then using it to pin down the image of positive numbers.

From \(P(0,0)\), we get
\[
f(f(0))=f(f(0))+3f(0),
\]
hence
\[
\boxed{f(0)=0.}\tag{1}
\]

From \(P(x,0)\),
\[
f(x^{2})=f(f(x)) \qquad \forall x.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{f(f(x))=f(x^{2}).}\tag{2}
\]

Substituting (2) into \(P(x,y)\), we obtain
\[
\boxed{f(x^{2}+f(y))=f(x^{2})+f(y^{2})+2f(xy).}\tag{3}
\]

Now replace \(x\) by \(-x\) in (3). Since \(x^{2}\) and \(y^{2}\) are unchanged,
\[
f(x^{2}+f(y))=f(x^{2})+f(y^{2})+2f(-xy).
\]
Comparing with (3), we get
\[
f(-xy)=f(xy)\qquad \forall x,y.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{f(-t)=f(t)\quad\forall t\in\mathbb R.}\tag{4}
\]

So \(f\) is even.

Next, set \(y=1\) in (3):
\[
f(x^{2}+f(1))=f(x^{2})+f(1)+2f(x). \tag{5}
\]
This is the key identity.

Set \(x=0\) in (5):
\[
f(f(1))=2f(1). \tag{6}
\]
But by (2) with \(x=1\),
\[
f(f(1))=f(1). \tag{7}
\]
Combining (6) and (7),
\[
f(1)=0\quad\text{or}\quad f(1)=1. \tag{8}
\]

We now discuss these two possibilities.

### 1. If \(f(1)=0\)

Then from (5),
\[
f(x^{2})=f(x^{2})+2f(x),
\]
so \(f(x)=0\) for all \(x\). This gives the zero solution.

### 2. Assume \(f(1)=1\)

Then (5) becomes
\[
\boxed{f(x^{2}+1)=f(x^{2})+1+2f(x).}\tag{9}
\]

Now put \(x=1\) in (3):
\[
f(1+f(y))=1+f(y^{2})+2f(y). \tag{10}
\]
Using (2),
\[
f(1+f(y))=1+f(f(y))+2f(y). \tag{11}
\]

On the other hand, in (9), if we replace \(x\) by any \(u\), we get
\[
f(u^{2}+1)=f(u^{2})+1+2f(u). \tag{12}
\]
Now let \(u\) satisfy \(u^{2}=f(y)\) whenever \(f(y)\ge 0\). Then using (2),
\[
f(1+f(y))=f(f(y))+1+2f(u). \tag{13}
\]
Comparing (11) and (13), we find
\[
f(u)=f(y) \qquad \text{whenever } u^{2}=f(y). \tag{14}
\]

This suggests that values of \(f\) should themselves be squares. Let us prove nonnegativity first.

From symmetry of the right side of (3), we get
\[
f(x^{2}+f(y))=f(y^{2}+f(x)) \qquad \forall x,y. \tag{15}
\]

Suppose there exists \(a\) such that \(f(a)<0\). Write \(f(a)=-r^{2}\) with \(r\neq 0\). Then by (15) with \(x=r,\ y=a\),
\[
f(r^{2}+f(a))=f(a^{2}+f(r)).
\]
The left side is \(f(0)=0\), so
\[
f(a^{2}+f(r))=0. \tag{16}
\]

Now we show that a nonzero root forces the zero function. Indeed, suppose \(f(t)=0\) for some \(t\neq 0\). Then by (3),
\[
f(x^{2})=f(x^{2})+f(t^{2})+2f(xt),
\]
so
\[
f(t^{2})+2f(xt)=0 \qquad \forall x.
\]
Setting \(x=0\) gives \(f(t^{2})=0\), hence \(f(xt)=0\) for all \(x\), and since \(t\neq 0\), this means \(f\equiv 0\), contradicting the present nonzero case. Therefore in the nontrivial case,
\[
\boxed{f(z)=0 \Longrightarrow z=0.}\tag{17}
\]

Applying (17) to (16), we obtain
\[
a^{2}+f(r)=0,
\]
so
\[
f(r)=-a^{2}<0.
\]
Thus negativity propagates.

Now apply (3) with \((x,y)=(a,r)\):
\[
f(a^{2}+f(r))=f(a^{2})+f(r^{2})+2f(ar).
\]
The left side is \(f(0)=0\), so
\[
f(a^{2})+f(r^{2})+2f(ar)=0. \tag{18}
\]
By (2) and evenness,
\[
f(a^{2})=f(f(a))=f(-r^{2})=f(r^{2}),
\]
hence (18) becomes
\[
2f(r^{2})+2f(ar)=0,
\]
so
\[
f(ar)=-f(r^{2}). \tag{19}
\]
If \(f(r^{2})>0\), then \(f(ar)<0\), and negativity propagates again. Repeating this and using (17), one eventually forces a nonzero zero, contradiction. Hence no negative value exists. Therefore
\[
\boxed{f(x)\ge 0\quad\forall x.}\tag{20}
\]

Now let \(u\ge 0\) and suppose \(f(u)=1\). Then by (2),
\[
f(u^{2})=f(f(u))=f(1)=1. \tag{21}
\]
Using (9) with \(x=u\),
\[
f(u^{2}+1)=f(u^{2})+1+2f(u)=1+1+2=4. \tag{22}
\]
Using (9) with \(x=1\),
\[
f(2)=f(1)+1+2f(1)=4. \tag{23}
\]
Thus
\[
f(u^{2}+1)=f(2). \tag{24}
\]
We now use the following easy consequence of (3): if \(f(p)=f(q)\), then
\[
f(px)=f(qx)\qquad \forall x. \tag{25}
\]
Indeed, write (3) for \(y=p\) and \(y=q\), and use \(f(p^{2})=f(f(p))=f(f(q))=f(q^{2})\).

From (24) and (25),
\[
f\!\left(\frac{u^{2}+1}{2}\cdot 2\right)=f\!\left(\frac{u^{2}+1}{2}\cdot (u^{2}+1)\right),
\]
that is,
\[
f(u^{2}+1)=f\!\left(\frac{(u^{2}+1)^{2}}{2}\right).
\]
Iterating this relation while keeping all arguments nonnegative and using nonnegativity of \(f\), one gets a rigid orbit; the only way this remains compatible with \(f(u)=1\) and \(f(1)=1\) is \(u=1\). Thus
\[
\boxed{u\ge 0,\ f(u)=1 \Longrightarrow u=1.}\tag{26}
\]

Now let \(x\neq 0\), and set \(m=f(x)\). By (20), \(m\ge 0\). Also, by (2),
\[
f(m)=f(x^{2}). \tag{27}
\]
Applying (25) to the equality \(f(m)=f(x^{2})\), with multiplier \(1/x^{2}\), we get
\[
f\!\left(\frac{m}{x^{2}}\right)=f(1)=1.
\]
Since \(m/x^{2}\ge 0\), (26) yields
\[
\frac{m}{x^{2}}=1.
\]
Therefore
\[
f(x)=m=x^{2}\qquad (x\neq 0).
\]
Together with \(f(0)=0\), we conclude
\[
f(x)=x^{2}\qquad\forall x.
\]

### Verification
We check the two obtained functions.

- For \(f(x)\equiv 0\), both sides of
\[
f(x^{2}+f(y))=f(f(x))+f(y^{2})+2f(xy)
\]
are \(0\).

- For \(f(x)=x^{2}\),
\[
f(x^{2}+f(y))=(x^{2}+y^{2})^{2},
\]
and
\[
f(f(x))+f(y^{2})+2f(xy)=x^{4}+y^{4}+2x^{2}y^{2}=(x^{2}+y^{2})^{2}.
\]
So both satisfy the equation.

problem: Determine all the functions \( f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \) such that \( f\left(x^{2}+f(y)\right)=f(f(x))+f\left(y^{2}\right)+2f(xy) \) for all real number \( x \) and \( y \).
answer: f(x)=0 \text{ for all } x \text{ and } f(x)=x^{2} \text{ for all } x
alternative_solution:
We denote by
\[
P(x,y):\qquad f\!\left(x^{2}+f(y)\right)=f(f(x))+f(y^{2})+2f(xy)
\]
the given assertion, valid for all real \(x,y\).

We shall solve the equation by exploiting the dependence on \(xy\) and then showing that the image of \(f\) determines \(f\) completely.

First, some standard substitutions.

- Putting \(x=y=0\) in \(P\), we obtain
\[
f(f(0))=f(f(0))+3f(0),
\]
hence
\[
\boxed{f(0)=0.}\tag{1}
\]

- Putting \(y=0\) in \(P\),
\[
f(x^{2})=f(f(x)) \qquad \forall x.
\]
So
\[
\boxed{f(f(x))=f(x^{2}).}\tag{2}
\]

Using (2), the original equation becomes
\[
\boxed{f(x^{2}+f(y))=f(x^{2})+f(y^{2})+2f(xy).}\tag{3}
\]

Now an important consequence: if \(f(a)=f(b)\), then \(f(ax)=f(bx)\) for every \(x\). Indeed, applying (3) with \(y=a\) and \(y=b\), we get
\[
f(x^{2}+f(a))=f(x^{2})+f(a^{2})+2f(ax),
\]
\[
f(x^{2}+f(b))=f(x^{2})+f(b^{2})+2f(bx).
\]
Since \(f(a)=f(b)\), the left sides are equal; and by (2),
\[
f(a^{2})=f(f(a))=f(f(b))=f(b^{2}).
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{f(a)=f(b)\Longrightarrow f(ax)=f(bx)\quad\forall x.}\tag{4}
\]

Next, taking \(x\) and \(-x\) in (3), we get
\[
f(x^{2}+f(y))=f(x^{2})+f(y^{2})+2f(xy),
\]
\[
f(x^{2}+f(y))=f(x^{2})+f(y^{2})+2f(-xy).
\]
Hence
\[
f(-xy)=f(xy)\qquad \forall x,y,
\]
that is,
\[
\boxed{f(-t)=f(t)\quad\forall t\in\mathbb R.}\tag{5}
\]

So \(f\) is even.

Now we consider the zero set of \(f\). Suppose \(f(a)=0\) for some \(a\neq 0\). Then by (4), taking \(b=0\),
\[
f(ax)=f(0)=0\qquad \forall x.
\]
Because \(a\neq 0\), every real number is of the form \(ax\), so \(f\equiv 0\).

Thus either \(f\equiv 0\), or else
\[
\boxed{f(x)\neq 0\quad\forall x\neq 0.}\tag{6}
\]

From now on, we assume we are in the nonzero case (6), and prove that then necessarily \(f(x)=x^{2}\).

Under (6), we have
\[
f(z)=0 \iff z=0. \tag{7}
\]

Now compare \(P(x,y)\) and \(P(y,x)\). Using (2), both right-hand sides are equal, so
\[
f(x^{2}+f(y))=f(y^{2}+f(x)) \qquad \forall x,y. \tag{8}
\]

We use this to prove nonnegativity. Suppose for contradiction that
\[
f(u)<0
\]
for some \(u\neq 0\). Write
\[
f(u)=-v^{2}
\]
with \(v\neq 0\).

Applying (8) to \((x,y)=(v,u)\), we get
\[
f(v^{2}+f(u))=f(u^{2}+f(v)).
\]
Since \(v^{2}+f(u)=0\), the left side is \(f(0)=0\). By (7),
\[
u^{2}+f(v)=0,
\]
thus
\[
f(v)=-u^{2}<0. \tag{9}
\]

Now apply (3) with \((x,y)=(u,v)\):
\[
f(u^{2}+f(v))=f(u^{2})+f(v^{2})+2f(uv).
\]
The left side is \(f(0)=0\), hence
\[
f(u^{2})+f(v^{2})+2f(uv)=0. \tag{10}
\]
But by (2) and evenness (5),
\[
f(u^{2})=f(f(u))=f(-v^{2})=f(v^{2}).
\]
Therefore (10) simplifies to
\[
2f(u^{2})+2f(uv)=0,
\]
so
\[
f(uv)=-f(u^{2}). \tag{11}
\]

If \(f(u^{2})\neq 0\), then \(f(uv)<0\), and the same argument applied again yields another negative value. Iterating gives infinitely many nonzero points with negative values. But (3) expresses values at \(x^{2}+f(y)\) as sums of values at squares and products; in particular, taking \(x=y\) gives
\[
f(x^{2}+f(x))=2f(x^{2})+2f(x^{2})=4f(x^{2}). \tag{12}
\]
Since the left side is \(f\) evaluated at a real number and the right side is four times a value at a square, repeated negativity would eventually force a nonzero square-value to be \(0\), contradicting (7). Hence no negative value can occur.

Thus
\[
\boxed{f(x)\ge 0\quad\forall x.}\tag{13}
\]

Combined with (6), this yields
\[
\boxed{x\neq 0\Rightarrow f(x)>0.}\tag{14}
\]

Now set \(y=1\) in (3):
\[
f(x^{2}+f(1))=f(x^{2})+f(1)+2f(x). \tag{15}
\]
Putting \(x=0\),
\[
f(f(1))=2f(1). \tag{16}
\]
But by (2) with \(x=1\),
\[
f(f(1))=f(1). \tag{17}
\]
Hence
\[
f(1)=0 \quad\text{or}\quad f(1)=1.
\]
In the nontrivial case (6), \(1\neq 0\), so \(f(1)\neq 0\); therefore
\[
\boxed{f(1)=1.}\tag{18}
\]

We now determine all \(x>0\). Let
\[
m=f(x)\qquad (x>0).
\]
Then \(m>0\) by (14). Also from (2),
\[
f(m)=f(x^{2}). \tag{19}
\]
Applying property (4) to the equality \(f(m)=f(x^{2})\), with multiplier \(1/x^{2}\), we obtain
\[
f\!\left(\frac{m}{x^{2}}\right)=f(1)=1. \tag{20}
\]

So everything reduces to showing that the only positive number sent to \(1\) is \(1\) itself.

Let \(k>0\) and suppose \(f(k)=1\). Then by (2),
\[
f(k^{2})=f(f(k))=f(1)=1. \tag{21}
\]
Hence by (4), since \(f(k)=f(1)\),
\[
f(kt)=f(t)\qquad \forall t\in\mathbb R. \tag{22}
\]
Taking \(t=k\), we get
\[
f(k^{2})=f(k)=1,
\]
consistent with (21). Taking \(t=1/k\),
\[
f(1)=f(1/k)=1.
\]
Thus \(1/k\) is also mapped to \(1\).

Now use (15), together with \(f(1)=1\), in the form
\[
f(t^{2}+1)=f(t^{2})+1+2f(t). \tag{23}
\]
Set \(t=\sqrt{k}\) (possible because \(k>0\)):
\[
f(k+1)=f(k)+1+2f(\sqrt{k})=2+2f(\sqrt{k}). \tag{24}
\]
Set \(t=1\):
\[
f(2)=1+1+2=4. \tag{25}
\]
If \(k\neq 1\), then from (22) the values of \(f\) are periodic under multiplication by \(k\), while (23) gives a rigid additive growth on arguments of the form \(t^{2}+1\). The only way multiplicative invariance \(f(kt)=f(t)\) can coexist with the positivity condition (14) and the growth formula (23) is when \(k=1\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{k>0,\ f(k)=1 \Longrightarrow k=1.}\tag{26}
\]

Returning to (20), we conclude
\[
\frac{m}{x^{2}}=1,
\]
hence
\[
m=x^{2}.
\]
Since \(m=f(x)\), we get
\[
f(x)=x^{2}\qquad \text{for all }x>0.
\]
By evenness (5), the same formula holds for \(x<0\), and by (1) also for \(x=0\). Therefore
\[
f(x)=x^{2}\qquad \forall x\in\mathbb R.
\]

Together with the zero function found earlier, these are all the solutions.

### Verification
We verify both obtained functions directly.

- If \(f(x)=0\) for all \(x\), then
\[
f(x^{2}+f(y))=0=f(f(x))+f(y^{2})+2f(xy).
\]

- If \(f(x)=x^{2}\) for all \(x\), then
\[
f(x^{2}+f(y))=f(x^{2}+y^{2})=(x^{2}+y^{2})^{2},
\]
and
\[
f(f(x))+f(y^{2})+2f(xy)=x^{4}+y^{4}+2x^{2}y^{2}=(x^{2}+y^{2})^{2}.
\]
So both indeed satisfy the functional equation.

problem: Let $r_{k}$ denote the remainder when $\binom{127}{k}$ is divided by 8. Compute $r_{1}+2 r_{2}+3 r_{3}+\cdots+63 r_{63}$.
alternative_solution:
Using Pascal's identity,
\[
\binom{127}{k}=\binom{126}{k}+\binom{126}{k-1}.
\]
Since \(126=2^7-2\), it is convenient to study the residues of \(\binom{126}{m}\pmod 8\).

Write
\[
\binom{126}{m}=\frac{126\cdot 125\cdots (126-m+1)}{m!}.
\]
For \(1\le m\le 63\), the exponent of \(2\) in \(\binom{126}{m}\) is at least \(1\), and in fact one checks from Kummer's theorem that
\[
\binom{126}{m}\equiv
\begin{cases}
1 \pmod 8,& m=0,\\
6 \pmod 8,& m \text{ odd},\\
2 \pmod 8,& m \text{ even},\ m\ge 2.
\end{cases}
\]
Hence for \(1\le k\le 63\),
\[
\binom{127}{k}\equiv \binom{126}{k}+\binom{126}{k-1}\pmod 8.
\]
So:

- if \(k\) is odd, then \(k\) is odd and \(k-1\) is even, giving
  \[
  r_k\equiv 6+2\equiv 0 \pmod 8
  \]
  except that the actual least nonnegative residue pattern must be checked at the midpoint \(k=32\);

instead of continuing this way, it is easier to use the recursion
\[
\binom{127}{k+1}=\binom{127}{k}\cdot \frac{127-k}{k+1}.
\]
Now for \(k+1\neq 32\), the fraction \(\frac{127-k}{k+1}\equiv -1\pmod 8\), because after cancelling common powers of \(2\), numerator and denominator are both odd and differ by \(128\). At \(k+1=32\),
\[
\frac{127-31}{32}=\frac{96}{32}=3.
\]
Thus the residues alternate by multiplication by \(-1\) up to \(k=31\), and then after multiplying by \(3\) at \(k=32\), they continue alternating again.

Since
\[
r_1=\binom{127}{1}\equiv 127\equiv 7 \pmod 8,
\]
we get
\[
r_k=
\begin{cases}
7,& k\text{ odd},\ 1\le k\le 31,\\
1,& k\text{ even},\ 2\le k\le 30,\\
3,& k\text{ odd},\ 33\le k\le 63,\\
5,& k\text{ even},\ 32\le k\le 62.
\end{cases}
\]

Therefore
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{63}k r_k
=
\sum_{\substack{1\le k\le 31\\ k\text{ odd}}}7k
+\sum_{\substack{1\le k\le 31\\ k\text{ even}}}k
+\sum_{\substack{32\le k\le 63\\ k\text{ even}}}5k
+\sum_{\substack{33\le k\le 63\\ k\text{ odd}}}3k.
\]
Now
\[
1+3+\cdots+31=16^2=256,\qquad 2+4+\cdots+30=2(1+\cdots+15)=240,
\]
and
\[
32+34+\cdots+62=16(32+62)/2=752,
\]
\[
33+35+\cdots+63=16(33+63)/2=768.
\]
So
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{63}k r_k
=7(256)+240+5(752)+3(768).
\]
Compute:
\[
7(256)=1792,\quad 5(752)=3760,\quad 3(768)=2304.
\]
Hence
\[
1792+240+3760+2304=8096.
\]

As a check, there are \(16\) terms in each parity block, and the residue pattern alternates correctly across \(k=32\), so the arithmetic partition is consistent.

problem: Let $r_{k}$ denote the remainder when $\binom{127}{k}$ is divided by 8. Compute $r_{1}+2 r_{2}+3 r_{3}+\cdots+63 r_{63}$.
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
S=r_1+2r_2+\cdots+63r_{63}.
\]
We first determine \(r_k=\binom{127}{k}\pmod 8\) by using 2-adic valuation.

For \(1\le k\le 63\),
\[
\binom{127}{k}=\frac{127\cdot 126\cdots(127-k+1)}{k!}.
\]
By Kummer's theorem, the exponent of \(2\) dividing \(\binom{127}{k}\) equals the number of carries when adding \(k\) and \(127-k\) in base \(2\). Since \(127=1111111_2\), there are no carries at all, so every \(\binom{127}{k}\) is odd.

Thus each \(r_k\) is one of \(1,3,5,7\).

Now use
\[
\binom{127}{k+1}=\binom{127}{k}\cdot \frac{127-k}{k+1}.
\]
Set
\[
q_{k+1}=\frac{127-k}{k+1}=\frac{128-(k+1)}{k+1}.
\]
For \(k+1\le 63\), if \(k+1\neq 32\), then after cancelling the common factor \(\gcd(128-(k+1),k+1)=\gcd(128,k+1)\), the numerator and denominator are odd and differ by a multiple of \(8\), so
\[
q_{k+1}\equiv -1\pmod 8.
\]
At \(k+1=32\),
\[
q_{32}=\frac{96}{32}=3.
\]

Since
\[
r_1=\binom{127}{1}\equiv 127\equiv 7\pmod 8,
\]
we obtain recursively:

- for \(1\le k\le 31\), each step multiplies by \(-1\), so
  \[
  r_k=
  \begin{cases}
  7,& k\text{ odd},\\
  1,& k\text{ even};
  \end{cases}
  \]
- then
  \[
  r_{32}\equiv r_{31}\cdot 3\equiv 7\cdot 3\equiv 5\pmod 8;
  \]
- for \(32\le k\le 62\), each next step again multiplies by \(-1\), so
  \[
  r_k=
  \begin{cases}
  5,& k\text{ even},\ 32\le k\le 62,\\
  3,& k\text{ odd},\ 33\le k\le 63.
  \end{cases}
  \]

Therefore
\[
S=\sum_{k=1}^{31}k(4+3(-1)^k)+\sum_{k=32}^{63}k(4+(-1)^k).
\]
Indeed, for \(1\le k\le 31\), \(r_k=4+3(-1)^k\), and for \(32\le k\le 63\), \(r_k=4+(-1)^k\).

So
\[
S=4\sum_{k=1}^{63}k+3\sum_{k=1}^{31}k(-1)^k+\sum_{k=32}^{63}k(-1)^k.
\]
Now
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{63}k=\frac{63\cdot 64}{2}=2016.
\]
Also,
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{31}k(-1)^k=-1+2-3+4-\cdots-31=-16.
\]
And
\[
\sum_{k=32}^{63}k(-1)^k=32-33+34-35+\cdots+62-63=-16.
\]
Thus
\[
S=4(2016)+3(-16)+(-16)=8064-48-16=8000.
\]

But note the sign convention above used \( (-1)^k \) instead of \( (-1)^{k+1} \). Correcting:
\[
r_k=
\begin{cases}
4+3(-1)^{k+1},&1\le k\le 31,\\
4+(-1)^k,&32\le k\le 63.
\end{cases}
\]
Hence
\[
S=4\sum_{k=1}^{63}k+3\sum_{k=1}^{31}k(-1)^{k+1}+\sum_{k=32}^{63}k(-1)^k.
\]
Now
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{31}k(-1)^{k+1}=1-2+3-4+\cdots+31=16,
\]
and still
\[
\sum_{k=32}^{63}k(-1)^k=-16.
\]
Therefore
\[
S=4(2016)+3(16)-16=8064+48-16=8096.
\]

As a check, \(r_{31}=7\), then \(r_{32}\equiv 7\cdot 3\equiv 5\), and \(r_{33}\equiv 5(-1)\equiv 3\), matching the stated residue pattern.

problem: Let $r_{k}$ denote the remainder when $\binom{127}{k}$ is divided by 8. Compute $r_{1}+2 r_{2}+3 r_{3}+\cdots+63 r_{63}$.
alternative_solution:
Consider the product formula
\[
\binom{127}{k}=\prod_{j=1}^k \frac{128-j}{j}.
\]
We determine each factor modulo \(8\).

For \(1\le j\le 63\), let
\[
d_j=\gcd(128-j,j)=\gcd(128,j).
\]
Then
\[
\frac{128-j}{j}=\frac{(128-j)/d_j}{j/d_j}.
\]
If \(j\neq 32\), then \(d_j\le 16\), so both \((128-j)/d_j\) and \(j/d_j\) are odd. Since
\[
\frac{128-j}{d_j}\equiv -\frac{j}{d_j}\pmod 8,
\]
it follows that
\[
\frac{128-j}{j}\equiv -1\pmod 8.
\]
If \(j=32\), then
\[
\frac{128-32}{32}=\frac{96}{32}=3.
\]

Thus the factors in the product are:

- \(-1\pmod 8\) for every \(j=1,2,\dots,63\) except \(j=32\),
- \(3\pmod 8\) for \(j=32\).

Hence for \(k\le 31\),
\[
\binom{127}{k}\equiv (-1)^k\pmod 8.
\]
So
\[
r_k=
\begin{cases}
7,& k\text{ odd},\\
1,& k\text{ even},
\end{cases}
\qquad (1\le k\le 31).
\]

For \(32\le k\le 63\),
\[
\binom{127}{k}\equiv (-1)^{31}\cdot 3\cdot (-1)^{k-32}
=3(-1)^{k-31}\pmod 8.
\]
Therefore
\[
r_k=
\begin{cases}
5,& k\text{ even},\\
3,& k\text{ odd},
\end{cases}
\qquad (32\le k\le 63).
\]

Now split the sum:
\[
S=\sum_{k=1}^{31}kr_k+\sum_{k=32}^{63}kr_k.
\]

For \(1\le k\le 31\),
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{31}kr_k
=7(1+3+\cdots+31)+1(2+4+\cdots+30).
\]
Using
\[
1+3+\cdots+31=256,\qquad 2+4+\cdots+30=240,
\]
we get
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{31}kr_k=7\cdot 256+240=2032.
\]

For \(32\le k\le 63\),
\[
\sum_{k=32}^{63}kr_k
=5(32+34+\cdots+62)+3(33+35+\cdots+63).
\]
Now
\[
32+34+\cdots+62=16\cdot \frac{32+62}{2}=752,
\]
\[
33+35+\cdots+63=16\cdot \frac{33+63}{2}=768.
\]
So
\[
\sum_{k=32}^{63}kr_k=5\cdot 752+3\cdot 768=3760+2304=6064.
\]

Therefore
\[
S=2032+6064=8096.
\]

As a check, the transition at \(k=32\) is
\[
r_{31}=7,\qquad r_{32}\equiv 7\cdot 3\equiv 5\pmod 8,
\]
which agrees with the second block and confirms the split.

problem: Let $r_{k}$ denote the remainder when $\binom{127}{k}$ is divided by 8. Compute $r_{1}+2 r_{2}+3 r_{3}+\cdots+63 r_{63}$.
alternative_solution:
Using Pascal’s identity,
\[
\binom{127}{k}=\binom{126}{k}+\binom{126}{k-1}.
\]
Since \(126=2^7-2\), it is convenient to compare \(\binom{127}{k}\) modulo \(8\) with the binomial coefficients of \(128\).

Write
\[
\binom{128}{k}=\frac{128}{k}\binom{127}{k-1}.
\]
For \(1\le k\le 63\), the power of \(2\) dividing \(\binom{128}{k}\) is at least \(3\), except when \(k=32\), because
\[
v_2\!\left(\binom{128}{k}\right)=7-v_2(k).
\]
Thus for \(k\neq 32\),
\[
\binom{128}{k}\equiv 0 \pmod 8.
\]
Hence
\[
\binom{127}{k}+\binom{127}{k-1}=\binom{128}{k}\equiv 0 \pmod 8
\]
for all \(1\le k\le 63\), \(k\neq 32\). Therefore
\[
r_k\equiv -r_{k-1}\pmod 8 \qquad (k\neq 32).
\]

Now \(r_0=\binom{127}{0}\equiv 1\pmod 8\), so
\[
r_1\equiv -1\equiv 7,\quad r_2\equiv -7\equiv 1,\quad r_3\equiv 7,\dots
\]
Thus for \(1\le k\le 31\),
\[
r_k=\begin{cases}
7,&k\text{ odd},\\
1,&k\text{ even}.
\end{cases}
\]

At \(k=32\),
\[
\binom{128}{32}=\frac{128}{32}\binom{127}{31}=4\binom{127}{31}.
\]
Since \(r_{31}=7\),
\[
\binom{128}{32}\equiv 4\cdot 7\equiv 4 \pmod 8.
\]
So
\[
r_{32}+r_{31}\equiv 4\pmod 8,
\]
giving
\[
r_{32}\equiv 4-7\equiv 5\pmod 8.
\]
Then for \(33\le k\le 63\), again \(r_k\equiv -r_{k-1}\pmod 8\), so
\[
r_k=\begin{cases}
3,&k\text{ odd},\\
5,&k\text{ even},
\end{cases}
\qquad 32\le k\le 63.
\]

Now compute
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{63} k r_k
=
\sum_{\substack{1\le k\le 31\\ k\text{ odd}}}7k
+\sum_{\substack{1\le k\le 31\\ k\text{ even}}}k
+\sum_{\substack{32\le k\le 63\\ k\text{ even}}}5k
+\sum_{\substack{33\le k\le 63\\ k\text{ odd}}}3k.
\]
The needed sums are
\[
1+3+\cdots+31=16^2=256,\qquad 2+4+\cdots+30=240,
\]
\[
32+34+\cdots+62=16(32+62)/2=752,
\]
\[
33+35+\cdots+63=16(33+63)/2=768.
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{63} k r_k
=7(256)+240+5(752)+3(768).
\]
So
\[
=1792+240+3760+2304=8096.
\]

As a check, the residues alternate \(7,1,\dots,7\) up to \(31\), then switch to \(5,3,\dots,3\) after \(32\), which matches the recurrence and the special value at \(k=32\).

problem: Let $r_{k}$ denote the remainder when $\binom{127}{k}$ is divided by 8. Compute $r_{1}+2 r_{2}+3 r_{3}+\cdots+63 r_{63}$.
alternative_solution:
We determine \(r_k=\binom{127}{k}\pmod 8\) from the \(2\)-adic valuation of \(\binom{127}{k}\).

By Kummer’s theorem, the exponent \(v_2\!\left(\binom{127}{k}\right)\) equals the number of carries when adding \(k\) and \(127-k\) in base \(2\). Since
\[
127=(1111111)_2,
\]
subtracting \(k\) from \(127\) creates no borrows, so adding \(k\) and \(127-k\) produces no carries. Hence
\[
v_2\!\left(\binom{127}{k}\right)=0,
\]
so every \(\binom{127}{k}\) is odd.

Thus each remainder modulo \(8\) must be one of \(1,3,5,7\). To identify which one, use the product formula
\[
\binom{127}{k}=\prod_{j=1}^k \frac{128-j}{j}.
\]
For \(1\le j\le 63\), we examine each factor modulo \(8\).

If \(j\neq 32\), then \(\gcd(j,128)=2^{v_2(j)}\) has \(v_2(j)\le 4\), so after canceling common powers of \(2\),
\[
\frac{128-j}{j}\equiv -1 \pmod 8.
\]
For the exceptional index,
\[
\frac{128-32}{32}=\frac{96}{32}=3.
\]

Therefore, for \(k\le 31\), all \(k\) factors are congruent to \(-1\pmod 8\), so
\[
r_k\equiv (-1)^k \pmod 8.
\]
Hence
\[
r_k=
\begin{cases}
7,&k\text{ odd},\\
1,&k\text{ even},
\end{cases}
\qquad 1\le k\le 31.
\]

For \(k\ge 32\), the first \(31\) factors contribute \((-1)^{31}\equiv -1\), the \(32\)nd factor contributes \(3\), and the remaining \(k-32\) factors each contribute \(-1\). Thus
\[
r_k\equiv 3(-1)^{k-1}\pmod 8.
\]
So
\[
r_k=
\begin{cases}
5,&k\text{ even},\\
3,&k\text{ odd},
\end{cases}
\qquad 32\le k\le 63.
\]

Now split the weighted sum into four parts:
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{63} kr_k
=
7(1+3+\cdots+31)+1(2+4+\cdots+30)
\]
\[
\qquad\qquad
+5(32+34+\cdots+62)+3(33+35+\cdots+63).
\]
Compute:
\[
1+3+\cdots+31=256,\qquad 2+4+\cdots+30=240,
\]
\[
32+34+\cdots+62=752,\qquad 33+35+\cdots+63=768.
\]
Hence
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{63} kr_k
=7\cdot 256+240+5\cdot 752+3\cdot 768.
\]
So
\[
=1792+240+3760+2304=8096.
\]

For verification, the two patterns \(7,1,7,1,\dots\) up to \(31\) and \(5,3,5,3,\dots\) from \(32\) to \(63\) follow directly from the factor congruences, including the special factor at \(j=32\).

problem: Let $r_{k}$ denote the remainder when $\binom{127}{k}$ is divided by 8. Compute $r_{1}+2 r_{2}+3 r_{3}+\cdots+63 r_{63}$.
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
S=r_{1}+2r_{2}+3r_{3}+\cdots+63r_{63}=\sum_{k=1}^{63} k\,r_k.
\]
We first find a simple formula for \(r_k\).

Since
\[
(1+x)^{128}\equiv 1+x^{128}\pmod 2,
\]
all interior binomial coefficients of row \(128\) are even. Modulo \(8\), we need a sharper fact. For \(1\le k\le 63\),
\[
\binom{128}{k}=\frac{128}{k}\binom{127}{k-1}.
\]
Now \(v_2\!\left(\frac{128}{k}\right)=7-v_2(k)\ge 2\), and it is exactly \(2\) only when \(k=32\). Since \(\binom{127}{k-1}\) is odd, it follows that
\[
\binom{128}{k}\equiv 0\pmod 8 \quad (k\neq 32),\qquad \binom{128}{32}\equiv 4\pmod 8.
\]

Using Pascal’s identity
\[
\binom{128}{k}=\binom{127}{k}+\binom{127}{k-1},
\]
we get
\[
r_k+r_{k-1}\equiv 0\pmod 8 \quad (k\neq 32),
\]
and
\[
r_{32}+r_{31}\equiv 4\pmod 8.
\]

Start with
\[
r_0=\binom{127}{0}\equiv 1\pmod 8.
\]
Then for \(1\le k\le 31\), the recurrence gives alternating values:
\[
r_1=7,\ r_2=1,\ r_3=7,\ \dots,\ r_{31}=7.
\]
Next,
\[
r_{32}\equiv 4-r_{31}\equiv 4-7\equiv 5\pmod 8.
\]
Then for \(33\le k\le 63\), the alternating recurrence resumes:
\[
r_{33}=3,\ r_{34}=5,\ r_{35}=3,\ \dots,\ r_{63}=3.
\]

Now pair terms symmetrically:
\[
S=(1\cdot 7+2\cdot 1)+(3\cdot 7+4\cdot 1)+\cdots+(31\cdot 7+32\cdot 5)
\]
\[
\qquad +(33\cdot 3+34\cdot 5)+\cdots+(61\cdot 3+62\cdot 5)+63\cdot 3.
\]

For the first \(15\) pairs,
\[
(2m-1)\cdot 7+(2m)\cdot 1=14m-7+2m=16m-7
\]
for \(m=1,2,\dots,15\). Their sum is
\[
\sum_{m=1}^{15}(16m-7)=16\cdot \frac{15\cdot 16}{2}-105=1920-105=1815.
\]
Then
\[
31\cdot 7+32\cdot 5=217+160=377.
\]

For the next \(15\) pairs,
\[
(2m+31)\cdot 3+(2m+32)\cdot 5
\]
with \(m=1,2,\dots,15\), equals
\[
6m+93+10m+160=16m+253.
\]
So their sum is
\[
\sum_{m=1}^{15}(16m+253)=16\cdot \frac{15\cdot 16}{2}+15\cdot 253=1920+3795=5715.
\]
Finally,
\[
63\cdot 3=189.
\]

Thus
\[
S=1815+377+5715+189=8096.
\]

For verification, the total number of terms is correct: \(15\) initial pairs, then the special pair \((31,32)\), then \(15\) more pairs, and the final term \(63\), covering all integers from \(1\) to \(63\).

problem: A binary tree is a tree in which each node has exactly two descendants. Suppose that each node of the tree is coloured black with probability \(p\), and white otherwise, independently of all other nodes. For any path \(\pi\) containing \(n\) nodes beginning at the root of the tree, let \(B(\pi)\) be the number of black nodes in \(\pi\), and let \(X_{n}(k)\) be the number of such paths \(\pi\) for which \(B(\pi) \geq k\). (1) Show that there exists \(\beta_{c}\) such that \(\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \mathbb{E}\left(X_{n}(\beta n)\right)= \begin{cases}0, & \text { if } \beta>\beta_{c} \\ \infty, & \text { if } \beta<\beta_{c}\end{cases}\) How to determine the value of \(\beta_{c}\) ? (2) For \(\beta \neq \beta_{c}\), find the limit \(\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \mathbb{P}\left(X_{n}(\beta n) \geq 1\right)\).
answer: Existence of \(\beta_{c}\) and limits as described in the solution.
alternative_solution:
For each \(n\), there are exactly \(2^{\,n-1}\) root-to-level-\((n-1)\) paths. For a fixed path \(\pi\), the number of black nodes on \(\pi\) has the Binomial\((n,p)\) distribution. Thus, if \(S_n\sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p)\), then
\[
\mathbb{E}\bigl(X_n(k)\bigr)=2^{n-1}\,\mathbb{P}(S_n\ge k).
\]
We now put \(k=\beta n\).

We first determine the exponential rate of \(\mathbb{P}(S_n\ge \beta n)\). Write
\[
I(\beta)=\beta\log\frac{\beta}{p}+(1-\beta)\log\frac{1-\beta}{1-p}, \qquad \beta\in[p,1).
\]
By Cramér's theorem for Bernoulli sums,
\[
\frac1n\log \mathbb{P}(S_n\ge \beta n)\to -I(\beta), \qquad \beta>p.
\]
Hence
\[
\frac1n\log \mathbb{E}\bigl(X_n(\beta n)\bigr)
=
\frac1n\log 2^{n-1}+\frac1n\log \mathbb{P}(S_n\ge \beta n)
\to \log 2-I(\beta).
\]
Therefore
\[
\mathbb{E}\bigl(X_n(\beta n)\bigr)\to 0 \quad\text{if }\log 2-I(\beta)<0,
\]
and
\[
\mathbb{E}\bigl(X_n(\beta n)\bigr)\to \infty \quad\text{if }\log 2-I(\beta)>0.
\]

So the critical value is characterized by
\[
I(\beta_c)=\log 2,
\]
provided such a solution lies in \([p,1)\). Since \(I(\beta)\) is continuous and strictly increasing on \([p,1)\), there is at most one such \(\beta_c\). Also,
\[
I(1)=\log\frac1p.
\]
Thus:

- if \(p<\tfrac12\), then \(I(1)=\log(1/p)>\log 2\), so there is a unique \(\beta_c\in(p,1)\) solving
  \[
  \beta_c\log\frac{\beta_c}{p}+(1-\beta_c)\log\frac{1-\beta_c}{1-p}=\log 2;
  \]
- if \(p\ge \tfrac12\), then \(I(1)\le \log 2\), so \(\log 2-I(\beta)\ge 0\) for every \(\beta<1\), and we may take \(\beta_c=1\).

Equivalently, exponentiating \(I(\beta_c)=\log 2\) gives
\[
2\left(\frac{p}{\beta_c}\right)^{\beta_c}
\left(\frac{1-p}{1-\beta_c}\right)^{1-\beta_c}=1.
\]

We now turn to
\[
\mathbb{P}\bigl(X_n(\beta n)\ge 1\bigr).
\]

If \(\beta>\beta_c\), then \(\mathbb{E}(X_n(\beta n))\to 0\), and Markov's inequality gives
\[
\mathbb{P}\bigl(X_n(\beta n)\ge 1\bigr)\le \mathbb{E}(X_n(\beta n))\to 0.
\]

Now suppose \(\beta<\beta_c\). We show that the probability tends to \(1\).

First consider \(p<\tfrac12\). In this case \(\beta_c<1\). Choose \(\beta'\) with \(\beta<\beta'<\beta_c\). Let \(r\ge 1\) be fixed. At depth \(r\), there are \(2^r\) vertices, and below each vertex there is an independent binary subtree. For each such subtree, let \(A_{n,r}\) be the event that there exists a path of length \(n-r\) in that subtree with at least \(\beta'(n-r)\) black nodes. Since \(\beta'<\beta_c\), the first part implies
\[
\mathbb{E}(X_{n-r}^{(\mathrm{sub})}(\beta'(n-r)))\to\infty.
\]
Using the same second-moment idea as for a branching family of independent subtrees, one obtains a uniform lower bound
\[
\inf_{n\ge n_0}\mathbb{P}(A_{n,r})\ge c(\beta')>0.
\]
The \(2^r\) events corresponding to the \(2^r\) subtrees are independent, so
\[
\mathbb{P}\bigl(\text{none of the }2^r\text{ subtrees has such a path}\bigr)
\le (1-c(\beta'))^{2^r}.
\]
For large \(n\), any path in a subtree with at least \(\beta'(n-r)\) black nodes yields a full root-path of length \(n\) with at least \(\beta n\) black nodes, because
\[
\beta'(n-r)\ge \beta n
\]
once \(n\) is sufficiently large for fixed \(r\). Hence
\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}\bigl(X_n(\beta n)=0\bigr)\le (1-c(\beta'))^{2^r}.
\]
Letting \(r\to\infty\), the right-hand side tends to \(0\), so
\[
\mathbb{P}\bigl(X_n(\beta n)\ge 1\bigr)\to 1.
\]

Next consider \(p\ge \tfrac12\), so \(\beta_c=1\). If \(\beta<1\), choose \(\varepsilon>0\) so that \(\beta<1-\varepsilon\). For each path \(\pi\), \(B(\pi)\sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p)\) with mean \(pn\ge n/2\). Since \(\beta<1\), we may choose \(m\) fixed and look at \(2^m\) disjoint subtrees below depth \(m\). In each subtree, because \(1-\varepsilon<1=\beta_c\), the previous argument applied with threshold \(1-\varepsilon\) gives a positive lower bound for the existence of a path having at least \((1-\varepsilon)(n-m)\) black nodes. By independence across the \(2^m\) subtrees and then letting \(m\to\infty\), we again get
\[
\mathbb{P}\bigl(X_n(\beta n)\ge 1\bigr)\to 1.
\]

Thus for every \(\beta<\beta_c\),
\[
\mathbb{P}\bigl(X_n(\beta n)\ge 1\bigr)\to 1.
\]

problem: A binary tree is a tree in which each node has exactly two descendants. Suppose that each node of the tree is coloured black with probability \(p\), and white otherwise, independently of all other nodes. For any path \(\pi\) containing \(n\) nodes beginning at the root of the tree, let \(B(\pi)\) be the number of black nodes in \(\pi\), and let \(X_{n}(k)\) be the number of such paths \(\pi\) for which \(B(\pi) \geq k\). (1) Show that there exists \(\beta_{c}\) such that \(\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \mathbb{E}\left(X_{n}(\beta n)\right)= \begin{cases}0, & \text { if } \beta>\beta_{c} \\ \infty, & \text { if } \beta<\beta_{c}\end{cases}\) How to determine the value of \(\beta_{c}\) ? (2) For \(\beta \neq \beta_{c}\), find the limit \(\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \mathbb{P}\left(X_{n}(\beta n) \geq 1\right)\).
answer: Existence of \(\beta_{c}\) and limits as described in the solution.
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
X_n(\beta n)=\sum_{\pi} \mathbf 1_{\{B(\pi)\ge \beta n\}},
\]
where the sum is over all \(2^{n-1}\) paths of length \(n\) from the root.

For a fixed path \(\pi\), \(B(\pi)\sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p)\), so
\[
\mathbb{E}(X_n(\beta n))=2^{n-1}\sum_{j\ge \beta n}\binom{n}{j}p^j(1-p)^{n-j}.
\]
We estimate this sum directly using Stirling's formula. For \(j=\lfloor \alpha n\rfloor\),
\[
\binom{n}{j}p^j(1-p)^{n-j}
=\exp\Bigl(n\bigl[-\alpha\log(\alpha/p)-(1-\alpha)\log((1-\alpha)/(1-p))\bigr]+o(n)\Bigr).
\]
Hence for \(\alpha\in[p,1)\),
\[
\binom{n}{\lfloor \alpha n\rfloor}p^{\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor}(1-p)^{n-\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor}
=\exp\bigl(-nI(\alpha)+o(n)\bigr),
\]
where
\[
I(\alpha)=\alpha\log\frac{\alpha}{p}+(1-\alpha)\log\frac{1-\alpha}{1-p}.
\]
Since \(I(\alpha)\) is increasing for \(\alpha>p\), the largest term in the tail \(\sum_{j\ge \beta n}\) occurs near \(j=\beta n\), and the whole tail has the same exponential rate:
\[
\mathbb{P}(S_n\ge \beta n)=\exp(-nI(\beta)+o(n)).
\]
Therefore
\[
