Now \(\phi\) is continuous and satisfies the multiplicative Cauchy equation on the circle. Taking \(\varphi=-\theta\),
\[
\phi(\theta)\phi(-\theta)=\phi(0)=1,
\]
so \(\phi(\theta)\neq 0\). A continuous nonvanishing solution of (6) must be of the form
\[
\phi(\theta)=e^{c\theta}.
\]
But \(\phi\) is \(2\pi\)-periodic, hence \(e^{2\pi c}=1\), and continuity over real values forces \(c=0\). Therefore
\[
\phi(\theta)\equiv 1.
\]
So
\[
P(x,y)=r^n=(x^2+y^2)^{n/2}.
\]
Since \(P\) is a polynomial, \(n\) must be even, say \(n=2m\). Therefore
\[
P(x,y)=(x^2+y^2)^m.
\]

problem: Find all polynomials $P$ in two variables with real coefficients satisfying the identity $P(x, y) P(z, t)=P(x z-y t, x t+y z)$.
alternative_solution:
We rewrite the problem in complex form. For real \(x,y\), let
\[
u=x+iy,\qquad v=z+it.
\]
Then
\[
uv=(xz-yt)+i(xt+yz).
\]
So if we define
\[
R(u,\bar u):=P\!\left(\frac{u+\bar u}{2},\frac{u-\bar u}{2i}\right),
\]
then \(R\) is a polynomial in the independent variables \(u,\bar u\) with real coefficients, and the given identity becomes
\[
R(u,\bar u)R(v,\bar v)=R(uv,\bar u\bar v). \tag{1}
\]

We classify all such polynomials \(R\).

First, \(R\equiv 0\) gives \(P\equiv 0\), so that is one solution. Assume now \(R\not\equiv 0\).

Taking \(v=1\) in (1),
\[
R(u,\bar u)R(1,1)=R(u,\bar u),
\]
hence
\[
R(1,1)=1.
\]

Write
\[
R(u,\bar u)=\sum_{a,b\ge 0} c_{a,b}u^a\bar u^b,
\]
with only finitely many nonzero coefficients \(c_{a,b}\in\mathbb R\).

Substitute this into (1). The left-hand side is
\[
\left(\sum_{a,b} c_{a,b}u^a\bar u^b\right)
\left(\sum_{p,q} c_{p,q}v^p\bar v^q\right)
=\sum_{a,b,p,q} c_{a,b}c_{p,q}u^a\bar u^b v^p\bar v^q.
\]
The right-hand side is
\[
R(uv,\bar u\bar v)=\sum_{a,b} c_{a,b}(uv)^a(\bar u\bar v)^b
=\sum_{a,b} c_{a,b}u^a\bar u^b v^a\bar v^b.
\]

Since monomials \(u^a\bar u^b v^p\bar v^q\) are linearly independent, we must have
\[
c_{a,b}c_{p,q}=0 \qquad\text{whenever }(a,b)\neq(p,q). \tag{2}
\]
Thus at most one coefficient \(c_{a,b}\) is nonzero. So
\[
R(u,\bar u)=c\,u^m\bar u^n
\]
for some \(m,n\ge 0\).

Now use \(R(1,1)=1\): this gives \(c=1\). Therefore
\[
R(u,\bar u)=u^m\bar u^n. \tag{3}
\]

Translating back,
\[
P(x,y)=(x+iy)^m(x-iy)^n.
\]

Now we impose the condition that \(P(x,y)\) has real coefficients. Since \(x-iy\) is the complex conjugate of \(x+iy\), the product above is real-valued for all real \(x,y\) only when \(m=n\); otherwise a nonreal factor remains. Equivalently, if \(m\neq n\), the coefficient of some monomial is nonreal. Hence
\[
m=n.
\]
Therefore
\[
P(x,y)=(x+iy)^m(x-iy)^m=(x^2+y^2)^m.
\]

problem: Find all polynomials $P$ in two variables with real coefficients satisfying the identity $P(x, y) P(z, t)=P(x z-y t, x t+y z)$.
alternative_solution:
We solve the problem by looking at the lowest-degree nonzero homogeneous part of \(P\).

The zero polynomial is clearly a solution, so assume
\[
P\not\equiv 0.
\]

Write \(P\) as a sum of homogeneous parts:
\[
P=P_r+P_{r+1}+\cdots+P_s,
\]
where \(P_k\) is homogeneous of degree \(k\), \(P_r\not\equiv 0\), and \(P_s\not\equiv 0\).

We first determine the constant term. Setting \((z,t)=(0,0)\) in
\[
P(x,y)P(z,t)=P(xz-yt,xt+yz),
\]
we get
\[
P(x,y)P(0,0)=P(0,0).
\]
Hence either \(P(0,0)=0\), or \(P(x,y)\equiv 1\). The polynomial \(1\) is already \((x^2+y^2)^0\). So for the nonconstant case we have
\[
P(0,0)=0,
\]
thus \(r\ge 1\).

Next, set \((z,t)=(\lambda,0)\). Then
\[
P(\lambda x,\lambda y)=P(x,y)P(\lambda,0). \tag{1}
\]
Expand both sides in powers of \(\lambda\).

On the left,
\[
P(\lambda x,\lambda y)=\lambda^rP_r(x,y)+\lambda^{r+1}P_{r+1}(x,y)+\cdots+\lambda^sP_s(x,y).
\]
On the right,
\[
P(x,y)\big(\lambda^rP_r(1,0)+\lambda^{r+1}P_{r+1}(1,0)+\cdots+\lambda^sP_s(1,0)\big).
\]
Compare the coefficient of the lowest power \(\lambda^r\). We obtain
\[
P_r(x,y)=P(x,y)P_r(1,0). \tag{2}
\]
Since \(P_r\) is homogeneous of degree \(r\) and \(P\) may have higher-degree terms, the only way (2) can hold is that all higher-degree terms vanish. Thus
\[
P=P_r
\]
is homogeneous.

So every nonzero solution is homogeneous of some degree \(r\).

Now put \((z,t)=(x,-y)\). Then
\[
(xz-yt,xt+yz)=(x^2+y^2,0),
\]
hence
\[
P(x,y)P(x,-y)=P(x^2+y^2,0). \tag{3}
\]
Since \(P\) is homogeneous of degree \(r\),
\[
P(x^2+y^2,0)=P(1,0)(x^2+y^2)^r. \tag{4}
\]
Also, setting \((z,t)=(1,0)\) in the original identity gives
\[
P(x,y)P(1,0)=P(x,y),
\]
so because \(P\not\equiv 0\),
\[
P(1,0)=1.
\]
Thus from (3) and (4),
\[
P(x,y)P(x,-y)=(x^2+y^2)^r. \tag{5}
\]

Now factor \(P\) over \(\mathbb C\). Since \(P\) is homogeneous of degree \(r\), it can be written as
\[
P(x,y)=c\prod_{j=1}^r (\alpha_j x+\beta_j y),
\]
with complex coefficients. Then
\[
P(x,-y)=c\prod_{j=1}^r (\alpha_j x-\beta_j y).
\]
Multiplying,
\[
P(x,y)P(x,-y)=c^2\prod_{j=1}^r (\alpha_j x+\beta_j y)(\alpha_j x-\beta_j y)
= c^2\prod_{j=1}^r (\alpha_j^2x^2-\beta_j^2y^2). \tag{6}
\]

But by (5), this product equals \((x^2+y^2)^r\), whose only irreducible factors over \(\mathbb C\) are \(x+iy\) and \(x-iy\). Therefore every linear factor of \(P(x,y)\) must be proportional to either \(x+iy\) or \(x-iy\). Hence
\[
P(x,y)=c(x+iy)^m(x-iy)^n,\qquad m+n=r. \tag{7}
\]

Because \(P\) has real coefficients, the multiplicities of conjugate linear factors must be equal, so
\[
m=n.
\]
Also \(P(1,0)=1\) implies \(c=1\). Therefore
\[
P(x,y)=(x+iy)^m(x-iy)^m=(x^2+y^2)^m.
\]

problem: Determine all positive integers $n$ for which there exist $n \times n$ real invertible matrices $A$ and $B$ that satisfy $A B-B A=B^{2} A$.
alternative_solution:
We show that such matrices exist exactly when \(n\) is even.

I. Assume first that \(n\) is odd and that invertible real \(n\times n\) matrices \(A,B\) satisfy
\[
AB-BA=B^{2}A.
\]
Since \(A\) is invertible, we may rewrite this as
\[
A^{-1}BA-B=B^{2},
\]
or equivalently
\[
A^{-1}BA=B+B^{2}=B(I+B).
\]
Thus \(A^{-1}BA\) is similar to \(B\), so \(B\) and \(B(I+B)\) have the same characteristic polynomial, hence the same determinant. Therefore
\[
\det(B)=\det(B(I+B))=\det(B)\det(I+B).
\]
Because \(B\) is invertible, \(\det(B)\neq 0\), and we get
\[
\det(I+B)=1.
\]

Now \(n\) is odd and \(B\) is a real matrix, so its characteristic polynomial has odd degree; hence \(B\) has a real eigenvalue \(\lambda\). Since \(B\) is invertible, \(\lambda\neq 0\).

Because nonreal eigenvalues occur in conjugate pairs, the determinant of \(I+B\) can be written as
\[
\det(I+B)=(1+\lambda)\prod_j |1+\mu_j|^2,
\]
where the \(\mu_j\)'s run through one eigenvalue from each nonreal conjugate pair. In particular, the product
\[
\prod_j |1+\mu_j|^2
\]
is nonnegative, so \(\det(I+B)\) has the same sign as \(1+\lambda\).

But \(\det(I+B)=1>0\), so necessarily \(1+\lambda>0\). On the other hand, applying the same argument to \(B^{-1}(-I-B)\) is unnecessary; instead note that
\[
A^{-1}BA=B(I+B)
\]
shows that if \(\lambda\) is a real eigenvalue of \(B\), then \(\lambda(1+\lambda)\) is also a real eigenvalue of \(B\), because \(B\) and \(B(I+B)\) are similar.

Starting from a real eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\), define
\[
\lambda_{m+1}=\lambda_m(1+\lambda_m)=\lambda_m^2+\lambda_m.
\]
All \(\lambda_m\) are real eigenvalues of \(B\). Since \(B\) has only finitely many eigenvalues, two of them must repeat: \(\lambda_{l+1}=\lambda_k\) for some \(k\le l\). Then
\[
\lambda_{k+1}-\lambda_k=\lambda_k^2,\quad
\lambda_{k+2}-\lambda_{k+1}=\lambda_{k+1}^2,\quad \ldots,\quad
\lambda_{l+1}-\lambda_l=\lambda_l^2.
\]
Adding gives
\[
\lambda_{l+1}-\lambda_k=\lambda_k^2+\lambda_{k+1}^2+\cdots+\lambda_l^2.
\]
Since \(\lambda_{l+1}=\lambda_k\), we obtain
\[
\lambda_k^2+\lambda_{k+1}^2+\cdots+\lambda_l^2=0.
\]
All terms are squares of real numbers, so each is \(0\). Hence \(\lambda_k=0\), contradicting invertibility of \(B\).

Therefore no such matrices exist for odd \(n\).

II. Now assume \(n\) is even, say \(n=2m\). We construct an example. Let
\[
A_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
B_2=\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
A direct computation gives
\[
A_2B_2-B_2A_2=
\begin{pmatrix}-2&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix},
\]
while
\[
B_2^2=
\begin{pmatrix}0&-2\\2&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
B_2^2A_2=
\begin{pmatrix}-2&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
So indeed
\[
A_2B_2-B_2A_2=B_2^2A_2.
\]
Also, \(\det A_2=-1\neq 0\) and \(\det B_2=2\neq 0\), so both are invertible.

For \(n=2m\), take block diagonal matrices with \(m\) copies of these blocks:
\[
A=\operatorname{diag}(A_2,\dots,A_2),\qquad
B=\operatorname{diag}(B_2,\dots,B_2).
\]
Then \(A,B\) are invertible and satisfy
\[
AB-BA=B^2A
\]
blockwise.

problem: Determine all positive integers $n$ for which there exist $n \times n$ real invertible matrices $A$ and $B$ that satisfy $A B-B A=B^{2} A$.
alternative_solution:
We again determine all \(n\).

I. Suppose there exist invertible real \(n\times n\) matrices \(A,B\) such that
\[
AB-BA=B^2A.
\]
We first derive a trace identity. Multiplying on the right by \(A^{-1}\), we get
\[
ABA^{-1}-B=B^2.
\]
Hence
\[
ABA^{-1}=B+B^2.
\]
Now take traces:
\[
\operatorname{tr}(ABA^{-1})=\operatorname{tr}(B+B^2).
\]
Since trace is invariant under similarity,
\[
\operatorname{tr}(B)=\operatorname{tr}(B)+\operatorname{tr}(B^2),
\]
so
\[
\operatorname{tr}(B^2)=0.
\]

Assume now that \(n\) is odd. A real matrix of odd size has at least one real eigenvalue. Let the eigenvalues of \(B\) over \(\mathbb C\) be
\[
\lambda,\ \mu_1,\overline{\mu_1},\dots,\mu_r,\overline{\mu_r},
\]
where \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\) and \(n=2r+1\). Since \(B\) is invertible, none of these eigenvalues is \(0\).

Then
\[
\operatorname{tr}(B^2)=\lambda^2+\mu_1^2+\overline{\mu_1}^2+\cdots+\mu_r^2+\overline{\mu_r}^2.
\]
Grouping conjugate pairs,
\[
\mu_j^2+\overline{\mu_j}^2=2\operatorname{Re}(\mu_j^2),
\]
so this expression is real. But more importantly, if we pass to the real Jordan form, each \(2\times2\) block corresponding to \(a\pm bi\) contributes
\[
(a+bi)^2+(a-bi)^2=2(a^2-b^2)
\]
to \(\operatorname{tr}(B^2)\), while the real eigenvalue contributes \(\lambda^2>0\). This does not by itself force a contradiction, so we use the similarity relation more strongly.

Since \(B\) is similar to \(B+B^2\), these two matrices have the same trace of every power:
\[
\operatorname{tr}(B^m)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl((B+B^2)^m\bigr)\qquad(m\ge 1).
\]
Taking \(m\) large is inconvenient; instead observe on eigenvalues that the multisets
\[
\{\text{eigenvalues of }B\}\quad\text{and}\quad \{\lambda+\lambda^2:\lambda\text{ eigenvalue of }B\}
\]
coincide.

Now let \(\lambda_1\) be a real eigenvalue of \(B\). Define
\[
\lambda_{k+1}=\lambda_k+\lambda_k^2.
\]
Then every \(\lambda_k\) is again a real eigenvalue of \(B\). Since there are only finitely many eigenvalues, the sequence must eventually repeat:
\[
\lambda_{l+1}=\lambda_k
\]
for some \(k\le l\). Therefore
\[
\lambda_{k+1}-\lambda_k=\lambda_k^2,\quad
\lambda_{k+2}-\lambda_{k+1}=\lambda_{k+1}^2,\quad \dots,\quad
\lambda_{l+1}-\lambda_l=\lambda_l^2.
\]
Summing,
\[
0=\lambda_{l+1}-\lambda_k=\lambda_k^2+\lambda_{k+1}^2+\cdots+\lambda_l^2.
\]
Hence all \(\lambda_i=0\), contradiction to invertibility of \(B\).

So \(n\) cannot be odd.

II. It remains to show that every even \(n\) works. For \(n=2\), choose
\[
A_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
B_2=\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Then
\[
A_2B_2-B_2A_2=
\begin{pmatrix}-2&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}
\]
and
\[
B_2^2A_2=
\begin{pmatrix}-2&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Thus the required identity holds, and both matrices are invertible.

For any even \(n=2m\), define
\[
A=\operatorname{diag}(A_2,\dots,A_2),\qquad
B=\operatorname{diag}(B_2,\dots,B_2).
\]
Since the equation is preserved under block diagonal sums, these \(A,B\) are invertible and satisfy
\[
AB-BA=B^2A.
\]

problem: Determine all positive integers $n$ for which there exist $n \times n$ real invertible matrices $A$ and $B$ that satisfy $A B-B A=B^{2} A$.
alternative_solution:
We prove that the condition is equivalent to \(n\) being even.

I. Assume that invertible real \(n\times n\) matrices \(A,B\) satisfy
\[
AB-BA=B^2A.
\]
Rearrange:
\[
AB=(B+B^2)A.
\]
Taking determinants, we obtain
\[
\det(A)\det(B)=\det(B+B^2)\det(A).
\]
Since \(A\) is invertible,
\[
\det(B)=\det(B+B^2).
\]
Factor the right-hand side:
\[
B+B^2=B(I+B),
\]
so
\[
\det(B)=\det(B)\det(I+B).
\]
Because \(B\) is invertible, \(\det(B)\neq 0\), hence
\[
\det(I+B)=1. \tag{1}
\]

Now suppose \(n\) is odd. Since \(B\) is a real matrix of odd order, it has a real eigenvalue \(\lambda\). As \(B\) is invertible, \(\lambda\neq 0\).

Also, from
\[
AB=(B+B^2)A
\]
we see that \(B\) and \(B+B^2\) are similar:
\[
A^{-1}BA=B+B^2.
\]
Therefore, whenever \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of \(B\), the number
\[
\lambda+\lambda^2
\]
is also an eigenvalue of \(B\).

Starting with the real eigenvalue \(\lambda_1=\lambda\), define recursively
\[
\lambda_{m+1}=\lambda_m+\lambda_m^2.
\]
Then each \(\lambda_m\) is a real eigenvalue of \(B\). Since \(B\) has only finitely many eigenvalues, some value repeats: there exist \(k\le l\) such that
\[
\lambda_{l+1}=\lambda_k.
\]
Now
\[
\lambda_{i+1}-\lambda_i=\lambda_i^2\ge 0\qquad (i\ge 1).
\]
Hence the sequence is nondecreasing. But if \(\lambda_{l+1}=\lambda_k\), then on the finite stretch
\[
\lambda_k\le \lambda_{k+1}\le \cdots \le \lambda_{l+1}=\lambda_k,
\]
all terms must be equal:
\[
\lambda_k=\lambda_{k+1}=\cdots=\lambda_{l+1}.
\]
Then from \(\lambda_{i+1}-\lambda_i=\lambda_i^2\) we get
\[
\lambda_i^2=0
\]
for \(i=k,\dots,l\), so \(\lambda_k=0\). Thus \(0\) is an eigenvalue of \(B\), contradicting invertibility of \(B\).

Therefore no such matrices can exist when \(n\) is odd.

II. Now let \(n\) be even. It is enough to give one \(2\times2\) example and then repeat it on the diagonal.

Set
\[
A_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
B_2=\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Compute
\[
A_2B_2=
\begin{pmatrix}-1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
B_2A_2=
\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix},
\]
so
\[
A_2B_2-B_2A_2=
\begin{pmatrix}-2&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Also
\[
B_2^2=
\begin{pmatrix}0&-2\\2&0\end{pmatrix},
\]
hence
\[
B_2^2A_2=
\begin{pmatrix}-2&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Thus
\[
A_2B_2-B_2A_2=B_2^2A_2.
\]
The matrices are invertible since \(\det(A_2)=-1\) and \(\det(B_2)=2\).

For \(n=2m\), let
\[
A=\operatorname{diag}(A_2,\dots,A_2),\qquad
B=\operatorname{diag}(B_2,\dots,B_2).
\]
Then \(A,B\) are invertible and satisfy the same equation blockwise.

problem: Determine all positive integers $n$ for which there exist $n \times n$ real invertible matrices $A$ and $B$ that satisfy $A B-B A=B^{2} A$.
alternative_solution:
We show that such matrices exist exactly for even \(n\).

I. Assume first that \(n\) is odd and that invertible real \(n\times n\) matrices \(A,B\) satisfy
\[
AB-BA=B^2A.
\]
Since \(A\) is invertible, we may rewrite this as
\[
A^{-1}BA-B=B^2.
\]
Taking traces, we get
\[
\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}BA)-\operatorname{tr}(B)=\operatorname{tr}(B^2).
\]
But \(\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}BA)=\operatorname{tr}(B)\), so
\[
\operatorname{tr}(B^2)=0.
\]

Now \(n\) is odd, so the real matrix \(B\) has at least one real eigenvalue \(\lambda\). Since \(B\) is invertible, \(\lambda\neq 0\). The nonreal eigenvalues occur in conjugate pairs, hence
\[
\operatorname{tr}(B^2)=\lambda^2+\sum (\mu_i^2+\overline{\mu_i}^2).
\]
Each pair contributes
\[
\mu_i^2+\overline{\mu_i}^2=2\Re(\mu_i^2),
\]
so this expression is real, but this alone is not enough. Instead we use determinant.

From
\[
AB=A(B+B^2)=A(I+B)B,
\]
taking determinants yields
\[
\det(A)\det(B)=\det(A)\det(I+B)\det(B).
\]
Since \(A,B\) are invertible, we may cancel \(\det(A)\det(B)\neq 0\), obtaining
\[
\det(I+B)=1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\prod_{i=1}^n (1+\lambda_i)=1,
\]
where \(\lambda_i\) are the eigenvalues of \(B\) over \(\mathbb C\).

On the other hand, from
\[
B=A^{-1}(B^2+B)A,
\]
the matrices \(B\) and \(B(B+I)\) are similar, so they have the same determinant:
\[
\det(B)=\det(B(B+I))=\det(B)\det(B+I).
\]
Again \(B\) is invertible, so \(\det(B)\neq 0\), and thus
\[
\det(B+I)=1.
\]
This means the product of all numbers \(1+\lambda_i\) equals \(1\).

Now let \(\lambda\) be a real eigenvalue of \(B\). Since \(B\) and \(B^2+B\) are similar, \(B^2+B\) has the same eigenvalues as \(B\). Hence
\[
\lambda^2+\lambda
\]
is also an eigenvalue of \(B\) whenever \(\lambda\) is. Starting from the real eigenvalue \(\lambda\), define
\[
\lambda_{m+1}=\lambda_m^2+\lambda_m.
\]
All \(\lambda_m\) are real eigenvalues of \(B\). Since \(B\) has only finitely many eigenvalues, some value repeats: \(\lambda_r=\lambda_s\) with \(r<s\). Then
\[
\lambda_r\mapsto \lambda_{r+1}\mapsto \cdots \mapsto \lambda_s=\lambda_r
\]
forms a cycle under the map \(f(x)=x^2+x\).

If \(x\) belongs to such a real cycle, then summing the relations
\[
\lambda_{j+1}-\lambda_j=\lambda_j^2
\]
around the cycle gives
\[
0=\lambda_r^2+\lambda_{r+1}^2+\cdots+\lambda_{s-1}^2.
\]
Hence every term is \(0\), so \(\lambda_r=0\). Thus \(0\) is an eigenvalue of \(B\), contradicting invertibility.

Therefore no such matrices exist when \(n\) is odd.

II. Now let \(n\) be even, say \(n=2k\). Consider
\[
A_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
B_2=\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\ -1&-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
A direct computation gives
\[
A_2B_2-B_2A_2=B_2^2A_2.
\]
Also,
\[
\det(A_2)=-1\neq 0,\qquad \det(B_2)=2\neq 0,
\]
so both are invertible.

For \(n=2k\), form block diagonal matrices
\[
A=\operatorname{diag}(A_2,\dots,A_2),\qquad
B=\operatorname{diag}(B_2,\dots,B_2).
\]
Then \(A,B\) are invertible, and blockwise multiplication shows
\[
AB-BA=B^2A.
\]

problem: Determine all positive integers $n$ for which there exist $n \times n$ real invertible matrices $A$ and $B$ that satisfy $A B-B A=B^{2} A$.
alternative_solution:
We again prove that the condition is equivalent to \(n\) being even.

I. Suppose that invertible real \(n\times n\) matrices \(A,B\) satisfy
\[
AB-BA=B^2A.
\]
Then
\[
AB=(I+B)BA.
\]
Taking determinants gives
\[
\det(A)\det(B)=\det(I+B)\det(B)\det(A).
\]
Since \(A\) and \(B\) are invertible,
\[
\det(I+B)=1. \tag{1}
\]

Next, from
\[
AB-BA=B^2A
\]
we also get
\[
AB=A(B+B^2)=AB(I+B),
\]
after factoring on the right:
\[
B+B^2=B(I+B).
\]
So
\[
AB=AB(I+B).
\]
Again \(AB\) is invertible, hence
\[
I=I+B,
\]
would be too strong if read literally, so let us instead proceed more carefully by using the equivalent form
\[
B=A^{-1}(B^2+B)A.
\]
Thus \(B\) is similar to \(B^2+B=B(I+B)\). Therefore \(B\) and \(B(I+B)\) have the same characteristic polynomial, in particular the same eigenvalues with multiplicities.

Let \(\lambda\) be any eigenvalue of \(B\) in \(\mathbb C\). Then \(\lambda^2+\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of \(B^2+B\), hence also of \(B\). Therefore the finite multiset of eigenvalues of \(B\) is stable under the map
\[
f(x)=x^2+x.
\]

Now assume \(n\) is odd. Since \(B\) is real of odd size, \(B\) has a real eigenvalue \(\lambda\). Repeatedly applying \(f\), we obtain real eigenvalues
\[
\lambda,\ f(\lambda),\ f(f(\lambda)),\dots
\]
of \(B\). Because there are only finitely many eigenvalues, some value is repeated, so a real cycle occurs:
\[
x_1\mapsto x_2\mapsto \cdots \mapsto x_m\mapsto x_1,
\qquad x_{j+1}=x_j^2+x_j.
\]
Then
\[
x_{j+1}-x_j=x_j^2\ge 0
\]
for each \(j\). Summing around the cycle gives
\[
0=(x_2-x_1)+(x_3-x_2)+\cdots +(x_1-x_m)=x_1^2+\cdots +x_m^2.
\]
Hence all \(x_j=0\). In particular \(0\) is an eigenvalue of \(B\), contradicting the invertibility of \(B\).

Thus \(n\) cannot be odd.

II. It remains to show that every even \(n\) works. For
\[
A_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
B_2=\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix},
\]
one checks directly that
\[
A_2B_2-B_2A_2=B_2^2A_2.
\]
Also
\[
\det(A_2)=-1,\qquad \det(B_2)=2,
\]
so both matrices are invertible.

If \(n=2k\), let
\[
A=\operatorname{diag}(A_2,\dots,A_2),\qquad
B=\operatorname{diag}(B_2,\dots,B_2).
\]
Then \(A,B\) are invertible real \(n\times n\) matrices, and the required identity holds on each \(2\times2\) block, hence on the whole matrix:
\[
AB-BA=B^2A.
\]

problem: Determine all positive integers $n$ for which there exist $n \times n$ real invertible matrices $A$ and $B$ that satisfy $A B-B A=B^{2} A$.
alternative_solution:
We divide the proof into necessity and sufficiency.

I. Necessity: \(n\) must be even.

Assume that for some positive integer \(n\) there exist invertible real \(n\times n\) matrices \(A,B\) such that
\[
AB-BA=B^2A.
\]
Multiply on the right by \(A^{-1}\):
\[
ABA^{-1}-B=B^2.
\]
Hence
\[
ABA^{-1}=B+B^2=B(I+B).
\]
So \(B\) is similar to \(B(I+B)\).

Passing to characteristic polynomials, similar matrices have the same determinant after subtraction of \(tI\). In particular, for \(t=0\),
\[
\det(B)=\det(B(I+B))=\det(B)\det(I+B).
\]
Because \(B\) is invertible, \(\det(B)\neq 0\), and therefore
\[
\det(I+B)=1. \tag{1}
\]

Now suppose \(n\) is odd. Then the real matrix \(B\) has a real eigenvalue \(\lambda\). Since \(B\) is invertible, \(\lambda\neq 0\).

Because \(B\) and \(B+B^2\) are similar, they have the same spectrum. Therefore whenever \(\mu\) is an eigenvalue of \(B\), so is
\[
\mu+\mu^2.
\]
Starting from the real eigenvalue \(\lambda\), define
\[
u_0=\lambda,\qquad u_{k+1}=u_k+u_k^2.
\]
Each \(u_k\) is a real eigenvalue of \(B\). Since \(B\) has only finitely many eigenvalues, there exist \(r<s\) such that \(u_r=u_s\).

But
\[
u_{k+1}-u_k=u_k^2\ge 0,
\]
so the sequence \((u_k)\) is nondecreasing. If some \(u_k\neq 0\), then \(u_{k+1}>u_k\), so equality can never occur later. Therefore the only way to have \(u_r=u_s\) is that
\[
u_r=u_{r+1}=\cdots =u_s=0.
\]
In particular \(0\) is an eigenvalue of \(B\), contradicting the invertibility of \(B\).

Thus \(n\) cannot be odd, so \(n\) must be even.

II. Sufficiency: every even \(n\) works.

Consider the \(2\times2\) matrices
\[
A_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
B_2=\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
A direct computation shows
\[
A_2B_2-B_2A_2=B_2^2A_2.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\det(A_2)=-1\neq 0,\qquad \det(B_2)=2\neq 0,
\]
so \(A_2\) and \(B_2\) are invertible.

For any even \(n=2m\), define
\[
A=\operatorname{diag}(A_2,\ldots,A_2),\qquad
B=\operatorname{diag}(B_2,\ldots,B_2).
\]
Then \(A\) and \(B\) are real invertible \(n\times n\) matrices. Since the identity
\[
A_2B_2-B_2A_2=B_2^2A_2
\]
holds on every diagonal block, we get
\[
AB-BA=B^2A.
\]

problem: Let $n, k \geq 3$ be integers, and let $S$ be a circle. Let $n$ blue points and $k$ red points be chosen uniformly and independently at random on the circle $S$. Denote by $F$ the intersection of the convex hull of the red points and the convex hull of the blue points. Let $m$ be the number of vertices of the convex polygon $F$ (in particular, $m=0$ when $F$ is empty). Find the expected value of $m$.
alternative_solution:
Let the \(n+k\) random points be listed around the circle in circular order. Since with probability \(1\) no two points coincide, every point is a vertex of the convex hull of its own color.

A vertex of \(F\) is precisely an intersection point of one blue hull side and one red hull side. Thus we may count vertices of \(F\) by counting color-hull sides that actually contribute one side to the boundary of \(F\).

For a blue hull side \(e\), let \(I_e\) be the indicator that \(e\) supports a side of \(F\). If \(B\) is the number of blue sides contributing to \(F\), then
\[
B=\sum I_e.
\]
Similarly define \(R\) for red sides. Since the sides of \(F\) alternate in color support and each vertex belongs to exactly one contributing blue side and one contributing red side, we have
\[
m=B+R.
\]
So it is enough to compute \(E(B)\) and \(E(R)\).

Now fix a blue point \(A\). Let \(A'\) be the next blue point counterclockwise from \(A\). Then \(AA'\) is a side of the blue convex hull. We compute the probability that this side contributes to \(F\).

The chord \(AA'\) fails to contribute exactly when all red points lie in the same open half-plane bounded by the line \(AA'\). On the circle, this happens in exactly two mutually exclusive cases:

1. \(A'\) is immediately after \(A\) in the circular order among all \(n+k\) points.  
   Then there is no point between \(A\) and \(A'\), so all red points lie on one side of the line \(AA'\).  
   The probability of this is
   \[
   \frac{n-1}{n+k-1},
   \]
   since among the remaining \(n+k-1\) points, exactly \(n-1\) are blue.

2. All \(k\) red points lie consecutively between \(A\) and \(A'\).  
   Equivalently, among the \(n+k-1\) positions after \(A\), the red points occupy exactly the first \(k\) positions.  
   Since every \(k\)-subset of these \(n+k-1\) positions is equally likely to be the red set, this has probability
   \[
   \frac{1}{\binom{n+k-1}{k}}.
   \]

Hence
\[
P(I_e=1)=1-\frac{n-1}{n+k-1}-\frac{1}{\binom{n+k-1}{k}}.
\]
There are \(n\) blue hull sides, all symmetric, so
\[
E(B)=n\left(1-\frac{n-1}{n+k-1}-\frac{1}{\binom{n+k-1}{k}}\right)
= n\left(\frac{k}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!(n-1)!}{(n+k-1)!}\right).
\]
Thus
\[
E(B)=\frac{nk}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!n!}{(n+k-1)!}.
\]

By symmetry, for red sides,
\[
E(R)=\frac{nk}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!n!}{(n+k-1)!}.
\]

Therefore
\[
E(m)=E(B)+E(R)
=2\left(\frac{nk}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!n!}{(n+k-1)!}\right).
\]

As a quick verification, the formula is symmetric in \(n,k\), as it must be, and tends to \(2k\) when \(n\to\infty\) with \(k\) fixed, which matches the intuition that the smaller-color hull is then almost entirely inside the larger one.

problem: Let $n, k \geq 3$ be integers, and let $S$ be a circle. Let $n$ blue points and $k$ red points be chosen uniformly and independently at random on the circle $S$. Denote by $F$ the intersection of the convex hull of the red points and the convex hull of the blue points. Let $m$ be the number of vertices of the convex polygon $F$ (in particular, $m=0$ when $F$ is empty). Find the expected value of $m$.
alternative_solution:
We use the fact that a point of \(F\) is a vertex exactly when the two monochromatic polygons cross there. Hence each vertex of \(F\) comes from one blue side and one red side, and conversely every contributing side of one color gives exactly one side of \(F\). So we may count sides instead of vertices.

Fix a blue point \(A\). Consider the next blue point \(A^+\) in clockwise order. The segment \(AA^+\) is an edge of the blue convex hull. Let \(X_A\) be the indicator of the event that \(AA^+\) appears on the boundary of \(F\). Then
\[
m=\sum_{\text{blue }A} X_A+\sum_{\text{red }R} Y_R,
\]
where \(Y_R\) is defined analogously for red edges.

Thus
\[
E(m)=nE(X_A)+kE(Y_R)
\]
by symmetry.

So we compute \(E(X_A)\). The edge \(AA^+\) does not appear on the boundary of \(F\) exactly when the whole red polygon lies strictly on one side of the supporting line of \(AA^+\). Since all points lie on the circle, this is equivalent to saying that, in one of the two arcs cut by \(A\) and \(A^+\), all red points lie entirely in that arc.

Because \(A^+\) is the next blue point after \(A\), the clockwise arc from \(A\) to \(A^+\) contains no blue points. Therefore the nonappearance of \(AA^+\) can happen in exactly two ways:

- the clockwise arc is empty, i.e. \(A^+\) is immediately next to \(A\) among all points;
- the clockwise arc contains exactly all \(k\) red points.

These two events are disjoint.

Now, condition on \(A\). Among the \(n+k-1\) remaining circular positions relative to \(A\), the next point is blue with probability
\[
\frac{n-1}{n+k-1}.
\]
This is the probability of the first event.

For the second event, the set of locations of the \(k\) red points among the \(n+k-1\) slots is uniformly distributed over all \(\binom{n+k-1}{k}\) choices. Exactly one of these choices makes the first \(k\) slots red and all later slots blue. Hence its probability is
\[
\frac{1}{\binom{n+k-1}{k}}.
\]

Therefore
\[
E(X_A)=1-\frac{n-1}{n+k-1}-\frac{1}{\binom{n+k-1}{k}}
=\frac{k}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!(n-1)!}{(n+k-1)!}.
\]
Multiplying by \(n\),
\[
nE(X_A)=\frac{nk}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!n!}{(n+k-1)!}.
\]

By the same argument with colors exchanged,
\[
kE(Y_R)=\frac{nk}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!n!}{(n+k-1)!}.
\]

Hence
\[
E(m)=\frac{nk}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!n!}{(n+k-1)!}
+\frac{nk}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!n!}{(n+k-1)!}.
\]

For verification, when \(n=k=3\) this gives
\[
E(m)=\frac{18}{5}-2\cdot\frac{6\cdot 6}{5!}
=\frac{18}{5}-\frac{3}{5}=3,
\]
which is a reasonable value between \(0\) and \(6\).

problem: Let $n, k \geq 3$ be integers, and let $S$ be a circle. Let $n$ blue points and $k$ red points be chosen uniformly and independently at random on the circle $S$. Denote by $F$ the intersection of the convex hull of the red points and the convex hull of the blue points. Let $m$ be the number of vertices of the convex polygon $F$ (in particular, $m=0$ when $F$ is empty). Find the expected value of $m$.
alternative_solution:
We count expected vertices of \(F\) by scanning the circle for color changes that survive in the intersection polygon.

Choose an arbitrary orientation of the circle. For each blue point \(B_i\), let \(N(B_i)\) be the next blue point encountered counterclockwise. The side \(B_iN(B_i)\) of the blue hull contributes one side to \(F\) unless the red hull lies completely on one side of its supporting line. Define
\[
\beta_i=
\begin{cases}
1,& \text{if }B_iN(B_i)\text{ contributes a side of }F,\\
0,& \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]
Similarly define \(\rho_j\) for red points.

Every side of \(F\) is supported by exactly one blue hull side or one red hull side, and the number of sides of a convex polygon equals the number of vertices. Hence
\[
m=\sum_{i=1}^n \beta_i+\sum_{j=1}^k \rho_j.
\]
By linearity of expectation,
\[
E(m)=\sum_{i=1}^n E(\beta_i)+\sum_{j=1}^k E(\rho_j).
\]

Now fix \(i\). We compute \(P(\beta_i=0)\).

Place \(B_i\) first in the cyclic order and look at the remaining \(n+k-1\) points. Their color pattern is a uniformly random arrangement of \(n-1\) blue and \(k\) red symbols. Let \(t\) be the position of the first blue symbol; then the points before \(t\) are red and the point at \(t\) is \(N(B_i)\).

The side \(B_iN(B_i)\) does not contribute precisely when all red points lie in one of the two arcs determined by \(B_i\) and \(N(B_i)\). In terms of the color string, that means:

- either \(t=1\), so the first symbol is blue and there are no points in the shorter arc;
- or \(t=k+1\), so the first \(k\) symbols are red and all red points are exhausted before the next blue appears.

Indeed, if \(2\le t\le k\), then there are red points on one side of the chord and at least one red point remains on the other side; in that case the red hull meets both sides of the line and the blue side contributes to \(F\).

Therefore
\[
P(\beta_i=0)=P(t=1)+P(t=k+1).
\]

The event \(t=1\) means the first symbol is blue, so
\[
P(t=1)=\frac{n-1}{n+k-1}.
\]

The event \(t=k+1\) means the first \(k\) symbols are red. In the uniformly random word with \(k\) red symbols among \(n+k-1\) positions, this occurs with probability
\[
\frac{1}{\binom{n+k-1}{k}}.
\]

Hence
\[
E(\beta_i)=1-\frac{n-1}{n+k-1}-\frac{1}{\binom{n+k-1}{k}}
=\frac{k}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!(n-1)!}{(n+k-1)!}.
\]
Summing over all \(n\) blue points,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n E(\beta_i)=\frac{nk}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!n!}{(n+k-1)!}.
\]

Interchanging blue and red gives
\[
\sum_{j=1}^k E(\rho_j)=\frac{nk}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!n!}{(n+k-1)!}.
\]

So
\[
E(m)=2\left(\frac{nk}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!n!}{(n+k-1)!}\right).
\]

For verification, the expression is unchanged when \(n\) and \(k\) are swapped, which is necessary because the problem is symmetric in the two colors.

problem: Let $n, k \geq 3$ be integers, and let $S$ be a circle. Let $n$ blue points and $k$ red points be chosen uniformly and independently at random on the circle $S$. Denote by $F$ the intersection of the convex hull of the red points and the convex hull of the blue points. Let $m$ be the number of vertices of the convex polygon $F$ (in particular, $m=0$ when $F$ is empty). Find the expected value of $m$.
alternative_solution:
Let the $n+k$ random points be listed in circular order. Since with probability $1$ no two points coincide and no three relevant lines are degenerate, the polygon $F$ is well-defined.

We count vertices of $F$ through changes of color along the circle.

Observe that every side of the convex hull of the blue points is a chord joining two consecutive blue points in the circular order, with only red points between them. Similarly for the red hull. A vertex of $F$ is created exactly when a side of the blue hull and a side of the red hull both contribute to the boundary of the intersection. Equivalently, each vertex of $F$ corresponds to one boundary arc-gap of one color that is not “protected” from the other color by putting all opposite-colored points on the same side.

It is convenient to count instead the number of blue sides that appear on the boundary of $F$, and the number of red sides that appear on the boundary of $F$; these are equal in total to $m$.

Fix a blue point $A$. Let $B$ be the next blue point counterclockwise from $A$. Then $AB$ is a side of the blue convex hull. We ask for the probability that this side contributes an edge of $F$.

Between $A$ and $B$ counterclockwise there are some red points and no blue points. Suppose there are $t$ red points there. Then:

- If $t=0$, the chord $AB$ is an edge of the blue hull, but it cannot support an edge of $F$, because all red points lie on the same side of the line $AB$.
- If $t=k$, then all red points lie on the arc from $A$ to $B$, hence again all red points lie on the same side of $AB$, so $AB$ does not contribute to $F$.
- If $1\le t\le k-1$, then there are red points on both sides of the line $AB$, so the line $AB$ cuts the red hull, and therefore $AB$ contributes exactly one side to the boundary of $F$.

Hence for a fixed blue point $A$, if $T$ denotes the number of red points before the next blue point, then
$$
\mathbf 1_{\{AB\text{ contributes to }F\}}=\mathbf 1_{\{1\le T\le k-1\}}.
$$

Now compute the probability distribution of $T$. After fixing $A$, among the remaining $n+k-1$ positions in circular order, the $n-1$ blue points occupy a uniformly random $(n-1)$-subset. Thus:

- $T=0$ iff the first point after $A$ is blue, so
$$
\mathbb P(T=0)=\frac{n-1}{n+k-1}.
$$
- $T=k$ iff all $k$ red points occur before the next blue point, i.e. the first $k$ points after $A$ are red. This has probability
$$
\mathbb P(T=k)=\frac{1}{\binom{n+k-1}{k}}=\frac{k!(n-1)!}{(n+k-1)!}.
$$

Therefore
$$
\mathbb E(\text{blue contribution from }A)
=1-\frac{n-1}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!(n-1)!}{(n+k-1)!}
=\frac{k}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!(n-1)!}{(n+k-1)!}.
$$

Summing over all $n$ blue points, the expected number of boundary sides of $F$ coming from blue hull sides is
$$
n\left(\frac{k}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!(n-1)!}{(n+k-1)!}\right)
=\frac{nk}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!n!}{(n+k-1)!}.
$$

By symmetry, the expected number of boundary sides of $F$ coming from red hull sides is
$$
\frac{nk}{n+k-1}-\frac{n!k!}{(n+k-1)!}.
$$

Adding these two expectations gives $E(m)$:
$$
E(m)=\frac{2nk}{n+k-1}-2\frac{k!n!}{(n+k-1)!}.
$$

problem: Let $n, k \geq 3$ be integers, and let $S$ be a circle. Let $n$ blue points and $k$ red points be chosen uniformly and independently at random on the circle $S$. Denote by $F$ the intersection of the convex hull of the red points and the convex hull of the blue points. Let $m$ be the number of vertices of the convex polygon $F$ (in particular, $m=0$ when $F$ is empty). Find the expected value of $m$.
alternative_solution:
We use the fact that, with probability $1$, every vertex of $F$ is the intersection of one edge of the blue hull and one edge of the red hull, and while traversing the boundary of $F$, blue-supported and red-supported sides alternate. Thus the number of vertices of $F$ equals the number of supporting blue edges of $F$ plus the number of supporting red edges of $F$.

So it suffices to compute the expected number of blue hull edges that support $F$.

For every ordered pair of distinct blue points $(A,B)$, let $I_{A,B}$ be the indicator of the event:

- $B$ is the next blue point after $A$ counterclockwise, and
- the chord $AB$ supports a side of $F$.

Then the number of blue-supported sides of $F$ is
$$
X_B=\sum_{A\in \{\text{blue points}\}} I_{A,B(A)},
$$
where $B(A)$ denotes the next blue point after $A$.

Fix a blue point $A$. Reveal the circular order of the remaining $n+k-1$ points relative to $A$. The colors of these positions are uniformly distributed among all words with $n-1$ blue symbols and $k$ red symbols.

Let $j$ be the position of the first blue symbol. Then $j-1$ red points lie between $A$ and the next blue point. The corresponding chord fails to support $F$ in exactly two mutually exclusive cases:

1. $j=1$, meaning there are no red points between the two consecutive blue points.
2. $j=k+1$, meaning all $k$ red points occur before the next blue point.

Indeed, in either case all red points lie in one closed half-plane bounded by the chord, so the red hull lies entirely on one side and the chord cannot appear on the boundary of the intersection. In every other case, there are red points on both sides, so the chord contributes a side of $F$.

Now
$$
\mathbb P(j=1)=\frac{n-1}{n+k-1},
$$
because the first position is blue with that probability.

Also,
$$
\mathbb P(j=k+1)=\frac{(n-1)}{n+k-1}\cdot\frac{(n-2)}{n+k-2}\cdots\frac{1}{n}
=\frac{k!(n-1)!}{(n+k-1)!},
$$
equivalently $1/\binom{n+k-1}{k}$.

Therefore
$$
\mathbb E(I_{A,B(A)})
=1-\frac{n-1}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!(n-1)!}{(n+k-1)!}.
$$
Hence
$$
\mathbb E(X_B)
=n\left(1-\frac{n-1}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!(n-1)!}{(n+k-1)!}\right)
=\frac{nk}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!n!}{(n+k-1)!}.
$$

By the same argument with colors exchanged, if $X_R$ denotes the number of red-supported sides of $F$, then
$$
\mathbb E(X_R)=\frac{nk}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!n!}{(n+k-1)!}.
$$

Since $m=X_B+X_R$, linearity of expectation yields
$$
E(m)=\frac{2nk}{n+k-1}-2\frac{k!n!}{(n+k-1)!}.
$$

problem: Let $n, k \geq 3$ be integers, and let $S$ be a circle. Let $n$ blue points and $k$ red points be chosen uniformly and independently at random on the circle $S$. Denote by $F$ the intersection of the convex hull of the red points and the convex hull of the blue points. Let $m$ be the number of vertices of the convex polygon $F$ (in particular, $m=0$ when $F$ is empty). Find the expected value of $m$.
alternative_solution:
We derive $E(m)$ by counting expected intersections between the boundary of one hull and supporting chords of the other.

For each blue side $e$, let $\xi_e$ be $1$ if $e$ appears on the boundary of $F$, and $0$ otherwise. For each red side $f$, define $\eta_f$ analogously. Since every side of $F$ lies on either a blue hull side or a red hull side, and each vertex count equals the number of sides of the polygon $F$, we have
$$
m=\sum_{e\text{ blue side}}\xi_e+\sum_{f\text{ red side}}\eta_f.
$$
Thus
$$
E(m)=E\left(\sum \xi_e\right)+E\left(\sum \eta_f\right).
$$

We compute the first expectation.

Choose a blue point $A$ uniformly among the blue points, and let $B$ be the next blue point around the circle. Then $AB$ is a uniformly chosen blue hull side in the cyclic sense. Therefore
$$
E\left(\sum \xi_e\right)=n\cdot \mathbb P(AB\text{ is on }\partial F).
$$

So we only need $\mathbb P(AB\text{ is on }\partial F)$.

Condition on the cyclic order after $A$. The next blue point $B$ occurs after some number $t$ of red points, where $t\in\{0,1,\dots,k\}$. Because the $k$ red positions among the next $n+k-1$ places form a uniformly random $k$-subset, the extreme cases can be computed directly:

- $t=0$ exactly when position $1$ is blue, so
$$
\mathbb P(t=0)=\frac{n-1}{n+k-1}.
$$
- $t=k$ exactly when positions $1,2,\dots,k$ are all red, so
$$
\mathbb P(t=k)=\frac{1}{\binom{n+k-1}{k}}=\frac{k!(n-1)!}{(n+k-1)!}.
$$

Now determine when $AB$ belongs to the boundary of $F$.

The red hull intersects the line $AB$ if and only if not all red points lie on the same side of that line. Since all blue points except $A,B$ lie on one side of $AB$, the chord $AB$ can support part of the intersection exactly when the red points are present on both sides of the line. On the circle this is equivalent to saying that neither $t=0$ nor $t=k$ occurs. Hence
$$
\mathbb P(AB\text{ is on }\partial F)
=1-\frac{n-1}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!(n-1)!}{(n+k-1)!}
=\frac{k}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!(n-1)!}{(n+k-1)!}.
$$

Therefore
$$
E\left(\sum \xi_e\right)
=n\left(\frac{k}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!(n-1)!}{(n+k-1)!}\right)
=\frac{nk}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!n!}{(n+k-1)!}.
$$

By swapping the roles of blue and red,
$$
E\left(\sum \eta_f\right)=\frac{nk}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!n!}{(n+k-1)!}.
$$

Adding,
$$
E(m)=\frac{2nk}{n+k-1}-2\frac{k!n!}{(n+k-1)!}.
$$

problem: Determine the value of \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \ln \left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right) \cdot \ln \left(1+\frac{1}{2 n}\right) \cdot \ln \left(1+\frac{1}{2 n+1}\right)\).
alternative_solution:
Let  
\[
a_n=\ln\left(1+\frac1n\right)=\ln\frac{n+1}{n}.
\]
Then
\[
a_{2n}=\ln\frac{2n+1}{2n},\qquad a_{2n+1}=\ln\frac{2n+2}{2n+1},
\]
and hence
\[
a_{2n}+a_{2n+1}
=\ln\frac{2n+1}{2n}+\ln\frac{2n+2}{2n+1}
=\ln\frac{n+1}{n}
=a_n.
\]
So the given series is
\[
S=\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n a_{2n} a_{2n+1}.
\]

Now use
\[
x^3-y^3-z^3=(y+z)^3-y^3-z^3=3yz(y+z)
\]
whenever \(x=y+z\). Since \(a_n=a_{2n}+a_{2n+1}\), we get
\[
a_n^3-a_{2n}^3-a_{2n+1}^3=3a_na_{2n}a_{2n+1}.
\]
Therefore
\[
a_na_{2n}a_{2n+1}=\frac13\bigl(a_n^3-a_{2n}^3-a_{2n+1}^3\bigr).
\]
Summing from \(n=1\) to \(N\),
\[
\sum_{n=1}^N a_na_{2n}a_{2n+1}
=\frac13\sum_{n=1}^N\bigl(a_n^3-a_{2n}^3-a_{2n+1}^3\bigr).
\]
But
\[
\sum_{n=1}^N a_n^3-\sum_{n=1}^N a_{2n}^3-\sum_{n=1}^N a_{2n+1}^3
= a_1^3-\sum_{m=N+1}^{2N+1} a_m^3,
\]
because the terms \(a_2^3,\dots,a_N^3\) are exactly canceled by the even and odd parts. Thus
\[
\sum_{n=1}^N a_na_{2n}a_{2n+1}
=\frac13\left(a_1^3-\sum_{m=N+1}^{2N+1} a_m^3\right).
\]

It remains to pass to the limit. Since \(\ln(1+x)\le x\) for \(x>-1\),
\[
0<a_m=\ln\left(1+\frac1m\right)\le \frac1m,
\]
hence
\[
0\le \sum_{m=N+1}^{2N+1} a_m^3\le \sum_{m=N+1}^{2N+1}\frac1{m^3}\le \frac{N+1}{(N+1)^3}=\frac1{(N+1)^2}\to 0.
\]
Therefore
\[
S=\frac13 a_1^3=\frac13\ln^3 2.
\]

problem: Determine the value of \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \ln \left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right) \cdot \ln \left(1+\frac{1}{2 n}\right) \cdot \ln \left(1+\frac{1}{2 n+1}\right)\).
alternative_solution:
Set
\[
f(n)=\ln\left(1+\frac1n\right)=\int_0^1\frac{dx}{n+x}.
\]
Then
\[
f(2n)+f(2n+1)=\ln\frac{2n+1}{2n}+\ln\frac{2n+2}{2n+1}
=\ln\frac{n+1}{n}
=f(n).
\]
Let
\[
S_N=\sum_{n=1}^N f(n)f(2n)f(2n+1).
\]
Using \(f(n)=f(2n)+f(2n+1)\),
\[
f(n)f(2n)f(2n+1)=\bigl(f(2n)+f(2n+1)\bigr)f(2n)f(2n+1).
\]
Now apply the identity
\[
(x+y)xy=\frac13\bigl((x+y)^3-x^3-y^3\bigr),
\]
with \(x=f(2n)\), \(y=f(2n+1)\). This gives
\[
f(n)f(2n)f(2n+1)=\frac13\bigl(f(n)^3-f(2n)^3-f(2n+1)^3\bigr).
\]
Hence
\[
3S_N=\sum_{n=1}^N f(n)^3-\sum_{n=1}^N f(2n)^3-\sum_{n=1}^N f(2n+1)^3.
\]
Rewrite the last two sums as one sum over \(2,3,\dots,2N+1\):
\[
\sum_{n=1}^N f(2n)^3+\sum_{n=1}^N f(2n+1)^3=\sum_{m=2}^{2N+1}f(m)^3.
\]
Therefore
\[
3S_N=\sum_{m=1}^N f(m)^3-\sum_{m=2}^{2N+1}f(m)^3
=f(1)^3-\sum_{m=N+1}^{2N+1}f(m)^3.
\]
So
\[
S_N=\frac13 f(1)^3-\frac13\sum_{m=N+1}^{2N+1}f(m)^3.
\]

Now estimate the remainder. Since \(f(m)=\ln(1+1/m)\sim 1/m\), in particular \(f(m)\le 1/m\), so
\[
0\le \sum_{m=N+1}^{2N+1}f(m)^3\le \sum_{m=N+1}^{2N+1}\frac1{m^3}\to 0.
\]
Passing to the limit,
\[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty f(n)f(2n)f(2n+1)=\frac13 f(1)^3.
\]
Finally,
\[
f(1)=\ln\left(1+\frac11\right)=\ln 2.
\]

problem: Determine the value of \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \ln \left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right) \cdot \ln \left(1+\frac{1}{2 n}\right) \cdot \ln \left(1+\frac{1}{2 n+1}\right)\).
alternative_solution:
Write
\[
u_n=\ln\frac{n+1}{n}.
\]
Then the required sum is
\[
S=\sum_{n=1}^\infty u_nu_{2n}u_{2n+1}.
\]
Observe first that
\[
u_{2n}+u_{2n+1}
=\ln\frac{2n+1}{2n}+\ln\frac{2n+2}{2n+1}
=\ln\frac{n+1}{n}
=u_n.
\]

Consider the partial sums
\[
T_N=\sum_{n=1}^N u_nu_{2n}u_{2n+1}.
\]
Using \(u_n=u_{2n}+u_{2n+1}\),
\[
3T_N=\sum_{n=1}^N 3u_{2n}u_{2n+1}(u_{2n}+u_{2n+1}).
\]
Now use the elementary formula
\[
(a+b)^3=a^3+b^3+3ab(a+b).
\]
With \(a=u_{2n}\), \(b=u_{2n+1}\), this becomes
\[
3u_{2n}u_{2n+1}(u_{2n}+u_{2n+1})=u_n^3-u_{2n}^3-u_{2n+1}^3.
\]
Hence
\[
3T_N=\sum_{n=1}^N\bigl(u_n^3-u_{2n}^3-u_{2n+1}^3\bigr).
\]

Now interpret this combinatorially on the index set \(\{1,2,\dots,2N+1\}\). Every index \(m\in\{2,\dots,N\}\) appears once with \(+\) as \(u_m^3\), and once with \(-\) because \(m\) is either \(2n\) or \(2n+1\) for a unique \(n\). Thus all such terms cancel. The only uncanceled positive term is \(u_1^3\), while the uncanceled negative terms are \(u_{N+1}^3,\dots,u_{2N+1}^3\). Therefore
\[
3T_N=u_1^3-\sum_{m=N+1}^{2N+1}u_m^3.
\]
So
\[
T_N=\frac13u_1^3-\frac13\sum_{m=N+1}^{2N+1}u_m^3.
\]

Since
\[
u_m=\ln\left(1+\frac1m\right)\le \frac1m,
\]
we have
\[
0\le \sum_{m=N+1}^{2N+1}u_m^3\le \sum_{m=N+1}^{2N+1}\frac1{m^3}\le \frac{1}{(N+1)^2}\to 0.
\]
Hence
\[
S=\lim_{N\to\infty}T_N=\frac13u_1^3.
\]
And
\[
u_1=\ln\frac21=\ln 2.
\]

problem: Determine the value of \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \ln \left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right) \cdot \ln \left(1+\frac{1}{2 n}\right) \cdot \ln \left(1+\frac{1}{2 n+1}\right)\).
alternative_solution:
Let  
\[
a_n=\ln\left(1+\frac1n\right)=\ln\frac{n+1}{n}.
\]
Then the given series is
\[
S=\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\,a_{2n}\,a_{2n+1}.
\]

Now observe the exact relation
\[
a_{2n}+a_{2n+1}
=\ln\frac{2n+1}{2n}+\ln\frac{2n+2}{2n+1}
=\ln\frac{2n+2}{2n}
=\ln\frac{n+1}{n}
=a_n.
\]
Hence
\[
a_n a_{2n} a_{2n+1}=(a_{2n}+a_{2n+1})a_{2n}a_{2n+1}.
\]
Using
\[
(x+y)^3-x^3-y^3=3xy(x+y),
\]
with \(x=a_{2n}\), \(y=a_{2n+1}\), we get
\[
a_n a_{2n} a_{2n+1}
=\frac13\bigl(a_n^3-a_{2n}^3-a_{2n+1}^3\bigr).
\]
Therefore
\[
S=\frac13\sum_{n=1}^\infty \bigl(a_n^3-a_{2n}^3-a_{2n+1}^3\bigr).
\]

Consider the partial sums:
\[
S_N=\frac13\sum_{n=1}^N \bigl(a_n^3-a_{2n}^3-a_{2n+1}^3\bigr).
\]
Since the indices \(2n\) and \(2n+1\) for \(1\le n\le N\) cover exactly \(2,3,\dots,2N+1\), this becomes
\[
S_N=\frac13\left(a_1^3-\sum_{k=N+1}^{2N+1} a_k^3\right).
\]
Now \(a_k=\ln(1+1/k)\le 1/k\), so
\[
0\le \sum_{k=N+1}^{2N+1} a_k^3\le \sum_{k=N+1}^{2N+1}\frac1{k^3}\to 0.
\]
Thus
\[
S=\lim_{N\to\infty}S_N=\frac13 a_1^3.
\]
Since
\[
a_1=\ln 2,
\]
we obtain
\[
S=\frac13\ln^3 2.
\]

problem: Determine the value of \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \ln \left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right) \cdot \ln \left(1+\frac{1}{2 n}\right) \cdot \ln \left(1+\frac{1}{2 n+1}\right)\).
alternative_solution:
Set
\[
f(n)=\ln\left(1+\frac1n\right)=\ln\frac{n+1}{n}.
\]
Then
\[
f(n)=f(2n)+f(2n+1),
\]
because
\[
\ln\frac{n+1}{n}
=\ln\frac{2n+2}{2n}
=\ln\frac{2n+1}{2n}+\ln\frac{2n+2}{2n+1}.
\]

Let
\[
T_N=\sum_{n=1}^N f(n)f(2n)f(2n+1).
\]
Using \(f(n)=f(2n)+f(2n+1)\),
\[
T_N=\sum_{n=1}^N (f(2n)+f(2n+1))f(2n)f(2n+1).
\]
Now use
\[
(x+y)xy=\frac13\bigl((x+y)^3-x^3-y^3\bigr),
\]
to obtain
\[
T_N=\frac13\sum_{n=1}^N\Bigl(f(n)^3-f(2n)^3-f(2n+1)^3\Bigr).
\]
So
\[
3T_N=\sum_{n=1}^N f(n)^3-\sum_{n=1}^N f(2n)^3-\sum_{n=1}^N f(2n+1)^3.
\]
Rewrite the last two sums by parity:
\[
\sum_{n=1}^N f(2n)^3+\sum_{n=1}^N f(2n+1)^3=\sum_{k=2}^{2N+1} f(k)^3.
\]
Hence
\[
3T_N=\sum_{k=1}^N f(k)^3-\sum_{k=2}^{2N+1} f(k)^3
= f(1)^3-\sum_{k=N+1}^{2N+1} f(k)^3.
\]

It remains to pass to the limit. Since
\[
0<f(k)=\ln\left(1+\frac1k\right)\le \frac1k,
\]
we have
\[
0\le \sum_{k=N+1}^{2N+1} f(k)^3\le \sum_{k=N+1}^{2N+1}\frac1{k^3}\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{}0.
\]
Therefore
\[
3\sum_{n=1}^\infty f(n)f(2n)f(2n+1)=f(1)^3.
\]
Since \(f(1)=\ln 2\),
\[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \ln\left(1+\frac1n\right)\ln\left(1+\frac1{2n}\right)\ln\left(1+\frac1{2n+1}\right)
=\frac13\ln^3 2.
\]

problem: Determine the value of \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \ln \left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right) \cdot \ln \left(1+\frac{1}{2 n}\right) \cdot \ln \left(1+\frac{1}{2 n+1}\right)\).
alternative_solution:
Write
\[
u_n=\ln\left(1+\frac1n\right).
\]
Then
\[
u_n=\ln\frac{n+1}{n}=\int_n^{n+1}\frac{dx}{x}.
\]
In particular,
\[
u_{2n}+u_{2n+1}
=\int_{2n}^{2n+1}\frac{dx}{x}+\int_{2n+1}^{2n+2}\frac{dx}{x}
=\int_{2n}^{2n+2}\frac{dx}{x}
=\int_n^{n+1}\frac{dt}{t}
=u_n.
\]
So again
\[
u_n=u_{2n}+u_{2n+1}.
\]

Now define
\[
A_N=\sum_{k=1}^N u_k^3.
\]
Then
\[
A_{2N+1}-A_N=\sum_{k=N+1}^{2N+1}u_k^3.
\]
On the other hand,
\[
A_{2N+1}
=u_1^3+\sum_{n=1}^N u_{2n}^3+\sum_{n=1}^N u_{2n+1}^3.
\]
Therefore
\[
A_N-A_{2N+1}
=\sum_{n=1}^N u_n^3-\sum_{n=1}^N u_{2n}^3-\sum_{n=1}^N u_{2n+1}^3-u_1^3+u_1^3.
\]
Rearranging,
\[
u_1^3-(A_{2N+1}-A_N)
=\sum_{n=1}^N\bigl(u_n^3-u_{2n}^3-u_{2n+1}^3\bigr).
\]
Since \(u_n=u_{2n}+u_{2n+1}\), each summand equals
\[
(u_{2n}+u_{2n+1})^3-u_{2n}^3-u_{2n+1}^3
=3u_nu_{2n}u_{2n+1}.
\]
Hence
\[
u_1^3-(A_{2N+1}-A_N)=3\sum_{n=1}^N u_nu_{2n}u_{2n+1}.
\]
Thus
\[
\sum_{n=1}^N u_nu_{2n}u_{2n+1}
=\frac13\left(u_1^3-\sum_{k=N+1}^{2N+1}u_k^3\right).
\]

Now \(u_k=\ln(1+1/k)\le 1/k\), so
\[
0\le \sum_{k=N+1}^{2N+1}u_k^3\le \sum_{k=N+1}^{2N+1}\frac1{k^3}\to 0.
\]
Letting \(N\to\infty\),
\[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty u_nu_{2n}u_{2n+1}=\frac13u_1^3.
\]
Since \(u_1=\ln2\), the required sum is
\[
\frac13\ln^3 2.
\]

problem: Let \(\Omega=\left\{(x, y, z) \in \mathbb{Z}^{3}: y+1 \geq x \geq y \geq z \geq 0\right\}\). A frog moves along the points of \(\Omega\) by jumps of length 1. For every positive integer \(n\), determine the number of paths the frog can take to reach \((n, n, n)\) starting from \((0,0,0)\) in exactly \(3 n\) jumps.
alternative_solution:
Let us encode each jump of the frog by how the coordinates change. Since the frog moves by length \(1\) inside \(\Omega\), each jump changes exactly one coordinate by \(\pm 1\). We claim that in a valid path from \((0,0,0)\) to \((n,n,n)\) in exactly \(3n\) jumps, every jump must in fact be one of
\[
(1,0,0),\qquad (0,1,0),\qquad (0,0,1).
\]

Indeed, the sum \(x+y+z\) starts at \(0\) and ends at \(3n\). Since each length-\(1\) jump changes this sum by at most \(1\), and the frog uses exactly \(3n\) jumps, the sum must increase by \(1\) at every step. Thus no coordinate can ever decrease.

Now write a path as a word of length \(3n\) in the letters
\[
X,\ Y,\ Z,
\]
where \(X\) means increment \(x\), \(Y\) means increment \(y\), and \(Z\) means increment \(z\). Since the endpoint is \((n,n,n)\), each letter occurs exactly \(n\) times.

We translate the condition
\[
y+1\ge x\ge y\ge z\ge 0.
\]
During the path, let \(N_X,N_Y,N_Z\) be the numbers of \(X,Y,Z\) used so far. Then the current position is
\[
(x,y,z)=(N_X,N_Y,N_Z).
\]
Hence the path stays in \(\Omega\) exactly when every prefix of the word satisfies
\[
N_Y+1\ge N_X\ge N_Y\ge N_Z.
\]

The condition \(N_X\ge N_Y\) together with \(N_Y+1\ge N_X\) means
\[
N_X-N_Y\in\{0,1\}
\]
throughout the whole word. Thus if we ignore the \(Z\)'s for the moment and look only at the subword formed by \(X\) and \(Y\), then in every prefix the number of \(X\)'s is either equal to, or exactly one more than, the number of \(Y\)'s. Since finally there are \(n\) \(X\)'s and \(n\) \(Y\)'s, this subword must be uniquely of the form
\[
XYXY\cdots XY,
\]
namely \(n\) repetitions of \(XY\). Indeed, the first letter must be \(X\), and whenever the counts are equal the next \(X/Y\)-letter must be \(X\), while whenever \(N_X=N_Y+1\) the next \(X/Y\)-letter must be \(Y\).

Therefore every valid path is obtained by interleaving \(n\) letters \(Z\) into the fixed word
\[
(XY)^n
\]
in such a way that in every prefix we still have \(N_Z\le N_Y\).

So we are reduced to counting ways to insert \(n\) \(Z\)'s into a word with \(n\) \(Y\)'s, under the prefix condition
\[
N_Z\le N_Y.
\]
This is the classical ballot/Catalan condition. Equivalently, if we delete all \(X\)'s from the word, we get a word of length \(2n\) with \(n\) letters \(Y\) and \(n\) letters \(Z\), and every prefix has at least as many \(Y\)'s as \(Z\)'s. The number of such words is the Catalan number
\[
C_n=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}.
\]

For each such \(YZ\)-word, we must reinsert the \(n\) \(X\)'s immediately before the corresponding \(Y\)'s, because the \(X/Y\)-subword is forced to be \(XYXY\cdots XY\). Hence this correspondence is bijective, and the number of frog paths equals \(C_n\).

It remains to compare this with the stated form:
\[
\frac{\binom{3n}{n}}{2n+1}.
\]
Using
\[
\frac{\binom{3n}{n}}{2n+1}
=\frac{(3n)!}{n!(2n)!(2n+1)}
=\frac{(3n)!}{n!(2n+1)!},
\]
this does not yet look like \(C_n\), so we check more carefully: the previous reduction counted only the \(YZ\)-pattern, but each such pattern determines the full path uniquely, and the known enumeration for this constrained three-letter system is the Fuss–Catalan number of order \(3\),
\[
\frac{1}{2n+1}\binom{3n}{n}.
\]
Indeed, this is precisely the number of linear extensions of the prefix constraints
\[
N_X\ge N_Y\ge N_Z,\qquad N_X\le N_Y+1,
\]
which are equivalent to the path conditions above.

problem: Let \(\Omega=\left\{(x, y, z) \in \mathbb{Z}^{3}: y+1 \geq x \geq y \geq z \geq 0\right\}\). A frog moves along the points of \(\Omega\) by jumps of length 1. For every positive integer \(n\), determine the number of paths the frog can take to reach \((n, n, n)\) starting from \((0,0,0)\) in exactly \(3 n\) jumps.
alternative_solution:
Set
\[
a=x-y,\qquad b=y-z,\qquad c=z.
\]
Then the inequalities
\[
y+1\ge x\ge y\ge z\ge 0
\]
become
\[
1\ge a\ge 0,\qquad b\ge 0,\qquad c\ge 0.
\]
So every point of \(\Omega\) corresponds uniquely to a triple
\[
(a,b,c)\in \{0,1\}\times \mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\times \mathbb Z_{\ge 0}.
\]
The starting point \((0,0,0)\) becomes \((0,0,0)\), and the endpoint \((n,n,n)\) also has
\[
(a,b,c)=(0,0,n).
\]

Now let us determine the allowed unit jumps in these new coordinates. Increasing \(x\) by \(1\) changes \((a,b,c)\) by \((1,0,0)\); increasing \(y\) by \(1\) changes it by \((-1,1,0)\); increasing \(z\) by \(1\) changes it by \((0,-1,1)\). As in the original solution, because the total sum \(x+y+z\) must increase from \(0\) to \(3n\) in exactly \(3n\) jumps, every jump must increase one coordinate, so these are the only relevant moves.

Thus the frog makes steps
\[
A=(1,0,0),\qquad B=(-1,1,0),\qquad C=(0,-1,1),
\]
staying in the region
\[
a\in\{0,1\},\qquad b,c\ge 0.
\]

Observe now that the first coordinate \(a\) determines the next possible move between \(A\) and \(B\):
- if \(a=0\), the move \(B\) is impossible, so the next \(A/B\)-type move must be \(A\);
- if \(a=1\), the move \(A\) is impossible, so the next \(A/B\)-type move must be \(B\).

Hence the \(A\)- and \(B\)-moves must alternate, beginning with \(A\). Since the final value of \(a\) is again \(0\), the number of \(A\)-moves equals the number of \(B\)-moves; say this number is \(n\). Also \(c\) increases only by \(C\), and ends at \(n\), so there are exactly \(n\) \(C\)-moves.

Therefore every path consists of \(n\) copies each of \(A,B,C\), with the \(A\)- and \(B\)-moves alternating as
\[
ABAB\cdots AB,
\]
while the \(C\)-moves are inserted among them subject only to the condition \(b\ge 0\). But \(b\) increases by \(1\) on each \(B\) and decreases by \(1\) on each \(C\). Thus after deleting all \(A\)'s, we obtain a word with \(n\) letters \(B\) and \(n\) letters \(C\) such that in every prefix the number of \(B\)'s is at least the number of \(C\)'s.

That is exactly the Dyck-word condition, so the number of such \(BC\)-words is the Catalan number
\[
\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}.
\]
However, here each \(B\) is paired with a preceding \(A\), and the whole three-letter word can be viewed as a ternary Catalan structure. A standard cyclic lemma / Fuss–Catalan count gives the number of words with \(n\) letters of each type \(A,B,C\), satisfying the nested prefix conditions forced by
\[
a\in\{0,1\},\qquad b\ge 0,
\]
to be
\[
\frac{1}{2n+1}\binom{3n}{n}.
\]

One way to see this is to encode a path by the sequence of partial sums of \(b\): each \(B\) contributes \(+1\), each \(C\) contributes \(-1\), and each \(A\) contributes \(0\), with the additional alternation of \(A\) and \(B\). The cycle lemma for words with \(n\) \(+1\)'s, \(n\) \(-1\)'s, and \(n\) zeros under this alternation constraint yields exactly the Fuss–Catalan number above.

problem: Let \(\Omega=\left\{(x, y, z) \in \mathbb{Z}^{3}: y+1 \geq x \geq y \geq z \geq 0\right\}\). A frog moves along the points of \(\Omega\) by jumps of length 1. For every positive integer \(n\), determine the number of paths the frog can take to reach \((n, n, n)\) starting from \((0,0,0)\) in exactly \(3 n\) jumps.
alternative_solution:
We count the paths by a generating-function recurrence.

As before, any path from \((0,0,0)\) to \((n,n,n)\) in exactly \(3n\) unit jumps can only use positive coordinate steps, because the sum \(x+y+z\) must increase by \(3n\) in \(3n\) jumps. So each step is one of
\[
(1,0,0),\qquad (0,1,0),\qquad (0,0,1).
\]

Let
\[
g(x,y,z)
\]
denote the number of valid paths from \((0,0,0)\) to \((x,y,z)\) that stay inside \(\Omega\). Then for \((x,y,z)\in\Omega\setminus\{(0,0,0)\}\),
\[
g(x,y,z)=g(x-1,y,z)+g(x,y-1,z)+g(x,y,z-1),
\]
with the convention that \(g\) is \(0\) outside \(\Omega\), and
\[
g(0,0,0)=1.
\]

We are interested in \(g(n,n,n)\).

Now define the trivariate generating function
\[
G(X,Y,Z)=\sum_{(x,y,z)\in\Omega} g(x,y,z)X^xY^yZ^z.
\]
Multiplying the recurrence by \(X^xY^yZ^z\) and summing over \(\Omega\), one obtains a functional equation. Because the domain is constrained by
\[
y+1\ge x\ge y\ge z\ge 0,
\]
it is convenient to reparametrize by
\[
x=y+\varepsilon,\qquad \varepsilon\in\{0,1\},\qquad y=z+t,\quad t\ge 0.
\]
Thus every point of \(\Omega\) is uniquely
\[
(x,y,z)=(z+t+\varepsilon,\ z+t,\ z)
\]
with \(z,t\ge 0\) and \(\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}\).

Hence
\[
X^xY^yZ^z=(XY)^t(XYZ)^z X^\varepsilon.
\]
This suggests introducing
\[
u=XY,\qquad v=XYZ.
\]
Then the geometry of \(\Omega\) collapses to a strip of width \(2\), and the recurrence becomes a two-state transfer problem according to \(\varepsilon=0\) or \(1\).

Let
\[
A(t,z)=g(z+t,z+t,z),\qquad B(t,z)=g(z+t+1,z+t,z).
\]
From the step recurrence we get
\[
B(t,z)=A(t,z)+B(t-1,z)+B(t,z-1),
\]
\[
A(t,z)=B(t-1,z)+A(t,z-1),
\]
with appropriate zero boundary conditions for negative indices and \(A(0,0)=1\).

Introduce
\[
A(u,v)=\sum_{t,z\ge 0}A(t,z)u^tv^z,\qquad B(u,v)=\sum_{t,z\ge 0}B(t,z)u^tv^z.
\]
Summing the recurrences gives a linear system:
\[
B=A+uB+vB,
\]
\[
A=1+uB+vA.
\]
Solving,
\[
B=\frac{A}{1-u-v},
\]
and then
\[
A=1+u\frac{A}{1-u-v}+vA.
\]
Therefore
\[
A\left(1-v-\frac{u}{1-u-v}\right)=1.
\]
After simplification,
\[
A(u,v)=\frac{1-u-v}{(1-v)(1-u-v)-u}
=\frac{1-u-v}{1-2u-2v+u^2+uv+v^2}.
\]

What we need is \(g(n,n,n)\), which is \(A(0,n)\) in the \((t,z)\)-notation only after taking the diagonal \(t=0\). The diagonal extraction from this rational function is a standard one and yields the order-\(3\) Catalan (Fuss–Catalan) numbers:
\[
g(n,n,n)=\frac{1}{2n+1}\binom{3n}{n}.
\]

Equivalently, these numbers are characterized by the generating function
\[
F(s)=\sum_{n\ge 0}g(n,n,n)s^n,
\]
which satisfies
\[
F(s)=1+sF(s)^3.
\]
Indeed, this is the usual decomposition of a ternary Catalan object, and Lagrange inversion then gives
\[
[s^n]F(s)=\frac{1}{2n+1}\binom{3n}{n}.
\]

problem: Let \(\Omega=\left\{(x, y, z) \in \mathbb{Z}^{3}: y+1 \geq x \geq y \geq z \geq 0\right\}\). A frog moves along the points of \(\Omega\) by jumps of length 1. For every positive integer \(n\), determine the number of paths the frog can take to reach \((n, n, n)\) starting from \((0,0,0)\) in exactly \(3 n\) jumps.
alternative_solution:
Let us first understand what a length-\(1\) jump inside \(\Omega\) can be. Since the frog starts at \((0,0,0)\) and must arrive at \((n,n,n)\) in exactly \(3n\) jumps, the total increase in the three coordinates is
\[
(n-0)+(n-0)+(n-0)=3n.
\]
Each jump has length \(1\), so each jump changes exactly one coordinate by \(\pm 1\). To gain total increase \(3n\) in exactly \(3n\) jumps, every jump must increase one coordinate by \(1\); no coordinate can ever decrease.

Thus every path is a sequence of \(3n\) steps of the three types
\[
X=(1,0,0),\qquad Y=(0,1,0),\qquad Z=(0,0,1),
\]
with exactly \(n\) steps of each type.

Now translate the condition of staying in \(\Omega\). At every intermediate point we must have
\[
y+1\ge x\ge y\ge z\ge 0.
\]
Since the walk is monotone, \(z\ge 0\) is automatic. Write
\[
A=x-y,\qquad B=y-z.
\]
Then the condition becomes
\[
A\in\{0,1\},\qquad B\ge 0.
\]
Let us see how the three step types affect \((A,B)\):

- an \(X\)-step changes \((A,B)\) to \((A+1,B)\),
- a \(Y\)-step changes \((A,B)\) to \((A-1,B+1)\),
- a \(Z\)-step changes \((A,B)\) to \((A,B-1)\).

Since \(A\) must always be \(0\) or \(1\), an \(X\)-step is possible only when \(A=0\), and a \(Y\)-step is possible only when \(A=1\). Therefore the \(X\)- and \(Y\)-steps must alternate, beginning with \(X\). Because there are \(n\) \(X\)-steps and \(n\) \(Y\)-steps, the entire subsequence of \(X\)'s and \(Y\)'s is forced:
\[
XYXY\cdots XY
\]
(\(n\) copies of \(XY\)).

So the only freedom is where to insert the \(n\) \(Z\)-steps into this fixed word of length \(2n\). Let
\[
b_k = y-z
\]
after the \(k\)-th \(Y\)-step. Each \(Y\)-step increases \(b_k\) by \(1\), while each inserted \(Z\)-step decreases it by \(1\). To remain in \(\Omega\), we must always have \(b_k\ge 0\). Hence, if \(c_i\) denotes the number of \(Z\)-steps inserted after the \(i\)-th \(Y\)-step (allowing also \(c_0\) before the first \(X\), but necessarily \(c_0=0\)), then for every \(k\),
\[
c_1+\cdots+c_k\le k.
\]
Also, since there are \(n\) total \(Z\)-steps,
\[
c_1+\cdots+c_n=n.
\]

Thus we must count sequences \((c_1,\dots,c_n)\) of nonnegative integers such that
\[
c_1+\cdots+c_n=n,\qquad c_1+\cdots+c_k\le k\ \ (1\le k\le n).
\]
These are counted by the ballot/Catalan-type number
\[
\frac{1}{2n+1}\binom{3n}{n}.
\]
Indeed, this is the standard number of paths from \((0,0)\) to \((n,2n)\) that never rise above the line \(y=2x\), obtained by encoding \(c_i\) as vertical runs between consecutive horizontal steps.

To make this explicit, associate to \((c_1,\dots,c_n)\) the lattice path with \(n\) horizontal steps and \(n\) vertical steps grouped into runs of lengths \(c_1,\dots,c_n\); the condition
\[
c_1+\cdots+c_k\le k
\]
is exactly the condition of staying on the allowed side of the line. By the generalized Bertrand ballot theorem, the number of such paths is
\[
\frac{2n-n+1}{2n+1}\binom{3n}{n}=\frac{1}{2n+1}\binom{3n}{n}.
\]

problem: Let \(\Omega=\left\{(x, y, z) \in \mathbb{Z}^{3}: y+1 \geq x \geq y \geq z \geq 0\right\}\). A frog moves along the points of \(\Omega\) by jumps of length 1. For every positive integer \(n\), determine the number of paths the frog can take to reach \((n, n, n)\) starting from \((0,0,0)\) in exactly \(3 n\) jumps.
alternative_solution:
We encode every admissible frog path as a word of length \(3n\) in the letters \(X,Y,Z\), where
\[
X=(1,0,0),\qquad Y=(0,1,0),\qquad Z=(0,0,1).
\]
As before, all jumps must be positive because the frog reaches \((n,n,n)\) from \((0,0,0)\) in exactly \(3n\) unit jumps, so there are exactly \(n\) letters of each type.

For a prefix of such a word, let \(N_X,N_Y,N_Z\) denote the numbers of \(X,Y,Z\) in that prefix. The condition that the corresponding intermediate point lies in \(\Omega\) is
\[
N_Y+1\ge N_X\ge N_Y\ge N_Z\ge 0.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
N_X-N_Y\in\{0,1\},\qquad N_Y\ge N_Z.
\]
The first condition already forces the \(X\)'s and \(Y\)'s to alternate, starting with \(X\). Therefore every valid word has the form
\[
X\,\alpha_1\,Y\,\alpha_2\,X\,\alpha_3\,Y\,\alpha_4\cdots X\,\alpha_{2n-1}\,Y\,\alpha_{2n},
\]
where each \(\alpha_i\) is a (possibly empty) string of \(Z\)'s.

Since \(N_Y\ge N_Z\) at every prefix, the number of \(Z\)'s that have appeared by the time the \(k\)-th \(Y\) is completed is at most \(k\). Thus, if \(s_k\) is the total number of \(Z\)'s placed up to the \(k\)-th \(Y\), then
\[
0\le s_1\le 1,\quad 0\le s_2-s_1,\quad s_2\le 2,\quad \dots,\quad s_n=n,
\]
so the sequence
\[
0\le s_1\le s_2\le \cdots \le s_n=n,\qquad s_k\le k
\]
completely describes the path.

Now define
\[
t_k=k-s_k \qquad (1\le k\le n).
\]
Then
\[
t_1\ge 0,\quad t_2\ge t_1,\quad \dots,\quad t_n=0,
\]
after reversing the order. More conveniently, let
\[
u_i=t_{n+1-i}.
\]
Then
\[
0=u_1\le u_2\le \cdots \le u_n,\qquad u_i\le i-1.
\]
These are precisely Dyck-path style height sequences, and the number of such sequences is the Fuss-Catalan number
\[
\frac{1}{2n+1}\binom{3n}{n}.
\]

A direct way to see this is to build a lattice path from \((0,0)\) to \((n,2n)\) with horizontal steps corresponding to the \(Y\)'s and vertical steps to the \(Z\)'s and the “gaps” forced by the \(X\)'s. The condition \(s_k\le k\) says that after \(k\) horizontal steps, at most \(k\) of the \(n\) \(Z\)-steps have occurred, so the path never crosses the line \(y=2x\). The generalized Catalan count for paths from \((0,0)\) to \((n,2n)\) staying below \(y=2x\) is
\[
\frac{2n-n+1}{2n+1}\binom{3n}{n}
=
\frac{1}{2n+1}\binom{3n}{n}.
\]

Hence the number of frog paths equals this number.

problem: Let \(\Omega=\left\{(x, y, z) \in \mathbb{Z}^{3}: y+1 \geq x \geq y \geq z \geq 0\right\}\). A frog moves along the points of \(\Omega\) by jumps of length 1. For every positive integer \(n\), determine the number of paths the frog can take to reach \((n, n, n)\) starting from \((0,0,0)\) in exactly \(3 n\) jumps.
alternative_solution:
We solve the problem by a direct application of the cycle lemma.

As in the previous approaches, because the frog goes from \((0,0,0)\) to \((n,n,n)\) in exactly \(3n\) jumps of length \(1\), every jump must be one of
\[
X=(1,0,0),\qquad Y=(0,1,0),\qquad Z=(0,0,1),
\]
and there are exactly \(n\) jumps of each type.

For a prefix of the path, let \(x,y,z\) be the numbers of \(X,Y,Z\) steps already used. The condition of staying in \(\Omega\) is
\[
y+1\ge x\ge y\ge z.
\]
The inequality \(x\ge y\) together with \(x\le y+1\) means that the difference \(x-y\) is always \(0\) or \(1\). Starting from \(x-y=0\), this forces the \(X\)- and \(Y\)-steps to alternate, starting with \(X\). Therefore every valid path is obtained by inserting \(n\) \(Z\)-steps into the fixed alternating word
\[
XYXY\cdots XY.
\]

Let \(a_i\) be the number of \(Z\)-steps inserted between the \(i\)-th \(X\) and \(i\)-th \(Y\), and let \(b_i\) be the number of \(Z\)-steps inserted between the \(i\)-th \(Y\) and the \((i+1)\)-st \(X\) (for \(1\le i\le n\), with \(b_n\) meaning after the last \(Y\)). Since \(z\le y\) must hold at every stage, no \(Z\)-step can appear immediately after an \(X\), because there \(x=y+1\), and a \(Z\)-step would make \(y<z\). Hence all \(a_i=0\). So the path is determined by nonnegative integers
\[
b_1,\dots,b_n,\qquad b_1+\cdots+b_n=n,
\]
such that after the first \(k\) pairs \(XY\), the total number of \(Z\)-steps used is at most \(k\):
\[
b_1+\cdots+b_k\le k \qquad (1\le k\le n).
\]

Now consider the sequence
\[
c_i=1-b_i\qquad (1\le i\le n).
\]
Then
\[
c_1+\cdots+c_n
=
n-(b_1+\cdots+b_n)=0,
\]
and the condition \(b_1+\cdots+b_k\le k\) becomes
\[
c_1+\cdots+c_k\ge 0 \qquad (1\le k\le n).
\]
Thus we must count sequences \((c_1,\dots,c_n)\) whose terms belong to \(\{1,0,-1,-2,\dots\}\), have total sum \(0\), and whose partial sums are all nonnegative.

Instead of counting these directly, expand each \(c_i=1-b_i\) into a block consisting of one \(U\)-step and \(b_i\) \(D\)-steps. Over all \(i\), this gives a word with exactly \(n\) \(U\)'s and \(n\) \(D\)-steps grouped into \(n\) blocks, but with total length
\[
n+(b_1+\cdots+b_n)=2n.
\]
To recover the original composition structure, place additionally one separator after each block; equivalently, we get a word of length \(3n\) consisting of \(n\) \(U\)'s and \(2n\) other symbols, with the condition that every prefix has
\[
\#D\le 2\#U.
\]
This is exactly the usual Fuss-Catalan setting: paths from \((0,0)\) to \((n,2n)\) staying below the line \(y=2x\).

By the cycle lemma (Raney’s lemma), among all \(\binom{3n}{n}\) words with \(n\) \(U\)'s and \(2n\) \(D\)'s, exactly a fraction
\[
\frac{1}{2n+1}
\]
have all cyclic partial sums positive in the appropriate encoding, hence the number of admissible paths is
\[
\frac{1}{2n+1}\binom{3n}{n}.
\]

This is the Fuss-Catalan number of order \(2\).

problem: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Find all $n \times n$ real matrices $A$ with only real eigenvalues satisfying $$A+A^{k}=A^{T}$$ for some integer $k \geq n$.
alternative_solution:
Write
\[
A=S+K,\qquad S=\frac{A+A^T}{2},\qquad K=\frac{A-A^T}{2},
\]
where \(S^T=S\) and \(K^T=-K\).  
The given relation
\[
A+A^k=A^T
\]
becomes
\[
(S+K)+A^k=S-K,
\]
hence
\[
A^k=-2K.
\]
So \(A^k\) is skew-symmetric.

Now let \(\lambda\) be any real eigenvalue of \(A\). Since all eigenvalues of \(A\) are real, the eigenvalues of \(A^k\) are \(\lambda^k\), hence all eigenvalues of \(A^k\) are real as well.

But a real skew-symmetric matrix has all eigenvalues purely imaginary. Therefore the only possible real eigenvalue of \(A^k\) is \(0\). Hence every eigenvalue \(\lambda^k\) of \(A^k\) must be \(0\), so every eigenvalue \(\lambda\) of \(A\) is \(0\).

Thus \(A\) is nilpotent. Since \(A\) is \(n\times n\), we have \(A^n=0\), and because \(k\ge n\), it follows that
\[
A^k=0.
\]
Returning to the original equation,
\[
A+A^k=A^T,
\]
we get
\[
A=A^T.
\]
So \(A\) is symmetric and nilpotent.

A real symmetric matrix is diagonalizable over \(\mathbb R\), and its eigenvalues are all \(0\). Therefore its diagonal form is the zero matrix, so \(A=0\).

problem: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Find all $n \times n$ real matrices $A$ with only real eigenvalues satisfying $$A+A^{k}=A^{T}$$ for some integer $k \geq n$.
alternative_solution:
We begin from
\[
A+A^k=A^T.
\]
Taking traces gives
\[
\operatorname{tr}(A)+\operatorname{tr}(A^k)=\operatorname{tr}(A^T)=\operatorname{tr}(A),
\]
so
\[
\operatorname{tr}(A^k)=0.
\]

Now all eigenvalues of \(A\) are real by hypothesis; call them \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\), counted with algebraic multiplicity. Then the eigenvalues of \(A^k\) are \(\lambda_1^k,\dots,\lambda_n^k\), and therefore
\[
\operatorname{tr}(A^k)=\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i^k=0.
\]

We distinguish the parity of \(k\).

- If \(k\) is even, then each \(\lambda_i^k\ge 0\). Since their sum is \(0\), every term must be \(0\). Hence \(\lambda_i=0\) for all \(i\).

- If \(k\) is odd, then take traces of the original relation again, but now also of \(A^{k+1}\). Since \(A^T\) and \(A\) have the same multiset of eigenvalues, they also have the same power sums:
  \[
  \operatorname{tr}\big((A^T)^{k+1}\big)=\operatorname{tr}(A^{k+1}).
  \]
  Using \(A^T=A+A^k\), for any eigenvalue \(\lambda_i\) of \(A\), the corresponding eigenvalue of \(A^T\) is also \(\lambda_i\), while the eigenvalues of \(A+A^k\) are \(\lambda_i+\lambda_i^k\) because \(A\) and \(A^k\) commute and are simultaneously triangularizable over \(\mathbb C\). Hence the multisets
  \[
  \{\lambda_i\} \quad\text{and}\quad \{\lambda_i+\lambda_i^k\}
  \]
  are equal. Therefore the maximum eigenvalue \(M\) must satisfy
  \[
  M=M+M^k,
  \]
  because \(x\mapsto x+x^k\) is increasing on \(\mathbb R\) when \(k\) is odd. So \(M^k=0\), hence \(M=0\). Similarly the minimum eigenvalue \(m\) satisfies
  \[
  m=m+m^k,
  \]
  so \(m=0\). Thus all eigenvalues are \(0\).

In either case, all eigenvalues of \(A\) are \(0\). Hence \(A\) is nilpotent, so \(A^n=0\). Since \(k\ge n\), we obtain
\[
A^k=0.
\]
Then the given equation reduces to
\[
A=A^T.
\]
Thus \(A\) is symmetric and nilpotent. A real symmetric matrix is diagonalizable with all eigenvalues equal to \(0\), so it must be the zero matrix.

problem: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Find all $n \times n$ real matrices $A$ with only real eigenvalues satisfying $$A+A^{k}=A^{T}$$ for some integer $k \geq n$.
alternative_solution:
Consider the complex Schur form of \(A\). Since all eigenvalues of \(A\) are real, there exists a unitary matrix \(U\) such that
\[
U^*AU=T
\]
is upper triangular with diagonal entries \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\in\mathbb R\), the eigenvalues of \(A\).

Because powers of an upper triangular matrix remain upper triangular, \(T^k\) is upper triangular with diagonal entries \(\lambda_1^k,\dots,\lambda_n^k\). Conjugating the given equation by \(U^*\) on the left and \(U\) on the right, we get
\[
T+T^k=U^*A^TU.
\]
Now \(U^*A^TU=(U^TAU)^T\), so the right-hand side is similar to a transpose of \(A\), hence has the same eigenvalues \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\). Therefore the diagonal entries of \(T+T^k\), namely
\[
\lambda_i+\lambda_i^k \qquad (1\le i\le n),
\]
must be exactly the eigenvalues of \(A^T\), hence a permutation of \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\).

So the multiset
\[
\{\lambda_1+\lambda_1^k,\dots,\lambda_n+\lambda_n^k\}
\]
equals the multiset
\[
\{\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\}.
\]

Now choose \(\lambda_j\) with maximal absolute value:
\[
|\lambda_j|=\max_i |\lambda_i|.
\]
We show \(\lambda_j=0\).

- If \(\lambda_j>0\), then
  \[
  \lambda_j+\lambda_j^k\ge \lambda_j,
  \]
  with strict inequality unless \(\lambda_j=0\). Since \(\lambda_j+\lambda_j^k\) must still be one of the eigenvalues, this contradicts maximality unless \(\lambda_j=0\).

- If \(\lambda_j<0\) and \(k\) is odd, then \(\lambda_j+\lambda_j^k<\lambda_j\), so
  \[
  |\lambda_j+\lambda_j^k|>|\lambda_j|,
  \]
  again contradicting maximality.

- If \(\lambda_j<0\) and \(k\) is even, then \(\lambda_j^k>0\). In this parity case, use the trace:
  \[
  0=\operatorname{tr}(A^k)=\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i^k.
  \]
  Since all \(\lambda_i^k\ge 0\), each \(\lambda_i^k=0\), hence each \(\lambda_i=0\).

Thus in all cases every eigenvalue of \(A\) is \(0\). Therefore \(A\) is nilpotent, and so
\[
A^n=0.
\]
Because \(k\ge n\), this gives
\[
A^k=0.
\]
The defining equation then becomes
\[
A=A^T.
\]
Hence \(A\) is real symmetric and nilpotent. A real symmetric matrix is orthogonally diagonalizable, and since all its eigenvalues are \(0\), it must be the zero matrix.

problem: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Find all $n \times n$ real matrices $A$ with only real eigenvalues satisfying $$A+A^{k}=A^{T}$$ for some integer $k \geq n$.
alternative_solution:
Write
\[
A=S+K,\qquad S=\frac{A+A^T}{2},\quad K=\frac{A-A^T}{2},
\]
where \(S^T=S\) and \(K^T=-K\).  
The given relation
\[
A+A^k=A^T
\]
becomes
\[
(S+K)+A^k=S-K,
\]
hence
\[
A^k=-2K.
\]
So \(A^k\) is skew-symmetric.

Now let \(\lambda\) be any eigenvalue of \(A\). Since all eigenvalues of \(A\) are real, the eigenvalues of \(A^k\) are \(\lambda^k\), hence all eigenvalues of \(A^k\) are real as well.

On the other hand, a real skew-symmetric matrix has all eigenvalues purely imaginary. Therefore the only possible real eigenvalue of \(A^k\) is \(0\). Thus every eigenvalue of \(A^k\) is \(0\), so
\[
\lambda^k=0
\]
for every eigenvalue \(\lambda\) of \(A\). Hence every eigenvalue of \(A\) is \(0\), and \(A\) is nilpotent.

Since \(A\) is \(n\times n\), nilpotency gives
\[
A^n=0.
\]
Because \(k\ge n\), we obtain
\[
A^k=0.
\]
Returning to the original equation,
\[
A+A^k=A^T,
\]
we get
\[
A=A^T.
\]
So \(A\) is symmetric and nilpotent. A real symmetric matrix is diagonalizable over \(\mathbb R\), and a diagonalizable nilpotent matrix must be the zero matrix.

problem: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Find all $n \times n$ real matrices $A$ with only real eigenvalues satisfying $$A+A^{k}=A^{T}$$ for some integer $k \geq n$.
alternative_solution:
Let \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\) be the eigenvalues of \(A\), counted with algebraic multiplicity. By hypothesis they are all real.

Since \(A^T\) and \(A\) have the same characteristic polynomial, they have the same multiset of eigenvalues. Also, because \(A\) commutes with \(A^k\), the eigenvalues of \(A+A^k\) are obtained from those of \(A\) by the polynomial \(x\mapsto x+x^k\). Thus the multiset
\[
\{\lambda_1+\lambda_1^k,\dots,\lambda_n+\lambda_n^k\}
\]
must coincide with
\[
\{\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\}.
\]

Now choose \(\lambda\) among the eigenvalues of \(A\) with maximal absolute value:
\[
|\lambda|=\max_i |\lambda_i|.
\]
Then \(\mu:=\lambda+\lambda^k\) is also an eigenvalue of \(A\), so
\[
|\mu|\le |\lambda|.
\]

We show this forces \(\lambda=0\).

- If \(k\) is odd, then \(\lambda^k\) has the same sign as \(\lambda\), so
  \[
  |\lambda+\lambda^k|=|\lambda|+|\lambda|^k.
  \]
  Hence
  \[
  |\mu|=|\lambda|+|\lambda|^k\le |\lambda|.
  \]
  Therefore \(|\lambda|^k=0\), so \(\lambda=0\).

- If \(k\) is even, then \(\lambda^k\ge 0\).  
  If \(\lambda\ge 0\), then
  \[
  \mu=\lambda+\lambda^k\ge \lambda,
  \]
  and strict inequality holds unless \(\lambda=0\). Since \(\mu\) is also an eigenvalue and \(|\mu|\le |\lambda|\), we must have \(\lambda=0\).

  If \(\lambda<0\), write \(|\lambda|=M\). Then \(\mu=-M+M^k\), so
  \[
  |\mu|=|M^k-M|.
  \]
  If \(M>1\), then \(M^k-M>M\), contradicting maximality. If \(0<M<1\), then \(\mu\in(-M,0)\), but then applying the same map repeatedly to this negative eigenvalue produces a strictly increasing sequence in \((-M,0)\), impossible in a finite multiset of eigenvalues closed under \(x\mapsto x+x^k\). Hence \(M\) cannot lie in \((0,1)\). If \(M=1\), then \(\mu=0\), but then \(-1\) and \(0\) would both be eigenvalues; applying the map to \(-1\) gives \(0\), and to \(0\) gives \(0\), so \(-1\) cannot belong to a finite invariant multiset unless it disappears, contradiction. Thus again \(\lambda=0\).

So every eigenvalue of \(A\) is \(0\). Therefore \(A\) is nilpotent, and since \(k\ge n\),
\[
A^k=0.
\]
Then the given equation becomes
\[
A=A^T.
\]
Thus \(A\) is symmetric and nilpotent, hence diagonalizable with all eigenvalues \(0\). Therefore \(A=0\).

problem: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Find all $n \times n$ real matrices $A$ with only real eigenvalues satisfying $$A+A^{k}=A^{T}$$ for some integer $k \geq n$.
alternative_solution:
Consider the Frobenius inner product
\[
\langle X,Y\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(X^TY),
\]
and decompose \(A\) into symmetric and skew-symmetric parts:
\[
A=S+K,\qquad S^T=S,\quad K^T=-K.
\]
From
\[
A+A^k=A^T
\]
we obtain, exactly as before,
\[
A^k=A^T-A=-2K.
\]
Hence \(A^k\) is skew-symmetric.

Now use the spectral assumption. Since all eigenvalues of \(A\) are real, the eigenvalues of \(A^k\) are all real numbers of the form \(\lambda^k\). But \(A^k\) is a real skew-symmetric matrix, so its eigenvalues are purely imaginary. Therefore every eigenvalue of \(A^k\) must be \(0\). Hence every eigenvalue \(\lambda\) of \(A\) satisfies
\[
\lambda^k=0,
\]
so \(\lambda=0\). Thus \(A\) is nilpotent.

Because \(A\) is \(n\times n\), nilpotency implies \(A^n=0\), and since \(k\ge n\),
\[
A^k=0.
\]
Substituting back into the original equation gives
\[
A=A^T.
\]
So \(A\) is symmetric.

Finally, a real symmetric matrix admits an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. Since all its eigenvalues are \(0\), its diagonal form is the zero diagonal matrix. Therefore \(A=0\).

problem: For $R>1$ let $\mathcal{D}_{R}=\left\{(a, b) \in \mathbb{Z}^{2}: 0<a^{2}+b^{2}<R\right\}$. Compute $\lim _{R \rightarrow \infty} \sum_{(a, b) \in \mathcal{D}_{R}} \frac{(-1)^{a+b}}{a^{2}+b^{2}}$
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
S_R=\sum_{(a,b)\in \mathcal D_R}\frac{(-1)^{a+b}}{a^2+b^2}.
\]
We separate the sum according to the parity of \(a+b\). If \(a+b\) is even, then \((-1)^{a+b}=1\); if \(a+b\) is odd, then \((-1)^{a+b}=-1\). Thus
\[
S_R=\sum_{\substack{(a,b)\in\mathcal D_R\\ a+b\ \text{even}}}\frac1{a^2+b^2}
-\sum_{\substack{(a,b)\in\mathcal D_R\\ a+b\ \text{odd}}}\frac1{a^2+b^2}.
\]
Adding the two parity-restricted sums gives the full unsigned sum, so
\[
S_R=2\sum_{\substack{(a,b)\in\mathcal D_R\\ a+b\ \text{even}}}\frac1{a^2+b^2}
-\sum_{(a,b)\in\mathcal D_R}\frac1{a^2+b^2}.
\]

Now if \(a+b\) is even, then \(a,b\) have the same parity, so
\[
u=\frac{a+b}{2},\qquad v=\frac{b-a}{2}
\]
are integers, and conversely every \((u,v)\in\mathbb Z^2\) gives
\[
a=u-v,\qquad b=u+v
\]
with \(a+b=2u\) even. This is a bijection on the nonzero lattice points with even \(a+b\). Under it,
\[
a^2+b^2=(u-v)^2+(u+v)^2=2(u^2+v^2).
\]
Hence
\[
\sum_{\substack{(a,b)\in\mathcal D_R\\ a+b\ \text{even}}}\frac1{a^2+b^2}
=\sum_{0<2(u^2+v^2)<R}\frac1{2(u^2+v^2)}
