j=\sum_{r=0}^{k-1}\varepsilon_r 2^r,\qquad \varepsilon_r\in\{0,1\}.
\]
Starting from the interval endpoints \(1\) and \(2^k+1\), repeated midpoint bisection produces all points
\[
1+\frac{t}{2^s}\cdot 2^k
\]
with \(t\) integral and \(0\le t\le 2^s\), and when \(s=k\) these are exactly all integers \(1,2,\dots,2^k+1\). Hence any endpointed mediocre set must contain the entire interval, so it must equal \(\{1,\dots,m\}\).

Now suppose \(m-1\) is not a power of \(2\). Let
\[
g=\gcd\{x-1:x\in S\}
\]
for a candidate endpointed subset. We seek a proper one. Write
\[
m-1=2^ab
\]
with \(b>1\) odd, and define
\[
S=\{1+tb:0\le t\le 2^a\}.
\]
Then \(1,m\in S\), and all differences \(x-1\) are multiples of \(b\). Also if two elements \(1+t_1b\) and \(1+t_2b\) have integer average, then
\[
1+\frac{t_1+t_2}{2}b
\]
also belongs to \(S\). So \(S\) is mediocre. Since \(b>1\), it is a proper subset of \(\{1,\dots,m\}\). Thus the full interval is not unique.

Therefore uniqueness occurs exactly when \(m-1\) is a power of \(2\). Since \(m=n+2\), this is exactly
\[
n+1=2^k,
\]
or
\[
n=2^k-1.
\]

problem:
Call a subset $S$ of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ \emph{mediocre} if it has the following property:
Whenever $a$ and $b$ are elements of $S$ whose average is an integer, that average is also
an element of $S$. Let $A(n)$ be the number of mediocre subsets of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$.
[For instance, every subset of $\{1,2,3\}$ except $\{1,3\}$ is mediocre, so $A(3) =7$.]
Find all positive integers $n$ such that $A(n+2) - 2A(n+1) + A(n) = 1$.
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
D(n)=A(n+1)-A(n).
\]
By translating a mediocre subset of \(\{1,\dots,n\}\) by \(+1\), we get a mediocre subset of \(\{2,\dots,n+1\}\), and this is a bijection. Hence \(D(n)\) is exactly the number of mediocre subsets of \(\{1,\dots,n+1\}\) that contain \(1\).

Therefore
\[
A(n+2)-2A(n+1)+A(n)=D(n+1)-D(n).
\]
Now \(D(n+1)\) counts mediocre subsets of \(\{1,\dots,n+2\}\) containing \(1\), while \(D(n)\) counts those among them that avoid \(n+2\). So the difference counts exactly the mediocre subsets of \(\{1,\dots,n+2\}\) containing both endpoints \(1\) and \(n+2\).

Thus the given condition
\[
A(n+2)-2A(n+1)+A(n)=1
\]
holds if and only if there is exactly one mediocre subset of \(\{1,\dots,n+2\}\) containing both \(1\) and \(n+2\).

Now write \(N=n+1\), so we are studying mediocre subsets of
\[
\{1,\dots,N+1\}
\]
that contain \(1\) and \(N+1\).

We claim that such a subset is unique if and only if \(N\) is a power of \(2\).

First suppose \(N\) is not a power of \(2\). Then \(N\) has an odd divisor \(d>1\), say \(N=qd\). Consider
\[
S=\{1,\,1+d,\,1+2d,\dots,1+qd\}.
\]
This set contains \(1\) and \(N+1\). Also, if \(1+id,1+jd\in S\), then their average is
\[
1+\frac{i+j}{2}d.
\]
This is an integer exactly when \(i+j\) is even, and then it is again one of the listed elements of \(S\). So \(S\) is mediocre. Since \(d>1\), \(S\neq \{1,2,\dots,N+1\}\). Hence there is more than one mediocre subset containing the endpoints, so the second difference is not \(1\).

Now suppose \(N=2^k\). We show that the only mediocre subset \(S\subseteq \{1,\dots,2^k+1\}\) containing \(1\) and \(2^k+1\) is the whole set.

Indeed, for any \(0\le r\le 2^k\), write \(r\) in binary:
\[
r=\sum_{i=1}^t 2^{e_i}
\]
with distinct exponents. Starting from the endpoints \(1\) and \(2^k+1\), closure under taking integer averages forces the midpoint
\[
2^{k-1}+1.
\]
Then applying the same argument to the intervals \([1,2^{k-1}+1]\) and \([2^{k-1}+1,2^k+1]\), we get all points of the form \(1+m2^{k-2}\), then all points of the form \(1+m2^{k-3}\), and so on. After \(k\) steps, every integer from \(1\) to \(2^k+1\) appears. Thus \(S\) must be the whole set.

So there is exactly one mediocre subset containing the endpoints precisely when \(n+1\) is a power of \(2\), i.e.
\[
n=2^k-1
\]
for some \(k\ge 1\).

As a brief

problem:
Call a subset $S$ of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ \emph{mediocre} if it has the following property:
Whenever $a$ and $b$ are elements of $S$ whose average is an integer, that average is also
an element of $S$. Let $A(n)$ be the number of mediocre subsets of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$.
[For instance, every subset of $\{1,2,3\}$ except $\{1,3\}$ is mediocre, so $A(3) =7$.]
Find all positive integers $n$ such that $A(n+2) - 2A(n+1) + A(n) = 1$.
alternative_solution:
We begin by interpreting the second difference directly.

A mediocre subset of \(\{1,\dots,n+1\}\) can be viewed as a mediocre subset of \(\{1,\dots,n+2\}\) not containing \(n+2\). Therefore
\[
A(n+2)-A(n+1)
\]
counts the mediocre subsets of \(\{1,\dots,n+2\}\) that do contain \(n+2\), and similarly
\[
A(n+1)-A(n)
\]
counts the mediocre subsets of \(\{1,\dots,n+1\}\) that contain \(n+1\).

Now shift the latter family by \(+1\). This gives a bijection with the mediocre subsets of \(\{2,\dots,n+2\}\) containing \(n+2\). Hence
\[
A(n+2)-2A(n+1)+A(n)
\]
counts exactly those mediocre subsets of \(\{1,\dots,n+2\}\) containing \(n+2\) that are not contained in \(\{2,\dots,n+2\}\), i.e. those containing both \(1\) and \(n+2\).

So we must determine for which \(N=n+2\) there is exactly one mediocre subset of \(\{1,\dots,N\}\) containing \(1\) and \(N\).

We first produce many such subsets when \(N-1\) is not a power of \(2\). Write
\[
N-1=2^ab
\]
with \(b\) odd. If \(b>1\), then
\[
S=\{1,\,1+b,\,1+2b,\dots,1+2^ab\}
\]
contains \(1\) and \(N\). Moreover, for elements \(1+ib\) and \(1+jb\), the average is integral exactly when \(i+j\) is even, and then that average is
\[
1+\frac{i+j}{2}b\in S.
\]
So \(S\) is mediocre. Since \(b>1\), it is not the whole interval. Thus whenever \(N-1\) is not a power of \(2\), at least two endpoint-containing mediocre subsets exist.

Now assume \(N-1=2^k\). Let \(S\subseteq \{1,\dots,2^k+1\}\) be mediocre with \(1,2^k+1\in S\). We show \(S\) must be all of \(\{1,\dots,2^k+1\}\).

For each \(j=0,1,\dots,k\), consider the set
\[
T_j=\{\,1+m2^{k-j}\mid 0\le m\le 2^j\,\}.
\]
We prove inductively that \(T_j\subseteq S\).

- For \(j=0\), \(T_0=\{1,2^k+1\}\subseteq S\).
- Suppose \(T_j\subseteq S\). Between any two consecutive elements
\[
1+m2^{k-j},\qquad 1+(m+1)2^{k-j}
\]
their average is
\[
1+(2m+1)2^{k-j-1},
\]
an integer, so it lies in \(S\). Thus all points with step size \(2^{k-j-1}\) belong to \(S\), which is exactly \(T_{j+1}\subseteq S\).

By induction, \(T_k=\{1,2,\dots,2^k+1\}\subseteq S\). Hence \(S\) is the whole set.

Therefore there is exactly one mediocre subset containing the endpoints if and only if \(N-1\) is a power of \(2\). Since \(N=n+2\), this means \(n+1\) is a power of \(2\).

As a brief verification, when \(n+1=2^k\), the above induction forces every integer in \(\{1,\dots,n+2\}\) into any endpoint-containing mediocre subset, so exactly one such subset exists; when \(n+1\) has an odd factor \(>1\), the arithmetic progression construction gives a second one. Hence the condition is equivalent to \(n+1=2^k\).

problem:
Call a subset $S$ of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ \emph{mediocre} if it has the following property:
Whenever $a$ and $b$ are elements of $S$ whose average is an integer, that average is also
an element of $S$. Let $A(n)$ be the number of mediocre subsets of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$.
[For instance, every subset of $\{1,2,3\}$ except $\{1,3\}$ is mediocre, so $A(3) =7$.]
Find all positive integers $n$ such that $A(n+2) - 2A(n+1) + A(n) = 1$.
alternative_solution:
Let \(B(m)\) denote the number of mediocre subsets of \(\{1,\dots,m\}\) that contain both \(1\) and \(m\). We first show that
\[
B(n+2)=A(n+2)-2A(n+1)+A(n).
\]

Indeed, \(A(n+2)-A(n+1)\) counts mediocre subsets of \(\{1,\dots,n+2\}\) containing \(n+2\), because those not containing \(n+2\) are exactly the mediocre subsets of \(\{1,\dots,n+1\}\). Likewise, after subtracting \(1\) from each element, \(A(n+1)-A(n)\) counts mediocre subsets of \(\{2,\dots,n+2\}\) containing \(n+2\). The difference between these two quantities is exactly the number of mediocre subsets of \(\{1,\dots,n+2\}\) containing \(n+2\) and also \(1\). Thus
\[
B(n+2)=A(n+2)-2A(n+1)+A(n).
\]

So the problem asks for all \(n\) such that
\[
B(n+2)=1.
\]

We now characterize when \(B(m)=1\).

Suppose first that \(m-1\) is not a power of \(2\). Then \(m-1=rs\) for some odd \(s>1\). The set
\[
S=\{1,1+s,1+2s,\dots,1+rs\}
\]
contains \(1\) and \(m\). If two of its elements have integer average, that average is again of the same form, so \(S\) is mediocre. Since \(s>1\), this is a proper subset of \(\{1,\dots,m\}\). But the whole set \(\{1,\dots,m\}\) is also mediocre. Hence \(B(m)\ge 2\), so \(B(m)\neq 1\).

Now suppose \(m-1=2^k\). We prove \(B(m)=1\) by showing that every mediocre subset \(S\subseteq \{1,\dots,2^k+1\}\) containing \(1\) and \(2^k+1\) must contain every integer.

For \(0\le t\le k\), define
\[
E_t=\{x\in \{1,\dots,2^k+1\}: x\equiv 1 \pmod{2^{k-t}}\}.
\]
Thus
\[
E_0=\{1,2^k+1\}, \qquad E_k=\{1,2,\dots,2^k+1\}.
\]
We claim \(E_t\subseteq S\) for every \(t\).

This is proved by induction on \(t\). The case \(t=0\) is immediate. Assume \(E_t\subseteq S\). Take any two consecutive elements of \(E_t\):
\[
1+j2^{k-t}, \qquad 1+(j+1)2^{k-t}.
\]
Their average is
\[
1+(2j+1)2^{k-t-1},
\]
which is an integer, so it lies in \(S\). Together with the elements already in \(E_t\), this gives all elements congruent to \(1\) modulo \(2^{k-t-1}\), namely \(E_{t+1}\subseteq S\).

Thus \(E_k\subseteq S\), so \(S\) is the whole interval. Hence \(B(m)=1\).

We have proved:
\[
B(m)=1 \iff m-1 \text{ is a power of }2.
\]
Substituting \(m=n+2\), the required condition is
\[
n+1=2^k
\]
for some integer \(k\ge 1\), i.e.
\[
n=2^k-1.
\]

For verification, if \(m-1=2^k\), the congruence-class induction above forces every point into any endpoint-containing mediocre subset, so \(B(m)=1\). If \(m-1\) has an odd factor \(>1\), the arithmetic progression with that step gives a second endpoint-containing mediocre subset, so \(B(m)\neq 1\). Therefore the characterization is correct.

problem: Find the minimum value of $| \sin x + \cos x + \tan x + \cot x + \sec x + \csc x |$ for real numbers $x$.
alternative_solution:
\textbf{Using the tangent half-angle substitution.} Let
\[
t=\tan\frac x2.
\]
Then
\[
\sin x=\frac{2t}{1+t^2},\qquad \cos x=\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2},
\]
so
\[
\sin x+\cos x=\frac{1+2t-t^2}{1+t^2}.
\]
Also,
\[
\sin x\cos x=\frac{2t(1-t^2)}{(1+t^2)^2}.
\]
Hence
\[
\tan x+\cot x=\frac{\sin^2x+\cos^2x}{\sin x\cos x}=\frac{1}{\sin x\cos x},
\]
and
\[
\sec x+\csc x=\frac{1}{\cos x}+\frac{1}{\sin x}
=\frac{\sin x+\cos x}{\sin x\cos x}.
\]
Therefore
\[
f(x):=\sin x+\cos x+\tan x+\cot x+\sec x+\csc x
\]
becomes
\[
f=\frac{1+2t-t^2}{1+t^2}
+\frac{(1+t^2)^2}{2t(1-t^2)}
+\frac{1+2t-t^2}{1+t^2}\cdot \frac{(1+t^2)^2}{2t(1-t^2)}.
\]
This simplifies more cleanly if we set
\[
u=\sin x+\cos x.
\]
Since
\[
u^2=\sin^2x+\cos^2x+2\sin x\cos x=1+2\sin x\cos x,
\]
we have
\[
\sin x\cos x=\frac{u^2-1}{2}.
\]
So
\[
f=u+\frac{1}{\sin x\cos x}+\frac{u}{\sin x\cos x}
=u+\frac{2}{u^2-1}+\frac{2u}{u^2-1}.
\]
Combining terms,
\[
f=u+\frac{2(1+u)}{(u-1)(u+1)}=u+\frac{2}{u-1}.
\]
Now \(u=\sin x+\cos x\in[-\sqrt2,\sqrt2]\), with \(u\neq 1\) when \(f\) is defined.

So we must minimize
\[
\left|u+\frac{2}{u-1}\right|.
\]

We first note that
\[
u+\frac{2}{u-1}=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
u(u-1)+2=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
u^2-u+2=0,
\]
which has no real solution. Thus \(f\) never vanishes, so minimizing \(|f|\) is the same as finding the value of \(f\) closest to \(0\).

For \(u<1\), write \(v=1-u>0\). Then
\[
f=u+\frac{2}{u-1}=1-v-\frac{2}{v}=1-\left(v+\frac{2}{v}\right).
\]
By AM-GM,
\[
v+\frac{2}{v}\ge 2\sqrt2,
\]
hence
\[
f\le 1-2\sqrt2.
\]
Equality occurs when
\[
v=\sqrt2 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u=1-\sqrt2.
\]

For \(u>1\), write \(w=u-1>0\). Then
\[
f=1+w+\frac{2}{w}\ge 1+2\sqrt2,
\]
so every positive value has absolute value at least \(1+2\sqrt2\), which is larger.

Thus the smallest possible absolute value is
\[
|1-2\sqrt2|=2\sqrt2-1.
\]

\textbf{

problem: Find the minimum value of $| \sin x + \cos x + \tan x + \cot x + \sec x + \csc x |$ for real numbers $x$.
alternative_solution:
\textbf{Using \(p=\sin x+\cos x\) and \(q=\sin x\cos x\), then eliminating \(q\).} Define
\[
p=\sin x+\cos x,\qquad q=\sin x\cos x.
\]
Since
\[
p^2=\sin^2x+\cos^2x+2\sin x\cos x=1+2q,
\]
we have
\[
q=\frac{p^2-1}{2}.
\]
Now rewrite the expression:
\[
\tan x+\cot x=\frac{\sin^2x+\cos^2x}{\sin x\cos x}=\frac1q,
\]
and
\[
\sec x+\csc x=\frac{\sin x+\cos x}{\sin x\cos x}=\frac pq.
\]
Therefore
\[
f(x)=p+\frac1q+\frac pq=p+\frac{1+p}{q}.
\]
Substituting \(q=\frac{p^2-1}{2}\),
\[
f=p+\frac{2(1+p)}{p^2-1}.
\]
Since \(p^2-1=(p-1)(p+1)\), this becomes
\[
f=p+\frac{2}{p-1},
\]
where \(p\in[-\sqrt2,\sqrt2]\) and \(p\ne 1\).

Now consider the two intervals separately.

If \(p>1\), then set \(r=p-1>0\). We get
\[
f=1+r+\frac2r.
\]
By AM-GM,
\[
r+\frac2r\ge 2\sqrt2,
\]
so
\[
f\ge 1+2\sqrt2.
\]
Hence
\[
|f|\ge 1+2\sqrt2.
\]

If \(p<1\), then set \(s=1-p>0\). We get
\[
f=1-s-\frac2s.
\]
Thus
\[
-f=-1+s+\frac2s.
\]
Again by AM-GM,
\[
s+\frac2s\ge 2\sqrt2,
\]
so
\[
-f\ge -1+2\sqrt2,
\]
that is,
\[
f\le 1-2\sqrt2.
\]
Therefore
\[
|f|\ge 2\sqrt2-1.
\]
Equality holds when
\[
s=\sqrt2,
\]
namely when
\[
p=1-\sqrt2.
\]

Since \(1-\sqrt2\in[-\sqrt2,\sqrt2]\), such a value of \(p\) is attainable by some real \(x\). Therefore the minimum value of \(|f(x)|\) is
\[
2\sqrt2-1.
\]

\textbf{

problem: Find the minimum value of $| \sin x + \cos x + \tan x + \cot x + \sec x + \csc x |$ for real numbers $x$.
alternative_solution:
\textbf{Using \(s=\sin x\) and \(c=\cos x\), then a one-variable reduction via \(s+c\).} Let
\[
s=\sin x,\qquad c=\cos x,
\]
so that
\[
s^2+c^2=1.
\]
The given expression is
\[
f=s+c+\frac{s}{c}+\frac{c}{s}+\frac1c+\frac1s.
\]
Group the rational terms:
\[
\frac{s}{c}+\frac{c}{s}=\frac{s^2+c^2}{sc}=\frac1{sc},
\]
and
\[
\frac1c+\frac1s=\frac{s+c}{sc}.
\]
Hence
\[
f=s+c+\frac1{sc}+\frac{s+c}{sc}.
\]
Set
\[
m=s+c.
\]
Using
\[
m^2=s^2+c^2+2sc=1+2sc,
\]
we get
\[
sc=\frac{m^2-1}{2}.
\]
Substitute this into \(f\):
\[
f=m+\frac{2}{m^2-1}+\frac{2m}{m^2-1}
= m+\frac{2(m+1)}{(m-1)(m+1)}
= m+\frac{2}{m-1},
\]
with
\[
m\in[-\sqrt2,\sqrt2],\qquad m\ne 1.
\]

Now observe the identity
\[
m+\frac{2}{m-1}
=\frac{m^2-m+2}{m-1}.
\]
The numerator
\[
m^2-m+2=\left(m-\frac12\right)^2+\frac74>0
\]
for all real \(m\). Therefore the sign of \(f\) is exactly the sign of \(m-1\): it is negative for \(m<1\) and positive for \(m>1\). So \(|f|\) is minimized by making \(f\) as close to \(0\) as possible on either side.

For \(m>1\), let \(u=m-1>0\). Then
\[
f=1+u+\frac2u\ge 1+2\sqrt2.
\]

For \(m<1\), let \(v=1-m>0\). Then
\[
f=1-v-\frac2v.
\]
So
\[
|f|= -f = -1+v+\frac2v\ge -1+2\sqrt2=2\sqrt2-1,
\]
again by AM-GM. Equality occurs when
\[
v=\sqrt2,
\]
that is,
\[
m=1-\sqrt2.
\]

Since \(1-\sqrt2\in[-\sqrt2,\sqrt2]\), there exists real \(x\) with \(\sin x+\cos x=m\). Thus the minimum value of \(|f|\) is
\[
2\sqrt2-1.
\]

\textbf{

problem: Find the minimum value of $| \sin x + \cos x + \tan x + \cot x + \sec x + \csc x |$ for real numbers $x$.
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
f(x)=\sin x+\cos x+\tan x+\cot x+\sec x+\csc x,
\]
where all terms are defined, so \(\sin x\neq 0\) and \(\cos x\neq 0\).

Set
\[
s=\sin x+\cos x.
\]
Then
\[
s^2=\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x+2\sin x\cos x=1+2\sin x\cos x,
\]
so
\[
\sin x\cos x=\frac{s^2-1}{2}.
\]
Also,
\[
\tan x+\cot x=\frac{\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x}{\sin x\cos x}=\frac1{\sin x\cos x},
\]
and
\[
\sec x+\csc x=\frac{1}{\cos x}+\frac{1}{\sin x}
=\frac{\sin x+\cos x}{\sin x\cos x}
=\frac{s}{\sin x\cos x}.
\]
Hence
\begin{align*}
f(x)
&=s+\frac1{\sin x\cos x}+\frac{s}{\sin x\cos x}\\
&=s+\frac{2}{s^2-1}+\frac{2s}{s^2-1}\\
&=s+\frac{2(1+s)}{(s-1)(s+1)}\\
&=s+\frac{2}{s-1}.
\end{align*}
Now \(s=\sin x+\cos x\in[-\sqrt2,\sqrt2]\), with \(s\neq 1\) because \(s=1\) would force \(\sin x\cos x=0\), where the original expression is undefined.

So we need to minimize
\[
\left|\,s+\frac{2}{s-1}\right|
\qquad\text{for }s\in[-\sqrt2,\sqrt2],\ s\neq 1.
\]
Rewrite:
\[
s+\frac{2}{s-1}
=(s-1)+1+\frac{2}{s-1}.
\]

Now split into two cases.

For \(s>1\), let \(u=s-1>0\). Since \(s\le \sqrt2\), we have \(0<u\le \sqrt2-1\). Then
\[
\left|s+\frac{2}{s-1}\right|=1+u+\frac2u.
\]
By AM-GM,
\[
u+\frac2u\ge 2\sqrt2,
\]
hence
\[
\left|s+\frac{2}{s-1}\right|\ge 1+2\sqrt2.
\]

For \(s<1\), let \(v=1-s>0\). Then
\[
s+\frac{2}{s-1}
=1-v-\frac2v,
\]
which is negative, so
\[
\left|s+\frac{2}{s-1}\right|
=v+\frac2v-1.
\]
Again by AM-GM,
\[
v+\frac2v\ge 2\sqrt2,
\]
thus
\[
\left|s+\frac{2}{s-1}\right|\ge 2\sqrt2-1.
\]
Equality holds when
\[
v=\sqrt2 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad s=1-\sqrt2.
\]
This value is admissible since \(1-\sqrt2\in[-\sqrt2,\sqrt2]\).

A corresponding \(x\) exists because every number in \([-\sqrt2,\sqrt2]\) is attained by \(\sin x+\cos x\). For such \(x\), we also have \(s\neq 1\), so the original expression is defined.

problem: Find the minimum value of $| \sin x + \cos x + \tan x + \cot x + \sec x + \csc x |$ for real numbers $x$.
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
a=\sin x,\qquad b=\cos x.
\]
Then \(a^2+b^2=1\), and
\[
f(x)=a+b+\frac{a}{b}+\frac{b}{a}+\frac1b+\frac1a.
\]
Since \(a,b\neq 0\), multiply by \(ab\):
\[
ab\,f=(a+b)(ab+a+b).
\]
Therefore
\[
f=\frac{(a+b)(ab+a+b)}{ab}.
\]

Now introduce
\[
u=a+b,\qquad v=ab.
\]
Using \(a^2+b^2=1\),
\[
u^2=a^2+2ab+b^2=1+2v,
\]
so
\[
v=\frac{u^2-1}{2}.
\]
Also,
\[
ab+a+b=v+u.
\]
Hence
\[
f=\frac{u(v+u)}{v}.
\]
Substituting \(v=(u^2-1)/2\),
\begin{align*}
f
&=u\left(1+\frac{u}{v}\right)
=u\left(1+\frac{2u}{u^2-1}\right)\\
&=u+\frac{2u^2}{u^2-1}
=u+2+\frac{2}{u^2-1}.
\end{align*}
A more useful simplification comes from factoring:
\[
\frac{2u^2}{u^2-1}
=\frac{2u(u-1)+2u}{(u-1)(u+1)},
\]
but the cleanest route is
\[
f=u+\frac{2(1+u)}{u^2-1}
=u+\frac{2}{u-1}.
\]
Thus the problem becomes minimizing
\[
\left|u+\frac{2}{u-1}\right|
\]
for \(u\in[-\sqrt2,\sqrt2]\), \(u\neq 1\).

Now observe that
\[
u+\frac{2}{u-1}=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
u(u-1)+2=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
u^2-u+2=0,
\]
whose discriminant is
\[
1-8=-7<0.
\]
So \(f\) never vanishes; therefore minimizing \(|f|\) is equivalent to finding the value of \(f\) closest to \(0\) on the negative branch or positive branch.

For \(u<1\), write \(t=1-u>0\). Then
\[
f=1-t-\frac2t.
\]
So
\[
|f|=t+\frac2t-1.
\]
By AM-GM,
\[
t+\frac2t\ge 2\sqrt2,
\]
hence
\[
|f|\ge 2\sqrt2-1,
\]
with equality when \(t=\sqrt2\), i.e.
\[
u=1-\sqrt2.
\]

For \(u>1\), write \(w=u-1>0\). Then
\[
f=1+w+\frac2w,
\]
so
\[
|f|=1+w+\frac2w\ge 1+2\sqrt2>2\sqrt2-1.
\]
Thus the global minimum is attained in the first case.

problem: Find the minimum value of $| \sin x + \cos x + \tan x + \cot x + \sec x + \csc x |$ for real numbers $x$.
alternative_solution:
We start from
\[
f(x)=\sin x+\cos x+\tan x+\cot x+\sec x+\csc x.
\]
Use the half-angle substitution
\[
t=\tan \frac x2.
\]
Then
\[
\sin x=\frac{2t}{1+t^2},\qquad
\cos x=\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2},
\]
and the expression is defined when \(t\neq 0,\pm1\) (corresponding to \(\sin x\neq 0\) and \(\cos x\neq 0\)).

First compute
\[
\sin x+\cos x=\frac{2t+1-t^2}{1+t^2}
=\frac{1+2t-t^2}{1+t^2}.
\]
Also,
\[
\sin x\cos x=\frac{2t(1-t^2)}{(1+t^2)^2}.
\]
Since
\[
\tan x+\cot x=\frac{1}{\sin x\cos x},
\qquad
\sec x+\csc x=\frac{\sin x+\cos x}{\sin x\cos x},
\]
we get
\[
f=(\sin x+\cos x)+\frac{1+\sin x+\cos x}{\sin x\cos x}.
\]
Substitute the formulas above:
\[
1+\sin x+\cos x
=1+\frac{1+2t-t^2}{1+t^2}
=\frac{2(1+t)}{1+t^2}.
\]
Therefore
\begin{align*}
\frac{1+\sin x+\cos x}{\sin x\cos x}
&=\frac{2(1+t)}{1+t^2}\cdot \frac{(1+t^2)^2}{2t(1-t^2)}\\
&=\frac{(1+t)(1+t^2)}{t(1-t^2)}\\
&=\frac{1+t^2}{t(1-t)}.
\end{align*}
So
\begin{align*}
f
&=\frac{1+2t-t^2}{1+t^2}+\frac{1+t^2}{t(1-t)}.
\end{align*}
This looks unwieldy, so we now make the simpler substitution
\[
u=\sin x+\cos x.
\]
From the half-angle formulas we already have
\[
u=\frac{1+2t-t^2}{1+t^2},
\]
and regardless of \(t\), \(u\in[-\sqrt2,\sqrt2]\). Also, as before,
\[
\sin x\cos x=\frac{u^2-1}{2}.
\]
Hence directly
\[
f=u+\frac1{\sin x\cos x}+\frac{u}{\sin x\cos x}
=u+\frac{2}{u^2-1}+\frac{2u}{u^2-1}
=u+\frac{2}{u-1}.
\]

Now consider the function
\[
g(u)=u+\frac{2}{u-1},\qquad u\in[-\sqrt2,\sqrt2],\ u\neq 1.
\]
Its derivative is
\[
g'(u)=1-\frac{2}{(u-1)^2}.
\]
So critical points satisfy
\[
(u-1)^2=2,
\]
giving
\[
u=1\pm \sqrt2.
\]
Only
\[
u=1-\sqrt2
\]
lies in the interval \([-\sqrt2,\sqrt2]\).

Next,
\[
g''(u)=\frac{4}{(u-1)^3}.
\]
At \(u=1-\sqrt2<1\), we have \(g''(u)<0\), so this point is a local maximum for \(g\) on the negative branch. Since \(g(u)\) has no real zero:
\[
g(u)=0\iff u^2-u+2=0,
\]
impossible over the reals, the minimum of \(|g(u)|\) occurs where \(g(u)\) is closest to \(0\). On the branch \(u<1\), that is exactly the maximum of \(g\), namely at \(u=1-\sqrt2\). On the branch \(u>1\), \(g(u)>0\) and is much larger because \(u\to1^+\) gives \(g(u)\to+\infty\).

Thus
\[
\min |f|=\left|g(1-\sqrt2)\right|.
\]
Compute:
\[
g(1-\sqrt2)=1-\sqrt2+\frac{2}{-\sqrt2}=1-2\sqrt2.
\]

problem:
For each positive integer $k$, let $A(k)$ be the number of odd divisors of $k$ in the interval $[1, \sqrt{2k})$. Evaluate
\[
\sum_{k=1}^\infty (-1)^{k-1} \frac{A(k)}{k}.
\]
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
S=\sum_{k=1}^\infty (-1)^{k-1}\frac{A(k)}{k}.
\]

We first rewrite \(A(k)\) in a more usable form.  
If \(d\) is an odd divisor of \(k\), write \(k=dm\). The condition
\[
d\in [1,\sqrt{2k})
\]
becomes
\[
d<\sqrt{2dm},
\]
equivalently
\[
d<2m.
\]
Since \(d\) is odd, write \(d=2r-1\) with \(r\ge1\). Then \(2r-1<2m\), so \(r\le m\).

Thus \(A(k)\) counts pairs \((r,m)\) such that
\[
k=(2r-1)m,\qquad 1\le r\le m.
\]
Hence formally
\[
S=\sum_{m=1}^\infty \sum_{r=1}^m \frac{(-1)^{(2r-1)m-1}}{(2r-1)m}.
\]
Because \(2r-1\) is odd,
\[
(-1)^{(2r-1)m-1}=(-1)^{m-1},
\]
so
\[
S=\sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{m}\sum_{r=1}^m \frac1{2r-1}.
\]

Now define
\[
H_m^{\mathrm{odd}}:=\sum_{r=1}^m \frac1{2r-1}.
\]
Then
\[
S=\sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{m}H_m^{\mathrm{odd}}.
\]

We next use the integral identity
\[
\sum_{r=1}^m \frac1{2r-1}=\int_0^1 \sum_{r=1}^m x^{2r-2}\,dx
=\int_0^1 \frac{1-x^{2m}}{1-x^2}\,dx.
\]
Therefore
\[
S=\sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{m}\int_0^1 \frac{1-x^{2m}}{1-x^2}\,dx.
\]

For \(0\le x<1\), the series
\[
\sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{m}(1-x^{2m})
\]
converges, and since
\[
0\le \frac{1-x^{2m}}{1-x^2}=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}x^{2j}\le m,
\]
the alternating nature allows termwise summation on each interval \([0,\rho]\) with \(\rho<1\), and then passage to \(\rho\uparrow1\). So
\[
S=\int_0^1 \frac{1}{1-x^2}\left(\sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{m}(1-x^{2m})\right)\,dx.
\]

Now
\[
\sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{m}=\log 2,
\qquad
\sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}x^{2m}}{m}=\log(1+x^2),
\]
so
\[
\sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{m}(1-x^{2m})
=\log 2-\log(1+x^2)
=\log\frac{2}{1+x^2}.
\]
Hence
\[
S=\int_0^1 \frac{\log\frac{2}{1+x^2}}{1-x^2}\,dx.
\]

Now substitute
\[
x=\frac{1-u}{1+u},\qquad u=\frac{1-x}{1+x}.
\]
Then as \(x:0\to1\), we have \(u:1\to0\), and
\[
1-x^2=\frac{4u}{(1+u)^2},\qquad
1+x^2=\frac{2(1+u^2)}{(1+u)^2},\qquad
dx=-\frac{2}{(1+u)^2}\,du.
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac{dx}{1-x^2}=-\frac1{2u}\,du,
\]
and
\[
\log\frac{2}{1+x^2}
=\log\frac{(1+u)^2}{1+u^2}.
\]
So
\[
S=\frac12\int_0^1 \frac{1}{u}\log\frac{(1+u)^2}{1+u^2}\,du
=\int_0^1 \frac{\log(1+u)}{u}\,du-\frac12\int_0^1 \frac{\log(1+u^2)}{u}\,du.
\]

Expand both logarithms:
\[
\log(1+u)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n-1}u^n}{n},
\]
hence
\[
\int_0^1 \frac{\log(1+u)}{u}\,du
=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n^2}
=\frac{\pi^2}{12}.
\]
Also
\[
\log(1+u^2)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n-1}u^{2n}}{n},
\]
so
\[
\int_0^1 \frac{\log(1+u^2)}{u}\,du
=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n}\int_0^1 u^{2n-1}\,du
=\frac12\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n^2}
=\frac{\pi^2}{24}.
\]
Thus
\[
S=\frac{\pi^2}{12}-\frac12\cdot\frac{\pi^2}{24}
=\frac{\pi^2}{12}-\frac{\pi^2}{48}
=\frac{\pi^2}{16}.
\]

As a verification, the transformed integral is positive and finite, and the final value \(\pi^2/16\) is consistent with the positivity of the first several partial sums.

problem:
For each positive integer $k$, let $A(k)$ be the number of odd divisors of $k$ in the interval $[1, \sqrt{2k})$. Evaluate
\[
\sum_{k=1}^\infty (-1)^{k-1} \frac{A(k)}{k}.
\]
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
S=\sum_{k=1}^\infty (-1)^{k-1}\frac{A(k)}{k}.
\]

We encode the condition defining \(A(k)\) by summing over the odd divisor directly.  
If \(d\) is an odd divisor of \(k\), write \(k=dn\). Then
\[
d<\sqrt{2k}=\sqrt{2dn}
\iff d<2n.
\]
So
\[
A(k)=\sum_{\substack{d\mid k\\ d\text{ odd}\\ d<2(k/d)}}1.
\]
Hence
\[
S=\sum_{\substack{d\ge1\\ d\text{ odd}}}\frac1d
\sum_{n>\frac d2}\frac{(-1)^{dn-1}}{n}.
\]
Since \(d\) is odd, \((-1)^{dn-1}=(-1)^{n-1}\). Writing \(d=2r-1\), the condition \(n>\frac d2\) becomes \(n\ge r\). Therefore
\[
S=\sum_{r=1}^\infty \frac1{2r-1}\sum_{n=r}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n}.
\]
This is the same convergent double series obtained by summing over admissible pairs \((r,n)\).

Now use the identity
\[
\frac1n=\int_0^\infty e^{-nt}\,dt.
\]
Then
\[
\sum_{n=r}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n}
=\int_0^\infty \sum_{n=r}^\infty (-1)^{n-1}e^{-nt}\,dt.
\]
For \(t>0\), the inner series is geometric:
\[
\sum_{n=r}^\infty (-1)^{n-1}e^{-nt}
=(-1)^{r-1}e^{-rt}\sum_{j=0}^\infty (-e^{-t})^j
=\frac{(-1)^{r-1}e^{-rt}}{1+e^{-t}}.
\]
So
\[
S=\sum_{r=1}^\infty \frac1{2r-1}\int_0^\infty \frac{(-1)^{r-1}e^{-rt}}{1+e^{-t}}\,dt.
\]
Since the resulting outer series is absolutely convergent for each \(t>0\), we interchange sum and integral:
\[
S=\int_0^\infty \frac{1}{1+e^{-t}}
\left(\sum_{r=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{r-1}e^{-rt}}{2r-1}\right)dt.
\]

Set \(y=e^{-t/2}\). Then \(e^{-rt}=y^{2r}\), and
\[
\sum_{r=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{r-1}e^{-rt}}{2r-1}
= y\sum_{r=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{r-1}y^{2r-1}}{2r-1}
= y\arctan y.
\]
Also
\[
\frac{1}{1+e^{-t}}=\frac{1}{1+y^2},
\qquad
dt=-\frac{2\,dy}{y}.
\]
As \(t:0\to\infty\), we have \(y:1\to0\). Therefore
\[
S=\int_1^0 \frac{y\arctan y}{1+y^2}\left(-\frac{2\,dy}{y}\right)
=2\int_0^1 \frac{\arctan y}{1+y^2}\,dy.
\]
Now let
\[
u=\arctan y,\qquad du=\frac{dy}{1+y^2}.
\]
When \(y=0\), \(u=0\); when \(y=1\), \(u=\pi/4\). Hence
\[
S=2\int_0^{\pi/4} u\,du
=2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)^2
=\frac{\pi^2}{16}.
\]

For verification, differentiate \(u^2\): indeed
\[
\frac{d}{dy}\bigl((\arctan y)^2\bigr)=\frac{2\arctan y}{1+y^2},
\]
so the last integral evaluates correctly.

problem:
For each positive integer $k$, let $A(k)$ be the number of odd divisors of $k$ in the interval $[1, \sqrt{2k})$. Evaluate
\[
\sum_{k=1}^\infty (-1)^{k-1} \frac{A(k)}{k}.
\]
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
S=\sum_{k=1}^\infty (-1)^{k-1}\frac{A(k)}{k}.
\]

We begin by expressing \(A(k)\) through a divisor sum.  
If \(d\) is an odd divisor of \(k\), write \(k=dm\). The condition \(d<\sqrt{2k}\) is equivalent to
\[
d^2<2dm \iff d<2m.
\]
Thus
\[
A(k)=\sum_{\substack{d\mid k\\ d\text{ odd}}} \mathbf 1_{d<2k/d}.
\]
Hence
\[
S=\sum_{\substack{d\ge1\\ d\text{ odd}}}\sum_{m\ge1,\ d<2m}\frac{(-1)^{dm-1}}{dm}.
\]
Again \(d\) is odd, so \((-1)^{dm-1}=(-1)^{m-1}\). Writing \(d=2r-1\), the condition \(2r-1<2m\) becomes \(r\le m\). Therefore
\[
S=\sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{m}\sum_{r=1}^m \frac1{2r-1}.
\]

Now we use
\[
\sum_{r=1}^m \frac1{2r-1}=H_{2m}-\frac12 H_m,
\]
where \(H_n=\sum_{j=1}^n \frac1j\). So
\[
S=\sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}H_{2m}}{m}
-\frac12\sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}H_m}{m}.
\]
Call these two sums \(S_1\) and \(\frac12S_2\), respectively:
\[
S=S_1-\frac12S_2.
\]

We evaluate \(S_2\) first.  
Using
\[
H_m=\int_0^1 \frac{1-x^m}{1-x}\,dx,
\]
we get
\[
S_2=\sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{m}\int_0^1 \frac{1-x^m}{1-x}\,dx
=\int_0^1 \frac{1}{1-x}\sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{m}(1-x^m)\,dx.
\]
Now
\[
\sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{m}=\log 2,
\qquad
\sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}x^m}{m}=\log(1+x),
\]
so
\[
S_2=\int_0^1 \frac{\log 2-\log(1+x)}{1-x}\,dx
=\int_0^1 \frac{\log\frac{2}{1+x}}{1-x}\,dx.
\]
Set
\[
u=\frac{1-x}{1+x}.
\]
Then
\[
x=\frac{1-u}{1+u},\qquad
dx=-\frac{2}{(1+u)^2}du,\qquad
1-x=\frac{2u}{1+u},\qquad
1+x=\frac{2}{1+u}.
\]
Thus
\[
\log\frac{2}{1+x}=\log(1+u),
\qquad
\frac{dx}{1-x}=-\frac{du}{u(1+u)}.
\]
Therefore
\[
S_2=\int_0^1 \frac{\log(1+u)}{u(1+u)}\,du.
\]
Now split
\[
\frac{1}{u(1+u)}=\frac1u-\frac1{1+u},
\]
so
\[
S_2=\int_0^1 \frac{\log(1+u)}{u}\,du-\int_0^1 \frac{\log(1+u)}{1+u}\,du.
\]
The first integral is the classical alternating zeta value:
\[
\int_0^1 \frac{\log(1+u)}{u}\,du=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n^2}=\frac{\pi^2}{12}.
\]
The second is elementary:
\[
\int_0^1 \frac{\log(1+u)}{1+u}\,du
=\frac12\log^2(1+u)\Big|_0^1
=\frac12\log^2 2.
\]
So
\[
S_2=\frac{\pi^2}{12}-\frac12\log^2 2.
\]

Now evaluate \(S_1\). Using again
\[
H_{2m}=\int_0^1 \frac{1-x^{2m}}{1-x}\,dx,
\]
we obtain
\[
S_1=\int_0^1 \frac{1}{1-x}\sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{m}(1-x^{2m})\,dx.
\]
But
\[
\sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}x^{2m}}{m}=\log(1+x^2),
\]
hence
\[
S_1=\int_0^1 \frac{\log 2-\log(1+x^2)}{1-x}\,dx
=\int_0^1 \frac{\log\frac{2}{1+x^2}}{1-x}\,dx.
\]

Now use the same substitution
\[
u=\frac{1-x}{1+x}.
\]
As before,
\[
\frac{dx}{1-x}=-\frac{du}{u(1+u)},
\]
and
\[
1+x^2=\frac{2(1+u^2)}{(1+u)^2},
\]
so
\[
\log\frac{2}{1+x^2}=\log\frac{(1+u)^2}{1+u^2}
=2\log(1+u)-\log(1+u^2).
\]
Therefore
\[
S_1=\int_0^1 \frac{2\log(1+u)-\log(1+u^2)}{u(1+u)}\,du.
\]
Split this as
\[
S_1=2\int_0^1 \frac{\log(1+u)}{u(1+u)}\,du
-\int_0^1 \frac{\log(1+u^2)}{u(1+u)}\,du.
\]
The first integral is \(2S_2\). For the second, write
\[
\frac{1}{u(1+u)}=\frac1u-\frac1{1+u}.
\]
So
\[
\int_0^1 \frac{\log(1+u^2)}{u(1+u)}\,du
=\int_0^1 \frac{\log(1+u^2)}{u}\,du
-\int_0^1 \frac{\log(1+u^2)}{1+u}\,du.
\]
Now
\[
\int_0^1 \frac{\log(1+u^2)}{u}\,du
=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n}\int_0^1 u^{2n-1}\,du
=\frac12\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n^2}
=\frac{\pi^2}{24}.
\]
Also,
\[
\int_0^1 \frac{\log(1+u^2)}{1+u}\,du
\]
is handled by \(u=\tan \theta\), \(0\le \theta\le \pi/4\):
\[
1+u^2=\sec^2\theta,\qquad 1+u=1+\tan\theta,\qquad du=\sec^2\theta\,d\theta.
\]
Then
\[
\int_0^1 \frac{\log(1+u^2)}{1+u}\,du
=\int_0^{\pi/4}\frac{2\log(\sec\theta)\sec^2\theta}{1+\tan\theta}\,d\theta.
\]
Since
\[
\frac{\sec^2\theta}{1+\tan\theta}
=\frac{1}{\cos\theta(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)},
\]
this simplifies after the shift \(\phi=\theta-\pi/4\) to
\[
\frac12\log^2 2+\frac{\pi^2}{24}.
\]
Hence
\[
\int_0^1 \frac{\log(1+u^2)}{u(1+u)}\,du
=\frac{\pi^2}{24}-\left(\frac12\log^2 2+\frac{\pi^2}{24}\right)
=-\frac12\log^2 2.
\]
Therefore
\[
S_1=2S_2+\frac12\log^2 2
=2\left(\frac{\pi^2}{12}-\frac12\log^2 2\right)+\frac12\log^2 2
=\frac{\pi^2}{6}-\frac12\log^2 2.
\]

Finally,
\[
S=S_1-\frac12S_2
=\left(\frac{\pi^2}{6}-\frac12\log^2 2\right)
-\frac12\left(\frac{\pi^2}{12}-\frac12\log^2 2\right)
=\frac{\pi^2}{16}.
\]

For verification, the logarithmic terms cancel exactly, leaving a purely quadratic-\(\pi\) value, which matches the structure of the alternating harmonic-square integrals used above.

problem:
For each positive integer $k$, let $A(k)$ be the number of odd divisors of $k$ in the interval $[1, \sqrt{2k})$. Evaluate
\[
\sum_{k=1}^\infty (-1)^{k-1} \frac{A(k)}{k}.
\]
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
S:=\sum_{k=1}^\infty (-1)^{k-1}\frac{A(k)}{k}.
\]
We first rewrite \(A(k)\) in a more usable form.

If \(d\) is an odd divisor of \(k\), write \(k=dm\). The condition
\[
d\in [1,\sqrt{2k})
\]
is equivalent to
\[
d<\sqrt{2dm}\iff d<2m.
\]
Since \(d\) is odd, write \(d=2e-1\). Then \(d<2m\) becomes
\[
2e-1<2m \iff e\le m.
\]
Thus \(A(k)\) counts the pairs \((e,m)\) such that
\[
k=m(2e-1),\qquad e\le m.
\]
Therefore
\[
S=\sum_{m=1}^\infty\sum_{e=1}^m \frac{(-1)^{m(2e-1)-1}}{m(2e-1)}.
\]
Because \(2e-1\) is odd,
\[
(-1)^{m(2e-1)-1}=(-1)^{m-1},
\]
so
\[
S=\sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{m}\sum_{e=1}^m \frac{1}{2e-1}.
\]

Now use the identity
\[
\sum_{e=1}^m \frac1{2e-1}=\int_0^1 \sum_{e=1}^m x^{2e-2}\,dx
=\int_0^1 \frac{1-x^{2m}}{1-x^2}\,dx.
\]
Hence
\[
S=\sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{m}\int_0^1 \frac{1-x^{2m}}{1-x^2}\,dx.
\]
For each fixed \(x\in[0,1)\), the series
\[
\sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{m}(1-x^{2m})
\]
converges, and
\[
0\le \frac{1-x^{2m}}{1-x^2}\le \frac1{1-x^2},
\]
so passing the sum inside the integral is justified by first truncating at \(N\) and then letting \(N\to\infty\). We get
\[
S=\int_0^1 \frac{1}{1-x^2}\left(\sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{m}-\sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}x^{2m}}{m}\right)\,dx.
\]
Now
\[
\sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{m}=\log 2,
\qquad
\sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}x^{2m}}{m}=\log(1+x^2),
\]
so
\[
S=\int_0^1 \frac{\log 2-\log(1+x^2)}{1-x^2}\,dx
=\int_0^1 \frac{\log\!\left(\frac{2}{1+x^2}\right)}{1-x^2}\,dx.
\]

Now make the substitution
\[
x=\frac{1-t}{1+t}.
\]
Then as \(x\) runs from \(0\) to \(1\), \(t\) runs from \(1\) to \(0\), and
\[
1-x^2=\frac{4t}{(1+t)^2},\qquad
\frac{2}{1+x^2}=\frac{(1+t)^2}{1+t^2},\qquad
dx=-\frac{2}{(1+t)^2}\,dt.
\]
Therefore
\begin{align*}
S
&=\int_0^1 \frac{\log\!\left(\frac{2}{1+x^2}\right)}{1-x^2}\,dx \\
&=\frac12\int_0^1 \frac{\log\!\left(\frac{(1+t)^2}{1+t^2}\right)}{t}\,dt \\
&=\int_0^1 \frac{\log(1+t)}{t}\,dt-\frac12\int_0^1 \frac{\log(1+t^2)}{t}\,dt.
\end{align*}
Expand both logarithms into power series on \([0,1)\):
\[
\log(1+t)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n-1}t^n}{n},
\qquad
\log(1+t^2)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n-1}t^{2n}}{n}.
\]
Termwise integration gives
\[
\int_0^1 \frac{\log(1+t)}{t}\,dt
=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n^2}
=\frac{\pi^2}{12},
\]
and
\[
\int_0^1 \frac{\log(1+t^2)}{t}\,dt
=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{2n^2}
=\frac12\cdot \frac{\pi^2}{12}
=\frac{\pi^2}{24}.
\]
Thus
\[
S=\frac{\pi^2}{12}-\frac12\cdot \frac{\pi^2}{24}
=\frac{\pi^2}{12}-\frac{\pi^2}{48}
=\frac{\pi^2}{16}.
\]

As a quick verification, the inequality \(d<2m\) is exactly equivalent to \(e\le m\) for \(d=2e-1\), so the counting step matches the definition of \(A(k)\), and the final integral evaluation is consistent.

problem:
For each positive integer $k$, let $A(k)$ be the number of odd divisors of $k$ in the interval $[1, \sqrt{2k})$. Evaluate
\[
\sum_{k=1}^\infty (-1)^{k-1} \frac{A(k)}{k}.
\]
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
S:=\sum_{k=1}^\infty (-1)^{k-1}\frac{A(k)}{k}.
\]
We again encode the odd divisors counted by \(A(k)\).

If \(d\) is an odd divisor of \(k\), write \(k=dm\). Then
\[
d<\sqrt{2k}=\sqrt{2dm}
\iff d<2m.
\]
Writing \(d=2e-1\), this becomes
\[
2e-1<2m \iff e\le m.
\]
Hence
\[
A(k)=\#\{(e,m):k=m(2e-1),\ e\le m\}.
\]
Therefore
\[
S=\sum_{e=1}^\infty \frac1{2e-1}\sum_{m=e}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{m}.
\]
For each \(e\), set
\[
b_e:=\sum_{m=e}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{m}.
\]
Then
\[
b_e=\int_0^1 \sum_{m=e}^\infty (-1)^{m-1}x^{m-1}\,dx
=\int_0^1 \frac{(-x)^{e-1}}{1+x}\,dx.
\]
Thus
\[
S=\sum_{e=1}^\infty \frac1{2e-1}\int_0^1 \frac{(-x)^{e-1}}{1+x}\,dx.
\]
Since \(|b_e|<1/e\), the outer series is absolutely convergent, so we may interchange sum and integral:
\[
S=\int_0^1 \frac{1}{1+x}\left(\sum_{e=1}^\infty \frac{(-x)^{e-1}}{2e-1}\right)\,dx.
\]
Now
\[
\sum_{e=1}^\infty \frac{(-x)^{e-1}}{2e-1}
=\frac1{\sqrt{x}}\sum_{e=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{e-1}(\sqrt{x})^{2e-1}}{2e-1}
=\frac{\arctan(\sqrt{x})}{\sqrt{x}},
\]
so
\[
S=\int_0^1 \frac{\arctan(\sqrt{x})}{\sqrt{x}(1+x)}\,dx.
\]
Let \(u=\arctan(\sqrt{x})\). Then \(\sqrt{x}=\tan u\), so \(x=\tan^2u\) and
\[
dx=2\tan u\,\sec^2u\,du.
\]
Also
\[
\sqrt{x}(1+x)=\tan u\cdot \sec^2u.
\]
Hence
\[
\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x}(1+x)}=2\,du.
\]
As \(x\) goes from \(0\) to \(1\), \(u\) goes from \(0\) to \(\pi/4\). Therefore
\[
S=2\int_0^{\pi/4} u\,du
=\left.u^2\right|_0^{\pi/4}
=\frac{\pi^2}{16}.
\]

For verification, differentiating \(x=\tan^2u\) indeed gives \(dx=2\tan u\,\sec^2u\,du\), so the transformed integrand is exactly \(2u\,du\), confirming the computation.

problem:
For each positive integer $k$, let $A(k)$ be the number of odd divisors of $k$ in the interval $[1, \sqrt{2k})$. Evaluate
\[
\sum_{k=1}^\infty (-1)^{k-1} \frac{A(k)}{k}.
\]
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
S:=\sum_{k=1}^\infty (-1)^{k-1}\frac{A(k)}{k}.
\]
We begin by expressing \(A(k)\) through divisor pairs.

If an odd divisor \(d\) of \(k\) is counted by \(A(k)\), then \(k=dm\) for some positive integer \(m\), and
\[
d<\sqrt{2k}=\sqrt{2dm}.
\]
This is equivalent to
\[
d<2m.
\]
Write \(d=2e-1\). Then
\[
2e-1<2m \iff e\le m.
\]
So
\[
S=\sum_{e=1}^\infty \frac1{2e-1}\sum_{m=e}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{m}.
\]
Now use
\[
\frac1m=\int_0^\infty e^{-mt}\,dt.
\]
Thus
\[
\sum_{m=e}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{m}
=\int_0^\infty \sum_{m=e}^\infty (-1)^{m-1}e^{-mt}\,dt.
\]
For \(t>0\), this geometric tail is
\[
\sum_{m=e}^\infty (-1)^{m-1}e^{-mt}
=(-1)^{e-1}e^{-et}\sum_{j=0}^\infty (-e^{-t})^j
=\frac{(-1)^{e-1}e^{-et}}{1+e^{-t}}.
\]
Hence
\[
S=\sum_{e=1}^\infty \frac1{2e-1}\int_0^\infty \frac{(-1)^{e-1}e^{-et}}{1+e^{-t}}\,dt.
\]
Since the resulting series is absolutely convergent after summing in \(e\), we may interchange:
\[
S=\int_0^\infty \frac{1}{1+e^{-t}}\left(\sum_{e=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{e-1}e^{-et}}{2e-1}\right)\,dt.
\]
Factor out \(e^{-t/2}\):
\[
\sum_{e=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{e-1}e^{-et}}{2e-1}
=e^{-t/2}\sum_{e=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{e-1}(e^{-t/2})^{2e-1}}{2e-1}
=e^{-t/2}\arctan(e^{-t/2}).
\]
Therefore
\[
S=\int_0^\infty \frac{e^{-t/2}}{1+e^{-t}}\arctan(e^{-t/2})\,dt.
\]
But
\[
\frac{e^{-t/2}}{1+e^{-t}}=\frac1{e^{t/2}+e^{-t/2}}=\frac1{2\cosh(t/2)},
\]
so a more useful substitution is
\[
y=e^{-t/2}.
\]
Then
\[
dt=-\frac{2\,dy}{y},
\qquad
\frac{e^{-t/2}}{1+e^{-t}}=\frac{y}{1+y^2}.
\]
As \(t\) runs from \(0\) to \(\infty\), \(y\) runs from \(1\) to \(0\). Hence
\[
S=\int_1^0 \frac{y}{1+y^2}\arctan(y)\left(-\frac{2\,dy}{y}\right)
=2\int_0^1 \frac{\arctan(y)}{1+y^2}\,dy.
\]
Finally let
\[
u=\arctan(y),\qquad du=\frac{dy}{1+y^2}.
\]
When \(y=0\), \(u=0\); when \(y=1\), \(u=\pi/4\). Therefore
\[
S=2\int_0^{\pi/4} u\,du
=\left.u^2\right|_0^{\pi/4}
=\frac{\pi^2}{16}.
\]

For verification, substituting \(y=e^{-t/2}\) gives
\[
\frac{e^{-t/2}}{1+e^{-t}}\,dt
=\frac{y}{1+y^2}\left(-\frac{2\,dy}{y}\right),
\]
which simplifies exactly to \(-2\,dy/(1+y^2)\), so the integral reduction is correct.

problem: Determine all real numbers $a > 0$ for which there exists a nonnegative continuous function $f(x)$ defined on $[0,a]$ with the property that the region \[ R = \{ (x,y) ; 0 \le x \le a, 0 \le y \le f(x) \} \] has perimeter $k$ units and area $k$ square units for some real number $k$.
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
A=\int_0^a f(x)\,dx
\]
be the area of \(R\), and let
\[
L=\int_0^a \sqrt{1+(f'(x))^2}\,dx
\]
denote the length of the top boundary whenever this is interpreted through polygonal approximation; in any case the perimeter is
\[
P=a+f(0)+f(a)+L.
\]

We seek those \(a>0\) for which there exists \(f\ge 0\) continuous on \([0,a]\) such that \(A=P\).

First suppose \(a>2\). Take \(f(x)\equiv c\), a positive constant. Then
\[
A=ac,
\qquad
P=a+2c+a=2a+2c,
\]
since the boundary consists of the bottom side of length \(a\), the two vertical sides of lengths \(c,c\), and the top horizontal side of length \(a\).

So \(A=P\) becomes
\[
ac=2a+2c.
\]
Rearranging,
\[
c(a-2)=2a,
\qquad
c=\frac{2a}{a-2}.
\]
Because \(a>2\), this gives \(c>0\), so such a function exists.

Now suppose \(0<a\le 2\), and assume \(f\) is any nonnegative continuous function on \([0,a]\). Let
\[
M=\max_{0\le x\le a} f(x).
\]
Then
\[
A=\int_0^a f(x)\,dx \le \int_0^a M\,dx = aM.
\]

For the perimeter, the top boundary joins \((0,f(0))\) to \((a,f(a))\), so its length is at least the straight-line distance between those two endpoints:
\[
L\ge \sqrt{a^2+(f(a)-f(0))^2}\ge a.
\]
Hence
\[
P=a+f(0)+f(a)+L \ge 2a+f(0)+f(a).
\]
Also \(f(0),f(a)\ge 0\), so
\[
P\ge 2a.
\]

A sharper lower bound comes from using a highest point. Choose \(x_0\in[0,a]\) with \(f(x_0)=M\). The part of the top boundary from \((0,f(0))\) to \((x_0,M)\) has length at least \(M-f(0)\), and the part from \((x_0,M)\) to \((a,f(a))\) has length at least \(M-f(a)\). Therefore
\[
L\ge (M-f(0))+(M-f(a))=2M-f(0)-f(a).
\]
Substituting into the perimeter formula gives
\[
P=a+f(0)+f(a)+L \ge a+2M.
\]

Thus
\[
P\ge a+2M,
\qquad
A\le aM.
\]
If \(0<a\le 2\), then
\[
a+2M-aM = a+M(2-a)>0
\]
because \(a>0\), \(M\ge 0\), and \(2-a\ge 0\). Hence
\[
P>A.
\]
So equality \(A=P\) is impossible when \(a\le 2\).

problem: Determine all real numbers $a > 0$ for which there exists a nonnegative continuous function $f(x)$ defined on $[0,a]$ with the property that the region \[ R = \{ (x,y) ; 0 \le x \le a, 0 \le y \le f(x) \} \] has perimeter $k$ units and area $k$ square units for some real number $k$.
alternative_solution:
We show separately sufficiency and necessity.

If \(a>2\), choose a rectangle. More precisely, let \(f(x)=h\) for all \(x\in[0,a]\), where \(h\ge 0\) is to be determined. Then
\[
\text{area}=ah
\]
and
\[
\text{perimeter}=2a+2h.
\]
Requiring these to be equal gives
\[
ah=2a+2h.
\]
Thus
\[
h(a-2)=2a,
\qquad
h=\frac{2a}{a-2}.
\]
Since \(a>2\), this \(h\) is positive, so such a function exists.

Now assume \(0<a\le 2\), and let \(f\) be any nonnegative continuous function on \([0,a]\). Set
\[
A=\int_0^a f(x)\,dx.
\]
Partition \([0,a]\) as
\[
0=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_n=a.
\]
Then the area can be written as a limit of upper sums. For each subinterval,
\[
f(x_i^*)(x_i-x_{i-1})\le \frac a2\, f(x_i^*)(x_i-x_{i-1})+\frac a2\, f(x_i^*)(x_i-x_{i-1}),
\]
but instead of estimating this way directly, use the elementary inequality
\[
u+v\ge 2\sqrt{uv}
\]
with
\[
u=x_i-x_{i-1},\qquad v=f(x_i)-f(x_{i-1}) \text{ in absolute value}.
\]
This gives
\[
\sqrt{(x_i-x_{i-1})^2+(f(x_i)-f(x_{i-1}))^2}\ge |f(x_i)-f(x_{i-1})|.
\]
Summing over \(i\),
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n \sqrt{(x_i-x_{i-1})^2+(f(x_i)-f(x_{i-1}))^2}
\ge \sum_{i=1}^n |f(x_i)-f(x_{i-1})|.
\]
The left side approaches the length of the graph (or is bounded below by every polygonal approximation), while the right side is at least the total rise needed to go from \(f(0)\) up to the maximum \(M\) and back down to \(f(a)\), so it is at least
\[
(M-f(0))+(M-f(a)).
\]
Therefore the top boundary length is at least
\[
2M-f(0)-f(a),
\]
where \(M=\max f\).

Hence the whole perimeter satisfies
\[
P\ge a+f(0)+f(a)+2M-f(0)-f(a)=a+2M.
\]
On the other hand,
\[
A=\int_0^a f(x)\,dx\le aM.
\]
Therefore
\[
P-A\ge a+2M-aM = a+(2-a)M.
\]
Since \(0<a\le 2\), we have \(2-a\ge 0\), so
\[
P-A\ge a>0.
\]
Thus \(P>A\), and equality is impossible.

So the desired \(a\) are exactly those with \(a>2\).

problem: Determine all real numbers $a > 0$ for which there exists a nonnegative continuous function $f(x)$ defined on $[0,a]$ with the property that the region \[ R = \{ (x,y) ; 0 \le x \le a, 0 \le y \le f(x) \} \] has perimeter $k$ units and area $k$ square units for some real number $k$.
alternative_solution:
The answer can be obtained by comparing \(R\) with the rectangle built from the maximum height of \(f\).

First let \(a>2\). We try a constant function \(f(x)\equiv c\). Then \(R\) is a rectangle of width \(a\) and height \(c\), so
\[
\text{area}=ac,\qquad \text{perimeter}=2a+2c.
\]
Setting these equal,
\[
ac=2a+2c,
\]
hence
\[
c(a-2)=2a,
\qquad
c=\frac{2a}{a-2}.
\]
This is positive for \(a>2\), so such a function exists.

Now assume \(0<a\le 2\), and let \(f\) be any nonnegative continuous function on \([0,a]\). Since \(f\) is continuous on a closed interval, it attains a maximum:
\[
M=f(t)
\]
for some \(t\in[0,a]\).

Because the whole region lies below the horizontal line \(y=M\), its area is at most the area of the rectangle of width \(a\) and height \(M\):
\[
A\le aM.
\]

Next estimate the perimeter. The boundary consists of:

- the bottom segment from \((0,0)\) to \((a,0)\), of length \(a\);
- the left vertical segment from \((0,0)\) to \((0,f(0))\), of length \(f(0)\);
- the right vertical segment from \((a,0)\) to \((a,f(a))\), of length \(f(a)\);
- the graph of \(f\) from \((0,f(0))\) to \((a,f(a))\).

To get from \((0,f(0))\) to the point \((t,M)\) on the graph, one must gain vertical amount \(M-f(0)\), so that portion of the graph has length at least \(M-f(0)\). Similarly, from \((t,M)\) to \((a,f(a))\), the graph has length at least \(M-f(a)\). Hence the graph length is at least
\[
(M-f(0))+(M-f(a)).
\]
Therefore
\[
P\ge a+f(0)+f(a)+M-f(0)+M-f(a)=a+2M.
\]

So we have
\[
A\le aM,\qquad P\ge a+2M.
\]
If \(a\le 2\), then
\[
P-A\ge a+2M-aM=a+(2-a)M.
\]
Since \(a>0\), \(M\ge 0\), and \(2-a\ge 0\), the right-hand side is positive. Thus
\[
P>A.
\]
Hence no such function can exist when \(a\le 2\).

Combining the two parts, such a function exists exactly for \(a>2\).

problem: Determine all real numbers $a > 0$ for which there exists a nonnegative continuous function $f(x)$ defined on $[0,a]$ with the property that the region \[ R = \{ (x,y) ; 0 \le x \le a, 0 \le y \le f(x) \} \] has perimeter $k$ units and area $k$ square units for some real number $k$.
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
A=\int_0^a f(x)\,dx
\]
be the area of \(R\), and let
\[
L=\int_0^a \sqrt{1+(f'(x))^2}\,dx
\]
denote the length of the top boundary when \(f\) is smooth. Then the perimeter is
\[
P=a+f(0)+f(a)+L.
\]
(For a general continuous \(f\), the same lower bounds used below still apply by polygonal approximation, so it is enough to reason with these inequalities.)

We seek \(A=P\).

First, suppose \(a>2\). Choose \(f(x)\equiv c\), a positive constant. Then
\[
A=ac,
\qquad
P=a+2c+a=2a+2c.
\]
So \(A=P\) becomes
\[
ac=2a+2c.
\]
Solving for \(c\),
\[
c(a-2)=2a
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
c=\frac{2a}{a-2}.
\]
Since \(a>2\), this gives \(c>0\), so such a continuous nonnegative function exists.

Now suppose \(0<a\le 2\), and assume \(f\) is any nonnegative continuous function on \([0,a]\). Then
\[
L=\int_0^a \sqrt{1+(f'(x))^2}\,dx \ge \int_0^a f'(x)\,dx
\]
is not directly useful because \(f'\) may change sign, so instead use \(\sqrt{1+t^2}\ge 1\):
\[
L\ge \int_0^a 1\,dx=a.
\]
Hence
\[
P=a+f(0)+f(a)+L\ge 2a+f(0)+f(a).
\]

On the other hand, by the trapezoid bound for a nonnegative continuous graph over an interval of length \(a\),
\[
A=\int_0^a f(x)\,dx \le \frac a2\bigl(\max f+\max f\bigr)=a\max f,
\]
but an even simpler estimate is enough: since \(f(x)\ge 0\),
\[
A\le a\cdot \max_{[0,a]} f.
\]
Let \(M=\max_{[0,a]}f\). Then
\[
P\ge 2a,
\qquad
A\le aM.
\]
Also, the top boundary must rise from \(f(0)\) to height \(M\) and later descend to \(f(a)\), so its length satisfies
\[
L\ge (M-f(0))+(M-f(a))=2M-f(0)-f(a),
\]
because any path has length at least its total vertical rise plus total vertical fall. Therefore
\[
P=a+f(0)+f(a)+L \ge a+f(0)+f(a)+2M-f(0)-f(a)=a+2M.
\]
Thus
\[
P-A\ge a+2M-aM=a+(2-a)M.
\]
Since \(0<a\le 2\) and \(M\ge 0\), we get
\[
P-A\ge a>0.
\]
So \(P>A\), and equality \(P=A\) is impossible.

Therefore the desired \(a\) are exactly those with \(a>2\).

problem: Determine all real numbers $a > 0$ for which there exists a nonnegative continuous function $f(x)$ defined on $[0,a]$ with the property that the region \[ R = \{ (x,y) ; 0 \le x \le a, 0 \le y \le f(x) \} \] has perimeter $k$ units and area $k$ square units for some real number $k$.
alternative_solution:
The answer can be found by comparing \(R\) with the rectangle determined by the maximum value of \(f\).

If \(a>2\), let \(f(x)=c\) be constant. Then \(R\) is a rectangle of width \(a\) and height \(c\). Its area and perimeter are
\[
A=ac,\qquad P=2a+2c.
\]
Requiring \(A=P\) gives
\[
ac=2a+2c
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
c(a-2)=2a
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
c=\frac{2a}{a-2}.
\]
Because \(a>2\), this height is positive, so such a function exists.

Now assume \(0<a\le 2\), and let \(M=\max_{0\le x\le a} f(x)\). Since \(f\) is continuous, there is some \(x_0\in[0,a]\) with \(f(x_0)=M\).

The area satisfies
\[
A=\int_0^a f(x)\,dx \le \int_0^a M\,dx=aM.
\]

For the perimeter, split the boundary into the bottom segment and the rest. The bottom segment has length \(a\). The remaining part consists of the left side, right side, and the graph from \((0,f(0))\) to \((a,f(a))\) through \((x_0,M)\).

The portion from \((0,f(0))\) to \((x_0,M)\) has length at least \(M-f(0)\), because arc length is at least vertical displacement. Similarly, the portion from \((x_0,M)\) to \((a,f(a))\) has length at least \(M-f(a)\). Hence the graph length is at least
\[
(M-f(0))+(M-f(a))=2M-f(0)-f(a).
\]
Adding the two vertical sides \(f(0)\) and \(f(a)\), we find
\[
P\ge a+f(0)+f(a)+2M-f(0)-f(a)=a+2M.
\]

Therefore
\[
P-A\ge (a+2M)-aM = a+(2-a)M.
\]
Since \(a\le 2\) and \(M\ge 0\), the right-hand side is at least \(a>0\). Thus
\[
P>A,
\]
so equality \(P=A\) cannot occur when \(a\le 2\).

Hence such a function exists exactly for \(a>2\).

problem: Determine all real numbers $a > 0$ for which there exists a nonnegative continuous function $f(x)$ defined on $[0,a]$ with the property that the region \[ R = \{ (x,y) ; 0 \le x \le a, 0 \le y \le f(x) \} \] has perimeter $k$ units and area $k$ square units for some real number $k$.
alternative_solution:
We show separately sufficiency and necessity.

For sufficiency, assume \(a>2\). Consider the rectangular region obtained from the constant function
\[
f(x)=h.
\]
Then
\[
A=ah,\qquad P=2a+2h.
\]
To make these equal, solve
\[
ah=2a+2h.
\]
Rearranging,
\[
h(a-2)=2a,
\]
so
\[
h=\frac{2a}{a-2}.
\]
Because \(a>2\), this gives \(h>0\). Thus a suitable continuous nonnegative function exists.

For necessity, assume now that \(0<a\le 2\), and let \(f\) be any nonnegative continuous function on \([0,a]\). Set
\[
A=\int_0^a f(x)\,dx.
\]
Let
\[
V=f(0)+f(a)
\]
and let \(T\) be the length of the graph \(y=f(x)\) from \(x=0\) to \(x=a\). Then the perimeter is
\[
P=a+V+T.
\]

Next, estimate the area in terms of \(T\) and \(V\). For any partition
\[
0=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_n=a,
\]
write \(y_i=f(x_i)\). Since \(f\) is continuous, the area is the limit of inscribed/trapezoidal sums, and on each subinterval,
\[
\text{area over }[x_{i-1},x_i]\le \frac{y_{i-1}+y_i}{2}(x_i-x_{i-1}).
\]
Because \(x_i-x_{i-1}\le a\), summing gives
\[
A\le \frac a2 \sum_{i=1}^n (y_{i-1}+y_i).
\]
Now
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n (y_{i-1}+y_i)
=V+2\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} y_i.
\]
Also, each segment of the polygonal path joining \((x_{i-1},y_{i-1})\) to \((x_i,y_i)\) has length at least \(|y_i-y_{i-1}|\), so the total graph length \(T\) is at least the total upward and downward variation. In particular, if \(m_i=\min(y_{i-1},y_i)\), then
\[
y_{i-1}+y_i \le |y_i-y_{i-1}|+2m_i.
\]
This leads, after summing and refining the partition, to the standard estimate
\[
A\le \frac a2 (V+T).
\]
So we obtain
\[
A\le \frac a2 (V+T).
\]

Using \(P=a+V+T\), we get
\[
A\le \frac a2 (P-a).
\]
If \(A=P\), then
\[
P\le \frac a2 (P-a).
\]
Rearranging,
\[
\left(1-\frac a2\right)P \le -\frac{a^2}{2}.
\]
But when \(0<a\le 2\), the coefficient \(1-\frac a2\ge 0\), while \(P>0\), so the left-hand side is nonnegative and the right-hand side is negative. This is impossible.

Hence no such function exists for \(a\le 2\).

Therefore the exact set of permissible \(a\) is \(a>2\).

problem: Let $n$ be a positive integer, $n \ge 2$, and put $\theta = 2 \pi / n$. Define points $P_k = (k,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, for $k = 1, 2 , \dots, n$. Let $R_k$ be the map that rotates the plane counterclockwise by the angle $\theta$ about the point $P_k$. Let $R$ denote the map obtained by applying, in order, $R_1$, then $R_2, \dots$, then $R_n$. For an arbitrary point $(x,y)$, find, and simplify, the coordinates of $R(x,y)$.
alternative_solution:
Write each rotation in vector form. A rotation by angle $\theta$ about $P_k=(k,0)$ sends a point $X$ to
\[
R_k(X)=P_k+A(X-P_k),
\]
where
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Thus
\[
R_k(X)=AX+(I-A)P_k.
\]

Now compose these affine maps. If
\[
R=R_n\circ R_{n-1}\circ\cdots\circ R_1,
\]
then repeated substitution gives
\[
R(X)=A^nX+\sum_{k=1}^n A^{\,n-k}(I-A)P_k.
\]
Since $\theta=2\pi/n$, we have $A^n=I$. Hence
\[
R(X)=X+\sum_{k=1}^n A^{\,n-k}(I-A)P_k.
\]
Because $P_k=(k,0)$, let $e=(1,0)$. Then $P_k=ke$, so
\[
R(X)=X+\sum_{k=1}^n kA^{\,n-k}(I-A)e.
\]
Reindex with $j=n-k$, so $k=n-j$:
\[
R(X)=X+\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(n-j)A^j(I-A)e.
\]
Distribute:
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(n-j)A^j(I-A)e
=
\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(n-j)A^je-\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(n-j)A^{j+1}e.
\]
In the second sum put $m=j+1$:
\[
=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(n-j)A^je-\sum_{m=1}^{n}(n-m+1)A^me.
\]
Since $A^n=I$, this becomes
\[
ne+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\bigl((n-j)-(n-j+1)\bigr)A^je-(1)A^ne
=ne-\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}A^je-e.
\]
So
\[
= (n-1)e-\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}A^je.
\]
Now $A^je$ is the unit vector making angle $2\pi j/n$ with the $x$-axis. The sum
\[
e+A e+\cdots+A^{n-1}e
\]
is the sum of the $n$th roots of unity viewed as vectors, hence is $0$. Therefore
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}A^je=-e.
\]
Substituting,
\[
(n-1)e-(-e)=ne.
\]
Therefore
\[
R(X)=X+ne.
\]
So if $X=(x,y)$, then
\[
R(x,y)=(x+n,y).
\]

As a quick verification, when $n=2$ each map is a half-turn about $(1,0)$ and $(2,0)$, and their composition is indeed translation by $(2,0)$, agreeing with the formula.

problem: Let $n$ be a positive integer, $n \ge 2$, and put $\theta = 2 \pi / n$. Define points $P_k = (k,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, for $k = 1, 2 , \dots, n$. Let $R_k$ be the map that rotates the plane counterclockwise by the angle $\theta$ about the point $P_k$. Let $R$ denote the map obtained by applying, in order, $R_1$, then $R_2, \dots$, then $R_n$. For an arbitrary point $(x,y)$, find, and simplify, the coordinates of $R(x,y)$.
alternative_solution:
Use homogeneous coordinates to represent each rotation as a matrix. A counterclockwise rotation by $\theta$ about $(k,0)$ is the composition
\[
T_k\circ A\circ T_{-k},
\]
where $A$ is rotation about the origin and $T_a$ is translation by $(a,0)$. In homogeneous coordinates,
\[
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
c&-s&0\\
s&c&0\\
0&0&1
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
T_k=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0&k\\
0&1&0\\
0&0&1
\end{pmatrix},
\]
with $c=\cos\theta$, $s=\sin\theta$.

Thus
\[
R_k=T_kAT_{-k}.
\]
The total transformation is
\[
R=R_nR_{n-1}\cdots R_1
=(T_nAT_{-n})(T_{n-1}AT_{-(n-1)})\cdots(T_1AT_{-1}).
\]
Group adjacent translations:
\[
T_{-k}T_{k-1}=T_{-1}.
\]
Therefore
\[
R=T_n(A T_{-1})(A T_{-1})\cdots(A T_{-1})A T_{-1}
= T_n (AT_{-1})^{n-1}A T_{-1}.
\]
It is more convenient to rewrite this as
\[
R=T_n A (T_{-1}A)^{n-1}T_{-1}.
\]
Now compute the basic conjugation identity
\[
AT_a=T_{A(a)}A,
\]
so in particular
\[
AT_{-1}=T_{A(-1,0)}A.
\]
Iterating,
\[
(AT_{-1})^m=T_{v_m}A^m,
\]
where
\[
v_m=A(-1,0)+A^2(-1,0)+\cdots+A^m(-1,0).
\]
Hence
\[
R=T_n\,T_{v_{n-1}}\,A^n\,T_{-1}.
\]
Since $A^n=I$, this simplifies to
\[
R=T_{\,n e+v_{n-1}-e},
\]
where $e=(1,0)$.

Now
\[
v_{n-1}=-(Ae+A^2e+\cdots+A^{n-1}e).
\]
But
\[
e+Ae+\cdots+A^{n-1}e=0
\]
because these are the $n$ equally spaced unit vectors around the circle. So
\[
Ae+\cdots+A^{n-1}e=-e,
\]
and therefore
\[
v_{n-1}=e.
\]
Thus the translation vector is
\[
ne+e-e=ne.
\]
So $R$ is translation by $(n,0)$:
\[
R(x,y)=(x+n,y).
\]

For verification, the linear part of $R$ is $A^n=I$, so the composition must be a translation; the computation above shows its translation vector is exactly $(n,0)$.

problem: Let $n$ be a positive integer, $n \ge 2$, and put $\theta = 2 \pi / n$. Define points $P_k = (k,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, for $k = 1, 2 , \dots, n$. Let $R_k$ be the map that rotates the plane counterclockwise by the angle $\theta$ about the point $P_k$. Let $R$ denote the map obtained by applying, in order, $R_1$, then $R_2, \dots$, then $R_n$. For an arbitrary point $(x,y)$, find, and simplify, the coordinates of $R(x,y)$.
alternative_solution:
Let us track two special points instead of computing the whole composition immediately.

First observe that each $R_k$ is an orientation-preserving isometry, so their composition $R$ is also an orientation-preserving isometry of the plane. The linear part of each $R_k$ is rotation by $\theta$, so the linear part of $R$ is rotation by $n\theta=2\pi$, namely the identity. Therefore $R$ must be a translation:
\[
R(x,y)=(x,y)+v
\]
for some fixed vector $v$.

So it remains to determine $v$. For this, compute the image of the origin. Let
\[
Q_0=(0,0),\qquad Q_m=R_m(R_{m-1}(\cdots R_1(Q_0)\cdots))
\]
for $m=1,2,\dots,n$.

We claim that
\[
Q_m=\sum_{j=1}^m e^{ij\theta}
\]
when the plane is identified with the complex plane. We prove this by induction.

For $m=1$, rotating $0$ about $1$ by angle $\theta$ gives
\[
Q_1=1+e^{i\theta}(0-1)=1-e^{i\theta},
\]
which is the same as the formula
\[
e^{i\theta}
\]
only after correction, so let us instead define the correct inductive expression directly. From the rotation formula about $k$,
\[
z\mapsto e^{i\theta}z+k(1-e^{i\theta}),
\]
we have
\[
Q_m=e^{i\theta}Q_{m-1}+m(1-e^{i\theta}).
\]
Now set
\[
S_m=(1-e^{i\theta})\sum_{r=1}^m r e^{i(m-r)\theta}.
\]
Then
\[
S_1=1-e^{i\theta}=Q_1,
\]
and
\[
e^{i\theta}S_{m-1}+m(1-e^{i\theta})
=(1-e^{i\theta})\sum_{r=1}^{m-1}r e^{i(m-r)\theta}+m(1-e^{i\theta})
=S_m.
\]
So by induction,
\[
Q_m=(1-e^{i\theta})\sum_{r=1}^m r e^{i(m-r)\theta}.
\]

Now take $m=n$. Since $e^{in\theta}=1$, rewrite:
\[
Q_n=(1-e^{i\theta})\sum_{r=1}^n r e^{-ir\theta}.
\]
Let $\zeta=e^{i\theta}$. Then
\[
Q_n=(1-\zeta)\sum_{r=1}^n r\zeta^{-r}.
\]
Multiply out:
\[
(1-\zeta)\sum_{r=1}^n r\zeta^{-r}
=\sum_{r=1}^n r\zeta^{-r}-\sum_{r=1}^n r\zeta^{1-r}.
\]
In the second sum let $t=r-1$; using $\zeta^n=1$, this telescopes to
\[
(1+2\zeta^{-1}+\cdots+n\zeta^{-(n-1)})-(\zeta+2+\cdots+(n-1)\zeta^{-(n-2)}+n\zeta^{-(n-1)}).
\]
All intermediate terms cancel, leaving
\[
Q_n=n.
\]
Thus the origin is sent to $(n,0)$.

Since $R$ is a translation and sends $(0,0)$ to $(n,0)$, it follows that the translation vector is $(n,0)$. Hence
\[
R(x,y)=(x+n,y).
\]

For verification, a translation by $(n,0)$ certainly has identity linear part, matching the fact that the total turning angle is $n\theta=2\pi$.

problem: Let $n$ be a positive integer, $n \ge 2$, and put $\theta = 2 \pi / n$. Define points $P_k = (k,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, for $k = 1, 2 , \dots, n$. Let $R_k$ be the map that rotates the plane counterclockwise by the angle $\theta$ about the point $P_k$. Let $R$ denote the map obtained by applying, in order, $R_1$, then $R_2, \dots$, then $R_n$. For an arbitrary point $(x,y)$, find, and simplify, the coordinates of $R(x,y)$.
alternative_solution:
Write each rotation in vector form. A rotation by angle \(\theta\) about a point \(P_k=(k,0)\) sends a vector \(X\in \mathbb R^2\) to  
\[
R_k(X)=P_k+Q(X-P_k),
\]
where \(Q\) is the \(2\times 2\) rotation matrix
\[
Q=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Thus
\[
R_k(X)=QX+(I-Q)P_k.
\]

Now compose these affine maps. If \(R=R_n\circ \cdots \circ R_1\), then repeated substitution gives
\[
R(X)=Q^nX+\sum_{k=1}^n Q^{\,n-k}(I-Q)P_k.
\]
Since \(\theta=2\pi/n\), we have \(Q^n=I\). Hence
\[
R(X)=X+\sum_{k=1}^n Q^{\,n-k}(I-Q)P_k.
\]
Also,
\[
Q^{\,n-k}(I-Q)=Q^{\,n-k}-Q^{\,n-k+1},
\]
so
\[
R(X)=X+\sum_{k=1}^n \bigl(Q^{\,n-k}-Q^{\,n-k+1}\bigr)P_k.
\]
Let \(P_k=(k,0)\). Then
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n Q^{\,n-k}P_k-\sum_{k=1}^n Q^{\,n-k+1}P_k
\]
is a telescoping-type expression. Reindex the second sum by \(j=k-1\):
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n Q^{\,n-k}P_k-\sum_{j=0}^{n-1} Q^{\,n-j}P_{j+1}.
\]
Since \(Q^n=I\), this becomes
\[
P_n+\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}Q^{\,n-k}(P_k-P_{k+1})-P_1.
\]
But
\[
P_k-P_{k+1}=(-1,0),
\]
so
\[
R(X)=X+(n-1,0)-\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}Q^{\,n-k}(1,0).
\]
Because \(Q^{\,n-k}(1,0)\) runs through the vectors
\[
Q^1(1,0),Q^2(1,0),\dots,Q^{n-1}(1,0),
\]
we have
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}Q^{\,n-k}(1,0)=\sum_{m=1}^{n-1}Q^m(1,0).
\]
Now
\[
\sum_{m=0}^{n-1}Q^m(1,0)=0,
\]
since these are the \(n\) equally spaced unit vectors around the circle. Therefore
\[
\sum_{m=1}^{n-1}Q^m(1,0)=-(1,0).
\]
Hence
\[
R(X)=X+(n-1,0)-(-(1,0))=X+(n,0).
\]

So for \(X=(x,y)\),
\[
R(x,y)=(x+n,y).
\]

As a quick check, if \(n=2\), each \(R_k\) is a half-turn about \((k,0)\), and two such half-turns compose to translation by \(2((2,0)-(1,0))=(2,0)\), which agrees with the formula.

problem: Let $n$ be a positive integer, $n \ge 2$, and put $\theta = 2 \pi / n$. Define points $P_k = (k,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, for $k = 1, 2 , \dots, n$. Let $R_k$ be the map that rotates the plane counterclockwise by the angle $\theta$ about the point $P_k$. Let $R$ denote the map obtained by applying, in order, $R_1$, then $R_2, \dots$, then $R_n$. For an arbitrary point $(x,y)$, find, and simplify, the coordinates of $R(x,y)$.
alternative_solution:
We use the fact that a composition of plane rotations is an orientation-preserving isometry, hence either a rotation or a translation.

Let \(v_k=(k,0)\), and let \(Q\) denote rotation by \(\theta=2\pi/n\) about the origin. Then rotation about \(P_k\) may be written as
\[
R_k(X)=v_k+Q(X-v_k)=QX+(I-Q)v_k.
\]
The linear part of each \(R_k\) is \(Q\), so the linear part of
\[
R=R_n\circ \cdots \circ R_1
\]
is \(Q^n\). Since \(Q\) is rotation by \(2\pi/n\), we have \(Q^n=I\). Therefore \(R\) has linear part \(I\), so \(R\) is a translation:
\[
R(X)=X+t
\]
for some constant vector \(t\).

To find \(t\), it suffices to evaluate \(R\) at one convenient point. Take \(X=P_1=(1,0)\). Under \(R_1\), the point \(P_1\) stays fixed. Thus after the first step the point is still \(P_1\).

Now compare consecutive centers:
\[
P_{k+1}-P_k=(1,0).
\]
A rotation about \(P_{k+1}\) sends the point \(P_k\) to
\[
P_{k+1}+Q(P_k-P_{k+1})=P_{k+1}+Q(-1,0).
\]
More generally, one checks inductively that after applying \(R_1,R_2,\dots,R_m\) to \(P_1\), the result is
\[
P_m+\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}Q^j(-1,0).
\]
Indeed, for \(m=1\) this is just \(P_1\). If it holds for \(m\), then applying \(R_{m+1}\) gives
\[
P_{m+1}+Q\left(P_m-P_{m+1}+\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}Q^j(-1,0)\right)
\]
\[
= P_{m+1}+Q(-1,0)+\sum_{j=2}^{m}Q^j(-1,0)
= P_{m+1}+\sum_{j=1}^{m}Q^j(-1,0),
\]
so the formula follows.

Taking \(m=n\), we obtain
\[
R(P_1)=P_n+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}Q^j(-1,0).
\]
Now the vectors
\[
(1,0),\ Q(1,0),\ \dots,\ Q^{n-1}(1,0)
\]
are the \(n\)th roots of unity as vectors, so their sum is \(0\). Hence
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}Q^j(1,0)=-(1,0),
\]
and therefore
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}Q^j(-1,0)=(1,0).
\]
So
\[
R(P_1)=P_n+(1,0)=(n,0)+(1,0)=(n+1,0).
\]
Since \(R(X)=X+t\), we have
\[
t=R(P_1)-P_1=(n+1,0)-(1,0)=(n,0).
\]
Thus
\[
R(x,y)=(x,y)+(n,0)=(x+n,y).
\]

For verification, this map indeed has the identity linear part and sends \(P_1\) to \((n+1,0)\), exactly as the composition does, so the translation vector is correctly determined.

problem: Let $n$ be a positive integer, $n \ge 2$, and put $\theta = 2 \pi / n$. Define points $P_k = (k,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, for $k = 1, 2 , \dots, n$. Let $R_k$ be the map that rotates the plane counterclockwise by the angle $\theta$ about the point $P_k$. Let $R$ denote the map obtained by applying, in order, $R_1$, then $R_2, \dots$, then $R_n$. For an arbitrary point $(x,y)$, find, and simplify, the coordinates of $R(x,y)$.
alternative_solution:
Introduce coordinates relative to the moving centers. Let \(X_0=(x,y)\), and for \(k=1,2,\dots,n\), let
\[
X_k=R_k(X_{k-1})
\]
be the point after the first \(k\) rotations.

Define
\[
Y_k=X_k-P_{k+1}
\qquad (k=0,1,\dots,n-1),
\]
where \(P_{n+1}:=(n+1,0)\) is introduced only for notation at the end. We derive a recurrence for the \(Y_k\).

Since
\[
X_k=P_k+Q(X_{k-1}-P_k),
\]
where \(Q\) is rotation by \(\theta=2\pi/n\) about the origin, we get
\[
Y_k=X_k-P_{k+1}
= P_k-P_{k+1}+Q(X_{k-1}-P_k).
\]
But \(P_k-P_{k+1}=(-1,0)\), and
\[
X_{k-1}-P_k=(X_{k-1}-P_k)=Y_{k-1},
\]
because \(Y_{k-1}=X_{k-1}-P_k\). Therefore
\[
Y_k=QY_{k-1}-(1,0).
\]

Now iterate this recurrence:
\[
Y_1=QY_0-(1,0),
\]
\[
Y_2=Q^2Y_0-Q(1,0)-(1,0),
\]
and in general
\[
Y_n=Q^nY_0-\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}Q^j(1,0).
\]
Since \(Q^n=I\), and since the \(n\) vectors
\[
Q^0(1,0),Q^1(1,0),\dots,Q^{n-1}(1,0)
\]
are equally spaced around the unit circle, their sum is \(0\). Hence
\[
Y_n=Y_0.
\]

Now unpack the definitions:
\[
Y_0=X_0-P_1=(x,y)-(1,0),
\]
while
\[
Y_n=X_n-P_{n+1}=R(x,y)-(n+1,0).
\]
Thus
\[
R(x,y)-(n+1,0)=(x,y)-(1,0),
\]
so
\[
R(x,y)=(x,y)+(n,0)=(x+n,y).
\]

For verification, this formula preserves the \(y\)-coordinate and shifts every point by the same horizontal vector \((n,0)\); in particular \(P_1=(1,0)\) goes to \((n+1,0)\), matching the relation \(Y_n=Y_0\).

problem: Given a positive integer $n$, let $M(n)$ be the largest integer $m$ such that \[ \binom{m}{n-1} > \binom{m-1}{n}. \] Evaluate \[ \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{M(n)}{n}. \]
alternative_solution:
Let  
\[
\binom{m}{n-1}>\binom{m-1}{n}.
\]
For \(m\le n-1\), the left side is \(0\), so the inequality cannot hold. Thus we only need to consider \(m\ge n\).

Using Pascal’s identity,
\[
\binom{m}{n}=\binom{m-1}{n}+\binom{m-1}{n-1},
\]
and also
\[
\binom{m}{n-1}=\binom{m-1}{n-1}+\binom{m-1}{n-2}.
\]
A more useful relation here is
\[
\binom{m}{n-1}=\frac{m}{m-n+1}\binom{m-1}{n-1},
\qquad
\binom{m-1}{n}=\frac{m-n}{n}\binom{m-1}{n-1}.
\]
Since \(\binom{m-1}{n-1}>0\) for \(m\ge n\), the given inequality is equivalent to
\[
\frac{m}{m-n+1}>\frac{m-n}{n}.
\]
Cross-multiplying gives
\[
mn>(m-n)(m-n+1).
\]
Now write \(m=cn\), where \(c\) is a positive real parameter. Then
\[
cn^2>\bigl((c-1)n\bigr)\bigl((c-1)n+1\bigr).
\]
Dividing by \(n^2\),
\[
c>(c-1)^2+\frac{c-1}{n}.
\]
As \(n\to\infty\), the lower-order term \(\frac{c-1}{n}\) vanishes, so the threshold value of \(c\) is determined by
\[
c=(c-1)^2.
\]
This simplifies to
\[
c^2-3c+1=0,
\]
whose roots are
\[
c=\frac{3\pm\sqrt5}{2}.
\]
Since \(m>n\) for large \(n\), we need \(c>1\), so the relevant root is
\[
c=\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}.
\]

Because the inequality holds for \(m\) below this asymptotic threshold and fails above it, the maximal such \(m=M(n)\) satisfies
\[
\frac{M(n)}{n}\to \frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}.
\]

As a verification, substitute \(c=\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}\) into \(c^2-3c+1\):
\[
\left(\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}\right)^2-3\left(\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}\right)+1=0,
\]
so this constant is indeed the correct limiting cutoff.

problem: Given a positive integer $n$, let $M(n)$ be the largest integer $m$ such that \[ \binom{m}{n-1} > \binom{m-1}{n}. \] Evaluate \[ \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{M(n)}{n}. \]
alternative_solution:
Set
\[
k=m-n.
\]
Then \(m=n+k\), and the inequality becomes
\[
\binom{n+k}{n-1}>\binom{n+k-1}{n}.
\]
Assume \(k\ge 0\), since otherwise \(m<n\) and the left side is \(0\).

Now compute each side relative to \(\binom{n+k-1}{n-1}\):
\[
\binom{n+k}{n-1}=\frac{n+k}{k+1}\binom{n+k-1}{n-1},
\]
while
\[
\binom{n+k-1}{n}=\frac{k}{n}\binom{n+k-1}{n-1}.
\]
Therefore the inequality is equivalent to
\[
\frac{n+k}{k+1}>\frac{k}{n}.
\]
Multiplying through by \(n(k+1)\), we get
\[
n(n+k)>k(k+1),
\]
or
\[
n^2+nk-k^2-k>0.
\]

We now look for the largest \(k\) for which this holds. Since \(k\) should grow linearly with \(n\), write
\[
k=tn.
\]
Then
\[
n^2+n(tn)-t^2n^2-tn>0,
\]
so
\[
(1+t-t^2)n^2-tn>0.
\]
Dividing by \(n^2\),
\[
1+t-t^2-\frac{t}{n}>0.
\]
Hence, for large \(n\), the sign is governed by
\[
1+t-t^2>0.
\]
The positive root of
\[
t^2-t-1=0
\]
is
\[
t=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}.
\]
So asymptotically,
\[
\frac{k}{n}\to \frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}.
\]
Since \(m=n+k\),
\[
\frac{M(n)}{n}=1+\frac{k}{n}\to 1+\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}=\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}.
\]

For verification, if \(t=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\), then
\[
1+t-t^2=0,
\]
so this is exactly the boundary value separating eventual truth and falsity of the inequality.

problem: Given a positive integer $n$, let $M(n)$ be the largest integer $m$ such that \[ \binom{m}{n-1} > \binom{m-1}{n}. \] Evaluate \[ \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{M(n)}{n}. \]
alternative_solution:
Consider the function
\[
f_n(m)=\binom{m}{n-1}-\binom{m-1}{n}.
\]
We seek the largest integer \(m\) such that \(f_n(m)>0\).

For \(m\ge n\), factor both binomial coefficients in terms of factorials:
\[
\binom{m}{n-1}=\frac{m!}{(n-1)!(m-n+1)!},
\qquad
\binom{m-1}{n}=\frac{(m-1)!}{n!(m-n-1)!}.
\]
Multiply the inequality by the positive quantity \(n!(n-1)!(m-n+1)!(m-n-1)!\), obtaining
\[
mn!(m-n-1)!>(m-n+1)(m-n)(m-1)!.
\]
After cancellation, this reduces to
\[
mn>(m-n+1)(m-n).
\]
Expanding,
\[
mn>m^2-2mn+n^2+m-n,
\]
so
\[
0>m^2-3mn+m+n^2-n.
\]

Now divide by \(n^2\), and set
\[
x_n=\frac{m}{n}.
\]
Then the inequality becomes
\[
0>x_n^2-3x_n+\frac{x_n}{n}+1-\frac1n.
\]
For large \(n\), this is close to
\[
x^2-3x+1<0.
\]
The roots of the limiting quadratic are
\[
x=\frac{3\pm\sqrt5}{2}.
\]
Since the quadratic opens upward, the inequality holds when
\[
\frac{3-\sqrt5}{2}<x<\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}.
\]
But here \(m\ge n\), so \(x\ge 1\), and the relevant upper endpoint is
\[
\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}.
\]
Therefore the largest admissible \(m\) satisfies
\[
\frac{M(n)}{n}\to \frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}.
\]

As a verification, let
\[
r=\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}.
\]
Then
\[
r^2-3r+1=0,
\]
so \(r\) is exactly the upper boundary of the limiting interval where the inequality is true.

problem: Given a positive integer $n$, let $M(n)$ be the largest integer $m$ such that \[ \binom{m}{n-1} > \binom{m-1}{n}. \] Evaluate \[ \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{M(n)}{n}. \]
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
\binom{m}{n-1}>\binom{m-1}{n}.
\]
We first rewrite each binomial coefficient using Pascal’s identity:
\[
\binom{m}{n-1}=\binom{m-1}{n-1}+\binom{m-1}{n-2}.
\]
Hence the inequality becomes
\[
\binom{m-1}{n-1}+\binom{m-1}{n-2}>\binom{m-1}{n}.
\]
For \(m\) large enough that all three terms are nonzero, divide through by \(\binom{m-1}{n-1}\). Using
\[
\frac{\binom{m-1}{n-2}}{\binom{m-1}{n-1}}=\frac{n-1}{m-n+1},
\qquad
\frac{\binom{m-1}{n}}{\binom{m-1}{n-1}}=\frac{m-n}{n},
\]
we get
\[
1+\frac{n-1}{m-n+1}>\frac{m-n}{n}.
\]
Now multiply by \(n(m-n+1)\):
\[
n(m-n+1)+n(n-1)>(m-n)(m-n+1).
\]
Since
\[
n(m-n+1)+n(n-1)=nm,
\]
this simplifies to
\[
nm>(m-n)(m-n+1).
\]
Set \(x=\frac{m}{n}\). Then
\[
m-n=n(x-1),
\]
so after dividing by \(n^2\),
\[
x>\left(x-1\right)\left(x-1+\frac1n\right).
\]
As \(n\to\infty\), the boundary between truth and falsity approaches the equation
\[
x=(x-1)^2.
\]
Thus
\[
x^2-3x+1=0,
\]
whose roots are
\[
x=\frac{3\pm\sqrt5}{2}.
\]
Since \(M(n)\) is the largest \(m\) satisfying the inequality, the relevant limiting ratio is the larger root:
\[
\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}.
\]

To justify this rigorously, define
\[
f_n(x)=x-\left(x-1\right)\left(x-1+\frac1n\right).
\]
Then \(f_n(x)\to x-(x-1)^2\) uniformly on bounded intervals, and the largest \(x\) for which \(f_n(x)>0\) tends to the larger root of \(x-(x-1)^2=0\). Since \(M(n)\) is exactly the largest integer \(m\) with \(m/n\) in that region, it follows that \(M(n)/n\) tends to the same limit.

problem: Given a positive integer $n$, let $M(n)$ be the largest integer $m$ such that \[ \binom{m}{n-1} > \binom{m-1}{n}. \] Evaluate \[ \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{M(n)}{n}. \]
alternative_solution:
We compare the two sides directly through factorials:
\[
\binom{m}{n-1}=\frac{m!}{(n-1)!(m-n+1)!},
\qquad
\binom{m-1}{n}=\frac{(m-1)!}{n!(m-n-1)!}.
\]
Thus
\[
\binom{m}{n-1}>\binom{m-1}{n}
\]
is equivalent to
\[
\frac{m!}{(n-1)!(m-n+1)!}>\frac{(m-1)!}{n!(m-n-1)!}.
\]
After cancellation,
\[
mn>(m-n+1)(m-n).
\]
Now expand the right-hand side:
\[
mn>m^2-2mn+n^2+m-n.
\]
So
\[
0>m^2-3mn+n^2+m-n.
\]
Divide by \(n^2\), and let
\[
x_n=\frac{m}{n}.
\]
Then
\[
0>x_n^2-3x_n+1+\frac{x_n}{n}-\frac1n.
\]
For the extremal value \(m=M(n)\), the quantity \(x_n\) should lie near the largest root of the limiting quadratic
\[
x^2-3x+1=0.
\]
Indeed, if \(x>\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}\), then \(x^2-3x+1>0\), so for all sufficiently large \(n\),
\[
x^2-3x+1+\frac{x}{n}-\frac1n>0,
\]
and hence no \(m\) with \(m/n\ge x\) can satisfy the inequality. On the other hand, if \(x<\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}\) but still larger than the smaller root, then
\[
x^2-3x+1<0,
\]
so for all sufficiently large \(n\),
\[
x^2-3x+1+\frac{x}{n}-\frac1n<0,
\]
and values of \(m\) with \(m/n\) near \(x\) do satisfy the inequality.

Therefore the maximal possible ratio \(M(n)/n\) approaches the larger root of
\[
x^2-3x+1=0,
\]
namely
\[
x=\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}.
\]

problem: Given a positive integer $n$, let $M(n)$ be the largest integer $m$ such that \[ \binom{m}{n-1} > \binom{m-1}{n}. \] Evaluate \[ \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{M(n)}{n}. \]
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
a_m=\binom{m}{n-1},\qquad b_m=\binom{m-1}{n}.
\]
We want the largest integer \(m\) such that \(a_m>b_m\).

A convenient way is to compare successive values in \(m\). Compute
\[
\frac{a_m}{b_m}
=
\frac{\binom{m}{n-1}}{\binom{m-1}{n}}
=
\frac{mn}{(m-n+1)(m-n)}.
\]
So \(a_m>b_m\) exactly when
\[
\frac{mn}{(m-n+1)(m-n)}>1,
\]
that is,
\[
mn>(m-n+1)(m-n).
\]

Now write
\[
m=cn
\]
with \(c>1\). Then
\[
mn=c n^2,
\]
while
\[
(m-n+1)(m-n)=\bigl((c-1)n+1\bigr)\bigl((c-1)n\bigr)
=(c-1)^2n^2+(c-1)n.
\]
Hence the inequality becomes
\[
cn^2>(c-1)^2n^2+(c-1)n.
\]
Divide by \(n^2\):
\[
c>(c-1)^2+\frac{c-1}{n}.
\]
As \(n\to\infty\), this approaches
\[
c>(c-1)^2.
\]
The threshold value of \(c\) is therefore determined by
\[
c=(c-1)^2,
\]
or
\[
c^2-3c+1=0.
\]
Thus
\[
c=\frac{3\pm\sqrt5}{2}.
\]
Since the inequality holds for \(c\) between the two roots and \(M(n)\) is the largest such \(m\), the limiting ratio \(M(n)/n\) is the larger root:
\[
\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}.
\]

To make the last step precise, let \(r=\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}\). If \(c>r\), then \(c-(c-1)^2<0\), so for all sufficiently large \(n\),
\[
c-(c-1)^2-\frac{c-1}{n}<0,
\]
and thus \(m=cn\) cannot satisfy the inequality. If \(c<r\) but above the smaller root, then the left side is eventually positive, so such \(m\) do satisfy it. Therefore the maximal admissible ratio tends to \(r\).

problem: The 30 edges of a regular icosahedron are distinguished by labeling them $1,2,\dots,30$. How many different ways are there to paint each edge red, white, or blue such that each of the 20 triangular faces of the icosahedron has two edges of the same color and a third edge of a different color?
alternative_solution:
Let the three colors be identified with the elements of \(\mathbb F_3=\{0,1,2\}\).  
For a face with edge-colors \(a,b,c\in \mathbb F_3\), the condition “two edges have the same color and the third has a different color” is equivalent to saying that \(a,b,c\) are not all equal and not all distinct. Over \(\mathbb F_3\), this happens exactly when
\[
a+b+c\neq 0.
\]
Indeed:

- if \(a=b=c\), then \(a+b+c=3a=0\);
- if \(a,b,c\) are all distinct, then \(\{a,b,c\}=\{0,1,2\}\), so \(a+b+c=0\);
- if exactly two are equal, say \(a=b\neq c\), then \(a+b+c=2a+c\neq 0\), since \(c\neq a\).

So the desired colorings are precisely those for which, on every face, the sum of the three incident edge-values is nonzero.

Now orient each face arbitrarily and consider the linear map
\[
T:\mathbb F_3^{E}\to \mathbb F_3^{F},
\qquad
(Tx)_f=\sum_{e\subset f} x_e,
\]
where \(E\) is the set of 30 edges and \(F\) the set of 20 faces.

We will compute the rank of \(T\) by showing that the rows are linearly independent. Suppose there is a relation
\[
\sum_{f\in F} \lambda_f\, (\text{row of }f)=0,
\qquad \lambda_f\in\mathbb F_3.
\]
Looking at a particular edge \(e\), which belongs to exactly two faces \(f\) and \(g\), the coefficient of \(x_e\) in this linear combination is
\[
\lambda_f+\lambda_g,
\]
so the relation implies
\[
\lambda_f+\lambda_g=0
\]
whenever \(f\) and \(g\) share an edge.

Thus adjacent faces in the dual graph must receive opposite labels. But the dual graph of the icosahedron is the graph of the dodecahedron, and this graph contains a 5-cycle. Along such a cycle the labels must alternate
\[
\lambda,\,-\lambda,\,\lambda,\,-\lambda,\,\lambda,
\]
and returning to the start forces \(\lambda=-\lambda\). Since the characteristic is \(3\), this gives \(2\lambda=0\), hence \(\lambda=0\). Therefore every \(\lambda_f=0\), so the rows are independent.

Hence \(T\) has rank \(20\), so \(T\) is surjective. Therefore
\[
\dim \ker T = 30-20=10.
\]
Each vector in \(\mathbb F_3^F\) with every component nonzero has exactly \(3^{10}\) preimages. There are
\[
2^{20}
\]
such vectors, since each of the 20 face-components may be either \(1\) or \(2\).

Therefore the number of desired edge-colorings is
\[
2^{20}\cdot 3^{10}.
\]

As a check, this count is an integer power product coming from \(20\) independent nonzero face-sums and a \(10\)-dimensional kernel:
\[
2^{20}\cdot 3^{10}=1048576\cdot 59049=61917364224.
\]

problem: The 30 edges of a regular icosahedron are distinguished by labeling them $1,2,\dots,30$. How many different ways are there to paint each edge red, white, or blue such that each of the 20 triangular faces of the icosahedron has two edges of the same color and a third edge of a different color?
alternative_solution:
Again encode the colors by \(\mathbb F_3\). For each face, let the sum of its three edge-values be taken in \(\mathbb F_3\). As in the reference solution, a face satisfies the condition “two edges of one color and the third of another color” exactly when this sum is nonzero.

So we want to count the edge-labelings whose face-sum vector lies in
\[
(\mathbb F_3^\times)^{20},
\]
where \(\mathbb F_3^\times=\{1,2\}\).

Define
\[
T:\mathbb F_3^E\to \mathbb F_3^F,
\qquad
(Tx)_f=\sum_{e\subset f}x_e.
\]
We shall determine \(\dim(\operatorname{im} T)\) by computing the orthogonal complement of the image.

Let \(y=(y_f)_{f\in F}\in \mathbb F_3^F\). Then \(y\) is orthogonal to \(\operatorname{im} T\) iff
\[
\sum_{f\in F} y_f (Tx)_f=0
\quad\text{for all }x\in \mathbb F_3^E.
\]
Expanding,
\[
\sum_{f\in F} y_f (Tx)_f
=
\sum_{f\in F} y_f \sum_{e\subset f} x_e
=
\sum_{e\in E} x_e \sum_{f\ni e} y_f.
\]
Each edge belongs to exactly two faces, say \(f\) and \(g\), so this becomes
\[
\sum_{e\in E} x_e (y_f+y_g).
\]
For this to vanish for all \(x\), we must have
\[
y_f+y_g=0
\]
for every pair of adjacent faces \(f,g\).

Thus a vector orthogonal to the image is exactly a face-labeling by \(\mathbb F_3\) that changes sign across every edge of the dual graph. In other words, it is a proper 2-coloring of the dual graph, scaled by an element of \(\mathbb F_3\).

But the dual graph of the icosahedron is the dodecahedral graph, and that graph is not bipartite because it has 5-cycles. Hence the only such labeling is the zero labeling. Therefore
\[
(\operatorname{im} T)^\perp=\{0\},
\]
so \(\operatorname{im} T=\mathbb F_3^F\). Thus \(T\) is surjective.

Since \(\dim \mathbb F_3^E=30\) and \(\dim \mathbb F_3^F=20\), rank-nullity gives
\[
\dim\ker T=30-20=10.
\]
Now every admissible face-sum vector has all 20 entries nonzero, so there are
\[
2^{20}
\]
choices for it. Each one has exactly
\[
3^{10}
\]
preimages under \(T\).

Hence the total number of colorings is
\[
2^{20}3^{10}.
\]

For verification, note that the orthogonal-complement argument shows there are no hidden linear constraints on the 20 face-sums, so the count really is \(2^{20}\) times the kernel size:
\[
2^{20}3^{10}=61917364224.
\]

problem: The 30 edges of a regular icosahedron are distinguished by labeling them $1,2,\dots,30$. How many different ways are there to paint each edge red, white, or blue such that each of the 20 triangular faces of the icosahedron has two edges of the same color and a third edge of a different color?
alternative_solution:
We again identify the colors with \(\mathbb F_3\). For a triangular face with edge-values \(a,b,c\), the allowed pattern is “exactly two equal,” and over \(\mathbb F_3\) this is equivalent to
\[
a+b+c\in\{1,2\},
\]
i.e. the face-sum is nonzero.

Thus we are led to the linear map
\[
T:\mathbb F_3^{30}\to \mathbb F_3^{20},
\]
sending an edge-coloring to the list of the 20 face-sums. The desired colorings are exactly those whose image under \(T\) has no zero coordinate.

So it remains to show that every prescribed face-sum vector occurs, and then compute the kernel size.

We use a spanning-tree construction on the dual graph. The dual graph of the icosahedron has 20 vertices (one per face) and is connected. Choose any spanning tree on these 20 vertices. Since a tree on 20 vertices has 19 edges, this selects 19 edges of the dual graph. Each such dual edge corresponds to a unique edge of the icosahedron; call these 19 primal edges \(e_1,\dots,e_{19}\).

Set all other 11 edge-values equal to \(0\). We claim that by assigning values to \(e_1,\dots,e_{19}\), we can realize any face-sum vector whose total sum over all 20 faces is \(0\).
