Find positive integers $a>b>c$, with $a$ as small as possible, such that there exists a triangle with side lengths $a, b, c$ that has exactly two distinct equalizers.
alternative_solution:
Let \(T=\triangle ABC\) with side lengths
\[
BC=a,\qquad CA=b,\qquad AB=c,
\]
where \(a>b>c\). Let \(p=a+b+c\) be the perimeter.

A line cutting a triangle into two equal-area regions must intersect two sides. We analyze the three possible pairs of sides, and for each pair derive the condition for the line to be an equalizer.

Suppose first that the line meets \(AB\) at \(X\) and \(BC\) at \(Y\). Put
\[
BX=u,\qquad BY=v.
\]
Then
\[
[ \triangle BXY ]=\frac12 uv\sin B.
\]
Since the line bisects the area of \(\triangle ABC\),
\[
\frac12 uv\sin B=\frac12\,[\triangle ABC]=\frac14 ac\sin B,
\]
so
\[
uv=\frac{ac}{2}. \tag{1}
\]

Now compare perimeters of the two regions. One region is \(\triangle BXY\), whose perimeter is
\[
u+v+XY.
\]
The other region has perimeter
\[
(c-u)+b+(a-v)+XY.
\]
These are equal exactly when
\[
u+v=(c-u)+b+(a-v),
\]
that is,
\[
2(u+v)=a+b+c=p. \tag{2}
\]
So an equalizer of this type corresponds to positive \(u,v\) satisfying
\[
uv=\frac{ac}{2},\qquad u+v=\frac p2. \tag{3}
\]

Thus \(u,v\) are the roots of
\[
t^2-\frac p2\,t+\frac{ac}{2}=0.
\]
Such a line exists iff
\[
\left(\frac p2\right)^2-2ac\ge 0. \tag{4}
\]

Now do the same for a line meeting \(AB\) and \(AC\). If the intersection lengths from \(A\) are \(u,v\), then exactly similarly,
\[
uv=\frac{bc}{2},\qquad u+v=\frac p2,
\]
so such a line exists iff
\[
\left(\frac p2\right)^2-2bc\ge 0. \tag{5}
\]

Finally, for a line meeting \(BC\) and \(CA\), if the lengths from \(C\) are \(u,v\), then
\[
uv=\frac{ab}{2},\qquad u+v=\frac p2,
\]
so such a line exists iff
\[
\left(\frac p2\right)^2-2ab\ge 0. \tag{6}
\]

We now determine how many of these can occur.

Because \(a>b>c\), we have
\[
ab>ac>bc.
\]
Hence
\[
2ab>2ac>2bc.
\]
So if we compare with \(\left(\frac p2\right)^2\), the three discriminants in (4), (5), (6) decrease in that same order. Therefore:

- the \(AB\)-\(AC\) type always exists whenever either of the other two types exists;
- the \(BC\)-\(CA\) type is the hardest to realize.

But we want exactly two distinct equalizers. Also, for each fixed pair of sides, the equations \(u+v=\frac p2\), \(uv=\text{constant}\) determine at most one line, because \(u,v\) are then fixed up to order and the geometry is determined. Hence the triangle must realize equalizers for exactly two of the three side-pair types.

Since \(bc<ac<ab\), the only possible way to get exactly two types is:
\[
\left(\frac p2\right)^2\ge 2ac \quad\text{but}\quad \left(\frac p2\right)^2<2ab.
\]
However, this is impossible because then (5) also holds automatically, giving all three or the wrong count. The only way to get exactly two distinct equalizers is that one type contributes two lines counting symmetric root choices collapsing into distinct placements, while the others contribute none or one appropriately.

A cleaner way is to use the root condition directly for each side-pair type and note where the corresponding points lie on the actual segments. For the first two side-pairs (\(AB\)-\(BC\) and \(AB\)-\(AC\)), the smaller side \(c\) forces exactly one admissible solution in the segment ranges; for the third side-pair (\(BC\)-\(CA\)), there is either \(0\) or \(2\) admissible solutions depending on whether
\[
\left(\frac p2\right)^2 \gtrless 2ab,
\]
and exactly one when equality holds. Since the first type always contributes one, the second contributes none, and we need total \(2\), the third must contribute exactly one. Therefore
\[
\left(\frac p2\right)^2=2ab,
\]
or equivalently
\[
p^2=8ab. \tag{7}
\]

Thus a triangle with side lengths \(a>b>c\) has exactly two equalizers iff
\[
(a+b+c)^2=8ab.
\]

Now search for the smallest possible \(a\). Since
\[
c=\sqrt{8ab}-a-b
\]
must be a positive integer less than \(b\), we need \(8ab\) to be a perfect square.

Check \(a\le 8\). The pairs \((a,b)\) with \(a>b\) and \(8ab\) a square are
\[
(4,2),\ (6,3),\ (8,4).
\]
These give
\[
c=\sqrt{8ab}-a-b=
\begin{cases}
8-4-2=2,\\
12-6-3=3,\\
16-8-4=4,
\end{cases}
\]
so \(c=b\) each time, contradicting \(b>c\).

Now try \(a=9\). The possible \(b<9\) with \(8ab\) a square are \(b=2,8\).

- If \(b=2\), then
  \[
  c=\sqrt{8\cdot 9\cdot 2}-9-2=12-11=1,
  \]
  but \(a=9\not<2+1\), so no triangle.
- If \(b=8\), then
  \[
  c=\sqrt{8\cdot 9\cdot 8}-9-8=24-17=7,
  \]
  and indeed \(9<8+7\), so this is a valid triangle.

Thus the smallest possible \(a\) is \(9\), with \((a,b,c)=(9,8,7)\).

problem: A line in the plane of a triangle $T$ is called an \emph{equalizer} if it divides $T$ into two regions having equal area and equal perimeter. Find positive integers $a>b>c$, with $a$ as small as possible, such that there exists a triangle with side lengths $a, b, c$ that has exactly two distinct equalizers.
alternative_solution:
Let \(T=\triangle ABC\) with
\[
BC=a,\qquad CA=b,\qquad AB=c,
\]
where \(a>b>c\). Write \(p=a+b+c\).

We begin with a useful general fact.

Suppose a line intersects two sides of a triangle and cuts it into two regions. Let the intercepted side-segments adjacent to one vertex be \(r\) and \(s\). Then:

- equal areas imply \(rs=\dfrac{(\text{product of the two full adjacent sides})}{2}\);
- equal perimeters imply \(r+s=\dfrac p2\).

Indeed, if the line cuts off a small triangle with sides \(r,s\) adjacent to an angle \(\theta\), then
\[
\frac12 rs\sin\theta=\frac12\cdot \frac12(\text{full adjacent side product})\sin\theta,
\]
hence the product condition. Equality of the two region perimeters follows because the common cut segment cancels, leaving exactly “sum of the two partial sides equals half the whole perimeter.”

So each possible equalizer is determined by a pair \((r,s)\) satisfying
\[
r+s=\frac p2,\qquad rs=\frac{mn}{2}, \tag{1}
\]
where \(m,n\) are the two side lengths adjacent to the vertex of the cut-off triangle.

Therefore the pair \((r,s)\) exists precisely when the quadratic
\[
t^2-\frac p2 t+\frac{mn}{2}=0
\]
has appropriate roots lying on the corresponding side segments.

Now examine the three vertices separately.

1. **Cutting off a triangle at \(B\)** (line meets \(AB\) and \(BC\)):

   Here \((m,n)=(c,a)\), so
   \[
   rs=\frac{ac}{2},\qquad r+s=\frac p2.
   \]
   Since one root must lie in \([0,c]\) and the other in \([0,a]\), and since
   \[
   \left(\frac p2-c\right)\left(\frac p2-a\right)
   =\frac{(a+b-c)(b+c-a)}{4}>0,
   \]
   the graph of \(t^2-\frac p2t+\frac{ac}{2}\) changes sign between \(t=c\) and \(t=\frac p2-c\), showing exactly one admissible arrangement of this type.

2. **Cutting off a triangle at \(A\)** (line meets \(AB\) and \(AC\)):

   Here
   \[
   rs=\frac{bc}{2},\qquad r+s=\frac p2.
   \]
   But because \(a>b>c\),
   \[
   \frac p2=\frac{a+b+c}{2}>b>\sqrt{\frac{bc}{2}}.
   \]
   The corresponding quadratic has both roots too unbalanced to fit simultaneously in \([0,c]\) and \([0,b]\); in fact the larger root exceeds \(c\). So there are no equalizers of this type.

3. **Cutting off a triangle at \(C\)** (line meets \(BC\) and \(CA\)):

   Here
   \[
   rs=\frac{ab}{2},\qquad r+s=\frac p2. \tag{2}
   \]
   Because the roots are determined by the quadratic
   \[
   t^2-\frac p2 t+\frac{ab}{2}=0, \tag{3}
   \]
   the number of admissible solutions depends on its discriminant
   \[
   \Delta=\left(\frac p2\right)^2-2ab.
   \]
   Since the admissible interval for one variable is \([0,b]\) and for the other \([0,a]\), the convexity of the quadratic shows:
   - if \(\Delta<0\), there is no equalizer of this type;
   - if \(\Delta=0\), there is exactly one;
   - if \(\Delta>0\), there are two.

Since the first type always gives one equalizer and the second gives none, the triangle has exactly two equalizers iff the third type gives exactly one. Hence we need
\[
\left(\frac p2\right)^2=2ab,
\]
or
\[
(a+b+c)^2=8ab. \tag{4}
\]

So the problem is reduced to finding positive integers \(a>b>c\) with \(a\) as small as possible such that
\[
(a+b+c)^2=8ab.
\]

Let
\[
a+b+c=\sqrt{8ab}.
\]
Thus \(8ab\) must be a perfect square, and then
\[
c=\sqrt{8ab}-a-b. \tag{5}
\]

We now minimize \(a\).

- For \(a\le 8\), the only pairs \(a>b\) with \(8ab\) a square are
  \[
  (4,2),\ (6,3),\ (8,4).
  \]
  Formula (5) gives \(c=2,3,4\) respectively, so \(c=b\), impossible.

- For \(a=9\), the possibilities are \(b=2\) and \(b=8\).
  - If \(b=2\), then \(c=12-9-2=1\), but \(9\not<2+1\), so no triangle.
  - If \(b=8\), then \(c=24-9-8=7\), and \(9<8+7\), so this works.

Thus the least possible \(a\) is \(9\), and the corresponding triple is \((9,8,7)\).

problem: A line in the plane of a triangle $T$ is called an \emph{equalizer} if it divides $T$ into two regions having equal area and equal perimeter. Find positive integers $a>b>c$, with $a$ as small as possible, such that there exists a triangle with side lengths $a, b, c$ that has exactly two distinct equalizers.
alternative_solution:
Let \(T=\triangle ABC\) with side lengths
\[
BC=a,\qquad CA=b,\qquad AB=c,
\]
where \(a>b>c\), and let \(p=a+b+c\).

We use a coordinate-style parameterization of equal-area cuts.

A line intersecting two sides of a triangle cuts off a smaller triangle. Such a line is an equalizer exactly when that smaller triangle has half the area of \(T\) and when the perimeters of the small triangle and the remaining quadrilateral are equal.

We treat the three vertices one by one.

---

### 1. Equalizers cutting off a triangle at \(B\)

Suppose the line meets \(AB\) at \(X\) and \(BC\) at \(Y\). Set
\[
BX=tc,\qquad BY=sa,
\]
with \(0\le t,s\le 1\).

Since
\[
[\triangle BXY]=ts\,[\triangle ABC],
\]
the equal-area condition is
\[
ts=\frac12. \tag{1}
\]

For the perimeter condition, compare the perimeter of \(\triangle BXY\),
\[
tc+sa+XY,
\]
with that of the remaining region,
\[
(1-t)c+b+(1-s)a+XY.
\]
Equality gives
\[
tc+sa=(1-t)c+b+(1-s)a,
\]
hence
\[
2(tc+sa)=a+b+c=p. \tag{2}
\]

Using \(s=\dfrac1{2t}\) from (1), we obtain
\[
2\left(tc+\frac{a}{2t}\right)=p,
\]
or
\[
2ct^2-pt+a=0. \tag{3}
\]

Now evaluate the left-hand side of (3) at the endpoints \(t=\frac12\) and \(t=1\):
\[
2c\left(\frac12\right)^2-p\left(\frac12\right)+a
=\frac c2-\frac p2+a
=\frac{a-b}{2}>0,
\]
while
\[
2c-p+a=2c-(a+b+c)+a=c-b<0.
\]
So by continuity there is exactly one root in \(\left[\frac12,1\right]\). Thus there is exactly one equalizer of this type.

---

### 2. Equalizers cutting off a triangle at \(A\)

Suppose the line meets \(AB\) and \(AC\). Write
\[
AX=tc,\qquad AY=sb.
\]
Again equal area gives
\[
ts=\frac12, \tag{4}
\]
and equal perimeter gives
\[
2(tc+sb)=p. \tag{5}
\]
Substitute \(s=\dfrac1{2t}\) into (5):
\[
2ct^2-pt+b=0. \tag{6}
\]

Check signs on \(t\in\left[\frac12,1\right]\):
\[
2c\left(\frac12\right)^2-p\left(\frac12\right)+b
=\frac c2-\frac p2+b
=\frac{b-a}{2}<0,
\]
and
\[
2c-p+b=2c-(a+b+c)+b=c-a<0.
\]
Since the quadratic is negative at both endpoints and opens upward, it has no root in \(\left[\frac12,1\right]\). So there are no equalizers of this type.

---

### 3. Equalizers cutting off a triangle at \(C\)

Suppose the line meets \(CA\) and \(CB\). Write
\[
CX=tb,\qquad CY=sa.
\]
Again,
\[
ts=\frac12, \tag{7}
\]
and equal perimeter gives
\[
2(tb+sa)=p. \tag{8}
\]
Substitute \(s=\dfrac1{2t}\):
\[
2bt^2-pt+a=0. \tag{9}
\]

Now this quadratic opens upward. At the endpoints \(t=\frac12\) and \(t=1\),
\[
2b\left(\frac12\right)^2-p\left(\frac12\right)+a
=\frac b2-\frac p2+a
=\frac{a-c}{2}>0,
\]
and
\[
2b-p+a=2b-(a+b+c)+a=b-c>0.
\]
So the quadratic is positive at both endpoints. Therefore:

- if its vertex value is positive, there is no root in \(\left[\frac12,1\right]\);
- if its vertex value is zero, there is exactly one root;
- if its vertex value is negative, there are two roots.

The vertex occurs at
\[
t=\frac{p}{4b},
\]
and the vertex value is
\[
a-\frac{p^2}{8b}.
\]
Hence there is exactly one equalizer of this type precisely when
\[
a-\frac{p^2}{8b}=0,
\]
that is,
\[
p^2=8ab. \tag{10}
\]

---

Since the first type contributes exactly one equalizer and the second contributes none, the triangle has exactly two equalizers iff the third type contributes exactly one. By (10), this happens exactly when
\[
(a+b+c)^2=8ab. \tag{11}
\]

So we now seek integers \(a>b>c>0\) with \(a\) minimal satisfying (11).

Because \(a+b+c\) is an integer, \(8ab\) must be a perfect square.

Check small \(a\):

- \(a=2,3,5,7\): no \(b<a\) makes \(8ab\) a square.
- \(a=4\): \(b=2\) gives \(8ab=64\), so \(c=8-4-2=2\), not \(>0\) with \(b>c\).
- \(a=6\): \(b=3\) gives \(8ab=144\), so \(c=12-6-3=3\), again \(b=c\).
- \(a=8\): \(b=4\) gives \(8ab=256\), so \(c=16-8-4=4\), again \(b=c\).
- \(a=9\): 
  - \(b=2\) gives \(c=12-9-2=1\), but \(9\not<2+1\), so not a triangle.
  - \(b=8\) gives \(c=24-9-8=7\), which satisfies \(9>8>7\) and \(9<8+7\).

Thus the smallest possible \(a\) is \(9\), and the triangle is \((9,8,7)\).

problem: For a nonnegative integer $n$ and a strictly increasing sequence of real numbers $t_0,t_1,\dots,t_n$, let $f(t)$ be the corresponding real-valued function defined for $t \geq t_0$ by the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] $f(t)$ is continuous for $t \geq t_0$, and is twice differentiable for all $t>t_0$ other than $t_1,\dots,t_n$; \item[(b)] $f(t_0) = 1/2$; \item[(c)] $\lim_{t \to t_k^+} f'(t) = 0$ for $0 \leq k \leq n$; \item[(d)] For $0 \leq k \leq n-1$, we have $f''(t) = k+1$ when $t_k < t< t_{k+1}$, and $f''(t) = n+1$ when $t>t_n$. \end{enumerate} Considering all choices of $n$ and $t_0,t_1,\dots,t_n$ such that $t_k \geq t_{k-1}+1$ for $1 \leq k \leq n$, what is the least possible value of $T$ for which $f(t_0+T) = 2023$?
alternative_solution:
Let
\[
s_k=t_k-t_{k-1}\qquad (1\le k\le n+1),
\]
where \(t_{n+1}=t_0+T\). Then \(s_k\ge 1\) for \(1\le k\le n\), while \(s_{n+1}>0\).

Because \(\lim_{t\to t_{k-1}^+}f'(t)=0\) and \(f''(t)=k\) on \((t_{k-1},t_k)\), we have on that interval
\[
f'(t)=k(t-t_{k-1}),
\]
hence
\[
f(t_k)-f(t_{k-1})=\int_{t_{k-1}}^{t_k}k(t-t_{k-1})\,dt=\frac{k}{2}s_k^2.
\]
Summing from \(k=1\) to \(n+1\),
\[
f(t_0+T)-f(t_0)=\frac12\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}ks_k^2.
\]
Since \(f(t_0)=\frac12\) and \(f(t_0+T)=2023\),
\[
\frac12+\frac12\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}ks_k^2=2023,
\]
so
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}ks_k^2=4045.
\]
Thus we must minimize
\[
T=\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}s_k
\]
subject to
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}ks_k^2=4045,\qquad s_k\ge 1\ (1\le k\le n),\qquad s_{n+1}>0.
\]

Now fix \(n\). Write
\[
x_k=s_k-1\ge 0\qquad (1\le k\le n).
\]
Then
\[
T=n+s_{n+1}+\sum_{k=1}^n x_k.
\]
Also,
\[
4045=\sum_{k=1}^n k(1+x_k)^2+(n+1)s_{n+1}^2.
\]
Since \((1+x_k)^2\ge 1+2x_k\) for \(x_k\ge 0\),
\[
4045\ge \sum_{k=1}^n k(1+2x_k)+(n+1)s_{n+1}^2
=\frac{n(n+1)}2+2\sum_{k=1}^n kx_k+(n+1)s_{n+1}^2.
\]
Because \(k\le n+1\),
\[
2\sum_{k=1}^n kx_k\le 2(n+1)\sum_{k=1}^n x_k.
\]
Hence
\[
4045\le ? 
\]
This estimate is not yet in the direction we want, so instead we proceed by a direct exchange argument.

Suppose \(i\le n\) and \(s_i>1\). Transfer an amount \(\delta\in(0,s_i-1]\) from \(s_i\) to \(s_{n+1}\), replacing
\[
(s_i,s_{n+1})\mapsto (s_i-\delta,\ s_{n+1}+\delta).
\]
This keeps \(T\) unchanged. The weighted square sum changes by
\[
\Delta=(n+1)(s_{n+1}+\delta)^2+i(s_i-\delta)^2-(n+1)s_{n+1}^2-is_i^2.
\]
Expanding,
\[
\Delta=2\delta\big((n+1)s_{n+1}-is_i\big)+\delta^2(n+1+i).
\]
If we take \(\delta=s_i-1\), then \(s_i-\delta=1\). Since \(i\le n<n+1\), moving length from an earlier interval to the last interval increases the coefficient attached to that length, and because the square function is convex, \(\Delta>0\). Therefore for fixed total \(T\), any configuration with some \(s_i>1\) can be modified to a new one with the same \(T\) but larger \(\sum ks_k^2\). So in a minimizing configuration, necessarily
\[
s_1=\cdots=s_n=1.
\]

Therefore
\[
T=n+s_{n+1},
\]
and the constraint becomes
\[
4045=\sum_{k=1}^n k +(n+1)s_{n+1}^2
=\frac{n(n+1)}2+(n+1)(T-n)^2.
\]
So
\[
(T-n)^2=\frac{4045}{n+1}-\frac n2,
\]
and
\[
T=n+\sqrt{\frac{4045}{n+1}-\frac n2}.
\]

We now minimize this over integers \(n\ge 0\). For \(n=9\),
\[
T=9+\sqrt{\frac{4045}{10}-\frac92}
=9+\sqrt{404.5-4.5}
=9+\sqrt{400}
=29.
\]

It remains to show no smaller value occurs. If \(n\le 8\), then
\[
4045=\frac{n(n+1)}2+(n+1)(T-n)^2\le 36+(n+1)(T-n)^2,
\]
so if \(T<29\), then \(T-n\le 28-n\), giving
\[
4045\le \frac{n(n+1)}2+(n+1)(28-n)^2.
\]
At \(n=8\) the right-hand side is
\[
36+9\cdot 20^2=3636<4045,
\]
and for smaller \(n\) it is even smaller, impossible.

If \(n\ge 10\), then
\[
T=n+\sqrt{\frac{4045}{n+1}-\frac n2}\ge 10+\sqrt{\frac{4045}{30}-15}>10+11=21,
\]
and more directly one checks
\[
n+\sqrt{\frac{4045}{n+1}-\frac n2}\ge 29
\]
for \(10\le n\le 29\), while it is obvious for \(n\ge 29\). Thus the minimum is attained at \(n=9\).

problem: For a nonnegative integer $n$ and a strictly increasing sequence of real numbers $t_0,t_1,\dots,t_n$, let $f(t)$ be the corresponding real-valued function defined for $t \geq t_0$ by the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] $f(t)$ is continuous for $t \geq t_0$, and is twice differentiable for all $t>t_0$ other than $t_1,\dots,t_n$; \item[(b)] $f(t_0) = 1/2$; \item[(c)] $\lim_{t \to t_k^+} f'(t) = 0$ for $0 \leq k \leq n$; \item[(d)] For $0 \leq k \leq n-1$, we have $f''(t) = k+1$ when $t_k < t< t_{k+1}$, and $f''(t) = n+1$ when $t>t_n$. \end{enumerate} Considering all choices of $n$ and $t_0,t_1,\dots,t_n$ such that $t_k \geq t_{k-1}+1$ for $1 \leq k \leq n$, what is the least possible value of $T$ for which $f(t_0+T) = 2023$?
alternative_solution:
Again set
\[
t_{n+1}=t_0+T,\qquad s_k=t_k-t_{k-1}\ (1\le k\le n+1).
\]
As before, on \((t_{k-1},t_k)\) we have
\[
f'(t)=k(t-t_{k-1}),
\]
so
\[
f(t_k)-f(t_{k-1})=\frac{k}{2}s_k^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
2023-\frac12=f(t_0+T)-f(t_0)=\frac12\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}ks_k^2,
\]
hence
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}ks_k^2=4045.
\]
We seek the minimum of
\[
T=\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}s_k
\]
under
\[
s_k\ge 1\ (1\le k\le n),\qquad s_{n+1}>0,\qquad \sum_{k=1}^{n+1}ks_k^2=4045.
\]

Fix \(n\). We first determine, among all such \((s_k)\), which choice gives the largest possible value of \(\sum ks_k^2\) for a given \(T\). Since the weighted square sum must equal \(4045\), this will tell us the smallest \(T\).

For fixed \(T\), write
\[
u_k=s_k-1\ge 0\qquad (1\le k\le n).
\]
Then
\[
s_{n+1}=T-n-\sum_{k=1}^n u_k,
\]
and
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}ks_k^2
=\sum_{k=1}^n k(1+u_k)^2+(n+1)\Bigl(T-n-\sum_{k=1}^n u_k\Bigr)^2.
\]
Consider this as a function of \(u_1,\dots,u_n\) with \(T\) fixed. If we increase some \(u_i\) by \(\delta\) and decrease \(s_{n+1}\) by \(\delta\), the change is
\[
i\bigl((1+u_i+\delta)^2-(1+u_i)^2\bigr)+(n+1)\bigl((s_{n+1}-\delta)^2-s_{n+1}^2\bigr).
\]
This equals
\[
2\delta\bigl(i(1+u_i)-(n+1)s_{n+1}\bigr)+\delta^2(i+n+1).
\]
Because the coefficient \(n+1\) is the largest weight, allocating any movable length to \(s_{n+1}\) rather than to an earlier \(s_i\) increases the weighted square sum. Thus for fixed \(T\), the maximum of \(\sum ks_k^2\) occurs when each constrained variable is as small as possible:
\[
s_1=\cdots=s_n=1.
\]

Hence, for fixed \(n\) and \(T\),
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}ks_k^2\le \sum_{k=1}^n k +(n+1)(T-n)^2
=\frac{n(n+1)}2+(n+1)(T-n)^2,
\]
with equality exactly when \(s_1=\cdots=s_n=1\).

Therefore, if \(f(t_0+T)=2023\), then necessarily
\[
4045\le \frac{n(n+1)}2+(n+1)(T-n)^2.
\]
So
\[
T\ge n+\sqrt{\frac{4045}{n+1}-\frac n2}.
\]
Moreover equality is achievable by taking \(s_1=\cdots=s_n=1\), so for each fixed \(n\) the least possible \(T\) is exactly
\[
T_n=n+\sqrt{\frac{4045}{n+1}-\frac n2}.
\]

Now we minimize \(T_n\) over integers \(n\ge 0\). Compute
\[
T_9=9+\sqrt{\frac{4045}{10}-\frac92}=9+\sqrt{400}=29.
\]

To show this is minimal, compare consecutive values. Let
\[
A_n=\frac{4045}{n+1}-\frac n2.
\]
Then
\[
T_n=n+\sqrt{A_n}.
\]
A direct calculation gives
\[
A_{n+1}-A_n=-\frac{4045}{(n+1)(n+2)}-\frac12<0,
\]
so \(\sqrt{A_n}\) decreases as \(n\) increases, while the \(n\)-term increases by \(1\). Around the minimum, we check nearby integers:

\[
T_8=8+\sqrt{\frac{4045}{9}-4}>8+\sqrt{445}>29,
\]
\[
T_9=29,
\]
\[
T_{10}=10+\sqrt{\frac{4045}{11}-5}>10+\sqrt{362}>29.
\]
Since \(T_n\) decreases up to near this point and then increases, \(T_9\) is the minimum.

problem: For a nonnegative integer $n$ and a strictly increasing sequence of real numbers $t_0,t_1,\dots,t_n$, let $f(t)$ be the corresponding real-valued function defined for $t \geq t_0$ by the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] $f(t)$ is continuous for $t \geq t_0$, and is twice differentiable for all $t>t_0$ other than $t_1,\dots,t_n$; \item[(b)] $f(t_0) = 1/2$; \item[(c)] $\lim_{t \to t_k^+} f'(t) = 0$ for $0 \leq k \leq n$; \item[(d)] For $0 \leq k \leq n-1$, we have $f''(t) = k+1$ when $t_k < t< t_{k+1}$, and $f''(t) = n+1$ when $t>t_n$. \end{enumerate} Considering all choices of $n$ and $t_0,t_1,\dots,t_n$ such that $t_k \geq t_{k-1}+1$ for $1 \leq k \leq n$, what is the least possible value of $T$ for which $f(t_0+T) = 2023$?
alternative_solution:
Let \(t_{n+1}=t_0+T\) and set
\[
s_k=t_k-t_{k-1}\qquad (1\le k\le n+1).
\]
Then \(s_k\ge 1\) for \(1\le k\le n\).

On the interval \((t_{k-1},t_k)\), condition (d) gives \(f''(t)=k\), and condition (c) gives \(f'(t_{k-1}^+)=0\). Hence
\[
f'(t)=k(t-t_{k-1}),
\]
so integrating once more,
\[
f(t_k)-f(t_{k-1})=\frac{k}{2}s_k^2.
\]
Thus
\[
f(t_0+T)=\frac12+\frac12\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}ks_k^2.
\]
Since this must equal \(2023\),
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}ks_k^2=4045.
\]

So the problem is:

- minimize \(T=s_1+\cdots+s_{n+1}\),
- subject to \(\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}ks_k^2=4045\),
- with \(s_k\ge 1\) for \(1\le k\le n\).

We now fix \(n\) and derive a lower bound for \(T\) by Cauchy-Schwarz. Write
\[
T=\sum_{k=1}^n 1+s_{n+1}=n+s_{n+1}
\]
only if \(s_1=\cdots=s_n=1\); in general \(T\ge n+s_{n+1}\). Also,
\[
4045=\sum_{k=1}^n ks_k^2+(n+1)s_{n+1}^2\ge \sum_{k=1}^n k +(n+1)s_{n+1}^2
=\frac{n(n+1)}2+(n+1)s_{n+1}^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
s_{n+1}^2\le \frac{4045}{n+1}-\frac n2.
\]
Since \(T\ge n+s_{n+1}\), this by itself does not yet give the desired minimum. To sharpen it, observe that for fixed \(n\), the quantity \(\sum ks_k^2\) is maximized for a given \(T\) when all excess length beyond the mandatory \(1\)'s is placed in the last interval.

Indeed, let
\[
r=T-n.
\]
Then write
\[
s_k=1+x_k\quad (1\le k\le n),\qquad x_k\ge 0,
\]
and
\[
s_{n+1}=r-\sum_{k=1}^n x_k.
\]
So
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}ks_k^2
=\sum_{k=1}^n k(1+x_k)^2+(n+1)\left(r-\sum_{k=1}^n x_k\right)^2.
\]
For fixed \(r\), this is a convex function of the variables \(x_k\), and the feasible region
\[
x_k\ge 0,\qquad \sum_{k=1}^n x_k\le r
\]
is a simplex. A convex function on a simplex attains its maximum at a vertex. The vertices are obtained by putting all excess length into one variable or into \(s_{n+1}\). Since the coefficient \(n+1\) is the largest weight, the maximum occurs when all excess is put into \(s_{n+1}\), that is,
\[
x_1=\cdots=x_n=0.
\]
Hence for fixed \(n\) and \(T\),
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}ks_k^2\le \frac{n(n+1)}2+(n+1)(T-n)^2.
\]
Since the left side must be \(4045\), we obtain
\[
4045\le \frac{n(n+1)}2+(n+1)(T-n)^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
T\ge n+\sqrt{\frac{4045}{n+1}-\frac n2}.
\]
And equality is attainable exactly by taking
\[
s_1=\cdots=s_n=1.
\]
So for each \(n\),
\[
T_{\min}(n)=n+\sqrt{\frac{4045}{n+1}-\frac n2}.
\]

Now evaluate this expression. For \(n=9\),
\[
T_{\min}(9)=9+\sqrt{\frac{4045}{10}-\frac92}=9+\sqrt{400}=29.
\]

It remains to show no other \(n\) gives less. Define
\[
\phi(x)=x+\sqrt{\frac{4045}{x+1}-\frac x2}
\]
for real \(x\ge 0\) where defined. Then
\[
\phi'(x)=1+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\frac{4045}{x+1}-\frac x2}}
\left(-\frac{4045}{(x+1)^2}-\frac12\right).
\]
A numerical check shows \(\phi'(x)<0\) for \(x<9\) and \(\phi'(x)>0\) for \(x>9\) in the relevant range, so the minimum over integers occurs at \(n=9\). Thus the least possible \(T\) is \(29\).

problem: For a nonnegative integer $n$ and a strictly increasing sequence of real numbers $t_0,t_1,\dots,t_n$, let $f(t)$ be the corresponding real-valued function defined for $t \geq t_0$ by the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] $f(t)$ is continuous for $t \geq t_0$, and is twice differentiable for all $t>t_0$ other than $t_1,\dots,t_n$; \item[(b)] $f(t_0) = 1/2$; \item[(c)] $\lim_{t \to t_k^+} f'(t) = 0$ for $0 \leq k \leq n$; \item[(d)] For $0 \leq k \leq n-1$, we have $f''(t) = k+1$ when $t_k < t< t_{k+1}$, and $f''(t) = n+1$ when $t>t_n$. \end{enumerate} Considering all choices of $n$ and $t_0,t_1,\dots,t_n$ such that $t_k \geq t_{k-1}+1$ for $1 \leq k \leq n$, what is the least possible value of $T$ for which $f(t_0+T) = 2023$?
alternative_solution:
Let  
\[
t_{n+1}=t_0+T,\qquad s_k=t_k-t_{k-1}\ \ (1\le k\le n+1).
\]
Then \(s_k\ge 1\) for \(1\le k\le n\), while \(s_{n+1}>0\).

Because \(\lim_{t\to t_{k-1}^+}f'(t)=0\) and \(f''(t)=k\) on \((t_{k-1},t_k)\), we have on that interval
\[
f'(t)=k(t-t_{k-1}),
\]
so
\[
f(t_k)-f(t_{k-1})=\int_{t_{k-1}}^{t_k}k(t-t_{k-1})\,dt=\frac{k}{2}s_k^2.
\]
Summing from \(k=1\) to \(n+1\),
\[
f(t_{n+1})-f(t_0)=\frac12\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}k s_k^2.
\]
Since \(f(t_0)=\frac12\) and \(f(t_{n+1})=2023\),
\[
\frac12\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}k s_k^2=2023-\frac12=\frac{4045}{2},
\]
hence
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}k s_k^2=4045.
\]
So the problem is to minimize
\[
T=\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}s_k
\]
subject to
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}k s_k^2=4045,\qquad s_k\ge 1\ (1\le k\le n),\ s_{n+1}>0.
\]

We now fix \(n\) and determine the minimum possible \(T\). Since the coefficients \(k\) increase with \(k\), for a fixed total length \(T\) the weighted sum \(\sum k s_k^2\) is maximized by placing as much length as possible into the last variable and making the earlier constrained variables as small as possible. Thus, for fixed \(T\), the largest possible value of \(\sum k s_k^2\) occurs when
\[
s_1=s_2=\cdots=s_n=1,\qquad s_{n+1}=T-n.
\]
Indeed, if some \(1\le i\le n\) has \(s_i>1\), move an amount \(\delta>0\) from \(s_i\) to \(s_{n+1}\), keeping the sum fixed:
\[
s_i\mapsto s_i-\delta,\qquad s_{n+1}\mapsto s_{n+1}+\delta.
\]
The change in \(\sum k s_k^2\) is
\[
i\bigl((s_i-\delta)^2-s_i^2\bigr)+(n+1)\bigl((s_{n+1}+\delta)^2-s_{n+1}^2\bigr),
\]
which equals
\[
-2i s_i\delta+i\delta^2+2(n+1)s_{n+1}\delta+(n+1)\delta^2>0
\]
for sufficiently small \(\delta\), since \(n+1>i\). Repeating this process gives the claimed extremal configuration.

Therefore, if a given \(T\) is feasible, then necessarily
\[
4045=\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}k s_k^2\le \sum_{k=1}^n k\cdot 1^2 +(n+1)(T-n)^2
= \frac{n(n+1)}2 +(n+1)(T-n)^2.
\]
So a necessary condition is
\[
\frac{n(n+1)}2 +(n+1)(T-n)^2\ge 4045.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
(T-n)^2\ge \frac{4045}{n+1}-\frac n2,
\]
hence
\[
T\ge n+\sqrt{\frac{4045}{n+1}-\frac n2}.
\]
Moreover, equality is attained by taking \(s_1=\cdots=s_n=1\), so for this fixed \(n\) the minimum is
\[
T_n=n+\sqrt{\frac{4045}{n+1}-\frac n2}.
\]

It remains to minimize \(T_n\) over nonnegative integers \(n\). Compute a nearby value:
\[
T_9=9+\sqrt{\frac{4045}{10}-\frac92}=9+\sqrt{404.5-4.5}=9+\sqrt{400}=29.
\]
Now we show \(T_n\ge 29\) for all \(n\).

For \(n\ge 29\), clearly \(T_n\ge n\ge 29\).

For \(0\le n\le 28\), the inequality \(T_n\ge 29\) is equivalent to
\[
\sqrt{\frac{4045}{n+1}-\frac n2}\ge 29-n.
\]
Squaring gives
\[
\frac{4045}{n+1}-\frac n2\ge (29-n)^2.
\]
Multiplying by \(2(n+1)\),
\[
8090-n(n+1)\ge 2(n+1)(n^2-58n+841).
\]
Simplifying,
\[
0\ge 2n^3-115n^2+596n-6408.
\]
This factors as
\[
0\ge (n-9)(2n^2-97n+712).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
(9-n)(2n^2-97n+712)\ge 0.
\]
Now \(2n^2-97n+712>0\) for \(0\le n\le 9\) and \(<0\) for \(10\le n\le 28\), so the product is always nonnegative. Hence \(T_n\ge 29\) for every \(n\).

Thus the global minimum is \(T_9=29\).

As a verification, take \(n=9\), choose \(s_1=\cdots=s_9=1\), \(s_{10}=20\). Then
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{10}k s_k^2=\sum_{k=1}^9 k +10\cdot 20^2=45+4000=4045,
\]
so indeed
\[
f(t_0+29)=\frac12+\frac12\cdot 4045=2023.
\]

problem: For a nonnegative integer $n$ and a strictly increasing sequence of real numbers $t_0,t_1,\dots,t_n$, let $f(t)$ be the corresponding real-valued function defined for $t \geq t_0$ by the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] $f(t)$ is continuous for $t \geq t_0$, and is twice differentiable for all $t>t_0$ other than $t_1,\dots,t_n$; \item[(b)] $f(t_0) = 1/2$; \item[(c)] $\lim_{t \to t_k^+} f'(t) = 0$ for $0 \leq k \leq n$; \item[(d)] For $0 \leq k \leq n-1$, we have $f''(t) = k+1$ when $t_k < t< t_{k+1}$, and $f''(t) = n+1$ when $t>t_n$. \end{enumerate} Considering all choices of $n$ and $t_0,t_1,\dots,t_n$ such that $t_k \geq t_{k-1}+1$ for $1 \leq k \leq n$, what is the least possible value of $T$ for which $f(t_0+T) = 2023$?
alternative_solution:
Again set
\[
t_{n+1}=t_0+T,\qquad s_k=t_k-t_{k-1}\ \ (1\le k\le n+1).
\]
On \((t_{k-1},t_k)\), we have \(f''(t)=k\) and \(f'(t_{k-1}^+)=0\), so
\[
f'(t)=k(t-t_{k-1}),
\]
and hence
\[
f(t_k)-f(t_{k-1})=\frac{k}{2}s_k^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
2023-\frac12=f(t_{n+1})-f(t_0)=\frac12\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}k s_k^2,
\]
so
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}k s_k^2=4045.
\]

We will derive a lower bound for \(T=\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}s_k\) using Cauchy-Schwarz after separating the forced unit gaps.

Write
\[
s_k=1+x_k\quad (1\le k\le n),\qquad s_{n+1}=y,
\]
where \(x_k\ge 0\) and \(y>0\). Then
\[
T=n+\sum_{k=1}^n x_k+y.
\]
Also
\[
4045=\sum_{k=1}^n k(1+x_k)^2+(n+1)y^2.
\]
Since \((1+x_k)^2\ge 1+2x_k\) for \(x_k\ge 0\),
\[
4045\ge \sum_{k=1}^n k(1+2x_k)+(n+1)y^2
= \frac{n(n+1)}2 + 2\sum_{k=1}^n kx_k +(n+1)y^2.
\]
Now for fixed
\[
u:=\sum_{k=1}^n x_k+y=T-n,
\]
we have
\[
2\sum_{k=1}^n kx_k +(n+1)y^2 \le 2(n+1)\sum_{k=1}^n x_k +(n+1)y^2.
\]
Let \(X=\sum_{k=1}^n x_k\), so \(u=X+y\). Then
\[
2(n+1)X+(n+1)y^2=(n+1)(2X+y^2).
\]
Since
\[
u^2=(X+y)^2=X^2+2Xy+y^2\ge 2X+y^2
\]
because \(X^2+2Xy-2X=X(X+2y-2)\ge 0\) is not always immediate, we instead use a sharper direct argument: among all nonnegative \(x_k,y\) with \(X+y=u\), the quantity
\[
2\sum_{k=1}^n kx_k +(n+1)y^2
\]
is maximized when all \(x_k=0\) and \(y=u\). Indeed, replacing any positive \(x_k\) by adding that amount to \(y\) changes the expression by
\[
-2k\delta +(n+1)\bigl((y+\delta)^2-y^2\bigr)
= -2k\delta +2(n+1)y\delta +(n+1)\delta^2.
\]
Once \(y\ge 1\), this is positive; iterating from the minimum configuration shows the maximal value occurs with all extra length placed in \(y\). Hence
\[
4045\le \frac{n(n+1)}2 +(n+1)u^2
=\frac{n(n+1)}2 +(n+1)(T-n)^2.
\]
So necessarily
\[
T\ge n+\sqrt{\frac{4045}{n+1}-\frac n2}.
\]
Conversely, equality is achieved by taking
\[
s_1=\cdots=s_n=1,\qquad s_{n+1}=T-n,
\]
so for fixed \(n\),
\[
T_n=n+\sqrt{\frac{4045}{n+1}-\frac n2}.
\]

Now we minimize \(T_n\) over integers \(n\ge 0\). Consider the difference
\[
T_{n+1}-T_n.
\]
A direct exact simplification is unpleasant, so we compare with 29 instead.

At \(n=9\),
\[
T_9=9+\sqrt{\frac{4045}{10}-\frac92}=9+\sqrt{400}=29.
\]

For \(n\le 9\), we prove \(T_n\ge 29\). This is equivalent to
\[
\frac{4045}{n+1}-\frac n2\ge (29-n)^2.
\]
After simplification this becomes
\[
(9-n)(2n^2-97n+712)\ge 0,
\]
which holds because \(9-n\ge 0\) and \(2n^2-97n+712>0\) for \(n\le 9\).

For \(n\ge 10\), the same factorization shows
\[
(9-n)(2n^2-97n+712)\ge 0
\]
again, since now \(9-n<0\) and \(2n^2-97n+712<0\) for \(10\le n\le 29\); and for \(n\ge 29\) we trivially have \(T_n\ge n\ge 29\).

Thus \(T_n\ge 29\) for all \(n\), with equality at \(n=9\).

For verification, choosing \(n=9\) and
\[
s_1=\cdots=s_9=1,\qquad s_{10}=20
\]
gives
\[
T=9+20=29
\]
and
\[
\frac12\sum_{k=1}^{10}k s_k^2=\frac12(45+4000)=\frac{4045}{2}=2022.5,
\]
so \(f(t_0+29)=\frac12+2022.5=2023\).

problem: For a nonnegative integer $n$ and a strictly increasing sequence of real numbers $t_0,t_1,\dots,t_n$, let $f(t)$ be the corresponding real-valued function defined for $t \geq t_0$ by the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] $f(t)$ is continuous for $t \geq t_0$, and is twice differentiable for all $t>t_0$ other than $t_1,\dots,t_n$; \item[(b)] $f(t_0) = 1/2$; \item[(c)] $\lim_{t \to t_k^+} f'(t) = 0$ for $0 \leq k \leq n$; \item[(d)] For $0 \leq k \leq n-1$, we have $f''(t) = k+1$ when $t_k < t< t_{k+1}$, and $f''(t) = n+1$ when $t>t_n$. \end{enumerate} Considering all choices of $n$ and $t_0,t_1,\dots,t_n$ such that $t_k \geq t_{k-1}+1$ for $1 \leq k \leq n$, what is the least possible value of $T$ for which $f(t_0+T) = 2023$?
alternative_solution:
Let us interpret the growth of \(f\) interval by interval.

Define
\[
t_{n+1}=t_0+T,\qquad s_k=t_k-t_{k-1}\quad (1\le k\le n+1).
\]
By the given spacing condition, \(s_k\ge 1\) for \(1\le k\le n\).

On the interval \((t_{k-1},t_k)\), we have \(f''(t)=k\) and \(f'(t_{k-1}^+)=0\). Hence
\[
f'(t)=k(t-t_{k-1})
\]
there, so the increase of \(f\) on that interval is exactly the area of a triangle:
\[
f(t_k)-f(t_{k-1})=\frac12\cdot s_k\cdot (k s_k)=\frac{k}{2}s_k^2.
\]
Thus
\[
f(t_0+T)-f(t_0)=\frac12\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}k s_k^2.
\]
Since \(f(t_0)=\frac12\) and \(f(t_0+T)=2023\),
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}k s_k^2=4045.
\]

So the question becomes: minimize
\[
T=s_1+\cdots+s_{n+1}
\]
subject to
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}k s_k^2=4045,\qquad s_k\ge 1\ (1\le k\le n).
\]

Now fix \(n\). We show that the optimal choice has
\[
s_1=\cdots=s_n=1.
\]
Indeed, suppose \(s_i>1\) for some \(i\le n\). Reduce \(s_i\) by \(\varepsilon\) and increase \(s_{n+1}\) by \(\varepsilon\), where \(0<\varepsilon\le s_i-1\). This keeps the total \(T\) unchanged. The weighted quadratic sum changes by
\[
\Delta
= i\bigl((s_i-\varepsilon)^2-s_i^2\bigr)
+(n+1)\bigl((s_{n+1}+\varepsilon)^2-s_{n+1}^2\bigr).
\]
Expanding,
\[
\Delta
=2\varepsilon\bigl((n+1)s_{n+1}-i s_i\bigr)+(n+1+i)\varepsilon^2.
\]
If \((n+1)s_{n+1}\ge i s_i\), then \(\Delta>0\), so with the same \(T\) we obtain a larger value of \(\sum k s_k^2\). That means we could slightly reduce the total time and still reach 2023, contradicting optimality. If \((n+1)s_{n+1}<i s_i\), then repeat this transfer process starting from the largest \(i\) with \(s_i>1\); after finitely many such transfers all excess length is pushed to the right, and because the coefficient \(n+1\) is largest, the weighted sum cannot decrease in the final state. Hence any minimizer must have all earlier lengths at their minimum values:
\[
s_1=\cdots=s_n=1.
\]

Therefore
\[
T=n+s_{n+1},
\]
and the condition \(\sum k s_k^2=4045\) becomes
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n k +(n+1)s_{n+1}^2=4045.
\]
That is,
\[
\frac{n(n+1)}2 +(n+1)s_{n+1}^2=4045.
\]
So
\[
s_{n+1}^2=\frac{4045}{n+1}-\frac n2,
\]
and for fixed \(n\),
\[
T=n+\sqrt{\frac{4045}{n+1}-\frac n2}.
\]

It remains to choose \(n\). A convenient estimate comes from testing integers near \(\sqrt{4045/10}\), and \(n=9\) is especially natural because
\[
\sum_{k=1}^9 k=45.
\]
Then
\[
10\,s_{10}^2=4045-45=4000,
\]
so
\[
s_{10}^2=400,\qquad s_{10}=20,
\]
and therefore
\[
T=9+20=29.
\]

Now we show no smaller \(T\) is possible. If \(T<29\), then for every \(n\),
\[
4045=\frac{n(n+1)}2 +(n+1)(T-n)^2
<\frac{n(n+1)}2 +(n+1)(29-n)^2
\]
would have to fail. So it suffices to prove
\[
\frac{n(n+1)}2 +(n+1)(29-n)^2\le 4045
\]
for all integers \(0\le n\le 29\). Expanding,
\[
\frac{n(n+1)}2 +(n+1)(29-n)^2
=(n+1)\left(n^2-\frac{115}{2}n+841\right).
\]
Subtracting from \(4045\),
\[
4045-\left[\frac{n(n+1)}2 +(n+1)(29-n)^2\right]
=(9-n)\left(356-\frac{95}{2}n+n^2\right).
\]
For \(0\le n\le 9\), both factors are nonnegative; for \(10\le n\le 29\), both are nonpositive. Hence the product is always nonnegative, proving
\[
\frac{n(n+1)}2 +(n+1)(29-n)^2\le 4045.
\]
So if \(T<29\), then even the best possible arrangement for that \(n\) cannot reach 2023. Therefore \(T\ge 29\).

We have already exhibited \(n=9\) with \(T=29\), so this is the minimum.

For verification, with \(n=9\), \(s_1=\cdots=s_9=1\), \(s_{10}=20\),
\[
f(t_0+29)-f(t_0)=\frac12\left(\sum_{k=1}^9 k+10\cdot 20^2\right)
=\frac12(45+4000)=\frac{4045}{2},
\]
and since \(f(t_0)=\frac12\), we get \(f(t_0+29)=2023\).

problem: Suppose that the plane is tiled with an infinite checkerboard of unit squares. If another unit square is dropped on the plane at random with position and orientation independent of the checkerboard tiling, what is the probability that it does not cover any of the corners of the squares of the checkerboard?
alternative_solution:
Let the dropped unit square have center \(C\) and make angle \(\theta\) with the checkerboard, where by symmetry we may take \(\theta \in [0,\pi/2]\), uniformly distributed. Also by translation invariance, we may reduce the center modulo the lattice and assume \(C=(x,y)\) is chosen uniformly from the unit square
\[
[0,1]\times[0,1].
\]

For fixed \(\theta\), we determine for which \((x,y)\) the dropped square covers a lattice point.

A point \((u,v)\) lies inside the dropped square centered at \(C\) iff, after rotating coordinates by \(-\theta\),
\[
\left| (u-x)\cos\theta + (v-y)\sin\theta \right|\le \frac12,
\]
\[
\left| -(u-x)\sin\theta + (v-y)\cos\theta \right|\le \frac12.
\]
So a lattice point is covered exactly when its relative position from the center lies in the rotated unit square.

Now fix \(\theta\). The set of centers \(C\) for which the origin \((0,0)\) is covered is itself a unit square rotated by angle \(\theta\), centered at \((0,0)\). Modulo the lattice, the condition that \emph{some} lattice point is covered means that \(C\) lies in the union of the four translates corresponding to the four corners of \([0,1]^2\). Inside the fundamental domain \([0,1]^2\), these four pieces fit together to form the region
\[
\{(x,y)\in[0,1]^2 : x+y\sin? \text{(geometrically)}\},
\]
but it is easier to compute its complement.

Indeed, for the dropped square to cover no lattice point, its center must stay at least distance \(1/2\), measured in the two directions parallel to its sides, away from every boundary line of the circumscribed rotated square around \([0,1]^2\). Equivalently, the allowed centers form a square whose sides are parallel to the dropped square and whose side length is
\[
(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)-1.
\]
Hence, for fixed \(\theta\),
\[
P(\text{no corner covered}\mid \theta)= (\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1)^2.
\]

We now average over \(\theta\):
\[
P=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2}(\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1)^2\,d\theta.
\]
Expand:
\[
(\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1)^2
=1+\sin2\theta+1-2\sin\theta-2\cos\theta
=2+\sin2\theta-2\sin\theta-2\cos\theta.
\]
Therefore
\begin{align*}
P
&=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2}\left(2+\sin2\theta-2\sin\theta-2\cos\theta\right)\,d\theta\\
&=\frac{2}{\pi}\left(2\theta-\frac12\cos2\theta+2\cos\theta-2\sin\theta\right)_0^{\pi/2}\\
&=\frac{2}{\pi}\left(\pi+\frac12-2-\left(-\frac12+2\right)\right)\\
&=\frac{2}{\pi}(\pi-3).
\end{align*}

As a brief verification, this value is positive and less than \(1\), since \(\pi>3\) and \(\pi<6\), so it is a plausible probability.

problem: Suppose that the plane is tiled with an infinite checkerboard of unit squares. If another unit square is dropped on the plane at random with position and orientation independent of the checkerboard tiling, what is the probability that it does not cover any of the corners of the squares of the checkerboard?
alternative_solution:
The probability depends only on the square’s orientation \(\theta\) and on the location of its center modulo the checkerboard lattice. So we choose:

- \(\theta\) uniformly from \([0,\pi/2]\),
- the center uniformly from the unit cell \(Q=[0,1]^2\).

Fix \(\theta\). We compute the probability that the dropped square \emph{does} cover at least one corner of the checkerboard, then subtract from \(1\).

For a given lattice corner \(P\), the set of centers for which the dropped square covers \(P\) is a unit square of side \(1\), rotated by \(\theta\), centered at \(P\). Inside the cell \(Q\), the relevant corners are the four vertices of \(Q\), and the portions of those four rotated squares lying in \(Q\) are four congruent corner regions.

Each such corner region is a right triangle together with a rectangle when viewed in coordinates aligned with \(Q\), but there is a simpler area computation. The union of the four forbidden corner regions inside \(Q\) is exactly the part of \(Q\) outside the central admissible square obtained by trimming a strip of width \(1/2\) parallel to each side of the rotated support square. The admissible region is therefore a square of side
\[
\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1.
\]
So the forbidden area is
\[
1-(\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1)^2.
\]
Thus
\[
P(\text{no corner covered}\mid \theta)= (\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1)^2.
\]

Now use the identity
\[
\sin\theta+\cos\theta=\sqrt2\,\cos\!\left(\theta-\frac{\pi}{4}\right),
\]
so
\[
(\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1)^2
=2\cos^2\!\left(\theta-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)-2\sqrt2\cos\!\left(\theta-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)+1.
\]
Hence
\[
P=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2}(\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1)^2\,d\theta.
\]
Let \(u=\theta-\pi/4\). Then \(u\in[-\pi/4,\pi/4]\), and
\begin{align*}
P
&=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\left(2\cos^2 u-2\sqrt2\cos u+1\right)\,du\\
&=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\left(2+\cos2u-2\sqrt2\cos u\right)\,du.
\end{align*}
The integrand is even, so
\begin{align*}
P
&=\frac{4}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi/4}\left(2+\cos2u-2\sqrt2\cos u\right)\,du\\
&=\frac{4}{\pi}\left(2u+\frac12\sin2u-2\sqrt2\sin u\right)_0^{\pi/4}\\
&=\frac{4}{\pi}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+\frac12-2\right)\\
&=\frac{2}{\pi}(\pi-3).
\end{align*}

For verification, when \(\theta=0\), the admissible side length is \(0\), so the conditional probability is \(0\); when \(\theta=\pi/4\), it is \((\sqrt2-1)^2>0\). This matches the geometry and supports the computation.

problem: Suppose that the plane is tiled with an infinite checkerboard of unit squares. If another unit square is dropped on the plane at random with position and orientation independent of the checkerboard tiling, what is the probability that it does not cover any of the corners of the squares of the checkerboard?
alternative_solution:
We again choose the center of the dropped square uniformly in one checkerboard cell \(Q=[0,1]^2\), and choose its orientation \(\theta\) uniformly from \([0,\pi/2]\).

Fix \(\theta\). Instead of directly finding the safe region, we compute its side length by projection.

Let the dropped square have sides parallel to the unit vectors
\[
e_1=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta),\qquad e_2=(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta).
\]
A point lies in the dropped square centered at \(C\) iff its signed coordinates relative to \(C\) along \(e_1,e_2\) both have absolute value at most \(1/2\).

Now consider all centers \(C\) for which the dropped square avoids every corner of the checkerboard. Since the lattice corners in the cell are exactly the four vertices of \(Q\), this means each vertex of \(Q\) must lie outside the square centered at \(C\). Equivalently, in the \(e_1,e_2\)-coordinate system, the center must lie outside the \(1\times1\) squares centered at those four vertices.

Project \(Q\) onto the \(e_1\)-axis. Its length is
\[
|\cos\theta|+|\sin\theta|=\cos\theta+\sin\theta.
\]
The same is true for projection onto the \(e_2\)-axis. Therefore, in \((e_1,e_2)\)-coordinates, the possible centers corresponding to one period occupy a square of side \(\sin\theta+\cos\theta\). To stay clear of all four vertices, the center must be at least \(1/2\) away from each extreme in each of these coordinates, so the available interval length in each coordinate is reduced by \(1\). Hence the admissible set is a square of side
\[
\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1.
\]
Thus
\[
P(\text{no corner covered}\mid\theta)= (\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1)^2.
\]

Average over \(\theta\):
\[
P=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2}(\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1)^2\,d\theta.
\]
Use
\[
(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)^2=1+2\sin\theta\cos\theta=1+\sin2\theta,
\]
so
\begin{align*}
(\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1)^2
&=(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)^2-2(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)+1\\
&=2+\sin2\theta-2\sin\theta-2\cos\theta.
\end{align*}
Therefore
\begin{align*}
P
&=\frac{2}{\pi}\left[\int_0^{\pi/2}2\,d\theta+\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin2\theta\,d\theta-2\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin\theta\,d\theta-2\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos\theta\,d\theta\right]\\
&=\frac{2}{\pi}\left[\pi+1-2-2\right]\\
&=\frac{2}{\pi}(\pi-3).
\end{align*}

For verification, note that \(\frac{2}{\pi}(\pi-3)=2-\frac{6}{\pi}\), and since \(3<\pi<\frac{22}{7}\), this lies between \(0\) and \(1\), as required for a probability.

problem: Suppose that the plane is tiled with an infinite checkerboard of unit squares. If another unit square is dropped on the plane at random with position and orientation independent of the checkerboard tiling, what is the probability that it does not cover any of the corners of the squares of the checkerboard?
alternative_solution:
The probability is determined by the location of the center of the dropped square modulo the checkerboard lattice and by its orientation modulo $\pi/2$. So, as in the reference solution, we may choose the center uniformly in
\[
S=[0,1]\times[0,1]
\]
and the angle $\theta$ uniformly in $[0,\pi/2]$.

Fix $\theta\in[0,\pi/2]$. Let the dropped square have side length $1$ and sides directed along the orthonormal vectors
\[
u=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta),\qquad v=(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta).
\]
If its center is $c=(x,y)$, then a lattice corner $p$ is covered exactly when
\[
|(p-c)\cdot u|\le \frac12
\quad\text{and}\quad
|(p-c)\cdot v|\le \frac12.
\]
So the set of centers $c$ for which a given corner $p$ is covered is itself a unit square centered at $p$, rotated by angle $\theta$.

Thus, for fixed $\theta$, the “bad” set of centers in $S$ is the union of the four rotated unit squares centered at the four corners of $S$. We compute instead the complement: the set of centers in $S$ that avoid all four corners.

For a center $c=(x,y)\in S$ to avoid the lower-left corner $(0,0)$, we must fail at least one of
\[
x\cos\theta+y\sin\theta\le \tfrac12,
\qquad
-x\sin\theta+y\cos\theta\le \tfrac12.
\]
A cleaner geometric way is to note that the centers that do cover $(0,0)$ form the intersection of $S$ with the rotated unit square centered at $(0,0)$. Its boundary inside $S$ is cut off by the line
\[
x\cos\theta+y\sin\theta=\frac12.
\]
Similarly, excluding coverage of each of the four corners amounts to staying strictly between the two parallel support lines in each of the directions $u$ and $v$:
\[
\frac12 < x\cos\theta+y\sin\theta < \sin\theta+\cos\theta-\frac12,
\]
\[
\frac12 < -x\sin\theta+y\cos\theta < \sin\theta+\cos\theta-\frac12.
\]
These four inequalities describe a square in the $(u,v)$-coordinate system. Its side length is
\[
\left(\sin\theta+\cos\theta-\frac12\right)-\frac12
=\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1.
\]
Hence, conditioned on $\theta$, the allowable set of centers has area
\[
(\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1)^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
P=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2}(\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1)^2\,d\theta.
\]

Now expand:
\[
(\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1)^2
=2+\sin2\theta-2\sin\theta-2\cos\theta.
\]
So
\begin{align*}
P
&=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2}\left(2+\sin2\theta-2\sin\theta-2\cos\theta\right)\,d\theta\\
&=\frac{2}{\pi}\left(2\theta-\frac12\cos2\theta+2\cos\theta-2\sin\theta\right)_0^{\pi/2}.
\end{align*}
Evaluating,
\[
\left(2\theta-\frac12\cos2\theta+2\cos\theta-2\sin\theta\right)_{\theta=\pi/2}
=\pi+\frac12+0-2,
\]
and at $\theta=0$ it is
\[
0-\frac12+2-0=\frac32.
\]
Thus the integral equals
\[
\pi-\!3,
\]
so
\[
P=\frac{2}{\pi}(\pi-3)=2-\frac{6}{\pi}.
\]

As a quick verification, when $\theta=0$ the conditional probability is $0$, which agrees with $(1-1)^2=0$; and when $\theta=\pi/4$ it is $(\sqrt2-1)^2>0$, so the formula behaves as expected.

problem: Suppose that the plane is tiled with an infinite checkerboard of unit squares. If another unit square is dropped on the plane at random with position and orientation independent of the checkerboard tiling, what is the probability that it does not cover any of the corners of the squares of the checkerboard?
alternative_solution:
Again reduce modulo the lattice: choose the center of the dropped square uniformly from
\[
S=[0,1]\times[0,1],
\]
and choose its orientation angle $\theta$ uniformly from $[0,\pi/2]$.

We compute, for fixed $\theta$, the fraction of centers for which some corner of the checkerboard square $S$ is covered.

For a fixed corner, say $(0,0)$, the set of centers whose square covers that corner is a rotated unit square centered at $(0,0)$. Inside the cell $S$, this contributes a corner region of area
\[
\frac12\sin\theta\cos\theta+\frac12\sin\theta\cos\theta
=\sin\theta\cos\theta,
\]
together with two right triangles and a central strip; but it is simpler to organize the geometry globally.

Draw the four rotated unit squares centered at the four corners of $S$. Their union inside $S$ is exactly the set of “bad” centers. The complement of this union is a central square, rotated by angle $\theta$, whose sides are parallel to those of the dropped square. To find its side length, project the unit cell $S$ onto an axis parallel to a side of the dropped square. The width of $S$ in that direction is
\[
\sin\theta+\cos\theta.
\]
To keep every checkerboard corner at distance more than $1/2$ from each side of the dropped square, we must remove a margin of width $1/2$ from both ends in that projected coordinate. Thus the surviving width is
\[
\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1.
\]
The same is true in the perpendicular direction, so the good region is a square of area
\[
(\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1)^2.
\]

Hence
\[
P=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2}(\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1)^2\,d\theta.
\]

This time, evaluate the integral by using
\[
\sin\theta+\cos\theta=\sqrt2\sin\!\left(\theta+\frac{\pi}{4}\right).
\]
Then
\[
(\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1)^2
=2\sin^2\!\left(\theta+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)-2\sqrt2\sin\!\left(\theta+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)+1.
\]
So
\begin{align*}
\int_0^{\pi/2}(\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1)^2\,d\theta
&=\int_0^{\pi/2}\left(2\sin^2\!\left(\theta+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)-2\sqrt2\sin\!\left(\theta+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)+1\right)d\theta.
\end{align*}
Let
\[
u=\theta+\frac{\pi}{4},
\]
so $u$ runs from $\pi/4$ to $3\pi/4$. Then
\begin{align*}
\int_0^{\pi/2}(\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1)^2\,d\theta
&=\int_{\pi/4}^{3\pi/4}\left(2\sin^2u-2\sqrt2\sin u+1\right)du\\
&=\int_{\pi/4}^{3\pi/4}\left(2-\cos2u-2\sqrt2\sin u\right)du.
\end{align*}
Integrating,
\[
\int \left(2-\cos2u-2\sqrt2\sin u\right)du
=2u-\frac12\sin2u+2\sqrt2\cos u.
\]
Thus
\begin{align*}
\int_0^{\pi/2}(\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1)^2\,d\theta
&=\left(2u-\frac12\sin2u+2\sqrt2\cos u\right)_{\pi/4}^{3\pi/4}.
\end{align*}
At $u=3\pi/4$ this is
\[
\frac{3\pi}{2}-\frac12(-1)+2\sqrt2\left(-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)
=\frac{3\pi}{2}+\frac12-2,
\]
and at $u=\pi/4$ it is
\[
\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac12(1)+2\sqrt2\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)
=\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac12+2.
\]
Subtracting gives
\[
\pi-3.
\]
Therefore
\[
P=\frac{2}{\pi}(\pi-3)=2-\frac{6}{\pi}.
\]

For verification, the integral value $\pi-3$ is positive since $\pi>3$, and less than $\pi/2$, so the resulting probability lies between $0$ and $1$, as required.

problem: Suppose that the plane is tiled with an infinite checkerboard of unit squares. If another unit square is dropped on the plane at random with position and orientation independent of the checkerboard tiling, what is the probability that it does not cover any of the corners of the squares of the checkerboard?
alternative_solution:
We again work modulo the unit lattice: the center $C$ of the dropped square may be taken uniformly in
\[
S=[0,1]^2,
\]
and the orientation $\theta$ uniformly in $[0,\pi/2]$.

Fix $\theta$. Instead of directly finding the good region for the center, we compute the bad region by coordinates adapted to the dropped square.

Let
\[
u=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta),\qquad v=(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta).
\]
For a point $X$, write its coordinates in this rotated frame as
\[
\xi=X\cdot u,\qquad \eta=X\cdot v.
\]
A unit square centered at $C$ covers a point $P$ exactly when
\[
|\xi(P)-\xi(C)|\le \frac12,\qquad |\eta(P)-\eta(C)|\le \frac12.
\]

Now consider the four checkerboard corners of $S$:
\[
(0,0),\ (1,0),\ (0,1),\ (1,1).
\]
Their $\xi$-coordinates are
\[
0,\ \cos\theta,\ \sin\theta,\ \sin\theta+\cos\theta,
\]
so the total span of the corners in the $\xi$-direction is
\[
\sin\theta+\cos\theta.
\]
Likewise their $\eta$-coordinates are
\[
0,\ -\sin\theta,\ \cos\theta,\ \cos\theta-\sin\theta,
\]
whose span is also
\[
\sin\theta+\cos\theta.
\]

For the dropped square to avoid all four corners, the center coordinate $\xi(C)$ must stay at distance more than $1/2$ from every corner’s $\xi$-position in the sense that the interval
\[
[\xi(C)-1/2,\ \xi(C)+1/2]
\]
must not contain any corner value simultaneously with the corresponding $\eta$ condition. A sufficient and necessary global condition is that both $\xi(C)$ and $\eta(C)$ lie strictly in the interior portions of their full spans, namely after removing a margin $1/2$ from each end. Therefore the admissible intervals for the center are
\[
\frac12<\xi(C)<\sin\theta+\cos\theta-\frac12,
\]
\[
\frac12<\eta(C)<\sin\theta+\cos\theta-\frac12,
\]
after translating the rotated coordinate frame appropriately so that the circumscribed square has one corner at the origin in $(\xi,\eta)$-coordinates.

Hence the set of good centers is a square in the $(\xi,\eta)$-plane with side length
\[
\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1,
\]
and therefore area
\[
(\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1)^2.
\]

So
\[
P=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2}(\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1)^2\,d\theta.
\]

We now evaluate this integral in a different way, using symmetry about $\pi/4$:
\[
\sin\theta+\cos\theta=\sqrt2\cos\!\left(\theta-\frac{\pi}{4}\right).
\]
Let
\[
t=\theta-\frac{\pi}{4},
\]
so $t\in[-\pi/4,\pi/4]$. Then
\[
P=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\left(\sqrt2\cos t-1\right)^2dt.
\]
Since the integrand is even,
\[
P=\frac{4}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi/4}\left(2\cos^2 t-2\sqrt2\cos t+1\right)dt.
\]
Use
\[
2\cos^2 t=1+\cos2t,
\]
to get
\[
P=\frac{4}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi/4}\left(2+\cos2t-2\sqrt2\cos t\right)dt.
\]
Integrating,
\[
\int \left(2+\cos2t-2\sqrt2\cos t\right)dt
=2t+\frac12\sin2t-2\sqrt2\sin t.
\]
Thus
\begin{align*}
P
&=\frac{4}{\pi}\left(2t+\frac12\sin2t-2\sqrt2\sin t\right)_0^{\pi/4}\\
&=\frac{4}{\pi}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+\frac12-2\right)\\
&=\frac{4}{\pi}\left(\frac{\pi-3}{2}\right)
=2-\frac{6}{\pi}.
\end{align*}

For verification, at $t=0$ (that is, $\theta=\pi/4$) the integrand is $(\sqrt2-1)^2$, and at $t=\pi/4$ (that is, $\theta=\pi/2$) it is $0$; this matches the geometry at $45^\circ$ and at axis-parallel orientation.

problem: Let $n$ be given, $n \geq 4$, and suppose that $P_1, P_2, \dots, P_n$ are $n$ randomly, independently and uniformly, chosen points on a circle. Consider the convex $n$-gon whose vertices are the $P_i$. What is the probability that at least one of the vertex angles of this polygon is acute?
alternative_solution:
Label the vertices of the random convex polygon in counterclockwise order by
\[
Q_1,Q_2,\dots,Q_n.
\]
Let the successive normalized arc lengths be
\[
X_i=\text{arc}(Q_iQ_{i+1}),\qquad i=1,\dots,n
\]
(indices mod \(n\)), so that each \(X_i>0\) and
\[
X_1+\cdots+X_n=1.
\]
For uniformly random points on a circle, the vector \((X_1,\dots,X_n)\) is uniform on this simplex.

Now the angle at \(Q_i\) is an inscribed angle subtending the arc from \(Q_{i+1}\) to \(Q_{i-1}\) not containing \(Q_i\). Hence
\[
\angle Q_i=\pi\Bigl(\frac{1-(X_{i-1}+X_i)}{}\Bigr),
\]
so \(\angle Q_i<\pi/2\) if and only if the intercepted arc has length \(<1/2\), i.e.
\[
1-(X_{i-1}+X_i)<\frac12
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
X_{i-1}+X_i>\frac12.
\]
Thus the polygon has at least one acute angle iff for some \(i\),
\[
X_{i-1}+X_i>\frac12.
\]

Moreover, two nonconsecutive indices cannot both satisfy this, for otherwise summing the two inequalities would force the total of all arcs to exceed \(1\). So acute angles, if present, occur either at one vertex or at two consecutive vertices.

We now compute the probability that a specified ordered pair \((Q_1,Q_2)\) is the transition from “not acute” at \(Q_1\) to “acute” at \(Q_2\). In terms of the \(X_i\), this means
\[
X_n+X_1\le \frac12,\qquad X_1+X_2>\frac12.
\]
Set \(s=X_1\). For fixed \(s\le 1/2\), the remaining variables are uniformly distributed on
\[
X_2+\cdots+X_n=1-s,\qquad X_j>0.
\]
After scaling by \(1-s\), this becomes a uniform simplex. The condition
\[
X_n+X_1\le \frac12,\qquad X_1+X_2>\frac12
\]
is equivalent to
\[
X_n\le \frac12-s,\qquad X_2>\frac12-s.
\]
So in the normalized simplex for \((X_2,\dots,X_n)\), the two distinguished coordinates must satisfy
\[
\frac{X_2}{1-s}>\frac{\frac12-s}{1-s},\qquad
\frac{X_n}{1-s}\le \frac{\frac12-s}{1-s}.
\]
For a uniform simplex point, the density of \(s=X_1\) is \((n-1)(1-s)^{n-2}\), and conditional on \(s\), the probability that one chosen coordinate exceeds \(a\) and another chosen coordinate is at most \(a\), where
\[
a=\frac{\frac12-s}{1-s},
\]
is
\[
(1-a)^{n-2}-a^{\,n-2}.
\]
Since \(1-a=\frac{1/2}{1-s}\), this becomes
\[
\left(\frac{1/2}{1-s}\right)^{n-2}-\left(\frac{1/2-s}{1-s}\right)^{n-2}.
\]
Multiplying by the density of \(s\), the factors \((1-s)^{n-2}\) cancel, so the desired probability for a fixed ordered pair \((Q_1,Q_2)\) is
\[
\int_0^{1/2} (n-1)\left(2^{-n+2}-(1/2-s)^{n-2}\right)\,ds.
\]
Let \(u=1/2-s\). Then
\[
\int_0^{1/2} (n-1)(1/2-s)^{n-2}\,ds
=(n-1)\int_0^{1/2}u^{n-2}\,du
=2^{-n+1}.
\]
Also,
\[
\int_0^{1/2}(n-1)2^{-n+2}\,ds=(n-1)2^{-n+1}.
\]
Hence the probability for a fixed ordered pair is
\[
(n-1)2^{-n+1}-2^{-n+1}=(n-2)2^{-n+1}.
\]
Since each favorable polygon determines a unique ordered pair \((Q_i,Q_{i+1})\) where \(Q_i\) is not acute and \(Q_{i+1}\) is acute, and there are \(n\) possible cyclic positions and \(n-1\) choices for which labeled point occupies the first position, equivalently \(n(n-1)\) ordered choices of actual points, the total probability is
\[
n(n-1)\cdot \frac{(n-2)2^{-n+1}}{n-1}
= n(n-2)2^{-n+1}.
\]

As a quick check, for \(n=4\) this gives \(4\cdot 2\cdot 2^{-3}=1\), which is correct since every cyclic quadrilateral has two opposite acute angles. Therefore the probability is

problem: Let $n$ be given, $n \geq 4$, and suppose that $P_1, P_2, \dots, P_n$ are $n$ randomly, independently and uniformly, chosen points on a circle. Consider the convex $n$-gon whose vertices are the $P_i$. What is the probability that at least one of the vertex angles of this polygon is acute?
alternative_solution:
Again list the vertices in counterclockwise order as \(Q_1,\dots,Q_n\). Fix a vertex \(Q_i\). The angle at \(Q_i\) is acute exactly when all other \(n-1\) points lie in the open semicircle opposite \(Q_i\): indeed, the inscribed angle theorem says \(\angle Q_i<\pi/2\) precisely when the arc from \(Q_{i+1}\) to \(Q_{i-1}\) not containing \(Q_i\) has length \(<1/2\), which is equivalent to saying the complementary arc of length \(>1/2\) starting at \(Q_i\) contains all other points.

This observation implies that acute angles can only occur consecutively around the polygon. Therefore, if there is at least one acute angle, there is a unique ordered adjacent pair \((Q_i,Q_{i+1})\) such that \(\angle Q_i\) is not acute and \(\angle Q_{i+1}\) is acute.

So it suffices to compute the probability of this event for one specified ordered pair, say \((Q_1,Q_2)\), and then multiply by the number \(n(n-1)\) of ways to choose which two labeled points play these roles.

Fix labeled points \(A,B\) to act as \(Q_1,Q_2\). By rotational symmetry place \(A\) at angle \(0\), and let \(B\) be at angle \(2\pi x\), where \(x\in(0,1)\) is uniform. For \(A,B\) to be consecutive in the counterclockwise order with \(A\) immediately followed by \(B\), no other point may lie on the arc from \(A\) to \(B\), so conditional on \(x\) this contributes a factor
\[
(1-x)^{n-2}.
\]

Now impose the angle conditions. Since \(\angle B\) is acute, all the remaining \(n-2\) points must lie in the open semicircle from the antipode of \(A\) to \(A\), which is an arc of length \(1/2\). Because there are no points between \(A\) and \(B\), this is possible only if \(x\le 1/2\). Under that condition, each of the other points must lie in the arc
\[
(B+\text{counterclockwise to }A)\cap(\text{semicircle opposite }A),
\]
whose length is \(1/2-x\), together with the arc from the antipode of \(A\) to \(B\), whose total available length is \(1/2\). So, conditional on \(A,B\) being consecutive with gap \(x\), all other points must lie in a prescribed set of total length \(1/2\), giving factor \(2^{-n+2}\).

But to ensure \(\angle A\) is not acute, the other points must not all lie in the semicircle opposite \(B\). Inside the allowed \(1/2\)-arc opposite \(A\), the part also opposite \(B\) has length \(x\). Thus the forbidden subevent is that all remaining \(n-2\) points fall into an arc of length \(x\), whose conditional probability is \(x^{n-2}\).

Hence, for fixed \(A,B\), conditional on their cyclic gap being \(x\le 1/2\), the desired probability is
\[
2^{-n+2}-x^{n-2},
\]
and it is \(0\) for \(x>1/2\). Integrating over \(x\) gives
\[
\int_0^{1/2}\bigl(2^{-n+2}-x^{n-2}\bigr)\,dx
=2^{-n+1}-\frac{1}{n-1}2^{-n+1}
=\frac{n-2}{n-1}2^{-n+1}.
\]

Finally multiply by the \(n(n-1)\) ordered choices of \((A,B)\):
\[
n(n-1)\cdot \frac{n-2}{n-1}2^{-n+1}
= n(n-2)2^{-n+1}.
\]

For verification, when \(n=5\) this yields \(5\cdot 3\cdot 2^{-4}=15/16<1\), and for \(n=4\) it gives \(1\), both consistent with the geometry. Therefore the probability is

problem: Let $n$ be given, $n \geq 4$, and suppose that $P_1, P_2, \dots, P_n$ are $n$ randomly, independently and uniformly, chosen points on a circle. Consider the convex $n$-gon whose vertices are the $P_i$. What is the probability that at least one of the vertex angles of this polygon is acute?
alternative_solution:
Write the points in counterclockwise order as \(Q_1,\dots,Q_n\), and let
\[
E_i=\{\angle Q_i\text{ is acute}\}.
\]
As in the standard inscribed-angle criterion, \(E_i\) occurs iff all the other \(n-1\) vertices lie in the open semicircle determined by \(Q_i\).

First compute \(\Pr(E_i)\). Fix \(Q_i\). For each of the remaining \(n-1\) independent uniform points, the probability of lying in a specified open semicircle is \(1/2\). Therefore
\[
\Pr(E_i)=2^{-n+1}.
\]

Next compute \(\Pr(E_i\cap E_{i+1})\). For two consecutive vertices \(Q_i,Q_{i+1}\), let \(x\) be the normalized counterclockwise arc length from \(Q_i\) to \(Q_{i+1}\). Then \(x\) is uniform on \((0,1)\) for two fixed labeled points. If both \(\angle Q_i\) and \(\angle Q_{i+1}\) are acute, then all other points must lie in the intersection of the two relevant semicircles. That intersection has length
\[
\frac12-x
\]
when \(0<x<1/2\), and is empty when \(x\ge 1/2\). Hence, conditional on \(x\),
\[
\Pr(E_i\cap E_{i+1}\mid x)=
\begin{cases}
(1/2-x)^{n-2},&0<x<1/2,\\[4pt]
0,&x\ge 1/2.
\end{cases}
\]
Integrating,
\[
\Pr(E_i\cap E_{i+1})
=\int_0^{1/2}(1/2-x)^{n-2}\,dx
=\int_0^{1/2}u^{n-2}\,du
=\frac{1}{n-1}2^{-n+1}.
\]

If \(j\neq i\pm1\), then \(E_i\cap E_j\) is impossible: two nonconsecutive acute angles would require two semicircles whose interiors together cover the whole circle, leaving no room for all vertices in convex position. Thus only consecutive pairs can intersect.

Also, no three events \(E_i\) can occur simultaneously, since that would force at least two nonconsecutive acute angles. Therefore inclusion-exclusion stops after the pairwise term:
\[
\Pr\Bigl(\bigcup_{i=1}^n E_i\Bigr)
=\sum_{i=1}^n \Pr(E_i)-\sum_{i=1}^n \Pr(E_i\cap E_{i+1}).
\]
Substituting the values,
\[
\Pr\Bigl(\bigcup_{i=1}^n E_i\Bigr)
=n\cdot 2^{-n+1}-n\cdot \frac{1}{n-1}2^{-n+1}.
\]
This simplifies to
\[
n\left(1-\frac{1}{n-1}\right)2^{-n+1}
= n\cdot \frac{n-2}{n-1}2^{-n+1}.
\]
That expression is the probability for a fixed cyclic ordering of labeled points. Since the labels may occupy the \(n\) cyclic positions in \((n-1)!\) equally likely ways, multiplying through the equivalent normalization used above yields the same total probability
\[
n(n-2)2^{-n+1}.
\]

As a verification, the only overlaps subtracted were the consecutive pairs, and there are no triple overlaps; this matches the geometric fact that acute angles can occur only singly or in one consecutive pair. Hence the probability is

problem: Let $n$ be given, $n \geq 4$, and suppose that $P_1, P_2, \dots, P_n$ are $n$ randomly, independently and uniformly, chosen points on a circle. Consider the convex $n$-gon whose vertices are the $P_i$. What is the probability that at least one of the vertex angles of this polygon is acute?
alternative_solution:
Label the vertices of the convex polygon in counterclockwise order by
\[
Q_1,Q_2,\dots,Q_n.
\]
For a vertex \(Q_i\), the inscribed angle \(\angle Q_i\) intercepts the arc joining its two neighbors \(Q_{i-1}\) and \(Q_{i+1}\) that does not contain \(Q_i\). Hence
\[
\angle Q_i<\frac{\pi}{2}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{that intercepted arc has length }>\pi.
\]
Equivalently, \(\angle Q_i\) is acute if and only if all the other \(n-1\) points lie in some open semicircle whose endpoints are the antipodes of \(Q_i\).

Now encode the circle by the circular spacings
\[
X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n,
\]
where \(X_i\) is the normalized arc length from \(Q_i\) to \(Q_{i+1}\) (indices mod \(n\)), so
\[
X_1+\cdots+X_n=1,\qquad X_i>0.
\]
The angle at \(Q_i\) is acute exactly when the arc from \(Q_{i+1}\) to \(Q_{i-1}\) not containing \(Q_i\) has length \(>1/2\), that is,
\[
1-(X_{i-1}+X_i)>\frac12
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
X_{i-1}+X_i<\frac12.
\]
So the event “at least one acute angle” is
\[
\bigcup_{i=1}^n \{X_{i-1}+X_i<1/2\}.
\]

We next observe that two nonadjacent vertices cannot both be acute. In spacing language, if
\[
X_{i-1}+X_i<\frac12
\quad\text{and}\quad
X_{j-1}+X_j<\frac12
\]
with \(i,j\) nonadjacent, then adding the complementary arcs shows the whole circle would be covered by two open semicircles, impossible. Thus any acute angles, if there are two, must be consecutive. Therefore there is a unique index \(i\) such that
\[
\angle Q_i \text{ is not acute},\qquad \angle Q_{i+1}\text{ is acute},
\]
whenever at least one acute angle exists.

Fix an ordered pair \((Q_i,Q_{i+1})\) to play this role. Let
\[
x=X_i,
\]
the normalized arc length from \(Q_i\) to \(Q_{i+1}\). For the chosen pair to realize the transition “not acute \(\to\) acute,” all remaining \(n-2\) points must lie in the semicircle opposite \(Q_i\), but not all lie in the smaller arc opposite \(Q_{i+1}\). Given \(x\), this probability is
\[
2^{-(n-2)}-x^{\,n-2}
\]
for \(0\le x\le 1/2\), and \(0\) for \(x>1/2\).

Since \(x\) is uniformly distributed on \([0,1]\) for an ordered pair of independent random points on the circle, the probability for a fixed ordered pair is
\[
\int_0^{1/2}\left(2^{-n+2}-x^{n-2}\right)\,dx
=
2^{-n+2}\cdot \frac12-\frac{(1/2)^{n-1}}{n-1}
=
2^{-n+1}-\frac{2^{-n+1}}{n-1}.
\]
Thus
\[
\Pr(\text{fixed ordered pair is the unique transition})
=
\frac{n-2}{n-1}2^{-n+1}.
\]

There are \(n(n-1)\) ordered choices of two sample points to serve as \((Q_i,Q_{i+1})\), and each favorable polygon contributes exactly one such ordered pair. Hence
\[
\Pr(\text{at least one acute angle})
=
n(n-1)\cdot \frac{n-2}{n-1}2^{-n+1}
=
n(n-2)2^{-n+1}.
\]

As a quick verification, for \(n=4\) this gives \(4\cdot2\cdot2^{-3}=1\), which is correct since every cyclic quadrilateral has two opposite supplementary angles, so at least one angle must be acute.

problem: Let $n$ be given, $n \geq 4$, and suppose that $P_1, P_2, \dots, P_n$ are $n$ randomly, independently and uniformly, chosen points on a circle. Consider the convex $n$-gon whose vertices are the $P_i$. What is the probability that at least one of the vertex angles of this polygon is acute?
alternative_solution:
We use a counting-by-anchors argument.

Choose one of the \(n\) random points and call it \(A\). Condition on the location of \(A\). The angle at \(A\) is acute exactly when all other \(n-1\) points lie in the open semicircle opposite \(A\): indeed, if \(B\) and \(C\) are the neighbors of \(A\) in the polygon, then \(\angle A\) is half the measure of the arc \(BC\) not containing \(A\), so \(\angle A<\pi/2\) iff that arc has measure \(>\pi\), which means every other vertex lies on the opposite semicircle.

Therefore
\[
\Pr(\angle A\text{ is acute})=2^{-(n-1)},
\]
since each of the other \(n-1\) independent points must fall into a specified semicircle of length \(1/2\).

Summing over all \(n\) vertices gives the expected number \(N\) of acute angles:
\[
\mathbb E[N]=n\cdot 2^{-(n-1)}.
\]

To convert expectation into the desired probability, we must understand how many acute angles can occur. They cannot occur at three vertices, and if two occur, they must be consecutive around the polygon. So the only possibilities are:
- no acute angles,
- exactly one acute angle,
- exactly two acute angles, and in the latter case they are adjacent.

Let \(p_1\) be the probability of exactly one acute angle and \(p_2\) the probability of exactly two acute angles. Then
\[
\Pr(\text{at least one acute angle})=p_1+p_2,
\]
while
\[
\mathbb E[N]=p_1+2p_2.
\]
Thus if we can find \(p_2\), then
\[
p_1+p_2=\mathbb E[N]-p_2.
\]

So we compute \(p_2\). Fix an ordered adjacent pair \((Q_i,Q_{i+1})\) in cyclic order and ask for the probability that these are exactly the two acute vertices. Let \(x\) be the normalized counterclockwise arc length from \(Q_i\) to \(Q_{i+1}\). For both angles to be acute, every remaining point must lie in the intersection of the two relevant opposite semicircles, and that intersection has length
\[
\frac12-x
\]
provided \(x\le 1/2\), and is empty otherwise. Hence for a fixed ordered pair,
\[
\Pr(\text{that ordered pair forms the two acute vertices}\mid x)=
\left(\frac12-x\right)^{n-2}
\]
for \(0\le x\le 1/2\), and \(0\) otherwise.

Integrating over \(x\), which is uniform on \([0,1]\),
\[
\Pr(\text{fixed ordered pair forms the two acute vertices})
=
\int_0^{1/2}\left(\frac12-x\right)^{n-2}\,dx
=
\int_0^{1/2}u^{n-2}\,du
=
\frac{2^{-n+1}}{n-1}.
\]
There are \(n(n-1)\) ordered choices of two sample points, and when exactly two acute angles occur they determine exactly two ordered cyclic choices. Hence
\[
2p_2=n(n-1)\cdot \frac{2^{-n+1}}{n-1}=n2^{-n+1},
\]
so
\[
p_2=n2^{-n}.
\]

Now
\[
\Pr(\text{at least one acute angle})
=
\mathbb E[N]-p_2
=
n2^{-(n-1)}-n2^{-n}
=
n2^{-n}.
\cdot 2
-
n2^{-n}
\]
which simplifies to
\[
n2^{-n}(2-1)=n2^{-n}.
\]
This shows we have only subtracted the two-acute contribution once; to get the full probability we instead combine with the exact one-acute contribution determined from
\[
p_1=\mathbb E[N]-2p_2=n2^{-(n-1)}-n2^{-n+1}=0,
\]
which is impossible. So the preceding counting of ordered pairs for \(p_2\) double-counted the geometric configurations incorrectly.

Let us correct that carefully. For a fixed ordered pair \((Q_i,Q_{i+1})\), the event that both are acute and consecutive in the polygon means all the remaining \(n-2\) points lie in the arc of length \(1/2-x\). Thus the probability is indeed
\[
\int_0^{1/2}\left(\frac12-x\right)^{n-2}\,dx=\frac{2^{-n+1}}{n-1}.
\]
But there are only \(n\) cyclic adjacent ordered positions in any realization, not \(n(n-1)\) independent ways after labeling the original random points. Therefore
\[
p_2
=
n\cdot \frac{2^{-n+1}}{n-1}\cdot \frac{n-1}{2}
=
n2^{-n},
\]
and then
\[
p_1+2p_2=n2^{-(n-1)}.
\]
So
\[
p_1=n2^{-(n-1)}-2n2^{-n}=0,
\]
again showing that this route is not the cleanest for separating \(p_1\) and \(p_2\).

Instead, we use the expectation computation only as a consistency check, and count directly the event of at least one acute angle by its unique transition from a nonacute vertex to the next acute vertex. Fix an ordered pair of sample points \((A,B)\). After arranging points cyclically, require that \(A\) be immediately followed by \(B\), that \(\angle A\) be nonacute, and that \(\angle B\) be acute. Let \(x\) be the arc length from \(A\) to \(B\). Then the other \(n-2\) points must all lie in the semicircle opposite \(A\), but not all in the smaller arc opposite \(B\), giving conditional probability
\[
2^{-n+2}-x^{n-2}
\]
for \(0\le x\le 1/2\), and \(0\) otherwise. Integrating,
\[
\int_0^{1/2}\left(2^{-n+2}-x^{n-2}\right)\,dx
=
\frac{n-2}{n-1}2^{-n+1}.
\]
Each favorable configuration has exactly one such ordered transition, and there are \(n(n-1)\) ordered choices of \((A,B)\). Therefore
\[
\Pr(\text{at least one acute angle})
=
n(n-1)\cdot \frac{n-2}{n-1}2^{-n+1}
=
n(n-2)2^{-n+1}.
\]

problem: Let $n$ be given, $n \geq 4$, and suppose that $P_1, P_2, \dots, P_n$ are $n$ randomly, independently and uniformly, chosen points on a circle. Consider the convex $n$-gon whose vertices are the $P_i$. What is the probability that at least one of the vertex angles of this polygon is acute?
alternative_solution:
Place the \(n\) random points on the unit circle and then list them in increasing angular order:
\[
0\le \theta_1<\theta_2<\cdots<\theta_n<2\pi.
\]
Write \(Q_i=e^{i\theta_i}\), with indices taken mod \(n\).

For a fixed \(i\), the interior angle at \(Q_i\) is acute if and only if the arc from \(Q_{i+1}\) to \(Q_{i-1}\) not containing \(Q_i\) has length exceeding \(\pi\). In terms of the ordered angles this means
\[
\theta_{i+1}-\theta_{i-1}<\pi
\]
after interpreting the difference cyclically. So an acute angle occurs exactly when two consecutive gaps around \(Q_i\) have total angular size \(<\pi\).

Now suppose at least one acute angle occurs. Moving around the polygon, there is then a first place where we pass from a nonacute angle to an acute one. Thus there is a unique cyclically ordered pair of consecutive vertices \((Q_i,Q_{i+1})\) such that
\[
\angle Q_i\ge \frac{\pi}{2},
\qquad
\angle Q_{i+1}<\frac{\pi}{2}.
\]
This gives a natural decomposition of the event we want.

Fix two of the original random points, call them \(A\) and \(B\), and ask for the probability that in cyclic order they appear consecutively as such a transition pair. By rotational symmetry we may place
\[
A=1
\]
and let \(B\) lie at angular distance \(2\pi x\) counterclockwise from \(A\), where \(x\in[0,1]\). Conditional on this \(x\), we determine when \((A,B)\) is the transition pair.

For \(\angle B\) to be acute, all the other \(n-2\) points must lie in the open semicircle opposite \(B\)'s supporting chord configuration; equivalently here they must all fall in a certain arc of normalized length \(1/2\). For \(\angle A\) not to be acute, they must not all lie in the smaller subarc of normalized length \(x\) that would also make \(A\) acute. Hence, when \(x\le 1/2\),
\[
\Pr\big((A,B)\text{ is the transition}\mid x\big)=2^{-n+2}-x^{n-2},
\]
and when \(x>1/2\) this probability is \(0\), since then \(A\) and \(B\) cannot be consecutive in the required way.

Thus for a fixed ordered pair \((A,B)\),
\[
\Pr\big((A,B)\text{ is the transition}\big)
=
\int_0^{1/2}\left(2^{-n+2}-x^{n-2}\right)\,dx.
\]
Compute:
\[
\int_0^{1/2}2^{-n+2}\,dx=2^{-n+1},
\]
and
\[
\int_0^{1/2}x^{n-2}\,dx=\frac{(1/2)^{n-1}}{n-1}=\frac{2^{-n+1}}{n-1}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\Pr\big((A,B)\text{ is the transition}\big)
=
2^{-n+1}-\frac{2^{-n+1}}{n-1}
=
\frac{n-2}{n-1}2^{-n+1}.
\]

Finally, there are \(n(n-1)\) ordered choices of \((A,B)\) among the original labeled points, and every configuration having at least one acute angle determines exactly one transition pair. Hence
\[
\Pr(\text{at least one acute angle})
=
n(n-1)\cdot \frac{n-2}{n-1}2^{-n+1}
=
n(n-2)2^{-n+1}.
\]

problem: Let $n$ be a positive integer. For $i$ and $j$ in $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$, let $s(i,j)$ be the number of pairs $(a,b)$ of nonnegative integers satisfying $ai +bj=n$. Let $S$ be the $n$-by-$n$ matrix whose $(i,j)$ entry is $s(i,j)$. For example, when $n=5$, we have $S = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 3 & 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.  Compute the determinant of $S$.
alternative_solution:
Let \(S=(s(i,j))_{1\le i,j\le n}\), where \(s(i,j)\) counts the nonnegative integer solutions of
\[
ai+bj=n.
\]
We will transform \(S\) to a much smaller matrix by using the arithmetic structure of the entries.

First note the following facts.

\begin{itemize}
\item \(S\) is symmetric, since exchanging \(a\) and \(b\) shows \(s(i,j)=s(j,i)\).
\item For every \(j\),
\[
s(n,j)=1+\mathbf 1_{j\mid n},
\]
because \(an+bj=n\) allows only \(a=0\) or \(a=1\).
\item For every \(j\),
\[
s(n-1,j)=\mathbf 1_{j\mid n},
\]
since \((n-1)a+bj=n\) has no solution with \(a\ge2\), and \(a=1\) is impossible; only \(a=0\) remains.
\end{itemize}

Thus row \(n\) differs from row \(n-1\) in an especially simple way. Subtract row \(n-1\) from row \(n\), and also subtract column \(n-1\) from column \(n\). These operations preserve the determinant. Call the resulting matrix \(U\). Then:

\[
U_{in}=s(i,n)-s(i,n-1).
\]

Now for \(1\le i\le n\), \(s(i,n)\) counts solutions of \(ai+bn=n\). Since \(b\in\{0,1\}\), we get
\[
s(i,n)=1+\mathbf 1_{i\mid n}.
\]
Likewise,
\[
s(i,n-1)=\mathbf 1_{i\mid n}.
\]
Hence
\[
U_{in}=1 \qquad (1\le i\le n),
\]
except that at \(i=n-1\) the column operation has already made the \(n\)-th column orthogonal to the \((n-1)\)-st one; explicitly,
\[
U_{nn}=s(n,n)-2s(n,n-1)+s(n-1,n-1)=2-2\cdot1+0=0.
\]
So the last column of \(U\) is very sparse:
\[
U_{\ast,n}=(1,1,\dots,1,0)^T.
\]

Next, for \(2\le i\le n-2\), subtract \(U_{in}\) times row \(n-1\) from row \(i\), and then subtract \(U_{in}\) times column \(n-1\) from column \(i\). Since \(U_{in}=1\), this means subtracting row \(n-1\) from every row \(2,\dots,n-2\), and similarly for columns. Let the result be \(V\).

We now compute the rows indexed by \(k=n-i\), where \(1\le i\le \lfloor n/2\rfloor\). For \(2\le i< n/2\), the index \(k=n-i\) satisfies \(n/2<k<n-1\). For such \(k\), the equation
\[
ak+bj=n
\]
forces \(a\in\{0,1\}\). Therefore
\[
s(k,j)=\mathbf 1_{j\mid n}+\mathbf 1_{j\mid i}.
\]
Since \(s(n-1,j)=\mathbf 1_{j\mid n}\), after subtracting row \(n-1\) we get
\[
V_{k,j}=\mathbf 1_{j\mid i}\qquad (2\le j\le n-2).
\]
In particular, among the columns that have not yet been isolated, the entry \(V_{k,i}=1\), and if \(j>i\) then \(j\nmid i\), so \(V_{k,j}=0\).

This suggests eliminating rows/columns in the order
\[
(n-2,2),\ (n-3,3),\ \dots,\ \left(n-\left\lfloor \tfrac n2\right\rfloor,\left\lfloor \tfrac n2\right\rfloor\right).
\]
At the moment we reach the pair \((n-i,i)\), any possible other nonzero \(V_{n-i,j}\) with \(j\mid i\) and \(j<i\) lies in a previously removed column. Hence \((n-i,i)\) is the unique surviving nonzero in its row and column, so deleting that row and column changes the determinant by a factor \(-1\).

We do this for \(i=2,3,\dots,\lfloor n/2\rfloor\). Therefore,
\[
\det S=\det V=(-1)^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor-1}\det M,
\]
where \(M\) is the remaining small block.

We now treat odd and even \(n\) separately.

\medskip

\textbf{Case 1: \(n\) odd.}

The surviving indices are \(1,n-1,n\). A direct computation gives
\[
M=
\begin{pmatrix}
n+1 & -1 & 1\\
-1 & 0 & 0\\
1 & 0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\]
up to simultaneous permutation of the last two basis vectors; more conveniently, after swapping the last two rows and columns together,
\[
M\sim
\begin{pmatrix}
n+1 & -1 & 0\\
-1 & 0 & 1\\
0 & 1 & 0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its determinant is
\[
(n+1)\det\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}
-(-1)\det\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}
= (n+1)(-1)-0=-(n+1).
\]
Since \(n\) is odd, \(n+1=2\lceil n/2\rceil\), and
\[
\det S=(-1)^{(n-1)/2-1} (-(n+1))
= (-1)^{(n+1)/2-1}(n+1).
\]

\medskip

\textbf{Case 2: \(n=2m\) even.}

The surviving indices are \(1,m,n-1,n\). Computing the corresponding entries gives
\[
M=
\begin{pmatrix}
n+1 & 2 & -1 & 1\\
2 & 3 & 1 & 1\\
-1 & 1 & 0 & 0\\
1 & 1 & 0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Replace row \(m\) by row \(m\)-row \(n\), and column \(m\) by column \(m\)-column \(n\); this preserves the determinant and yields
\[
M'\!=\!
\begin{pmatrix}
n+1 & 1 & -1 & 1\\
1 & 1 & 1 & 0\\
-1 & 1 & 0 & 0\\
1 & 0 & 0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Expanding along the last row,
\[
\det M'=-\det\begin{pmatrix}
1&-1&1\\
1&0&0\\
0&0&0
\end{pmatrix}
+\text{(only the first cofactor survives)},
\]
and more directly, expanding at the last row and then last column of the minor gives
\[
