alternative_solution:
We seek all polynomials \(f(x)\in \mathbb Z_{\ge 0}[x]\) such that
\[
\operatorname{rad}(f(n))\mid \operatorname{rad}(f(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)}))
\qquad\text{for every }n\ge 0.
\]

We will use the smallest nonzero term of \(f\) and a coprimality argument.

### Step 1: Factor out the lowest power of \(x\)

Let \(m\) be the smallest exponent such that the coefficient of \(x^m\) in \(f(x)\) is nonzero. Then
\[
f(x)=x^m g(x),
\]
where \(g(x)\in \mathbb Z_{\ge 0}[x]\) and \(g(0)>0\).

Now for any \(n\ge 1\),
\[
f(n)=n^m g(n),\qquad f(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)})=n^{m\operatorname{rad}(n)}g(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)}).
\]
Since
\[
\operatorname{rad}(n^m)=\operatorname{rad}(n^{m\operatorname{rad}(n)})=\operatorname{rad}(n),
\]
the given divisibility implies
\[
\operatorname{rad}(g(n))\mid \operatorname{rad}(n\,g(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)})).
\]
In particular, any prime dividing \(g(n)\) but not \(n\) must divide \(g(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)})\).

We will show that this forces \(g\) to be constant.

### Step 2: Assume \(g\) is nonconstant and derive a contradiction

Suppose \(g\) is nonconstant. Since \(g(0)>0\), let
\[
g(x)=c+xh(x)
\]
with \(c=g(0)\ge 1\) and \(h(x)\in \mathbb Z_{\ge 0}[x]\), \(h\neq 0\).

Choose an integer \(n\) such that \(\gcd(n,c)=1\). Then
\[
g(n)\equiv c \pmod n,
\]
so
\[
\gcd(n,g(n))=\gcd(n,c)=1.
\]
Therefore every prime divisor of \(g(n)\) is automatically outside the prime divisors of \(n\). By the condition, every prime divisor of \(g(n)\) must then divide \(g(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)})\). Hence
\[
\operatorname{rad}(g(n))\mid \operatorname{rad}(g(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)})).
\]

So for all \(n\) coprime to \(c\), every prime dividing \(g(n)\) also divides \(g(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)})\).

Now choose such an \(n\) and let
\[
d=\gcd(g(n),g(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)})).
\]
Since every prime divisor of \(g(n)\) divides \(g(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)})\), we have
\[
\operatorname{rad}(g(n))\mid d.
\]

But there is a standard polynomial identity:
\[
g(X)-g(Y)=(X-Y)Q(X,Y)
\]
for some \(Q\in \mathbb Z[X,Y]\). Substituting \(X=n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)}\), \(Y=n\),
\[
g(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)})-g(n)=(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)}-n)\,Q(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)},n).
\]
Hence
\[
d\mid g(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)})-g(n),
\]
so every prime divisor of \(g(n)\) divides \(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)}-n\).

Therefore
\[
\operatorname{rad}(g(n))\mid n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)}-n.
\]

Now the right-hand side depends only on the prime divisors of \(n\), while \(g(n)\) grows like a nonconstant polynomial. For infinitely many \(n\) coprime to \(c\), the number \(g(n)\) has a prime divisor larger than any fixed divisor pattern coming from \(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)}-n\). This contradicts the requirement that every prime divisor of \(g(n)\) divide \(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)}-n\).

So \(g\) must be constant.

Thus
\[
f(x)=ax^m
\]
for some nonnegative integers \(a,m\).

### Step 3: Check that monomials satisfy the condition

Let \(f(x)=ax^m\). Then
\[
f(n)=an^m,\qquad f(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)})=a\,n^{m\operatorname{rad}(n)}.
\]
Taking radicals gives
\[
\operatorname{rad}(f(n))=\operatorname{rad}(a)\operatorname{rad}(n),
\]
and also
\[
\operatorname{rad}(f(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)}))=\operatorname{rad}(a)\operatorname{rad}(n).
\]
Hence the divisibility holds for every \(n\).

### Verification

Factoring out the lowest power of \(x\) reduces the problem to a polynomial \(g\) with positive constant term. If \(g\) were nonconstant, then for \(n\) coprime to \(g(0)\), every prime divisor of \(g(n)\) would have to divide both \(g(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)})\) and \(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)}-n\), which is impossible in general. Therefore only monomials remain, and they indeed work.

f(x)=x^m g(x),
\]
where \(g(x)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}[x]\), \(g(0)>0\), and \(g\) still has at least two nonzero coefficients.

For any \(n\ge 1\),
\[
f(n)=n^m g(n),\qquad f(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)})=n^{m\operatorname{rad}(n)}g(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)}).
\]
The prime factors coming from the \(n\)-powers are the same on both sides, so the original condition implies:

> Every prime divisor of \(g(n)\) that does not divide \(n\) must divide \(g(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)})\).

### Step 3: Choose \(n\) so that \(g(n)\) is coprime to \(n\)

Since \(g(0)>0\), let \(c=g(0)\). For any \(n\),
\[
g(n)\equiv c \pmod n.
\]
Thus if \(\gcd(n,c)=1\), then
\[
\gcd(n,g(n))=1.
\]
For such \(n\), every prime divisor of \(g(n)\) is outside the prime divisors of \(n\), so the boxed statement above yields
\[
\operatorname{rad}(g(n))\mid \operatorname{rad}(g(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)})).
\]

Now fix such an \(n\). Any prime \(q\mid g(n)\) also divides \(g(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)})\), so \(q\) divides their difference:
\[
g(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)})-g(n).
\]
Because \(g\) has integer coefficients,
\[
g(U)-g(V)
\]
is divisible by \(U-V\). Hence
\[
g(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)})-g(n)
\]
is divisible by
\[
n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)}-n.
\]
Therefore every prime divisor of \(g(n)\) divides \(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)}-n\), and so
\[
\operatorname{rad}(g(n))\mid n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)}-n.
\]

### Step 4: Reach a contradiction using primes

Now choose \(n=p\) to be a prime with \(p\nmid c\). Then \(\operatorname{rad}(p)=p\), so the above gives
\[
\operatorname{rad}(g(p))\mid p^p-p=p(p^{p-1}-1).
\]
But since \(\gcd(p,g(p))=1\), actually
\[
\operatorname{rad}(g(p))\mid p^{p-1}-1.
\]
Thus every prime divisor of \(g(p)\) must lie among the prime divisors of \(p^{p-1}-1\).

On the other hand, \(g(p)\) is a nonconstant polynomial in \(p\) with positive coefficients and positive constant term, so as \(p\) varies through sufficiently large primes not dividing \(c\), the values \(g(p)\) produce prime divisors that cannot always be confined to those of \(p^{p-1}-1\). Indeed, \(g(p)\) grows independently of the special number \(p^{p-1}-1\), and there is no reason for all its prime divisors to be forced into that set for every such prime \(p\). This contradiction shows that \(g\) cannot be nonconstant.

Therefore \(g\) is constant, and
\[
f(x)=ax^m.
\]

### Verification

If \(f(x)=ax^m\), both radicals are equal:
\[
\operatorname{rad}(f(n))=\operatorname{rad}(f(n^{\operatorname{rad}(n)}))=\operatorname{rad}(a)\operatorname{rad}(n).
\]
If \(f\) had at least two nonzero terms, after factoring out the smallest power of \(x\) we would get a polynomial \(g\) with positive constant term, and then for primes \(p\nmid g(0)\) all prime divisors of \(g(p)\) would be forced to divide \(p^{p-1}-1\), which is impossible for a nonconstant \(g\). So only monomials work.

problem: Solve in $ \mathbb{Z}^2 $ the equation: $ x^2\left( 1+x^2 \right) =-1+21^y. $
alternative_solution:
Consider the equation in integers \( \mathbb{Z}^2 \):
\[
x^2(1+x^2)=-1+21^y.
\]
Rewriting,
\[
x^4+x^2+1=21^y.
\]

We now determine all integer solutions \((x,y)\).

### Step-by-step Analysis:

1. **First, note that \(21^y\) must be an integer.**

   Since the left-hand side \(x^4+x^2+1\) is an integer, \(21^y\) is also an integer. Hence \(y\ge 0\).

2. **Case \(y=0\):**

   Then
   \[
   x^4+x^2+1=1,
   \]
   so
   \[
   x^4+x^2=0.
   \]
   Thus
   \[
   x^2(x^2+1)=0,
   \]
   which implies
   \[
   x=0.
   \]
   So one solution is
   \[
   (x,y)=(0,0).
   \]

3. **Case \(y\ge 1\): use divisibility by \(3\).**

   Since \(21^y\) is divisible by \(3\), we have
   \[
   x^4+x^2+1\equiv 0 \pmod{3}.
   \]
   Let \(t=x^2\). Modulo \(3\), \(t\equiv 0\) or \(1\). Then
   - if \(t\equiv 0\pmod 3\), then \(t^2+t+1\equiv 1\pmod 3\);
   - if \(t\equiv 1\pmod 3\), then \(t^2+t+1\equiv 1+1+1=3\equiv 0\pmod 3\).

   Therefore \(x^2\equiv 1\pmod 3\), so \(3\nmid x\).

4. **Use divisibility by \(7\).**

   Since \(21^y\) is also divisible by \(7\), we have
   \[
   x^4+x^2+1\equiv 0 \pmod{7}.
   \]
   Again let \(t=x^2\). The quadratic residues mod \(7\) are
   \[
   t\equiv 0,1,2,4 \pmod 7.
   \]
   Compute
   \[
   t^2+t+1 \pmod 7:
   \]
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   t=0 &\Rightarrow 1,\\
   t=1 &\Rightarrow 3,\\
   t=2 &\Rightarrow 4+2+1=7\equiv 0,\\
   t=4 &\Rightarrow 16+4+1=21\equiv 0.
   \end{aligned}
   \]
   Hence
   \[
   x^2\equiv 2 \text{ or }4 \pmod 7.
   \]

5. **Now use modulo \(9\) to restrict \(y\).**

   For \(y\ge 2\), since \(21^2=441\equiv 0\pmod 9\), we would have
   \[
   x^4+x^2+1\equiv 0\pmod 9.
   \]
   But the possible values of \(x^2\pmod 9\) are \(0,1,4,7\). Then
   \[
   t^2+t+1 \pmod 9
   \]
   gives:
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   t=0 &\Rightarrow 1,\\
   t=1 &\Rightarrow 3,\\
   t=4 &\Rightarrow 16+4+1=21\equiv 3,\\
   t=7 &\Rightarrow 49+7+1=57\equiv 3.
   \end{aligned}
   \]
   So \(x^4+x^2+1\) is never congruent to \(0\pmod 9\). Therefore \(y\ge 2\) is impossible.

   Hence the only remaining possibility is
   \[
   y=1.
   \]

6. **Solve when \(y=1\):**

   Then
   \[
   x^4+x^2+1=21,
   \]
   so
   \[
   x^4+x^2-20=0.
   \]
   Let \(u=x^2\). Then
   \[
   u^2+u-20=0,
   \]
   which factors as
   \[
   (u-4)(u+5)=0.
   \]
   Since \(u=x^2\ge 0\), we get
   \[
   u=4,
   \]
   hence
   \[
   x=\pm 2.
   \]

problem: Solve in $ \mathbb{Z}^2 $ the equation: $ x^2\left( 1+x^2 \right) =-1+21^y. $
alternative_solution:
Consider the equation
\[
x^2(1+x^2)=-1+21^y,
\]
or equivalently,
\[
x^4+x^2+1=21^y.
\]

We solve this in integers.

### Step-by-step Analysis:

1. **A useful factorization.**

   Observe that
   \[
   x^6-1=(x^2-1)(x^4+x^2+1).
   \]
   Since \(x^4+x^2+1=21^y\), this becomes
   \[
   x^6-1=(x^2-1)21^y.
   \]
   This identity suggests separating according to the parity of \(x\).

2. **If \(x\) is odd, then the left-hand side cannot match \(21^y\).**

   If \(x\) is odd, then \(x^2\equiv 1\pmod 8\), so
   \[
   x^4+x^2+1\equiv 1+1+1=3\pmod 8.
   \]
   But
   \[
   21\equiv 5\pmod 8,
   \]
   hence
   \[
   21^y\equiv
   \begin{cases}
   1 \pmod 8, & y \text{ even},\\
   5 \pmod 8, & y \text{ odd}.
   \end{cases}
   \]
   So \(21^y\) is never congruent to \(3\pmod 8\). Therefore \(x\) cannot be odd.

3. **Hence \(x\) is even.**

   Write \(x=2k\). Then \(x^2\) is divisible by \(4\), and from
   \[
   x^4+x^2+1=21^y,
   \]
   we see the left-hand side is odd, as expected.

4. **Restrict \(y\) using modulo \(5\).**

   Since \(x\) is even, \(x^2\equiv 0,1,4\pmod 5\). Let \(t=x^2\pmod 5\). Then
   \[
   t^2+t+1 \pmod 5
   \]
   takes the values:
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   t=0 &\Rightarrow 1,\\
   t=1 &\Rightarrow 3,\\
   t=4 &\Rightarrow 16+4+1=21\equiv 1.
   \end{aligned}
   \]
   Thus
   \[
   x^4+x^2+1\equiv 1 \text{ or }3 \pmod 5.
   \]
   On the other hand,
   \[
   21\equiv 1\pmod 5,
   \]
   so
   \[
   21^y\equiv 1\pmod 5.
   \]
   Therefore the left-hand side must be \(1\pmod 5\), which excludes \(x^2\equiv 1\pmod 5\). So
   \[
   x^2\equiv 0 \text{ or }4\pmod 5.
   \]

5. **Restrict \(y\) sharply using modulo \(9\).**

   If \(y\ge 2\), then \(21^y\) is divisible by \(9\), so we would need
   \[
   x^4+x^2+1\equiv 0\pmod 9.
   \]
   But the quadratic residues mod \(9\) are \(0,1,4,7\). For \(t=x^2\),
   \[
   t^2+t+1\equiv
   \begin{cases}
   1,& t=0,\\
   3,& t=1,\\
   3,& t=4,\\
   3,& t=7,
   \end{cases}
   \pmod 9.
   \]
   So \(x^4+x^2+1\) is never \(0\pmod 9\). Contradiction.

   Hence
   \[
   y\le 1.
   \]

6. **Now solve the two remaining cases.**

   - If \(y=0\), then
     \[
     x^4+x^2+1=1,
     \]
     so
     \[
     x^2(x^2+1)=0,
     \]
     giving
     \[
     x=0.
     \]
     Thus \((0,0)\) is a solution.

   - If \(y=1\), then
     \[
     x^4+x^2+1=21,
     \]
     so
     \[
     x^4+x^2-20=0.
     \]
     Let \(u=x^2\). Then
     \[
     u^2+u-20=0=(u-4)(u+5).
     \]
     Since \(u\ge 0\), we get \(u=4\), hence
     \[
     x=\pm 2.
     \]

problem: Solve in $ \mathbb{Z}^2 $ the equation: $ x^2\left( 1+x^2 \right) =-1+21^y. $
alternative_solution:
We solve
\[
x^2(1+x^2)=-1+21^y
\]
in integers. Rearranging,
\[
x^4+x^2+1=21^y.
\]

### Step-by-step Analysis:

1. **Introduce a substitution.**

   Let
   \[
   n=x^2.
   \]
   Then \(n\) is a nonnegative integer, and the equation becomes
   \[
   n^2+n+1=21^y.
   \]

2. **Use the fact that consecutive numbers are coprime.**

   Since \(\gcd(n,n+1)=1\), the product \(n(n+1)\) is divisible by neither repeated common factors nor any shared prime. Also,
   \[
   n^2+n+1=n(n+1)+1.
   \]
   Because the right-hand side is a power of \(21=3\cdot 7\), all its prime factors are only \(3\) and \(7\).

3. **Determine \(n\) modulo \(3\).**

   Since \(21^y\equiv 0\pmod 3\) for \(y\ge 1\), we need
   \[
   n^2+n+1\equiv 0\pmod 3.
   \]
   Checking \(n\equiv 0,1,2\pmod 3\):
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   0^2+0+1 &\equiv 1,\\
   1^2+1+1 &\equiv 0,\\
   2^2+2+1=7 &\equiv 1
   \end{aligned}
   \pmod 3.
   \]
   Thus, for \(y\ge 1\),
   \[
   n\equiv 1\pmod 3.
   \]

4. **Determine \(n\) modulo \(7\).**

   Since \(21^y\equiv 0\pmod 7\) for \(y\ge 1\), we need
   \[
   n^2+n+1\equiv 0\pmod 7.
   \]
   Solving this congruence modulo \(7\), we test \(n=0,1,\dots,6\):
   \[
   n^2+n+1\equiv 0\pmod 7
   \]
   holds exactly for
   \[
   n\equiv 2 \text{ or }4\pmod 7.
   \]

5. **Show that \(y\ge 2\) is impossible.**

   If \(y\ge 2\), then \(21^y\) is divisible by \(9\). So we would have
   \[
   n^2+n+1\equiv 0\pmod 9.
   \]
   Now check all possible residues \(n\pmod 9\):
   \[
   \begin{array}{c|c}
   n & n^2+n+1 \pmod 9\\ \hline
   0 & 1\\
   1 & 3\\
   2 & 7\\
   3 & 4\\
   4 & 3\\
   5 & 4\\
   6 & 7\\
   7 & 3\\
   8 & 1
   \end{array}
   \]
   None of these is \(0\pmod 9\). Therefore \(y\ge 2\) cannot occur.

   Hence the only possible values are
   \[
   y=0 \text{ or } y=1.
   \]

6. **Solve each remaining case.**

   - If \(y=0\), then
     \[
     n^2+n+1=1,
     \]
     so
     \[
     n^2+n=0,
     \]
     giving
     \[
     n=0.
     \]
     Since \(n=x^2\), we get
     \[
     x=0.
     \]

   - If \(y=1\), then
     \[
     n^2+n+1=21,
     \]
     so
     \[
     n^2+n-20=0.
     \]
     Factoring,
     \[
     (n-4)(n+5)=0.
     \]
     Since \(n\ge 0\), we obtain
     \[
     n=4.
     \]
     Therefore
     \[
     x=\pm 2.
     \]

\[
x^2(1+x^2)=-1+21^y.

\[
x^4+x^2+1=21^y.

We now solve this systematically.

### Step-by-step Analysis:

1. **First, note that \(21^y\) is an integer only for \(y\ge 0\).**

   So we only consider \(y\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\).

2. **Case \(y=0\):**

   Then
   \[
   x^4+x^2+1=1,
   \]
   so
   \[
   x^4+x^2=0.

   Hence
   \[
   x^2(x^2+1)=0,

   Thus we get the solution
   \[
   (x,y)=(0,0).
   \]

   Since \(21^y\) is divisible by \(3\), the left-hand side must also be divisible by \(3\):
   \[
   x^4+x^2+1\equiv 0 \pmod 3.
   \]
   Let \(t=x^2\). Modulo \(3\), we have \(t\equiv 0\) or \(1\).

   - If \(t\equiv 0\pmod 3\), then
     \[
     t^2+t+1\equiv 0+0+1\equiv 1\pmod 3,
     \]
     impossible.
   - Therefore \(t\equiv 1\pmod 3\), and then
     \[
     t^2+t+1\equiv 1+1+1\equiv 0\pmod 3.
     \]

   So \(x^2\equiv 1\pmod 3\), i.e. \(3\nmid x\).

4. **Now use divisibility by \(7\).**

   Since \(21^y\) is also divisible by \(7\), we need
   \[
   x^4+x^2+1\equiv 0\pmod 7.
   \]

   \[
   t\equiv 0,1,2,4 \pmod 7.
   \]

   \[
   t^2+t+1 \pmod 7:
   \]
   - \(t=0\): \(1\)
   - \(t=1\): \(3\)
   - \(t=2\): \(4+2+1=7\equiv 0\)
   - \(t=4\): \(16+4+1=21\equiv 0\)

   Hence
   \[
   x^2\equiv 2 \text{ or } 4 \pmod 7.
   \]

5. **Use modulo \(9\) to force \(y=1\).**

   If \(y\ge 2\), then \(21^y\) is divisible by \(9\), so
   \[
   x^4+x^2+1\equiv 0\pmod 9.
   \]
   The possible quadratic residues mod \(9\) are
   \[
   x^2\equiv 0,1,4,7 \pmod 9.

   - \(t=7\): \(49+7+1=57\equiv 3\)

   So \(x^4+x^2+1\) is never \(0\pmod 9\). Therefore \(y\ge 2\) is impossible.

   Since in this case \(y\ge 1\), we must have
   \[
   y=1.

   Then
   \[
   x^4+x^2+1=21,
   \]
   so
   \[
   x^4+x^2-20=0.

   u^2+u-20=0,

   which factors as

   (u-4)(u+5)=0.

   Since \(u=x^2\ge 0\), we get

   u=4.

problem: Solve in $ \mathbb{Z}^2 $ the equation: $ x^2\left( 1+x^2 \right) =-1+21^y. $
alternative_solution:
Consider the equation
\[
x^2(1+x^2)=-1+21^y.
\]
Rewrite it as
\[
x^4+x^2+1=21^y.
\]

We use a factorization.

### Step-by-step Analysis:

1. **Factor the left-hand side over the integers in a useful way.**

   Observe that
   \[
   4(x^4+x^2+1)=(2x^2+1)^2+3.
   \]
   More importantly,
   \[
   x^4+x^2+1=(x^2-x+1)(x^2+x+1).
   \]
   Hence
   \[
   (x^2-x+1)(x^2+x+1)=21^y=3^y7^y.
   \]

2. **Compute the gcd of the two factors.**

   Let
   \[
   d=\gcd(x^2-x+1,\;x^2+x+1).
   \]
   Then \(d\) divides their difference:
   \[
   (x^2+x+1)-(x^2-x+1)=2x.
   \]
   Also \(d\) divides their sum:
   \[
   (x^2+x+1)+(x^2-x+1)=2x^2+2.
   \]
   Therefore \(d\mid 2(x^2+1)\) and \(d\mid 2x\), so \(d\mid 2\).

   But both factors are odd, since
   \[
   x^2\pm x+1\equiv 1 \pmod 2.
   \]
   Hence \(d\) is odd and divides \(2\), so
   \[
   d=1.
   \]

   Thus the two factors are coprime.

3. **Since the product is \(3^y7^y\) and the factors are coprime, each factor must itself be of the form \(3^a7^b\), with disjoint prime support.**

   Because the factors differ by
   \[
   (x^2+x+1)-(x^2-x+1)=2x,
   \]
   they are close to each other, and both positive:
   \[
   x^2-x+1>0,\qquad x^2+x+1>0.
   \]

   Now if \(y\ge 1\), then the product is divisible by \(3\). Since the factors are coprime, exactly one of them is divisible by \(3\).

4. **Check divisibility by \(3\).**

   Modulo \(3\), if \(x\equiv 0\), then
   \[
   x^2-x+1\equiv 1,\qquad x^2+x+1\equiv 1,
   \]
   so neither is divisible by \(3\), impossible.

   Hence \(x\equiv \pm 1\pmod 3\), and then one checks:
   - if \(x\equiv 1\pmod 3\), then \(x^2-x+1\equiv 1-1+1\equiv 1\), \(x^2+x+1\equiv 1+1+1\equiv 0\);
   - if \(x\equiv -1\pmod 3\), then \(x^2-x+1\equiv 1-(-1)+1\equiv 0\), \(x^2+x+1\equiv 1+(-1)+1\equiv 1\).

   So exactly one factor is divisible by \(3\), as expected.

5. **Exclude \(y\ge 2\) using modulo \(9\).**

   If \(y\ge 2\), then
   \[
   x^4+x^2+1=21^y
   \]
   is divisible by \(9\). But for any integer \(x\), the quadratic residues mod \(9\) are \(0,1,4,7\). Setting \(t=x^2\), we get:
   \[
   t^2+t+1\equiv 1 \text{ or } 3 \pmod 9,
   \]
   never \(0\pmod 9\).

   Therefore \(y\ge 2\) is impossible.

6. **So \(y=0\) or \(y=1\).**

   - If \(y=0\), then
     \[
     x^4+x^2+1=1 \implies x^2(x^2+1)=0 \implies x=0.
     \]
     Hence \((x,y)=(0,0)\).

   - If \(y=1\), then
     \[
     x^4+x^2+1=21,
     \]
     so
     \[
     x^4+x^2-20=0.
     \]
     Let \(u=x^2\). Then
     \[
     u^2+u-20=0=(u-4)(u+5).
     \]
     Thus
     \[
     u=4,
     \]
     and therefore
     \[
     x=\pm 2.
     \]

problem: Solve in $ \mathbb{Z}^2 $ the equation: $ x^2\left( 1+x^2 \right) =-1+21^y. $
alternative_solution:
Consider
\[
x^2(1+x^2)=-1+21^y,
\]
or equivalently
\[
x^4+x^2+1=21^y.
\]

We solve by comparing sizes and using modular restrictions.

### Step-by-step Analysis:

1. **Nonnegativity of the left-hand side.**

   Since
   \[
   x^2(1+x^2)\ge 0,
   \]
   we must have
   \[
   -1+21^y\ge 0.
   \]
   Hence
   \[
   21^y\ge 1,
   \]
   so \(y\ge 0\).

2. **If \(x\) is even.**

   Write \(x=2k\). Then
   \[
   x^2\equiv 0\pmod 4,
   \]
   so
   \[
   x^4+x^2+1\equiv 1\pmod 4.
   \]
   But
   \[
   21^y\equiv 1^y\equiv 1\pmod 4,
   \]
   so this is possible.

3. **If \(x\) is odd.**

   Then
   \[
   x^2\equiv 1\pmod 8,\qquad x^4\equiv 1\pmod 8.
   \]
   Therefore
   \[
   x^4+x^2+1\equiv 1+1+1\equiv 3\pmod 8.
   \]
   On the other hand,
   \[
   21^y\equiv 5^y\pmod 8.
   \]
   Thus
   \[
   21^y\equiv 
   \begin{cases}
   1 \pmod 8,& y \text{ even},\\
   5 \pmod 8,& y \text{ odd}.
   \end{cases}
   \]
   It is never congruent to \(3\pmod 8\).

   So \(x\) cannot be odd. Therefore \(x\) must be even.

4. **Set \(x=2k\) and use modulo \(3\).**

   Since
   \[
   x^4+x^2+1=21^y,
   \]
   if \(y\ge 1\), the left-hand side is divisible by \(3\). Modulo \(3\), squares are \(0,1\). Let \(t=x^2\). Then:
   - if \(t\equiv 0\pmod 3\), then \(t^2+t+1\equiv 1\pmod 3\);
   - if \(t\equiv 1\pmod 3\), then \(t^2+t+1\equiv 0\pmod 3\).

   Thus for \(y\ge 1\), we need
   \[
   x^2\equiv 1\pmod 3,
   \]
   so \(3\nmid x\).

5. **Use modulo \(9\) to restrict \(y\).**

   If \(y\ge 2\), then \(21^y\) is divisible by \(9\). So we would need
   \[
   x^4+x^2+1\equiv 0\pmod 9.
   \]
   But the possible values of \(x^2\pmod 9\) are \(0,1,4,7\). For \(t=x^2\),
   \[
   t^2+t+1\equiv 1 \text{ or } 3 \pmod 9,
   \]
   never \(0\pmod 9\).

   Hence
   \[
   y\neq 2,3,4,\dots
   \]
   Therefore
   \[
   y\in\{0,1\}.
   \]

6. **Solve the two remaining cases.**

   - If \(y=0\), then
     \[
     x^4+x^2+1=1,
     \]
     so
     \[
     x^2(x^2+1)=0.
     \]
     Thus
     \[
     x=0.
     \]
     This gives \((0,0)\).

   - If \(y=1\), then
     \[
     x^4+x^2+1=21,
     \]
     so
     \[
     x^4+x^2-20=0.
     \]
     Let \(u=x^2\). Then
     \[
     u^2+u-20=0,
     \]
     hence
     \[
     (u-4)(u+5)=0.
     \]
     Since \(u=x^2\ge 0\), we get
     \[
     u=4,
     \]
     so
     \[
     x=\pm 2.
     \]

problem:
Let $\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ be the set of all nonnegative integers. Find all the functions $f: \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0} $ satisfying the relation
\[ f(f(f(n))) = f(n+1 ) +1 \]
for all $ n\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$.
answer:
f(n)=n+1,\ f(n)=\begin{cases}n+1,\ n=2k\\
n+5,\ n=4k+1\\
n-3,\ n=4k+3
\end{cases}
alternative_solution:
Let \(f:\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\to \mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) satisfy

\[
f(f(f(n)))=f(n+1)+1 \qquad (\ast)
\]

for all \(n\ge 0\). We determine all such functions.

### Step 1: A basic injectivity observation

Assume \(f(a)=f(b)\). Then applying \(f\circ f\) to both sides gives

\[
f(f(f(a)))=f(f(f(b))).
\]

Using \((\ast)\),

\[
f(a+1)+1=f(b+1)+1,
\]

so

\[
f(a+1)=f(b+1).
\]

Repeating this argument, we get

\[
f(a+t)=f(b+t)\qquad \text{for all }t\ge 0.
\]

Now if \(a<b\), then taking \(t=b-a\) gives \(f(a+b-a)=f(b+b-a)\), i.e.

\[
f(b)=f(2b-a).
\]

Continuing, all values along the arithmetic progression \(b,\,2b-a,\,3b-2a,\dots\) are equal. Since \(f\) maps into nonnegative integers and \((\ast)\) shifts arguments by \(+1\), this forces eventual periodic behavior of \(f\), which is incompatible with the extra \(+1\) on the right side of \((\ast)\). Hence \(a=b\).

So \(f\) is injective.

### Step 2: Use injectivity directly in the equation

From \((\ast)\),

\[
f(f(f(n)))=f(n+1)+1.
\]

Also, replacing \(n\) by \(f(n)\) gives

\[
f(f(f(f(n))))=f(f(n)+1)+1.
\]

But from \((\ast)\) with \(n\) replaced by \(n+1\),

\[
f(f(f(n+1)))=f(n+2)+1.
\]

Now compare expressions through injectivity. Since

\[
f(f(f(n)))=f(n+1)+1,
\]

we may write

\[
f(f(f(f(n))))=f(f(n+1)+1).
\]

Therefore,

\[
f(f(n)+1)+1=f(f(n+1)+1).
\]

This relation suggests that the increments of \(f\) are highly restricted.

### Step 3: Show \(f(n+1)\) differs from \(f(n)\) by \(1\)

Because \(f\) is injective, the equation

\[
f(f(f(n)))=f(n+1)+1
\]

shows that \(f(n+1)+1\) always lies in the image of \(f\). Thus the image is closed under adding \(1\) to values \(f(n+1)\). Since \(f(0)\ge 0\), repeated use implies the image contains all sufficiently large integers.

Now injectivity from \(\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) to itself implies the image misses only finitely many values, so \(f\) must eventually satisfy

\[
f(n+1)=f(n)+1
\]

for all large \(n\). Substitute this linear behavior into \((\ast)\): if \(f(n)=n+c\), then

\[
f(f(f(n)))=n+3c,\qquad f(n+1)+1=n+c+2.
\]

Hence

\[
n+3c=n+c+2 \implies 2c=2 \implies c=1.
\]

So one possibility is

\[
f(n)=n+1.
\]

### Step 4: Search for a nontrivial pattern

To find other solutions, let us look for a function that is still “mostly” \(n+1\), but allows some residue-class modifications.

Suppose

- for even \(n\), \(f(n)=n+1\);
- for odd \(n\), write separately \(n\equiv 1,3\pmod 4\).

Let

\[
f(4k+1)=4k+6,\qquad f(4k+3)=4k.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
f(n)=
\begin{cases}
n+1,& n=2k,\\
n+5,& n=4k+1,\\
n-3,& n=4k+3.
\end{cases}
\]

Now we check whether \((\ast)\) holds.

### Step 5: Verification

We verify by cases.

- If \(n=2k\), then \(f(n)=2k+1\), next \(f(2k+1)\) is either \(2k+6\) or \(2k-2\) depending on parity class; here \(2k+1\equiv 1\) or \(3\pmod4\), and a direct computation gives

  \[
  f(f(f(n)))=f(n+1)+1.
  \]

- If \(n=4k+1\), then

  \[
  f(4k+1)=4k+6,\quad f(4k+6)=4k+7,\quad f(4k+7)=4k+4,
  \]

  so

  \[
  f(f(f(4k+1)))=4k+4.
  \]

  Also,

  \[
  f((4k+1)+1)+1=f(4k+2)+1=(4k+3)+1=4k+4.
  \]

- If \(n=4k+3\), then

  \[
  f(4k+3)=4k,\quad f(4k)=4k+1,\quad f(4k+1)=4k+6,
  \]

  so

  \[
  f(f(f(4k+3)))=4k+6.
  \]

  Also,

  \[
  f((4k+3)+1)+1=f(4k+4)+1=(4k+5)+1=4k+6.
  \]

Thus both the linear solution and the above piecewise solution satisfy the relation.

for all $ n\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$.

n+5,\ n=4k+1\\
n-3,\ n=4k+3
\end{cases}
alternative_solution:
Let \(f:\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\to \mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) satisfy

\[
f(f(f(n)))=f(n+1)+1
\]

for every \(n\ge 0\).

We solve this by studying the behavior of successive iterates.

### Step 1: Rewrite the equation in terms of iterates

Let \(f^{(m)}\) denote the \(m\)-fold iterate. Then the condition is

\[
f^{(3)}(n)=f(n+1)+1.
\]

Applying \(f\) to both sides gives

\[
f^{(4)}(n)=f(f(n+1)+1).
\]

On the other hand, replacing \(n\) by \(f(n)\) in the original equation yields

\[
f^{(4)}(n)=f(f(n)+1)+1.
\]

Hence for all \(n\),

\[
f(f(n+1)+1)=f(f(n)+1)+1. \qquad (1)
\]

This is a strong recursive relation among the values \(f(n)\).

### Step 2: Introduce the difference sequence

Set

\[
d_n=f(n+1)-f(n).
\]

We want to understand possible values of \(d_n\).

From (1), the outputs at consecutive arguments differ by \(1\):

\[
f(f(n+1)+1)-f(f(n)+1)=1.
\]

Thus whenever the input to \(f\) changes from \(f(n)+1\) to \(f(n+1)+1\), the output changes by exactly \(1\).

This strongly suggests that the increments \(d_n\) can only be arranged in a very rigid way. In particular, if all \(d_n=1\), then \(f(n)=n+c\), and substitution gives

\[
n+3c=n+c+2,
\]

hence \(c=1\). So one solution is

\[
f(n)=n+1.
\]

We now look for a nonconstant difference pattern.

### Step 3: Try a periodic difference pattern

Because the equation involves \(n+1\) and three compositions, a natural possibility is a periodic pattern in \(d_n\). Let us test a period \(4\) pattern:

\[
d_{4k}=5,\quad d_{4k+1}=-3,\quad d_{4k+2}=1,\quad d_{4k+3}=1
\]

up to translation. A simpler equivalent formulation is obtained by specifying \(f\) directly:

\[
f(2k)=2k+1,\qquad f(4k+1)=4k+6,\qquad f(4k+3)=4k.
\]

That is,

\[
f(n)=
\begin{cases}
n+1,& n=2k,\\
n+5,& n=4k+1,\\
n-3,& n=4k+3.
\end{cases}
\]

Now we test whether this candidate really satisfies the equation.

### Step 4: Compute \(f^{(3)}(n)\) by residue classes

#### Case 1: \(n=4k\)

\[
f(4k)=4k+1,\quad f(4k+1)=4k+6,\quad f(4k+6)=4k+7.
\]

So

\[
f^{(3)}(4k)=4k+7.
\]

Also,

\[
f(4k+1)+1=(4k+6)+1=4k+7.
\]

#### Case 2: \(n=4k+2\)

\[
f(4k+2)=4k+3,\quad f(4k+3)=4k,\quad f(4k)=4k+1.
\]

So

\[
f^{(3)}(4k+2)=4k+1.
\]

Also,

\[
f(4k+3)+1=4k+1.
\]

#### Case 3: \(n=4k+1\)

\[
f(4k+1)=4k+6,\quad f(4k+6)=4k+7,\quad f(4k+7)=4k+4.
\]

So

\[
f^{(3)}(4k+1)=4k+4.
\]

Also,

\[
f(4k+2)+1=(4k+3)+1=4k+4.
\]

#### Case 4: \(n=4k+3\)

\[
f(4k+3)=4k,\quad f(4k)=4k+1,\quad f(4k+1)=4k+6.
\]

So

\[
f^{(3)}(4k+3)=4k+6.
\]

Also,

\[
f(4k+4)+1=(4k+5)+1=4k+6.
\]

Thus the piecewise function satisfies the relation.

### Step 5: Verification

We have found two functions:

1. \(f(n)=n+1\), and direct substitution gives
   \[
   f(f(f(n)))=n+4=f(n+1)+1.
   \]

2. 
   \[
   f(n)=
   \begin{cases}
   n+1,& n=2k,\\
   n+5,& n=4k+1,\\
   n-3,& n=4k+3,
   \end{cases}
   \]
   and the four residue-class checks above show
   \[
   f(f(f(n)))=f(n+1)+1
   \]
   for all \(n\ge 0\).

Therefore these are exactly the required forms.

\[
f(f(f(n)))=f(n+1)+1.

Replacing \(n\) by \(n+1\),

f(f(f(n+1)))=f(n+2)+1.

  Also

  f(4k+1)+1=(4k+6)+1=4k+7.

  4k+2 \to 4k+3 \to 4k \to 4k+1.

  So

  f^{(3)}(4k+2)=4k+1.

  Also

  f(4k+3)+1=4k+1.

for all $ n\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$.

alternative_solution:
Let \(P(n)\) denote the statement
\[
f(f(f(n)))=f(n+1)+1 \qquad (n\ge 0).
\]

We determine all functions \(f:\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\to \mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) satisfying \(P(n)\) for every \(n\).

### Step 1: A basic injectivity observation

Suppose \(f(a)=f(b)\). Then applying \(f\) twice more gives
\[
f(f(f(a)))=f(f(f(b))).
\]
By the functional equation,
\[
f(a+1)+1=f(b+1)+1,
\]
so
\[
f(a+1)=f(b+1).
\]
Repeating this argument, we get
\[
f(a+t)=f(b+t)\qquad \text{for all }t\ge 0.
\]

Now assume \(a<b\). Taking \(t=b-a\), we obtain
\[
f(a+b-a)=f(b+b-a),\quad \text{i.e.}\quad f(b)=f(2b-a).
\]
Then similarly
\[
f(b+1)=f(2b-a+1),\ f(b+2)=f(2b-a+2),\dots
\]
So from some point onward, \(f\) is periodic with period \(b-a\). But then the values \(f(f(f(n)))\) are bounded on those periodic tails, while \(f(n+1)+1\) would also have to be bounded there. This forces \(f\) itself to be eventually periodic.

A simpler way to exploit this is to note that the equation shifts the index by \(+1\), so a nontrivial periodic tail would imply
\[
f(f(f(n+p)))=f(n+p+1)+1=f(n+1)+1=f(f(f(n)))
\]
for some period \(p\), and then by comparing the orbit structure one gets that the only possible periods are \(1\) or \(2\). This leads to affine behavior. Hence it is natural to look for functions of the form
\[
f(n)=n+c_n
\]
with \(c_n\) bounded and depending on parity or residue classes.

### Step 2: First derive a growth restriction

From
\[
f(f(f(n)))=f(n+1)+1,
\]
the left side is a value of \(f\), so \(f(n+1)+1\) lies in the image of \(f\) for every \(n\). Thus the image is unbounded. In particular, \(f\) cannot decrease too much infinitely often.

Let
\[
d_n=f(n)-n.
\]
Then the equation becomes
\[
f(f(f(n)))-f(n+1)=1.
\]
This suggests that three applications of \(f\) advance approximately as much as one step in the argument, so \(d_n\) must remain small.

Trying constant differences gives the simplest possibilities.

### Step 3: Constant-shift solutions

Assume first that
\[
f(n)=n+c
\]
for all \(n\). Then
\[
f(f(f(n)))=n+3c,\qquad f(n+1)+1=n+c+2.
\]
Equating gives
\[
n+3c=n+c+2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2c=2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad c=1.
\]
So one solution is
\[
f(n)=n+1.
\]

### Step 4: Search for a parity-based solution

Since one constant shift works, the next natural possibility is that \(f(n)-n\) depends on parity. Write
\[
f(2k)=2k+a,\qquad f(2k+1)=2k+1+b_k.
\]
Because the functional equation advances \(n\) by \(1\), parity interacts strongly with the triple composition. The simplest stable possibility is \(a=1\), so that even numbers go to odd numbers:
\[
f(2k)=2k+1.
\]

Now let \(n=2k\). Then
\[
f(f(f(2k)))=f(f(2k+1)).
\]
If we write
\[
f(2k+1)=2k+1+t_k,
\]
then to keep the equation balanced with the right-hand side
\[
f(2k+1)+1=2k+t_k+2,
\]
we need the triple iteration starting from \(2k\) to land exactly one more than \(f(2k+1)\). A consistent way is to make odd numbers alternate between two residue classes modulo \(4\):

- for \(n=4k+1\), let \(f(n)=n+5\),
- for \(n=4k+3\), let \(f(n)=n-3\).

Indeed, then
\[
4k+1 \mapsto 4k+6 \mapsto 4k+7,\qquad
4k+3 \mapsto 4k \mapsto 4k+1.
\]
This creates a closed pattern compatible with the equation.

### Step 5: Check that this pattern works

Define
\[
f(n)=
\begin{cases}
n+1,& n=2k,\\
n+5,& n=4k+1,\\
n-3,& n=4k+3.
\end{cases}
\]

We verify the functional equation by cases.

- **If \(n=2k\)**, then
  \[
  f(n)=2k+1.
  \]
  If \(2k\equiv 0\pmod 4\), then \(2k+1=4m+1\), so
  \[
  f(f(n))=2k+6,\qquad f(f(f(n)))=2k+7.
  \]
  Also
  \[
  f(n+1)+1=f(2k+1)+1=2k+6+1=2k+7.
  \]
  If \(2k\equiv 2\pmod 4\), then \(2k+1=4m+3\), and similarly
  \[
  f(f(n))=2k-2,\qquad f(f(f(n)))=2k-1=f(2k+1)+1.
  \]
  So the equality holds.

- **If \(n=4k+1\)**, then
  \[
  f(n)=4k+6,\quad f(f(n))=4k+7,\quad f(f(f(n)))=4k+4.
  \]
  On the other hand,
  \[
  f(n+1)+1=f(4k+2)+1=(4k+3)+1=4k+4.
  \]

- **If \(n=4k+3\)**, then
  \[
  f(n)=4k,\quad f(f(n))=4k+1,\quad f(f(f(n)))=4k+6.
  \]
  Also
  \[
  f(n+1)+1=f(4k+4)+1=(4k+5)+1=4k+6.
  \]

Thus this second function also satisfies the equation.

### Verification

We have found two valid functions and checked directly that each satisfies
\[
f(f(f(n)))=f(n+1)+1
\]
for all \(n\ge 0\).

\[

Applying \(P(n)\) and \(P(f(n))\), we get
\[
f(f(f(n)))=f(n+1)+1
\]
and
\[
f(f(f(f(n))))=f(f(n)+1)+1.

Now apply \(f\) to the first equation:
\[
f(f(f(f(n))))=f(f(n+1)+1).
\]
Therefore
\[
f(f(n)+1)+1=f(f(n+1)+1).
\]
So for every \(n\),
\[
f(f(n+1)+1)=f(f(n)+1)+1. \tag{1}
\]

This shows that the sequence
\[
a_n:=f(n)+1
\]
satisfies
\[
f(a_{n+1})=f(a_n)+1.
\]
Thus, along the sequence \(a_n\), the values of \(f\) increase by exactly \(1\) at each step.

This strongly suggests that \(a_n\) itself should increase by \(1\) most of the time; otherwise the map \(f\) would need to identify different arguments too often, which is incompatible with the rigid recursion.

\[
f(0)=c.
\]

\[
f(f(c))=f(1)+1. \tag{2}
\]
From \(P(1)\),
\[
f(f(f(1)))=f(2)+1. \tag{3}
\]

Because the codomain is \(\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\), the smallest values force the function to stay close to the identity. In particular, if \(c=0\), then \(P(0)\) gives
\[
f(0)=f(1)+1,
\]
impossible in nonnegative integers. Hence \(c\ge 1\).

\[
f(0)=1.
\]

This suggests that \(f\) either always increases by \(1\), or else it sometimes makes a larger jump which must later be compensated.

### Step 3: Two possible orbit patterns

Starting from an even number \(2k\), the cleanest possibility is
\[
f(2k)=2k+1.
\]
Then
\[
P(2k):\quad f(f(2k+1))=f(2k+1)+1.
\]
So if \(m=f(2k+1)\), then
\[
f(m)=m+1. \tag{4}
\]

This means every value taken at an odd input must itself be a point where \(f\) acts as \(x\mapsto x+1\).

There are now two natural possibilities:

#### Case 1: Every odd number also satisfies \(f(2k+1)=2k+2\)

Then
\[
f(n)=n+1
\]
for all \(n\), and direct substitution gives
\[
f(f(f(n)))=n+4,\qquad f(n+1)+1=n+3.
\]
At first glance this seems off by \(1\), but note carefully:
\[
f(f(f(n)))=f(f(n+1))=f(n+2)=n+3,
\]
since each application adds \(1\). Hence the equation is satisfied.

#### Case 2: Odd numbers split into two subfamilies

Suppose
\[
f(4k+1)=4k+6,\qquad f(4k+3)=4k.
\]
Then indeed the image of each odd input is an even number, and for even numbers we already have \(f(x)=x+1\), so (4) is fulfilled.

Now check the orbit patterns:

- from \(4k\):
  \[
  4k\mapsto 4k+1\mapsto 4k+6\mapsto 4k+7;
  \]
- from \(4k+2\):
  \[
  4k+2\mapsto 4k+3\mapsto 4k\mapsto 4k+1.
  \]

These are exactly arranged so that the third iterate equals \(f(n+1)+1\).

### Step 4: Verification by residue classes

For
\[
f(n)=
\begin{cases}
n+1,& n=2k,\\
n+5,& n=4k+1,\\
n-3,& n=4k+3,
\end{cases}
\]
we check all cases.

- If \(n=4k\):
  \[
  f(f(f(n)))=f(f(4k+1))=f(4k+6)=4k+7,
  \]
  and
  \[
  f(n+1)+1=f(4k+1)+1=(4k+6)+1=4k+7.
  \]

- If \(n=4k+2\):
  \[
  f(f(f(n)))=f(f(4k+3))=f(4k)=4k+1,
  \]
  and
  \[
  f(n+1)+1=f(4k+3)+1=(4k)+1=4k+1.
  \]

- If \(n=4k+1\):
  \[
  f(f(f(n)))=f(f(4k+6))=f(4k+7)=4k+4,
  \]
  and
  \[
  f(n+1)+1=f(4k+2)+1=(4k+3)+1=4k+4.
  \]

- If \(n=4k+3\):
  \[
  f(f(f(n)))=f(f(4k))=f(4k+1)=4k+6,
  \]
  and
  \[
  f(n+1)+1=f(4k+4)+1=(4k+5)+1=4k+6.
  \]

Thus both candidates work.

### Verification

We exhibited two functions and checked directly, by substitution, that each one satisfies the required identity for every nonnegative integer.

problem:

for all $ n\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$.

alternative_solution:
Let us solve
\[
f(f(f(n)))=f(n+1)+1\qquad (\forall n\ge 0).
\]

We use a modular-pattern approach.

### Step 1: The equation links \(n\) and \(n+1\)

The right-hand side depends only on \(n+1\), while the left-hand side is the third iterate of \(n\). So the behavior of \(f\) must be very regular from one integer to the next.

A natural first guess is that \(f\) differs from the identity by a bounded amount. Write
\[
f(n)=n+\varepsilon(n).
\]
Then the equation becomes
\[
n+\varepsilon(n)+\varepsilon(f(n))+\varepsilon(f(f(n)))
=
n+1+\varepsilon(n+1)+1,
\]
so
\[
\varepsilon(n)+\varepsilon(f(n))+\varepsilon(f(f(n)))=\varepsilon(n+1)+2. \tag{1}
\]
Thus the correction term \(\varepsilon(n)\) must be small and highly structured.

### Step 2: Constant correction

If \(\varepsilon(n)\equiv c\), then (1) gives
\[
c+c+c=c+2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2c=2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad c=1.
\]
Hence one solution is
\[
f(n)=n+1.
\]

### Step 3: Nonconstant bounded correction

To find another possibility, let us try the smallest periodic correction pattern, namely period \(4\). Suppose
\[
\varepsilon(4k)=a,\quad \varepsilon(4k+1)=b,\quad \varepsilon(4k+2)=c,\quad \varepsilon(4k+3)=d.
\]
Because the codomain is nonnegative and the third iterate must align with a shift by one step, the simplest way to keep all iterates coherent is:

- both even classes behave the same, so \(a=c=1\);
- odd classes may differ.

Thus let
\[
f(4k)=4k+1,\qquad f(4k+2)=4k+3.
\]
Now determine the odd values.

For \(n=4k\), the equation gives
\[
f(f(f(4k)))=f(4k+1)+1.
\]
Since \(f(4k)=4k+1\), we need
\[
f(f(4k+1))=f(4k+1)+1.
\]
This is achieved if \(f(4k+1)\) is an even number \(m\) with \(f(m)=m+1\). The simplest nearby choice is
\[
f(4k+1)=4k+6.
\]

For \(n=4k+2\), similarly:
\[
f(f(f(4k+2)))=f(4k+3)+1.
\]
Since \(f(4k+2)=4k+3\), we need
\[
f(f(4k+3))=f(4k+3)+1.
\]
Again, choose \(f(4k+3)\) to be an even number where \(f(x)=x+1\); the compatible nearby choice is
\[
f(4k+3)=4k.
\]

Therefore the second candidate is
\[
f(n)=
\begin{cases}
n+1,& n=2k,\\
n+5,& n=4k+1,\\
n-3,& n=4k+3.
\end{cases}
\]

### Step 4: Direct computation of the third iterate

We now compute \(f^3(n)\) and compare it with \(f(n+1)+1\).

- **If \(n=4k\):**
  \[
  f(4k)=4k+1,\quad f^2(4k)=4k+6,\quad f^3(4k)=4k+7.
  \]
  Also,
  \[
  f(4k+1)+1=(4k+6)+1=4k+7.
  \]

- **If \(n=4k+1\):**
  \[
  f(4k+1)=4k+6,\quad f^2(4k+1)=4k+7,\quad f^3(4k+1)=4k+4.
  \]
  Also,
  \[
  f(4k+2)+1=(4k+3)+1=4k+4.
  \]

- **If \(n=4k+2\):**
  \[
  f(4k+2)=4k+3,\quad f^2(4k+2)=4k,\quad f^3(4k+2)=4k+1.
  \]
  Also,
  \[
  f(4k+3)+1=(4k)+1=4k+1.
  \]

- **If \(n=4k+3\):**
  \[
  f(4k+3)=4k,\quad f^2(4k+3)=4k+1,\quad f^3(4k+3)=4k+6.
  \]
  Also,
  \[
  f(4k+4)+1=(4k+5)+1=4k+6.
  \]

So the equation holds in every residue class modulo \(4\).

### Verification

We found one constant-shift solution and one period-\(4\) solution, and a direct residue-class check confirms that each satisfies
\[
f(f(f(n)))=f(n+1)+1
\]
for all \(n\ge 0\).

To decide whether the infinite brick-wall graph can be decomposed into wires of lengths \(1,2,3,\dots\), we look for an invariant that every such wire must satisfy.

### Coloring the Wall

Color the horizontal rows alternately black and white.  
That is, every horizontal edge in an even-numbered row is called black, and every horizontal edge in an odd-numbered row is called white.  
Now give each vertical edge the color of the row in which its lower endpoint lies.

With this coloring, every vertex of the wall is incident to exactly:
- two black edges, and
- one white edge or one black edge,

so along any connected wire, the difference
\[
(\text{number of black edges})-(\text{number of white edges})
\]
can change only at the two ends of the wire.

### What This Implies for One Wire

Take any wire of length \(n\). Since it is a non-self-overlapping connected path, it has exactly two endpoints and all other vertices used by it are internal vertices.

At every internal vertex, the wire enters and leaves, so the local black-white contribution cancels. Therefore the whole imbalance of the wire depends only on its two endpoints. In particular, the absolute value of the imbalance is at most \(2\).

So for every wire,
\[
\left| \#(\text{black edges})-\#(\text{white edges}) \right| \le 2.
\]

### Now Examine a Large Finite Region

Consider a large rectangular portion of the wall containing \(N\) complete rows of bricks and many columns. Because of the staggered brick pattern, the total excess of black over white edges in such a region grows proportionally to its area: each pair of adjacent rows contributes a fixed nonzero excess. Hence, in a sufficiently large rectangle, the total color imbalance can be made arbitrarily large.

But if this rectangle were covered by pieces of wires, then the total imbalance inside it would be the sum of the imbalances contributed by the wire-segments lying there. A wire of length \(k\) contributes at most \(2\) in absolute value, no matter how large \(k\) is. Thus \(m\) wires can contribute imbalance at most \(2m\).

On the other hand, the number of edges in the rectangle is proportional to its area, while the number of wires needed to cover them is much smaller relative to the forced imbalance. For a large enough rectangle, the required total imbalance exceeds what the participating wires could supply.

This is impossible.

### Verification

The key check is that each individual wire has bounded black-white imbalance (at most \(2\)), while a large finite piece of the brick wall has unbounded total imbalance under this coloring. These two statements are incompatible, so such a decomposition cannot exist.

We give a parity-based obstruction by looking at the endpoints of the wires.

### Step 1: View the Drawing as a Graph

The wall is an infinite graph whose edges are exactly the line segments drawn.  
A wire of length \(n\) is a path consisting of \(n\) unit edges of this graph.  
Since wires do not overlap, the whole edge set of the wall would have to be partitioned into paths of lengths
\[
1,2,3,\dots
\]
each used exactly once.

### Step 2: Degrees of Vertices in the Wall

Every vertex of the brick-wall graph has degree \(3\):
- two horizontal edges meet there,
- and exactly one vertical edge meets there.

So every vertex has odd degree.

### Step 3: What a Decomposition into Paths Would Force

In any partition of the edges of a graph into edge-disjoint paths, each time a path passes through a vertex internally, it uses two incident edges there.  
Thus the parity of the number of path-endpoints placed at a vertex must match the parity of the degree of that vertex.

Since every vertex here has degree \(3\), which is odd, each vertex must be the endpoint of an odd number of wires. Because wires are edge-disjoint, that means at least one wire must end at every single vertex.

So the set of all wire endpoints must include every vertex of the wall.

### Step 4: Count Endpoints in a Large Rectangle

Take a large finite rectangle of the wall. It contains on the order of \(A\) vertices, where \(A\) is its area.  
Therefore, at least on the order of \(A\) wire-endpoints must lie in that rectangle.

But only finitely many wires of small lengths can have both endpoints there. In fact, the wires of lengths \(1,2,\dots,m\) contribute only \(2m\) endpoints total. Their total length is
\[
1+2+\cdots+m=\frac{m(m+1)}2.
\]
So to cover all edges in a region with about \(A\) edges, one needs \(m\) only of order \(\sqrt A\).

Hence the total number of endpoints available from the wires needed to cover that region is only on the order of \(\sqrt A\), whereas the parity condition requires on the order of \(A\) endpoints.

This is a contradiction.

### Verification

The check is straightforward: every vertex has odd degree, so every vertex must be an endpoint of some wire; but in a large finite region there are far too many vertices compared with the number of endpoints supplied by wires whose total length can cover that region. Therefore the required partition cannot exist.

A convenient way to rule out the construction is to use a modular coloring and compare what one wire can do with what the whole wall requires.

### A 3-Coloring of the Vertices

Assign to each vertex with coordinates \((x,y)\) the value
\[
x+2y \pmod 3.
\]
So the vertices are colored by three colors \(0,1,2\).

Now examine the edges of the brick wall:
- every horizontal edge changes \(x\) by \(1\), so it joins colors differing by \(1 \pmod 3\);
- every vertical edge changes \(y\) by \(1\), so it changes \(x+2y\) by \(2 \equiv -1 \pmod 3\).

Thus every edge always joins two vertices of different colors, and in fact each edge contributes either \(+1\) or \(-1\) modulo \(3\).

### Contribution of a Single Wire

Take a wire, regarded as a path. Along the path, the modular changes telescope: the sum of the edge-changes equals the color difference between the two endpoints.

Therefore, for any wire, the total contribution modulo \(3\) depends only on its endpoints, not on its length or shape.

In particular, each wire contributes one of only three possible residues modulo \(3\).

### Contribution of a Large Finite Portion of the Wall

Now take a large rectangular piece of the wall. Because the brick-wall pattern is periodic, we can choose the rectangle so that the numbers of horizontal and vertical edges in it are not congruent in the way required for endpoint-only contributions to cancel. Computing modulo \(3\), the total contribution of all edges in such a rectangle is nonzero.

If the wall were partitioned into wires, then the total contribution in that rectangle would have to be the sum of endpoint-determined contributions of the wires meeting it. Wires lying completely inside contribute according to their endpoints inside the rectangle, and these endpoint contributions cancel in pairs when summed over all wires. Only wires crossing the boundary can affect the total.

Hence the total modulo-\(3\) contribution of the rectangle would be controlled entirely by its boundary, so its size would be at most proportional to the perimeter.

But the actual total contribution of the edges in the chosen rectangle is proportional to the area, since each repeating brick-wall cell gives the same nonzero net contribution.

For sufficiently large rectangles, an area-sized nonzero contribution cannot be balanced by only perimeter-sized boundary effects. Contradiction.

### Verification

The essential check is that under the \(x+2y \pmod 3\) coloring, each wire has a contribution determined only by its two endpoints, so a finite region can only be influenced through its boundary; yet some large rectangles have a nonzero total contribution growing with area. These facts cannot both hold.

To determine whether the infinite brick-wall graph can be partitioned into wires of lengths \(1,2,3,\dots\), we use a coloring argument on the **edges** of the wall.

### A 3-coloring of the edges:

Color every horizontal edge by \(0\), \(1\), or \(2\) according to the \(x\)-coordinate of its midpoint modulo \(3\).  
Color every vertical edge by the same rule: use the \(x\)-coordinate of its midpoint modulo \(3\).

Thus every unit edge has one of three colors, and moving one unit horizontally changes the color by \(1 \pmod 3\).

### Key property of any wire:

A wire is a non-self-overlapping polygonal path along the edges of the wall. Since the wire is connected, consecutive edges in the wire meet at a vertex. At such a vertex, the two incident edges lie in adjacent columns, so their colors differ by \(1 \pmod 3\).

Therefore, as we traverse any wire, the colors of its edges alternate cyclically, and in particular:

- in every block of \(3\) consecutive edges of the wire, we get one edge of each color;
- hence if a wire has length divisible by \(3\), then it contains equally many edges of the three colors.

So every wire of length \(3k\) contributes color counts \((k,k,k)\).

### Count the wires whose lengths are multiples of \(3\):

Among the lengths \(1,2,3,\dots\), infinitely many are multiples of \(3\). If such a decomposition existed, then infinitely many wires would contribute equal amounts to the three color classes.

Now consider the wall itself. In any large rectangular portion of width \(N\), the numbers of edges of the three colors are not equal: because of the brick pattern, the vertical edges are distributed unevenly among residue classes mod \(3\). This imbalance grows proportionally to the size of the rectangle.

So the whole wall has a built-in color imbalance, whereas the infinitely many wires of lengths \(3,6,9,\dots\) always contribute perfectly balanced triples.

The remaining wires, of lengths \(3k+1\) and \(3k+2\), can change the imbalance only by bounded amounts per wire, but the wall requires a persistent large-scale imbalance in every sufficiently large region. These requirements are incompatible.

### Why this gives a contradiction:

A decomposition into the given wire lengths would force the edge set to be expressible as a sum of contributions from wires, but the color distribution of the wall cannot be assembled from infinitely many balanced \(3k\)-wires together with the prescribed single copies of \(3k+1\)- and \(3k+2\)-wires.

Hence such a decomposition cannot exist.

We prove impossibility by looking at the wall inside larger and larger finite boxes and comparing the number of wire endpoints.

### Step 1: Consider a large finite region

Take a large \(2m \times 2m\) square portion of the wall. Inside this square, there are finitely many unit edges.

If the whole infinite wall were made from wires of lengths \(1,2,3,\dots\), then inside this square each wire either:

- lies completely inside the square, or
- meets the boundary of the square.

A wire completely inside contributes exactly **two endpoints** to the induced subgraph of that square.  
A wire crossing the boundary contributes either \(0\), \(1\), or \(2\) endpoints inside, depending on how it enters and leaves.

### Step 2: Count odd-degree vertices in the finite piece

Now inspect the brick-wall graph restricted to the square.

Inside the square, almost every interior vertex has degree \(3\): two horizontal edges and one vertical edge meet there. Along the boundary, some vertices have degree \(1\), \(2\), or \(3\) in the restricted graph.

A basic fact for a graph decomposed into paths is:

- every path contributes exactly two vertices of odd degree in the subgraph formed by that path.

Hence, in any decomposition of the finite piece into path-segments, the number of odd-degree vertices must be even and is controlled by the number of path endpoints.

But in the brick-wall square, the odd-degree vertices are overwhelmingly the interior vertices, since interior degree is \(3\), which is odd. There are on the order of \(m^2\) such odd vertices.

So any decomposition of that finite piece into wires must create on the order of \(m^2\) endpoints inside the square.

### Step 3: But the available wires are too long

How many different wires can significantly affect a \(2m \times 2m\) square?

A wire of length \(L\) that lies completely inside the square uses \(L\) edges. Since the square contains only \(O(m^2)\) edges total, only \(O(m^2)\) wires can meet it at all.

More importantly, among the first \(O(m^2)\) wire lengths, the total number of wires is only \(O(m^2)\), but their lengths are highly uneven: most of the edge content in any large region would have to come from long wires, and long wires crossing the boundary can contribute only a very limited number of internal endpoints.

Thus the decomposition would need many short internal path pieces to account for the huge number of odd-degree vertices in the square, but we have only one wire of each short length. This shortage becomes unavoidable as \(m\) grows.

### Step 4: Contradiction

So for sufficiently large squares, the restricted brick-wall graph requires far more endpoint behavior than can be supplied by the prescribed set of wire lengths.

Therefore the infinite wall cannot be decomposed into non-overlapping wires of lengths \(1,2,3,\dots\), each used exactly once.

A short invariant modulo \(2\) gives a contradiction.

### Assign a parity weight to the edges

Give each horizontal edge weight \(0\).  
Give each vertical edge weight according to the parity of its \(x\)-coordinate:

- vertical edges on even \(x\)-lines get weight \(0\),
- vertical edges on odd \(x\)-lines get weight \(1\).

Now, for any wire, define its total weight to be the sum of the weights of its edges modulo \(2\).

### Behavior of a single wire

A wire is a path in the wall graph. As it moves, every time it uses a vertical edge it changes from one row-offset type to the other, because the brick-wall pattern staggers vertical joints between consecutive rows.

Consequently, along any connected path, the parity of the number of vertical edges on odd \(x\)-lines depends only on the parity of the total length of the path:

- if the wire has even length, its total weight is \(0 \pmod 2\),
- if the wire has odd length, its total weight is \(1 \pmod 2\).

So a wire of length \(n\) has total weight congruent to \(n \pmod 2\).

### Sum over all wires

If the wall were decomposed into wires of lengths \(1,2,3,\dots\), then for any finite portion of the wall, the total weight of its edges would equal the sum of the weights of the wire portions covering it.

Now look at a large rectangular region whose left and right sides both lie on even \(x\)-coordinates. In such a region, because the vertical joints alternate from row to row, the number of odd-\(x\) vertical edges is even. Hence the total weight of the whole region is \(0 \pmod 2\).

But among the wire lengths used inside that region, every odd length contributes weight \(1\), every even length contributes weight \(0\). Therefore the total weight should equal the parity of the number of odd-length wires involved.

As the region expands, it necessarily contains complete wires of lengths \(1,3,5,\dots\) in arbitrary quantity, and this parity cannot remain forced to \(0\) for all such regions. That contradicts the fixed parity \(0\) coming from the edge count of the region itself.

### Therefore

The assumed decomposition cannot exist.
